1A · Urban Spatio-Temporal LearningFull ResearchTeatro StudioMonday 10:30 – 12:308 talksChair: Aurora Rossi (University of Bonn)
FULLUniRoad: Unifying Road Representations Across Cities and Tasks
Jie Zhao (Department of Electronic Engineering, Tsinghua University) · Jiazhi Liu (College of Computer Science, Chongqing University) · Wanyi Zhang (College of Computer Science, Chongqing University) · Chao Chen (College of Computer Science, Chongqing University)
Abstract
Learning generalizable road representations is essential for urban computing, yet remains challenging due to heterogeneous urban signals, city-specific road characteristics, and diverse downstream tasks. Existing methods often encode multi-source information jointly, causing functional, structural, and mobility semantics to be entangled in a single representation space. We propose UniRoad, a unified multi-view framework for cross-city road representation learning. UniRoad decomposes road semantics into three complementary views: an LLM-based profile view that captures functional semantics from road attributes and POI contexts, a prototype-based structure view that learns transferable structural roles from local topology, and a trajectory-informed mobility view that models travel patterns from road sequences. UniRoad further introduces confidence-guided fusion to adaptively integrate these views according to their reliability. Extensive experiments on four cities and four downstream tasks demonstrate that UniRoad consistently outperforms strong baselines and achieves robust cross-city transferability. Code and data are available at: https://github.com/csjiezhao/UniRoad.
FULLCoST: Semantic-Aware Urban Understanding via Spatial-Temporal Alignment
Yutian Jiang (The Hong Kong University of Science and Technology (Guangzhou)) · Jiabo Liu (The Hong Kong University of Science and Technology (Guangzhou)) · Xixuan Hao (The Hong Kong University of Science and Technology (Guangzhou)) · Yuxuan Liang (The Hong Kong University of Science and Technology (Guangzhou))
Abstract
Geospatial representation learning from satellite imagery is a fundamental problem for large-scale urban analysis and real-world applications. Despite recent advances, current methods struggle with cross-region generalization and semantic interpretability due to their reliance on region-specific auxiliary data and the neglect of semantic alignment within multi-temporal urban imagery. Therefore, we present CoST, a novel Contrastive-based Spatial-Temporal framework that aligns spatial context with multi-temporal semantics to extract universal geographic regularities shared across regions. Specifically, CoST explicitly models spatial correlations to capture transferable geographic structures and exploits multi-year urban change semantics to align learned representations with high-level geo-semantics. Extensive experiments demonstrate that CoST consistently achieves superior performance across various downstream tasks and in unseen scenario, yielding an average relative gain of 8.7% over the strongest competing methods across eight city-indicator settings. The code is available in this repo (https://github.com/Arandinglv/CoST).
FULLCRAFT: Cross-Region Adaptive Federated Transfer Learning for Urban Spatiotemporal Prediction
Zhehao Dai (Zhejiang University of Technology) · Xiao Han (Zhejiang University of Technology) · Zhaolin Deng (Zhejiang University of Technology) · Xuyuan Hu (Zhejiang University of Technology) · Zijian Zhang (Jilin University) · Guojiang Shen (Zhejiang University of Technology) · Xiangjie Kong (Zhejiang University of Technology)
Abstract
Urban spatiotemporal prediction is crucial for smart city management, yet fragmented data across administrative boundaries significantly impedes effective model training. To overcome data limitations and leverage knowledge from data-rich regions while preserving data privacy, federated transfer learning has emerged as a promising approach for cross-regional urban prediction tasks. However, traditional learning methods encounter the dual challenge: (1) intra-regional knowledge acquisition difficulties due to missing boundaries that weaken spatiotemporal dependencies and cause data sparsity; and (2) cross-regional knowledge transfer bias, where distribution differences between source and target regions trigger negative transfer and reduce model robustness. To address these issues, we propose CRAFT: a novel federated transfer learning framework that integrates Large Language Models (LLMs) for urban spatiotemporal prediction. Leveraging LLMs' powerful semantic understanding and contextual reasoning abilities, CRAFT captures complex spatiotemporal dependencies and uncovers latent regional connections from heterogeneous data sources, thus alleviating boundary-induced data sparsity. Additionally, to address inter-regional data heterogeneity, we employ a mixture-of-experts (MoE) model with parameter decoupling, which excels at handling diverse data distributions while minimizing federated communication costs. Experimental results on real-world datasets from multiple cities demonstrate the effectiveness of CRAFT in cross-regional federated transfer learning. The code is publicly available at: https://github.com/Jasonxx4/CRAFT.
FULLBPR-Net: Bin-Resolved Temporal Responses for Frequency-Aware Prototype Routing in Spatiotemporal Forecasting
Giseong Hong (Graduate School of Data Science, Chonnam National University) · Collins Botambu (Graduate School of Data Science, Chonnam National University) · Jin-Taek Seong (Graduate School of Data Science, Chonnam National University)
Abstract
Spatiotemporal forecasting requires modeling temporal dynamics and spatial dependencies across multiple spatial units. Existing approaches construct spatial relations from graph structures, latent representations, or attention weights. This work uses frequency-bin-level temporal responses in the prototype routing cost before spatial-unit-level aggregation. We propose BPR-Net (Bin-aware Prototype Routing Network), a frequency-bin-aware prototype routing model for spatiotemporal forecasting. BPR-Net explicitly represents frequency-bin-level temporal responses before they are aggregated into spatial-unit-level representations and uses them for prototype-based spatial relation learning. Specifically, BPR-Net represents each spatial unit through bin-resolved temporal responses, incorporates them into the prototype routing cost via Bin-Prototype Affinity, and modulates the routed representation using a spectral signature. Experiments on nine datasets across mobile traffic, air quality, taxi flow, and traffic sensor domains show that BPR-Net achieves the best result in 26 out of 28 dataset–metric settings against 19 baselines. Additional analyses show that BPR-Net achieves low forecasting error with short inference time in the reported efficiency settings and maintains low forecasting errors for spatial units with different spectral properties.
FULLSTAAR: Spatio-Temporal Attention over Adaptive Regions for Traffic Forecasting
Jeongwoo Son (Korea Advanced Institute of Science and Technology (KAIST)) · Jihye Na (Korea Advanced Institute of Science and Technology (KAIST)) · Uimin Lee (Korea Advanced Institute of Science and Technology (KAIST)) · Jae-Gil Lee (Korea Advanced Institute of Science and Technology (KAIST))
Abstract
Accurate traffic forecasting is essential for Intelligent Transportation Systems (ITS). Attention-based Spatio-Temporal Graph Neural Networks (STGNNs) have been widely adopted to capture long-range spatial dependencies, but their node-level attention incurs quadratic complexity and limits scalability in large-scale traffic networks. Although sparse and hierarchical attention mechanisms reduce this cost by restricting node pairs, they still rely on node-level modeling. Through empirical analysis on a 2,352-node benchmark, we find that removing node-level attention from representative baselines does not consistently degrade performance, suggesting that its additional predictive benefit may be marginal in large-scale settings. In contrast, region-level attention appears useful for modeling traffic propagation, which is also consistent with classical traffic engineering models that represent traffic dynamics over aggregated spatial units. Motivated by these observations, we propose STAAR, a Spatio-Temporal Attention over Adaptive Regions framework that dynamically constructs soft traffic regions and models dependencies among them. Specifically, adaptive region assignment assigns each node to multiple regions with normalized weights, while spatio-temporal attention captures time-lagged dependencies by flattening region tokens across time steps into a unified sequence. Extensive experiments on large-scale traffic benchmarks demonstrate that our model achieves competitive accuracy with substantial efficiency gains, reducing training time by 3.5×–29× and inference time by 2.8×–28× compared with existing attention-based STGNNs. The source code of STAAR is publicly available at https://github.com/kaist-dmlab/STAAR.
FULLCPTIF: Continuous-Time Perception Traffic Forecasting based on Spatio-Temporal Graph Learning
Huijun Tang (Durham University) · Junlong Zhao (Hangzhou Dianzi University) · Pinlong Zhao (Hangzhou Dianzi University) · Pengfei Jiao (Hangzhou Dianzi University) · Huaming Wu (Tianjin University) · Hongjian Sun (Durham University)
Abstract
Intelligent transportation systems (ITS) increasingly deploy roadside units (RSUs) equipped with sensors for environmental perception. Each RSU captures the surrounding traffic scene as a stream of point clouds, whose volume varies with vehicle density, mutual occlusion, and scene geometry. Since downstream tasks such as object detection, tracking, and cooperative perception depend on these streams, accurately predicting future perception volume is necessary for proactive resource provisioning in real-time ITS applications. However, this volume cannot be reliably determined from conventional traffic variables alone, as the same number of vehicles can produce substantially different amounts of point cloud data under different sensing conditions. Moreover, the perception influence between road sections shifts continuously as vehicles move and alter occlusion conditions, and vehicle arrivals introduce time-varying propagation delays that a fixed road-topology graph cannot capture. To address these challenges, we propose CPTIF, a continuous-time spatiotemporal forecasting framework that models each RSU as a node on a dynamic graph with adaptive edge weights fusing learnable structural priors and state-dependent dynamic relations. Temporal evolution and spatial propagation are unified through a cascaded neural controlled differential equation architecture, where discrete observations are first interpolated into continuous control paths and latent states evolve along these paths, enabling prediction at arbitrary future timestamps without retraining. We construct a perception traffic forecasting benchmark by coupling SUMO-driven traffic simulation with CARLA-rendered sensor perception across five topologically distinct maps. Experiments demonstrate that CPTIF outperforms representative baselines in prediction accuracy and multi-step stability.
FULLRegion-Guided Slow-Fast Graph ODEs for Traffic Flow Forecasting
Wenjun Li (Shenyang Aerospace University) · Huaijun Qiu (Shenyang Aerospace University) · Cuiwei Liu (Shenyang Aerospace University)
Abstract
Traffic flow forecasting requires modeling rapidly changing local fluctuations and slowly evolving regional trends. Existing Neural Ordinary Differential Equation (Neural ODE)-based traffic forecasting models usually evolve states at a single spatial granularity, which may entangle node-level volatility with macroscopic evolution and lead to over-smoothed peak predictions under volatile traffic conditions. To capture such mixed-scale dynamics, we propose Hierarchical Slow-Fast Spatial-Temporal Graph ODE (HSF-STGODE), a region-guided slow-fast continuous framework for traffic flow forecasting. HSF-STGODE decomposes traffic evolution into two coupled continuous processes: a Fast Graph ODE modeling node-level short-term fluctuations on the sensor graph, and a Slow Graph ODE capturing region-level trends on a learnable latent region graph. The two processes are connected through bottom-up aggregation and top-down guidance, enabling regional trends to provide stable context for fine-grained node evolution. To further model lagged propagation and irregular local variations, we incorporate a delay-aware pattern module, a flow-consistency regularizer, and a dual-gated fusion mechanism for scale-specific multi-period initialization. Experiments on four widely used PeMS benchmarks show HSF-STGODE achieves the best or tied-best RMSE across all datasets, with strong MAPE performance and competitive MAE results against representative and strong baselines. These results suggest region-guided slow-fast continuous modeling is particularly effective in reducing large forecasting deviations for traffic flow forecasting. Code is available at https://github.com/KYasmaine/HSF-STGODE.
FULLRiskTraf: Risk-Extrapolated Residual Learning for Multi-Variate Traffic Flow Prediction
Guangyu Wang (Dongbei University of Finance & Economics) · Zhidan Liu (Hong Kong University of Science and Technology (Guangzhou))
Abstract
Traffic sensors commonly record flow, speed, and occupancy, but standard traffic flow forecasting benchmarks and models rarely exploit all three raw measurements reliably. Although speed and occupancy provide sensor-native traffic-state information beyond flow alone, existing releases often omit these variables, replace them with proxies, or contain logically inconsistent records. Moreover, direct empirical risk minimization over three-variable inputs may exploit regime-dependent shortcuts, as the relationships among flow, speed, and occupancy vary substantially between free-flow and congested states. We introduce PEMSB-3V, a public benchmark suite that preserves raw flow, speed, and occupancy measurements from PeMS detectors for flow prediction. We also propose RiskTraf, a model-agnostic risk-extrapolated residual plug-in. For each trained spatio-temporal backbone, RiskTraf freezes the selected checkpoint and learns a lightweight zero-start residual head from historical speed and occupancy. The residual head constructs ordered traffic-risk environments and optimizes horizon-wise flow corrections with a risk extrapolation objective, thereby mitigating regime-specific shortcut correlations without modifying the backbone. Extensive experiments demonstrate that RiskTraf consistently improves diverse forecasting backbones and outperforms debiasing and distribution-shift adaptation methods. Our code and benchmark are available at https://github.com/Guangyu4/RiskTraf.
1B · Sequential RecommendationFull ResearchSala SinopoliMonday 10:30 – 12:308 talksChair: Alberto Carlo Maria Mancino (Politecnico di Bari)
FULLThe Prism of Interest: Refracting User Needs in Session-Based Recommendation
Yu Qing (University of Electronic Science and Technology of China) · Xiao Wang (University of Electronic Science and Technology of China) · Zhe Wang (University of Electronic Science and Technology of China) · Xiurui Xie (University of Electronic Science and Technology of China) · Ke Qin (University of Electronic Science and Technology of China) · Shuang Liang (University of Electronic Science and Technology of China)
Abstract
Session-based Recommendation (SBR) aims to predict users' next interaction based on short-term anonymous behavior sequences. Yet accurately modeling the dynamic switching and hierarchical dependency of user intent remains a critical challenge. Existing methods typically treat intents as parallel signals thus ignoring the dynamic shift in the dominant decision-making pattern layer within a session. However, we argue that the dominant decision-making pattern shifts across hierarchical intent layers over time, and treating these layers as static or independent inevitably causes mismodeling. To address these issues, we propose a Pyramid Routing for Intent Sequence Modeling framework (PRISM), which constructs an intent pyramid to parse user decision-making processes. Specifically, we first devise a Hierarchical Vector Quantization module to progressively compress actions into theme and goals. We then employ a Multi-Intent Routing Network to model the cross-layer dependency and information propagation among different intent layers. Finally, to adapt to the dynamic shifting of decision dominance, we design a Mixture of Intent Module that adaptively weights the prediction distributions from different layers, and introduce a Goal-Aware Contrastive Regularizer to ensure the consistency of hierarchical intent representations. Experimental results on three real-world datasets exhibit that PRISM achieves state-of-the-art performance.
FULLMAPLE: Mamba-Based Adaptive Prototype Learning for Intent Disentanglement in Sequential Recommendation
Yue Xie (Soochow University) · Yan Zhang (Soochow University) · Guo Chen (Soochow University) · Li Zhang (Soochow University) · Lei Zhao (Soochow University)
Abstract
Sequential recommender systems struggle to simultaneously capture persistent long-term preferences and volatile short-term intentions, while existing dual-stream architectures are computationally inefficient when handling long sequences and suffer from feature entanglement between the two interest streams. To address these issues, we propose a Mamba-based Adaptive Prototype LEarning and cross-intent contrastive alignment framework (MAPLE). MAPLE employs Mamba as the long-term encoder; its selective state space mechanism selectively retains important historical signals across the entire interaction sequence, making it well-suited for capturing stable long-term interest features with linear computational complexity. Meanwhile, the GRU-based short-term encoder focuses on a local tail window to model recent preference shifts. To decouple these two interest streams, we maintain a set of global semantic prototypes for each interest type and extract soft proxies as personalized semantic anchors through attention-weighted aggregation, thereby leveraging global intent consensus to enrich individual user representations. These proxies are further applied as contrastive anchors in a novel cross-intent InfoNCE loss, which treats proxies of the complementary intent stream as cross-intent contrastive anchors to promote semantic differentiation between long and short-term representations. Finally, we introduce an asymmetric dynamic gated fusion module that prioritizes long-term features as the main component and incorporates short-term features as the auxiliary component for next-item prediction. Experiments on four real-world benchmark datasets demonstrate that MAPLE achieves highly competitive performance, significantly outperforming state-of-the-art models on rank-aware metrics.
FULLDART: Residual Trust and Tail-Aware Dual-View Alignment for Sequential Recommendation
Song Yu (Central South University) · Yanbo Wang (Central South University) · Lei Cao (Central South University) · Zhifang Liao (Central South University) · Yuelan Qi (Central South University)
Abstract
Sequential recommender systems commonly learn item representations from interaction data. This paradigm works well for frequent items, but becomes unreliable for long-tail items whose ID embeddings receive limited updates. Offline semantic embeddings derived from large language models provide useful item-side knowledge beyond interaction logs. They can therefore compensate for the insufficient interaction supervision of long-tail items. However, directly optimizing such semantic priors for recommendation may distort their original semantic structure. Moreover, semantic information should not be injected uniformly across all items, since head items are already well supported by interactions while long-tail items require semantic compensation more urgently. In this paper, we propose DART, a constrained semantic enhancement framework that couples Residual Trust Semantic Adaptation with Tail-Aware Dual-View Alignment for sequential recommendation. DART treats offline LLM-derived item embeddings as frozen semantic anchors and injects collaborative signals through a trust-region-constrained residual pathway. This design allows item representations to absorb useful collaborative information while limiting semantic drift. To further improve long-tail recommendation, DART introduces a tail-aware dual-view alignment mechanism that concentrates cross-view transfer on long-tail items instead of aligning all items uniformly. Experiments on three public benchmarks show that DART achieves strong overall performance and consistent gains in long-tail settings. Further ablation and representation analyses verify the effectiveness of residual-trust adaptation and tail-aware semantic transfer.
FULLLSF-SR: Latent Semantic Fusion for Sequential Recommendation via Flow-based Conditional Variational Autoencoders
Shih-Hong Chen (National Yang Ming Chiao Tung University) · Josh Jia-Ching Ying (National Chung Hsing University) · Vincent S. Tseng (National Yang Ming Chiao Tung University)
Abstract
Sequential recommendation aims to predict users' future interests from their historical interactions. Although Large Language Models (LLMs) capture rich item semantics, existing methods often struggle to align collaborative signals with textual semantic knowledge. As a result, the learned item representations fail to capture the complementary strengths of both signals, leading to suboptimal recommendation quality. To address this limitation, we propose Latent Semantic Fusion for Sequential Recommendation via Flow-based Conditional Variational Autoencoders (LSF-SR), a novel framework that uses a Conditional Variational Autoencoder (CVAE) with Normalizing Flows to fuse item ID embeddings and LLM-generated semantic signals. At the core of LSF-SR is a conditional fusion module augmented with planar or radial flows. This module learns a flexible latent space that encourages items with similar semantic profiles to cluster together within the latent manifold. Through extensive experiments on five public benchmark datasets, we demonstrate that LSF-SR consistently outperforms state-of-the-art baselines, achieving gains of up to 12.98% and 14.13% in Recall@20 and NDCG@20, respectively.
FULLCaLR: Context-Aware Latent Reasoning for Sequential Recommendation
Minxuan Shan (University of Science and Technology of China) · Shuxian Bi (University of Science and Technology of China) · Ziye Zhang (Kuaishou Technology) · Sunhao Dai (Renmin University of China) · Chuyuan Wang (Kuaishou Technology) · Yu Li (Kuaishou Technology) · Xiaoshuang Chen (Kuaishou Technology) · Yongqi Liu (Kuaishou Technology) · Kaiqiao Zhan (Kuaishou Technology) · Wenjie Wang (University of Science and Technology of China)
Abstract
Sequential recommendation aims to model users’ evolving preferences from their historical interactions. Recent latent reasoning methods improve sequential recommenders by extending inferencetime computation in continuous representation space, refining user representations without generating explicit reasoning text. However, existing methods mainly reason over the encoded history itself and make limited use of contextual feedback from users’ recent interactions. Such feedback, especially positive and negative signals in the latest session, can not only complement the long-term user representation but also provide directional guidance for latent reasoning by indicating which preference patterns should be strengthened or suppressed. In this paper, we propose Context-Aware Latent Reasoning (CaLR), a model-agnostic framework that grounds latent reasoning in session-level context. From the input perspective, CaLR selects informative positive and negative items from users’ recent sessions as reasoning anchors. From the architecture perspective, it injects these anchors into each reasoning step through a Cross-Attention-based module. From the optimization perspective, it introduces Process Supervision Loss (PSL) to supervise intermediate reasoning states according to anchor feedback polarity. Experiments on two real-world public benchmarks show that CaLR consistently improves multiple sequential recommendation backbones and outperforms strong latent reasoning baselines. Ablation and further analyses verify the effectiveness of each component in CaLR. Moreover, a seven-day online A/B test on Kuaishou Lite demonstrates its effectiveness in real-world industrial deployment. Our code is available at https://github.com/Ak4ne-windsky/CaLR.
FULLBuilding Sequential Recommendation Models upon Thermoelastic Spectral Operators
Juntao Hu (Chongqing University) · Ruyue Dong (The Hong Kong Polytechnic University) · Xiao Du (Chongqing University) · Huayi Shen (Chongqing University) · Wei Zhou (Chongqing University) · Junhao Wen (Chongqing University)
Abstract
Sequential recommendation aims to predict the next item a user will interact with from behavioral history. Frequency-domain methods emerge as a promising approach to capture different behavioral patterns by decomposing user sequences into frequency components with various filters. However, existing spectral filters mainly emphasize or suppress frequency components, without explicitly modeling how preference signals evolve in the spectral domain. To overcome this limitation, we propose TelaRec, a novel physics-inspired sequential recommendation model built upon the Thermoelastic Spectral Operator (TSO). TSO treats user behavior sequences as preference fields and models their evolution through heat conduction and elastic wave propagation, where heat conduction extracts stable preferences and elastic wave propagation captures short-term interests. Derived from partial differential equations, TSO enables analytical spectral operations beyond conventional static or adaptive filtering. We further introduce User-aware Frequency Calibration (UFC) to adjust the propagation scale of each frequency mode according to the current user's spectral response for personalized spectral evolution. Experiments on six benchmark datasets demonstrate that TelaRec achieves competitive recommendation performance and high computational efficiency. Our source code is available at https://github.com/TBI805/TelaRec.
FULLClosing the Long-Short View Gap in Sequential Recommendation without Cached History
Lingfeng Shi (Texas A&M University) · Chengkai Huang (University of New South Wales) · Lina Yao (University of New South Wales) · James Caverlee (Texas A&M University)
Abstract
Sequential recommenders are typically trained on long user histories to capture rich behavioral signals, yet serving with training-length sequences is often impractical due to real-time efficiency constraints. Directly using only recent behaviors leads to a severe performance drop. To bridge this gap, existing approaches compress user histories into persistent per-user states, storing and retrieving them at inference time; while effective, they impose non-trivial infrastructure overhead and offer little remedy in cold-start scenarios. In this paper, we empirically identify two structural flaws rooted in geometric properties and dataset sparsity, and propose a novel two-stage framework to close the long-short-view performance gap. Specifically, in the first stage, we replace the commonly used dot-product with angular similarity scoring and leverage a modified softmax to counter prefix position bias. In the second stage, we fine-tune only bias and LayerNorm components—universal to standard sequential backbones—for further improvement. Both stages are guided by carefully designed learning objectives. Extensive experiments on two representative backbones across three public datasets demonstrate the effectiveness of our proposed framework.
FULLGOD: Enhancing Generalization via Deep Grafting for Sequential Recommendation
WooJoo Kim (Pohang University of Science and Technology) · JunYoung Kim (Pohang University of Science and Technology) · JaeHyung Lim (Pohang University of Science and Technology) · HwanJo Yu (Pohang University of Science and Technology)
Abstract
Sequential recommenders often struggle with sparse and noisy histories, limiting generalization to unseen interactions. Knowledge distillation mitigates this by transferring dense supervision from a teacher to a student. However, most distillation methods run teacher and student independently, then match student outputs or representations to the teacher. Such supervision entangles student-component effects, blurring whether weak generalization stems from unreliable embeddings, overfitted encoding, or co-adaptation to sparse histories. In this paper, we propose Graft-Oriented Distillation (GOD), a component-level distillation framework for improved generalization through grafting. Grafting denotes replacing selected frozen-teacher components with trainable student counterparts to build hybrid source models. GOD uses these hybrid models to evaluate student embeddings with the teacher encoder and the student encoder with teacher embeddings, providing component-level feedback. At inference, GOD uses only the student, incurring no additional cost. Across three real-world datasets, GOD outperforms state-of-the-art baselines by up to 13.92%.
