Hanqi Yang (Guangdong University of Technology) · Jiahao Lian (Guangdong University of Technology) · Yuyan Qiu (Guangdong University of Technology) · Kexin Xie (Guangdong University of Technology) · Baoyao Yang (Guangdong University of Technology)
Abstract
Time series forecasting with variable missing is a pervasive yet challenging real-world problem. Missing values from sensor malfunctions or communication disruptions severely degrade the performance of conventional models designed for complete data, limiting their practical utility. To tackle the dual challenge of simultaneous imputation and forecasting, we propose EvoGNN, a novel Mutually Evolving Graph Neural Network, centered on a Node-Edge Co-Evolution mechanism that moves beyond merely capturing time-varying dynamics. Its core innovation lies in establishing a closed-loop, iterative refinement process where adjacency relations (edge) and node representations dynamically and mutually enhance each other. This is realized through two synergistic modules: an Edge-Driven State Refinement (ESR) module, which fuses static prior knowledge with a dynamically learned graph to update node states, and a Node-Driven Adjacency Evolution (NAE) module, which evolves the graph adjacency by reasoning over refined node increments and global temporal contexts. A Recurrent Equilibrium Gate (REG) is further introduced to regulate the evolution dynamics, ensuring stable and convergent learning. Extensive experiments demonstrate that EvoGNN consistently outperforms SOTA baselines across various missing scenarios. We theoretically demonstrate the convergence, effectiveness and efficiency of the co-evolutionary process, providing analytical insight into reliability and scalability.

FULLBRAD: Enhancing Code summarization with Bytecode Retrieval-Augmented Deliberation model
Jian Wang (Xinjiang University) · Wendong Zhang (Xinjiang University) · Zhifang Liao (Central South University) · Peng Lan (Central South University)
Abstract
Comments and summaries play a critical role in program comprehension. However, high-quality summaries are often missing in large codebases. Existing code summarization methods improve linguistic fluency but still fall short in capturing program execution semantics. Furthermore, source-level retrieval methods struggle to identify code examples that are syntactically different but functionally relevant. To address these limitations, we propose BRAD (Bytecode Retrieval-Augmented Deliberation), a novel retrieval-augmented deliberation model for code summarization that integrates bytecode-level semantics with multi-pass deliberation. Specifically, BRAD (1) encodes bytecode control-flow graphs (CFG) with a Graph Attention Network (GAT) to preserve control flow semantics, and (2) retrieves exemplar drafts in the bytecode text space to capture execution-oriented functional cues. These are then fused with textual encodings in a deliberative refinement process to generate the final summary. We evaluate BRAD on a public Java dataset, and the results show that compared with the strong baselines, BRAD increases BLEU-1 by 18.7%, BLEU-2 by 16.2%, BLEU-3 by 8.5%, BLEU-4 by 2.8%, ROUGE-L by 13.4%, BERTScore-F1 by 6.3%, and CIDEr by 10.0%.
FULLCARE: When Not to Retrieve—Conflict-Aware Empathetic Dialogue via Intent-Gated Retrieval and Latent Critique
Chengwei Wu (Sun Yat-sen University) · Shaoling Liang (Guangxi Zhuang Autonomous Region Information Center) · Jian Huang (Guangxi Zhuang Autonomous Region Information Center) · Shangsong Liang (Sun Yat-sen University)
Abstract
Retrieval-Augmented Generation (RAG) can undermine empathetic dialogue when retrieved content is tonally or emotionally misaligned with the user's expressed state: standard models forward the retrieved advice mechanically even when it is factually correct, eroding the supportive rapport the conversation calls for—a failure mode we term knowledge intrusion. We propose CARE (Conflict-Aware Reasoning for Empathy), which reframes retrieval-augmented generation as a decision to withhold: rather than treating retrieved documents as mandatory inputs to the generator, CARE introduces an explicit rejection action and learns when to take it. CARE cascades three mechanisms: Intent-Gated Retrieval, a probabilistic gate that suppresses retrieval when the user only needs emotional validation; Latent Critique, an explicit chain-of-thought step that decides whether to use or withhold the retrieved document on tonal and emotional grounds; and Conflict-Aware DPO, a preference objective trained on teacher-distilled robust/compliant response pairs to sharpen the rejection decision. At 50% injected noise, CARE improves Gating F1 over Standard RAG by up to 33.1 points, achieves a Context Rejection Score (CRS) above 70, and preserves generation quality. Our code is available at https://github.com/Zhizitan76/CARE-CIKM2026.

Seonho An (KAIST) · Chaejeong Hyun (KAIST) · Min-Soo Kim (KAIST)
Abstract
Graph RAG on corpus graphs enhances retrieval by leveraging intermediate node content as contextual clues to uncover unretrieved oracle nodes. However, existing methods suffer from two critical blind spots, namely semantically blind graph expansion and topology blind pruning, or else rely on prohibitively slow retrieval and generation interleaving. To address this, we formalize these limitations through an operational taxonomy and propose a retriever design that couples semantics-aware adding with graph-aware pruning under efficiency constraints. We instantiate this design as GraFine, which alternates between two refinement stages: Semantic Proximity eXpansion (SPX) for semantics-aware node addition, and a Graph Smoothing Reranker (GSR) for graph-aware pruning. Experiments on reference networks and text-rich knowledge graphs show that GraFine improves retrieval accuracy and generation quality while maintaining time-efficiency. Furthermore, we introduce Topological Recall (TR), a metric that quantifies the topological proximity between retrieved and oracle nodes. Our analysis using TR confirms that GraFine more effectively steers refinement toward undiscovered oracle nodes by leveraging intermediate contextual clues. Our code is available at this link: github.com/asmath472/GraFine (https://github.com/asmath472/GraFine).

Zafar Ali (Southeast University) · Asad Khan (Southeast University) · Aalia Malik (Southeast University) · Pavlos Kefalas (Aristotle University of Thessaloniki)
Abstract
Multimodal retrieval-augmented generation (RAG) systems often rely on long unstructured contexts or aggressively expanded evidence graphs, which can introduce noisy evidence, weaken multi-hop reasoning, and increase unsupported generation. Instead of injecting all retrieved evidence into the generator, GraphLoom performs reliability-aware subgraph retrieval with bounded expansion and selectively routes high-utility evidence through hierarchical graph memory slots and joint graph–sequence attention in a frozen language model. Experimental results show consistent gains in answer quality and evidence faithfulness over strong multimodal RAG, graph-retrieval, and open-source vision–language baselines, with improved retrieval quality on MultiModalQA and stable performance under noisy evidence pools. Additional analyses using MiniCheck-based verification, human evaluation, and latency profiling show that reliability-calibrated graph evidence routing provides an effective alternative to long-context multimodal evidence injection.

Meenu Ravi (Virginia Tech) · Shailik Sarkar (Florida Polytechnic Institute) · Lulwah Alkulaib (Kuwait University College of Science) · Yordanos Tessema (Virginia Tech) · Chang-Tien Lu (Virginia Tech)
Abstract
Current work on improving reliability in large language model (LLM)- generated answers has primarily leveraged Retrieval-Augmented Generation (RAG), knowledge-graph augmentation, and reinforcement learning. While these methods are adept at enhancing and measuring reliability through semantic similarity and faithfulness, they often struggle to distinguish semantic similarity from geographic validity. This is especially critical in natural hazard management domains where geographic granularity (i.e., town vs. city vs. state) is significant for decision-making, as responses valid in one municipality may not transfer to another. In such domains, a confidently wrong answer carries greater risk than abstaining. We present GeoRisk-RAG, a novel hierarchy-aware framework that addresses this geographic-validity gap through selective answering. This framework explicitly estimates geographic applicability using a Directed Acyclic Graph (DAG)-based distance for context retrieval before response generation. Experiments on a novel held-out wildfire-related question-answering (QA) dataset show that GeoRisk-RAG significantly reduces false confidence rates for location-dependent questions, lowering the rate to 0.009 compared with 0.090 for standard semantic similarity and reranking baselines, while consistently achieving higher human preference alignment. This work provides a more comprehensive assessment of end-to-end RAG pipelines by integrating geographic validity and selective-answering behavior for safer decision-making in geospatial domains.

Or Dado (Technion) · David Carmel (Technology Innovation Institute (TII)) · Oren Kurland (Technion)
Abstract
While retrieval-augmented generation has become a common approach for enhancing question answering systems, retrieval is not universally advantageous. We study the problem of predicting whether incorporating external retrieved information is likely to improve response quality for a given question. To this end, we evaluate a range of prediction methods that are based on retrieval signals, answer characteristics, and semantic consistency between generated responses and retrieved passages. We further devise a predictor that probes the LLM's internal state. Its prediction performance significantly narrows the performance gap between post-generation methods which are computationally demanding and pre-generation (post-retrieval) methods. We use the prediction methods to devise a selective retrieval framework that dynamically chooses between retrieval and non-retrieval generation modes per question. Experimental results demonstrate that selectively applying retrieval augmentation yields answer quality that transcends that of using retrieval for all queries.

Abstract
Retrieval-augmented generation (RAG) is typically optimized for topical relevance, yet its success ultimately depends on whether retrieved passages are useful for a large language model (LLM) to generate correct and complete answers. We argue that such utility is often LLM-specific rather than universal, due to differences in models’ knowledge, reasoning, and ability to leverage evidence. We formalize LLM-specific utility as the performance improvement of a target LLM when a passage is provided, compared to answering without evidence. Experiments show that existing utility-aware selection and scoring methods largely capture model-agnostic usefulness and struggle to reliably estimate LLM-specific utility. Xingnan Jin (Beijing University of Technology) · Yongping Du (Beijing University of Technology) · Mingyang Li (Beijing University of Technology) · Binrui Wang (Beijing University of Technology)
Abstract
Multi-hop retrieval-augmented question answering depends on compact evidence sets whose members complement one another rather than repeat already covered facts. In evidence selection over a candidate pool, prevailing relevance-based selectors score each candidate mainly as a standalone match to the question, which obscures its marginal role under the evidence already selected. A candidate that appears weak in isolation may complete missing support after another unit establishes a bridge, while a highly relevant candidate may become redundant once its fact has been covered. This paper introduces Marginal Evidence Coalition Selection (MECS), a state-conditioned evidence selector that treats the partially selected evidence set as a coalition and estimates the marginal value of adding each remaining candidate. MECS derives pairwise preferences from public supporting-fact annotations over partial evidence states, and its typed scoring channels align candidate value with support addability, bridge continuity, and coalition consistency. This formulation permits candidate value to vary across evidence states, promoting candidates that complete uncovered support while suppressing repeated or incompatible evidence. Evaluated as an evidence selector over shared candidate pools, MECS improves support recovery and downstream answer accuracy on HotpotQA, 2WikiMultihopQA, and MuSiQue with frozen readers. Mechanism and robustness diagnostics further support the role of state-conditioned marginal selection in recovering complementary evidence for multi-hop QA.

FULLEnd-to-End Delayed Matching Learning for Micro-View Order Dispatching in Ride-Hailing
Rongxiao Huang (Nanjing University) · Zhou Hao (Nanjing University) · Jiaqi Zheng (Nanjing University) · Jiecheng Guo (Didi Chuxing) · Guobin Wu (Didi Chuxing) · Qun Li (Didi Chuxing) · Guihai Chen (Nanjing University)
Abstract
Micro-view order dispatching (MICOD) is a critical task in ride-hailing platforms, aiming to optimize driver--order matching within limited spatiotemporal contexts. Prior works predominantly employ Reinforcement Learning (RL) to learn delayed matching policies. However, RL-based approaches often suffer from sample inefficiency and instability due to the need for extensive trial-and-error exploration. Furthermore, the combinatorial nature of dispatching typically breaks differentiability, preventing end-to-end alignment between prediction models and optimization objectives. In this paper, we propose DML, an End-to-End Delayed Matching Learning framework. Unlike RL, DML formulates order dispatching as a learning-from-expert problem inspired by imitation learning. By leveraging the insight that a global offline optimal matching (OPT) can be computed from historical data, DML constructs an expert in hindsight and avoids the need for online exploration. To effectively clone this expert behavior while enabling end-to-end training, we address two key challenges: expert decomposition and combinatorial differentiability. First, we construct a Delay-Augmented Bipartite Graph (DABG) and theoretically prove that the global OPT can be equivalently decomposed into local sequential learning targets. Second, we incorporate a differentiable optimization layer based on the Sinkhorn--Knopp (SK) algorithm and introduce a Batch-SK (B-SK) implementation to efficiently handle variable-sized graphs in parallel. Experiments on a real-world dataset collected from Didi Chuxing demonstrate that DML significantly outperforms state-of-the-art baselines in both matching quality and training efficiency.
FULLApproximate Pareto Frontiers for Submodular Utility and Cost Tradeoffs
Karan Vombatkere (Boston University) · Evimaria Terzi (Boston University)
Abstract
In many data-mining applications, including recommender systems, influence maximization, and team formation, the goal is to pick a subset of elements (e.g., items, nodes in a network, experts to perform a task) to maximize a monotone submodular utility function while simultaneously minimizing a cost function. Classical formulations model this tradeoff via cardinality or knapsack constraints, or by combining utility and cost into a single weighted objective. However, such approaches require committing to a specific tradeoff in advance and return only a single solution, offering limited insight into the space of viable utility–cost tradeoffs. In this paper, we depart from the single-solution paradigm and examine the problem of computing representative sets of high-quality solutions that expose different tradeoffs between submodular utility and cost. For this, we introduce (α1,α2)-approximate Pareto frontiers that provably approximate the achievable tradeoffs between submodular utility and cost. Specifically, we formalize the Pareto–⟨ f,c ⟩ problem and develop efficient algorithms for multiple instantiations arising from different combinations of submodular utility f and cost functions c. % Since the (α1,α2)-approximate Pareto % frontier can often have a large number of solutions, We also provide an adaptive search algorithm that computes only a small subset of points that collectively summarize the entire Pareto frontier. Our results offer a principled and practical framework for understanding and exploiting utility–cost tradeoffs in submodular optimization. Experiments on datasets from diverse application domains demonstrate that our algorithms efficiently compute approximate Pareto frontiers in practice.
FULLBASAR: Bidirectional Sparse-Attentive Autoregressive Learning for Dynamic Heterogeneous Multi-Agent Task Assignment
Wenjian Wu (Soochow University) · Zesheng Jia (Soochow University) · Benyuan Yang (Soochow University) · Jin Wang (Soochow University)
Abstract
Dynamic heterogeneous task assignment is a fundamental problem in graph-based decision systems, where a scheduler must allocate continuously arriving tasks to multiple agents with diverse capabilities under coalition feasibility, deadlines, and resource constraints. Existing optimization-based methods often incur high replanning costs, while learning-based solvers usually struggle with weak task-agent coupling, sparse delayed rewards, and limited generalization under dynamic arrivals and coalition requirements. This paper presents BASAR, an end-to-end autoregressive framework for dynamic heterogeneous multi-agent task assignment on graphs. BASAR combines bidirectional task-agent cross-domain fusion, sparse-attentive state refinement, and feasible-action masked pointer decoding to generate online assignments over revealed task nodes and agent-specific fallback actions. To improve learning in collaborative scheduling, BASAR introduces an cooperative reward that evaluates the revealed task set and redistributes team utility through marginal service credits. Experiments on dynamic task assignment benchmarks show that BASAR achieves strong deadline-aware performance under fixed task workloads and high task throughput under fixed makespan execution, while reducing total planning time by up to 98.7% compared with the optimization-based baseline. Our code is available at https://github.com/wuwenjianw/BASAR.
FULLA Multi-Agent Reinforcement Learning Approach for Dynamic Route Optimization of Customized Shuttle Bus Services
Jianqiang Yan (Northwest University) · Yufan Yang (Northwest University) · Yuan Gao (Northwest University) · Boting Qu (Northwest University)
Abstract
Real-time routing for customized shuttle buses presents a complex multi-agent control problem characterized by stochastic demands and strict topological constraints. However, efficient dispatching is frequently hindered by coarse-grained station representations, uncoordinated agent interactions, and the neglect of discrete operational constraints. To address these issues, HGA-PAC is presented as an event-driven framework where decisions are triggered upon vehicle arrival at stations. The framework operates through three synergistic components: a Heterogeneous Graph Attention encoder for fine-grained spatiotemporal dynamics, an attention-based communication module to mitigate resource competition, and a phaseaware decoder to ensure physical feasibility via dynamic masking. Experimental results demonstrate that our method significantly reduces operational costs and achieves a superior trade-off between service rate and travel efficiency compared to state-of-the-art baselines.

Gang Yan (Jilin University)
Abstract
Short-session personalization and contextual recommendation often must improve later decisions from only a few selected-feedback observations. Standard online evaluation makes this improvement hard to interpret, because post-prefix reward may reflect both credit already stored from early actions and new reward information acquired while evaluation continues. We study this attribution problem through frozen-state credit storage, an adapt-then-freeze view in which rewards may update episode-local state during a short prefix, but later decisions can only read the state left at the freeze point. This boundary changes the design target: selected feedback is useful only if it is written before freezing into a state that remains readable afterward. Building on this insight, we introduce ReBEP, a bounded episodic-plasticity family organized around the action-local structure of selected feedback. ReBEP pairs a shared context scorer with resettable action-local memory, writes reward evidence only to the selected action slot, and reads the same slot after freezing. Its local-evidence update extends a scalar reward trace while preserving bounded action-local execution. Across latent-context tasks, supervised-to-bandit anchors, stress settings, and a short-session recommendation anchor, ReBEP stores prefix feedback more effectively as frozen decision credit than scalar traces, recurrent states, plasticity baselines, and frozen-prefix sequence summaries under the same write-read boundary. Memory interventions and component ablations show that the advantage depends on the frozen memory itself, action-slot assignment, bounded projection, and local-evidence writing rather than generic state capacity.

Guhyeon Kang (Sungkyunkwan University) · Jaehwi Lee (Soongsil University) · Minhae Kwon (Sungkyunkwan University)
Abstract
Recent progress in offline reinforcement learning (RL) has been driven by expressive generative actors such as diffusion and flow-matching policies, which capture multimodal behavior in offline datasets. However, these actors require multiple denoising or integration steps per action and thus incur substantial overhead at every decision in deployment. In this work, we revisit where capacity should be invested in an offline actor--critic method. Since the critic is used only during training and is discarded at deployment while the actor runs at every decision step, allocating capacity to the critic rather than the actor is more favorable for inference-time efficiency. However, scaling MLP critics in offline RL is known to introduce several distinct instabilities that have, in practice, kept critics shallow. We identify three distinct failure modes that arise when critics are deepened in offline RL---optimization, bootstrap-noise amplification, and value-range drift---and address each with a corresponding ingredient: a residual MLP backbone, n-step bootstrap targets, and a categorical cross-entropy loss. Abstract
Auto-bidding is a crucial task in real-time advertising markets, where policies must optimize long-horizon value under delivery constraints (e.g., budget and CPA). Existing methods for auto-bidding rely on compact numerical state representations: while they can implicitly capture delivery dynamics, they offer limited support for explicitly representing and controlling high-level intent, evolving feedback, and operator-style strategic guidance in real campaigns. Meanwhile, Large Language Models (LLMs) offer a powerful method for encoding semantic information, it remains unclear when LLMs help and how to integrate them without sacrificing numerical precision. Through systematic preliminary studies, we find that (1) LLM embeddings contain bidding-relevant cues yet cannot replace numerical features, and (2) gains emerge only with careful semantic–numeric integration rather than naive concatenation. It injects these semantics as tokens alongside numerical trajectory tokens and uses self-attention to integrate them, improving controllability and generalization across objectives. Across diverse scenarios and budget regimes, SemBid outperforms competitive baselines from offline RL and generative sequence modeling, with more consistent gains in overall performance, constraint satisfaction, and robustness. Binglin Wu (Dalian University of Technology) · Yingyi Zhang (Dalian University of Technology) · Xianneng Li (Dalian University of Technology) · Ruyue Deng (Alibaba International Digital Commerce Group) · Chuan Yue (Alibaba International Digital Commerce Group) · Weiru Zhang (Alibaba International Digital Commerce Group) · Xiaoyi Zeng (Alibaba International Digital Commerce Group)
Abstract
Auto-bidding systems strive to maximize marketing value while maintaining high compliance with efficiency constraints, such as Target Cost-Per-Action (CPA). While Decision Transformers offer powerful sequence modeling capabilities, their application to this setting faces two challenges: 1) standard Return-to-Go conditioning causes state aliasing by ignoring the cost dimension, preventing precise resource pacing; and 2) standard regression constrains the policy to mimic historical averages, limiting its capacity to optimize performance near the high-efficiency boundary. By utilizing these high-utility outcomes as weighted regression targets, the model overcomes mean regression and approaches the empirical high-efficiency boundary. Extensive experiments on two public benchmarks and online A/B tests show that PRO-Bid achieves better constraint satisfaction and value acquisition than state-of-the-art baselines.

APPLIEDGenMRP: A General Multi-Route Planning Framework for Efficient and Personalized Real-Time Industrial Navigation
Chengzhang Wang (Alibaba Group) · Chao Chen (Alibaba Group) · Jun Tao (Alibaba Group) · Tengfei Liu (Southern University of Science and Technology) · He Bai (Alibaba Group) · Song Wang (Alibaba Group) · Longfei Xu (Alibaba Group) · Kaikui Liu (Alibaba Group) · Xiangxiang Chu (Alibaba Group)
Abstract
Existing industrial-scale navigation applications contend with massive road networks, typically employing two main categories of approaches for route planning. The first relies on precomputed road costs for optimal routing and heuristic algorithms for generating alternatives, while the second, generative methods, has recently gained significant attention. However, the former struggles with personalization and route diversity, while the latter fails to meet the efficiency requirements of large-scale real-time scenarios. To address these limitations, we propose GenMRP, a general framework for multi-route planning. In GenMRP, routes are generated iteratively. The first iteration identifies the optimal route, while the subsequent ones generate alternatives that balance quality and diversity using the newly proposed correctional boosting approach. Each iteration incorporates road features, user historical sequences, and previously generated routes into a Link Cost Model to update road costs, followed by route generation using the Dijkstra algorithm. Extensive experiments show that GenMRP achieves state-of-the-art performance with high efficiency in both offline and online environments. To facilitate further research, we have publicly released the training and evaluation dataset. GenMRP has been fully deployed on the Amap app for over a year, and it has brought a substantial improvement in user trajectory coverage, demonstrating its effectiveness and benefits.
APPLIEDNext-Generation ETA Prediction: Uncertainty-Aware Probabilistic Multi-Task Modeling for On-Demand Delivery
Chi Zhang (DoorDash) · Pierre Counathe (DoorDash) · Jaydeep Thik (DoorDash) · Jason Kim (DoorDash) · Ziqi Jiang (DoorDash) · Jie Qin (DoorDash) · Wesley Cheung (DoorDash) · Wen Ge (DoorDash) · Bailey Kobuke (DoorDash) · Lewis Warne (DoorDash) · Michael Polino (DoorDash) · Jianzhe Luo (DoorDash) · Pradeep Varma (DoorDash) · Sifeng Lin (DoorDash) · Gayatri Iyengar (DoorDash)
Abstract
Accurate estimated time of arrival (ETA) prediction is central to on-demand delivery platforms, yet it must operate under rapid distribution shifts, heterogeneous geographies, merchant partners, and consumers, as well as long-tailed operational edge cases. At marketplace scale, ETAs represent a promise, where even small errors can compound into substantial impacts on consumer experience and operational efficiency. We present DoorDash's next-generation ETA system, built on four contributions. First, a Feature-wise Linear Modulation (FiLM) based Base Model supporting point and probabilistic output heads. Second, a multi-task architecture that jointly produces consistent ETAs across surfaces and geographies. Third, we cast consumer-facing ETA window generation as a constrained optimization problem and decompose it into a two-layer architecture that separates accuracy-focused modeling from business-aware policy. Fourth, we pair probabilistic Base Models with an uncertainty-aware Decision Layer policy. The system is deployed in production at DoorDash's global marketplace scale and validated through large-scale online A/B experiments. Against our historical tree-based baseline, the deployed Base Model iterations reduce prediction mean absolute error by 34.6%, improve on-time accuracy by 19.9%, and improve ETA consistency by 37.6%, accompanied by material annual improvements in Gross Order Value. Layering the uncertainty-aware Decision Layer policy on top raises the error reduction to 35.0% and the on-time-accuracy gain to 20.9% in shadow deployment; online A/B validation of that policy is the next step in its rollout.
APPLIEDLAGAD: An LLM-Augmented Framework for Graph Anomaly Detection
Hao Lan (East China Normal University) · Li Han (East China Normal University) · Dawei Cheng (Tongji University)
Abstract
Graph anomaly detection (GAD) aims to identify nodes that deviate from normal structural or semantic patterns, with broad applications in financial transactions, network security, and online social platforms. However, existing GAD methods predominantly focus on sophisticated optimization within the graph domain, such as refining neighbor selection and aggregation strategies, and thus inevitably suffer from aggregation anomaly dilution. This issue is particularly pronounced under weak-information scenarios with sparse connectivity and ambiguous features. Moreover, such methods largely overlook the rich semantic cues in raw textual content. To unleash the textual modality for compensating insufficient graph signals and mitigating aggregation anomaly dilution, large language models (LLMs) have emerged as a promising solution given their strong semantic reasoning. Nevertheless, effectively fusing textual embeddings with graph structures remains challenging. In this paper, we propose LAGAD, the first framework that introduces the LLMs-as-Consultants paradigm into GAD. LAGAD leverages LLMs to extract external knowledge from textual information to compensate for the insufficiency of graph signals, thereby enhancing GAD performance. Specifically, LAGAD identifies low-confidence nodes via dual-phase selection and builds representative two-hop subgraphs via semantic similarity. The encoded subgraphs, together with node-level textual and structural descriptions, are fed into the LLM for structure–semantic joint prediction with natural-language explanations. The LLM predictions are then converted into pseudo-labels for local retraining, forming a closed feedback loop that refines the base model. Extensive experiments demonstrate that LAGAD effectively mitigates challenges under weak-information settings and significantly enhances the performance and robustness of underlying GNN models.

Yice Luo (Antgroup) · Yun Zhu (Antgroup) · Chen Xi (Antgroup) · Yongchao Liu (Antgroup) · Xintan Zeng (Antgroup) · Chengying Huan (Nanjing University) · Kai Zhang (Antgroup) · Jinrui Zhang (Antgroup) · Juelu Zhang (Antgroup) · Jiajun Zheng (Antgroup)
Abstract
Industrial fraud detection often relies on costly expert-crafted features that overlook graph-structured relational signals, while GNNs often do not meet the interpretability and deployment requirements of financial risk control. We propose GraphFAS (Graph Feature Automated Selection), a distributed feature selection procedure based on Boruta that bridges this gap through: (1) a non-parametric graph feature generation module that constructs explicit, interpretable structural features via multi-hop subgraph extraction and multi-scale aggregation without learned parameters; and (2) an automated distributed feature selection algorithm extending Boruta with median-based aggregation across partitions to robustly identify informative features at scale with minimal domain expertise. Compared with end-to-end GNN pipelines, GraphFAS decouples feature aggregation from model training, enabling direct integration with tabular models and direct compatibility with TreeSHAP-based explanations. Deployed in Alipay, GraphFAS delivers order-of-magnitude improvements in engineering efficiency while showing strong performance against expert-driven and graph-learning baselines on large-scale graphs.
APPLIEDCATeye: Coupled Attribute–Topology Invariance Learning for Voucher Abuse Detection
Tian Tian (Nanyang Technological University) · Shuaicheng Niu (Nanyang Technological University) · Hao Kuang (Lazada Inc.) · Yuanhang Hu (Lazada Inc.) · Dong Li (Alibaba Group) · Zhiqi Shen (Nanyang Technological University)
Abstract
Voucher abuse poses a major challenge in e-commerce, where malicious users exploit promotional vouchers for profit. Unfortunately, fraud patterns evolve rapidly over time and across regions, causing distribution shifts that degrade existing detection models unless retrained frequently. To tackle this, we propose the Coupled Attribute–Topology Invariance Learning framework (CATeye). The key challenge arises from coupled attribute–topology shift, where edges built from attribute proximity cause environment-driven attribute shift to induce shifted topology, thereby amplifying variant signals through GNN message passing. CATeye sees through such coupled shifts with two learnable selectors. First, an Attribute Invariance Selector (AIS) learns node-adaptive masks to filter out non-invariant attributes. Then, conditioned on retained invariant attributes, an Edge Invariance Selector (EIS) samples an invariant subgraph and isolates non-invariant edges. Using the resulting invariant and non-invariant components, CATeye constructs multiple views and applies view-specific objectives to emphasize domain-invariant representations while suppressing domain-specific variations. Experiments on both a proprietary dataset from Lazada, a major Southeast Asian e-commerce platform, and a public benchmark show that CATeye consistently outperforms nine strong domain generalization and graph anomaly detection baselines, achieving up to an 8.61% improvement in average F1 score over the strongest baseline. Source code is publicly available at https://github.com/Tian0426/CATeye.
APPLIEDRobust and Scalable Merchant Fraud Detection at Mastercard via Surrogate-Guided Neighbor Selection
Jahnavi Methukumalli (Mastercard) · Shivani Sharma (Mastercard) · Aditi Prasad (Mastercard) · Manasvi Aggarwal (Mastercard) · Rupam Kumawat (Indian Institute of Technology Delhi) · Suhas Powar (Mastercard) · Yatin Katyal (Mastercard) · Sahil Manchanda (Mastercard)
Abstract
Detecting merchant fraud is a critical challenge for global payment networks such as Mastercard, where data is inherently a hybrid of high-resolution tabular features and complex graph topology. While Graph Neural Networks (GNNs) based methods have shown promise in capturing the dependencies between nodes, deploying them at scale is challenging due to i) signal dilution under extreme heterophily, where extremely sparse fraudulent nodes are overwhelmed by benign neighborhoods, ii) prediction instability, where standard stochastic neighborhood sampling techniques for scalability leads to inconsistent risk estimates of merchants across inference runs undermining trustworthiness; and iii) high computational load at billion-edge scale. SGS introduces a dual-surrogate architecture, where lightweight gradient-boosted tree models are trained for merchants and cards to produce deterministic risk estimates. These strong dual surrogate scores jointly guide risk-aware deterministic neighborhood edge selection, and explicity accounts for node heterogeneity, yields task-aligned neighborhoods, produces consistent merchant representations, and naturally reduces the effective graph edge set. We evaluate SGS on Mastercard's production merchant-card network with 1.99 billion edges and 65 million nodes. SGS shows a 3.6% AUCPR lift over strong production baselines and consistently outperforms state-of-the-art fraud and heterophily-aware GNNs. Crucially, SGS achieves prediction stability while reducing total end-to-end running time by approximately 84%. Yuxuan Wang (Fudan University) · Yateng Tang (Tencent Weixin Group) · Renhong Huang (Zhejiang University) · Jingwen Zhou (Fudan University) · Siwei Zhang (Fudan University) · Yun Xiong (Fudan University) · Xuehao Zheng (Tencent Weixin Group) · Jiarong Xu (Fudan University)
Abstract
Online payment platforms generate massive transaction streams that contain rich behavioral signals for financial risk assessment. However, building a transaction foundation model for such tasks faces three major challenges. First, risk signals exhibit multi-scale temporal semantics, spanning immediate intents at the transaction level, short-term rhythms at the daily level, and long-term cycles at the monthly level. Second, financial transactions are inherently noisy and bursty. Third, an inherent objective gap exists between self-supervised reconstruction pre-training and downstream discriminative risk classification, often leading to inefficient adaptation and even negative transfer. In this paper, we propose a novel transaction foundation model, a pre-training and fine-tuning framework for large-scale financial risk assessment on transaction sequences. Specifically, we introduce a Hierarchical Transaction Transformer to explicitly model transaction sequences across transaction, daily, and monthly dimensions to comprehensively capture heterogeneous risk patterns at multiple granularities. To encourage the model to learn stable, essential behavioral representations, we design a Multi-scale Financial Summary Reconstruction Task that focuses on reconstructing aggregated statistical summaries rather than raw, noisy transaction values. To align the pre-trained representation space with downstream discriminative risk signals, we introduce an Intermediate Adaptation Stage that enables smooth knowledge transfer and significantly improves task adaptation. Extensive offline experiments and real-world online deployment on Tencent's large-scale payment platform demonstrate the effectiveness of our framework, providing a new paradigm for industrial transaction risk assessment.

Abstract
Corporate default prediction is a core problem in financial risk management, yet traditional credit models rely heavily on financial statements that are often sparse or unavailable for many firms. Corporate transaction networks offer a complementary view of real economic activity, but how risk propagates through buyer–seller relationships remains underexplored. We conduct a large-scale empirical study using real-world electronic tax-invoice data spanning six years that links transaction histories with default events, revealing that transaction-driven risk is both role-dependent (buyer or seller) and scale-dependent. Based on these findings, we construct multiplex buyer-view and seller-view transaction networks and propose DefaultGNN, a dual-perspective graph neural network-based framework for corporate default prediction. DefaultGNN integrates both views to model how risk flows through transactional relationships, achieving strong improvements over both attribute-based and graph-based baselines, especially for firms with limited intrinsic risk signals. We further provide interpretable network-based explanations by visualizing how distressed trading partners contribute to default risk. In collaboration with a licensed credit rating agency, we validate that DefaultGNN's predictions complement existing credit scoring models, improving approval rates by 7-11%p without increasing default risk among approved firms. The source code can be found at https://github.com/jhkim611/DefaultGNN.

Tires are critical components that directly influence core vehicle dynamics, and wet grip is a key performance criterion. To address this problem, we propose GRSWP, a GRaph-based Semi-supervised learning framework for Wet griP prediction designed for real-world development with scarce wet grip labels. GRSWP constructs a tire-graph whose nodes represent tires, footprint images form node features, and edges connect tires with similar design specifications. It then performs unsupervised graph contrastive pretraining on all available tires, followed by supervised fine-tuning on the limited labeled samples. Experiments on real-world tire development data show that GRSWP reduces prediction error by approximately 63.7% in terms of RMSE relative to FEA-based simulation, while accelerating prediction from over 10 hours to 1.5 milliseconds per sample. The source code is publicly available at https://github.com/Bigdasgit/GRSWP.
APPLIEDLabel-free Industrial Fault Detection via Adversarial Inverse Reinforcement Learning: A System for Run-to-Failure Prognostics
Dhiraj Neupane (Deakin University) · Mohamed Reda Bouadjenek (Deakin University) · Richard Dazeley (Deakin University) · Sunil Aryal (Deakin University)
Abstract
Machinery fault detection (MFD) remains heavily reliant on supervised learning, which struggles with the scarcity of fault labels in real-world settings. While reinforcement learning (RL) offers a framework to model the sequential nature of degradation, current “RL-based” MFD methods reduce the problem to a static contextual bandit (CB) formulation: by ignoring state transitions and discarding the temporal discount factor, they collapse to standard supervised classification. We propose an adversarial inverse reinforcement learning (AIRL) framework that treats MFD as an offline IRL problem. Unlike reconstruction-based approaches that rely on static error margins, or CBs that ignore dynamics, our method recovers an intrinsic “health” reward directly from observational state transitions, requiring neither manual reward engineering nor fault labels. On three run-to-failure benchmarks (HUMS2023, IMS, XJTU-SY), AIRL is the only method pairing within-window detection with non-saturated post-detection consistency across all datasets, while CB baselines fail to detect gradual degradation and reconstruction models collapse into always-anomalous states. Code and data: https://github.com/dhirajneupane/AIRL-MFD-DN.

Abstract
Multiplayer Online Battle Arena (MOBA) games rely on matchmaking to maintain competitive balance. Our prior work, CUPID, framed matchmaking as an assignment re-optimization problem and showed that a single-mode win-rate predictor can meaningfully rebalance teams. However, deploying such a system across diverse player populations exposes three practical bottlenecks: most queueing players lack sufficient in-mode match history (cold start), skill distributions shift drastically across rank tiers (distribution inconsistency), and extreme skill segments are severely data-starved. We present CHAMP, a cross-domain matchmaking framework that resolves these deployment bottlenecks. To address data sparsity and cold starts, CHAMP replaces the target-mode-only player profile with a hybrid domain feature collection: a timestamp-ordered cross-mode short-term sequence whose slices are annotated with target-domain features, plus per-mode breakdowns of long-term, real-time and team statistics. We further propose the Domain-Aware Win-rate Network (DAWN): a Domain-aware Knowledge Extractor (DAKE) compiles target-mode attributes into learnable representations that feed Domain-Aware Temporal/Spatial/Permutation OmniNet Encoders (DATOE/DASOE/DAPOE), so that mode-conditioned representations and per-mode debiasing are learned jointly inside a single shared network. Online, one trained DAWN serves every supported mode, with per-mode position-satisfaction thresholds as the only mode-specific knob. APPLIEDLithoFormer: A Robust Framework for Stratigraphic Inference via Geology-Informed Multi-Task Transformers
Shwetha Nagaraj Salimath (University Paris-Saclay, CNRS) · Francesca Bugiotti (University Paris-Saclay, CNRS) · Sylvain Wlodarczyk (SLB) · Sohaib Ouzineb (SLB)
Abstract
Accurate geological characterization of subsurface reservoirs from well log data is essential to support projects such as carbon capture and storage (CCS), geothermal development, and extraction of natural resources. Existing automated techniques for geological characterization primarily use sliding-window classification, which limits their ability to understand broader geological contexts, often leading to misaligned formation layers. To overcome these limitations, we introduce LithoFormer, a robust framework for stratigraphic inference using a Seq2Seq transformer model that ingests entire multivariate well logs in a single pass. It features a PatchTST backbone, rotary positional embeddings (RoPE), and a decoupled multi-task head for predicting geological zones and boundary probabilities simultaneously. To ensure robustness, we implement a constrained data augmentation strategy and a geology-informed loss function that enforces domain constraints. Validated and deployed on three real-world datasets, LithoFormer demonstrates a 90% reduction in median boundary error and eliminates stratigraphic order violations compared to traditional sliding-window baselines.

Abstract
User tracking aims to identify network activities belonging to the same user across websites and network environments, supporting applications such as personalized recommendation and targeted advertising. As dynamic address allocation and modern privacy protections constrain traditional tracking methods, traffic-based tracking techniques have emerged to link dynamic addresses through traffic patterns. However, existing methods usually rely on large-scale user labels for supervised training, while such labels are difficult to obtain in TLS encrypted traffic, severely limiting model generalization. In this paper, we propose SLATE, a self-supervised address linkage framework integrated with LLMs under limited labeled data. Specifically, SLATE introduces a homologous subgraph discrimination task based on address behavior partitioning, which encourages the encoder to capture stable behavior patterns across temporal evolution from large-scale unlabeled data. Moreover, SLATE develops a graph semantic projection module, which enables the LLM to better interpret behavior graph representations through graph-text matching and node semantic classification, and further leverages its reasoning capability to support address linkage decisions. We evaluate SLATE on two real-world user datasets. Experimental results show that SLATE substantially outperforms the strongest self-supervised methods, achieving an average improvement of over 15% in Hits@1, while remaining competitive with state-of-the-art supervised methods. These findings demonstrate the strong potential of combining self-supervised learning with LLMs for address linkage in tracking ecosystems.

Abstract
Multi-party data collaboration increasingly requires deduplicating datasets held by independent providers. Tingyu Fan (Institute of Information Engineering, Chinese Academy of Sciences) · Xiaojun Chen (Institute of Information Engineering, Chinese Academy of Sciences) · Xudong Chen (Institute of Information Engineering, Chinese Academy of Sciences)
Abstract
Cloud-hosted Large Language Models (LLMs) have become key knowledge sources for domain-specific model training. Prompt-driven Knowledge Distillation (KD) allows clients to leverage these models for student training, but client prompts often contain sensitive information that is exposed when sent in plaintext. Existing Differential Privacy (DP)-based methods protect teacher-side data rather than client prompts, while defenses that inject Gaussian noise into prompt embeddings remain vulnerable to reconstruction attacks and may degrade distillation utility. To address this gap, we propose VeilKD, a scalable framework for dual-private prompt-driven knowledge distillation that protects client prompts via secure inference while preserving server-side model confidentiality. Francesco Luigi De Faveri (University of Padova) · Guglielmo Faggioli (University of Padova) · Nicola Ferro (University of Padova)
Abstract
Modern Information Retrieval (IR) systems, including small and medium-scale ones, often search across millions of documents. In many cases, data owners outsource retrieval to a third-party host to keep the data accessible. Furthermore, IR has also moved toward semantic matching with dense embeddings; although these embeddings are less interpretable than sparse representations, they remain vulnerable to model inversion attacks. Sending document embeddings to a third-party retrieval provider can, therefore, create privacy risks. An honest-but-curious host may try to reconstruct the original documents and exploit their content. One option is to send encrypted or obfuscated embeddings instead of the original vectors. Existing methods, however, have important limits: Asymmetric Scalar Product-preserving Encryption (ASPE) is vulnerable to inversion, while homomorphic encryption is often too costly. Building on the ASPE literature, we propose the Pivot-based Intersection Noise Scheme (PINS), a noise-injection method designed for dense IR. Retrieval-Augmented Generation (RAG) is a promising technique for applying LLMs to proprietary domains. However, retrieved documents may contain sensitive knowledge, posing risks of privacy leakage in generative results. Thus, effectively erasing private information from retrieved documents is a key challenge for RAG. Unlike traditional text anonymization, RAG should consider: (1) the inherent multi-document reasoning may face de-anonymization attacks; (2) private knowledge varies by scenarios, so users should be allowed to customize which information to erase; (3) preserving sufficient publicly available knowledge for generation tasks. Abstract
The defining question for approximate machine unlearning is not how strongly to perturb the model, but which signal in its representation to perturb. Existing methods perturb both at once: the sample-specific detail that identifies the forget set and the semantic structure that supports generalization. The result is a familiar trade-off, where forgetting and utility move in opposite directions, with no principled rest point. We separate the two signals through feature-map quantization: the quantized feature retains the semantic structure while shedding the identifying detail, and therefore specifies what an unlearned representation should look like for each forget sample. Dimitrios Karapiperis (International Hellenic University) · George Papadakis (National and Kapodistrian University of Athens) · Manolis Koubarakis (National and Kapodistrian University of Athens) · Vassilios S. Verykios (Hellenic Open University)

Entity Resolution (ER) is a critical data cleaning task for identifying records that refer to the same real-world entity. In the era of Big Data, traditional batch ER is often infeasible due to volume and velocity constraints, which call for Progressive ER methods that maximize recall within a limited computational budget. However, existing progressive approaches fail to scale to high-velocity streams because they rely on deterministic sorting to prioritize candidate pairs, a process that incurs prohibitive super-linear complexity and heavy initialization costs. Yunhao Yao (University of Science and Technology of China) · Zhiqiang Wang (University of Science and Technology of China) · Ruiqi Li (University of Science and Technology of China) · Haoran Cheng (University of Science and Technology of China) · Puhan Luo (University of Science and Technology of China) · Xiang-Yang Li (University of Science and Technology of China)
Abstract
As the Internet of Things (IoT) becomes deeply embedded in daily life, users are increasingly concerned about privacy leakage, especially from video, which holds rich, sensitive information. While many techniques can protect privacy, frame-by-frame protection in large-scale video analytics (e.g., smart communities) introduces significant latency. A more efficient solution is to first detect frames containing privacy objects (e.g., faces) and then apply selective protection. However, pixel-domain detection requires fully decoding video frames, incurring decoding overhead. Compressed-domain approaches directly analyze compressed video streams to accelerate inference, but often sacrifice accuracy, and the per-frame processing remains inefficient. Therefore, we propose ComPrivDet, an efficient framework for detecting privacy objects in compressed video by reusing I-frame inference results. ComPrivDet provides a pixel-domain detector on I-frames and a lightweight compressed-domain detector on P/B-frames. Leveraging compressed-domain cues to determine the presence of new objects, ComPrivDet either reuses I-frame results to skip P/B-frame detections or refines them with a lightweight detector. We prototype ComPrivDet on an edge server with an NVIDIA GeForce RTX 3090 GPU. ComPrivDet maintains 99.75% accuracy for private face detection and 96.83% for private license plate detection while skipping over 80% of inferences. It averages 1.36% higher accuracy with 57.23% lower inference latency than pixel-domain baselines, and 10.93% higher accuracy with 44.65% lower latency than compressed-domain baselines.

Large-scale aerial imagery provides fine-grained visual information for urban analytics, traffic monitoring, emergency response, and geospatial data mining. A central challenge is to reliably detect tiny objects in high-resolution, dense, and cluttered scenes. PolyphaseDet also improves prediction stability under one-pixel input translations while maintaining real-time efficiency comparable to that of the RT-DETR baseline.

Text–text consistency and anti-collapse contrastive text–mask losses with negative queries close the loop without dense annotations or VLM fine-tuning. A variational EM formulation yields a per-step contraction result under regularity assumptions, distinguishing semantic faithfulness from verifier overfitting. Across seven test sets on GF2, QuickBird, WorldView-III, and WorldView-II, LANCE improves reduced-scale reference metrics by up to 11.7% (median 2.1%) over the strongest learning baseline. Independent evaluation using a held-out VLM and a supervised aerial detector yields gains of +6.4 mAP and +0.072 open-vocabulary F1 over the closest competitor. Text perturbations, cross-verifier transfer, and pseudo-RGB ablations examine the mechanisms underlying these gains. The framework connects image fusion to verifiable semantic representations for multimodal retrieval and knowledge management.
FULLSWORD: Scene-Grounded Wasserstein Object-Relation Distance for 3D Scene Graph Prediction
U-Chae Jun (Sookmyung Women's University) · Jaeeun Ko (Sookmyung Women's University) · Yoonhyuk Choi (Sookmyung Women's University) · Jiwoo Kang (Sookmyung Women's University)
Abstract
3D scene graph prediction is commonly optimized with object-node and relation-edge classification losses. These objectives encourage exact object and relation label recovery, but they do not directly optimize semantic proximity to the ground-truth scene graph: two wrong graphs can receive comparable penalties even when one is much closer in object roles and relation contexts. A direct graph-distance loss is difficult in general, since graph matching and graph edit distance require correspondence search and edit-cost design. Our key observation is that prior supervised 3D scene graph prediction protocols are conducted on fixed object-node indices and supervised edge slots. This can turn a scene graph comparison into a well-defined aligned graph-distance problem. To this end, we propose SWORD, a Scene-Grounded Wasserstein Object-Relation Distance that builds block-normalized object and relation ground distance metrics from training scene graph annotations through a deterministic base-to-context order, without external semantic priors. SWORD lifts these metrics to Wasserstein distances over aligned node and null-augmented edge marginals, providing semantic graph-distance supervision beyond exact-label penalties while preserving the ground-truth graph as the unique zero-distance solution in aligned marginal probability space. We prove that SWORD is a strict metric on aligned marginal probabilistic scene graphs, preserves scene-graph-grounded substitution ordering, controls additive graph-grounded semantic observables, and yields a surrogate upper-bounding decoded semantic error.
FULLVISRA: Vision-Language Induced Supervision and Representation Alignment for Long-Tailed Generalized Category Discovery
Yizhong Zhang (East China Normal University) · Hongzhe Shou (East China Normal University) · Guanyu Lu (East China Normal University) · Fang Zhou (East China Normal University)
Abstract
Generalized Category Discovery (GCD) aims to classify unlabeled data containing both known and novel classes, given only labels for known classes. Existing GCD methods typically assume a relatively balanced data distribution, an assumption that breaks down in realistic open-world scenarios. In this paper, we study Long-Tailed Generalized Category Discovery (LT-GCD), where both labeled and unlabeled data follow long-tailed distributions. Under such conditions, training signals are dominated by known categories; this imbalance biases representation learning and weakens novel-category discovery. To address these challenges, we propose VISRA, a semantic-driven framework for LT-GCD built upon a parametric GCD pipeline. Rather than relying solely on distribution debiasing, our framework leverages Vision-Language Models (VLMs) to provide additional semantic supervision for representative novel-class instances and guide visual representation learning. Experimental results on three long-tailed datasets demonstrate that VISRA achieves state-of-the-art performance, effectively alleviating novel-class supervision deficiency and learning more discriminative representations under severe imbalance. Our code and prompt are available at https://github.com/EileanZYZ/VISRA.
FULLAsymmetric Privileged Distillation for Weakly Supervised Video Anomaly Detection
Xusheng Li (Northwestern Polytechnical University) · Haotong Du (Northwestern Polytechnical University) · Binghan Chen (Northwestern Polytechnical University) · Xianghua Li (Northwestern Polytechnical University) · Chao Gao (Northwestern Polytechnical University)
Abstract
Recent advances in Large Language Models (LLMs) and vision–language models have introduced richer semantic guidance into Weakly Supervised Video Anomaly Detection (WS-VAD). However, video-dependent text generation or encoding during inference introduces substantial computational overhead and complicates deployment in resource-constrained scenarios. We propose APD-VAD, an Asymmetric Privileged Distillation framework that uses LVLM-generated descriptions as privileged information during training and deploys a visual student without dynamic text processing. A Privileged Language Cascade (PLC) supplies video- and snippet-level descriptions to the teacher, and a Background-Debiased Graph (BDG) attenuates scene-dominated relations before temporal graph reasoning. Semantic-distribution, feature, and topology distillation transfer the resulting class, snippet, and relational knowledge to the student. At inference, a dual-branch visual graph and Visual Prototype Memory (VPM) provide category-aware visual context through cached category prototypes and class-routed visual retrieval. Experiments on UCF-Crime and XD-Violence demonstrate competitive anomaly detection and improved fine-grained temporal localization, while deployment profiling confirms efficient inference without recurring LVLM processing. Code is available at https://github.com/cgao-comp/APD-VAD.
FULLFOCAL: Forgery-Centric One-Class Artifact Learning for Out-of-Distribution Deepfake Detection
Muhammad Shahid Muneer (Sungkyunkwan University) · Razaib Tariq (Sungkyunkwan University) · Simon S. Woo (Sungkyunkwan University)
Abstract
Existing deepfake detection methods learn facial representations that capture the identity, semantics, or geometric structure of real faces. We argue that such face-centric representations can introduce identity and semantic biases, encoding appearance attributes that correlate with a person’s identity rather than with the image’s manipulation, thereby limiting transferability to unseen forgery types. We propose Forgery-Centric One-Class Artifact Learning (FOCAL), a representation learning framework that models manipulation artifacts directly rather than generic facial semantics. FOCAL is trained exclusively on forged images: an encoder-decoder reconstructs spatial artifact maps from fake inputs, forcing the encoder to learn where and how manipulation has occurred. This reconstruction objective is complemented by spatial and frequency-domain contrastive losses that encourage invariance to input perturbations while preserving discriminative forgery cues. Because the encoder captures a compact forgery-artifact distribution, real faces unseen during training naturally fall outside. We exploit this property by proposing the Dynamic-Centroid Mahalanobis Distance (DCMD), which enables classifier-free, zero-shot detection with out target-domain adaptation. FOCAL surpasses state-of-the-art methods on standard cross-dataset benchmarks in both detection AUC and pixel-level forgery despite fake-only training. This clearly demonstrates that forgery-centric representations yield transfer- able features than approaches anchored to real-face distributions
FULLClosing Generalization Gaps in Continual Face Forgery Detection
Bohyun Moon (Sungkyunkwan University) · Minh Binh Le (Sungkyunkwan University) · Simon S. Woo (Sungkyunkwan University)
Abstract
Deepfake manipulations evolve rapidly across digital media platforms, requiring continual detector updates as the distributions of face forgeries shift. Unlike general class-incremental learning, continual face forgery detection is a domain-incremental binary task in which new manipulations of the same fake class are introduced. We demonstrate that existing continual deepfake detectors remain tied to distribution-specific cues, preserving performance on seen datasets while struggling to generalize to unseen manipulation domains. This observation suggests that effective continual adaptation should preserve transferable representations while retaining prior knowledge under sequential domain shifts. We further find that SVD-based parameter-efficient tuning improves transferability but requires regularization against forgetting. Accordingly, we propose TASER, an exemplar-free framework that couples this transferable basis with transport-guided regularization. Asymmetric Class-Wise Partial Optimal Transport (AC-POT) aligns real and fake manifolds separately for class-aware adaptation, while OT-guided Contrastive Separation (OTCon) strengthens the real/fake boundary using transport-selected positives and opposite-class negatives. TASER achieves state-of-the-art intra-dataset retention and cross-dataset generalization, with a final average AUC of 0.9787, a 0.0123 average forgetting AUC, and an overall cross-dataset AUC of 0.8626 across challenging continual face forgery benchmarks.

FULLUnveiling Color-induced Emotions latent in Image-Text Expressions from Dual Perceptual Pathways
Changrong Min (Criminal Investigation Police University of China) · Changchun Li (Jilin University) · Bing Wang (Jilin University) · You Lu (Shenzhen University of Advanced Technology) · Ximing Li (Jilin University)
Abstract
Image-text emotion detection (ITED) aims to identify the emotion expressed by a given pair of text and image. However, existing methods often overlook color, a fundamental visual cue that carries rich emotional information. From the perspective of human cognition, color expressions in images and texts can evoke emotions in both direct and indirect ways. Inspired by this observation, we design a Dynamic Emotion Semantic Enhancement Framework via Dual Color-induced Pathways for the ITED task. Specifically, our framework first builds a direct color-induced emotion (CIE) pathway based on general human color-emotion patterns and an indirect pathway through the generative imagination of color-similar scenes. Such rich CIE knowledge is then parameterized as multiple trainable experts within a mixture-of-CIE-experts module (MoCE) shared across the two modalities. However, as not all the color-induced emotions contribute positively to the final prediction, we design a dynamic expert selection mechanism that allows words in texts or regions in images to adaptively retrieve experts' knowledge consistent with the grounded emotions. Extensive experiments on three ITED datasets under different modality fusion strategies demonstrate the effectiveness, robustness, and generalization ability of the framework.
FULLMultimodal Aspect-Based Sentiment Analysis via Evidence-Guided Region Calibration
Baoxing Jiang (Sichuan University) · Xinpei Zhang (Sichuan University) · Yujie Wan (Sichuan University) · Renyue Zhang (New York University) · Shenggen Ju (Sichuan University)
Abstract
Multimodal Aspect-Based Sentiment Analysis (MABSA) aims to identify aspect-level sentiment from user-generated image-text posts. Although visual information can provide useful context for sentiment reasoning, it is not uniformly beneficial for aspect-level prediction. Different image regions may serve distinct roles: some provide content support for post understanding, some offer sentiment-related evidence, while others introduce irrelevant or misleading signals. To address this challenge, we propose VEGA, a MABSA framework that integrates visual evidence construction with evidence-guided region calibration. Specifically, VEGA first leverages a multimodal large language model to construct two complementary types of visual evidence from each image-text pair: content-aware visual evidence and context-aware sentiment evidence. These evidence streams are then used to calibrate region-level visual representations through a dual-support cross-attention mechanism, enabling image regions to contribute according to their roles in content understanding and sentiment inference. Finally, the calibrated visual features are integrated with the original text in a unified encoder-decoder architecture for both multimodal aspect sentiment classification and joint multimodal aspect-sentiment analysis subtasks. Experiments on public benchmarks demonstrate that VEGA consistently outperforms strong task-specific baselines. Further analyses confirm the effectiveness of visual evidence construction and evidence-guided region calibration.
FULLReasonGraph: Graph-Enhanced Reasoning Distillation for Aspect Sentiment Triplet Extraction
Shuchen Chen (Sun Yat-sen University) · Yunhe Pang (Sun Yat-sen University) · Keyi Chen (Sun Yat-sen University) · Daifeng Li (Sun Yat-sen University)
Abstract
Aspect Sentiment Triplet Extraction (ASTE) aims to extract aspect–opinion–sentiment triplets from review sentences and is a fundamental task in fine-grained sentiment analysis. Recent large language model-based chain-of-thought (CoT) methods improve instruction following and semantic reasoning for ASTE, but their verbose reasoning outputs introduce substantial inference overhead and often lack explicit structural grounding. We propose ReasonGraph, which integrates gold-guided CoT distillation with dependency-graph-based syntactic grounding. The distillation pipeline first trains the model with explicit reasoning chains and final answers, and then shifts to direct answer generation, allowing reasoning ability to be internalized while keeping inference compact. Meanwhile, a GATv2 dependency-graph encoder injects parsed syntactic structures as continuous prefix embeddings, enabling the LLM to adaptively balance syntactic and semantic cues. Experiments on four standard ASTE benchmarks show that ReasonGraph achieves strong performance with significantly faster inference than CoT-based reasoning methods. Further analysis indicates that our method effectively captures complementary semantic and syntactic information and focuses on the most informative cues for triplet extraction. Our code is available at https://github.com/cscsysu/aste-cikm.
FULLBoundary and Discourse-Aware Modeling for Dialogue-Level Aspect-Based Sentiment Quadruple Analysis
Siying Yu (Inner Mongolia University) · Lihong Shi (Inner Mongolia University) · Xianguo Zhang (Inner Mongolia University)
Abstract
Dialogue-level Aspect-based Sentiment Quadruple Analysis (DiaASQ) aims to extract all (target, aspect, opinion, sentiment) quadruples from multi-turn multi-party dialogues, where sentiment elements may be scattered across different speakers and turns. Despite exploiting dialogue structures, existing methods face two fundamental bottlenecks: First, span representations relying on average pooling treat all tokens equally, which inherently dilutes critical boundary cues and introduces semantic ambiguity—especially when boundaries carry sentiment-bearing modifiers. Second, existing methods model dialogue structures at the coarse utterance level, neglecting fine-grained span-pair interactions across turns—crucial for linking scattered sentiment elements. To address these limitations, we propose: (1) Boundary-Aware Bilinear Attention Pooling (BAP), which replaces uniform averaging with boundary-guided attention, using bilinear projections to dynamically weight span tokens based on their relevance to start/end boundaries; (2) Role-aware Dialogue Householder Projection (RDHP), which refines span-pair representations via geometry-aware partial projections, projecting away dialogue-irrelevant directions while preserving sentiment-bearing subspaces. Extensive experiments on Chinese and English DiaASQ benchmarks demonstrate competitive performance, establishing a new state-of-the-art on the English benchmark with substantial gains in cross-turn quadruple extraction.
FULLSchema-Driven Structured Information Extraction from Biomedical Literature via Large Language Models
Emanuele Cavalleri (University of Milano) · Ali Rastegar Mojarad (University of Milano) · J. Harry Caufield (Lawrence Berkeley National Lab) · Justin Reese (Lawrence Berkeley National Lab) · Christopher J. Mungall (Lawrence Berkeley National Lab) · Marco Mesiti (University of Milano)
Abstract
Named Entity Recognition and Relation Extraction are key Information Extraction tasks that enable the transformation of unstructured text into structured, machine-interpretable knowledge. In the biomedical domain, the extraction process must be guided by semantic constraints and domain knowledge to prevent the introduction of incorrect, inconsistent, or irrelevant information. In this paper, we propose a framework for constrained multi-stage information extraction pipelines guided by biomedical ontologies. The approach relies on the specification of a schema describing the entities, relations, constraints, and semantic dependencies relevant to the target domain. The schema is used to automatically generate a list of context-aware prompts that guide a general-purpose LLM during the extraction process (avoiding specific fine-tuning). The framework further supports mapping to ontology terms, extraction guidelines, and ontology-derived examples to improve extraction consistency and semantic validation. The proposed approach has been integrated into SchemaLink, an intelligent web platform supporting schema specification, prompt generation and execution, ontology-aware mapping, and visualization of extracted entities and relations. Extensive experiments on biomedical information extraction benchmarks show that our approach outperforms existing schema-guided prompt engineering methods by more effectively modeling dependencies between entity and relation extraction tasks, while achieving performance comparable to fine-tuned domain-specific models.
FULLMitigating the Morpheme Tokenization Bottleneck in Agglutinative Languages: A Korean Case Study with Interleave Attention
Hyunwook Yu (Chung-Ang University) · Minju Kim (Chung-Ang University) · Mucheol Kim (Chung-Ang University)
Abstract
Decoder-only language models score text through next-token likelihoods over tokenizer-induced token sequences. This scoring interface becomes unstable when tokenizer segmentation shapes candidate selection or passage relevance scores rather than contextual fit alone. Agglutinative languages expose this problem sharply because morphosyntactic information is densely packed into surface forms. Korean offers a representative agglutinative stress case through particles, endings, compounds, and spacing variation. We propose Interleave Attention, a decoder augmentation that injects morphology-aware auxiliary representations into the scoring path. Prefix-aligned interleaving integrates these representations into a fused causal sequence rather than a separate cross-attention memory. Under matched initialization, continued-pretraining corpus, objective, and scoring interface, Interleave continued pretraining (CPT) produces stable trajectory-level gains over a parameter-matched decoder-only baseline, improving the overall benchmark average by 3.34 points and the context-conditioned average by 7.12 points. Controlled relevance scoring shows improved rank-sensitive scoring under a fixed hard-negative pool, and Korean surface-form stress tests indicate additional Korean-side robustness under surface variation. These results support a bottleneck-mitigation interpretation that separates the general Interleave effect from the morphology-based auxiliary-tokenizer effect.
FULLDynamic Topic Modeling for Cross-Corpus Temporal Analysis
Ruoxuan Li (Columbia University) · Bruce Kogut (Columbia University)
Abstract
Dynamic Embedded Topic Models (D-ETM) provide an interpretable framework for modeling temporal semantic evolution, but cross-corpus comparison remains difficult because topics are often learned independently and aligned only after training, a process that does not guarantee stable topic correspondence across corpora and time. To address this problem, we propose a D-ETM framework that first learns a common dynamic topic space over a merged multi-corpus collection, which we call the shared backbone, then introduces corpus-specific residual adaptation around the frozen backbone without creating separate latent topic spaces. This design preserves a shared topic index for cross-corpus comparison while allowing each corpus to specialize lexically. We evaluate the framework on three temporally structured corpora spanning 97 years: the Corpus of Historical American English, Harvard Business Review, and International Labour Review. Residual adaptation improves corpus-specific fit relative to the shared backbone while preserving the same-index cross-corpus topic trajectories, achieving substantially stronger alignment than full fine-tuning from the same backbone, with (97.5 ± 0.7%) versus (17.9 ± 1.1%) trajectory Retrieval@1, as well as stronger alignment than independent training with post-hoc Hungarian matching. These results suggest that incorporating topic alignment into the model can support more stable over-time cross-corpus comparisons while retaining corpus-specific lexical variation.
FULLSeeing is Deciding: Evidence-Based Parallel Probing for LLM-based Web Agents
Hanxun Li (National University of Defense Technology) · Bin Li (Intelligent Game and Decision Lab (IGDL)) · Jingtao Qi (Intelligent Game and Decision Lab (IGDL)) · Enze Wang (Intelligent Game and Decision Lab (IGDL)) · Haoxiang Jin (Intelligent Game and Decision Lab (IGDL)) · Biao Han (National University of Defense Technology) · Jinshu Su (National University of Defense Technology)
Abstract
Autonomous agents powered by Large Language Models (LLMs) can automate complex web tasks, but their reliability is limited by uncertain action outcomes: the consequence of interacting with a web element is often known only after execution. Existing sequential methods are vulnerable to error propagation after wrong decisions, while tree-search approaches rely on speculative pre-execution scoring and incur substantial exploration cost. We introduce WebTactix, an evidence-based parallel probing framework that shifts web navigation from speculative prediction to grounded decision making. Rather than scoring actions before execution, WebTactix executes multiple candidate plans in parallel, observes their successor pages, and compares the resulting evidence to select the next branch while accounting for future continuation. This design enables the agent to explore multiple alternatives without committing prematurely to uncertain decisions or incurring the overhead of extensive tree search. Experiments on WebArena and Online-Mind2Web demonstrate consistent improvements in both task success and efficiency, with WebTactix achieving 76.8% success on WebArena while reducing average completion time by 56.2% relative to the strongest tree-search baseline.
