FULLCo-JDPRec: Collaborative Joint Dynamic Pruning for Efficient LLM-based Generative Recommendation
Shunhang Zheng (Hangzhou Dianzi University) · Pengfei Jiao (Hangzhou Dianzi University) · Pinlong Zhao (Hangzhou Dianzi University) · Haocheng Yang (Tsinghua Shenzhen International Graduate School) · Dalin Zhang (Hangzhou Dianzi University) · Yuling Wang (Hangzhou Dianzi University)
Abstract
Generative recommendation leverages Large Language Models (LLMs) to model item semantics and user preference dynamics through sequence-to-token generation, but deep Transformer layers and wide Feed Forward Network (FFN) dimensions introduce substantial memory and latency overhead in online recommendation scenarios. Existing LLM pruning methods are mainly designed to preserve general language modeling ability, often overlooking the recommendation-specific states shaped by item semantics, collaborative signals, and temporal preference dynamics. To address this limitation, we propose Co-JDPRec, a collaborative joint dynamic pruning framework that shifts the pruning objective from parameter removal to recommendation-state preservation. Specifically, Co-JDPRec introduces a task-aware saliency criterion that combines collaborative alignment and sequence-order sensitivity, enabling the model to identify neurons critical for user-item relations and evolving preference dynamics. Guided by this saliency, Co-JDPRec jointly searches FFN width and layer depth to derive a compact heterogeneous architecture, followed by distillation recovery to restore recommendation performance. Theoretically, Co-JDPRec characterizes structural importance via first-order Taylor sensitivity under recommendation-aware objectives. Empirically, it achieves superior accuracy–efficiency trade-offs on both title-based and semantic-ID-based generative recommendation backbones, validating the effectiveness of recommendation-state-aware pruning.
FULLMISTRec: Masked Item-Slot Token Modeling for LLM-based Generative Recommendation
Huaye Zhang (China University of Petroleum (East China)) · Tingting Chen (China University of Petroleum (East China)) · Shaojun Wang (China University of Petroleum (East China)) · Diqiong Jiang (China University of Petroleum (East China))
Abstract
Large Language Models (LLMs) have recently been explored for generative recommendation, where item tokenization plays a critical role. Existing studies design item identifiers such as discrete Semantic IDs, single-token identifiers, and multi-token or set identifiers. However, in many identifier-based methods, the item-level grounding of these introduced identifiers is not established during general-domain pre-training and must instead be learned during recommendation-specific adaptation. Consequently, LLMs may treat them as opaque prediction symbols rather than stable item representations. To address this issue, we propose MISTRec, a masked item-slot modeling framework for learning structured continuous item representations. MISTRec introduces three key designs. First, MISTRec decomposes each item into continuous CF-aware and latent semantic slots, reducing the entanglement between collaborative signals and metadata-derived item semantics. Second, it trains these slots with Masked Slot Autoencoding (MSA) by reconstructing corrupted historical slots and completing a fully masked future item. Third, it introduces False Negative Reweighting (FNR), which downweights semantically conflicting negatives during target alignment and improves the stability of full-catalog ranking. Experiments on three public benchmarks show that MISTRec consistently improves next-item recommendation over strong sequential and generative baselines, while yielding more stable item neighborhoods across random seeds.
FULLRethinking Item Tokenization in Generative Recommenders: From Fixed Atoms to Semantic Subwords
Xinrui Miao (University of Science and Technology of China) · Mingjia Yin (University of Science and Technology of China) · Jiaqing Zhang (University of Science and Technology of China) · Wei Guo (Huawei Technologies) · Yong Liu (Huawei Technologies) · Yuyang Ye (University of Science and Technology of China) · Hao Wang (University of Science and Technology of China) · Enhong Chen (University of Science and Technology of China)
Abstract
In generative recommender systems, items are typically tokenized into fixed-length semantic ID sequences for autoregressive next-item prediction. However, for user-context modeling, this fine-grained representation triggers Intra-item Attention Overload: excessive attention is spent on low-level intra-item dependencies rather than high-level inter-item behavioral transitions. To address this, we propose Semantic Subword Tokenization (SST), which represents historical items as variable-length semantic subwords while preserving fixed-length target decoding. SST first applies Item-level Subword Tokenization (IST) to merge stable adjacent atom tokens into compact semantic subword tokens, thereby reducing intra-item reassembly in the encoder. It then introduces Behavior-induced Co-occurrence Augmentation (BCA) to inject coarse-grained semantic prefix transition signals, guiding the freed modeling capacity toward inter-item behavioral regularities. Extensive experiments on three public datasets and three generative recommender backbones show empirical improvements of SST over fixed-length and transferable variable-length SID baselines. Code is available at https://github.com/mxrcandy/Semantic-Subword-Tokenization.
FULLBeyond Uniform Token Training: A Multi-Target Framework for Learning Token-Weighted Objectives in Generative Recommenders
Wei-Ning Chiu (Carnegie Mellon University) · Song-Duo Ma (National Taiwan University) · Han-Jay Shu (National Tsing Hua University) · Chuan-Ju Wang (Academia Sinica) · Pu-Jen Cheng (National Taiwan University)
Abstract
Recent generative recommendation models recast next-item prediction as the generation of a semantic identifier sequence. While this formulation enables autoregressive models to produce item IDs directly, the commonly used token-level likelihood objective does not distinguish between tokens that play different roles in item identification. This limitation is especially pronounced for semantic-ID representations, where prefix tokens often determine coarse item groups and later tokens provide finer-grained disambiguation. To better align training with the structure of semantic IDs, we study token-level learning signals from two complementary perspectives. First, we introduce a prefix-aware weighting scheme, Front-Greater Weighting, which emphasizes tokens according to their contribution to reducing semantic ambiguity among candidate items. Second, frequency weighting increases the learning emphasis on infrequent tokens, addressing the long-tailed distributions and popularity bias commonly observed in recommendation data. We further introduce a multi-target optimization framework with curriculum learning, which integrates the two token-weighted objectives with the standard likelihood and enables stable optimization with adaptive emphasis across training stages. Experiments on multiple benchmark datasets demonstrate that the proposed approach consistently improves generative recommendation performance over strong baselines and prior token-weighting methods. Additional analyses show that the method is robust across different semantic-ID constructions and backbone scales, and that it improves recommendation quality for both popular and long-tail items. Code is available at github repository.
FULLLearning to Reflect and Correct: Towards Better Decoding Trajectories for Large-Scale Generative Recommendation
Haibo Xing (Alibaba International Digital Commerce Group) · Hao Deng (Alibaba International Digital Commerce Group) · Lingyu Mu (Alibaba International Digital Commerce Group) · Jinxin Hu (Alibaba International Digital Commerce Group) · Yu Zhang (Alibaba International Digital Commerce Group) · Xiaoyi Zeng (Alibaba International Digital Commerce Group) · Jing Zhang (Wuhan University, School of Computer Science)
Abstract
Generative Recommendation (GR) has become a promising paradigm for large-scale recommendation systems, yet existing GR models typically perform single-pass decoding without explicit refinement, causing early deviations to accumulate and degrade recommendation quality. Recent work mitigates this via two reasoning paradigms: reason-then-generate, which refines intermediate states before producing the draft, and reason-while-generating, which interleaves reasoning with token generation. Both, however, reason before a complete draft exists and cannot diagnose or revise a finalized Semantic-ID (SID) trajectory. To this end, we propose GRC, to our knowledge the first structured reflection–correction paradigm for GR that performs reasoning on a complete draft via a Generation–Reflection–Correction process. GRC introduces a supervised reflection-correction template with multi-granular reflection labels in the SID space, and further optimizes the GRC trajectory via GRPO-based reinforcement learning with tailored rewards that jointly evaluate correction quality and reflection accuracy. For efficient online serving, we propose an Entropy-Guided Reflection Scheduling (EGRS) strategy that prioritizes high-uncertainty trajectories for correction under a fixed beam budget. Extensive experiments show that GRC consistently outperforms eight state-of-the-art baselines by up to 13.33%, and online A/B tests demonstrate its substantial practical value in large-scale industrial recommendation, delivering a 1.39% lift in advertising revenue with only modest latency overhead.
FULLRQ-Reg: A Residual-Quantization-Based Framework for Continuous Value Prediction in Recommender Systems
Runpeng Cui (Kuaishou Technology) · Zhipeng Sun (Kuaishou Technology) · Chi Lu (Kuaishou Technology) · Peng Jiang (Kuaishou Technology)
Abstract
Predicting continuous values such as watch-time and gross merchandise value (GMV) is a core problem in industrial recommendation systems. Its inherent difficulty stems from the highly complex and long-tailed distributions of the target signals, which are hard to model accurately. Existing regression methods typically rely on fixed parametric assumptions on the target distribution: overly simple assumptions underfit real-world data, whereas more intricate ones tend to sacrifice scalability and generalization. To address these limitations, we propose a sequence modeling framework based on residual quantization (RQ), in which the target continuous value is decomposed into a sequence of quantization codes that represent progressively finer approximations. The model autoregressively predicts these codes from coarse to fine granularity, with each step refining the residual error left by the previous one. To further improve the quality of the learned representations, we introduce an ordinal-aware representation learning objective that aligns the RQ code embedding space with the ordinal structure of target values, thereby yielding continuous representations of quantization codes and more accurate predictions. We conduct comprehensive experiments on public benchmarks for watch-time and lifetime value (LTV) prediction, together with a large-scale online A/B test for GMV prediction on an industrial short-video recommendation platform. Across all settings, the proposed method shows competitive performance among existing state-of-the-art approaches and generalizes well across diverse continuous value prediction scenarios.
FULLFAF: A Feature-Aware Adaptive Pre-training Framework for Bridging Gaps in CTR Prediction
Kai Cheng (University of Science and Technology of China) · Hao Wang (University of Science and Technology of China) · Kefan Wang (University of Science and Technology of China) · Luankang Zhang (University of Science and Technology of China) · Yiquan Lee (HUAWEI TECHNOLOGIES CO.LTD) · Wei Guo (HUAWEI TECHNOLOGIES CO.LTD) · Yong Liu (HUAWEI TECHNOLOGIES CO.LTD) · Yuyang Ye (University of Science and Technology of China) · Enhong Chen (University of Science and Technology of China)
Abstract
Self-supervised pre-training has emerged as an effective solution to data sparsity in Click-Through Rate (CTR) prediction. However, existing paradigms still face two critical limitations: (1) task degeneration in pre-training, where heuristic or random target construction may lead to trivial shortcuts; and (2) limited adaptivity in fine-tuning, where static transfer strategies fail to accommodate optimization heterogeneity across diverse feature fields and ID frequencies. To address these issues, we propose the Feature-aware Adaptive pre-training and fine-tuning Framework (FAF). The core of FAF lies in two coupled designs. First, we improve pre-training target construction from both token and feature levels. At the token level, we introduce a position-decayed future item prediction task to incorporate additional future behavior supervision while reducing the influence of noisy distant targets. At the feature level, we formulate masked feature selection as a combinatorial optimization problem and derive an entropy-redundancy scoring criterion, which selects informative target fields with low contextual redundancy to construct non-trivial reconstruction tasks. Second, we design an adaptive fine-tuning strategy that combines field-aware and item frequency-aware update regulation. This strategy dynamically adjusts embedding update magnitudes across heterogeneous feature fields and item frequencies, improving the compatibility between pre-trained representations and downstream task adaptation. Extensive experiments on three real-world datasets show that FAF brings consistent overall performance gains over strong baselines across multiple backbone models, demonstrating its effectiveness in representation learning and compatible knowledge transfer.
FULLFC-GNN: Unleashing Field Priors for Graph-based CTR Prediction
Huanyu Liu (Huazhong University of Science and Technology) · Hui Liu (Huazhong University of Science and Technology) · Hengjie Xie (Huazhong University of Science and Technology) · Wenyi Hu (Huazhong University of Science and Technology) · Zengyang Li (Central China Normal University)
Abstract
Graph Neural Networks (GNNs) have been adopted for click-through rate (CTR) prediction to explicitly capture and model feature interactions. However, existing graph evolution approaches with separate structural inference and feature aggregation face two key challenges in recommendation scenarios. On the one hand, recursively updated structural representations can suffer from degraded edge discriminability during graph evolution, destabilizing high-order topology learning. On the other hand, heterogeneous feature fields make conventional message passing prone to semantic misalignment. Consequently, the learned topology may not align with the semantic requirements of subsequent message propagation. In this paper, we propose Field-aware Compositional GNN (FC-GNN), which exploits field semantics as a dual-role inductive bias to stabilize graph learning. At the structure level, we introduce a Field Prior Matrix as a field-conditioned interaction operator, reducing the dependence of edge discrimination on feature representations. At the node level, we establish Field Semantic Anchors as shared semantic coordinates and employ a field-conditioned gating mechanism to calibrate heterogeneous feature representations before message passing. Moreover, we reuse the same field prior matrix during aggregation to form a feedback bridge between structure inference and semantic propagation. Experimental results on three public datasets demonstrate that FC-GNN consistently outperforms existing methods.
4B · Graph & Multimodal RecommendationFull ResearchSala SinopoliTuesday 16:00 – 18:008 talksChair: Keigo Sakurai (Hokkaido University)
FULLHard but Not Too Hard: Semi-Hard Negative Sampling for Implicit Collaborative Filtering
Junha Park (Sogang University) · Seyeon Choi (Sogang University) · Jihoon Yang (Sogang University) · Gordon Euhyun Moon (Sogang University)
Abstract
Negative sampling plays a pivotal role in implicit feedback-based collaborative filtering (CF) models optimized with pairwise ranking loss, as these models must learn to rank preferred items higher than non-preferred ones. As simply treating all unobserved interactions as negative samples may degrade model accuracy, previous studies have explored various negative sampling strategies, such as static and hard negative sampling, to select more informative negative samples. However, static negative sampling methods often fail to select informative samples because they do not account for training dynamics or the structure of user preferences, whereas hard negative sampling methods suffer from the false negative problem and may therefore introduce incorrect training signals. To address these limitations and provide a theoretical solution to the negative sampling problem, we conduct an in-depth analysis of implicit CF under the Bayesian Personalized Ranking loss. As a result, we find that sampling highly preferred items as negatives degrades recommendation performance, whereas more frequently sampling moderately preferred items improves it. Based on these findings, we propose Semi-Hard Negative Sampling (SHNS), a novel negative sampling method for implicit CF that selects moderately difficult negative samples while dynamically annealing the sampling difficulty to mitigate the risk of false negatives. Extensive experimental results show that SHNS achieves superior performance compared with 10 state-of-the-art negative sampling methods. Further empirical analysis demonstrates that SHNS effectively mitigates the false negative problem while maintaining the ability to select informative negative samples.
FULLDual-Tree LLM-Enhanced Negative Sampling for Implicit Collaborative Filtering
Jiayi Wu (Beijing Institute of Technology) · Zhengyu Wu (Beijing Institute of Technology) · Xunkai Li (Beijing Institute of Technology) · Rong-Hua Li (Beijing Institute of Technology) · Guoren Wang (Beijing Institute of Technology)
Abstract
Negative sampling is a pivotal technique in implicit collaborative filtering (CF), enabling efficient and effective training by contrasting observed interactions with sampled unobserved ones. Recently, large language models (LLMs) have shown promise in recommender systems, yet their use in negative sampling remains underexplored. Existing methods often rely on textual information and task-specific fine-tuning, which may limit their applicability in settings with scarce textual metadata or constrained computational resources. To this end, we propose a text-free and fine-tuning-free Dual-Tree LLM-enhanced Negative Sampling method (DTL-NS). It consists of two modules: (i) an offline false negative identification module that leverages hierarchical index trees to transform collaborative structural and latent semantic information into structured item-ID encodings for LLM inference, enabling accurate identification of false negatives; and (ii) a multi-view hard negative sampling module that combines user–item preference scores with item–item hierarchical similarities from these encodings to mine high-quality negatives, thus improving models’ discriminative ability. Extensive experiments demonstrate that DTL-NS consistently improves recommendation performance across different implicit CF models, negative sampling methods, and LLMs.
FULLDo All Nodes Benefit Equally from Knowledge Graphs? Adaptive Node-Aware KG Fusion for Recommendation
Jaehyun Park (Soongsil University) · Minseo Jeon (Soongsil University) · Daewon Gwak (Soongsil University) · Sunuk Kim (Soongsil University) · Hanvit Lee (Soongsil University) · Jinhong Jung (Soongsil University)
Abstract
KG-aware recommendation has been widely studied to alleviate data sparsity by using knowledge graphs (KGs), which represent items, entities, and their relations as graphs and provide item-side knowledge. However, existing methods incorporate item knowledge without considering how much each user or item node should rely on it. As a result, they apply KG signals indiscriminately across nodes, even to nodes whose collaborative filtering (CF) signals from the interaction graph (IG) are already reliable. In this paper, we propose AdaKG (Adaptive Node-Aware KG Fusion), a novel KG-aware recommendation method that adaptively adjusts the contribution of auxiliary knowledge for each node. Since user-item interactions and item knowledge provide different types of signals, directly mixing them can distort the CF signals. To avoid this, AdaKG separately encodes the IG and KG with view-specific encoders, allowing each view to capture its own information. It then estimates how strongly each node should rely on item knowledge by measuring the stability of its CF signals under small adversarial perturbations, assigning a larger KG contribution to less stable nodes. Finally, AdaKG adaptively aligns the IG and KG embeddings in a shared space and fuses them according to the estimated node-wise reliance. Through experiments, we show that AdaKG achieves strong performance compared with its baselines and the effectiveness of our adaptive fusion strategy.
FULLSocialKAN: Learning User Preferences on Signed Social Graphs with Kolmogorov-Arnold Networks
Anchen Li (Aalto University) · Elena Casiraghi (Aalto University) · Juho Rousu (Aalto University)
Abstract
User-user social networks are widely utilized as side information in recommendation and have been shown to improve performance. We argue that current social recommenders still have room for improvement. First, for social data utilization, most methods focus mainly on positive trust relations, while failing to effectively use negative distrust relations, which can also provide useful signals for recommendation. Second, in terms of modeling architecture, most methods rely on linear or nonlinear transformation structures (e.g., multi-layer perceptrons) as their foundational building blocks. Kolmogorov-Arnold Networks (KANs), recently introduced for their strong data-fitting ability, offer a promising alternative. To this end, in this paper, we propose SocialKAN, a novel KAN-based trust-distrust-aware social recommender method. Specifically, SocialKAN introduces three KAN-based graph learning channels to model the user-item interaction graph, user trust graph, and user distrust graph, respectively. To better enable effective cross-view adaptation among the three channels, we design a semantic routing module for knowledge sharing at the embedding level and an adaptive consensus knowledge distillation strategy for output alignment at the optimization level. Experimental results on the three datasets show that our proposed SocialKAN method achieves strong performance. Ablation studies further validate the rationality and effectiveness of the components designed in our SocialKAN.
FULLKG-ARMM: Residual Structural Fusion for Graph-Augmented Personalized Retrieval
Mohamed Elrfaey (University of Victoria) · Thomas Gulliver (University of Victoria)
Abstract
Dense multimodal retrieval scales well, but it can miss relational evidence from user histories, item neighborhoods, and domain entities. We present KG-ARMM, a retrieval-compatible Residual Structural Fusion (RSF) framework. A text-and-poster backbone supports approximate nearest-neighbor (ANN) candidate generation; an offline item graph and filtered knowledge graph (KG) supply evidence to a lightweight pairwise re-ranker. The primary configuration gives the learned score limited authority, combining it with normalized structural support, a popularity penalty, and a long-tail bonus. On a temporal MovieLens–The Movie Database (TMDB) benchmark evaluated against the full catalog, the balanced variant improves normalized discounted cumulative gain at 20 (NDCG@20) by 8.3% (0.04273 to 0.04628) and Recall@20 by 7.0% (0.09968 to 0.10666) over the multimodal backbone. A matched full-scale control without graph/KG features or the direct structural term reaches 0.04405 NDCG@20 and 0.10336 Recall@20; complete-model paired gains remain positive with 95% intervals [0.00205, 0.00241] and [0.00285, 0.00375], respectively. KGSupport@20 rises from 0.2704 in that control to 0.3128, with stable catalog behavior. Sparse-history users gain most, and validation-holdout ablations favor the filtered relation bundle. Unrestricted learned-score authority yields higher accuracy but collapses long-tail exposure. These results support structural evidence as a sparse, auditable correction layer over dense multimodal retrieval rather than as an unconstrained replacement for the base ranking signal.
FULLBRIDGE: Behavior-Guided Residual Integration with Dual-Frequency Graph Evidence
Zesheng Li (University of the Chinese Academy of Sciences) · Chengchang Pan (University of the Chinese Academy of Sciences) · Honggang Qi (University of the Chinese Academy of Sciences)
Abstract
Multimodal recommendation improves item representations by combining visual, textual, and collaborative signals, but stronger cross-view alignment does not always improve ranking. Our diagnostics on Amazon Baby show that direct consistency has an effective range: moderate alignment helps, while stronger alignment suppresses recommendation-specific variation. We also observe a clear spectral split: low-frequency components capture shared structure, whereas higher-frequency components retain more private ranking signal. Based on these findings, we propose BRIDGE, a behavior-guided residual integration framework built on dual-frequency graph evidence. BRIDGE separates the model into three parts: DFGE decomposes graph-smoothed ID, visual, and textual channels into spectral bands; BEN converts training-only co-user overlap into signed candidate evidence; and CRI applies that evidence only inside the base top-K candidate set during training and inference. This design keeps the multimodal backbone and localizes behavior evidence to candidate calibration. Experiments on Amazon Baby, Sports, and Electronics show that BRIDGE reaches 0.1128/0.1262/0.0778 Recall@20 and 0.0525/0.0594/0.0385 NDCG@20, outperforming baselines by up to 7.3% in Recall@20 and 14.9% in NDCG@20. Project materials are available at https://lizesheng13.github.io/bridge/.
FULLInformation-Guided Selective Modality Alignment for Multimodal Recommendation
Wenze Ma (Shanghai Jiao Tong University) · Chenyu Sun (Shanghai Jiao Tong University) · Yanmin Zhu (Shanghai Jiao Tong University) · Qiwen Gu (Shanghai Jiao Tong University) · Xuhao Zhao (Shanghai Jiao Tong University)
Abstract
Multimodal recommendation (MMRec) aims to enhance recommendation performance by leveraging rich item content from multiple modalities. However, directly incorporating all modality information does not necessarily lead to better preference modeling, since user interests are often more related to a subset of modality signals, while other signals may be weakly aligned with user preferences or even introduce noise. Although recent MMRec methods improve modality utilization through invariant learning, attention mechanisms, graph refinement, or contrastive learning, their alignment processes are often implicit or heuristic and lack a clear objective for selecting modality signals that better match user interests. In this paper, we propose AMUR, an information-guided selective modality-interest alignment framework for multimodal recommendation. Inspired by an information-theoretic view, AMUR aims to enhance modality information that is more related to user interests while reducing the influence of less aligned signals. Specifically, AMUR first refines modality graph structures towards user behavior, and then selectively aligns shared interest-related semantics across modalities. This enables AMUR to improve modality-interest alignment while preserving useful modality-specific complementary information. Extensive experiments on three real-world datasets demonstrate the effectiveness of AMUR over competitive baselines. The codes are available here. (https://github.com/Wenze1/AMUR)
FULLViSalRec: Visual and Saliency-Informed Reward Augmentation for Sequential Recommender Systems
Georgios Koutroumpas (Telefónica Scientific Research) · Jie Wang (University of Glasgow) · Sergi Abadal (Universitat Politècnica de Catalunya) · Joemon M. Jose (University of Glasgow) · Ioannis Arapakis (Telefónica Scientific Research)
Abstract
In Reinforcement Learning (RL)-based sequential recommendation, offline training often reduces user feedback to sparse binary rewards, weakening credit assignment and limiting policy optimisation. In visual recommendation settings, user choices are also shaped by product appearance, visual attention, and semantic impressions, which provide preference cues that binary outcomes cannot capture. However, how to transform such visual cues into reward supervision and how they impact recommendation performance remains underexplored. Therefore, we introduce ViSalRec, a unified visual-feedback reward augmentation framework for offline RL-based recommendation. ViSalRec treats visual preference cues as an additional reward layer that transforms item image, predicted saliency maps, and multimodal Large Language Model (LLM) judgements into dense reward signals, instantiated as saliency-based rewards, visually-conditioned LLM likeability rewards, and history-conditioned LLM purchase rewards. Within SA2C-style actor–critic recommenders, we study how these reward formulations interact with data characteristics, sequence encoders, and advantage-estimation strategies. Experiments on Amazon Review variants show that visual reward augmentation can improve recommendation performance, but its effectiveness depends on the proxy signal, data density, and reward-integration strategy. Overall, LLM-mediated and history-aware rewards are more reliable than raw saliency rewards, especially under denser data and value-based training. These findings provide an account of when visual preference feedback improves offline RL-based recommendation and how such rewards can be designed and integrated.
4C · Time Series & Trajectory MiningFull ResearchSala PetrassiTuesday 16:00 – 18:008 talksChair: Hakim Qahtan (Utrecht University)
FULLNext Token Prediction for Generalizable Human Activity Recognition
Yize Cai (The Hong Kong University of Science and Technology (Guangzhou)) · Anlan Yu (Peking University) · Baoshen Guo (Singapore-MIT Alliance for Research and Technology) · Yunhuai Liu (Peking University) · Zhiqing Hong (The Hong Kong University of Science and Technology (Guangzhou))
Abstract
One major challenge of sensor-based Human Activity Recognition (HAR) is data heterogeneity, where domain shifts between training and testing data could significantly degrade recognition performance. Recently, large language models (LLMs) have demonstrated strong cross-domain generalization capabilities by modeling language with next-token prediction, offering a promising paradigm for mitigating domain shifts in HAR. In this paper, we propose NextHAR, a novel self-supervised sensor pretraining framework for generalizable HAR. NextHAR first tokenizes sensor data in the frequency space, converting them into motion-semantic tokens. Then, to learn human motion dynamics, NextHAR jointly models inter-channel correlations and temporal dependencies by predicting the next sensor token groups. Furthermore, we introduce a comprehensive cross-domain HAR benchmark to enable systematic evaluation. Extensive experiments on this benchmark show that NextHAR outperforms state-of-the-art methods by 13.83% in accuracy and 15.00% in F1-score. Moreover, NextHAR achieves an average inference latency of 0.033 seconds on wearable devices, highlighting its efficiency for real-world applications. Our code and organized benchmark are publicly available at https://github.com/saiketa/NextHAR.
FULLExploring Semantics-Frequency Alignment in Diffusion Transformers for Financial Time Series Generation
Yingxiao Zhang (Peking University) · Jiaxin Duan (China Electronics Cloud Tech Co., Ltd) · Junfu Zhang (Peking University) · Yue Zou (Peking University) · Ke Feng (Peking University)
Abstract
Existing financial time series generation (FTSG) approaches predominantly model unconditional distributions, lacking the semantic controllability required to simulate deliberate market dynamics, such as macroeconomic shifts and geopolitical shocks. To bridge this gap, this paper studies text-conditioned FTSG that synthesizes realistic multivariate price sequences guided by natural language market descriptions. We propose Fin-CoDiT, a novel diffusion transformer framework engineered around a profound architectural inductive bias: the structural isomorphism between the hierarchical semantic depth of large language models (LLMs) and the spectral frequencies of time-series signals. To exploit this, Fin-CoDiT introduces a Semantics-Frequency Alignment mechanism via Grouped Routing Attention, which dynamically routes explicit LLM layers to their targeted frequency bands during the denoising process. To encode cross-variable dependencies of time series without violating the temporal arrow, we propose Time-Frequency Causal Variational Autoencoder, which strictly operates as a channel-wise bottleneck equipped with orthogonal causal convolutions to fundamentally eliminate future information leakage. Furthermore, it incorporates a branched decoder with in-network differentiable morphological projections, guaranteeing absolute physical market constraints (e.g., Pricehigh ≥ Pricelow). For the training and evaluation of this novel paradigm, we construct an automated multi-agent workflow that creates high-quality text-time series pairs from real-world market states spanning January 1, 2015, to December 31, 2025. Extensive experiments on treasury futures and ETFs demonstrate that Fin-CoDiT establishes a new state-of-the-art, significantly outperforming existing baselines in both generation fidelity and controllability.
FULLUPLOTS: A Unified Pretrained Language Model for Constrained Time-series Generation
Du Yin (The University of New South Wales) · Hao Xue (The Hong Kong University of Science and Technology Guangzhou (HKUST-GZ)) · Jinliang Deng (The Hong Kong University of Science and Technology) · Yang Yang (The University of New South Wales) · Shuang Ao (The University of New South Wales) · Arian Prabowo (The University of New South Wales) · Flora Salim (The University of New South Wales)
Abstract
Many time-series generation studies train a separate generator for each dataset. We study a complementary setting in which one shared, channel-independent generator is trained on several timestamp-derived scenario pools and a compact textual prompt selects the desired pool at inference. We propose UPLOTS, a Unified, Prompt-guided Language model framework fOr constrained Time-Series generation. UPLOTS combines a Diffusion-TS generator with a truncated pretrained language-model backbone, a Time-series Prompt Embedding Module, and two multi-dataset balancing mechanisms: Curriculum-Aware Loss Modulation and Rolling-Loss Dynamic Sampling. We evaluate four real-world datasets under morning- and evening-peak scenarios and extend the analysis to 14 prompt configurations on ETTh and Energy, covering temporal, calendar, load-level, and volatility subsets. The results support unified, in-distribution generation for the predefined datasets and scenario prompts. Downstream forecasting experiments further assess the utility of the generated samples for data augmentation. Our code is available at https://github.com/cruiseresearchgroup/UPLOTS.
FULLBeyond Node-Level Relations: Hybrid Hierarchical Graphs for Multivariate Time Series Imputation under Node Blackout
Jaehyun Bae (Sungkyunkwan University) · Hogun Park (Sungkyunkwan University)
Abstract
Missing data imputation in multivariate time series (MTS) becomes particularly challenging when an entire target node is unobserved throughout an input window, a setting we refer to as node blackout. This setting arises in both spatiotemporal sensing datasets and more general MTS benchmarks, where a node denotes the basic relational unit and may correspond to either a physical sensor stream or a feature/variable channel. Existing methods increasingly exploit inter-variable dependencies through graph structures or attention-based interactions, but most still depend primarily on flat node-level support. Such support becomes fragile when blackout targets have weak local relations or when multiple blackout nodes occur within the same local region, making immediate neighborhoods insufficient or ambiguous for reconstruction. To address this issue, we propose HHGI, a Hybrid Hierarchical Graph learning framework for MTS Imputation under node blackout. HHGI preserves a sparse local graph as a stable structural prior while introducing a higher-level support graph over subgraphs. The higher-level support graph is constructed from two complementary views: inherited topology, which preserves topology-consistent support from the local graph, and subgraph similarity, which retrieves support from structurally compatible local subsystems beyond immediate node-level neighborhoods. To make this higher-level support adaptive to each input window, we construct it from temporal representations and stabilize subgraph formation with shared node priors. We further introduce a missingness-aware adaptive fusion mechanism that balances local and hierarchical supports according to node missing ratio and local-support reliability. Experiments on five real-world MTS datasets demonstrate strong and consistent performance of HHGI across both explicit spatial settings and general multivariate benchmarks under node blackout. Our code is available at https://github.com/jhBae00/H2GI.
FULLViCO: Vision-Augmented Time Series Anomaly Detection with Prototype-Guided Coordination
Xuesong Zeng (Central South University) · Minjun Cao (Central South University) · Hao Miao (The Hong Kong Polytechnic University) · Chenxi Liu (Hong Kong Institute of Science & Innovation, Chinese Academy of Sciences) · Senzhang Wang (Central South University)
Abstract
Time series anomaly detection aims to identify time points or intervals that deviate from normal temporal behavior. In reconstruction-based detection, this requires errors that distinguish anomalies rather than merely accurate reconstruction. However, most existing methods rely solely on temporal modeling, while vision-augmented approaches focus primarily on forecasting, leaving the potential of structural visual cues for reconstruction-based detection underexplored. Moreover, bridging temporal and visual representations further remains challenging. To address these challenges, we propose a Vision-Augmented Coordination framework for time series anomaly detection, called ViCO. A decoupled visual teacher and temporal student characterize normal behavior from complementary views: tri-view visual representations capture structural regularities, whereas raw sequences model value-sensitive dynamics. Prototype-Guided Coordination retrieves normal structural prototypes and conditions the temporal decoder, translating visual structure into reconstruction guidance for anomaly scoring. Extensive experiments on five real-world datasets demonstrate that ViCO consistently outperforms strong baselines by up to 9.0%, while enabling teacher-free inference for lightweight deployment. Code is available at https://github.com/Cedarrr1/ViCO.
FULLOpenTAD: Detecting Open Set Anomalous Trajectory with Memory-Enhanced Distribution Drift Learning
Yida Li (Institute of Computing Technology, Chinese Academy of Sciences) · Shuo Liu (Institute of Computing Technology, Chinese Academy of Sciences) · Di Yao (Institute of Computing Technology, Chinese Academy of Sciences) · Jingping Bi (Institute of Computing Technology,Chinese Academy of Sciences)
Abstract
Detecting emerging anomalous trajectories of unseen types is a critical yet challenging problem for applications such as urban planning, traffic management, and public safety. Existing methods often rely on closed-set assumptions, i.e., they either assume all anomaly types are known or detect anomalous trajectories without using anomaly labels, limiting their ability to detect novel, unseen anomalies. In this paper, we propose OpenTAD, an open-set trajectory anomaly detection framework for identifying anomalous trajectories of both seen and unseen anomaly types. A pseudo-anomaly generation strategy is introduced to address label scarcity by enriching the anomaly manifold, enabling OpenTAD to learn compact normal boundaries even with limited anomaly samples. To tackle spatio-temporal complexity, a memory-augmented trajectory encoding module is designed to capture high-order spatio-temporal dependencies under complex dynamics. Moreover, OpenTAD leverages distribution shift learning to handle anomaly uncertainty by maximizing the separation between normal and anomalous distributions in the latent space, ensuring reliable detection of unseen anomalies. Extensive experiments on multiple real-world trajectory datasets with both synthetic and real anomalies demonstrate that OpenTAD outperforms state-of-the-art baselines, achieving an 8.88% improvement in detecting novel anomalies.
FULLOSTAR: Online Anomalous Sub-trajectory Detection via Topology-Aware Autoregressive Reasoning
Zixuan Liu (University of Electronic Science and Technology of China) · Zhichen Lai (Fuzhou University) · Liwei Deng (Aalborg University) · Hao Miao (University of Electronic Science and Technology of China) · Qingying Yu (Anhui Normal University) · Chao Li (University of Electronic Science and Technology of China) · Lei Jia (University of Electronic Science and Technology of China) · Yan Zhao (University of Electronic Science and Technology of China)
Abstract
Online anomalous sub-trajectory detection is a core technology for applications such as real-time traffic monitoring and fraud prevention. Existing methods primarily suffer from three key limitations: 1) weak capability in fine-grained anomaly localization, 2) insufficient constraints regarding road network topology, and 3) difficulties in interpreting the spatiotemporal physical logic of anomalous behaviors. To address these issues, we propose OSTAR, an online generative framework for anomalous sub-trajectory detection driven by topology-aware autoregressive reasoning. Specifically, OSTAR first utilizes a macro-micro-aware perception module to capture local movement dynamics. Building upon this, it embeds road network topology into its autoregressive modeling to capture physical movement constraints. During inference, rather than outputting an uninterpretable anomaly score, it dynamically constructs a physically coherent reference path to serve as a transparent baseline. Finally, by decoupling the detection into independent spatial and temporal dimensions, OSTAR explicitly pinpoints "spatial detours" and "temporal abnormal dwelling." This design effectively overcomes the opacity of traditional black-box scores. Extensive experiments on two real-world datasets demonstrate that OSTAR achieves excellent accuracy in fine-grained anomaly localization while maintaining competitive inference efficiency, meeting the real-time requirements of industrial deployment. The source code is publicly available at https://github.com/lzxcompute/OSTAR.
FULLELASTIC: Trajectory-Based Synchronization of Event and Tracking Data in Soccer
Hyunsung Kim (KAIST) · Hoyoung Choi (KAIST) · Kunhee Lee (KAIST) · Sangwoo Seo (KAIST) · Tom Boomstra (AFC Ajax) · Jinsung Yoon (Fitogether) · Chanyoung Park (KAIST)
Abstract
Combining event and tracking data is fundamental to modern soccer analytics, yet the two sources are rarely well aligned: event timestamps recorded by human annotators often miss the true moment of the action, distorting the spatiotemporal context that downstream models rely on. Existing synchronization methods depend on noisy human-annotated event locations and fail to detect ball receptions, obscuring when each player gains ball possession. To address these limitations, we propose ELASTIC (Event-Location-AgnoSTIC synchronizer), a framework that infers the start and end timestamps of events solely from player and ball trajectories, without relying on annotated event locations. To recover ball receptions, ELASTIC enriches the event sequence by inserting virtual termination events between consecutive events, so that the end of each event is detected jointly with its start. It then extracts a sparse set of candidate frames where ball touches are physically plausible, and aligns the termination-inserted event sequence with the candidate-frame sequence using an extended Needleman-Wunsch algorithm. For reproducible evaluation, we construct a publicly available benchmark by annotating ground-truth timestamps on the Sportec Open DFL Dataset, on which ELASTIC substantially outperforms existing methods. Through downstream task evaluation, we further show that improved synchronization translates into measurable gains in soccer analytics. The source code and benchmark are available at https://github.com/hyunsungkim-ds/elastic.git.
4D · Benchmarks, Datasets & ToolkitsResourcesSala OspitiTuesday 16:00 – 18:0017 talksChair: Stefano Marchesin (University of Padova)
RESOURCEMTUKG: A Multi-scale Temporal Urban Knowledge Graph Dataset for Knowledge-Enhanced Spatiotemporal Prediction
Jiahao Hu (Changchun University of Science and Technology) · Chaoran Zhou (Changchun University of Science and Technology) · Yang Tang (Changchun University of Science and Technology) · Xin Zhang (Changchun University of Science and Technology) · Hongwei Yang (Changchun University of Science and Technology)
Abstract
Integrating multi-source knowledge into urban knowledge graphs (UrbanKGs) has shown strong potential for improving urban spatiotemporal prediction (USTP). However, existing public UrbanKGs are often misaligned with the temporal and multi-scale nature of USTP. First, they usually represent urban facts as static triples, ignoring when facts become valid, expire, or change over time. Second, their functional-zone layers are typically derived from static POI clustering, which overlooks spatial boundaries, activity interactions, and event-driven temporal semantics. As a result, current datasets provide limited support for modeling temporally valid knowledge and its cross-scale effects on prediction. To address these limitations, we propose MTUKG, a multi-scale temporal urban knowledge graph dataset. MTUKG represents urban events as time-interval facts, enabling knowledge to be aligned with specific prediction windows. It further introduces a spatial unit-driven method that integrates spatial morphology, semantic distributions, spatial decay effects, and dynamic events to construct temporal functional zones and establish multi-scale temporal associations across micro, meso, and macro urban scales. Experiments on USTP and knowledge reasoning tasks demonstrate that MTUKG significantly enhances predictive performance and provides a structured knowledge resource for modeling the temporal dynamics, functional evolution, and multi-scale dependencies in urban systems. The dataset and source code are available at https://github.com/Jiahaohuhu/MTUKG.
RESOURCEStreamFuels: A Dynamic Resource for Time Series Benchmarking in Fuel Analytics
Lucas G M Castro (Pontifícia Universidade Católica do Paraná (PUCPR)) · André G R Ribeiro (Pontifícia Universidade Católica do Paraná (PUCPR)) · Jean Paul Barddal (Pontifícia Universidade Católica do Paraná (PUCPR)) · Alceu De Souza Britto Junior (Pontifícia Universidade Católica do Paraná (PUCPR)) · Vinícius M A Souza (Pontifícia Universidade Católica do Paraná (PUCPR))
Abstract
Fuels and petroleum derivatives (e.g., gasoline, diesel, and kerosene), remain essential energy sources for transportation systems, industrial operations, and residential use. Historical data on fuel sales, production, and pricing, typically represented as time series, enable tasks such as demand forecasting, pattern discovery, and anomaly detection, supporting data-driven decision-making in transportation logistics, production planning, and price regulation. However, these efforts are often hindered by the lack of accessible, well-structured datasets. To address this gap, we present StreamFuels, an open-source Python library that serves as a dynamic benchmarking resource for time series mining in the fuel sector. StreamFuels programmatically retrieves the most recent data from official government sources at access time, delivering five curated datasets with over 40,000 time series. The data are cleaned, standardized, and provided in the TSF format, ensuring compatibility with popular time series toolkits. We validate the resource by benchmarking state-of-the-art algorithms across three tasks: forecasting, classification, and pattern analysis (i.e., motif and discord discovery). Our results establish reproducible performance baselines and demonstrate the utility of StreamFuels for advancing research on time series mining and data-driven applications in the fuel sector.
RESOURCEDaily52: An Air-exposed Smell Dataset for Real-world Odor Classification
Xueyi Zhou (Hanyang University) · Qi Lu (Tsinghua University) · Dong-Kyu Chae (Hanyang University)
Abstract
Previous gas-sensing datasets were designed and collected in sealed environments primarily for laboratory research or domain-specific applications. The lack of air-exposed settings limits the study and modeling of the gas properties under natural volatilization. This work bridges this gap by building an unsealed gas-sensing dataset for real-world gas classification, dubbed Daily52, collected from 52 everyday items measured using a self-developed electronic nose (e-nose). We thoroughly benchmark various odor classification models as baselines, among which InceptionTime is found to achieve an impressive 88.24% accuracy in recognizing items. Comprehensive analysis further demonstrates that our dataset is high-resolution and effective for studying the olfactory modality. Potential olfactory research is also discussed beyond our dataset. To our knowledge, this is the first dataset that enables benchmarking methods for classifying real-world gas-sensing data of natural volatiles.
RESOURCELEMMA-RCA: A Large Multi-modal Multi-domain Dataset for Root Cause Analysis
Lecheng Zheng (University of Illinois Urbana Champaign) · Zhengzhang Chen (NEC Laboratories America) · Dongjie Wang (University of Kansas) · Chengyuan Deng (Rutgers University) · Reon Matsuoka (NEC Laboratories Japan) · Haifeng Chen (NEC Laboratories America)
Abstract
Root cause analysis (RCA) is crucial for enhancing the reliability and performance of complex systems. However, progress in this field has been hindered by the lack of large-scale, open-source datasets tailored for RCA. To bridge this gap, we introduce LEMMA-RCA, a large dataset designed for diverse RCA tasks across multiple domains and modalities. LEMMA-RCA features various real-world fault scenarios from Information Technology (IT) and Operational Technology (OT) systems, including microservices, water distribution, and water treatment systems, with hundreds of system entities involved. We evaluate the performance of six baseline methods on LEMMA-RCA across various settings, including offline and online models, as well as single and multi-modal settings. Our study demonstrates the utility of LEMMA-RCA in facilitating fair evaluation and promoting the development of more robust RCA techniques. The dataset is publicly available at https://www.lemmarca.info.
RESOURCEMemeChain: A Multimodal Cross-Chain Dataset for Meme Coin Forensics and Risk Analysis
Alberto Maria Mongardini (Technical University of Denmark) · Alessandro Mei (Sapienza University of Rome)
Abstract
The meme coin ecosystem has grown into one of the most active yet least observable segments of the cryptocurrency market, characterized by extreme churn and widespread fraudulent behavior. While countless meme coins are deployed across multiple blockchains, they rely heavily on off-chain web and social infrastructure to signal legitimacy. These very signals are largely absent from existing datasets, which are often limited to single-chain data or lack the multimodal artifacts required for comprehensive risk modeling. To address this gap, we introduce MemeChain, a large-scale, open-source, cross-chain dataset comprising 34,988 meme coins across Ethereum, BNB Smart Chain, Solana, and Base. MemeChain integrates on-chain data with off-chain artifacts, including website HTML source code, token logos, and linked social media accounts, enabling multimodal and forensic study of meme coin projects. By providing cross-chain coverage and rich off-chain context, MemeChain serves as a foundational resource for research in financial forensics, multimodal anomaly detection, and automated scam prevention in the meme coin ecosystem.
RESOURCENRCD: An Open Database of Collegiate Running with Unified Performance Standardization
Jonathan A. Karr (University of Notre Dame) · Ryan M. Fryer (University of Notre Dame) · Ben Darden (Virginia Tech) · Nicholas Pell (University of North Carolina at Chapel Hill) · Kayla Ambrose (University of Notre Dame) · Evan Hall (University of Notre Dame) · Ramzi K. Bualuan (University of Notre Dame) · Nitesh V. Chawla (University of Notre Dame)
Abstract
Collegiate running in the United States generates thousands of race results annually in cross country and track and field, yet no large-scale dataset has been publicly available for research. Existing websites such as Athletic.net, MileSplit, and TFRRS host results but do not support bulk download, restricting prior analyses to ~500 performances, often skewing studies toward male athletes. We introduce the National Running Club Database (NRCD), the first openly available collegiate running dataset at scale: 143,868 approved performances from 31,351 athletes across 1,423 meets in four sports (cross country (XC), indoor and outdoor track, and road races), 36.2% women, spanning 2003-2026. Meets from August 2023 onward carry comprehensive course distance, elevation gain and loss, weather at race time, and track venue metadata (99.9% of XC rows with weather fields). NRCD is community-governed through open submission and expert approval and is maintained as a live database whose meet volume has grown yearly. We release a unified performance standardization framework that operationalizes established distance, elevation, and heat adjustments in one pipeline; XC-only validation; heat is a Hadley-band heuristic. We recommend gender-stratified modeling. On XC, full standardization lowers median within-athlete cross-meet variability by 51.1% (women) and 35.4% (men) versus raw times. We release the dataset and pipeline with a Python package `nrcd' under FAIR principles, supporting longitudinal athlete modeling, environmental-confounder studies, and gender-equity research in collegiate sport.
RESOURCECT-bias: A Dataset for Auditing the Impact of Patients' Sensitive Information on Clinical Trial Matching
Maciej Rybinski (University of Málaga) · Aditya Joshi (University of New South Wales) · Nathan Inkiriwang (University of Sydney) · Sarvnaz Karimi (CSIRO)
Abstract
Medical advances are rooted in insights gathered from clinical trials. Technology plays a key role in clinical trial recruitment: patients use specialised platforms to search for clinical trials, and clinical trial recruiters search through patient records to find eligible patients. Existing research shows that personal characteristics of patients influence the outputs of models tasked with medical question answering. While similar classes of neural models are increasingly present in medical information-seeking pipelines, the scientific community lacks resources to investigate how well these models cope with bias in medical retrieval tasks. Here, we present CT-bias, a novel resource for auditing of bias for specific patients and groups of patients where private or sensitive information was recoded as a part of a medical note. To create the dataset, we perturb patient notes from an established patient-trial matching benchmark by inserting specific patient information (sexual orientation, occupation, education level) irrelevant to their medical condition. In an example experiment, we study the impact of this information on the retrieval results of 12 leading open source zero-shot dense retrieval models. We also propose a methodology to inspect models for biases, and observe that, while most models are generally robust to medically irrelevant information, some patient characteristics impact the retrieval results more than others. CT-bias will a useful resource to evaluate future ranking models and CT matching pipelines while the dataset creation protocol itself can be extended to several retrieval and prediction biomedical AI tasks.
RESOURCEAPEX-VW: A Document-Level English-Spanish Post-Editing Dataset in the Healthcare Domain
Marie Escribe (Hong Kong Baptist University) · Tharindu Ranasinghe (Lancaster University) · Amal Haddad Haddad (University of Granada) · Hansi Hettiarachchi (Lancaster University) · Damith Premasiri (Lancaster University)
Abstract
Post-Editing (PE) of Machine Translation (MT) output often involves repeating the same lexical and terminological corrections across many segments, especially in specialised and highly repetitive documents. Despite substantial work on Automatic Post-Editing (APE), most available corpora operate at the sentence level, others are synthetic, and overall not designed to study how corrections propagate in realistic Computer-Assisted Translation (CAT) workflows. This paper presents the APEX-VW (Automatic Post-Editing eXperiments on Virtual Wards) Corpus, a new open English-Spanish (EN-ES) dataset built from recent NHS virtual-ward documents and professional PE in Trados Studio, with controlled MT, terminology, and quality assurance settings. The corpus contains seven document-coherent source texts totalling 42k words, translated with four MT systems representing different paradigms and then post-edited by professional translators. Unlike prior resources such as WMT APE corpora, eSCAPE, MLQE-PE, or LangMark, the dataset preserves document order and CAT-tool context, making it suitable for research on terminology normalisation, correction propagation, and human-in-the-loop translation support. The paper describes the corpus design, data preparation, PE setup, and initial corpus statistics, and positions the resource as a benchmark for document-level APE and propagation-aware assistive tools.
RESOURCERecDistillery: A Framework for Teacher-Student Knowledge Distillation in Recommender Systems
Marialuisa Pisicchio (Politecnico di Bari) · Alberto Carlo Maria Mancino (Politecnico di Bari) · Leonardo Di Gioia (Politecnico di Bari) · Daniele Malitesta (LUISS Guido Carli University) · Fedelucio Narducci (Politecnico di Bari) · Tommaso Di Noia (Politecnico di Bari)
Abstract
Knowledge Distillation (KD) improves the efficiency of recommender systems by transferring knowledge from high-capacity teacher models to lightweight student architectures. Despite its growing popularity, KD research for recommendation remains fragmented, making reproducibility and fair comparison across distillation strategies difficult. We present <sc>RecDistillery</sc>, the first open-source, model-agnostic framework for standardizing teacher–student KD workflows in recommender systems. The framework provides a modular architecture unifying data preparation, teacher integration, student training, distillation, and evaluation. It supports both native PyTorch-based recommenders and externally trained models, enabling heterogeneous teacher–student distillation within a unified pipeline. <sc>RecDistillery</sc> facilitates both the reproduction of existing KD methods and the rapid prototyping of new approaches through reusable losses, data loaders, metrics, and configuration modules. We demonstrate its capabilities through representative case studies involving multiple recommendation frameworks and externally imported teachers. The framework code, documentation, and demo examples are publicly available at https://github.com/sisinflab/RecDistillery.
RESOURCEFranKGraphBench: Reproducible Benchmarking for Knowledge Graph-based Recommendation
Paulo Viviurka Do Carmo (Institute for Applied Informatics) · Alvaro José Lopes (Computer Science and Mathematics Institute, University of São Paulo) · Marcos Paulo Silva Gôlo (Computer Science and Mathematics Institute, University of São Paulo) · Edgard Marx (Institute for Applied Informatics)
Abstract
Knowledge Graphs (KGs) enable the integration of data across multiple domains and data types, supporting human interpretability, machine processing, and distributed data access. KGs have become especially valuable for enhancing recommender systems (RSs), which provide personalized user experiences and are now ubiquitous across platforms such as social media, streaming services, e-commerce, news, and search engines. However, reproducibility remains a persistent challenge in developing and evaluating machine learning methods for KG-based RSs, due to heterogeneous data sources and model complexity. Therefore, we introduce FranKGraphBench, a modular benchmarking framework that consolidates baseline models, datasets, and evaluation metrics into a standardized structure. Users can define experiments via configuration files, enabling reproducible sharing of model specifications, datasets, and evaluation settings. FranKGraphBench contains 6 KG-form RS datasets: 3 DBpedia-enriched, 1 Wikidata-enriched, and 2 unenriched. Finally, we validate its effectiveness through a small benchmark and an ablation study to showcase its capabilities and the importance of open settings for reproducible experimentation.
RESOURCEOffTrail: A Benchmark for Natural-Language Context in Recommendation beyond Interaction Histories
Nikita Sukhorukov (AXXX) · Danil Gusak (AXXX) · Alisa Petrova (MIRAI) · Alexey Kovalev (CogAI Lab) · Aleksandr I. Panov (CogAI Lab) · Evgeny Frolov (AXXX)
Abstract
Recommender systems are increasingly expected to combine interaction histories with language. In many cases, a user's next choice may depend on a temporary situation—such as their current mood, plans, or constraints—that is not visible in past behavior. Existing benchmarks, however, mostly evaluate average next-item accuracy, broad instruction following, or content understanding; they do not isolate recommendation episodes in which external situation context is plausibly needed. We introduce OffTrail, a benchmark built on MovieLens for situation-aware recommendation beyond interaction histories. It contains two complementary families of episodes: observed off-trail choices that are real user transitions but hard to infer from prior behavior, and neighbor-supported alternative continuations that represent plausible futures for similar recent histories. Each episode packages a user history, target item, item metadata, and generated life-situation context. The contexts are treated as plausible external circumstances rather than ground-truth user intentions. OffTrail supports controlled evaluation across sequential models, LLM-based recommenders, and hybrid systems by keeping the recommendation episode fixed while exposing or withholding the situation context. By releasing the artifacts, construction pipeline, and evaluation protocol, OffTrail provides a reproducible testbed for studying whether natural-language context improves ranking when interaction history is weak or ambiguous. Benchmark: https://doi.org/10.5281/zenodo.20560655.
RESOURCEEval4Sim: An Evaluation Framework for Persona Simulation
Eliseo Bao (IRLab, CITIC, Universidade da Coruña) · Anxo Perez (IRLab, CITIC, Universidade da Coruña) · Javier Parapar (IRLab, CITIC, Universidade da Coruña) · Xi Wang (University of Sheffield)
Abstract
Large Language Model personas, explicit profiles specifying a user's attributes, preferences, and behavioural tendencies, are increasingly used to simulate human conversations for user modelling, social reasoning, and behavioural analysis. Evaluating whether such simulations faithfully reflect human conversational behaviour is critical, yet current practice often relies on LLM-as-a-judge approaches that provide limited grounding in observable behaviour and produce opaque scalar scores. We present Eval4Sim, an evaluation framework that measures alignment between simulated and human conversations across three dimensions: adherence, whether persona traits are recoverable from dialogue via dense retrieval; consistency, whether a persona maintains a distinguishable stylistic identity via authorship verification; and naturalness, whether conversations exhibit human-like turn-to-turn flow via dialogue NLI. Unlike optimization-oriented metrics, each dimension takes a human corpus as a reference baseline and penalizes deviations in both directions, distinguishing insufficient persona encoding from over-optimized, unnatural behaviour. The framework is corpus-agnostic: any persona-annotated conversational dataset can serve as the reference. Evaluated over ten simulation corpora, Eval4Sim surfaces systematic trade-offs invisible to single-score methods.
RESOURCEIshigaki-IDS-Bench: A Benchmark for Generating Information Delivery Specification from BIM Information Requirements
Ryo Kanazawa (ONESTRUCTION Inc.) · Koyo Hidaka (ONESTRUCTION Inc.) · Teppei Miyamoto (ONESTRUCTION Inc.) · Takayuki Kato (ONESTRUCTION Inc.) · Tomoki Ando (ONESTRUCTION Inc.) · Chenguang Wang (AWS GenAI Innovation Center) · Dayuan Jiang (AWS GenAI Innovation Center) · Naofumi Fujita (ONESTRUCTION Inc.) · Shuhei Saitoh (ONESTRUCTION Inc.) · Atomu Kondo (ONESTRUCTION Inc.) · Koki Arakawa (ONESTRUCTION Inc.) · Daiho Nishioka (ONESTRUCTION Inc.)
Abstract
Building Information Modeling (BIM) projects increasingly use Information Delivery Specification (IDS) to formalize information requirements in a machine-checkable XML format. Because IDS conditions are grounded in the Industry Foundation Classes (IFC) vocabulary, authoring them requires expertise in IFC concepts, validation tools, and property set conventions. Existing benchmarks for structured generation do not adequately capture the additional burden of vocabulary conformance and external-validator agreement that IDS imposes. We present Ishigaki-IDS-Bench, the first publicly released benchmark for IDS generation from BIM information requirements. The benchmark contains 166 examples spanning 83 practical scenarios authored in Japanese and English by six BIM/IDS experts, each paired with a gold IDS file and metadata covering input format, turn setting, target IFC versions, and construction domain. Evaluation proceeds in two stages: (i) formal validity scored by the buildingSMART IDSAuditTool along Processability, Structure, and Content, and (ii) content fidelity scored by facet-level macro-F1 against the gold IDS. Across 10 LLMs in zero-shot, the highest Facet F1 is 65.6%, achieved by GPT-5.5, while the highest Content pass rate is only 33.1%, achieved by Claude Opus 4.5. Ishigaki-IDS-Bench is released on Hugging Face (DOI 10.57967/hf/8873) under CC BY 4.0, and the evaluation code is released on Zenodo (DOI 10.5281/zenodo.20550510) under Apache-2.0.
RESOURCEBWOR: A Bilingual Benchmark for Modeling and Solving Operations Research Problems from Natural Language
Bowen Zhang (Shanghai Jiao Tong University) · Pengcheng Luo (Shanghai Jiao Tong University) · Genke Yang (Shanghai Jiao Tong University) · Boon-Hee Soong (Nanyang Technological University) · Chau Yuen (Nanyang Technological University)
Abstract
We introduce BWOR, a benchmark of 82 textbook-style operations research (OR) problems with bilingual Chinese–English statements, verified numeric answers, and execution-based evaluation. It tests whether a large language model (LLM) can turn natural-language OR descriptions into executable solver code and correct solutions. Baselines distinguish non-reasoning, reasoning, and decomposed-agent systems. The release includes data, evaluation scripts, prompts, and baseline summaries for reproducible comparison.
RESOURCEGeese Belong in (Data) Lakes: An Index Lake for Anserini
Gijs Hendriksen (Radboud University) · Djoerd Hiemstra (Radboud University) · Jimmy Lin (University of Waterloo) · Arjen P. de Vries (Radboud University)
Abstract
We present an index lake for Anserini: a remote index representation of all inverted indexes from Anserini's reproducibility suite. Each index is represented as a set of Parquet files on remote object storage, and retrieval is performed through SQL with DuckDB. Through an extensive benchmark of 239 experiments across 50 collections, we empirically confirm our results are consistent with Anserini's. We analyze query latencies over the index lake and conclude that (1) most experiments can be run relatively efficiently, requiring only a couple of seconds per query; and (2) for large collections and learned sparse indexes, queries suffer from increased latency due to high overhead. We are also able to reduce total network transfer, since (1) index lakes are smaller than the corresponding prebuilt Lucene indexes; and (2) up to 90% of the index can be skipped by pushing filters on the postings table to the data lake. The index lake increases reproducibility and makes it easier to run new experiments on standard test collections and prebuilt indexes.
RESOURCERISE: A Rust Library for Inverted Index Search Engines
Angelo Savino (Seltz) · Rossano Venturini (University of Pisa)
Abstract
Inverted indexes are a crucial data structure for efficient information retrieval in large text corpora. They enable fast full-text search by mapping each term to the documents in which it appears, on top of which efficient algorithms quickly retrieve the documents relevant to a user query. We present RISE, a novel inverted index library implemented in Rust, designed to deliver high performance and efficiency for information retrieval tasks. RISE leverages Rust's safety and performance to provide a robust solution for building and querying inverted indexes, while offering accessible extensibility through its expressive trait system. While developing RISE, we revisited the inverted-index literature, thereby reproducing numerous prior works using this new test bench. We evaluated RISE against existing libraries, demonstrating competitive query performance across various datasets and workloads, with some algorithms achieving speedups of up to 2× over the current state of the art. Our results indicate that RISE is a promising tool for researchers and practitioners in the field of information retrieval.
RESOURCEPosIR: A Multilingual Benchmark for Diagnosing Position Bias in Information Retrieval
Ziyang Zeng (Beijing University of Posts and Telecommunications) · Dun Zhang (Prior Shape) · Yu Yan (Beijing University of Posts and Telecommunications) · Xu Sun (Orange Research) · Cuiqiaoshu Pan (Beijing University of Posts and Telecommunications) · Yudong Zhou (Prior Shape) · Yuqing Yang (Beijing University of Posts and Telecommunications)
Abstract
Position bias—the systematic effect of where key information is located on retrieval effectiveness—is a critical concern in information retrieval. Although recent studies have identified such bias in dense retrievers, existing analyses focus predominantly on monolingual English, fail to disentangle document length from information position, and lack a standardized framework for controlled evaluation. To address these limitations, we introduce PosIR, a benchmark to systematically diagnose position bias across diverse retrieval scenarios, comprising 310 language–domain dataset combinations spanning 10 languages and 31 domains. Each query is paired with a positive document, a localized reference span, and positional metadata, enabling controlled analysis of retrieval quality across evidence locations and length bins. PosIR provides a complete data generation pipeline with quality-control filtering, along with baseline evaluation scripts. Experiments with 10 widely-used dense retrievers reveal that position bias is pervasive in both multilingual and cross-lingual retrieval, and that it intensifies as documents grow longer. PosIR serves as a foundational resource to advance the development of position-robust retrieval systems.
