FULLNode Importance Estimation in Multiplex Networks
Siqi Ma (National Key Laboratory of Information Systems Engineering, National University of Defense Technology) · Yang Fang (National University of Defense Technology) · Pengming Zhu (Information Support Force Engineering University) · Changhong Jin (School of Computer Science, University College Dublin) · Ruihai Dong (School of Computer Science, University College Dublin) · Weidong Xiao (National Key Laboratory of Information Systems Engineering, National University of Defense Technology) · Xiang Zhao (National Key Laboratory of Big Data and Decision, National University of Defense Technology)
Abstract
Node importance estimation is an essential task in network science, with broad applications in recommendation systems and network dismantling. Existing GNN-based methods implicitly operate in a flattened relation space, where diverse interactions are either ignored or collapsed into a single propagation graph. However, real-world networks are far more complex. They comprise multiple types of nodes and edges, and are often multi-layered. As a result, single-layer methods fail to capture the intrinsic and extrinsic interactions among diverse relational categories. This study presents the first dedicated study on node importance estimation in multiplex networks, where a common set of nodes is connected through multiple relational layers. Our objective is to provide a comprehensive analysis by modeling distinct relationships as independent network layers while capturing both intra-layer connections and cross-layer dependencies. The proposed framework, namely HiGH, uses hypergraphs to learn intra-layer structures and capture higher-order interactions and grouping effects by modeling node influences. Specifically, an adaptive importance selector first identifies important nodes at each layer by integrating their local and global information. By constructing hyperedges from selected important nodes rather than from all nodes, the process becomes more targeted for importance-related tasks and reduces the complexity of hyperedge construction. Furthermore, a nested contrastive learning module with inter-layer bridge nodes facilitates cross-layer information transfer, allowing the model to discern node-level universality and specificity across layers. Extensive experiments on three real-world datasets show that HiGH outperforms twelve competing baselines, demonstrating its effectiveness.
FULLHAWKEYE: Seeing One Layer Deeper --- A Cohesion-Aware Structural Channel for Temporal Link Prediction
Jiacheng Ding (The University of Memphis) · Xiaofei Zhang (The University of Memphis)
Abstract
State-of-the-art temporal-link-prediction (TLP) models are, in essence, multi-channel information aggregators: they combine an interaction-history channel, a time-encoding channel, and a structure channel. The first two have been refined relentlessly; the structure channel remains a crude afterthought — DyGFormer encodes it as a 1–2-bit neighbour-cooccurrence count. We begin with a measurement: on sparse temporal graphs the classical 1-hop common-neighbour signal is near-random (discriminative AUC 0.50), because two nodes almost never share a direct neighbour; the genuinely discriminative signal lies one hop deeper — the 2-hop cohesive bridge, whose discAUC reaches 0.73–0.98, on both bipartite and non-bipartite graphs. Motivated by this, we propose HAWKEYE, a cohesion-aware structural channel that incrementally maintains the classical k-family of cohesiveness indicators (degree -> k-core -> k-truss) and forms 2-hop cohesive-bridge features. HAWKEYE is a drop-in replacement for a temporal-graph model's native structure channel, with no change to the backbone. Swapping HAWKEYE into DyGFormer improves test AP/MRR over the cooccurrence channel by +0.6 to +10.8 points across six multi-seed-validated datasets (uci, enron, USLegis, CanParl, reddit, mooc; wiki legacy single-seed). On the bipartite recommendation benchmark tgbl-subreddit, a 3-seed single-pass struct-only ablation shows HAWKEYE nearly doubling the baseline test MRR (0.103±0.003 -> 0.204±0.005, +10.1 points across all three seeds), demonstrating large-graph effectiveness; the streaming pipeline scales to the 67M-edge tgbl-flight in five minutes per pass. We further characterise when it helps: the gain tracks a graph's training-free 2-hop discAUC and vanishes on degenerate or saturated graphs — a predictable boundary. All code, data, drawio-editable figures, and figure-generation scripts are released.
FULLCCEC-TGN for Link Prediction in Large-Scale Continuous-Time Dynamic Graphs
Yuan Li (North China University of Technology) · Jinzhao Han (North China University of Technology) · Kaiyu Zhang (North China University of Technology) · Guoli Yang (Advanced Institute of Big Data) · Yuhai Zhao (Northeastern University)
Abstract
Temporal link prediction aims to forecast future connections from historical interactions. As a fundamental problem in temporal graph learning, existing methods exhibit three major limitations. (1) They usually focus on node-level interaction histories and information aggregated from temporal neighbors, while overlooking cohesive information from node-associated subgraphs. (2) They do not sufficiently integrate high-order topological information with temporal information. (3) They are susceptible to confounding factors, which may lead to spurious correlations. To address these limitations, we propose CCEC-TGN, a temporal graph neural network designed for continuous-time dynamic graphs (CTDGs). (1) We leverage continuous coreness to capture time-evolving cohesive information. (2) We use structural encoding, conditional structural interpolation, and gated residual fusion to integrate macro-level structural information with micro-level temporal information. (3) We apply counterfactual consistency regularization to mitigate confounding factors and improve robustness and generalization. Experiments on several real-world temporal graph datasets demonstrate the effectiveness and efficiency of CCEC-TGN, especially in inductive prediction settings. The source code is available at https://github.com/BJHanjz/CCEC-TGN.
FULLEdge Sparsification via Temporal Forman-Ricci Curvature for Dynamic Graph Learning
Poupak Azad (University of Manitoba) · Cuneyt Gurcan Akcora (University of Central Florida) · Kiarash Shamsi (University of Manitoba)
Abstract
Temporal graph learning has become essential for analyzing real-world systems whose interactions continuously evolve over time, including financial transaction networks, communication systems, and online social platforms. However, learning from large-scale temporal graphs remains computationally challenging when networks are dense and rapidly changing. To address this limitation, we propose a network-curvature-inspired edge sparsification framework for dynamic graph learning. Our proposed method, TRicci, extends classical Forman-Ricci curvature to directed weighted temporal graphs by capturing structural support, temporal recency, and local interaction competition. Experiments on 9 transaction networks and 3 temporal graph benchmark datasets demonstrate that the proposed framework preserves predictive performance across multiple graph-level prediction tasks. The results show that TRicci sparsifies temporal graphs by approximately 80% while reducing end-to-end downstream training and inference time by an average of 55.94%, without substantial degradation in predictive performance. Our findings suggest that temporal curvature can serve as a principled basis for scalable temporal graph learning by preserving predictive temporal-structural information under substantial sparsification.
FULLEvent-Aware Label Propagation Framework over Heterogeneous Graphs for Fake News Short-Video Detection
Hongyi Nie (Northwestern Polytechnical University) · Yaosong Bi (Northwestern Polytechnical University) · Bohan Qi (Northwestern Polytechnical University) · Shiqi Fan (The Hong Kong Polytechnic University) · Chao Gao (Northwestern Polytechnical University) · Xiaoyu Li (Northwestern Polytechnical University)
Abstract
Short video platforms have revolutionized information consumption but also accelerated the spread of fake news detection. Most existing detection methods use a single-sample paradigm, treating videos as independent instances and ignoring the macro-level event context. To address this issue, this paper proposes an Event-Aware Label Propagation framework over Heterogeneous Graphs for fake news video detection(EALP-HG). The framework constructs an event-centric heterogeneous graph that explicitly models hierarchical relationships among events, videos, and multimodal content, thereby enabling structured reasoning from event context to video evidence. A dual-level attention–based heterogeneous graph attention network is further employed to jointly aggregate node-and type-level information, enabling comprehensive representations for both event and videos. More importantly, EALP-HG introduces an explicit event-aware label propagation strategy, which uses predicted event labels as prior guidance to regularize video predictions. Extensive experiments on two real-world datasets demonstrate the superior performance of EALP-HG. Under 5-fold cross-validation, it outperforms state-of-the-art baselines by 4.73% and 3.29% in accuracy, respectively. These results verify the effectiveness of incorporating event-aware supervision into fake news video detection. The code of our work is available at https://github.com/cgao-comp/EALP-HG.
FULLEffective Heterophilous Heterogeneous Graph Learning via Decoupled Spectral Filtering and Curriculum Learning
Siqing Li (University of New South Wales) · Yong-Min Shin (Yonsei University) · Won-Yong Shin (Yonsei University) · Xin Cao (University of New South Wales)
Abstract
Heterogeneous graphs (HGs) are widely used to model complex relational data in domains such as traffic networks, biology, and recommendation systems. While heterogeneous graph neural networks (HGNNs) demonstrate strong performance on homophilous benchmarks, they struggle to generalize to heterophilous HGs where connected nodes often hold different labels. Recent spectral HGNNs attempt to address this by modeling complex shift operations by positive non-commutative polynomials, but they suffer from severe over-parameterization and overfitting, especially when data are limited. Furthermore, existing methods often neglect the internal conflict between meta-path subgraphs with diverging homophily ratios. In this paper, we propose CLS-HGNN, a Curriculum Learning enhanced Spectral Heterogeneous Graph Neural Network. To mitigate over-parameterization, we replace dense learnable weight matrices with Jacobi polynomial bases, which decouple the spectral filtering process and significantly reduce complexity while preserving expressiveness. To reduce the impact of conflicts arising from inconsistent homophily, we introduce a curriculum learning strategy that quantifies node difficulty via training loss dynamics and embedding deviations across meta-paths. This allows the model to progressively learn from consistent (easy) patterns to conflicting (hard) ones. Extensive experiments demonstrate that CLS-HGNN achieves state-of-the-art performance on heterophilous HGs and significantly improves training efficiency compared to existing spectral methods.
FULLHERDGNN: Hybrid Error-Guided Regularization with Deviation for Highly Imbalanced Classification in Dynamic Graphs
Vahid Shahrivari Joghan (Utrecht University) · Ramon Rico (Utrecht University) · Ioana Hulpus (Utrecht University) · Yannis Velegrakis (Utrecht University)
Abstract
Risk monitoring tasks like financial fraud detection, money laundering detection, and cybersecurity often involve graph-native datasets that are characterized by extreme class imbalance and evolving structure, as well as deployment constraints that require incremental model updates under bounded temporal memory. Despite recent efforts in graph representation learning, the state-of-the-art Dynamic Graph Neural Networks (DGNNs) have several limitations: They are either designed for class-balanced settings and (some) offer a bounded temporal memory footprint, or are designed for class-imbalanced settings but do not offer a bounded temporal memory footprint. To bridge this gap, we propose HERDGNN: the first DGNN tailored for class-imbalanced settings while keeping a bounded temporal memory footprint. To address class imbalance, HERDGNN integrates deviation-aware regularization pushing abnormal entities away from the distribution of normal ones. To maintain bounded temporal memory, HERDGNN captures temporal information through a compact hierarchical memory whose size is fixed and independent of graph size, enabling live-update training without storing node-level temporal states. We evaluate the effectiveness of HERDGNN on 7 large-scale real and synthetic financial networks, under a live-update protocol, against 3 GNN baselines and 5 state-of-the-art DGNNs. The results show that HERDGNN achieves competitive or superior performance compared to the competing methods, and overall strikes the best balance between classification performance and memory consumption.
FULLFrom Auxiliary Views to Actions: Edge Augmentation for Strict Cold-Start Fraud Screening
Qichao Wang (Nanyang Technological University) · Pengcheng Wu (Nanyang Technological University) · Zhiqi Shen (Nanyang Technological University)
Abstract
Fraudulent user detection in advance is crucial for risk control of real-world applications. One of the primary challenges lies in classifying new users as either benign or fraudulent when only limited user profile information is available. This scenario is often referred to as the Strict Cold Start (SCS) problem. Existing methods generally address this challenge by enhancing the topology or features of SCS nodes. However, these approaches can introduce task-irrelevant noise or require sharing raw cross-scenario features, which is operationally undesirable when scenarios are owned by different teams. To overcome these limitations, we propose a novel graph learning framework called CoMGL. This framework employs a multi-view learning strategy to effectively tackle SCS tasks on graphs. Specifically, the CoMGL regards the interaction bipartite graphs from different scenarios as the multi-views for separately learning user representation, yielding more comprehensive representation for SCS users. Each view encoder consumes only its own scenario-local features, and only the resulting user embeddings are fused, which limits cross-scenario raw feature transfer. Experimental results on real-world datasets demonstrate the effectiveness of the proposed framework compared with the state-of-the-art approaches.

FULLRTDBStream: Efficient DBSCAN in Data Streams with Ray Tracing Cores
Ziming Wang (Fudan University) · Kai Zhang (Fudan University) · Ruohan Li (Fudan University) · Zhigang Zhao (Qilu University of Technology) · Chunxiao Wang (Qilu University of Technology) · Zhenying He (Fudan University) · Yinan Jing (Fudan University) · X. Sean Wang (Fudan University)
Abstract
Density-based clustering has been widely used in various applications such as hot spot detection, image segmentation, and geo-social network analysis. DBSCAN, as a representative density-based clustering approach, is known for expensive computation overhead, especially when the data volume is large. Specifically, performing DBSCAN on high-speed continuous incoming data with stringent realtime requirement poses challenges for modern applications, such as traffic monitoring and industry sensor monitoring. This paper proposes RTDBStream, a high-performance DBSCAN approach that utilizes ray tracing cores (RT cores) in modern GPUs for acceleration. RTDBStream transforms DBSCAN in data streams into an efficient ray tracing job in a three-dimensional space. To efficiently utilize the RT cores, two optimization techniques are designed in RTDBStream, namely Identifying Cores by Gridding and Clustering by Creating Mixed-radius Spheres, to significantly accelerate the clustering process. Experimental results show that RTDBStream outperforms existing implementations on both CPUs and GPU CUDA cores, and it achieves up to 16.4× over existing RT-based implementations.
FULLVoronoiSCAN: Enhancing DBSCAN with Voronoi Tessellation for Distributed Clustering
Florian Siepe (Viessmann IT Service GmbH) · Thorsten Papenbrock (Marburg University)
Abstract
DBSCAN, one of the most widely used density-based clustering algorithms in both research and industry, has proven to be a powerful tool for discovering complex patterns. Its robustness against noise and outliers has made it a cornerstone of density-based clustering. On large-scale datasets, DBSCAN is costly to compute and, hence, many distributed solutions have been proposed. However, many of them use naive partitioning strategies leading to suboptimal runtimes. To address this limitation, we propose VoronoiSCAN, a novel parallel and exact clustering algorithm that combines the DBSCAN algorithm with Voronoi tessellation for Euclidean distance and low dimensional datasets. By partitioning the input space into cells using Voronoi tessellations, we divide the problem into balanced, local clusterings. The subsequent necessary merging process relies on a novel density connectivity graph construction, which represents the neighborhood of the Voronoi cells. We demonstrate the effectiveness of the proposed algorithm through comprehensive experiments on various datasets, showcasing its potential for large-scale clustering applications and its superior performance compared to other distributed DBSCAN algorithms.
FULLManifold Diffusion Stability-Based Cross-view Graph Supplementation for Incomplete Multi-view Clustering
Xi Chen (Guangdong University of Technology) · Yonghao Wu (Guangdong University of Technology) · Shuping Zhao (Guangdong University of Technology) · Lunke Fei (Guangdong University of Technology) · Bob Zhang (University of Macau)
Abstract
Incomplete multi-view clustering aims to partition unlabeled samples when some views are missing. Recent graph-guided contrastive methods improve clustering by exploiting neighborhood structures from observed views. However, existing methods usually describe local structures with discrete pairwise affinities estimated from incomplete observations. Such affinities are sensitive to view-specific noise, sparse local density, and missing views, where accidental neighbor relations may be transferred across views and further affect contrastive supervision. To address these limitations, we propose Manifold Diffusion Stability-guided Cross-view Graph Supplementation (MDSCGS), a confidence-guided graph supplementation framework for incomplete multi-view clustering. Specifically, MDSCGS estimates manifold diffusion stability from observed view graphs to characterize stable local connectivity beyond direct pairwise proximity, and calibrates this stability through cross-view diffusion-neighbor consistency. Guided by the calibrated stability, high-confidence auxiliary structures are selected to supplement missing target-view relations, while unreliable cross-view relations are suppressed. The augmented view graphs are further integrated into graph-guided contrastive representation learning, enabling the model to exploit complementary cross-view information while preserving stable local manifold geometry. Extensive experiments on four benchmark datasets under different missing rates demonstrate that MDSCGS consistently outperforms representative incomplete multi-view clustering methods.
FULLM2DNA: Multi-Modal Dual-Stream Representation Learning with Joint Relational Modeling for DNA Sequence Clustering
Bowen Liu (City University of Hong Kong) · Pengyue Jia (City University of Hong Kong) · Wanyu Wang (City University of Hong Kong) · Maolin Wang (City University of Hong Kong) · Xiao Han (Zhejiang University of Technology) · Xiangyu Zhao (City University of Hong Kong)
Abstract
Unsupervised DNA sequence clustering aims to group DNA sequences into biologically meaningful categories based on intrinsic similarities without relying on external annotations. While both global structural patterns and local sequential contextual information is essential for this task, existing methods predominantly rely on structural features, largely overlooking the rich biologically information embedded in the sequential context. To address this limitation, we propose M2DNA, a novel Asymmetric Dual-Stream framework designed for unsupervised clustering. Specifically, M2DNA converts DNA sequences into Frequency Chaos Game Representation (FCGR) images to extract structural priors via a Convolutional Neural Network (CNN), while treating sequences as text to capture local biologically information using a genomic foundation model. These multi-modal features are aggregated via a fusion layer to drive clustering. To mitigate modality laziness in this architecture, we further introduce a Probabilistic Module Dropout (PMD) strategy that compels the learnable branch to extract discriminative semantic features. Extensive experiments on 11 benchmark datasets demonstrate that structural and sequential information are highly complementary, enabling M2DNA to significantly outperform state-of-the-art baselines. To foster reproducibility, our code is publicly released (https://github.com/Applied-Machine-Learning-Lab/CIKM2026_M2DNA).
FULLVISTA: Variable-length Interpretable Scalable Temporal Analysis for Industrial Time Series Event Clustering
Hao Huang (GE Vernova) · Naresh Iyer (GE Vernova)
Abstract
Clustering multivariate time series by operational conditions or fault types is important across industrial domains, but existing methods struggle with long, variable-length recordings, localized signatures, and interpretability. We present VISTA (Variable-length Interpretable Scalable Temporal Analysis), an unsupervised time series clustering model for industrial events that jointly captures local and global structure. First, a convolutional encoder embeds each sliding window. Then an eviction-attention mechanism, trained end-to-end via a straight-through estimator, maintains a bounded pool of the top-P most informative embeddings per series, and truncated SVD on this pool produces a fixed-dimensional representation that captures the principal directions of variation across the pooled embeddings of each time series, naturally accommodating variable length. Finally, K-means is applied to all the representations to assign a label to each event time series. Window- and series-level contrastive losses train the pipeline end-to-end. The bounded pool keeps memory usage constant per series and computation linear with sequence length. Intra-pool self-attention scores yield faithful temporal localization (“when”), and a per-cluster channel-attribution score identifies the sensors most relevant to each cluster (“what”). On five industrial datasets, VISTA outperforms all twelve baselines in time series event clustering. Faithfulness tests confirm that these interpretable scores identify windows and channels relevant to VISTA's clustering output and align with domain-expert physical interpretations.
FULLCausal Tracing and Algorithmic Recourse for Multivariate Time Series Anomalies
Guangyu Li (Shandong Normal University) · Chao Luo (Shandong Normal University)
Abstract
Significant progress has been made in multivariate time series anomaly detection, enabling the effective identification of various anomalies. However, in time sensitive scenarios such as industrial control and microservice monitoring, a critical challenge remains: how to rapidly generate remediation measures that are both interpretable and incur low intervention cost after an anomaly is detected. To close this loop, a system must not only accurately identify anomalies but also trace their root causes. To this end, this paper focuses on algorithmic recourse in noisy multivariate time series and proposes a root cause localization mechanism that integrates causal inference, aiming to precisely identify the core variables that trigger anomalies. Based on the identified root cause variables, counterfactual windows are constructed, from which a downstream recourse generator produces repair suggestions that balance effectiveness with low intervention cost. We introduce a counterfactual based repair framework—CARE (Causal Algorithmic Recourse)—which not only reverses the anomalous time window but also provides causally interpretable remediation strategies. Experimental results on both synthetic and real world datasets demonstrate that CARE achieves precise root cause localization, maintains a high repair success rate, and significantly reduces the intervention cost. This work offers a feasible pathway toward shifting from passive anomaly monitoring to active, interpretable, and autonomous system repair.
FULLFrequency-Aware Anomaly Detection in Tabular Data
Ning Wang (Shanxi University) · Liang Du (Shanxi University) · Xi Ma (Unit 96901, PLA) · Yan Chen (Taiyuan University of Technology) · Xinye Wang (Tiangong University) · Zhiguo Hu (Shanxi University)
Abstract
The central challenge of one-class tabular anomaly detection lies not only in the absence of anomaly labels, but also in that abnormality can only be defined relative to normality. Such deviations do not have a fixed form in heterogeneous tabular spaces, and thus detection methods have to rely on implicit assumptions about anomaly patterns. For example, reconstruction-based paradigms expect anomalies hard to reconstruct through normal mappings, while distance-based paradigms expect anomalies to exhibit irregularity in local neighborhoods. However, real anomalies do not always follow these assumptions. They may be well reconstructed due to the generalization ability of deep models, or appear locally plausible. Therefore, this paper no longer seeks new reconstruction tricks or local constraints, but instead investigates whether discriminative cues can be discovered from the overall organization of normal patterns themselves. To this end, we analyze the inter-sample connection structure (T-Graph), and find that, under this data-dependent organization, anomalies induce stronger high-frequency responses. This suggests that spectral information captures structural changes induced by anomalous perturbations to normal connection patterns, thereby providing a new structural cue for distinguishing normal and anomalous data. Motivated by this, we propose FASEN (Frequency-Aware Spectral Encoding Network). It first employs wavelet filters to decouple graph signals into multi-scale spectral representations. Subsequently, we design a Frequency Selection module to adaptively learn the frequency preference of normal data, thereby guiding the model to reconstruct utilizing the topological features dominated by normal patterns. Extensive experiments on multiple benchmark datasets demonstrate that FASEN outperforms SOTA methods. Further analysis indicates that this mechanism behaves as a physically interpretable matched filter. The complete code is available at https://github.com/criticcc/FASEN.
FULLMitigating Convergence Collapse in Fixed-Target Anomaly Detectors via Kernel-Anchored Locality Regularization
José Lucas De Melo Costa (Université Paris-Saclay, CNRS, CentraleSupélec, LISN UMR 9015) · Fabrice Popineau (Université Paris-Saclay, CNRS, CentraleSupélec, Laboratoire Interdisciplinaire des Sciences du Numérique) · Arpad Rimmel (Université Paris-Saclay, CNRS, CentraleSupélec, Laboratoire Interdisciplinaire des Sciences du Numérique) · Bich-Liên Doan (Université Paris-Saclay, CNRS, CentraleSupélec, Laboratoire Interdisciplinaire des Sciences du Numérique)
Abstract
A family of tabular anomaly detectors trains a neural map toward a fixed target under squared-error loss and scores anomalies by the test-time residual; contraction matching, one-step rectified flow, and reconstruction autoencoders all fit this template. We characterize a convergence collapse: better optimization makes the detector worse. At convergence, the learned map tracks the target even off-distribution, so the residual signal vanishes on anomalies as well as on normal data. These detectors therefore rely on implicit non-convergence (early stopping, capacity caps) to retain signal. We argue this is structural: effective anomaly detection requires a locality constraint that blocks unconstrained extrapolation. Classical detectors (kNN, KDE, isolation forests, LOF) enforce locality explicitly; fixed-target neural detectors do not. We formalize the connection by showing that the kernel-regression analog of a fixed-target detector is a finite-bandwidth Nadaraya–Watson smoother, which we call Kernel Contraction Matching (KCM). KCM is closed-form, training-free, and CPU-efficient, yet matches established neural baselines on ADBench. Building on this bridge, we introduce the Kernel-Anchored Regularizer (KAR), which penalizes deviation of the neural prediction from a kernel-weighted average of training targets. Across collapse-prone ADBench datasets and three backbones, KAR mitigates collapse and improves AUROC under prolonged training.
4G · Adversarial Attacks & BackdoorsFull ResearchStudio 2Tuesday 16:00 – 18:008 talksChair: Saravanakumar Duraisamy (University of Luxembourg)
FULLAssessing Attack Surfaces in Generative Search Engines through Publisher Attributes: A Case Study in Political Domains
Riku Mochizuki (Keio University/QueryLift Inc.) · Shusuke Komatsu (QueryLift Inc.) · Souta Noguchi (QueryLift Inc.) · Kazuto Ataka (Keio University)
Abstract
We characterize the attack surface of generative search engines (GSEs) against poisoning attacks in the political domain, from the perspectives of citation selection and personalization. GSEs integrate web search and answer generation with user preferences and backgrounds using large language models (LLMs). They play a crucial role in how users access information on the web. Because anyone can publish content on the web, GSEs are vulnerable to poisoning attacks that manipulate citations to undermine reliable information delivery. Existing studies on citation evaluation focus on how faithfully answers reflect cited content. However, they leave unexamined the two critical aspects to capture the attack surface of GSEs against poisoning attacks: which publishers GSEs prefer to cite, and how personalization affects citation behavior. To fill this gap, we introduce an evaluation framework that characterizes the attack surface of GSEs against poisoning attacks. Our contributions are twofold: (1) we propose a novel metric, content-injection barrier, which quantifies the difficulty of injecting arbitrary content onto the web with a given level of publisher authority; and (2) we reveal how personalization affects citation behavior by embedding user profiles into GSEs. We conduct experiments on three major GSEs in the political domain of the United States and Japan. Our results show that (a) the attack surface differs across GSE models; (b) the web search functionality of GSEs shapes the attack surface; (c) ruling parties have a broader attack surface than opposition parties; and (d) user profiles have little influence on the attack surface.
FULLRetriever as an Attack Surface: Exploring Fairness Vulnerabilities in Retrieval-Augmented Generation
Yuzhe Liu (State Key Laboratory of AI Safety) · Ruqing Zhang (State Key Laboratory of AI Safety) · Yingchen Zhang (State Key Laboratory of AI Safety) · Jiafeng Guo (State Key Laboratory of AI Safety) · Xueqi Cheng (State Key Laboratory of AI Safety)
Abstract
Retrieval-augmented generation (RAG) systems have recently been shown to be vulnerable to fairness and bias manipulation, with prior attacks predominantly targeting the data layer via corpus poisoning. In this work, we expose a fundamentally different and largely unexplored attack surface: the retriever itself. Motivated by the widespread deployment of off-the-shelf neural retrievers as plug-and-play components in modular RAG pipelines, we formalize the Adversarial Fairness Attack against RAG (AFA-RAG), where an adversary manipulates only retriever parameters, leaving both the corpus and generator untouched, to systematically skew evidence exposure toward a target demographic while preserving semantic relevance and stealth. To instantiate this threat, we propose AFA-RL, a reinforcement learning framework that treats the retriever as a strategic ranking agent interacting with a RAG environment. AFA-RL learns adversarial ranking policies that subtly reshape retrieved evidence to bias downstream response generation, guided by a fairness-aware reward with strict relevance and distributional constraints. Experiments across multiple datasets and large language model backbones show that AFA-RL can cause disproportionate fairness degradation with negligible impact on standard retrieval metrics. Our results uncover a previously overlooked supply-chain vulnerability in modular RAG systems and underscore the urgent need for robustness guarantees at the retriever level.
FULLAnchoring Bias: A Persistent Fairness Backdoor Attack against MLLMs under Continual Learning
Yuyang Luo (Emory University) · Kai Shu (Emory University)
Abstract
Multimodal Large Language Models (MLLMs) are increasingly deployed in high-stakes domains where fairness is a critical safety requirement. In practice, these models are continually updated through continual learning (CL) to adapt to evolving tasks and data distributions. Prior work has shown that backdoor attacks can manipulate MLLM responses through hidden triggers, but naively implanted backdoors degrade as models undergo subsequent updates of CL. Although fairness has emerged as a central concern for MLLM deployment, whether backdoor-induced fairness violations can survive CL remains unexplored, leaving two critical questions unanswered: (1) whether a backdoor can reliably induce fairness violations in MLLMs, and (2) whether such fairness-targeted backdoors can persist through continual learning. We bridge this gap by proposing Persistent Fairness Backdoor Attack (PFBA) to inject persistent and group-specific discrimination into MLLMs. Specifically, PFBA achieves this through two novel mechanisms. The Latent Space Fairness Reinforcement reshapes the model's deep feature geometry by anchoring privileged-group representations to preserve utility while repelling and clustering targeted-group representations to sustain discrimination, and the Continual Learning Simulation iteratively optimizes the trigger against simulated parameter drift to ensure backdoor persistence across future updates. Extensive experiments demonstrate that PFBA induces severe fairness disparities that persist across continual learning rounds, evading standard backdoor defenses. The data and code are publicly available at https://github.com/lyygua/PFBA (https://github.com/lyygua/Persistent-Fairness-Backdoor-Attack-LVLM.git).
FULLMTBTime: Backdoor Attacks on Multi-objective Patterns under Multivariate Time Series Prediction
Guohui Ding (Shenyang Aerospace University) · Mingyang Xu (Shenyang Aerospace University) · Yimin Xu (Shenyang Aerospace University) · Rui Zhou (Swinburne University of Technology)
Abstract
Multivariate time series (MTS) prediction is widely used in safety-critical domains such as traffic management, energy systems, weather forecasting, and financial analysis. Recent studies have shown that MTS prediction models are vulnerable to backdoor attacks, where poisoned training samples with hidden triggers can manipulate model predictions at run time. However, existing backdoor attacks on MTS prediction mainly focus on a single target pattern, forcing attacked variables to follow the same predefined trend. This setting overlooks a more realistic and challenging threat: in real-world multivariate systems, different variables are often causally correlated, sometimes positively and sometimes negatively, so an attacker may need to manipulate multiple target variables toward different target patterns simultaneously while keep the predictions normal for unpoisoned data. To address this gap, we propose MTBTime, a backdoor attack framework for multi-objective target patterns in MTS prediction. MTBTime first identifies vulnerable poisoning positions by combining Granger causality, neural causality scores, and prediction-error-based screening. It then constructs an adaptive causal graph convolutional trigger generator to learn inter-variable dependencies and optimize stealthy triggers that can jointly manipulate multiple target variables toward their respective target patterns. Extensive experiments on multiple benchmark datasets and mainstream MTS prediction models show that MTBTime achieves stronger attack effectiveness than existing methods in multi-target scenarios, while maintaining clean prediction performance and attack stealthiness. These results reveal a previously underexplored vulnerability of MTS prediction models under multi-objective backdoor attacks.
FULLMind the Margins: Probing Link Prediction via Perturbations
Adel Memariani (Data Science Group (DICE), Heinz Nixdorf Institute, Paderborn University, Germany) · Arnab Sharma (Data Science Group (DICE), Heinz Nixdorf Institute, Paderborn University, Germany) · Michael Röder (Data Science Group (DICE), Heinz Nixdorf Institute, Paderborn University, Germany) · Axel-Cyrille Ngonga Ngomo (Data Science Group (DICE), Heinz Nixdorf Institute, Paderborn University, Germany)
Abstract
Adversarial attacks pose a major threat to link prediction models. Carefully chosen triple-level perturbations can exploit weaknesses in the learned representations and change the model's ranking decisions. Despite their importance, adversarial attacks on knowledge graph embeddings (KGE) models remain less studied than their counterparts in areas such as image classification. One reason is that KGE inputs are discrete relational triples, not continuous pixel values. Moreover, KGE scores are computed within multi-relational prediction settings, where each relation can produce a different score distribution. As a result, score-based attack strategies cannot be directly transferred to KGE models. Studying training-data perturbations therefore both exposes vulnerabilities and identifies informative graph edits that can improve performance. In this work, we use adversarial triple modifications as controlled probes of KGE decision behavior. We introduce a decision-margin perspective that measures how clearly each training triple is ranked above its strongest negative alternatives. Our results reveal systematic vulnerability patterns, as well as improvement opportunities, that are shared across different KGE models. At the same time, these effects are not determined by the embedding model alone. The impact of training data perturbations also depends on the structure of the underlying knowledge graph. Overall, our study reframes adversarial probes as diagnostic instruments for KGE models.
FULLGrAP³: A Data-free Model Extraction Attack Framework under Graph Pre-training and Prompt Learning Paradigm
Lingxiang Tian (Institute of Computing Technology, Chinese Academy of Sciences) · Yang Liu (Institute of Computing Technology, Chinese Academy of Sciences) · Xingtong Yu (The Chinese University of Hong Kong) · Zhuoer Xu (Independent Researcher) · Xiang Ao (Institute of Computing Technology, Chinese Academy of Sciences)
Abstract
Graph pre-training and prompt learning paradigm have recently achieved remarkable success by improving the adaptability of Graph Neural Networks (GNNs) and alleviating the reliance on large task-specific datasets. However, we find that this paradigm inadvertently increases the vulnerability of GNNs to model extraction, a type of attack in which adversaries replicate a target model by observing its outputs. A particularly challenging and realistic scenario arises when attackers cannot access any target training data, known as the data-free setting. To address this, we propose GrAP3, a novel framework that enables the reconstruction of high-fidelity surrogate models under this resource-constrained condition. We first conduct a formal risk analysis to examine the impact of pre-training and prompt learning on model extractability. The analysis shows that these paradigms jointly tighten the theoretical upper bound of surrogate–target discrepancy. They are achieved by reducing representation, classification, and distribution gaps, which is the barrier to model extraction. Building on this insight, GrAP3 generates structurally coherent and label-aware query graphs using a multi-class contextual stochastic block model. It further integrates a learnable prompt subgraph whose embeddings and structural connections are jointly optimized with a pre-trained surrogate through alternating optimization. Comprehensive experiments on six benchmark datasets demonstrate the superior model extraction performance of GrAP3 without any access to the training data.
FULLKernel-Complexity Edge Sanitization for Training-Free Defense against Structural Graph Attacks
Yaning Jia (Dartmouth College) · Shenyang Deng (Dartmouth College) · Yaoqing Yang (Dartmouth College) · Chiyu Ma (Dartmouth College) · Wenxuan Xu (Dartmouth College) · Soroush Vosoughi (Dartmouth College)
Abstract
Graph Neural Networks (GNNs) have achieved remarkable success across diverse applications, yet they remain highly vulnerable to adversarial attacks that maliciously perturb graph structure. Existing defenses often lack rigorous theoretical grounding, rely on attack-specific heuristics, or require costly retraining procedures such as adversarial training. To address these limitations, we propose Kernel-Complexity Edge Sanitization (KCES), a training-free and model-agnostic framework for defending against structural attacks. KCES is built upon Graph Kernel Complexity (GKC), a principled metric derived from the graph Gram matrix that appears in a generalization upper bound on the GNN test error. From this bound, we define an edge-specific KC score that quantifies each edge’s structural influence via its induced change in GKC. KCES then identifies and prunes high-KC edges, which are empirically enriched with adversarial perturbations under structural attacks, to mitigate their harmful impact. Computationally efficient and scalable, KCES operates as a lightweight preprocessing step without retraining and can be seamlessly integrated with existing defenses. Extensive experiments demonstrate that KCES consistently outperforms representative robust baselines across diverse attack settings and scales effectively to large graphs. Supported by theoretical analysis and extensive empirical validation, KCES provides a principled and efficient framework for securing GNNs. Our code is available at https://github.com/karpning/KCScore.
FULLTowards Black‑Box Model Inversion Attacks via Lightweight Latent Diffusion Fine‑tuning
Zetao Lin (Shenzhen University) · Qiao Yan (Shenzhen University)
Abstract
Model inversion attacks (MIAs) aim to reconstruct high-quality copies of inaccessible private training data from deep neural networks, thereby posing a severe threat to data privacy. Training-based MIAs are only applicable to reconstructing low-resolution grayscale images. Optimization-based MIAs suffer from complex training of attack models, reconstruction quality degradation caused by iterative optimization, and high query and time overhead. Although diffusion-based MIAs achieve significant advantages in reconstruction quality and generation efficiency, this paradigm still faces two major limitations: 1) Unfiltered public datasets, which severely constrains reconstruction quality. 2) Low execution efficiency, particularly the substantial computational and time overhead incurred by training conditional diffusion models from scratch in the image space. Thus, we propose Lightweight Latent Diffusion Fine-tuning for Model Inversion Attack (LLDF-MI), a novel method that fine-tunes the pre-trained latent diffusion models (LDMs) via Low-Rank Adaptation (LoRA) to achieve efficient and high-quality black-box MIA. Specifically, we first constructs a Top-K positive face fine-tuning dataset via head pose detection and target model confidence filtering for precise visual-identity mappings. On this basis, we design a Multi-Identity LoRA module with a "partially identity-specific + partially shared" parameter allocation strategy, combined with conditional encoding and substitute-based identity loss, to precisely guide the generated images toward the target identity feature space. Experiments show that its attack performance significantly outperforms existing black-box and label-only MIAs, and is comparable to advanced white-box MIAs. Furthermore, it substantially reduces the training time overhead of the attack model and effectively improves the generation efficiency of attack images.

FULLRich-Media Re-Ranker: A User Satisfaction-Driven LLM Re-ranking Framework for Rich-Media Search
Zihao Guo (SKLCCSE, School of Computer) · Ligang Zhou (Baidu Inc) · Zeyang Tang (Baidu Inc) · Feicheng Li (Baidu Inc) · Ying Nie (Baidu Inc) · Zhiming Peng (Baidu Inc) · Qingyun Sun (SKLCCSE, School of Computer) · Jianxin Li (SKLCCSE, School of Computer)
Abstract
Re-ranking plays a crucial role in modern information search systems by refining the ranking of initial search results to better satisfy user information needs. However, existing methods show two notable limitations in improving user search satisfaction: inadequate modeling of multifaceted user intents and neglect of rich side information such as visual perception signals. To address these challenges, we propose the Rich-Media Re-Ranker framework, which aims to enhance user search satisfaction through multi-dimensional and fine-grained modeling. Our approach begins with a Query Planner that analyzes the sequence of query refinements within a session, decomposing the query into clear and complementary subqueries to enable broader coverage of users’ potential intents. Subsequently, moving beyond primary text content, we integrate richer side information of candidate results, including signals modeling visual content generated by the VLM-based evaluator. These comprehensive signals are then processed alongside carefully designed re-ranking principle that considers multiple facets, including content relevance and quality, information gain, information novelty, and the visual presentation of cover images. Then, the LLM-based re-ranker performs the holistic evaluation based on these principles and integrated signals. To enhance the scenario adaptability of the VLM-based evaluator and the LLM-based re-ranker, we further enhance their capabilities through multi-task reinforcement learning.
FULLInference-Free Multimodal Learned Sparse Retrieval for Production-Scale Visual Document Search
Gyu-Hwung Cho (NAVER Corporation) · Youngjune Lee (NAVER Corporation) · Kiyoon Jeong (NAVER Corporation) · Siyoung Lee (NAVER Corporation) · Sanggyu Han (NAVER Corporation) · Hervé Déjean (Naver Labs Europe) · Stéphane Clinchant (Naver Labs Europe) · Seung-won Hwang (Seoul National University)
Abstract
As large-scale visual-document corpora such as arXiv papers and enterprise PDFs continue to grow, visual-document retrieval has gained attention; yet it still lacks a deployable system that lexically indexes visual documents to serve queries without neural encoding at scale. Existing methods either achieve strong retrieval quality with VLM-based dense or multi-vector models but require neural query encoding at serving time, or avoid query encoding with OCR- or caption-based BM25 at the cost of time-consuming text extraction or generation. To fill this missing serving regime, we present V-SPLADE, an inference-free sparse retriever for visual-document retrieval. However, such inference-free multimodal learned sparse retrieval systems remain underexplored and have not yet shown dense-level effectiveness under high sparsity. We attribute this limitation to a lexical grounding problem: visual sparse representations often fail to capture the lexical content embedded in document images. To address this, we introduce caption-gated token supervision, a training-only signal that uses VLM-generated captions as lexical cues to activate retrieval-relevant vocabulary dimensions. With this supervision, V-SPLADE improves average NDCG@5 across six benchmarks by +13.7pp over the same-scale dense baseline and by up to +6.2pp over OCR- or caption-based BM25 baselines. On an 18.7M-document corpus, it doubles R@5 over the same-scale dense baseline and further improves competing retrievers through score fusion by up to +1.6pp R@5. Code and model weights are available at github.com/naver/v-splade and huggingface.co/naver/v-splade-quality, respectively.
FULLSAFE-G: Structure-Aware Faithful Evidence-guided Generation for Knowledge-Based Visual Question Answering
Long Shu (University of Science and Technology of China) · Shuochen Liu (University of Science and Technology of China) · Wei Chen (University of Science and Technology of China) · Junda Lin (University of Science and Technology of China) · Zhi Zheng (University of Science and Technology of China) · Huijun Hou (NIO) · Tong Xu (University of Science and Technology of China)
Abstract
Knowledge-based Visual Question Answering (KB-VQA) aims to answer queries that necessitate reasoning over external knowledge sources beyond the visual content. Typically, current methods fuse multimodal features to retrieve external information, subsequently leveraging Multimodal Large Language Models (MLLMs) to derive answers from the retrieved evidence. However, these methods often struggle to capture structural associations within complex contexts to effectively filter noise. Furthermore, they frequently fail to ensure that the reasoning process remains strictly faithful to the retrieved evidence. To address these challenges, we propose SAFE-G, a Structure-Aware Faithful Evidence-guided Generation framework, which enables precise evidence localization and trustworthy reasoning. Specifically, we first employ a coarse-grained hybrid search fusing visual and textual modalities to recall candidate documents, and subsequently implement a structure-aware fine-grained graph retrieval that captures structural dependencies to filter noise and pinpoint precise evidence. Moreover, we introduce a reinforcement learning (RL) strategy with an evidence-grounded reward that assigns credit to correct answers only when the selected evidence is correct. This strict alignment constraint compels the model to anchor its response in the retrieved context, effectively enhancing its capability to locate evidence via multimodal features and perform faithful reasoning. Extensive experiments on the Encyclopedic-VQA and InfoSeek benchmarks demonstrate that SAFE-G outperforms prior methods by a margin of 8.9% and 3.5%, substantially enhancing the overall reasoning accuracy. Our source code is publicly available at: https://github.com/MINE-USTC/SAFE-G.
FULLMulti-View Hierarchical Graph Neural Network for Sketch-Based 3D Shape Retrieval
Hang Cheng (Tsinghua University) · Muyan He (Harbin Institute of Technology) · Mingyu Fan (Tsinghua University) · Chenfeng Xie (Harbin Institute of Technology) · Xi Cheng (Tsinghua University) · Chenxi Zhai (Tsinghua University) · Long Zeng (Tsinghua University)
Abstract
Sketch-based 3D shape retrieval (SBSR) aims to retrieve 3D shapes that are consistent with the category of the input hand-drawn sketch. The core challenge of this task lies in two aspects: existing methods typically employ simplified aggregation strategies for independently encoded 3D multi-view features, which ignore the geometric relationships between views and multi-level details, resulting in weak 3D representation. Simultaneously, traditional SBSR methods are constrained by visible category limitations, leading to poor performance in zero-shot scenarios. To address these challenges, we propose Multi-View Hierarchical Graph Neural Network (MV-HGNN), a novel framework for SBSR. Specifically, we construct a view-level graph and capture adjacent geometric dependencies and cross-view message passing via local graph convolution and global attention. A view selector is further introduced to perform hierarchical graph coarsening, enabling a progressively larger receptive field for graph convolution and mitigating the interference of redundant views, which leads to more discriminative hierarchical 3D representation. To enable category-agnostic alignment and mitigate overfitting to seen classes, we leverage CLIP text embeddings as semantic prototypes and project both sketch and 3D features into a shared semantic space. We use a two-stage training strategy for category-level retrieval and a one-stage strategy for zero-shot retrieval under the same model architecture. Under both category-level and zero-shot settings, extensive experiments on three public benchmarks demonstrate that MV-HGNN outperforms state-of-the-art methods.
FULLPrompt Contamination in Realistic Universal Cross-Domain Retrieval: Diagnosis and Text-Guided Rectification
Jiangyue Chen (Southeast University) · Li Yao (Southeast University) · Yuanyang Zhang (Southeast University) · Xinwei Li (Southeast University)
Abstract
Universal Cross-Domain Retrieval (UCDR) requires models to generalize to unseen domains and unseen categories at inference time. Recent prompt-learning methods for vision–language models have achieved strong performance on object-centric benchmarks, yet their behavior under cluttered multi-object scenes remains under-explored. In such scenes, co-occurring objects can act as contextual distractors and induce prompt contamination: visually salient distractors may dominate the candidate tokens used for instance-adaptive prompt generation, causing retrieval representations to drift away from the designated primary target. To diagnose this gap, we construct DomainCOCO, a Realistic UCDR benchmark with 180,000 images across six domains, where each sample contains a designated primary category and contextual distractors. DomainCOCO is intended as a controlled diagnostic benchmark for studying target-aware retrieval under multi-object clutter and stylized domain shifts. We further provide Text-Guided Rectification Network (TGR-Net), a practical rectification baseline that uses text embeddings as semantic guidance to re-weight patch-level visual evidence before prompt generation. Its Candidate Prompt Purification (CPP) module reduces distractor-dominated prompt synthesis, while a teacher–student strategy with a learnable null token enables label-free inference. Multi-scale feature fusion and gallery-side refinement are used as optional inference components for accuracy-oriented deployment. Experiments on DomainNet and DomainCOCO show that TGR-Net provides consistent gains over strong CLIP-based baselines, with larger gains in the more cluttered DomainCOCO setting. Code is available at https://github.com/YUEcjy13/TGR-Net.
FULLPRISM: Geometry-Aware Adaptation for Cross-Modal Retrieval under Distribution Shift
Zhijing Wang (University of Electronic Science and Technology of China) · Shanjun Cai (University of Electronic Science and Technology of China) · Xupeng Wang (University of Electronic Science and Technology of China) · Shengjie Min (Chengdu Jinfa Edge Intelligence Technology Co., Ltd.) · Aiguo Chen (University of Electronic Science and Technology of China)
Abstract
Cross-modal retrieval aims to identify semantically relevant instances from a gallery of another modality given queries of interest. Existing methods typically assume that online queries follow the same distribution as the source domain. However, due to the complexity and diversity of real-world queries, online query streams often substantially deviate from the source distribution; such deviations distort the geometry of the shared representation space and degrade retrieval performance. In this paper, we demonstrate that distribution shifts are inherently anisotropic within the representation space, where different geometric directions exhibit varying levels of semantic sensitivity and shift intensity. Leveraging this insight, we propose Projected Representation via Induced Spectral Metric (PRISM), which employs spectral decomposition to separate semantic-sensitive components from shift-intensive variations. During test-time adaptation, PRISM selectively confines adaptation updates to the subspace associated with high shift intensity but low semantic sensitivity, thereby suppressing distributional perturbations while preserving semantic consistency. We further show that PRISM achieves a tighter generalization bound under distribution shifts. Abstract
Large language models are increasingly used to search biomedical knowledge bases. In this setting, queries describe the desired biomedical entity in natural language, and the system retrieves matching candidates. Existing methods typically represent candidate entities through text, leaving out available structural information such as molecular structure or protein sequence. Text descriptions can omit fine-grained structural information, making it difficult for text-only representations to distinguish candidates with similar descriptions but different structures. A natural idea is to introduce structural modalities. However, structural and textual representations of the same entity can encode partially overlapping information, creating cross-modal redundancy. Naive fusion can then reinforce shared information and reduce the contribution of additional structural signals. We present OrthoMol, a multi-modal framework for biomedical entity retrieval whose entity-side fusion explicitly accounts for this redundancy. Its core step, Residual Orthogonal Projection (ROP), decomposes the structural embedding into two parts: a text-aligned component and an orthogonal residual. ROP then removes the text-aligned component and uses the orthogonal residual to augment the text embedding as a complementary structural signal. On both benchmarks, OrthoMol outperforms foundation-model retrieval baselines and improves over the text-only version of the same backbone. Notably, on ProtDescribe, it reduces the mean rank of the target protein by 29% relative to the text-only backbone.

Wooseong Syz Cho (Kookmin University) · Ha-Myung Park (Kookmin University)
Abstract
Retrieval-Augmented In-Context Learning (ICL) faces fundamental Information Retrieval (IR) bottlenecks when applied to continuous graph-structured data (e.g., molecules), as 1D textual representations (e.g., SMILES) fail to capture latent topological causalities. This representational bottleneck becomes catastrophic in Activity Cliff scenarios, where minor structural modifications trigger extreme target value divergences. In such environments, standard retrieval methods inject contradictory exemplars, causing LLMs to suffer from the Parroting effect—blindly mimicking the labels of retrieved neighbors rather than discerning true structural causality. Experimental results demonstrate that S3-Prompt achieves state-of-the-art performance (e.g. up to 2.8% improvement in ROC-AUC) on MoleculeNet classification tasks while maintaining highly competitive results and consistent architectural synergies across regression tasks. Notably, it exhibits significant improvements in prediction robustness within challenging activity cliff regions.

FULLEmbedding Surgery: Localized Updates for Adaptive Ranking Correction in Dense Retrieval
Maddalena Amendola (IIT-CNR) · Antonio Mallia (Seltz) · Raffaele Perego (ISTI-CNR)
Abstract
Dense retrieval systems are core components of modern search engines, recommendation platforms, and retrieval-augmented generation pipelines. They encode documents and queries into dense embeddings, enabling efficient semantic search via vector similarity. However, because document embeddings are computed offline and stored in static indexes, these systems struggle to adapt to user feedback or evolving search intent. To address this limitation, we introduce embedding surgery, a lightweight approach for adaptive ranking correction in dense retrieval. The method applies localized, minimal updates to selected document embeddings at query time, guided by editorial feedback, user interactions, or pseudo-labels from large language models. We formulate embedding surgery as a convex optimization problem that enforces ranking constraints while minimizing modifications to the affected document representations. We integrate embedding surgery into standard dense retrieval pipelines and evaluate it on TREC Deep Learning, TREC Robust, TREC CAsT, and MS MARCO benchmarks. Results show consistent improvements (e.g., up to +60.64% relative improvement in nDCG@10 on DL-Hard under editorial feedback), even under noisy feedback, with low computational cost and without disrupting the global structure of the embedding space. Extensive experiments show that ranking corrections propagate to semantically related queries and that embedding updates can be applied safely and efficiently to scalable Approximate Nearest Neighbor indexes via simple in-place overwriting, without requiring costly index reconstruction. Finally, embedding surgery complements query adaptation methods such as CoRocchio, yielding additional gains while being more robust to noisy feedback.

Abstract
Cross-encoders fine-tuned from Transformer backbones remain the standard for second-stage re-ranking, and recent knowledge-distillation strategies have closed much of the gap with LLM re-rankers. However, these strategies have not been compared under controlled conditions. In particular, it remains unclear how distillation from LLM rankers compares to distillation from strong cross-encoder teachers, or to purely supervised objectives. It is also unclear how much newer backbones (RoBERTa, ELECTRA, DeBERTaV3, ModernBERT) contribute compared to the original BERT. We release all 162 trained models on HuggingFace and a unified training codebase.
FULLCan LLM Annotations Replace User Clicks for Learning to Rank?
Lulu Yu (State Key Laboratory of AI Safety) · Keping Bi (State Key Laboratory of AI Safety) · Jiafeng Guo (State Key Laboratory of AI Safety) · Shihao Liu (Baidu Inc.) · Shuaiqiang Wang (Baidu Inc.) · Dawei Yin (Baidu Inc.) · Xueqi Cheng (State Key Laboratory of AI Safety)
Abstract
Large-scale supervision is essential for training modern ranking models, yet obtaining high-quality human relevance annotations remains costly. Click data has long been used as a low-cost alternative, and recent advances in large language models (LLMs) have introduced LLM-based relevance annotation as another promising source of supervision. Motivated by these findings, we explore two training strategies, annotation-aware data scheduling and frequency-aware multi-objective learning, to integrate both supervision signals. Both strategies improve ranking performance across queries at all frequency levels, with frequency-aware multi-objective learning achieving stronger results. Our code is available at https://github.com/Trustworthy-Information-Access/LLMAnn_Click.
FULLPageLLM: A Multi-Grained Reward Framework for Whole-Page Optimization with Large Language Models
Xinyuan Wang (Arizona State University) · Liang Wu (Nokia) · Dongjie Wang (Northeast Normal University) · Yanjie Fu (Arizona State University)
Abstract
Whole-page optimization (WPO) decides how search and recommendation results are surfaced to users, and large language models (LLMs) open a new route to it by treating page generation as sequence generation. Adapting LLMs to web-scale WPO, however, remains bottlenecked by the need for costly human annotations and by the mismatched granularity between page-level coherence and item-level placement. Abstract
Reranking is instrumental in multi-stage recommender systems as it produces the target sequence of items exposed to users. Generative models have shown promise in this field recently, surpassing traditional discriminative paradigms. However, current methods generally follow an item-level generation manner. They either construct a sequence by irreversible autoregression, or iteratively refine a given sequence through item swapping and replacements. Such item-level decision horizons may cause the solution to be trapped in a local optimum, and also limit the ability to capture dependencies within the sequence, thus failing to pursue a global optimal objective. Furthermore, these methods mainly rely on historical contexts for modeling. We argue that in addition to such "past descriptors", the generation of a target sequence also requires directional guidance related to the future. First, a self-guidance mechanism is designed to shape a future "guidance": (i) we enable the model to learn the correspondence between an exposed sequence and its own resulting future; (ii) at inference, the model is then equipped to self-control the future to be a desired one, therefore self-guiding the generation of a target sequence. Second, we present a holistic sequence generator for reranking. Specifically, a diffusion module is employed to progressively "picture" the permutation over candidate items in a sequence-level manner instructed by the above guidance, thereby avoiding local decision traps. Abstract
As a critical stage in the modern multi-stage recommendation pipeline, list-wise reranking determines the final exposed item sequence and directly shapes the user experience by modeling complex dependencies among candidate items within a list. Existing methods typically formulate this task as selecting indices from the local input list. However, this approach suffers from a semantically inconsistent action space: the same output neuron (logit) corresponds to different items across different samples, preventing the model from forming a stable, item-intrinsic representation. Specifically, we represent items as sequences of discrete tokens and reformulate reranking as a token generation task. Abstract
Modern industrial recommender systems have increasingly adopted the Generator-Evaluator (G-E) framework for the re-ranking stage. Within this paradigm, the generator produces candidate item lists from a pool filtered by upstream retrieval and ranking modules, while the evaluator scores these lists and selects the highest-scoring one for final exposure per request. However, on sequential platforms (e.g., short-video apps), users consume items continuously, ignoring artificial list boundaries. Conventional evaluators score lists by aggregating point-wise values, implicitly assuming exposure independence. Extensive experiments demonstrate that SWIM significantly outperforms baselines in listwise reranking tasks, yielding substantial improvements in overall recommendation engagement.

Zhuoran Wang (Beijing University of Technology) · Haozhe Jia (Beijing University of Technology) · Yunhui Lin (Beijing University of Technology) · Yuxuan Liang (The Hong Kong University of Science and Technology (Guangzhou)) · Guangyin Jin (Changan University)

FULLNo Logs, Only Catalogs: Catalog-to-Supervision Training for Recommendation with LLM-Simulated Preferences
Donghee Han (Korea Advanced Institute of Science and Technology) · Jiwon Jeong (Korea Advanced Institute of Science and Technology) · Hwanjun Song (Korea Advanced Institute of Science and Technology) · Mun Yong Yi (Korea Advanced Institute of Science and Technology)
Abstract
Most recommender systems remain fundamentally dependent on user–item interaction data for training. Recent studies suggest that LLMs can be used either as zero-shot recommenders or as user simulators, but whether LLM-generated signals can substitute for missing behavior data and train a recommender system remains an open question. We study Catalog-to-Supervision Training for recommendation: the model is trained using only the item catalog, with no user–item interaction logs or popularity statistics. Given only the catalog, CASTRec synthesizes catalog-grounded synthetic preference trajectories, grounds them in the actual catalog items, and trains a lightweight encoder for launch-time recommendation. Across benchmarks, CASTRec outperforms baselines, despite using zero interactions during training. It is especially effective in short-history and long-tail regimes, where interaction-trained models are most limited.
FULLBeyond Observed Auxiliary Relations: Environment-Conditioned Modeling for Multi-Behavior Recommendation
Seunghan Lee (Korea University) · Hyunsik Yoo (University of Illinois Urbana-Champaign) · Jian Kang (MBZUAI) · Susik Yoon (Korea University) · Seongku Kang (Korea University)
Abstract
Multi-behavior recommendation (MBR) leverages auxiliary behavioral signals, such as clicks and add-to-cart, to enhance target behavior prediction like purchases. While recent graph neural network–based approaches have achieved strong performance by systematically propagating auxiliary behavior signals, they still suffer from two fundamental challenges inherent to auxiliary behaviors: (1) missing auxiliary signals, which hinder generalization to items without auxiliary observations, and (2) unreliable auxiliary signals, which amplify noise misaligned with the target behavior. To address these challenges in a unified manner, we propose BOAR, an environment-conditioned MBR framework that addresses missing and unreliable auxiliary signals through two complementary modules conditioned on auxiliary observability. Extensive experiments demonstrate that BOAR consistently outperforms state-of-the-art baselines, achieving up to 7.82% gains in HR@10 overall and up to 44.2% gains for target items without auxiliary observations, highlighting its ability to capture hidden preferences beyond observed auxiliary relations. Our code is available at: https://github.com/LSH0411/BOAR.
FULLMoEFormer: A Unified Mixture-of-Experts and Transformer Architecture for Multi-Domain Recommendation

Multi-Domain Recommendation (MDR) aims to model user behaviors across multiple domains with heterogeneous distributions while balancing knowledge sharing and domain-specific specialization. Specifically, the MoEFormer consists of three key designs: (1) A Multi-Level Tokenization that converts heterogeneous multi-domain inputs into dimension-aligned tokens at the field, context, reasoning, and domain levels. (2) A Domain-Disentangled Mask that constrains token interactions to prevent negative transfer and enforce domain-aware information flow. Abstract
While Graph Neural Networks (GNNs) have established themselves as the state-of-the-art paradigm in recommender systems, their performance is often hampered by severe data sparsity. Cross-domain recommendation (CDR) offers a promising solution by leveraging multi-domain interactions. However, existing methods typically rely on specialized, end-to-end architectures. Moreover, these methods typically employ static or uniform transfer mechanisms, failing to capture the interest heterogeneity across domains and the personalized nature of cross-domain correlations. Instead of enforcing uniform constraints, this module learns user-specific affinity scores to dynamically gate knowledge transfer, accommodating users with varying degrees of cross-domain consistency. Abstract
Cross-Domain Sequential Recommendation (CDSR) mitigates data sparsity and cold-start issues by transferring user preferences across domains. Although Graph Neural Networks (GNNs) effectively capture collaborative signals, they struggle with the inherent structural sparsity present in individual domains. Specifically, users or items with few interactions become "isolated nodes". Traditional cross-domain methods fail to rescue these nodes because they rely on explicit, overlapping interaction topologies that are often missing, severely hindering message passing. In contrast, Large Language Models (LLMs) encode rich semantic knowledge yet lack the inherent ability to interpret collaborative graph structures. To address this limitation, we propose SGLP (Semantic-Guided Graph Structure Learning with LLM Structural Priors), a framework that leverages LLM knowledge as a structural prior to reconstruct sparse interaction graphs. Specifically, SGLP employs LLMs to generate Item Semantic Embeddings and User Global Semantic Profiles, establishing a robust semantic foundation. Abstract
Cross-Domain Sequential Recommendation (CDSR) has emerged as a promising paradigm for alleviating data sparsity by transferring user preferences across domains. However, existing methods typically rely on sparse overlapping users or static LLM-derived embeddings, leading to two challenges: the Overlap Dilemma, where fragmented cross-domain connectivity impedes effective knowledge transfer, and the Semantic Gap, where identical items lack domain-specific contextual interpretations. Specifically, we develop a Hierarchical Semantic Representation module that employs shared codebooks with domain-adaptive codeword refinements through Domain-adaptive Residual Quantization, thereby disentangling global static knowledge from layered dynamic semantics. Code is available at https://github.com/zaixiaxiaowu/DA-HSR.

Abstract
Jointly modeling search and recommendation has emerged as a promising paradigm to capture diverse user preferences. However, the undifferentiated integration of cross-domain behaviors often induces negative transfer, driven by intrinsic intent ambiguity and extrinsic cross-domain semantic interference. To address this, we propose DiffuSAR, a diffusion-based framework designed to purify cross-domain behavioral sequences. Yidan Fan (Nanjing University Of Aeronautics And Astronautics) · Tianzi Zang (Nanjing University Of Aeronautics And Astronautics) · Yicong Li (Nanjing University Of Aeronautics And Astronautics) · Juan Li (Nanjing University Of Aeronautics And Astronautics) · Wenze Ma (Shanghai Jiao Tong University)
Abstract
Cross-Domain Recommendation (CDR) mitigates sparsity by transferring knowledge from source to target domains, yet its performance heavily depends on the quality of negative samples. Uniform random sampling is dominated by easy negatives that yield vanishing gradients, while hard negative sampling based on point-wise scores may suffer from false negatives and limited coverage of the global item structure. (https://github.com/fanydan/SGNCDR)
