Zehua Cheng (University of Oxford) · Wei Dai (FLock.io) · Jiahao Sun (FLock.io)
Abstract
Training large Transformer language models is dominated by the cost of synchronous parameter updates: every block of weights is moved at every step using a gradient computed before any block has moved. The resulting trajectory is wasteful, because per-block updates are evaluated on a frozen snapshot of the rest of the network that the next step will already invalidate. Second-order methods such as Shampoo and K-FAC address this spatially through preconditioning, and sharpness-aware methods such as SAM trade compute for sharper minima, but both leave the temporal coupling between blocks untouched. We introduce Gradient Interaction Graph Optimization (GIGO), a meta-optimizer that estimates a sparse directed graph of cross-block gradient dependencies online, partitions each step into contiguous sequential stages along this graph, and refreshes downstream gradients using a stale-activation approximation. The framework wraps any base optimizer, adds one cached boundary activation per stage (∼32 MB at Tseq=1024, scaling linearly with sequence length), and is compatible with mixed precision and data parallelism. On GPT-2 Small through XL (124M–1.5B), GIGO-Adam reaches the same OpenWebText/C4 perplexity in 32.0–34.0 % fewer optimizer steps than synchronous AdamW — a lead of 8–22 percentage points over the strongest 2024-vintage baselines (SOAP, Muon, Sophia, Lion, GaLore) on the Small comparison cohort — with a per-step overhead of 32–38 % and a net wall-clock benefit ranging from +5.2 % (Small) to +16.2 % (XL) across the four sizes tested. The benefit vanishes or reverses where the method's preconditions do not hold: a synthetic block-diagonal control (SRR = 0.0 %), the overhead-dominated Penn Treebank stress test (-18.5 % wall-clock), and a weak-coupling small-vision-Transformer diagnostic (-12.4 % wall-clock on CIFAR-100). Ablations decompose the mechanism: the partial-re-forward refresh primitive alone (random partition) accounts for 9.4 % SRR, the interaction-graph schedule contributes a further ∼22 pp, and the layer-contiguity constraint controls overhead. Our convergence theorem matches the standard Adam O(T-1/4) rate uniformly in graph-estimation quality, providing a safety guarantee; the empirical step-reduction is reported as an empirical regularity not formally predicted by the theory.
FULLStrong Lottery Ticket Hypothesis for Quantum Neural Networks
HongKyun Kwon (Ulsan National Institute of Science and Technology) · Hyun Kyu Lee (Ulsan National Institute of Science and Technology) · Joongheon Kim (Korea University) · Sung Whan Yoon (Ulsan National Institute of Science and Technology)
Abstract
Quantum Neural Networks (QNNs) possess high expressivity via rich unitary transformations, offering abundant representational capacity while maintaining a parameter-effective architecture. In classical deep learning, the high expressivity of deep neural networks (DNNs) motivates the Strong Lottery Ticket Hypothesis (SLTH), which suggests that a randomly initialized DNN contains sparse subnetworks that achieve high performance immediately or serve as a warm start. On the quantum side, a key question is: Does a strong lottery ticket exist in QNNs? Our answer is, Quantum-Strong Lottery Ticket Hypothesis (Q-SLTH), i.e., the first theoretical analysis for the existence of high-performing subnetworks in random scratch of QNNs. We validate our theory by proposing a quantum edge-popup algorithm to find strong subnetworks and empirically identifying winning tickets in randomly initialized QNNs on the MNIST and Fashion-MNIST benchmarks. For practice, Q-SLTH suggests a way to compress QNNs, allowing them to use fewer gates and thereby mitigating quantum-noise-induced degradation that is amplified across multiple layers of quantum gates.
FULLFrom Redundancy to Efficiency: A Similarity-based Filter Sharing for Deep Model Compression
Parul Kukrety (Indian Institute of Technology Ropar) · Shashi Shekhar Jha (Indian Institute of Technology Ropar) · Sudeepta Mishra (Indian Institute of Technology Ropar)
Abstract
Deep CNNs have achieved significant performance across a variety of computer vision tasks. However, their effectiveness comes at a cost of overparameterization. This leads to extensive computation and memory requirements, thereby limiting practical deployment in resource-constrained environments. A growing body of evidence suggests that many of these parameters are redundant, motivating the need for compression strategies that go beyond parameter-level heuristics. To overcome these challenges, we propose a layerwise, similarity-based filter-sharing framework for optimizing parameters of deep models by identifying and exploiting redundancy among filters. By leveraging representational similarity of the filters measured via Centered Kernel Alignment (CKA), our approach enables efficient filter-sharing over layers, significantly reducing the number of parameters, FLOPs and overall memory footprint. We form clusters of filters by measuring their feature-map similarity scores on the dataset, enabling compression decisions guided by representational behaviour rather than raw parameter values. We further use an entropy- and energy-based scaling mechanism that adaptively determines the number of shared filters per layer. Additionally, we extend the framework with a class-conditional formulation, enabling the construction of specialized compressed sub-models tailored to different subsets of tasks. This provides insight into how representational redundancy varies with task difficulty and allows the model to allocate capacity in a data-dependent manner. We conduct extensive experiments over VGG16, AlexNet, ResNet and MobileNetV2 models across standard benchmark datasets. The results demonstrate the effectiveness of our proposed method in achieving substantial parameter and FLOP reductions, while maintaining competitive accuracy. We compare our framework against several state-of-the-art compression methods from the literature. Our proposed framework offers a simple and effective approach to exploiting redundancy in deep networks, with practical implications for efficient deployment and adaptive model design.
FULLEPTQ: Fast and Accurate 2-bit Post-Training Quantization via Factored E8 Lattice
Ha-Myung Park (Kookmin University) · Jungeun Park (Kookmin University) · Chaewon Jeong (Kookmin University) · Woncheol Son (Kookmin University) · Yunjun Kim (Kookmin University) · Junseo Youn (Kookmin University) · Ki Yeon Park (Kookmin University)
Abstract
Two-bit Post-Training Quantization (PTQ) offers an attractive path to deploying Large Language Models under strict memory budgets, yet scalar quantization suffers from catastrophic performance collapse at this extreme bit-width. While Vector Quantization (VQ) methods resolve the accuracy issue, existing approaches suffer from practical inefficiencies: complex optimization pipelines result in hours-long quantization, and some methods exhibit severely limited inference throughput. We propose EPTQ, a 2-bit PTQ framework available in two complementary variants (E8 and FE8), achieving high accuracy and practical efficiency through three contributions: (1) Factored E8 (FE8) lattice quantization, which decomposes the E8 codebook into a compact 4 KB structure that fits in the GPU L1 cache, enabling fast codebook lookup at inference time; (2) Lightweight scale normalization via row/column scaling vectors (g, h), which aligns weight distributions to maximize E8 quantization efficiency, requiring only element-wise per-token scaling at inference; and (3) Adaptive critical weight preservation via knee-point threshold detection, which more accurately identifies Hessian-sensitive weights than approaches relying on fixed global criteria, consistently improving perplexity across models, with zero bit-overhead by encoding the preservation mask into the existing codebook index space. Evaluated across multiple LLMs including Llama-2 and Llama-3 families, EPTQ (E8) achieves accuracy competitive with or surpassing QTIP on Llama-2 models, while EPTQ (FE8) surpasses competing VQ methods in decode throughput on most models, achieving up to 38% faster inference than FP16, with both variants reducing quantization time by over 80% compared to competing approaches.
FULLExploring Model Invariance with Discrete Search for Ultra-Low-Bit Quantization
Yuqiao Wen (University of Alberta) · Yanshuai Cao (RBC Borealis) · Lili Mou (University of Alberta, Alberta Machine Intelligence Institute (Amii), Canada CIFAR AI Chair)
Abstract
As language models continue to grow in size due to their success in a wide range of applications such as conversational agents and coding, there is a pressing need to make them more accessible. A popular technique is to reduce their memory footprint by post-training quantization, where we use fewer bits (e.g., 4--8 bits) to represent the model without retraining it. However, quantizing language models remains a challenging task, especially in the ultra-low-bit setup (e.g., 2 bits). In this paper, we propose InvarExplore, a unified framework that systematically explores different kinds of model invariance to maximize quantization performance. Importantly, InvarExplore features a discrete search algorithm that enables us to explore permutation invariance, which is under-studied as it cannot be optimized with gradient-based methods. Such exploration allows us to take advantage of the synergy between each type of invariance. Our results and in-depth analyses show that InvarExplore is compatible with existing state-of-the-art integer quantization methods, achieving an add-on performance improvement over strong competing methods.
FULLPay Where It Matters: Accurate and Versatile Bit-Level Stream Analytics with Nino-Sketch
Weihe Li (The University of Edinburgh) · Haoyu Liu (Tencent) · Zukai Li (The University of Edinburgh) · Paul Patras (The University of Edinburgh)
Abstract
Analyzing high-velocity data streams is critical for tasks like real-time monitoring, anomaly detection, and performance analysis, driving interest in sketches, probabilistic data structures that efficiently summarize fast streams. Traditional sketches often use large, fixed-size counters, leading to inefficient memory usage in skewed data distributions. Recent solutions, such as hierarchical structures and dynamic counters, attempt to improve memory efficiency but struggle to balance this with detection accuracy. In this work, we present Nino-Sketch, a memory-efficient and versatile sketch for data stream analysis. Nino-Sketch employs a flexible filter to exclude cold items (e.g., those with low frequency or persistence) while focusing on tracking hot items using variable-size counters. When a counter overflows, it reallocates memory by sacrificing the slot with the smallest counter value, enhancing the tracking of hot items. By using variable-length fingerprints (a short identifier derived from an item's key using hashing techniques) for different item types, Nino-Sketch further optimizes memory usage. Experimental results on various datasets show that Nino-Sketch surpasses existing methods, reducing relative error by up to 11.17× over prior baselines under tight memory conditions (e.g., 16KB) while retaining competitive update throughput. We further deploy Nino-Sketch as a synthesizable RTL design on a Xilinx Kintex-7 FPGA, confirming that the bit-level layout is implementable on reconfigurable hardware.
FULLAutoCSF: A Provably Safe Indexing Framework for Filter-Augmented Compressed Static Functions
Vihan Lakshman (MIT CSAIL) · David Torres Ramos (Distill) · Chen Luo (Amazon Search) · Bryce Kille (Illumina) · Todd J. Treangen (Rice University) · Benjamin Coleman (Google Deepmind)
Abstract
We consider the problem of building space-efficient indexes for static key-value datasets with highly skewed value distributions. A standard technique for this task is to augment a compressed static function (CSF) with an approximate set membership prefilter to handle a dominating value and break the one-bit-per-key barrier. However, we observe that prior approaches decide when to apply such a prefilter using idealized cost models or data-driven heuristics, and, as a result, can recommend using a prefilter in regimes where it actively increases space usage. We introduce AutoCSF, a principled algorithm for combining CSFs with prefiltering that comes with a provable safety guarantee: with high probability, it does not recommend a filter when doing so would harm space usage. Our key insight is that while modeling the absolute cost of each index appears intractable, the difference in cost between a CSF and a filter-augmented CSF admits clean analytical bounds via the optimality of Huffman codes. We derive a lower bound on this difference whose sign yields a provably safe decision criterion, along with a complementary upper bound on the maximum achievable savings from prefiltering. Because AutoCSF depends only on the dominant value fraction and a filter cost function, it applies to any approximate set membership structure with a known cost-versus-false-positive-rate tradeoff. We also validate our bounds empirically across three synthetic value distributions and four real-world genomics workloads, and show that the decision criterion never recommends a space-increasing filter while its parameter selection costs at most 0.02 bits per key more than an exhaustive search.

FULLTerminal-Optimal Graph Diffusion with Null-Model-Constrained and Structure-Preserving Noise
Yuchen Zhou (Beijing Electronic Science and Technology Institute) · Yuehong Yan (Independent) · Shubao Jin (Xidian University) · Jiaze Xin (Independent) · Jie Gao (Xidian University) · Rong Qian (Beijing Electronic Science and Technology Institute)
Abstract
Graph diffusion models have emerged as a promising approach for generating complex networks, yet they typically face two major drawbacks. First, terminating the forward process in pure Gaussian noise eliminates the intrinsic structural signatures of the original network, which leads to suboptimal generation quality. Second, the absence of constraints along the diffusion trajectory causes progressive degradation of topological features, ultimately resulting in complete structural collapse. To overcome these challenges, we introduce Null-Model-Constrained Graph Diffusion (NMC-GD), a principled framework incorporating specialized designs for graph generation. Specifically, we substitute the conventional isotropic prior with a null-model distribution as the new forward diffusion endpoint, explicitly preserving critical statistical properties of the network. In addition, we develop a null-model-guided continuous-time stochastic differential equation (SDE) and design a directional noise term that enforces a global structural constraint on the diffusion trajectory, striking a balance between stochasticity and structural invariance. Extensive experiments on three public datasets demonstrate that NMC-GD achieves superior generation quality and computational efficiency.
FULLEquivariant Graph Neural ODEs for Modeling Physical Dynamics
Jiawei Chen (Tianjin University) · Luxinming Yin (Elite Prep Academy) · Yuqi Li (Institute of Computing Technology, Chinese Academy of Sciences) · Bo Zhao (Yale University) · Huiran Duan (The City University of New York) · Wenjun Wang (Tianjin University)
Abstract
Modeling 3D dynamical systems is a fundamental challenge in the physical and engineering sciences, where Equivariant Graph Neural Networks (EGNNs) have emerged as a powerful paradigm by incorporating geometric symmetries. However, these models are fundamentally constrained by their discrete-time, Markovian framework, which neglects long-range temporal correlations and inevitably leads to error accumulation in long-horizon forecasting. To address this limitation, we introduce the Equivariant Graph Neural Ordinary Differential Equation (EG-NODE), a novel framework that directly learns the continuous-time evolution laws of physical systems. Instead of predicting discrete future states, EG-NODE leverages an equivariant GNN as its core to directly model the ordinary differential equation governing the system's instantaneous rate of change the physical laws of motion thereby natively preserving SE(3) symmetry within the learning process. This continuous-time paradigm enables high-precision predictions at arbitrary time points and allows for the use of adaptive step-size solvers to dynamically balance computational efficiency and accuracy. Extensive experiments on N-body, molecular, and fluid dynamics benchmarks demonstrate that EG-NODE significantly outperforms existing discrete models in long-horizon prediction accuracy and effectively suppresses error propagation. Our work establishes a more fundamental, first-principles-based paradigm for learning continuous physical laws from data. Our code is available at https://anonymous.4open.science/r/egno_egnn-436D/.
FULLDynamic Fusion of Topology and History: The AdaGPS Architecture with GatEdgeformer
Chenkai Hao (Northeastern University) · Ying Yin (Northeastern University) · Hexuan Lv (Northeastern University) · Yuan Li (North China University of Technology) · Yuhai Zhao (Northeastern University)
Abstract
Graph Transformers show immense potential in graph representation learning, yet adaptively capturing complex topological dependencies remains a critical challenge. This paper proposes AdaGPS, a novel adaptive architecture featuring three core improvements. First, the introduced GatEdgeformer module injects edge feature information through a dynamic gating mechanism, enhancing the global attention's perception of complex graph structures. Second, dynamically fusing local structure perception with global attention interaction effectively filters structural noise and accurately extracts long-range dependencies. Third, dynamically fusing historical representations from all previous layers enables the deep AdaGPS architecture to fully utilize rich positional and structural encodings preserved across preceding layers. Extensive experiments strongly demonstrate that the injection of edge features and historical information effectively improves model accuracy. Furthermore, the gated dynamic fusion of local and global features significantly enhances cross-domain generalization capability. Systematic ablations confirm robustness and stability, providing a highly expressive new paradigm for graph representation learning and potential computing power network applications.
FULLAdvancing Edge Classification through High-Dimensional Causal Modeling of Node-Edge Interplay
Duanyu Feng (Sichuan University) · Li Ding (Sichuan University) · Hongru Liang (Sichuan University) · Wenqiang Lei (Sichuan University)
Abstract
Edge classification, a crucial task for graph applications, remains relatively under-explored compared to link prediction. Current methods often overlook the potential causal influences of node features on edge features, leading to a loss of relevant prior information. In this work, we present an empirical exploration using the Causal Edge Classification Framework (CECF). Unlike conventional causal inference methods, CECF is the first framework to apply causal inference principles to the edge classification task and to explore modeling edge features as a high-dimensional treatment within a causal framework. Based on the node embedding of Graph Neural Network (GNN), CECF seeks to learn a balanced representation of high-dimensional edge features by mitigating the potential influence of node features. Then, a cross-attention network captures the complex dependencies between node and edge features for final edge classification. Extensive experiments demonstrate that CECF not only achieves superior performance but also serves as a flexible, plug-and-play enhancement for existing methods. We also provide empirical analyses, offering insights into when and how this high-dimensional causal modeling framework works for the edge classification.
FULLSeesaw Effect of Graph Neural Networks
Changlin Yu (University of Electronic Science and Technology of China) · Zhen Liu (University of Electronic Science and Technology of China) · Wen-Bo Xie (Southwest Petroleum University)
Abstract
Graph neural networks (GNNs) have achieved remarkable success in node classification tasks, but their performance often varies significantly across classes. Some classes benefit from highly accurate predictions, while others perform relatively poorly. Recent advances in imbalanced node classification have provided partial remedies, but often lead to a seesaw effect: improvements in the minority class come at the expense of the majority class. This phenomenon reflects a deeper problem of inter-class interference, where optimizing for some classes during training interferes with or inhibits learning in other classes. This imbalance is closely related to representation bias, where limited representational capacity is unevenly distributed across classes. To address this issue, we propose a graph balancing learning framework based on the structural rebalancing theory. Extensive node classification experiments demonstrate that our framework is applicable to various existing GNN models and effectively addresses the seesaw effect of GNNs. The code is available at https://github.com/linlin-oss/SSER-main.
FULLQuantifying and Optimizing Graph Neural Network Sparsification with An Approximation Framework
Ruixiao Zeng (Nanyang Technological University) · Ningyi Liao (Nanyang Technological University) · Siqiang Luo (Nanyang Technological University)
Abstract
Graph Neural Networks (GNNs) have shown promising performance in learning from graph-structured data, but at the cost of prohibitive computational overhead due to a series of graph-scale operators. To reduce redundant graph operations, previous studies attempt to sparsify the graph by pruning or sampling graph edges, which enables popular GNN deployments in realistic tasks. However, these methods are mostly empirical, lacking a theoretical framework for bounding approximation precision and guiding sparsification policy. In this work, we present the first approximation theory for GNN sparsification that unifies both pruning and sampling paradigms, directly characterizing the representation error deviation in a layer-wise manner. Our theoretical bounds reveal that the pattern of error accumulation throughout iterative graph operators varies with key GNN model properties. Based on our framework, we further derive an optimal sparsification policy that minimizes the layer-wise approximation error under fixed computational constraints. Experimental evaluations confirm our theoretical findings on layer approximation bounds. Remarkably, our proposed optimal sparsification allocation reduces the representation error by up to 10× and retains better prediction accuracy compared to canonical sampling strategies. The code is available at https://github.com/Rechard16/QuOS/.
FULLBPB-GNN: Resource-Efficient Distributed GNN Training via Boundary-Aware Prefetching and Cost-Balanced Batch Construction
Zhichao Chen (Northeastern University) · Xingwei Wang (Northeastern University) · Chu Zhao (Northeastern University) · Yuhai Zhao (Northeastern University) · Shangyang Wu (Northeastern University)
Abstract
Distributed graph neural network (GNN) training is essential for large-scale graph learning, but existing mini-batch frameworks still suffer from substantial inter-partition communication overhead and indirect, coarse-grained GPU memory control. In distributed mini-batch training, remote sampled neighbors cause frequent feature fetching, while fixed seed-node batch sizes cannot accurately reflect the computation graph expansion induced by multi-layer sampling. This paper presents BPB-GNN, a resource-efficient distributed GNN training system that jointly optimizes inter-partition feature access, hierarchical storage management, and mini-batch construction. First, BPB-GNN introduces a training-centric boundary-aware prefetching strategy to localize high-value remote neighbor features associated with boundary nodes in training-node receptive fields. Second, it uses a DRAM/NVMe SSD hierarchy with priority-aware placement and dynamic migration to manage prefetched features under limited DRAM capacity. Finally, it constructs seed-node batches according to estimated sampling-induced load costs rather than equal seed-node counts, thereby balancing batch-level workloads and reducing peak GPU memory usage and its inter-batch fluctuation. These resource-efficient mechanisms may also improve the efficiency of large-scale GNN computation in computing power networks and JointCloud environments. Experiments on real-world graph datasets show that BPB-GNN achieves up to 5× speedup over the baselines while reducing peak GPU memory usage by up to 36%.
FULLQ-Flow: Power-Balance-Aware Graph Learning for Power Flow Calculation with Partially Observed Reactive Power
Zhen Zhao (Shanghai AI Laboratory) · Ziyang Ding (Shanghai Jiao Tong University) · Linjian Meng (Shanghai AI Laborotory) · Lei Bai (Shanghai AI Laborotory)
Abstract
Classical AC power flow assumes that nodal active and reactive power injections are fully specified. In practice, however, reactive power at some PQ buses may be unavailable due to limited observability or implicit local control. In this paper, we study power flow calculation with partially observed reactive power, where network topology, bus types, active power, and only a subset of reactive-power injections are available as inputs. Specifically, we propose Q-Flow, a graph-based framework for predicting voltage states from such incomplete inputs. Q-Flow combines a Hierarchical Information Fusion (HI-Fuse) with a Multi-Order Gated Kolmogorov–Arnold Network (MoG-KAN), allowing the model to exploit local grid structure, bus-type information, and system-level context while modeling the nonlinear relationship between power injections and voltage states. AC power-flow equations are further incorporated as a physical consistency constraint during training. We evaluate Q-Flow on IEEE 39-, 118-, and 300-bus systems under fixed and sample-dependent reactive-power masks, as well as the complete-Q setting. Q-Flow consistently outperforms representative graph-learning baselines and maintains low voltage-state errors as reactive-power observability decreases.

FULLOutcome-aware Evaluation of Recommendation Rankings in Art Therapy Using Multimodal Physiological Utility
Saravanakumar Duraisamy (University of Luxembourg) · Bereket A. Yilma (University of Luxembourg) · Parvin Emami (University of Luxembourg) · Luis A. Leiva (University of Luxembourg)
Abstract
Recommender systems are often evaluated using observable behavioral signals as surrogate relevance measures of user experience. However, in well-being and mental health support applications, user experience is inherently non-observable. To address this limitation, we introduce a multimodal physiology-driven framework for evaluating recommendation rankings in art therapy using functional near-infrared spectroscopy (fNIRS) and eye-gaze signals. We define a physiological utility scalar that captures item-level internal response by combining prefrontal hemodynamic responses with attention and engagement dynamics derived from gaze behavior, enabling direct comparison between system-generated rankings and rankings induced by internal user responses. We show that fNIRS-derived utility exhibits moderate alignment with system rankings (Spearman’s ρ ≈ 0.40, pairwise accuracy ≈ 0.69), with inter-hemispheric functional connectivity showing the strongest alignment among the evaluated neural descriptors. Gaze-derived utility yields stronger observed alignment (ρ ≈ 0.55, pairwise accuracy ≈ 0.75), particularly for attention continuity and engagement-related representations. Multimodal integration yielded the highest observed agreement between recommendation rankings and physiology-derived utility (ρ ≈ 0.61, pairwise accuracy ≈ 0.77). Our findings provide exploratory evidence that multimodal physiological signals may offer complementary information for evaluating recommendation rankings in outcome-sensitive art therapy.
FULLBeyond Static Profiles: Intent-Aware Behavioural Control for LLM-based Recommendation Simulation
Xinye Wanyan (RMIT University) · Chenglong Ma (RMIT University) · Danula Hettiachchi (RMIT University) · Ziqi Xu (RMIT University) · Jeffrey Chan (RMIT University)
Abstract
Large language models (LLMs) are increasingly used in recommender systems for user modelling, ranking, and simulation. Among these applications, LLM-based user simulators provide a flexible way to evaluate recommender systems without relying on live user feedback. However, existing simulators typically reduce user behaviour to static preference matching based on fixed user profiles, overlooking the fact that real decisions may also reflect recent preference shifts and exploratory behaviour. To address this limitation, we propose IntRecSim (Intent-aware Recommendation Simulation), a plug-in behavioural control framework for LLM-based user simulation. IntRecSim introduces a lightweight intent mechanism that guides whether the simulated decision should follow long-term preferences, recent behavioural evidence, or exploratory behaviour. Since standard recommendation datasets lack explicit intent annotations, we construct pseudo-intent supervision from historical interactions using hybrid category and semantic preference signals. The inferred intent is injected into the LLM simulator as a dynamic control signal, making the framework compatible with different profile-generation backbones. Experiments on three benchmark datasets, covering discrimination and ranking tasks show that IntRecSim improves simulation performance in most evaluated settings. Further analysis highlights the importance of explicit behavioural control for modelling realistic user decisions in LLM-based recommender simulation.
FULLTMemAgent: Transferable Memory for Cross-Domain User Behaviour Simulation
Md Faisal Ahmed (RMIT University) · Estrid He (RMIT University) · Chenglong Ma (RMIT University) · Jeffrey Chan (RMIT University)
Abstract
Reliable evaluation of recommender systems (RSs) often requires user studies or online interaction logs, both of which are costly to obtain for new or low-resource platforms. User behaviour simulation offers a scalable alternative, but existing simulators are typically trained and deployed within a single domain. Thus, they cannot easily reuse the same user agent across domains and often conflate stable user traits with domain-specific interaction evidence. In this paper, we study cross-domain user behaviour simulation: given a user agent learned from a source domain, simulate the same user's behaviour in a target domain. We propose TMemAgent, a transferable memory-based user simulator. The key idea is to treat memory as an actively managed behavioural representation rather than a passive store of past interactions. TMemAgent maintains two complementary memory banks: a transferable memory bank that captures stable user characteristics across domains, and a domain-specific memory bank that preserves local contextual evidence. A memory learning and management (MLM) policy, trained with an actor-critic objective, dynamically decides when to retrieve, add, reflect, update, or forget memory entries. Experiments on three Amazon domains show that TMemAgent improves user-agent prediction performance, yielding gains of around 12% in same-domain settings and around 14% in cross-domain settings compared with the strongest baseline. Moreover, the transferred agents preserve behavioural diversity close to the ground truth, demonstrating that explicit MLM supports scalable, transferable, and behaviourally realistic user simulation for RS evaluation.
FULLBeyond States: Investigating the Effects of Context on User Modeling with Feature-Conditioned Markov Models
Jana Isabelle Friese (University of Duisburg-Essen) · Andreas Konstantin Kruff (TH Köln - University of Applied Sciences) · Timo Breuer (TH Köln - University of Applied Sciences) · Philipp Schaer (TH Köln - University of Applied Sciences) · Norbert Fuhr (University of Duisburg-Essen)
Abstract
User behavior simulation is widely used to evaluate interactive information retrieval systems, but classical state-based approaches (e.g., Markov models) have limited ability to incorporate contextual information relevant for decision-making. We address this limitation by introducing a feature-conditioned Markov-style user model, in which transition probabilities are modeled as functions of positional, content-based, and interaction-derived features, enabling context-aware decision making while preserving the structural simplicity and computational efficiency of state-based models. Applying a multi-level framework that assesses predictive fit and behavioral fidelity, we analyze how different sources of contextual information contribute to realistic user simulation across multiple datasets, search settings, and feature configurations. Our results show that incorporating contextual features improves the models' ability to reproduce key aspects of real user interactions, but that their effectiveness hinges on search scenario and modeling objective. Instead of a “one-size-fits-all” solution, effective simulation requires task- and setting-specific feature selection. Our framework provides a practical and interpretable basis for making these choices.
FULLRole of Personality in Conversational Information Seeking
Abdisalam Abukar (University of Glasgow) · Junchen Fu (University of Glasgow) · Chengli Zhai (University of Glasgow) · Joemon M. Jose (University of Glasgow)
Abstract
Large language models (LLMs) are increasingly used for information seeking, where users find, compare, and evaluate information through dialogue. In this role, the assistant does more than retrieve or generate content: it shapes how users articulate constraints, ask follow-up questions, verify claims, and decide when an answer is sufficient for action. Yet little is known about how user personality, assistant personality, and task context jointly influence these interactions. We examine personality as a controllable variable in conversational information seeking and study its effects on user behaviour and interaction quality. We conducted a controlled within-subject study in which assistant personality and task type were experimentally varied, while participant personality was measured using Big Five scores. Twenty-six participants each completed three information-seeking tasks under three assistant personality conditions: extraverted, conscientious, and neutral. Tasks covered exploratory travel planning, comparative smartphone shopping, and verification-sensitive health and diet information seeking. Data included conversation logs, behavioural traces, post-interaction questionnaires, an exit questionnaire, and Big Five measures. The assistant conditions were behaviourally distinct: the extraverted assistant produced longer turns, the conscientious assistant elicited higher user word share and more turns, and the neutral baseline fell between them. The strongest effect was a task-by-assistant interaction on trust and delegation, with preferred styles varying by task. No global winner emerged, but participants strongly preferred style choice or adaptation. These findings position assistant personality as a context-sensitive interactional design variable rather than a globally optimisable system property.
FULLHow Cultural Background and Cognitive Style Shape Responses to Sustainability-Aware Explanations in Healthy Food Recommender Systems
Thi Ngoc Trang Tran (Graz University of Technology) · Viet-Man Le (Graz University of Technology) · Alexander Felfernig (Graz University of Technology) · Sebastian Lubos (Graz University of Technology) · Thi Minh Ngoc Chau (School of Hospitality and Tourism - Hue University) · Li Chen (Hong Kong Baptist University) · Gerhard Leitner (University of Klagenfurt) · Mehrdad Rostami (University of Oulu) · Amir Mollazadeh Sardroudi (University of Oulu)
Abstract
Food recommender systems are increasingly expected to encourage healthier, more sustainable choices, often through sustainability-aware explanations that blend transparency with persuasive messaging. Yet little is known about how users' cultural backgrounds and cognitive styles shape their responses to these explanations. In this paper, we investigate the influence of cultural background and cognitive style on users' behavioral decisions and subjective evaluations of sustainability-aware explanations in food recommender systems. We conducted a user study using a web-based food recommendation prototype incorporating three Cialdini-inspired persuasive explanation strategies: Authority, Commitment, and Social Proof. The study compared Asian and European participants and further examined differences across cognitive-style groups. The results show that cultural background significantly influenced both recipe-selection behavior and users' perceptions of explanation quality, whereas cognitive style showed comparatively smaller effects that mainly affected subjective explanation evaluations. On the other hand, the persuasive explanation strategies themselves produced relatively stable behavioral effects across cultural and cognitive-style groups, with no significant interaction effects after multiple-comparison correction. These findings provide practical implications for designing food recommender systems that effectively balance persuasive support, transparency, and cultural adaptability to encourage healthier and more environmentally responsible consumption behaviors.
FULLOn Mitigating Data Sparsity in Conversational Recommender Systems
Sixiao Zhang (Nanyang Technological University) · Mingrui Liu (Nanyang Technological University) · Wei Yuan (The University of Queensland) · Hongzhi Yin (The University of Queensland) · Cheng Long (Nanyang Technological University)
Abstract
Conversational recommender systems (CRSs) infer user preferences from dialogue contexts, but they suffer from severe data sparsity in both dialogue and entity spaces. Dialogue data are linguistically diverse and open-ended, making it difficult to generalize across varied expressions. Meanwhile, existing CRS models often rely on large knowledge graphs, where only a small fraction of entities receive effective supervision during training, leaving the majority under-trained or entirely unseen at inference time. To address these challenges, we propose DACRS, a novel CRS framework consisting of three modules: Dialogue Augmentation, Knowledge-Guided Entity Modeling, and Dialogue–Entity Matching. The Dialogue Augmentation module adopts a two-stage augmentation pipeline to enrich dialogue contexts and improve robustness to linguistic variation. The Knowledge-Guided Entity Modeling module leverages knowledge graphs through entity substitution and an entity similarity constraint to enhance representation learning for sparsely supervised and unseen entities. Finally, the Dialogue–Entity Matching module integrates dialogue representations with mentioned entity embeddings via dialogue-guided attention aggregation, yielding user representations that capture both explicit and implicit preferences. Extensive experiments on two public benchmark datasets demonstrate that DACRS consistently outperforms state-of-the-art conversational recommender systems.

FULLPOLAR: Policy Optimization through Larger Reasoners
Ye Yuan (Peking University) · Zhiping Xiao (University of Washington) · Ming Zhang (Peking University)
Abstract
Reinforcement learning with verifiable rewards (RLVR) is a practical way to improve the reasoning and decision-making abilities of large language models, but its training signal is often sparse. When a policy faces prompts beyond its current ability, every sampled trajectory in a group may fail the verifier, resulting in an all-zero group. In this case, group-relative policy optimization gives little useful gradient even when the prompt contains valuable learning content. This capacity-difficulty mismatch is especially costly for smaller models used in knowledge-intensive and web-interaction tasks. We present POLAR, a difficulty-aware training framework that augments on-policy RL with conditional guidance from a larger reasoner. POLAR uses the standard GRPO branch when at least one sampled response succeeds, and switches to a supervised objective over verified teacher trajectories only when the whole student group receives zero reward. The method can turn otherwise wasted all-zero groups into targeted learning opportunities while keeping policy exploration on prompts the student can handle. We formalize the switching criterion, teacher selection objective, mixed RL/supervised loss, and compute overhead. We evaluate POLAR on WebShop, GAIA, and WebWalkerQA using Qwen2.5-7B-Instruct, Qwen3-4B, and Qwen3-8B policies. The results show consistent gains over matched GRPO baselines, with large improvements on hard web traversal questions for the two smaller policies. Ablations and diagnostics further show that the gains come from the proposed all-zero recovery mechanism.
FULLThe Compaction Cliff in Long-Running AI Agent Memory
Saber Zerhoudi (University of Passau) · Jelena Mitrović (University of Passau) · Michael Granitzer (University of Passau)
Abstract
A safety rule and an episodic log compete for the same tokens in an AI agent's context. When the budget overflows, both are summarized at the same rate; only the rule needs exact wording to remain enforceable. On 20 production agent configurations, Claude Code's /compact prompt on Sonnet 4.6 preserves 53% of safety rules after one compaction round and 10% after five. We name this the Compaction Cliff. We address it with Knowledge Triage, a framework that classifies each line of an agent's knowledge base by type and routes each type through its own retention policy. Three deterministic operators implement this triage across the three context-management operations: TypeCompact rewrites items in place under per-type fidelity, TypeDecompose partitions a topic too large to compact safely, replicating in-scope safety rules across partitions, and TypeRetrieve fetches items from external storage with in-scope rules pinned ahead of relevance. On five public corpora, TypeCompact preserves 2-4× more safety rules than the strongest single-shot LLM compactor at every ratio, with 96% recall over five rounds. TypeDecompose reaches 0% locality violations against 93% under uniform partitioning. TypeRetrieve reaches 100% recall@50 against 73% for the best single-shot LLM retriever. Abstract
For long-horizon LLM agents, forgetting is not a housekeeping detail: it determines whether the agent preserves commitments, updates stale beliefs, and reasons coherently under finite memory. Fangzheng Tian (University of Glasgow) · Debasis Ganguly (University of Glasgow) · Craig Macdonald (University of Glasgow)
Abstract
Agentic Retrieval-Augmented Generation (RAG) has become a promising paradigm for multi-hop question answering, where a reasoning model iteratively issues queries to a retriever and incorporates newly retrieved context into subsequent reasoning steps. Specifically, after each retrieval-reasoning iteration, we force an agentic model to stop reasoning and generate an intermediate answer based on its current state. This allows us to define two iteration-level measures: partial answer quality at each iteration, and partial utility as the change in partial answer quality across iterations. Accordingly, we formulate two prediction tasks, partial answer quality prediction and partial utility prediction, and study trajectory-derived signals from intra-iteration, inter-iteration, and query-iteration perspectives. Experiments show that partial answer quality is more predictable than partial utility, with supervised models achieving Pearson's r above 0.43 for quality prediction. Finally, using predicted answer quality and utility for early stopping reduces average iteration count by about 11% while preserving about 98% of the final answer quality achieved by natural stopping.

Sheng Zhang (City University of Hong Kong) · Junyi Li (City University of Hong Kong) · Wenlin Zhang (City University of Hong Kong) · Xiaowei Qian (City University of Hong Kong) · Yichao Wang (Huawei Technologies Ltd.) · Yingyi Zhang (City University of Hong Kong) · Maolin Wang (City University of Hong Kong) · Yong Liu (Huawei Technologies Ltd.) · Xiangyu Zhao (City University of Hong Kong)

Recent search agents for multi-hop reasoning often fail by either retrieving incomplete evidence or reasoning over irrelevant portions of the retrieved content, leading to a retrieval-reasoning boundary shift. Implementation code is available for reproducibility: https://github.com/Applied-Machine-Learning-Lab/CIKM2026_R2-Searcher.

Mingyue Cheng (State Key Laboratory of Cognitive Intelligence, University of Science and Technology of China) · Daoyu Wang (State Key Laboratory of Cognitive Intelligence, University of Science and Technology of China) · Qi Liu (State Key Laboratory of Cognitive Intelligence, University of Science and Technology of China) · Shuo Yu (State Key Laboratory of Cognitive Intelligence, University of Science and Technology of China, Hefei, China) · Xiaoyu Tao (State Key Laboratory of Cognitive Intelligence, University of Science and Technology of China) · Yuqian Wang (State Key Laboratory of Cognitive Intelligence, University of Science and Technology of China) · Chengzhong Chu (Artificial Intelligence Engineering Institute, iFLYTEK Co., Ltd) · Yu Duan (Artificial Intelligence Engineering Institute, iFLYTEK Co., Ltd) · Mingkang Long (Artificial Intelligence Engineering Institute, iFLYTEK Co., Ltd) · Enhong Chen (State Key Laboratory of Cognitive Intelligence, University of Science and Technology of China)
Abstract
Synthesizing informative commercial reports from massive and noisy web sources is critical for high-stakes business decisions. Although recent deep research agents (DRAs) achieve notable progress, their reports remain limited in quality, reliability, and coverage. These mainly stem from ambiguous intents that cause search drift, retrieved web content that rapidly saturates the context window, and single-pass synthesis that limits report comprehensiveness. In this work, we propose Mind2Report, a cognitive deep research agent that emulates commercial analysts to synthesize expert-level reports. Finally, Mind2Report iteratively synthesizes the report based on the evolving outline and accumulated evidence. Together, these designs enable reliable and context-efficient long-horizon commercial deep research. To rigorously evaluate commercial DRAs, we further construct QRC-Eval, comprising 200 real-world commercial tasks and a holistic evaluation framework covering report quality, reliability, and coverage. Extensive experiments demonstrate that Mind2Report consistently outperforms leading proprietary and open-source DRAs, while ablations verify the effectiveness of each module and further analyze the challenges they address. The implementation of Mind2Report and the QRC-Eval data are publicly available (https://github.com/ustc-ai4science/Mind2Report).

Peng Lan (Central South University) · Yutao Deng (Central South University) · Ruhao Deng (Central South University) · Yuhang Fang (Central South University) · Ke Wang (Central South University) · Zhifang Liao (Central South University)
Abstract
High-quality commit messages are crucial software knowledge that summarize the intent, scope, and rationale of code changes, which improves maintenance, code review, and repository traceability. As the Conventional Commits Specification (CCS) has been increasingly adopted in modern software development, commit header generation must produce not only fluent descriptions but also repository-appropriate structured header fields (type and scope). In this work, we study CCS-style commit header generation, focusing on the structural format <type>[optional scope]: <description>. To address these limitations, we propose HARE, a novel History-Aware Repository-level memory framework for generating conventional commit headers. Ablation studies verify the contributions of episodic memory, evolutionary memory, and PMI-based reranking, while robustness analyses show that HARE remains effective across repositories with both sparse and extensive histories. Our framework implementation and dataset are available at https://doi.org/10.5281/zenodo.22006538.
6C · Trustworthy RecommendationFull ResearchSala PetrassiWednesday 16:00 – 18:008 talksChair: Shashi Shekhar Jha (Indian Institute of Technology Ropar)
FULLCURE: Circuit-Aware Unlearning for LLM-based Recommendation
Ziheng Chen (Stony Brook University) · Zezhong Fan (Columbia University) · Jiali Cheng (University of Massachusetts Lowell) · Yunzhi Yao (Zhejiang University) · Hadi Amiri (University of Massachusetts Lowell) · Gabriele Tolomei (Sapienza University of Rome) · Xiangguo Sun (Southeast University) · Yang Zhang (National University of Singapore)
Abstract
Recent advances in large language models (LLMs) have opened new opportunities for recommender systems by enabling rich semantic understanding and reasoning about user interests and item attributes. However, as privacy regulations tighten, incorporating user data into LLM-based recommendation (LLMRec) introduces significant privacy risks, making unlearning algorithms increasingly crucial for practical deployment. Despite growing interest in LLMRec unlearning, most existing approaches formulate unlearning as a weighted combination of forgetting and retaining objectives while updating model parameters in a uniform manner. Such formulations inevitably induce gradient conflicts between the two objectives, leading to unstable optimization and resulting in either ineffective unlearning or severe degradation of model utility. Moreover, the unlearning procedure remains largely black-box, undermining its transparency and trustworthiness. </par> <par>To tackle these challenges, we propose CURE, a circuit-aware unlearning framework that disentangles model components into functionally distinct subsets and selectively updates them. Here, a circuit refers to a computational subgraph that is causally responsible for task-specific behaviors. Specifically, we extract the core circuits underlying item recommendation and analyze how individual modules within these circuits contribute to the forget and retain objectives. Based on this analysis, these modules are categorized into forget-specific, retain-specific, and task-shared groups, each subject to function-specific update rules to mitigate gradient conflicts during unlearning. Experiments on real-world datasets show that our approach achieves more effective unlearning than existing baselines.
FULLEchoTrace: Diagnosing Recursive Risks in LLM-Powered Recommender Systems
Donguk Park (Ulsan National Institute of Science and Technology (UNIST)) · Dongwon Lee (The Pennsylvania State University) · Yeon-Chang Lee (Ulsan National Institute of Science and Technology (UNIST))
Abstract
Large language models (LLMs) are increasingly integrated into recommender systems as data augmenters, profile generators, and recommendation modules. While these roles can enhance semantic understanding and recommendation quality, they also introduce LLM-specific risks such as bias and hallucination. These risks become more critical in feedback-loop settings, where LLM-generated signals and recommendations recursively shape future training data and recommendation dynamics. In this paper, we propose a role-aware, phase-wise diagnostic framework for analyzing how LLM-induced risks emerge, propagate, and accumulate in LLM-powered recommender systems. Our framework combines controlled feedback-loop simulation with longitudinal phase-wise diagnosis across LLM-generated content, recommendation outputs, feedback-loop dynamics, and ecosystem-level effects. Experiments on widely used benchmarks show that LLM-based components can amplify popularity bias, introduce spurious signals through hallucination, and gradually produce polarized and self-reinforcing exposure patterns over time. The code for EchoTrace is available at https://github.com/DongUk-Park/EchoTrace.
FULLDiffusion-guided Disentanglement with Causal Debiasing for Cross-Domain Recommendation
Jiaming Yang (Nanjing University of Science and Technology) · Shunmei Meng (Nanjing University of Science and Technology) · Qianmu Li (Nanjing University of Science and Technology) · Chentong Yu (Nanjing University of Science and Technology)
Abstract
Cross-Domain Recommendation (CDR) effectively alleviates data sparsity by transferring knowledge from auxiliary domains. To achieve fine-grained transfer, disentangled learning is increasingly adopted to decouple user interaction motivations. However, existing paradigms predominantly rely on shallow linear assumptions that fail to decouple complex non-linear semantic noise and structural biases during knowledge transfer. Furthermore, their static training-stage debiasing exposes the inference phase to structural popularity bias and propagates confounding effects into final rankings. To address these challenges, we propose Diffusion-guided Disentanglement with Causal Debiasing for Cross-Domain Recommendation (DiDC-CDR). Specifically, DiDC-CDR extracts robust single-domain priors from global and niche subgraphs to explicitly capture long-tail interests. Conditioned on these priors, a diffusion module iteratively purifies cross-domain shared item attributes, which subsequently guide a geometric orthogonal constraint to rigorously isolate intrinsic interests from conformity. Finally, causal counterfactual intervention is executed to eliminate popularity-induced spurious correlations during inference. Extensive experiments across six diverse real-world dual-target CDR scenarios demonstrate that DiDC-CDR significantly outperforms state-of-the-art baselines. Notably, in the Elec & Cloth task characterized by a substantial domain gap, our method achieves improvements of 14.32% and 16.33% in HR@10 and NDCG@10 for the target Cloth domain, respectively, thereby providing a novel generative and causal paradigm for robust knowledge transfer.
FULLPOPCORN: Popularity-decoupled Interest Matching for Personalized News Recommendation
Seongeun Ryu (Hanyang University) · Jaesung Hwang (Hanyang University) · Masoud Rehyani Hamedani (Hanyang University) · Sang-Wook Kim (Hanyang University)
Abstract
To alleviate the information overload problem on online news platforms, personalized news recommendation aims to provide news articles aligned with users' interests. Most conventional methods suffer from popularity bias. To mitigate this, popularity-aware methods regard popularity-driven clicks as bias. Although these methods show higher accuracy, they still face three challenges: (C1) discriminating click types on popular news, (C2) topic-unaware popularity modeling, and (C3) dealing with interest signal attenuation. To jointly address these challenges, we propose POPCORN, a novel model-agnostic framework for POPularity-deCOupled inteRest matching in personalized News recommendation, with three key strategies: (1) Popularity-decoupled news modeling to discriminate interest-driven and popularity-driven clicks, (2) Candidate-guided user modeling to amplify a user's interest signal for a candidate news based on its topic, and (3) Popularity-penalized interest matching to suppress popular news not genuinely interesting to the user. Extensive experiments with three real-world datasets and eight state-of-the-art methods demonstrate that the methods augmented with POPCORN consistently outperform their original versions.
FULLBeyond Dense Propagation: A Remove-and-Reintegrate Framework for Debiased Short-Video Recommendation
Aoran Chen (The University of Osaka) · Guanyu Cao (The University of Osaka) · Shengzhe Jiao (The University of Osaka) · Zhi Li (The University of Osaka) · Yihong Zhang (The University of Osaka) · Takahiro Hara (The University of Osaka)
Abstract
Graph neural network based recommender systems have achieved strong performance by propagating collaborative signals over user-item interaction graphs. However, in short-video recommendation platforms, the near-zero interaction cost produces substantially denser interaction graphs and amplifies popularity bias, where some high-degree nodes become connected to semantically heterogeneous neighborhoods and behave as incoherent hubs. These nodes propagate conflicting signals during message passing, degrading graph-based representation learning and recommendation performance. Existing methods reduce popularity bias by adjusting representations during or after graph propagation. However, in dense short-video graphs with high-degree nodes, conflicting signals can be repeatedly aggregated and amplified, making such adjustments less effective. Motivated by this observation, we propose a remove-and-reintegrate framework for short-video recommendation. To reduce popularity bias, we remove incoherent hubs and construct a purified interaction graph by analyzing the structure in an SVD-derived latent space. This is because SVD captures global interaction patterns and, thus, can identify such incoherent hubs. After that, we further design a lightweight reintegration module that aligns the removed nodes back into the recommendation space through ranking-aware optimization, allowing their representations to be preserved without reintroducing noisy propagation. Experiments on three public short-video recommendation datasets demonstrate that the proposed framework consistently improves multiple graph-based recommendation backbones and achieves superior performance on both recommendation accuracy and popularity-aware evaluation metrics.

Qinwen Ran (Sichuan University) · Guanmeng Xian (Sichuan University) · Ning Yang (Sichuan University) · Philip S Yu (University of Illinois at Chicago)
Abstract
Graph Contrastive Learning (GCL) enhances recommendation via embedding uniformity, yet this very property introduces a critical vulnerability exploitable by poisoning attacks. Existing defenses overlook this geometric weakness. In this paper, we propose GCL-Detox, a defense framework that mitigates such attacks by systematically regulating embedding uniformity. We provide a rigorous theoretical analysis showing that the proposed training dynamics guarantee a monotonic increase in embedding non-uniformity, establish strict superiority over conventional joint training, and yield an explicit robustness bound against poisoning attacks. Extensive experiments on three real-world datasets confirm that GCL-Detox significantly enhances robustness against state-of-the-art attacks while maintaining competitive accuracy, validating both our theoretical and empirical claims.

Yunfan Wu (Institute of Computing Technology, Chinese Academy of Sciences) · Qi Cao (Institute of Computing Technology, Chinese Academy of Sciences) · Kaike Zhang (Institute of Computing Technology, Chinese Academy of Sciences) · Fei Sun (Institute of Computing Technology, Chinese Academy of Sciences) · Huawei Shen (Institute of Computing Technology, Chinese Academy of Sciences)
Abstract
Recommender systems are essential tools for managing information overload. However, their vulnerability to data poisoning attacks presents substantial security concerns, where attackers can inject fake users to manipulate recommendations. Existing attacks, nevertheless, face two primary challenges, failing to fully reveal the vulnerabilities of recommender systems: First, representing fake users as a large constrained binary interaction matrix is hard to optimize, due to its high dimensionality and combinatorial nature. Second, modeling the poisoning effects of fake users across all training steps of the victim recommender is intractable. To address these two challenges, we propose FEO (Fake Embedding Optimization with Forward-looking), a novel poisoning attack with fake embedding optimization and single-step forward-looking. Moreover, we focus on the critical training step when fake users form positive pairs with target items, to examine the poisoning effects of fake users in manipulating target item embeddings, instead of modeling the entire training process. Extensive experiments across three real-world datasets, five victim models, and five scenarios demonstrate FEO's superior attack performance.
FULLEBD: Engagement-aware Bidirectional Debiasing with User Micro-Behaviors in E-commerce Recommendations
Weiqiu Wang (Taobao & Tmall Group of Alibaba) · Runfeng Zhang (Taobao & Tmall Group of Alibaba) · Yifei Liu (University of Chinese Academy of Sciences) · Anqi Zhu (Taobao & Tmall Group of Alibaba) · Jie Fang (Taobao & Tmall Group of Alibaba) · Mingming Pan (Taobao & Tmall Group of Alibaba) · Haihong Jiang (Taobao & Tmall Group of Alibaba) · Wen Xu (Taobao & Tmall Group of Alibaba) · Yipeng Yu (Taobao & Tmall Group of Alibaba) · Jiahao Yu (Taobao & Tmall Group of Alibaba) · Yijiao Wang (Taobao & Tmall Group of Alibaba) · Yeqiu Yang (Taobao & Tmall Group of Alibaba) · Fei Sun (State Key Laboratory of AI Safety, Institute of Computing Technology, CAS) · Jian Wu (Taobao & Tmall Group of Alibaba.) · Yuning Jiang (Taobao & Tmall Group of Alibaba) · Xu Liu (Taobao & Tmall Group of Alibaba) · Chengxiao Feng (Taobao & Tmall Group of Alibaba) · Bo Zheng (Taobao & Tmall Group of Alibaba)

Click-through Rate (CTR) prediction and Conversion Rate (CVR) prediction, as core tasks in modern e-commerce recommender systems, are conventionally formulated as binary classification tasks using click/purchase labels. However, this approach suffers from Intention-Action Divergence (IAD) bias, where users' explicit actions (e.g., click/purchase) misalign with their implicit interest levels inferred from fine-grained interactions (e.g., dwell time, swipe velocity). In this paper, we focus on mitigating the IAD bias by leveraging users' implicit intentions. Specifically, we first mine more than one hundred kinds of user-device interactions in their decision-making process, termed Micro-Behaviors (MBs). Instead of constructing resource-consuming sequential features, we compress MBs into a lightweight sample-level engagement score that scalably quantifies users' intentions for billions of samples. Second, considering the inaccessibility of MBs in online serving, we propose a Pointwise-and-Pairwise Engagement Debiasing (P2ED) approach to mitigate the IAD bias in the CVR task, which utilizes the predefined engagement scores only in model training process. Finally, we extend the P2ED method to the CTR task with a novel Engagement-aware Bidirectional Debiasing (EBD) framework to address the limitation of missing engagement scores in non-click samples. Our method improves CVR and CTR performance, delivering +2.2‰/+1.4‰ AUC gains offline and driving 4.27% GMV growth and 1.38% IPV lift in online A/B tests.
