APPLIEDPaper Espresso: From Paper Overload to Research Insight
Mingzhe Du (Nanyang Technological University) · Anh Tuan Luu (Nanyang Technological University) · Dong Huang (National University of Singapore) · See-Kiong Ng (National University of Singapore)
Abstract
The accelerating pace of scientific publishing makes it increasingly difficult for researchers to stay current. We present Paper Espresso, an open-source platform that automatically discovers, summarizes, and analyzes trending arXiv papers. The system uses large language models (LLMs) to generate structured summaries with topical labels and keywords, and provides multi-granularity trend analysis at daily, monthly, and lifecycle scales through LLM-driven topic consolidation. Over 36 months of continuous deployment, Paper Espresso has processed 13,388 papers and publicly released all structured metadata, revealing rich dynamics in the AI research landscape: a mid-2025 surge in reinforcement learning for LLM reasoning, non-saturating topic emergence (6,673 unique topics), and a positive correlation between topic novelty and community engagement (2.0× median upvotes for the most novel papers). The live demo and code are available at https://huggingface.co/spaces/Elfsong/Paper_Espresso.
APPLIEDOn the Influence of Hyperparameters in Tree-Based Linear Methods for Extreme Multi-Label Text Classification: Insights for Efficient and Effective Search
Kuan-Ting Chen (National Taiwan University) · Hung-Chih Chiang (National Taiwan University) · Chih-Jen Lin (National Taiwan University)
Abstract
Extreme multi-label text classification (XMTC) aims to assign each document the most relevant labels from a large label set. Tree-based linear methods based on bag-of-words features have proven to be strong baselines for XMTC in practice. These methods construct a tree structure over the label space to enable fast training and prediction. However, to search for the best model, the large hyperparameter search space makes the process difficult and time-consuming. This study innovatively analyzes the hyperparameters of tree-based linear methods. Based on our findings, we suggest an efficient and effective guideline. Experiments show that our proposed guideline leads to consistent improvements across datasets, thereby strengthening tree-based linear methods as a stronger XMTC baseline. Our proposed setting has been integrated into a multi-label library to facilitate practical usage.
APPLIEDCorrecting to Predict: Pseudo-Value Correction for Multimodal Attribute Value Extraction
Junhao Zhang (Alibaba International Digital Commerce Group) · Feiran Hu (Alibaba International Digital Commerce Group) · Xiao Hu (Alibaba International Digital Commerce Group) · Baoliang Cui (Alibaba International Digital Commerce Group) · Xiaoyi Zeng (Alibaba International Digital Commerce Group)
Abstract
Product attribute value extraction (AVE) is a fundamental task in e-commerce, aiming to identify specific values of predefined attributes from multimodal product profiles such as text and images. While multimodal large language models (MLLMs) have shown promise for AVE, they face challenges in extracting implicit attributes that require joint reasoning over visual and textual cues, often confusing semantically similar values. However, existing methods often fail to resolve such ambiguities because the correct value often depends on subtle multimodal cues that are easy to miss or override. To address this challenge, we propose Correcting to Predict (C2P), a framework that treats attribute extraction as a correction process. Given an initial pseudo-value such as a retrieved candidate or placeholder, the model learns to correct it using multimodal evidence. During training, diverse pseudo-values help the model learn evidence-based correction behavior, and a self-consistency refinement stage further reduces sensitivity to pseudo-value perturbations. At inference, a fixed placeholder triggers the learned correction behavior, enabling efficient single-pass prediction without online retrieval or iterative refinement. We evaluate C2P on a public benchmark and a large-scale industrial dataset. Offline results show that C2P outperforms strong baselines, with notable gains on ambiguous attributes. Online A/B tests on AliExpress further show consistent improvements in seller adoption, attribute completeness, and user engagement, validating C2P’s effectiveness and efficiency in real-world deployment.
APPLIEDSelf-Evolving Ontology via Cumulative Definition Enrichment for Entity Canonicalization
Seungtaek Oh (Korea Electronics Technology Institute) · Ilhwan Kim (Korea Electronics Technology Institute) · Jaewon Moon (Korea Electronics Technology Institute)
Abstract
Ontology grounding pipelines rely on expert-curated vocabularies, but citizens describe the same facilities in their own words. The Korean Safety e-Report platform, which routes over one million citizen complaints annually to responsible agencies, suffers from exactly this problem: its keyword-matching pipeline fails to recognize many citizen expressions, causing misrouted reports and delayed field response. We present Cumulative Definition Enrichment (CDE), which continually discovers synonym expressions from incoming complaints and incorporates them into entity definitions, producing embeddings that improve as the ontology absorbs real usage. Experts design the ontology structure, while CDE learns the vocabulary from the complaint stream. We define two evaluation metrics: Direct Link Rate (DLR), the fraction of complaints resolved through automatic ontology grounding, and Qualified DLR (Q-DLR), which combines DLR with synonym mapping accuracy. DLR alone can be misleading because adding incorrect synonyms still increases coverage; Q-DLR captures whether the added synonyms are actually correct. On 100K real complaints across two ontology versions and two initialization settings, CDE achieves the highest Q-DLR in every condition. Scalability experiments on 600K complaints confirm consistent performance. All processing runs on-premise with limited GPU resources under strict data sensitivity constraints, and the system is planned for government integration starting in 2027.
APPLIEDMicro vs. Macro Averaging for Link Prediction Evaluation in Knowledge Graphs
Lydia Klecan (Rochester Institute of Technology) · Carlos R. Rivero (Rochester Institute of Technology)
Abstract
Link prediction aims to infer missing (subject, predicate, object) triples in a knowledge graph. To evaluate link prediction, each test triple is transformed into two queries: (subject, predicate, ?) and (?, predicate, object), and the rank of the corresponding correct, singleton answer is recorded. However, current empirical studies largely ignore the fact that multiple test triples may share the same (subject, predicate) or (predicate, object) pairs, resulting in queries with multiple correct answers. These settings naturally correspond to micro and macro averaging in traditional machine learning and information retrieval. Despite its importance, the macro setting has received very little attention. Prior work is limited to a single study over two benchmarking datasets, FB15K-237 and WN18RR, using a limited set of ranking metrics. Other metrics specifically designed to capture multi-answer retrieval behavior, such as Bpref and RBP, have not yet been analyzed in the macro setting. In this paper, we present an empirical study of micro and macro averaging for link prediction evaluation in knowledge graphs. We analyze nine benchmarking datasets to characterize query imbalance and the distribution of correct answers per query. We further evaluate ten pre-trained link prediction models for each dataset under both micro and macro averaging using several metrics, including Bpref and RBP. Our results show that macro averaging tends to yield higher effectiveness scores than micro averaging, consistent with previous observations on FB15K-237. Non-singleton queries, those with multiple answers, exhibit distinct ranking behavior, revealing differences in how models find correct answers beyond the first one. We conclude that macro averaging and non-singleton queries deserve more attention in link prediction evaluation.
APPLIEDPre-retrieval Query Clustering for Adaptive Top-k Document Retrieval in RAG Systems
Ye Xia (Portland State University) · Emre Yamangil (EvenUp) · Haixun Wang (EvenUp)
Abstract
RAG systems commonly retrieve a fixed number of documents (top-k) to ground generation, but this static approach is brittle: simple queries suffer over-retrieval (adding noise and cost) while complex queries are under-retrieved, causing recall failures that cascade into incorrect answers. Motivated by the question of how many documents must be retrieved to answer an arbitrary query reliably, we propose a practical, general framework for query-adaptive retrieval depth. Offline, we estimate per-query retrieval difficulty by measuring NDCG under the default retriever and deriving a query-specific “saturation” point k* from the NDCG–k curve. Because computing these signals online is expensive, we cluster a large set of queries in embedding space and summarize each cluster with a recommended retrieval depth that targets high coverage (e.g., ~95%) using a mean-plus-variance rule. At runtime, the system assigns an incoming query to a cluster and selects the corresponding top-k in constant time. Compared with post-retrieval confidence methods that rely on clustering retrieved documents, our approach is pre-retrieval and query-centric, making it robust in heterogeneous, case-like corpora and applicable across domains such as legal, healthcare, finance, and enterprise search. Finally, this framework has been tested in full-traffic queries that improved F1 by over 36% while reducing token usage by 14% on low-complexity clusters without accuracy loss.
APPLIEDGraphMind: From Operational Traces to Self-Evolving Workflow Automation
Yiwen Zhu (Microsoft) · Joyce Cahoon (Microsoft) · Anna Pavlenko (Microsoft) · Qiushi Bai (Microsoft) · Nima Shahbazi (University of Illinois Chicago) · Divya Vermareddy (Microsoft) · Meina Wang (Microsoft) · Mathieu Demarne (Microsoft) · Swati Bararia (Microsoft) · Wenjing Wang (Microsoft) · Hemkesh Vijaya Kumar (Microsoft) · Hannah Lerner (Microsoft) · Katherine Lin (Microsoft) · Steve Toscano (Microsoft) · Miso Cilimdzic (Microsoft) · Subru Krishnan (Microsoft)
Abstract
Complex operational workflows are central to system operations, yet remain difficult to automate due to heavy human input and limited adaptability. We present GraphMind, a system that constructs, executes, and evolves action-centric workflow graphs with minimal human effort. The system operates in three phases. First, a *scalable offline pipeline* extracts structured workflow graphs from human resolution traces, capturing problems, actions, and their causal relationships. Second, an *online multi-agent traversal* engine navigates the graph to dynamically construct and execute workflows, combining graph-guided retrieval with LLM-driven reasoning. Third, *Adaptive Traversal Reinforcement* (ATR) reinforces successful traversal paths, enabling execution-informed graph adaptation. GraphMind has been deployed across four cloud database services for incident investigation. Evaluated on 93 held-out incidents and validated via blind expert review, the system outperforms an Agentic Summary-RAG baseline in mitigation reach, hallucination rate, and diagnostic throughput while requiring 8x less retrieval context. The ATR layer reduces hallucination rate by 26%, demonstrating that workflow graphs can learn from execution feedback. A 12-week field study confirms practical value: 97% of scored conversations yield actionable results within interactive latency.
RESOURCEQFR-RAG: A Multi-Level Evaluation Resource for Grounded RAG over Technical-Medical Documentation
Emma Bakker (University of Amsterdam) · Simon Lupart (University of Amsterdam) · Balazs Borsos (Medis Medical Imaging) · Dorottya Papp (Medis Medical Imaging)
Abstract
Technical-medical documentation poses a challenging setting for grounded retrieval-augmented generation (RAG): valid answers often depend on exact thresholds, workflow constraints and combinations of documented conditions. However, existing RAG benchmarks rarely provide the fine-grained evidence, completeness, citation, abstention and safety annotations needed to evaluate such behaviour. We introduce QFR-RAG, a multi-level evaluation resource for grounded RAG over Quantitative Flow Ratio (QFR) documentation for cardiology software used in angiography-based assessment of coronary disease. QFR-RAG comprises a 400-question benchmark: 50 technical extraction questions with reference answers and gold evidence, 50 multi-evidence questions annotated with 103 required evidence slots and 278 atomic answer nuggets and 300 paired adversarial questions targeting nonsensical requests, false premises and unsafe relaxation of documented constraints. Its layered evaluation protocol separates retrieval sufficiency, exact correctness, nugget-level completeness, citation grounding, abstention and safety-preserving refusal or correction, revealing empirically distinct failure modes across retrieval and generation. As a baseline validation, we benchmark retrieval pipelines and general-purpose and medically specialised language models of different sizes, showing that strong performance on exact technical extraction does not imply complete multi-evidence answering. QFR-RAG provides a deeply annotated framework for evaluating grounded, complete and safety-aware RAG in controlled technical-medical software documentation and illustrates an annotation design that can be adapted to similar parameter-dense domains.
RESOURCEReCaRe: A Bilingual Benchmark for Revision Candidate Retrieval in Evolving Legal Corpora
Takumi Ito (University of Tsukuba) · Yuma Kurokawa (University of Tsukuba) · Makoto P. Kato (University of Tsukuba) · Sumio Fujita (LY Corporation)
Abstract
Document corpora in organizational and public settings evolve as statutes, policies, specifications, and knowledge bases are revised. Maintaining such corpora requires identifying documents that should be inspected after a change, yet this candidate-identification step has not been directly addressed by existing benchmarks. We formalize this problem as Revision Candidate Retrieval (RCR): retrieving documents for expert inspection and possible revision. RCR consists of two complementary tasks: Rat2Rev, which retrieves articles given an amendment rationale, and Rev2Rev, which retrieves co-revised articles given an observed revision. To study RCR, we introduce ReCaRe, a bilingual benchmark built from EU and Japanese legislative amendments, containing 91,361 EU articles and 90,170 Japanese articles. Our analysis shows low lexical overlap, length asymmetry, and implicit cross-article revision relationships. Experiments show that BM25 remains a strong first-stage baseline, long-context dense retrievers improve recall, zero-shot listwise LLM reranking improves Rat2Rev rankings, and document expansion and dense-retriever domain adaptation provide complementary first-stage gains.
RESOURCELexskill: A Systematic Chinese Legal Skill Framework with High-Quality Annotations and an Execution Harness
Hu YiRan (University of Waterloo) · Rongxin Cheng (Tsinghua University) · Haitao Li (Tsinghua university) · Wenbo Lv (Tsinghua University) · Xin Meng (Peking University) · Qingjing Chen (University of Bologna) · Huanghai Liu (Tsinghua University) · Jing Xu (Tsinghua University) · Fuheng Jiang (Tsinghua University) · Xuanhang Wu (Tsinghua University) · Xinyu Wang (Tsinghua University) · Chong Wang (Tsinghua University) · Weihang Su (Tsinghua University) · Zibing Que (Renmin University) · Yun Liu (Tsinghua University) · Weixing Shen (Tsinghua University) · Qingyao Ai (Tsinghua University) · Yiqun Liu (Tsinghua University) · Charles Clarke (University of Waterloo)
Abstract
Agents in knowledge-intensive domains require not only knowledge retrieval, but also the skills to effectively use retrieved knowledge. Since domain knowledge is often highly complex, agents must possess strong reasoning capabilities in order to perform tasks effectively. In the legal domain, different legal systems exhibit substantial differences, and the reasoning logic for applying legal knowledge varies significantly across systems. Meanwhile, existing skill collections lack a systematic skill framework grounded in domain knowledge, limiting their scalability and extensibility. To address these challenges, we present LexSkill, a reasoning-oriented legal skill library for the Chinese legal system. Within this framework, legal experts construct 36 atomic skills, further organized into 180 sub-atomic skills and 2 compound skills. Since legal problem solving also requires grounded access to legal resources and coordinated reasoning across multiple steps, we further introduce Chinese-Law-Harness, which augments the skill library with MCP modules built over a case repository and a statutory repository, and incorporates a multi-agent system for skill orchestration and execution. Evaluations on existing legal AI benchmarks show that leveraging the skill library through the proposed harness significantly outperforms direct problem solving without structured support, verifying the effectiveness of our skills and harness.
RESOURCEMOSAIC: Unveiling the Moral, Social and Individual Dimensions of Large Language Models
Erica Coppolillo (ICAR-CNR) · Emilio Ferrara (University of Southern California)
Abstract
Large Language Models (LLMs) are increasingly deployed in sensitive applications including psychological support, healthcare, and high-stakes decision-making. Existing evaluation benchmarks rely almost exclusively on Moral Foundation Theory (MFT), neglecting other key dimensions such as social values, personality traits, and individual characteristics that shape human ethical reasoning. We introduce MOSAIC, the first large-scale benchmark designed to jointly assess the moral, social, and individual characteristics of LLMs. MOSAIC comprises nine validated questionnaires drawn from moral philosophy, psychology, and social theory, alongside four platform-based games designed to probe morally ambiguous scenarios, totaling over 600 curated items. We validate the benchmark across six models from different families, providing empirical evidence that MFT alone is insufficient for comprehensive ethical evaluation of LLMs. All resources are publicly available.
RESOURCERV-FLS: A Resource for Retrospective Verification of Forward-Looking Statements
Zhi-Hong Lin (Chaoyang University of Technology) · Shih-Hung Wu (Chaoyang University of Technology) · Chung-Chi Chen (National Institute of Informatics)
Abstract
Forward-looking statements (FLSs) influence decisions before their outcomes are known, yet they are rarely revisited systematically after relevant evidence becomes available. Retrospective verification of FLSs differs from conventional fact verification because supporting or contradicting evidence may emerge gradually, remain inaccessible, or be insufficient for a responsible judgment. We introduce RV-FLS, a resource for retrospective verification of scenario-level FLSs derived from financial analyst reports. RV-FLS contains 651 human-reviewed instances. Each instance links an original statement and publication date to post-publication evidence collected within a five-year verification window, an evidence-grounded rationale, an agent-generated judgment, a human review decision, and a final label. We construct the resource through an agent-first workflow in which a retrieval-augmented language model assembles evidence packages and proposes preliminary judgments for human adjudication. As standalone label predictors, a closed-book model and a retrieval-augmented agent achieve accuracies of 26.5% and 42.5%, respectively. Under agent-first construction, however, reviewers accept 74.5% of the generated judgments, while average verification time decreases from 12.89 to 3.34 minutes per scenario. RV-FLS supports research on evidence retrieval, evidence-conditioned classification, and end-to-end retrospective verification, while providing an auditable foundation for making future-oriented claims more transparent and accountable.
RESOURCESemiHS-Bench: A Semiconductor Benchmark for HS6 Classification from Sparse ERP-Style Text
Swapnil Bembde (Hitachi America, Ltd.) · Sai Rama Raju Penmatsa (Hitachi America, Ltd.)
Abstract
Large language models (LLMs) are increasingly used for product classification in trade compliance and supply-chain analytics. Their potential for Harmonized System (HS) classification is substantial, especially for automating six-digit code assignment over industrial records. One persistent challenge is input sparsity: enterprise systems often expose terse descriptions, abbreviated bill-of-material entries, or bare part numbers, forcing models to recover product identity before classification. Existing HS datasets rely on richer customs rulings, shipment descriptions, or synthetic product text, and cannot isolate this operational regime. To this end, we propose SemiHS-Bench, a benchmark for HS6 classification of semiconductor supply-chain products from real ERP-style text. Specifically, each product is represented through controlled input tiers derived from the same observation, with labels grounded in a held-out multilingual corpus of customs rulings. We evaluate LLM baselines on constrained and open classification, showing substantial degradation under sparse inputs. The benchmark, ruling corpus, and evaluation tools are available online at https://github.com/cti-iel/SemiHS-Bench.
RESOURCEGESIS KG: Enhancing Discovery, Interoperability and Reusability in Social Science Research through Knowledge Graphs
Debanjali Biswas (Heinrich Heine University) · Benjamin Zapilko (GESIS - Leibniz Institute for the Social Sciences, Cologne) · Yudong Zhang (GESIS - Leibniz Institute for the Social Sciences, Cologne) · Ran Yu (GESIS - Leibniz Institute for the Social Sciences, Cologne) · Endri Gupta (GESIS - Leibniz Institute for the Social Sciences, Cologne) · Peter Mutschke (GESIS - Leibniz Institute for the Social Sciences, Cologne) · Stefan Dietze (GESIS - Leibniz Institute for the Social Sciences, Cologne)
Abstract
Effective discovery and reuse of scholarly resources require machine-readable, semantically linked metadata - yet no knowledge graph exists that integrates the full range of social science scholarly resources. We present the GESIS Knowledge Graph (GESIS KG) a large-scale domain-specific knowledge graph interlinking and transforming social science metadata into an AI-ready knowledge graph to improve interoperability and automated discovery across global research ecosystems. Built on the GESIS KG Ontology, extending established vocabularies, the graph captures not only scholarly metadata but also the provenance of semantic link between these resources. GESIS KG supports semantic search, provenance-aware citation tracking, and metadata reuse through a SPARQL endpoint, OAI-PMH API, and bulk download. The resource is publicly available under CC BY 4.0 license at https://doi.org/10.7802/2969.
6E · Time Series Forecasting IIFull ResearchAuditoriumArteWednesday 16:00 – 18:008 talksChair: Seungeon Lee (Max Planck Institute for Software Systems)
FULLGraph Neural Delay Differential Equations for Continuous Epidemic Forecasting
Mingda Xu (Northwestern Polytechnical University) · Zhanwei Du (Southern University of Science and Technology) · Chao Gao (Northwestern Polytechnical University)
Abstract
Reliable epidemic forecasting is essential for early warning and proactive public health decision-making. Existing spatio-temporal forecasting methods often model regional interactions on fixed discrete grids and rely on instantaneous or uniformly delayed transmission assumptions, limiting their ability to capture asynchronous epidemic spread and irregular surveillance records. To address these limitations, we propose EpiDDE, a continuous-time delay-aware framework based on graph neural delay differential equations for epidemic forecasting. EpiDDE first estimates latent epidemic delay priors from surveillance sequences, including both within-region temporal delays and cross-region propagation delays. It then constructs a Delay-Aware Transmission Graph (DATG) by combining sequence-derived delay priors with learnable regional representations, enabling data-driven modeling of directed and heterogeneous delayed dependencies. Conditioned on the learned DATG, EpiDDE evolves regional epidemic states through a graph-coupled neural DDE driven by delayed self-region and cross-region messages. Extensive experiments on four real-world epidemic datasets show that EpiDDE achieves competitive epidemic forecasting performance across multiple prediction horizons. Further analyses demonstrate the effectiveness of delay estimation, DATG learning, and DDE-based continuous evolution, particularly for long-horizon forecasting and irregular observations.
FULLZoomLens Stock Forecasting: Adaptive Multi-Scale Modeling for Market-Aware Investment
Junting Zhang (School of Computer Science and Engineering, Northeastern University) · Yue Kou (School of Computer Science and Engineering, Northeastern University) · Derong Shen (School of Computer Science and Engineering, Northeastern University) · Dong Li (School of Information, Liaoning University) · Tiezheng Nie (School of Computer Science and Engineering, Northeastern University)
Abstract
Modern stock markets demand a sophisticated capability to simultaneously focus on fine-grained local volatility and perceive broader global trends. However, existing methods often remain limited by rigid temporal architectures and a neglect of dynamic cross-asset dependencies. To address these challenges, we propose an Adaptive Multi-scale signal Selection and Fusion Model (AMSFM). Functioning as an intelligent ZoomLens, AMSFM incorporates an adaptive temporal scale selector that dynamically aligns modeling horizons with real-time market regimes, effectively capturing both microscopic fluctuations and macroscopic contexts. Furthermore, we propose an interpretable attribution and interaction mechanism to decompose forecasts into transparent feature contributions. To capture broader market influences, our model employs a market-aware forecasting strategy that integrates global context to perceive panoramic spillover effects without relying on rigid prior knowledge. Extensive experiments on three real-world datasets demonstrate that AMSFM significantly outperforms state-of-the-art benchmarks. The source code is available at: https://github.com/yizhibeijibei/AMSFM.
FULLRetrieve the Right Signal: Decomposition-Guided Retrieval-Augmented Forecasting for Financial Markets
Yongdam Kim (Sogang University) · Hyeonji Park (Sogang University) · Dongwoo Lee (Sogang University) · Jeongseon Cho (Sogang University) · Yein Lee (Sogang University) · Jihoon Yang (Sogang University) · Sungwon Jung (Sogang University)
Abstract
Financial time-series forecasting is important for portfolio construction, risk management, and investment strategy design, but financial markets are highly nonstationary and often lack stable periodicity. Retrieval-augmented forecasting is attractive in this setting because similar market conditions can lead to similar historical market responses. However, when retrieval is performed over the raw signal, similarity can be dominated by level or trend rather than by detrended temporal patterns that are more relevant to future market reactions. We propose a decomposition-guided retrieval framework for financial time-series forecasting. It decomposes each input into a trend component and a detrended component using a strictly causal moving average, and performs retrieval in the detrended space. The retrieved detrended futures are used both as a direct retrieval-based forecasting component and as Retrieval-as-Context (RAC) tokens that provide additional context to the forecasting backbone. This design separates trend modeling from retrieval over detrended temporal patterns, reducing misleading raw-signal matches while preserving historical market responses that are relevant to the current query. It also allows retrieved information to influence representation learning, rather than being used only through output-level fusion. Across eight real-world financial datasets and two TFB financial-market benchmarks, the framework outperforms retrieval-augmented, decomposition-based, attention-based, patch-based, clustering-based, and classical statistical baselines. On the eight real-world datasets, the framework ranks first in 23 out of 48 settings under both MSE and MAE; on the TFB benchmarks, it ranks first in 7 out of 8 MSE configurations.
FULLAnomaly-Regularized Foundation Models for Robust Electricity Market Forecasting
Kaveh Karimadini (Macquarie University) · Xuyun Zhang (Macquarie University) · Amin Beheshti (Macquarie University)
Abstract
In recent cases of multivariate time series forecasting, models are facing challenges that are due to complex interactions between multiple variables, rapid regime shifts and extreme events that cause problems, especially in the domain of electricity markets like the Australian National Electricity Market (NEM). In our research, we tried to improve the existing singular value decomposition autoencoder (SVD-AE) by introducing a spectral aspect to the anomaly scoring and coming up with a regularisation framework aimed at increasing the accuracy of the time series foundation model (TSFM). We used 5-minute resolution NEM data to evaluate our framework; specifically, the anomaly detection part was done on multiple variables influencing the Regional Reference Price (RRP), such as demand, generation, interconnector, temporal and weather, but the zero-shot forecasting and fine-tuning of the forecasting part were done solely on raw and regularised RRP against the same original ground truth. The forecasting outputs from our Hybrid-Scored SVD-AE (HS-SVD-AE) are then compared to the existing baseline SVD-AE. The experiments showed that in the fine-tuned scenario of TSFM, our proposed framework outperforms the existing SVD-AE regularisation by a good margin, but in the zero-shot scenario, SVD-AE performs better by a slight difference. Our findings in this research show that explicitly scored spectral information structure can complement multivariate anomaly detection, which produces more robust foundation model forecasting.
FULLA Deep Learning Framework for Quantile Demand Forecasting in E-commerce with Doubly Censored Data
Ziwen Ye (Meituan) · Jiawen Wei (Meituan) · Teng Song (Meituan) · Chen Chen (Meituan) · Guangrui Ma (Meituan)
Abstract
In recent years, a growing number of online retail companies have embraced deep learning models for demand forecasting, leveraging their scalability in processing large-scale datasets. Accurate demand forecasts enable improved planning and allow operational flexibility to adjust sales accordingly. Moreover, quantile estimation has gained widespread application as it offers valuable uncertainty quantification, thereby enhancing the robustness of decision-making processes. However, limited research has addressed the effective quantification of uncertainty when target labels are ambiguous. In retail, actual sales can be capped by stock and boosted by temporary promotions, whereas the target is underlying demand. Such scenarios are characterized by double censoring and no deep-learning pipeline yet exists for such data. In this paper, we introduce a straightforward framework for learning quantiles from doubly-censored observations and propose a tailored evaluation metric. Our approach is supported by theoretical guarantees, and we empirically demonstrate that our metric correlates well with the oracle calibration measure. Experimental results show that our estimator surpasses existing baselines. Finally, inventory simulations and real-world applications confirm the practical utility of our method in retail operations.
FULLEarthOracle: A Self-Correcting World Model with Observational Feedback for Long-Horizon Earth Forecasting
Tanda Li (Institute of Computing Technology, Chinese Academy of Sciences) · Luxinming Yin (Elite Prep Academy) · Yuqi Li (Institute of Computing Technology, Chinese Academy of Sciences) · Huiran Duan (The City University of New York) · Bo Zhao (Yale University) · Chuanguang Yang (Institute of Computing Technology, Chinese Academy of Sciences)
Abstract
While deep learning models have achieved unprecedented success in short-to-medium-range weather forecasting, they universally suffer from error accumulation, spectral decay, and climate drift during long-horizon autoregressive rollouts. We argue that this stems from a fundamental paradigm flaw: treating forecasting as an open-loop “one-shot extrapolation” rather than the closed-loop “predict-observe-assimilate” cycle inherent in operational numerical systems. To address this, we propose EarthOracle, a self-correcting Earth World Model that explicitly embeds sparse observations into its inference loop. At its core lies a Differentiable Data Assimilation (Diff-DA) module, which dynamically injects heterogeneous and sparse observations (e.g., satellite radiances, buoy data, radiosondes) directly into the latent state using learnable uncertainty weights. Coupled with a novel self-correction training objective based on perturbation consistency, EarthOracle actively digests new information to suppress error amplification over long trajectories. Furthermore, we introduce a Cross-Scale Memory mechanism that disentangles fast-evolving weather signals from slow-varying ocean-atmosphere coupled modes in the latent space, ensuring that observation feedbacks modulate the system at physically appropriate timescales. Extensive experiments on ERA5 (1979–2024) and multi-source sparse observations demonstrate that EarthOracle significantly outperforms pure autoregressive baselines in Subseasonal-to-Decadal (S2D) forecasting. It maintains stable energy spectra and climatology over long rollouts, and matches the predictive skill of dynamical S2D models on critical teleconnection indices (e.g., ENSO, MJO) at less than 0.1% of their inference cost. By redefining long-term Earth forecasting from open-loop extrapolation to closed-loop assimilation, EarthOracle provides a scalable and robust new paradigm for real-world AI climate prediction.
FULLMemPerceiver: Adaptive Multi-Scale Memory Reveals Biome-Specific Temporal Fingerprints in Carbon Flux Prediction
Gaoshan Bi (The University of Sheffield) · Menghui Zhou (The University of Sheffield) · Xulong Wang (The University of Sheffield) · Zhipeng Yuan (The University of Sheffield) · Qing Xue (Mutus Tech Ltd) · Po Yang (The University of Sheffield)
Abstract
Terrestrial carbon flux prediction is critical for quantifying ecosystem carbon sources and sinks. However, current deep learning models still struggle with cross-ecosystem generalisation across the heterogeneous biomes covered by global eddy-covariance networks. A fundamental reason is that different ecosystems are shaped by past climate over very different timescales: climate may continue to influence ecosystem processes for only weeks in tropical savannas but for months in temperate forests, while existing models apply a single uniform temporal context window to all ecosystems. To address this challenge, we propose MemPerceiver, a multimodal framework that augments the EcoPerceiver backbone with six ecologically motivated memory scales (-180 to -7 days) and a per-scale gating network, allowing the model to learn which of the predefined temporal horizons are most informative for each prediction, without requiring biome-specific lag labels. On the CarbonSense benchmark of 385 eddy-covariance sites across 15 IGBP classes, MemPerceiver achieves state-of-the-art performance on both Net Ecosystem Exchange (NEE) and Gross Primary Production (GPP), with particularly large gains in data-scarce settings: relative to EcoPerceiver, it reduces RMSE by 23.0% on the one-shot WAT class and improves NSE by 24.0% on the zero-shot SNO class. Averaging the learned gate activations within each biome yields an interpretable temporal fingerprint, and within-biome consistency analysis shows that these fingerprints provide a stable, model-derived view of biome-specific ecological memory. The code is available at https://github.com/gaoshan-bi/MemPerceiver.
FULLAquaNord-SE: A Large-Scale Longitudinal Multimodal Benchmark for Swedish Inland Water Quality
Md Moinul Islam (University of Oulu) · Getnet Demil (University of Oulu) · Mourad Oussalah (University of Oulu)
Abstract
Predicting inland water quality reliably requires integrating water quality observations, satellite remote sensing, meteorological reanalysis, and catchment descriptors, yet no benchmark provides these modalities jointly under reproducible evaluation protocols for optically complex, seasonally ice-affected inland waters. We introduce AquaNord-SE, a longitudinal multimodal benchmark of 883,325 samples from 18,743 Swedish lake and river monitoring stations over 2000-2025, integrating 38 water quality parameters from SLU Miljödata MVM with observations from five satellite sensor streams, ERA5-Land and MESAN meteorological reanalysis, 64 HydroATLAS catchment attributes, and 13 derived water quality indices. The dataset is structured as station-aligned multimodal feature sets and spatial-temporal archives, accompanied by a five-tier modality ablation design and three orthogonal generalization splits across spatial, temporal, and latitudinal axes. Benchmarking across tabular, spatial-temporal, and multimodal baselines under split conformal prediction and quantile regression reveals that static catchment attributes alone (R2=0.303 Chlorophyll-a, R2=0.642 Secchi) consistently outperform all non-tabular models, while total phosphorus proves intractable across all families (best R2=0.118). Conformal calibration error increases from 0.062 to 0.225 across the oligotrophic-hypereutrophic gradient, co-locating with the eutrophic regime where atmospheric correction (AC) failure exceeds 65% of optical retrievals. We additionally release a gridded water quality index (WQI) NetCDF at 5 km resolution over 2000-2025, supporting Water Framework Directive (WFD) compliance and long-term trend analysis. The dataset and evaluation protocols are publicly available to support reproducible research in environmental knowledge management and data-driven water quality assessment and monitoring.
6F · Robust Graph Learning & Graph-LLMsFull ResearchStudio 1Wednesday 16:00 – 18:008 talksChair: Zeyd Boukhers (Fraunhofer FIT)
FULLMultilayer Network Backboning
Valerio Siniscalco (University of Milan) · Michele Coscia (IT University of Copenhagen)
Abstract
Data collection comes with some amount of measurement error and network data is not exempt from this issue. Once a network is collected, it is necessary to test whether an edge exists with some degree of statistical certainty. This is a process called “network backboning.” There are a number of approaches to perform network backboning, but the approaches in the literature only work for directed, bipartite networks, and/or hypergraphs. To the best of our knowledge, there is no network backboning approach that takes into account the additional information that comes from multilayer networks. In this paper, we provide the first such approach, by extending the popular noise-corrected backboning approach using a similar Bayesian framework to consider potential layer-layer (anti)correlations. In synthetic experiments, we show that using the additional information that comes from the multiple layers is beneficial to find more accurate network backbones, at a minimal additional time complexity cost. We provide an extensive case study using a network from Wikipedia to show the real world usefulness of extracting multilayer backbones.
FULLLearning to Preserve Structural Backbones for Robust Graph Neural Networks
Hanwen Xu (Nanjing University of Aeronautics and Astronautics) · Feng Hu (Nanjing University of Aeronautics and Astronautics) · Yicong Li (Nanjing University of Aeronautics and Astronautics) · Hao Sui (Nanjing University of Aeronautics and Astronautics)
Abstract
Graph Neural Networks (GNNs) are effective for modeling relational data, yet they remain vulnerable to adversarial structural perturbations. Existing defenses typically treat all edges equally, lacking targeted protection for the structural backbones, and struggle to balance robustness with clean accuracy. To address these issues, we propose PSB-GNN, a robust graph learning framework that learns to preserve structural backbones. Specifically, we leverage an explainer-derived prior to initialize a learnable defense policy, guiding a probabilistic structural denoising process that stochastically masks structural noise while preserving structural backbones. Additionally, we introduce a dual trust defense mechanism with a parallel feature-only pathway to enhance robustness without compromising clean accuracy, an asymmetric distillation framework to stabilize training, and a deterministic pruning strategy to filter adversarial edges during inference. Extensive experiments on three benchmarks show that PSB-GNN significantly outperforms state-of-the-art defenses, generalizes well across explainers, and maintains superior clean accuracy. The code is available at https://github.com/baxiansheng2/PSB-GNN.
FULLGradual Adversarial Graph Transfer: Stabilizing Alignment with Dual Transitional Domains
Xing Wei (Tongji University) · Jiayi Yang (Tongji University) · Chunchun Chen (Tongji University) · Chenrun Wang (Tongji University) · Xin Sun (City University of Macau) · Ming Li (Zhejiang Normal University) · Rui Fan (Tongji University) · Hanli Wang (Tongji University) · Wei Ye (Tongji University)
Abstract
Graph domain adaptation under large source-target shifts is challenging because direct endpoint alignment often causes unstable adversarial optimization, while explicit intermediate-graph generation may introduce topology distortion and semantic artifacts. To address this problem, we propose Gradual Adversarial Graph Transfer (GAGT), which formulates cross-domain graph transfer as constructing a semantically feasible latent transition pathway. GAGT first learns domain-invariant and domain-specific representations through contrastive disentangled representation learning with tolerance-bounded reconstruction, where the reconstruction tolerance regularizes a semantically feasible region rather than forcing exact recovery. Based on this, GAGT synthesizes dual transitional domains as bidirectional bridge states and performs gradual adversarial alignment along the pathway. In this way, a large source-target discrepancy is decomposed into smaller and semantically constrained local discrepancies, yielding smoother adversarial signals and more stable transfer. Extensive experiments on diverse graph domain adaptation benchmarks demonstrate that GAGT outperforms nearly all state-of-the-art methods, especially under large structural and feature distribution shifts. Our code is available at https://github.com/GEEX-Weixing/GAGT-CIKM.
FULLSA-GSL: Simulated Annealing for Graph Structure Learning
Alessandro Sbandi (Sapienza University of Rome) · Federico Siciliano (Sapienza University of Rome) · Fabrizio Silvestri (Sapienza University of Rome)
Abstract
Graph Neural Networks (GNNs) have become a cornerstone for applications involving graph data. However, the performance of GNNs is critically dependent on the underlying graph structure. This presents a fundamental challenge, as a predefined topology may not be optimal for the specific learning task, limiting the model's performance. This limitation is particularly pronounced in heterophilous settings, where the inherent homophily assumption of GNNs contradicts the actual graph structure, causing models that rely on raw topology to fail. Although Graph Structure Learning (GSL) aims to address this issue, most existing methods use continuous relaxations of the graph topology to enable gradient-based optimization. This approach can trap models in local optima and fail to capture the discrete nature of graph data. To address this issue, we introduce a novel GSL algorithm, Simulated Annealing for Graph Structure Learning (SA-GSL), that leverages Simulated Annealing (SA) to optimize the discrete graph structure, effectively adapting the topology to handle heterophily. The SA algorithm operates as a gradient-free refiner proposing new topologies, guided by a multi-objective energy function that uses a lightweight Label Propagation model as a proxy while simultaneously promoting sparsity. An ensemble of candidate structures is generated at each step and combined via majority voting. The final graph is weighted between the original topology and the SA refined ensemble structure. Our experiments reveal that SA-GSL is highly effective, achieving state-of-the-art results on several key node classification benchmarks (1.5% on Cora, 3% on Minesweeper). The code implementation is publicly available on our GitHub repository (https://github.com/ashba93/sa-gsl).
FULLRobust Node Classification via Noise-robust Views and Prototype Relabeling
Hoyoung Yoon (Seoul National University) · Junghun Kim (Seoul National University) · U Kang (Seoul National University)
Abstract
How do we classify nodes accurately on heterophilic graphs when training labels are infected by neighbors' majority classes? In many real-world applications, annotators lack sufficient evidence for each node in isolation and thus rely on its neighborhood context, causing labels to drift toward the neighborhood majority. We call this bias structural label infection, a graph-dependent corruption that makes supervision appear artificially homophilic even though the underlying graph remains heterophilic. This setting is particularly challenging because message passing quickly reinforces infected labels, making corrupted nodes look confident and rendering common loss- or agreement-based denoising methods unreliable. Structural label infection affects both hop selection and label correction. Because corrupted labels are aligned with neighborhood majorities, optimizing hop weights with these labels gives fake-homophilic neighborhoods an artificial advantage. This is especially harmful on heterophilic graphs, where useful propagation is not restricted to immediate neighbors. Moreover, predictions are produced by a model trained on infected labels, so directly copying them passes this infection to the next training round. We propose Recover (Robust nodE Classification under structural label nOise Via multi-score hop routing and prototypE Relabeling), a robust node classification framework that severs the feedback loop between infected supervision and structural propagation. Instead of allowing corrupted labels to dictate neighborhood aggregation, Recover secures robust representations by dynamically routing propagation through proxies based on static features and averaged task confidence. Subsequently, it directly rectifies the corrupted supervision by projecting these stabilized embeddings against reliable class prototypes. Extensive experiments demonstrate that Recover achieves up to 29.41 percentage-point improvement in accuracy under infected-label settings.
FULLLLMTGL: Large Language Models for Robust Text-Attributed Graph Learning under Missing Text and Label Noise

Text-attributed graphs have attracted considerable attention due to their extensive applications in domains such as social networks and citation networks. The code and anonymized datasets are publicly available at: https://github.com/mrjc12/GL-DataLeakage.

FULLCOTA: Confidence-aware Opinion and Trust Assessment

Abstract
Opinion consolidation is a common problem in crowdsourced knowledge collection and data integration, where multiple workers may provide conflicting opinions about the same statements. Accurately aggregating this knowledge is challenging, particularly when workers exhibit varying levels of reliability. Most existing approaches focus on binary or categorical inputs and ignore the confidence that workers assign to their own opinions, despite its potential to improve consolidation precision and robustness. In this paper, we introduce the Confidence-aware Opinion and Trust Assessment (COTA) algorithm, a confidence-aware opinion-consolidation method that aggregates numerical and binary opinions provided by multiple workers. Experimental results show that incorporating workers' self-reported confidence significantly improves consolidation quality. In particular, COTA outperforms state-of-the-art baselines and remains effective even with inconsistent worker accuracy, provided that confidence correlates with opinion reliability. These results highlight the potential of confidence-aware opinion consolidation for aggregating uncertain knowledge in collaborative settings.

Schema matching (SM) is a critical step in data integration pipelines and serves as a foundation for tasks such as Table Search and Entity Matching. However, applying Large Language Models (LLMs) to SM is prohibitively expensive due to the task's inherent quadratic complexity, which hinders scalable and cost-efficient deployment. Column Type Annotation (CTA) is a fundamental task in Semantic Table Interpretation that assigns semantic types to table columns. FULLCavity-Calibrated Prediction Sets

Conformal prediction equips black-box classifiers with finite-sample, distribution-free coverage guarantees, but its standard application to structured outputs over probabilistic graphical models is hampered by two issues: per-node nonconformity scores derived from approximate beliefs are inflated by self-reinforcing local potentials, and a naive Bonferroni correction over N output variables produces prediction sets that grow with the size of the graph. Closed-set hyperspectral image (HSI) classifiers are often deployed in scenes whose land-cover taxonomy is incomplete. In this setting, an unseen crop type, road material, or mixed surface may not look globally alien: it can lie near the known feature manifold and still be assigned to a known class with high confidence. Positive-unlabeled (PU) learning addresses weak-supervision settings where training data contain labeled positives and unlabeled samples, but no labeled negatives. However, aggregate control does not explicitly distinguish the two critical tails of the unlabeled distribution: high-score negative-like samples that drive false positives and weak positive modes that drive false negatives. Many business and clinical decisions depend on the conditional average treatment effect (CATE) of each of several continuous treatments that move together: advertising spend and discount levels driven by the same campaign, or drug doses adjusted in a common protocol. Several estimator families produce CATE at every query point with a confidence interval, including meta-learners, doubly robust learners, Causal Forests and Double Machine Learning (DML); DML in particular gives both in closed form and is widely deployed. Yu Zhang (Alibaba Group) · Zhihan Wang (Alibaba Group) · Guanlin Chen (Alibaba Group) · Min Jiang (Alibaba Group) · Shuai Li (Alibaba Group)
Abstract
Coupon campaigns aim to lift both conversion and revenue, but gross merchandise value (GMV) inherits a deterministic funnel structure from conversion and conditional order value and is typically zero-inflated and heavy-tailed. Shoki Yamao (Recruit Holdings Co., Ltd.) · Ryo Matsui (Recruit Co., Ltd.) · Kazuhide Nakata (Institute of Science Tokyo)
Abstract
Coupon allocation optimization can be formulated as a multiple-choice knapsack problem (MCKP) that maximizes total reward subject to a limited budget, using the expected reward and cost when each coupon is assigned to each customer as coefficients. Since these coefficients are unobservable before assignment, the standard two-stage method (TSM) first estimates them with a prediction model and then solves the MCKP. However, because the prediction model is trained to minimize prediction error (e.g., MSE), improving prediction accuracy does not necessarily improve the quality of the MCKP solution. To bridge this gap, decision-focused learning (DFL) has attracted attention as a framework that trains the prediction model using a loss defined by the quality of the MCKP solution itself. Existing DFL methods for marketing design their losses based on the priority ordering of coupon assignments for each customer, but evaluate each customer's coupon assignment independently, failing to properly account for the shared budget constraint that couples all customers' assignments. In this paper, we propose LEOM-DFL (Lagrangian EOM-based Decision-Focused Learning), a method that directly optimizes the quality of the overall MCKP solution, including inter-customer dependencies arising from the budget constraint. Since rewards and costs of unassigned coupons are unobserved, LEOM-DFL employs an expected outcome metric (EOM) based on doubly robust (DR) estimators to estimate the total reward and total cost for any given assignment from logged data. Solving the Lagrangian relaxation of the MCKP with these estimates yields a budget-dependent trade-off weight, which is incorporated into the loss to capture inter-customer dependencies. Furthermore, the combination of entropy regularization and the implicit function theorem yields a closed-form gradient computation. A001APPLIEDHiSAC: Hierarchical Sparse Activation Compression for Ultra-long Sequence Modeling in Recommendation Systems
Kun Yuan (Taobao & Tmall Group of Alibaba) · Junyu Bi (Taobao & Tmall Group of Alibaba) · Daixuan Cheng (Renmin University) · Changfa Wu (Taobao & Tmall Group of Alibaba) · Shuwen Xiao (Taobao & Tmall Group of Alibaba) · Binbin Cao (Taobao & Tmall Group of Alibaba) · Jian Wu (Taobao & Tmall Group of Alibaba) · Yuning Jiang (Taobao & Tmall Group of Alibaba)
Abstract
We introduce HiSAC (Hierarchical Sparse Activation Compression), a framework that compresses ultra-long user behavior sequences into compact, personalized interest representations for industrial recommendation. Modeling histories with thousands of interactions is essential for capturing dynamic user preferences, yet existing compression methods suffer from two fundamental limitations: they impose a fixed number of global interest centers that ignore per-user granularity, and they rely on hard assignment that introduces quantization error and discards long-tail behaviors. HiSAC addresses both via three tightly integrated components: (1)multimodal tokenization with Residual Quantized VAE that maps items to a hierarchical discrete codebook, (2)a hierarchical voting mechanism that sparsely activates user-specific interest-agents as adaptive preference centers, and (3)a Soft-Routing Attention that aggregates all historical signals in a debiased semantic space, weighting contributions by similarity to minimize quantization error and preserve sparse long-tail preferences. We validate HiSAC on a large-scale industrial dataset (200M users, 30B interactions) and the public Taobao-MM benchmark, where it consistently outperforms both generic compression baselines and state-of-the-art sequence models. Deployed on Taobao's “Guess What You Like” homepage serving hundreds of millions of daily active users, HiSAC delivers a 1.65% CTR uplift, 2.24% CTCVR improvement, and 2.56% increase in orders while reducing end-to-end inference latency by over 40% relative to the deployed compression baseline.
A002FULLConstrained Preference Dynamics: Energy-Based Minimization for Multi-Interest Recommendation
Yuhang Zhang (Peking University)
Abstract
In sequential recommendation, multi-interest models are widely deployed to capture diverse user preferences from behavioral histories. However, existing architectures typically extract multiple representation vectors and fuse them via conventional attention mechanisms. By computing a weighted sum, this paradigm implicitly assumes that distinct preferences are independent and can always be linearly combined. Consequently, when internal conflicts arise, such as budget constraints versus performance requirements, these feed-forward mechanisms compromise, yielding recommendations that combine incompatible signals. In this paper, we formulate conflicting preferences through explicit pairwise constraints. We propose Constrained Preference Dynamics (CPD), a framework that casts preference aggregation as a constrained dynamical system. CPD treats preference intensities as state variables evolving under learned pairwise constraints. By minimizing an energy function via unrolled gradient descent, the system moves preference states toward locally stable, low-energy configurations before scoring. On five real-world datasets, CPD improves overall accuracy while delivering larger gains under high-conflict scenarios. Specifically, on the Amazon Clothing conflict subset, CPD outperforms the strongest baseline MDGR by 19.8% in Recall@10 and 24.8% in NDCG@10. These results show that incorporating constrained dynamics improves recommendation performance under preference conflict.
A003FULLRouteRec: Behavior-Guided Sparse Routing for Sequential Recommendation
Junyeong Song (Korea Advanced Institute of Science and Technology) · Jaemin Yoo (Seoul National University)
Abstract
Sessionized interaction histories contain behavioral patterns that can improve sequential recommendation. However, existing models process all sessions through the same parameterized blocks, regardless of their behavioral differences. Mixture of Experts (MoE) enables conditional computation, but it leaves open what should guide expert allocation. We propose RouteRec, a sequential recommender that uses observed session behavior as the routing criterion. RouteRec summarizes four types of behavioral evidence from sessionized histories: interaction tempo, item-group focus, repetition and carryover, and popularity tendency. It uses these cues to route computation at macro, mid, and micro scopes. Cue-derived scores first select expert groups; within each selected group, the current backbone state then refines expert selection. Across six public datasets and 18 dataset–metric combinations, RouteRec ranks first in 12 and second in three, yielding the best overall average rank of 1.61 compared with 4.11 for the next-best baseline. Additional analyses suggest that the behavioral cues guide expert allocation beyond added capacity and produce routing patterns aligned with observed behavior. Our code is available at https://github.com/jy1559/RouteRec.
A004SHORTMitigating Negative Feedback in Sequential Recommendations with Barlow Twins
Veronika Ivanova (Yandex) · Evgeny Frolov (AXXX)
Abstract
Sequential recommender systems are commonly optimized for next-item prediction, but they often underutilize negative feedback such as dislikes, skips, or low ratings. As a result, items that a user is likely to reject may still be ranked highly, which can reduce user satisfaction. Effectively incorporating negative feedback is challenging because such signals are often sparse, noisy, and must be modeled without degrading positive-preference prediction. We propose NegBT, a non-contrastive framework for negative-feedback-aware sequential recommendation based on the Barlow Twins objective. The key idea is to construct two deterministic views of the same user's history: a positive-only sequence that captures core preferences and a full mixed-feedback sequence that preserves the original behavioral context. By encouraging consistency between these representations while reducing feature redundancy, NegBT incorporates mixed-feedback histories as an auxiliary regularizer without relying on hard negative sampling. Experiments on three datasets show that NegBT provides a strong balance between positive-item accuracy and negative-feedback avoidance. In particular, it improves over positive-only SASRec on positive-target ranking metrics while reducing the relative promotion of negative items, with especially clear gains on explicit-feedback datasets and long user histories.
A005SHORTEnriching Sequential Recommendation with Graph Laplacian Positional Embeddings
Ekaterina Trushkova (HSE University) · Artur Gimranov (HSE University) · Anton Lysenko (HSE University)
Abstract
Sequential recommenders typically rely on learnable positional embeddings to encode the order of user interactions. In this work, we ask whether this ordinal signal can be replaced by a structural one derived from the item space. We propose to use Laplacian positional embeddings in SASRec: we build an item co-occurrence graph from training interactions, compute eigenvectors of its symmetric normalized Laplacian, and use them as frozen graph-derived positional embeddings. The backbone architecture and training objective remain unchanged. Experiments on four public sequential-recommendation benchmarks show that this simple replacement improves SASRec performance on most ranking metrics and remains competitive with strong positional and temporal encoding baselines. These findings indicate that item-item graph structure can be an effective substitute for standard ordinal positional embeddings in sequential recommendation.
A006FULLSpikeRec: Accurate and Preference-Preserving Live-Streaming Recommendation under User-Sampled Signal Loss
Jeongmin An (Seoul National University) · Jaeri Lee (Seoul National University) · U Kang (Seoul National University)
Abstract
Given a user's past interactions and the set of channels that are currently live, how can a recommender choose the next channel when both channel availability and audience attention change within minutes? Live-streaming recommendation is difficult because the valid candidate set and each channel's audience state change continuously. In large-scale systems, an additional difficulty arises when training logs are subsampled at the user level for scalability: every interaction of the sampled users is kept and the rest are discarded. This user-level subsampling preserves each selected user's viewing history for learning personal preference, but removes many viewers from each channel's time series. As a result, standard sequential recommenders learn a user's revisit tendencies, but remain weak at detecting current channel-level signals such as sudden viewer-count surges. Simply boosting channels with global surges is also unsafe because many users return to channels they already know. In this paper, we propose SpikeRec (Spike-aware Recommender for live-streaming channels), an accurate recommender for live-streaming platforms. SpikeRec detects the spike of each live channel from the full streaming data, converting the viewer count into percentiles to make the spikes comparable across channels. It then enriches the representation of a user with the channels spiking around the recent interactions of the user, so that the spikes are reflected in the preference of the user. It finally adds a spike-scaled bonus to the channels that the user has watched before, so that the repeating tendency of the user is reflected as well. We also collect Chzzk, a new live-streaming dataset with de-identified chat and donation interactions together with the viewer counts of every channel. SpikeRec gives the best accuracy on every metric and every dataset, improving Hit@10 by up to 16.4% over the second-best method.
A007SHORTDebate4Rec: Multi-Agent Debate for List-Level Feedback and Selection in Generative Recommendation
Yiyang Li (Shanghai Jiao Tong University) · Zheli Zhou (Shanghai Jiao Tong University) · Weiwen Liu (Shanghai Jiao Tong University) · Bo Chen (Kuaishou Technology) · Jianghao Lin (Shanghai Jiao Tong University) · Weinan Zhang (Shanghai Jiao Tong University) · Chaoyi Ma (Kuaishou Technology) · Ruiming Tang (Kuaishou Technology) · Han Li (Kuaishou Technology) · Kun Gai (Kuaishou Technology)
Abstract
Generative recommendation has become a promising paradigm for producing complete recommendation lists, yet providing proper feedback to multiple candidates remains challenging. A key difficulty is the conflict between matching users' historical preferences and maintaining content diversity. Existing reward modeling and re-ranking methods usually rely on fixed objective aggregation or single-model judgment, which limits their flexibility and explainability in resolving such conflicts. To address this issue, we propose Debate4Rec, a multi-agent debate framework for feedback and candidate-list selection in generative recommendation. Debate4Rec acts as an external list-level feedback signal producer that provides interpretable feedback and selects the best candidate list. It decomposes list evaluation into two specialized agents: a Preference Agent for assessing alignment with user interests, and a Diversity Agent for evaluating category coverage, redundancy, and list richness. The agents first make independent judgments and then conduct a structured two-round debate to exchange evidence, revise decisions, and reach a final selection. Experiments on ML-1M and a Kuaishou short-video dataset show that Debate4Rec achieves competitive and often better performance than the LLM-based and traditional re-ranking baselines under the candidate-list selection setting. Ablation studies further confirm the effectiveness of role-specialized agents, structured debate, and the feedback-selector mechanism.
A008SHORTDistilling Post-Conversion Content for User Retention Modeling
Tianbao Ma (Kuaishou Technology) · Ruochen Yang (Kuaishou Technology) · Chengen Li (Kuaishou Technology) · Yuexin Shi (Kuaishou Technology) · Jiangxia Cao (Kuaishou Technology) · Linxun Chen (Kuaishou Technology) · Zhaojie Liu (Kuaishou Technology) · Yanan Niu (Kuaishou Technology) · Han Li (Kuaishou Technology) · Kun Gai (Kuaishou Technology)
Abstract
User retention is a key metric to measure long-term engagement in modern platforms. In real-time bidding (RTB) advertising system for user re-engagement, the retention model is required to predict future revisit probability at bidding time, before the user converts and consumes any content. Although post-conversion content, termed Onboarding Content, provides highly informative signals for retention prediction, directly using it in training causes severe feature leakage and creates a gap between training and serving. To address this issue, we propose OCARM, a two-stage distillation-aligned framework for Onboarding Content Augmented Retention Modeling, enabling the model to implicitly capture future content using only observable features during inference. In the first stage, we deliberately expose onboarding content to train a hierarchical encoder that produces teacher representations. In the second stage, a user encoder is aligned with the frozen teacher through distillation, allowing the model to approximate the inaccessible onboarding signals without leakage. Extensive offline experiments and online A/B tests demonstrate that our framework achieves consistent improvements in a real-world growth scenario.
A009FULLSmart Predict then Optimize for Constrained Learning to Rank
Zechun Niu (Renmin University of China) · Jiayu Chen (Kuaishou Technology) · Haozhe Duan (Renmin University of China) · Chunzhen Huang (Kuaishou Technology) · Han Wen (Kuaishou Technology) · Qing Tan (Kuaishou Technology) · Kaiqiao Zhan (Kuaishou Technology) · Kun Gai (Kuaishou Technology) · Jiaxin Mao (Renmin University of China)
Abstract
Ranking is a central problem in information retrieval. Traditional learning-to-rank methods aim to train a ranking model to predict the relevance of each item and then rank them according to the relevance scores. However, many real-world ranking systems must satisfy application-specific constraints to ensure the fairness, safety, or diversity of the ranking, so the ranking decision can no longer be obtained by decreasingly sorting the relevance scores. A straightforward solution is to utilize the predict-then-optimize paradigm: first training a ranking model to predict relevance scores and then feeding the predicted relevance into a downstream optimizer to generate a ranking list that satisfied the constraints. This paradigm can produce feasible rankings when the constrained problem is feasible, but its prediction training is separated from the optimization of the ranking objective, making it difficult to directly optimize the quality of the induced ranking. In this paper, we propose SPORank, a unified framework for constrained learning to rank. By adopting the SPO+ loss, SPORank jointly considers relevance prediction and constrained optimization during training, making it broadly applicable to constrained ranking problems. We instantiate SPORank on two concrete tasks. The experimental results demonstrate SPORank effectively improves ranking performance while satisfying the required constraints.
A010FULLSelf-Evolving Memory for Generative Recommendation
Xinyu Lin (National University of Singapore) · Zhuosong Jiang (National University of Singapore) · Zixiao Suo (National University of Singapore) · Siqin Wang (National University of Singapore) · Hanqing Zeng (Meta AI) · Hanchao Yu (Meta AI) · Yinglong Xia (Meta AI) · Jiang Zhang (Meta AI) · Aashu Singh (Meta AI) · Fei Liu (Meta AI) · Wenjie Wang (National University of Singapore) · Fuli Feng (National University of Singapore) · Yang Song (Meta AI) · Qifan Wang (Meta AI) · Tat-Seng Chua (National University of Singapore)
Abstract
Generative recommendation has emerged as a promising end-to-end paradigm for personalized recommendation. In real-world recommendation scenarios, however, user preferences continuously evolve over time, making self-evolving an essential capability for generative recommender systems. Existing evolving strategies, such as continual retraining and distillation-based adaptation, directly update the shared model parameters using streaming interactions. Nevertheless, we find that directly applying such strategies to generative recommendation introduces a critical issue, termed evolution conflict. Specifically, heterogeneous preference shifts from different users are optimized within a fully shared autoregressive parameter space, causing dominant behavioral patterns to progressively dominate the model evolution process while underrepresented patterns become increasingly overlooked. To address this issue, we propose a self-evolving memory paradigm for generative recommendation, aiming to enable effective evolution across heterogeneous behavioral patterns. We further identify three key principles for effective self-evolving recommendation systems, including isolated memorization, reinforced evolution, and scalable application. Guided by these principles, we develop LION, a simple yet effective framework centered on a sparse Key-Value memory layer. Specifically, LION introduces sparse memory activation to isolate the evolution of different behavioral patterns, while a consolidation loss is designed to reinforce the learning of underrepresented preference dynamics during continual adaptation. Extensive experiments on diverse real-world datasets demonstrate the effectiveness of LION under various continual evolution settings (e.g., per-period evaluation, user/item group evaluation, and evolution convergence analysis).
A011APPLIEDControllable Autoregressive Retrieval with Long-term Action Perception for Recommendations
Jinwei Luo (Tencent Music Entertainment) · Dugang Liu (Shenzhen University) · Xing Tang (Shenzhen Technology University) · Xiuqiang He (Shenzhen Technology University) · Renjie Wei (Tencent Music Entertainment) · Zhe Wu (Tencent Music Entertainment) · Xin Huang (Tencent Music Entertainment) · Siliang Huang (Tencent Music Entertainment) · Hongcheng Fu (Tencent Music Entertainment)
Abstract
Autoregressive retrieval (AR) has emerged as a leading paradigm for the first stage of industrial recommender systems. However, existing AR methods (i) overlook long-term action perception, training their generation only against the immediate next interaction, and (ii) lack the controllability needed to align candidate generation with diverse business goals without retraining. We propose Controllable Autoregressive Retrieval with long-term action perception (CAR), a simple yet deployable framework that addresses both issues. A long-term supervision module attaches multiple action-sliding prediction heads at different future horizons and transfers their knowledge to the main model via parameter sharing (P-CAR) or cascading (C-CAR), injecting a long-horizon perspective. An action-induced input module reorders the input as an action--item sequence and exposes a target action token at inference time, enabling goal-aware control over the recall set. Experiments on three public benchmarks and two industrial datasets, along with online A/B tests on QQ Music and WeSing, which now serve hundreds of millions of daily users in production, show consistent, statistically significant gains over strong AR baselines.
A012SHORTGryphon: A Unified Architecture for Semantic-ID Generation and Item-Level Scoring in Industrial Recommendations
Daria Tikhonovich (Yandex) · Oleg Sorokin (Yandex) · Vladislav Dodonov (Yandex) · Mariia Ulianova (Yandex) · Ilya Murzin (Yandex)
Abstract
Generative retrieval (GR) has become a scalable approach to candidate generation: each item is assigned a short hierarchical token sequence called a Semantic ID (SID), and the next item's SID is decoded autoregressively. A practical limitation is that the decoder's beam search optimizes the likelihood of token sequences, not the relevance of the underlying items. These objectives diverge when sequence likelihood is poorly calibrated due to beam search error accumulation, and when several items collapse onto a single SID and receive identical scores. We introduce Gryphon, an encoder-decoder generative recommendation architecture that adds a jointly trained item-level scoring component alongside SID generation, reusing the encoder's user representation computed in a single forward pass. Instead of ranking SIDs by accumulated token likelihood, Gryphon resolves each generated SID to its concrete items and re-scores those items directly, which sidesteps miscalibrated sequence scores and separates items that collide on the same identifier. On an industrial music service, with item-level scoring trained under a next-item-prediction objective, Gryphon attains the highest item-level Recall@1000, above the strongest baselines (+3.7% over vanilla GR and +2.5% over collision-resolved GR) at comparable parameter count and latency. Gryphon's item-level ranking also surpasses its beam-likelihood ranking of the same candidates (+4.2% gain), demonstrating the benefit of item-level scoring in GR. Deployed as the sole candidate source in a 7-day A/B test, Gryphon produced no statistically significant change in total listening time (+0.25%) while replacing a pipeline of more than 15 candidate generators and a separate preranking stage, substantially simplifying the candidate-generation system.
A013SHORTS²DGR: Stable-State Diffusion for Generative Recommendation
Ashish Kumar (Indian Institute of Technology Roorkee) · Prashant Kumar (Bennett University)
Abstract
Generative recommendation represents each item as a semantic ID (SID) sequence and predicts the next item by generating its tokens from user-item interaction history. Recent diffusion-based methods replace autoregressive decoding with masked denoising, enabling bidirectional SID modeling and generation without a fixed left-to-right order. However, masked-diffusion GenRec still depends on two main selection stages: which SID tokens are masked during training and which partial SID candidates are retained during inference. Existing noising strategies estimate token uncertainty from a single probe context, which can make masked views sensitive to context-specific uncertainty, while path-level decoding can retain redundant trajectories that lead to the same partial SID state. We propose S2DGR, a stable-state diffusion framework for generative recommendation. S2DGR introduces Stability-Aware Noising (SAN), which aggregates SID-token uncertainty across multiple probe contexts to construct stable masked training views, and State-Unique Denoising (SUD), which selects inference candidates according to partial SID states rather than only denoising paths. Experiments on multiple benchmark datasets show that S2DGR consistently improves over strong discriminative, generative, and diffusion-based recommendation baselines.
A014SHORTGRID: Generative Recommendation via Inpainting Diffusion
Jia Ma (Tencent) · Jun Cheng (Tencent) · Kangyi Lin (Tencent)
Abstract
Generative Recommendation (GR) utilizing discrete Semantic IDs (SIDs) has emerged as a promising paradigm for sequential recommendation. However, existing GR paradigms exhibit significant generation flaws: traditional autoregressive (AR) models suffer from strict left-to-right causal constraints leading to error accumulation, while current discrete diffusion adaptations rely on isolated next-item beam search, which causes "homogeneous stacking" and lacks explicit list-level coordination. Furthermore, these methods often compromise the interpretable, hierarchical structure of SIDs. To address these limitations, we propose GRID, a novel framework that reformulates generative top-K recommendation as a 2D discrete diffusion inpainting problem. By modeling the recommended item list and their multi-digit hierarchical SIDs along two orthogonal axes, GRID recovers the complete matrix of future items simultaneously via parallel decoding. To ensure structural validity and semantic diversity, we introduce a hierarchical SID construction method alongside a dual-regularized inpainting objective that enforces hierarchy consistency and intra-list uniqueness. Supported by a progressive curriculum training strategy, extensive experiments on three Amazon datasets demonstrate that GRID effectively overcomes homogeneous stacking, fundamentally resolving the limitations of traditional decoding, and achieves state-of-the-art performance across all benchmarks.
A015SHORTSPRIG: Semantic-ID-enhanced Paths for Knowledge Graph-based Generative Recommendation
Justin Hangöbl (Johannes Kepler University) · Marta Moscati (Johannes Kepler University) · Alessandro B. Melchiorre (Criteo AI Lab) · Shah Nawaz (Johannes Kepler University) · Markus Schedl (Johannes Kepler University)
Abstract
Recommender systems leveraging generative models often generate item identifiers directly, rather than ranking catalog items by a recommendation score. Recent work extends beyond pure sequential interaction signals by incorporating item content and structured relationships among items, with two distinct directions emerging. Semantic IDs (SIDs) enrich item representations by replacing opaque, randomly initialized embeddings with hierarchically quantized discrete codes derived from item content. Knowledge-graph (KG) path reasoning instead generates entity-relation paths that ground recommendations in structured relationships between items, attributes, and external entities, thereby enriching the relational context.
