These two lines have complementary limitations: SID-based models lack relational grounding, while KG-based generative recommenders still represent items as arbitrary, opaque tokens tied to large embedding tables, limiting parameter sharing and generalization. We propose SPRIG, a generative recommender that integrates content-derived SIDs into KG path reasoning. SPRIG is trained on information-rich KG paths that terminate in items represented as discrete, content-derived tokens, combining the advantages of both approaches. We evaluate SPRIG on movie and music recommendation datasets against baselines spanning sequential language models, KG-augmented methods, and SID-based approaches. Our results show that SPRIG achieves competitive performance over prior generative models while using fewer parameters and a lower compute cost. Code: https://github.com/justinhangoebl/semantic-id-knowledge-graph-recommender
A016FULLNeither Black nor White: Balancing Semantic and Collaborative Signals with Graph-Informed Semantic IDs (GrIS)
Aleksei Medvedev (Huawei Ireland Research Centre) · Alejandro Ariza-Casabona (Huawei Ireland Research Centre) · Steven Derby (Huawei Ireland Research Centre) · Gonzalo Fiz Pontiveros (Huawei Ireland Research Centre) · Xinyang Shao (Huawei Ireland Research Centre) · Florian Spiess (Huawei Ireland Research Centre)
Abstract
Existing work on Semantic IDs (SIDs) for generative recommendation treats SID construction as a representation learning problem: encode items into a quantised latent space and read off codes. We argue this view is incidental. SID construction is, at heart, a recursive clustering problem, and once stated this way the natural object to cluster is a graph whose nodes carry semantic content and whose edges carry collaborative signal; SID assignment becomes a hierarchical graph partition. This reframing yields a unified framework, Graph-Informed Semantic IDs (GrIS), that subsumes prior approaches rather than displacing them. RQ-VAE and RQ-KMeans are recovered as the special case where the graph is empty, exposing content-only quantisation as one corner of a larger design space along two so-far-collapsed axes: graph construction and recursive partition algorithm. We explore two contrasting instantiations: RecDMoN, which performs hierarchical assignment via differentiable graph pooling, and RQ-GAE, which extends RQ-VAE with graph-aware item representations and a graph reconstruction objective. On multiple real-world datasets, GrIS consistently improves over CF-aware SOTA, with gains of up to +52% Hit@10. Because graph construction and partition are explicit, separately configurable components, improvements on either axis can be combined and evaluated systematically.
A017FULLProfiling What Matters: Context-Aware Item Profiles from Large-Scale Metadata for LLM Recommenders
Dojun Hwang (Korea University) · Seunghan Lee (Korea University) · Cheonyoung Park (KT Corporation) · Sara Yu (KT Corporation) · SeongKu Kang (Korea University)
Abstract
While Large Language Models (LLMs) have significantly advanced reranking in recommendation, effectively leveraging item-side information remains challenging. Real-world items are described by vast, heterogeneous, and unstructured metadata, where decision-relevant signals are often implicit, noisy, or buried in long descriptions. Moreover, feature salience is highly context-dependent, varying not only across items but also across users. Existing methods often rely on item titles, fixed attributes, or static item summaries, which limit personalized and fine-grained item understanding. To bridge this gap, we propose CAIRO, a user context-aware item profiling framework for LLM-based reranking. CAIRO first structures raw metadata and reviews into objective features and subjective traits, and employs a lightweight profiler to select the most relevant information for each user–item pair with limited serving-time overhead. The resulting profiles are concise and context-specific, providing relevant item-side evidence for the LLM's ranking decision. Experiments show that CAIRO consistently improves LLM-based reranking, highlighting the importance of item profiling that effectively exploits vast item-side information.
A018FULLLiteUP4Rec: Efficient User Profiling from LLM-Derived Semantic Supervision
Donghee Han (Korea Advanced Institute of Science and Technology) · Daeyoung Roh (Korea Advanced Institute of Science and Technology) · Jiwon Jeong (Korea Advanced Institute of Science and Technology) · Mun Yong Yi (Korea Advanced Institute of Science and Technology)
Abstract
LLM-derived user profiles improve recommendation quality but are costly to keep up to date: each new interaction requires regenerating the profile with another LLM call. We present LiteUP4Rec, a framework that amortizes LLM-based user profiling into a surrogate model, reconstructing the LLM-derived user representation from item embeddings and removing per-user LLM calls from the serving path while preserving the underlying preference signal. An LLM is used only during offline data preparation to produce user profiles and item descriptions; a lightweight transformer profiler is then trained under mean squared error against the encoded profile, and an alignment projection concatenates its output with collaborative features inside a two-tower retrieval formulation that inherits precomputable item indices and scalable nearest-neighbor lookup. Across benchmarks and baselines, LiteUP4Rec yields an average 40% (up to 74%) improvement. Latency and memory costs are significantly reduced, enabling LLM-derived user profiling under real-time latency budgets.
A019APPLIEDTagLLM: A Fine-Grained Tag Generation Approach for Note Recommendation
Zhijian Chen (Tongji University) · Likai Wang (Dewu) · Lei Chen (Dewu) · Yaguang Dou (Dewu) · Jialiang Shi (Dewu) · Tian Qi (Dewu) · Dongdong Hao (Dewu) · Mengying Lu (Tsinghua University) · Cheng Ye (Dewu) · Chao Wei (Dewu)
Abstract
Large Language Models (LLMs) have shown promising potential in E-commerce community recommendation. While LLMs and Multimodal LLMs (MLLMs) are widely used to encode notes into implicit embeddings, leveraging their generative capabilities to represent notes with interpretable tags remains unexplored. In the field of tag generation, traditional close-ended methods heavily rely on the design of tag pools, while existing open-ended methods applied directly to note recommendations face two limitations: (1) MLLMs lack guidance during generation, resulting in redundant tags that fail to capture user interests; (2) The generated tags are often coarse and lack fine-grained representation of notes, interfering with downstream recommendations. To address these limitations, we propose TagLLM, a fine-grained tag generation method for note recommendation. TagLLM captures user interests across note categories through a User Interest Handbook and constructs fine-grained tag data using multimodal CoT Extraction. A Tag Knowledge Distillation method is developed to equip small models with competitive generation capabilities, enhancing inference efficiency and reducing costs. In online A/B test, TagLLM increases average view duration per user by 0.31%, average interactions per user by 0.96%, and page view click-through rate in cold-start scenario by 32.37%, demonstrating its effectiveness. TagLLM has been deployed in Dewu's community services, generating tag features for over 600,000 new notes daily.
A020FULLSAERec: Constructing Fine-grained Interpretable Intents Priors via Sparse Autoencoders for Recommendation
Jiangnan Xia (University of Georgia) · Xuansheng Wu (University of Georgia) · Yu Yang (The Education University of Hong Kong) · Yujun Fu (The Education University of Hong Kong) · Xin Wang (Jilin University) · Ninghao Liu (The Hong Kong Polytechnic University)
Abstract
Intent-based recommender systems have gained significant attention for enhancing accuracy and interpretability by modeling the underlying motivations behind user behaviors. Most existing models derive intents directly from user sequences via clustering or prototype learning. However, they are sensitive to the sequence quality, require presetting the number of intents and lack explicit semantic grounding. These issues lead to an incomplete and coarse intent set and limit the effectiveness of recommendation. In this paper, we propose the Sparse Autoencoder for intent-based recommendation (SAERec), a novel recommender that automatically constructs a fine-grained, interpretable intent space from a textual corpus to guide recommendation. Rather than treating texts as side signals, SAERec leverages them as high-information-density evidence for intent construction. Specifically, we first extract a comprehensive set of fine-grained interpretable intents from the latent space of Large Language Models (LLMs) by using a Sparse Autoencoder (SAE) to disentangle and interpret text embeddings, which isolates intent-related semantics from substantial textual noise. Then, for each user, we retrieve relevant intents from the set as priors to guide recommendation. These priors include personal intents that match each user’s current interests and public intents that capture general item patterns shared across users (e.g., “quality” and “price”). Finally, to integrate retrieved intents into sequence modeling, we propose a multi-branch attention mechanism that captures temporal dependencies and injects both personal and public intent signals, followed by an adaptive fusion layer to construct the final user representation for recommendation. Extensive experiments on public datasets demonstrate the superiority of SAERec, consistently outperforming state-of-the-art baselines while providing human-understandable explanations. Our code is available at https://github.com/jiangnanx129/SAERec.
A021RESOURCETE4 RS: Toward End-to-End Explanation Evaluation for Recommender Systems
Kathrin Wardatzky (University of Zurich) · Oana Inel (University of Zurich) · Abraham Bernstein (University of Zurich)
Abstract
Explanations in Recommender Systems (RS) play a crucial role in enhancing transparency, trust, and user satisfaction. Benchmarking such explanations, however, is not trivial, as existing evaluation frameworks typically do not assess all explanation stages (i.e., generation, abstraction, formatting, and communication) or evaluate them in isolation. In this paper, we present TE4 RS, an end-to-end explanation evaluation framework for RS that assesses explanation methods across all four stages: generation, abstraction, format, and communication. It contains 20 explanation methods covering seven categories and 31 evaluation metrics. We also integrate large language models to format the explainers' abstract outputs and to serve as proxy evaluators for human evaluation. TE4 RS allows to set up an evaluation pipeline that mimics a specific application scenario and compares multiple explanation methods, thereby fostering a holistic, structured evaluation of RS explanations. The code can be found at: https://gitlab.ifi.uzh.ch/DDIS-Public/te4-rs.
A022SHORTSplit Decisions: How Evaluation Protocols Change Recommender Model Selection
Mikhail Pechatov (T-bank)
Abstract
Offline recommender evaluation often treats the train/test split as a technical detail, even though different split protocols answer different deployment questions. We study how the split protocol changes not only absolute ranking metrics, but also the model that would be selected from a candidate set. We evaluate widely used recommender models on widely used public recommender benchmarks under global-temporal, leave-one-out, random-interaction, and per-user temporal splits. Our evidence uses full-catalog ranking and defines split-induced model-selection regret: the loss on a global-temporal target caused by selecting a model under another split. Across public datasets and bounded industrial stress tests, non-global protocols often select different models and transfer poorly to the chronological target. The pattern persists across metrics, cutoffs, split seeds, and model sanity checks, suggesting that split choice is a model-selection decision rather than a harmless preprocessing detail. The results suggest that chronological deployment claims should either select models under a global-temporal protocol or report the regret induced by alternative splits.
A023SHORTDo LLM Recommenders Know When They're Hallucinating? Auditing Confidence Calibration in Catalog Faithfulness
Srijith Ravikumar (Amazon.com LLC)
Abstract
LLM recommenders for top-K item suggestion regularly emit titles outside the target catalog. Prior audits report a binary out-of-domain rate; none ask whether the model knew. We jointly audit hallucination rate (OOD@10) and verbalized-confidence calibration (ECE, Brier, reliability) for four zero-shot LLM recommenders from four independent vendors (Mistral Large, Llama-3.3-70B, GPT-OSS-120B, Claude Sonnet 4.6), not grounded or fine-tuned systems, across three catalogs (MovieLens-25M, Amazon Reviews 2023 Toys, Yelp Open Dataset), stratified by item popularity. Measuring catalog membership is itself the hard part: on identical outputs the reported rate moves by an order of magnitude with the string matcher used, and F1 cannot separate the candidates. We validate the instrument against 201 human judgments and select on net bias, where the adopted one is off by -0.040 against +0.144 for the common fuzzy rule. Hallucination is then strongly catalog-dependent (0.6-2.7% on MovieLens, 11.6-38.7% on Yelp, 49.3-61.0% on Amazon Toys). Each model holds a near-constant confidence level barely responsive to the catalog, while the catalog-hit rate swings 60 points, so the sign of the error is set by where a model's constant lands against a catalog's accuracy: 7 of the twelve cells are under-confident and 5 over-confident, all four under-confident on MovieLens, all four over-confident on Amazon Toys. We read this as an elicitation mismatch: "Just Ask" elicits a generic quality rating, not a catalog-membership probability. A conformal abstention threshold over verbalized confidence changes hallucination by at most 1.65 pp across four alpha levels, because the channel cannot separate correct items from hallucinations. We recommend that audits report calibration alongside OOD, validate the matcher producing the OOD number, and use catalog-anchored elicitation.
A024FULLA Dual-Expert Strategy Integrating LLMs to Mitigate Negative Transfer in Cross-Domain Sequential Recommendation
Hyeongjun Yun (SK Telecom) · Kihyuk Song (SK Telecom) · Jaegul Choo (Korea Advanced Institute of Science and Technology (KAIST)) · Chung Park (SK Telecom)
Abstract
Cross-Domain Sequential Recommendation (CDSR) predicts the next item a user will interact with based on their historical interaction sequences across multiple domains. Recent approaches leverage Large Language Models (LLMs) finetuned on textual representations of cross-domain user sequences to retrieve the recommended items, referred to as LLMRec. However, LLMRec primarily models the autoregressive patterns of token-level item texts, while overlooking item-level collaborative signals. This semantic misalignment often leads to distorted knowledge transfer across domains—termed negative transfer—degrading performance in the CDSR task. To address this issue, we propose a novel LLM-based CDSR model, DuELRec: Domain-Gated Dual Experts with LLMs for Cross-Domain Sequential Recommendation. We propose a domain-gated dual-expert framework, equipped with an item-aware attention transformation module, which aggregates textual subtokens into item-level representations and enforces block-level attention masking. The single-domain expert restricts autoregressive attention to items within the same domain, while the cross-domain expert allows it across all domains. A gating mechanism adaptively fuses their outputs, using single-domain signals to reduce cross-domain noise that causes negative transfer. Second, we introduce a dual-sampling token-to-item contrastive learning objective that allows LLMs to capture the item-level collaborative signals from both single- and cross-domains. This is achieved by transforming token-level item texts into item-level representations and applying stochastic negative sampling from both single- and cross-domain item pools for contrastive learning. Extensive experiments on two real-world datasets across ten domains show that our model outperforms 26 state-of-the-art methods in recommendation performance. Its deployment in our personal assistant app led to a 47.6% relative increase in click-through rate, demonstrating real-world impact. Our code and appendices are available at https://github.com/cpark88/DuELRec.
A025FULLRecSoup: Efficient Model Merging Approach for Controllable Multi-Objective Recommendation
Zidong Jia (Renmin University of China) · Guofu Xie (Renmin University of China) · Xiao Zhang (Renmin University of China)
Abstract
Recommender systems often need to balance multiple conflicting objectives. Controllable Multi-Objective Recommendation (CMOR) enables dynamic adjustment of objective trade-offs at inference time without retraining, adapting to shifting user or system requirements. Existing CMOR approaches typically rely on output-level reranking or parameter-generating modules, which either limit the scope of feasible trade-offs or incur substantial training and inference cost. Model merging provides a promising alternative by reusing multiple objective-specific models via parameter combination. However, its direct application to recommender systems is challenging due to the lack of a shared linear regime and cross-objective interference. To address these issues, we propose RecSoup, a lightweight two-stage approach for effective CMOR via specialized model merging. RecSoup first mitigates parameter interference across objectives through a pruning strategy that jointly considers objective-specific importance and cross-objective relevance. It then performs adaptive parameter merging via a learnable preference-to-coefficient mapping, allowing dynamic trade-off control at inference time without joint retraining or additional generative modules. Theoretically, we prove that RecSoup outperforms the parameter generation paradigm in effectiveness and efficiency, as it can fully navigate the Pareto front without smoothness constraints. Extensive experiments on multiple benchmarks demonstrate that RecSoup achieves improved Pareto front quality and effective controllability while delivers 165–228× faster inference-time latency than parameter generation approaches. Code is available at https://github.com/35798642/RECSOUP.git.
A026SHORTGive Me MoE: Dynamic Expert Routing for Inductive Graph-based Recommendation
Liana Mardanova (Innopolis University) · Denis Krasilnikov (Moscow Institute of Physics and Technology) · Oleg Lashinin (Moscow Institute of Physics and Technology) · Marina Ananyeva (National Research University Higher School of Economics) · Ilya Makarov (National Research University Higher School of Economics)
Abstract
Graph-based recommender systems capture high-order user–item dependencies but often underperform in cold-start settings, especially for new items with limited interactions. Inductive graph models generalize to unseen users and items via node features and neighborhood aggregation. However, most rely on shared parameters that may be suboptimal for heterogeneous neighborhoods, which can limit cold-start performance. We propose MoE-IGR, a Mixture-of-Experts module for inductive graph-based recommendation that replaces the shared post-aggregation update with dynamic, layer-wise expert routing, enabling context-dependent message passing. We instantiate MoE-IGR on PinSage and evaluate it on three real-world datasets under temporal, cold-user, cold-item, and joint cold-start protocols. MoE-IGR yields substantial gains (up to 16% Recall@20), largest in cold-item recommendation (up to 34.4% NDCG@20). Routing analysis reveals expert specialization: cold items focus on a subset of experts, warm items prefer others, and semantically related item groups exhibit similar routing patterns, suggesting that experts capture both collaborative and semantic signals.
A027APPLIEDConnectionMind: Leveraging Social Networks and Large Language Models for Personalized Recommendation at Meta
Haoyu Han (Michigan State University) · Yuming Liu (Meta Platforms,Inc.) · Lei Huang (Meta Platforms, Inc.) · Lizhu Zhang (Meta Platforms, Inc.) · Jiliang Tang (Michigan State University) · Xiangjun Fan (Meta Platforms, Inc.)
Abstract
Modern recommendation systems on social media platforms such as Meta must model complex social relationships alongside massive and heterogeneous content such as text and video. Traditional recommendation models, however, often omit these signals or treat them independently, limiting their ability to integrate multi-relational context for fine-grained personalization. We present ConnectionMind, a production-ready recommendation framework that tightly integrates social network structure with large language models (LLMs) to enable scalable and reasoning-aware personalization at Meta. ConnectionMind constructs a heterogeneous graph connecting users, items, friends, groups, and creator pages, and formulates recommendation as a graph reasoning problem that discovers personalized paths from users to candidate items. An LLM-based policy reasons over these graph structures to guide recommendation decisions. To train the system at scale, ConnectionMind adopts a two-stage strategy: supervised fine-tuning (SFT) on large-scale user–item interaction trajectories to initialize the reasoning policy, followed by end-to-end reinforcement learning (RL) to further optimize personalized graph reasoning. Extensive experiments on multiple real-world datasets demonstrate consistent improvements over representative baselines. More importantly, ConnectionMind has been deployed in Meta's large-scale recommendation pipeline and evaluated through online A/B tests, achieving a 0.43% improvement in video watch time. These results demonstrate the effectiveness and measurable real-world impact of graph-based LLM reasoning for production recommendation.
A028FULLA Transformer Architecture via Lightweight Sigmoid Attention for Graph Collaborative Filtering
Hyungjin Kim (SK Inc.) · Seokho Ahn (Inha University) · Minhye Jeon (Inha University) · Sungbok Shin (Sogang University) · Young-Duk Seo (Inha University)
Abstract
Transformer architectures have achieved strong performance in graph collaborative filtering by modeling complex user-item relationships. However, existing studies often rely on row-wise softmax attention, auxiliary modules, or constrained architectures, leading to three key challenges: relation modeling, architectural coherence, and computational efficiency. To address these challenges, we propose LiSA, a Transformer via lightweight sigmoid attention. LiSA replaces row-wise softmax attention with an element-wise sigmoid scoring formulation, enabling observed user-item relations to be modeled without normalization against other elements in the same row. It further incorporates a scaling parameter for attention sensitivity and score calibration, together with gated residual connections that preserve structural information across layers. Experiments on five real-world benchmarks show that LiSA consistently outperforms baselines while maintaining lightweight computation. Code is available at https://github.com/Burf/LiSA.
A029FULLThe Edge Spectrum of Choice-Derived Item Graphs: Strong and Weak Edges Encode Different Relations in Collaborative Filtering
Keigo Sakurai (Hokkaido University) · Takahiro Ogawa (Hokkaido University) · Miki Haseyama (Hokkaido University)
Abstract
Graph collaborative filtering relies on item–item graphs whose edges are used for positive smoothing, under the implicit assumption that stronger edges encode more of the same relation as weaker ones. We show that this assumption fails for a practically important class of graphs: those whose edge weights come from a choice model. On such graphs, strong and weak edges encode qualitatively different relations, which we call an edge spectrum. Specifically, strong edges concentrate on the in-slate competitors of clicked items, exactly the pairs that the within-slate ranking gradient pushes apart, while weak edges do not. We formalize this as a sign mismatch between the smoothing operator and the ranking gradient, and prove that co-click graphs cannot exhibit the same misalignment by construction. This diagnosis explains three empirical observations on MIND and EB-NeRD: (i) drop-in choice-derived operators do not beat co-click, despite indexing structurally distinct neighborhoods; (ii) uniform scalar fixes (sign flip, in-slate margin loss) fail predictably, because the misalignment lives in the graph, not in the loss; (iii) only edge-magnitude-aware operators, with the regime boundary located by the diagnosis rather than by tuning, recover the predicted ordering. The neighbor cutoff k is therefore a semantic switch, not a sparsification hyperparameter. Our claim concerns which interventions fail or succeed and why, not absolute headline gains, which the diagnosis itself predicts to be small under the attenuated propagation channel we observe. We turn the diagnosis into a reusable protocol practitioners can run before deploying any choice-derived item-side operator. Code: https://github.com/kyomusso/Edge-Spectrum-in-CF.
A030FULLMixture-of-Experts Enhanced Parameter-free Hypergraph Contrastive Network for Next Point-of-Interest Recommendation
Guangteng Liu (Hubei University) · Wanli Li (Huazhong Agricultural University) · Ke Sun (Wuhan University of Science and Technology) · Feng Wang (Hubei University of Arts and Science) · Lu Liu (Hubei University of Arts and Science) · Ping Huang (Hubei University of Arts and Science)
Abstract
Next Point-of-Interest (POI) recommendation aims to predict a user's next destination based on historical check-in sequences. Existing works have achieved notable progress by capturing human mobility patterns through spatio-temporal context modeling and by injecting global collaborative signals via graph neural networks and hypergraph neural networks to alleviate data sparsity. However, indiscriminate fusion may leave heterogeneous mobility signals, such as spatial constraints, temporal habits, and categorical preferences, insufficiently differentiated. Additionally, learnable transformations in parameterized hypergraph convolutions may perturb topology-driven collaborative signals during multi-layer propagation, particularly on sparse interaction data. Moreover, the user's static preference representation and the sequence-encoded dynamic intent representation originate from different embedding spaces, resulting in semantic misalignment. To address these challenges, this paper proposes the Mixture-of-Experts Contrastive Parameter-free Hypergraph Network (M-CPHNet). Specifically, a relative time-gap encoding preserves diurnal rhythms via modulo-24 operations for fine-grained temporal intent modeling. A user-conditioned intent excitation gate coupled with an adaptive soft-routing mixture-of-experts module adaptively weights multiple experts to model complementary spatial, temporal, and categorical mobility patterns, yielding sequence intent representations. These are then fused with relative time-gap embeddings and absolute position embeddings, encoded by a Transformer, and aggregated via an attention query into a short-term dynamic intent. A parameter-free hypergraph convolution (Pf-HGConv) layer introduces no learnable weights in its propagation operator and performs normalized aggregation solely on the user–POI and category–POI co-occurrence matrices to obtain topology-enhanced global POI representations, thereby reducing parameterization-induced distortion. Hypergraph-sequence contrastive learning aligns the user's static preference representation with the short-term dynamic intent representation, mitigating semantic misalignment. Experiments on three real-world datasets show that M-CPHNet achieves higher observed performance than the evaluated baselines, with an average improvement of 4.8% in Acc@5 across the three datasets; under the reported experimental settings, its per-epoch training time on Foursquare-NYC is substantially shorter than that of STHGCN.
A031APPLIEDLLM Meets Traffic: Traffic-Aware Large Language Models for Next POI Recommendation in Vehicle Navigation Interfaces
Jongsoo Lee (Hanyang University) · Minwook Kim (Hanyang University) · Namhyuk Kim (Hyundai Motor Company) · Dong-Kyu Chae (Hanyang University)
Abstract
Next Point-of-Interest (POI) recommendation is a production-relevant task for modern in-car navigation interfaces. Given a user’s current and historical context, the system can suggest the next destination while accounting for both user preference and travel feasibility. However, existing Large Language Models (LLMs) for next POI recommendation (1) overlook real-time traffic conditions and thus fail to account for user-specific trade-offs between POI preferences and travel time, and (2) rely on text embedding-based POI candidate retrieval, which may surface semantically similar yet geographically implausible POIs. To address these limitations, we propose TraPOI, a Traffic-aware LLM for Next POI Recommendation. TraPOI consists of (i) a multimodal embedding alignment module to project POI, GPS, and traffic data into the LLM’s latent space, and (ii) a multi-view candidate retrieval module that retrieves distance-based and embedding-based candidates to facilitate spatially feasible and semantically relevant next POI recommendation. We also introduce (iii) multimodal prompting to explicitly incorporate traffic and spatial context into the LLM’s reasoning process. We constructed two novel datasets aligning check-in records with real-time traffic data from Seoul and California (CA) to validate our approach. Extensive experiments demonstrate that TraPOI significantly outperforms state-of-the-art baselines, achieving accuracy gains up to 11.61%. Our code and dataset are available at: https://github.com/kmw409722-svg/TraPOI.
A032FULLLearning Semantic Co-occurrence and Personalized Focused Representations for Multimodal Sequential Recommendation
Shujie Li (The University of Hong Kong) · Guanghu Yuan (South China University of Technology) · Jinfeng Xu (The University of Hong Kong) · Chengming Li (Shenzhen MSU-BIT University) · Feng Liang (Shenzhen MSU-BIT University) · Runhao Zeng (Shenzhen MSU-BIT University) · Edith C. H. Ngai (The University of Hong Kong) · Xiping Hu (Shenzhen MSU-BIT University)
Abstract
Multimodal sequential recommendation (MSR) leverages textual and visual content of items to capture the evolution of user interests over time. Prior efforts have largely concentrated on multimodal fusion strategies or downstream sequential modeling, while the question of how to obtain item representations genuinely aligned with the recommendation objective has received far less attention. Off-the-shelf encoders pretrained on generic corpora produce representations that emphasize broad semantic similarity rather than the specific cues that drive user choice in a recommendation scenario. In this work, we propose ScopeRec, a Semantic co-occurrence and personalized focus framework for multimodal sequential Recommendation, which reshapes multimodal representations from two complementary views. From the item view, items co-interacted within a behavior sequence carry rich sequence-level semantic associations, which we term semantic co-occurrence. ScopeRec mines such multi-level co-occurrence patterns directly from historical sequences and injects them back into the item representations, yielding embeddings that better reflect users' historical semantic preferences. From the user view, user attention typically concentrates on a few keywords in text or salient regions in images, which we term semantic focus. To exploit this property, ScopeRec employs a hierarchical mixture-of-experts (MoE) architecture in which different experts independently capture fine-grained interest from distinct semantic perspectives. A specialized fusion module then adaptively combines representations across modalities and semantic levels in a personalized manner. Experiments on three public MSR benchmarks show that ScopeRec consistently surpasses state-of-the-art baselines, with relative gains of 13.8% to 28.7% on NDCG and Hit Ratio.
A033FULLFedTGC: Trajectory-Guided Graph Collaboration for Federated Recommendation
Jinghao Tang (Shenzhen University) · Songbai Liu (Shenzhen University) · Lijia Ma (Shenzhen University) · Qiuzhen Lin (Shenzhen University) · Jianyong Chen (Shenzhen University) · Laizhong Cui (Shenzhen University)
Abstract
Federated recommendation preserves user privacy by keeping interaction data on local clients, but this decentralization limits direct access to cross-user collaborative signals. Existing graph-based federated recommendation methods attempt to recover such signals by constructing client relation graphs. However, our empirical analysis shows that under a temporally faithful evaluation protocol, in which negative sampling and candidate construction are restricted to information available at the recommendation cutoff, client relations constructed by existing graph-based methods can become increasingly unreliable in practice. Consequently, clients may collaborate with mismatched neighbors, thereby introducing harmful collaborative signals and causing negative transfer. To address this problem, we propose FedTGC, a trajectory-guided graph collaboration framework for reliable federated recommendation. FedTGC represents each client by its local item embedding update trajectory, constructs a dynamic client relation graph from compact trajectory descriptors, and adaptively personalizes the calibration of collaboration strength across clients. This design enables effective knowledge sharing among similar clients. Extensive experiments on five real-world datasets show that FedTGC consistently outperforms representative federated recommendation baselines under the Honest Setting. Further analyses reveal that the commonly adopted Original Setting can substantially overestimate recommendation performance, highlighting the importance of temporally faithful evaluation and validating the effectiveness of trajectory-guided collaboration. The source code is available at https://github.com/Charleston77/FedTGC.
A034FULLWhen Can Social Network Recommendations Improve Precision and Mitigate Inequality?
Elif Ece Erdem (University of Amsterdam) · Maarten de Rijke (University of Amsterdam) · Fernando P. Santos (University of Amsterdam)
Abstract
Link recommendation algorithms can reshape network topology and amplify structural inequalities through “rich-get-richer” dynamics: well-connected users may be disproportionately recommended, accumulating further connections at peripheral nodes' expense. Typical evaluations overlook how algorithmic choices interact with network topology behind this disparity. We introduce an auditing framework that isolates the effects of algorithmic design from those of network topology, on precision and structural equality. We define Equality Gain, a measure to quantify whether a recommender mitigates or amplifies structural disparities relative to a recommender-free baseline. To systematically vary topology, we introduce Counterfactual Graph Rewiring (CGR), which produces graphs with tunable clustering at a fixed degree sequence. We find that the precision–equality trade-off characterizing link-recommendation algorithms is contingent on network topology: sparse graphs exhibit a trade-off, whereas dense, highly clustered graphs admit a “win-win” regime in which models exploiting triadic closure around low-degree nodes attain both high precision and equality gains. These findings motivate a shift from model-centric optimization to network-aware link recommendation, aligning algorithmic mechanisms with network structure.
A035SHORTEvaluating Provider-Fairness Mitigation in Price-Aware Recommendation
Fernando Medina-Quispe (Universitat de Barcelona) · David Contreras Aguilar (La Salle-Universitat Ramon Llull) · Elizabeth Gómez (Fundación Universitaria María Cano) · Maria Salamó (Universitat de Barcelona) · Ludovico Boratto (University of Cagliari)
Abstract
Price-aware recommender systems incorporate economic signals into ranking, offering practical benefits but their implications for provider-side fairness remain largely unexplored. In this work, we present the first systematic evaluation of fairness mitigation in price-aware recommendation. We quantify provider-side exposure disparities across groups defined by continent, country, and price segment using three representative price-aware models on two datasets. Our analysis reveals systematic provider-side disparities, indicating that price-aware ranking can exhibit substantial provider imbalance. We then evaluate three post-processing re-ranking strategies (PFair, PFAR, and Calibration) applied to top-k recommendations to mitigate these disparities. Results show that mitigation effectiveness varies substantially across methods and settings. PFair achieves the strongest reductions for interaction-based exposure disparities, whereas PFAR is generally more effective under catalog-based reference distributions but exhibits substantial instability. Calibration remains comparatively conservative, producing only limited changes in disparity. These findings highlight the fairness risks of price-aware recommendation and show that the effectiveness of existing mitigation strategies is conditional on both the fairness reference distribution and the underlying ranking model.
A036SHORTOrthogonal Popularity Decomposition for Sequential Recommendation
Chen Yi Xu (The Chinese University of Hong Kong) · Hengyu Zhang (The Chinese University of Hong Kong) · Hong Cheng (The Chinese University of Hong Kong)
Abstract
Popularity bias is common in sequential recommenders, disproportionately favoring frequent items over long-tail ones. We identify representation anisotropy as a geometric manifestation of this bias: item embeddings collapse toward a cone whose dominant direction correlates with item frequency. To address this, we propose Orthogonal Popularity Decomposition (OPD), which introduces a learnable popularity direction and projects item embeddings onto it, isolating a popularity component from an orthogonal collaborative subspace. OPD produces a near-isotropic embedding subspace and provides an interpretable, controllable popularity prior that can be tuned at inference without retraining. Experiments on three benchmark datasets demonstrate that OPD enables controllable accuracy–fairness trade-offs and consistent performance gains across all datasets. The source code is available online.
A037SHORTT-MSDF: T-shaped Convolutional Multi-stream Discovery Framework with LLM-Driven Compatibility Priors
He Guo (Peking University) · Ruocong Tang (Alibaba Group) · Xing Fang (Alibaba Group) · Chenyi Yan (Alibaba Group) · Yang Huang (Alibaba Group) · Jing Wang (Alibaba Group) · Yipin Dai (Southeast University Nanjing) · Zhentao Song (Southeast University Nanjing)
Abstract
In modern recommender systems, the “filter bubble” effect remains a formidable challenge as models tend to over-exploit historical interactions at the expense of potential interest discovery. Although various exploration strategies have been proposed, effectively balancing prediction precision with serendipity within the ranking layer remains an open problem. To address this challenge, this paper introduces T-MSDF, a novel T-shaped convolutional Multi-stream Sequential Discovery Framework. T-MSDF leverages Large Language Models (LLMs) to construct a category affinity table that quantifies semantic complementarity between product categories, enabling the generation of augmented behavior sequences along exploration paths grounded in real-world common-sense logic. The framework consists of four synergistic components: (1) an LLM-constrained Sequence Expansion module that generates knowledge-augmented behavior streams; (2) a T-shaped Convolutional Fusion Network that harmonizes temporal evolution with spatial complementarity across behavior streams; (3) an Interest Decoupling and Alignment scheme, which disentangles convergent preferences from divergent exploration signals via residual extraction and discovery-aware contrastive learning; and (4) an Adaptive Gated Fusion Network, which dynamically weights the decoupled interest representations to prioritize serendipitous recommendations without compromising ranking precision. Extensive offline evaluations and online A/B tests on a large-scale industrial platform demonstrate that T-MSDF significantly improves key discovery metrics, achieving a +5.92% increase in Discovery Rate (DR) and a +6.15% lift in Discovery-CTR, alongside notable growth in CTR (+1.18%) and GMV (+2.30%).
A038SHORTCan Large Language Models Identify Meaningful Touchpoints in Conversion Attribution?
Jinqi Wu (Nanjing University) · Sishuo Chen (Taobao & Tmall Group of Alibaba) · Zhangming Chan (Taobao & Tmall Group of Alibaba) · Yong Bai (Taobao & Tmall Group of Alibaba) · Chao Yi (Taobao & Tmall Group of Alibaba) · Han Zhu (Taobao & Tmall Group of Alibaba) · Shuodian Yu (Taobao & Tmall Group of Alibaba) · Lei Zhang (Taobao & Tmall Group of Alibaba) · Sheng Chen (Taobao & Tmall Group of Alibaba) · Chenghuan Hou (Taobao & Tmall Group of Alibaba) · Jian Xu (Taobao & Tmall Group of Alibaba) · Chaoyou Fu (Nanjing University)
Abstract
Touchpoint selection in conversion attribution, namely identifying meaningful touchpoints contributing to conversions, is essential for e-commerce recommendation and online advertising. Current selection methods rely heavily on collaborative-filtering-based heuristics, which fail to align with user-perceived semantic intent. Through human annotation, we reveal a significant semantic gap: many implicitly-related, semantically relevant touchpoints remain undetected by existing rules. Therefore, we systematically evaluate the capability of Large Language Models (LLMs) in identifying these hidden associations. Our evaluation shows that while LLMs effectively uncover a substantial portion of implicitly-related touchpoints, significant room for improvement remains in their selection performance. Furthermore, we analyze the impact of different prompting strategies and foundation model choices on identification performance, providing valuable insights into their reasoning patterns and effectiveness. These insights offer a new roadmap for transitioning conversion attribution from mechanical rule-matching to human-aligned semantic reasoning. Moreover, we leverage the LLM-attributed conversion labels for enhancing industrial CVR model training and achieve significant offline performance gains, showing the potential of LLMs in conversion attribution.
A039FULLFollow the COMPASS: Reasoning-Guided Advertiser Bid Modeling for Campaign Simulation under Auction Dynamics
Xiaoyu Wang (The Graduate University for Advanced Studies, SOKENDAI) · Yonghui Guo (Tencent Advertising) · Sheng Yao (Tencent Advertising) · Zhikun Wang (Tencent Advertising) · Weikun Lin (Tencent Advertising) · Weicheng Feng (Tencent Advertising) · Angzhan Wen (Tencent Advertising) · Peiwen Pan (Tencent Advertising) · Pengyu Zheng (Tencent Advertising) · Gong Chen (Tencent Advertising) · Kensuke Fukuda (National Institute of Informatics) · Yusheng Ji (National Institute of Informatics)
Abstract
Advertisers launch ad campaigns to bid for potential customers and promote sales. In uncertain auction environments, accurate campaign performance forecasting (CPF) can help advertisers navigate toward efficient campaign configurations and successful marketing, much like a compass. However, existing CPF methods largely neglect auction dynamics, where competitors adjust their bids in response to evolving campaign states. Conventional log-driven models, which directly fit observable states to bid actions, overlook the deliberate reasoning process underlying advertiser behavior, leading to suboptimal forecasts. To fill the gap, we propose COMPASS, a reasoning-driven framework for modeling bid behavior during ad campaigns. COMPASS explicitly treats bid reasoning as a latent variable and progressively infers it under a Search-Optimization framework. Instead of a naive brute-force search, COMPASS adopts a hierarchical inference strategy: a high-capacity schema model searches over compact, high-level bid strategies, while a lightweight execution model expands them into concrete bid predictions and provides evaluation feedback. To simplify online deployment, we further propose an alignment-as-distillation mechanism with a self-evaluation trick. This avoids a separate knowledge distillation stage and produces a self-contained execution model that can be independently deployed without invoking the schema model at serving time. Extensive experiments on industrial and public datasets demonstrate the effectiveness of COMPASS. In large-scale online A/B tests, COMPASS achieves a 5.1% uplift in average revenue per user, validating its practical impact in real-world advertising systems.
A040FULLUncertainty-Triggered Test-Time Selective Inference for Click-Through Rate Prediction
Moyu Zhang (Alibaba Group) · Yun Chen (Alibaba Group) · Yujun Jin (Alibaba Group) · Jinxin Hu (Alibaba Group) · Yu Zhang (Alibaba Group) · Xiaoyi Zeng (Alibaba Group)
Abstract
Click-through rate (CTR) models estimate the probability of a user clicking on an item and exhibit varying prediction reliability across instances at inference time. Some feature combinations of model input are well-represented in training data and yield confident outputs, while others produce high uncertainty due to feature combination sparsity. Training-time approaches such as adaptive gating mechanisms learn a deterministic feature selection function, but this function is itself unreliable for under-observed combinations since it suffers from the same sparsity problem. More fundamentally, training and inference have asymmetric objectives: training benefits from diverse pattern exposure including sparse ones to learn generalizable representations, whereas inference should prioritize only combinations the model has already learned to evaluate reliably. This asymmetry motivates test-time optimization as a complementary paradigm. Rather than relying on a single learned function, test-time optimization explores multiple feature configurations per instance and aggregates predictions, deriving robustness from exploration diversity. By deferring computation decisions until the actual instance is observed, it further enables selective budget allocation that invests extra resources only in uncertain samples. However, CTR models with binary objectives lack built-in mechanisms for per-instance uncertainty assessment, and strict industrial latency constraints leave limited room for additional computation. Therefore, we propose a model-agnostic training-free Uncertainty-Triggered Test-Time Selective Inference framework (UTTSI) that operates directly on any already-trained CTR model without modifying its parameters. UTTSI estimates per-instance uncertainty via dual signals combining model logit confidence with a frequency-based prior, and selectively triggers feature path exploration only for uncertain samples, with the majority of confident instances served at zero additional cost. Finally, extensive experiments strongly validate the effectiveness of UTTSI.
A041SHORTContext-Aware User Intent Modeling for Relevant Recommendation in E-commerce
Dike Sun (Alibaba Group) · Zheng Zou (Alibaba Group) · Jingtong Zang (Alibaba Group) · Zhu Jiahui (Alibaba Group) · Qi Sun (Alibaba Group) · Rui Ma (Alibaba Group) · Huaipeng Zhao (Alibaba Group) · Tao Luo (Alibaba Group) · Xiaoyi Zeng (Alibaba Group)
Abstract
Relevant recommendation is essential for e-commerce conversion and is typically initiated by a user-clicked trigger item. However, user intent is inherently dynamic and multifaceted. Existing methods with static trigger representations cannot adequately capture real-time intent drift or disentangle fine-grained preferences such as brand versus category. We propose Context-Aware User Intent Modeling (CAIM) to address these limitations. CAIM incorporates an Intention Enhancement Module (IEM) that integrates real-time context to dynamically reconstruct the trigger representation, serving as an adaptive anchor. An Intention Retrieval Module (IRM) retrieves relevant long-term user behaviors, while a Sub-intention Extraction Module (SIEM) decomposes the overall intent into attribute-level sub-intentions. Experiments on industrial datasets show that CAIM outperforms state-of-the-art baselines. Deployed in a large-scale e-commerce platform under strict latency constraints, CAIM yields a 6.9% increase in orders and a 7.7% increase in Gross Merchandise Value (GMV), validating its effectiveness and practical applicability.
A042APPLIEDResolving Price-Segment Blindspot in Search Ranking for Value-Driven Marketplaces
Shubhendu Pandey (Meesho) · Satyendra Yadav (Meesho) · Virri Pranav (Meesho) · Sagnik Sarkar (Meesho) · Bhavuk Singhal (Meesho) · Abhay Shukla (Meesho) · Ravindra Kumar Yadav (Meesho) · Debdoot Mukherjee (Meesho)
Abstract
On value-driven marketplaces, user-product interactions concentrate heavily around affordable products. Search ranking systems trained on such engagement data therefore learn relevance patterns that primarily reflect the preferences of the dominant value conscious user cohort, limiting their ability to accurately personalize results for users whose intent aligns with relatively higher-priced products. We refer to this failure mode as the Price-Segment Blindspot. This challenge cannot be addressed through static promotion of higher-priced products, because price preference is highly contextual. A value-conscious user may occasionally search for an expensive “silk saree” before a wedding, while users with affinity toward high-priced products may still prefer inexpensive products for routine purchases. Effective ranking therefore requires modeling latent user affinity and real-time query intent to infer when different price segments are relevant. We address this challenge by incorporating user-level affinity and query-level intent signals into a production ranking system. However, on-platform interactions alone provide weak evidence of user's price-segment affinity due to sparse interactions in higher price segment. To address this sparsity, we augment the user affinity model with off-platform behavioral signals that better capture user spending patterns. In a three-week A/B experiment on the Meesho platform with ∼300 million monthly active users, our approach improved the GMVc (Gross Merchandise Value Contribution) of the High Price-Segment products by 5.92% and orders by 6.32%, while keeping the overall O/Vi (Orders-per-Viewer) nearly flat +0.06%.
A043SHORTLearning from What You Retrieve: Online RL Fine-Tuning for Semantic Retrieval
Shaowei Wei (Alibaba Group) · Chong Huang (Alibaba Group) · Songtao Fang (Alibaba Group) · Jin Zhang (Alibaba Group) · Zhuojun Wang (Alibaba Group) · Chengfu Huo (Alibaba Group)
Abstract
In large-scale e-commerce retrieval, dual-encoder retrievers are optimized for contrastive similarity, whereas downstream rerankers capture finer-grained relevance preferences; this objective mismatch limits end-to-end retrieval quality. Reinforcement Learning offers a way to use reward-model feedback for retriever adaptation, but we observe that standard policy-gradient updates can degrade embedding geometry, especially when the document index must remain frozen due to industrial constraints. To address this, we propose PAO (Positive-Advantage-Only), a selective RL optimization method. Our analysis reveals that indiscriminate penalization of negative samples (pushing away) in a frozen high-dimensional space disrupts pre-trained semantic manifolds. PAO selectively applies gradient updates only to retrieved items with positive advantages, effectively pulling query embeddings toward high-reward regions while preserving global topological stability. Experiments on both a massive industrial dataset and public benchmarks demonstrate that PAO significantly outperforms standard RL and distillation baselines.
A044SHORTUnleashing the Power of LLMs in Dense Retrieval with Query Likelihood Modeling
Hengran Zhang (State Key Laboratory of AI Safety) · Keping Bi (State Key Laboratory of AI Safety) · Jiafeng Guo (State Key Laboratory of AI Safety) · Xiaojie Sun (State Key Laboratory of AI Safety) · Shihao Liu (Baidu Inc) · Daiting Shi (Baidu Inc) · Dawei Yin (Baidu Inc) · Xueqi Cheng (Institute of Computing Technology, Chinese Academy of Sciences)
Abstract
Dense retrieval is a fundamental task in Information Retrieval (IR), forming the foundation for downstream applications such as re-ranking and augmenting generation. Recently, large language models (LLMs) have exhibited remarkable semantic understanding capabilities, drawing significant interest from researchers in dense retrieval. While LLMs, as decoder-style generative models, excel in language generation, they often struggle to capture global information due to their lack of attention to subsequent tokens. Motivated by the classical word-based language modeling approach in IR, particularly the query likelihood (QL) model, we seek to exploit the generative advantages of LLMs through QL maximization. Instead of using QL estimation directly for document ranking, we introduce QL maximization as an auxiliary task to strengthen the backbone, thereby facilitating the subsequent contrastive learning of the retriever. We introduce our model, LLM-QL, which incorporates two key components: Attention Block (AB) and Document Corruption (DC). AB blocks the attention of predictive tokens to the document tokens before the document's ending token, while DC corrupts a document by masking a portion of its tokens during prediction. Evaluations on the in-domain (MS MARCO) and out-of-domain dataset (BEIR) indicate LLM-QL's superiority over other LLM-based retrievers. Furthermore, comprehensive analyses also validate the efficacy of LLM-QL and its components.
A045FULLGenerate to Accelerate: Improved Reranking via LLM-Generated Pivot Documents
Nilanjan Sinhababu (Indian Institute of Technology Kharagpur) · Soumedhik Bharati (Mohamed bin Zayed University of Artificial Intelligence) · Debasis Ganguly (University of Glasgow) · Pabitra Mitra (Indian Institute of Technology Kharagpur)
Abstract
Common approaches to reduce the computational overhead of reranking models include identifying a candidate set of documents for reranking or constructing comparison graphs to minimize redundant comparisons. For pointwise rankers, determining a candidate set typically involves estimating a query-dependent cutoff based on the scores of the top-ranked documents. In contrast, comparison graphs for listwise approaches are often derived using heuristics, such as propagating local comparisons within sliding windows in a bottom-up fashion or reducing comparisons via pivot-based strategies in a top-down manner. In this work, we argue that restricting these processes to existing documents in the collection is unnecessary. Instead, we propose leveraging the generative capabilities of large language models to synthesize a pseudo-relevant document for a given query. We then adapt existing reranking approaches and also propose a novel parallel reranking approach to leverage this LLM-generated document as a pivot. Our experiments demonstrate that using LLM-generated pivots for ranked list truncation reduces the number of pointwise ranker inferences by up to 66%. In both in-domain and out-of-domain settings, we observe speedups of up to 2.95× in listwise reranking, while maintaining comparable or improved retrieval effectiveness.
A046SHORTOn Non-Relevance Signals in Pointwise LLM-based Reranking
Akihiro Katsuno (NTT, Inc.) · Yuichiro Okugawa (NTT, Inc.) · Toshimitsu Tanaka (NTT, Inc.) · Tomomi Nagao (NTT, Inc.) · Hiroaki Kawata (NTT, Inc.)
Abstract
Pointwise reranking with large language models (LLMs) evaluates query-document pairs independently and allows parallel processing, but it often struggles with absolute relevance estimation. In this work, we investigate whether non-relevance prompting provides a signal that differs from ordinary relevance prompting in LLM-based pointwise reranking. Specifically, we compute both relevance and non-relevance scores for each query-passage pair and examine two simple ways to combine them: (1) a simple product and (2) a probability-weighted RMSE to the ideal label targets. We evaluate these scores on 10 datasets from TREC and BEIR using nDCG@10 with GPT-4o-mini and Llama-3.1-8B-Instruct. With GPT-4o-mini, bidirectional scoring significantly improves over relevance-only scoring and achieves performance comparable to RankGPT, although gains over a two-prompt relevance-only control are not statistically significant. Further analysis on highly relevant DL19 pairs shows that flipped non-relevance scores often raise the scores of documents underestimated by the relevance prompt. In contrast, the effectiveness of using non-relevance scores for Llama varies across datasets, suggesting that the utility of non-relevance prompting is model-dependent.
A047FULLWhen Do Anchor-Based Pointwise LLM Rerankers Help? Retriever Quality, Statistical Scope, and Anchor Design
Utshab Kumar Ghosh (Missouri University of Science and Technology) · Shubham Chatterjee (Missouri University of Science and Technology)
Abstract
Anchor-based pointwise LLM reranking scores each candidate against a shared reference passage to recover cross-document context at pointwise cost. We study when this actually helps, using GCCP/PAGC as a representative method. Our study is reproduction-first. We use reproduction as a starting point for a controlled component-level stress test of anchor-based pointwise reranking. Our initial reimplementation, based only on the paper text, achieves 0.24 nDCG@10 instead of the reported 0.66, revealing that several undocumented implementation details are necessary to reproduce the method. After identifying and recovering eight such details, we reproduce the reported results within 1.6% and use the validated implementation for controlled analysis. We find that the core contrastive scoring idea is robust under rigorous statistical correction. However, two design choices held fixed in the original paper are less reliable. First, we find that combining the contrastive score with the standard pointwise relevance score helps when the first-stage retriever is BM25, but gives little or no benefit when the first-stage retriever is a stronger dense model such as E5. Second, the paper's more complex method for constructing the anchor is unnecessary. A much simpler anchor, built by interleaving the top-ranked sentences, matches or outperforms it across datasets. These findings are consistent across different LLM backbones, including a 4-bit quantized 72B model. Overall, anchor-based pointwise reranking is effective, but its gains come mainly from contrastive scoring rather than from the more complex aggregation and anchor-construction choices, and they appear under narrower conditions than the original evaluation suggests.
A048SHORTDifficulty-Gated Fusion of Reasoning Views for Temporal Retrieval
Jamie Holdcroft (UNSW Sydney) · Abdelrahman Abdallah (University of Innsbruck) · Adam Jatowt (University of Innsbruck)
Abstract
Reasoning-intensive temporal retrieval requires matching a query to documents whose relevance depends on shared temporal reasoning rather than lexical overlap. Expanding a query into several reformulations that make its temporal intent explicit, and retrieving with each, supplies this reasoning, but fusing the resulting rankings with equal weights wastes accuracy: for any single query, only some reformulations are reliable. We propose query-difficulty-gated fusion of reasoning views. From each view we read an eight-dimensional signature of its score distribution, built from query-performance-prediction quantities such as softmax entropy, score gaps, and dispersion, and a gate of roughly one thousand parameters maps these signatures to per-query view weights. The fused ranking uses no relevance labels at inference, no re-ranking, and no fine-tuning of the retriever; the gate is trained leave-one-task-out. On the Tempo benchmark, the method improves all six retrievers we evaluate, from BERT encoders to 7B decoder retrievers, with the largest gains on the weaker backbones. The strongest retrievers reach 0.297 and 0.303 nDCG@10, and the per-query gain over the original query is significant under a paired bootstrap (p<0.001). A per-query oracle reaches 0.364 against our realized 0.297, exposing headroom that identifies per-query view selection as a concrete next step (https://github.com/DataScienceUIBK/difficulty-gated-reasoning-view-fusion).
A049SHORTLearning to Act, Failing to Retrieve: Diagnosing Reward-Effectiveness Mismatch in Proactive Conversational Information Retrieval
Haoyan Zhang (Dublin City University) · Gareth J. F. Jones (Maynooth University)
Abstract
Proactive conversational information retrieval (CIR) requires an agent to decide not only what to retrieve, but how to act: when to ask the user for clarification, when to issue a new retrieval, and when to reuse evidence it has already gathered. We study this as a sequential dialogue-management problem over Ask, Push, and Reuse. We train the interaction policy with reinforcement learning in an LLM-driven environment providing user simulation, query reformulation, and a relevance judge that scores the training reward; evaluation instead uses held-out human relevance judgements (qrels). The resulting agent learns coherent, state-dependent behaviour and accumulates high shaped reward, yet its qrel-based retrieval effectiveness (nDCG, MAP) falls at or below simple non-learned baselines on iKAT. We argue that this reflects a reward–effectiveness mismatch: the shaped reward, scored by an LLM judge and crediting cheap reuse of buffered evidence, is only loosely coupled to held-out qrel effectiveness. We localize this mismatch to reward design and show that replacing the dialogue-shaped signal with a retrieval-gain-aligned reward recovers much of the gap to the strongest non-learned baseline—roughly doubling nDCG@10 and MAP, with the residual gap traced to clarification quality—suggesting that reward formulation is a key lever for aligning proactive dialogue behaviour with retrieval quality.
A050SHORTDistributional Approximate Nearest Neighbour Search for Uncertainty-Aware Retrieval
Olivier Jeunen (Independent Researcher)
Abstract
Approximate Nearest Neighbour search indices form the backbone of real-world recommender systems, enabling real-time candidate retrieval over million-item catalogues. Typically, a single point estimate embedding is learnt for every user and every item. At serving time, the user embedding queries the index for relevant items. Since these representations are learnt from sparse interaction data, they are noisy and might fail to capture all the nuances that contribute to “relevance”—ignoring the fundamental uncertainty that is inherent to them. The result is a retrieval pipeline that is systematically biased toward the small minority of popular head items with well-estimated embeddings, at the expense of the long-tail majority of niche, diverse, and serendipitous content. We propose dinosaur (Distributional Approximate Nearest Neighbour Search for Uncertainty-Aware Retrieval): a simple and infrastructure-compatible framework to incorporate embedding uncertainty into candidate generation. Rather than indexing point estimates, dinosaur samples Si embeddings per item and constructs an index on this augmented set. Analogously, at query time, a user embedding is sampled. This two-sided stochastic retrieval process implicitly marginalises over embedding uncertainty, without requiring changes to model architecture or ANN index infrastructure. On the analytical side, we show that dinosaur recovers standard point-estimate retrieval as uncertainty vanishes, and we characterise how increased embedding variance expands the regions of latent space in which uncertain items are retrievable. Reproducible empirical observations align with these expectations, showing large coverage gains with small losses in offline recall.
A051FULLASH: Asymmetric Scalar Hashing With Learned Dimensionality Reduction for High-Fidelity Vector Quantization
Mariano Tepper (Elastic) · Theodore Willke (IBM)
Abstract
For a long time, additive quantizers, such as product quantization, have been considered the gold standard in terms of accuracy and efficiency. Recently, scalar quantization has re-emerged from the depths of history with a new wave of data-agnostic techniques. Inscribed in this general framework, we turn our attention to data-driven methods, showing that new highs in recall and speed can be achieved by reducing the number of dimensions while increasing the bitrate per dimension. Critically, this dimensionality reduction needs to be learned from data to be successful. We present ASH (Asymmetric Scalar Hashing), a data-driven encoder-decoder framework that applies dimensionality reduction to database vectors via a learned orthonormal projection, followed by scalar quantization, while keeping queries in their original form. This asymmetric design enables higher accuracy than the best additive and scalar quantizers at iso-compression, while admitting highly efficient similarity computations via SIMD operations. ASH has short learning and encoding times, making it attractive for real-world deployment. Extensive experiments on a variety of datasets demonstrate that ASH achieves state-of-the-art ANN recall and speeds across all compression regimes.
A052RESOURCEA Resource for Evaluating Creative Search on the Infinite Index
Niklas Deckers (University of Kassel and hessian.AI) · Aleyna Albayrak (University of Kassel) · Klara M. Gutekunst (University of Kassel and hessian.AI) · Paul Hahn (University of Münster) · Henry Plutz (Bauhaus-Universität Weimar) · Moritz Wirth (University of Kassel) · Martin Potthast (University of Kassel, hessian.AI and ScaDS.AI)
Abstract
Iterative generative systems can refine generated content, such as images or text, based on an initial prompt and user feedback. Iterative refinement helps users solve creative tasks that cannot be addressed reliably through ad-hoc prompt engineering alone. However, reproducible evaluation of such systems is challenging because user interactions induce branching during annotation. We propose a method for formulating topic descriptions for interactive scenarios, inspired by classic Cranfield-style topics. We also provide guidelines for creating reproducible topics that pose meaningful challenges to the evaluated systems and build a dataset of abstract concepts that are used to formulate topics on the domain of creative image generation. We formulate a workflow for the validation of these topics and enable the evaluation of current and future iterative generative systems.
A053FULLTransforming User Actions into Audit Signals: Participatory Auditing to Improve Search Results
Zeyan Liang (University of Glasgow) · Graham McDonald (University of Glasgow) · Iadh Ounis (University of Glasgow)
Abstract
Regulatory frameworks, such as the European Union's Digital Services Act (DSA), have established new directives for the governance of online platforms, including Information Retrieval (IR) systems. In particular, the DSA mandates that IR systems should enable stakeholders, such as users, to independently audit the outputs of the system, for example, with respect to ranking quality or fairness. Moreover, users should be able to provide actionable feedback to the system's providers. In this work, we introduce a participatory audit strategy that transforms natural user interactions into actionable signals for identifying and correcting ranking errors, i.e., documents that have been systematically undervalued in the search results. We show that our strategy provides actionable feedback that can be used to improve the overall relevance of highly ranked documents. Our strategy uses a 3x3 grid presentation with 9x9 Latin-square counterbalancing as an unbiased audit interface, enabling auditors to identify ranking errors through their natural search behaviours. We evaluate our strategy with 108 participants across a Participatory Audit and separate Evaluation, complemented by an independent offline evaluation. Our findings show that our approach enables users to easily identify relevant documents that are ranked at lower positions by the system. We also show that these audit signals (the user's clicks and brief passage selections, collected while participants engage with the audit interface) can be used to rerank the results, and that the reranking elicits deeper user engagement. Our audit strategy produces measurable improvements in both online (user engagement) and offline (nDCG@10) evaluations. For example, participants preferred 6.7% of low-ranked documents identified by our strategy over every top-ranked document from the original ranking. We show that a reranking based on the obtained audit signals resulted in a statistically significant 6.81% relative gain in nDCG@10, according to a Bonferroni-corrected paired bootstrap test, with passage selection rates rising 6.1 percentage points in our online evaluation.
A054RESOURCELLMJudge: Meta-Evaluating Automatic Relevance Judgments
Hossein A. Rahmani (University College London) · Clemencia Siro (University of Amsterdam) · Mohammad Aliannejadi (University of Amsterdam) · Nick Craswell (Microsoft) · Charles L. A. Clarke (University of Waterloo) · Guglielmo Faggioli (University of Padua) · Bhaskar Mitra (Independent Researcher) · Paul Thomas (Microsoft) · Emine Yilmaz (University College London)
Abstract
Large language models (LLMs) are increasingly used to produce the relevance labels that underpin the evaluation of information retrieval (IR) and retrieval-augmented generation systems. Yet delegating relevance assessment to an LLM raises a meta-evaluation question that is hard to answer with existing resources: when, and how much, can we trust an automatic judge? We present LLMJudge, a resource for meta-evaluating LLM-generated relevance judgments. LLMJudge collects 42 complete judgment sets over the TREC 2023 Deep Learning track, spanning fine-tuned, proprietary, and open-source models and a wide range of prompting strategies. Each judgment set is paired with official human qrels, enabling two complementary axes of analysis: label agreement with human assessors (e.g., Cohen’s κ, Krippendorff’s α) and system-ranking fidelity (e.g., Kendall’s τ, Spearman’s ρ). Beyond the data, we release a standardized format, baselines, and an evaluation harness so that new judges can be plugged in and compared reproducibly. Our analysis shows that high label agreement is neither necessary nor sufficient for faithful system ranking, that open-source judges are markedly more stable than proprietary ones, and that fine-tuning improves correlation at the cost of reliability. LLMJudge is publicly available and provides a reusable testbed for auditing the judges who increasingly judge our systems. Full resources, data, and detailed results are available at https://llm4eval.github.io/LLMJudge-benchmark/.
A055RESOURCELEDGER: A Long-Context Benchmark of Corporate Annual Reports for Grounded Financial Retrieval and Extraction
Charles Moslonka (Artefact Research Center) · Amaury de Vitry (Artefact Research Center) · Arthur Garnier (Ardian) · Hicham Randrianarivo (Artefact Research Center) · Emmanuel Malherbe (Artefact Research Center)
Abstract
Finance reporting is a natural proving ground for large language models, and the very-long-context capabilities of recent models across all sizes make rigorous evaluation in this domain an increasingly pressing need. Yet most public financial resources reduce the task to plain-text SEC 10-K filings paired with a handful of question–answer items. We release Ledger (Long-context Evaluation of Documents for Grounded Extraction and Retrieval), a corpus of 4,999 digitized corporate annual reports — full documents with figures, tables, and narrative, not just regulatory filings. Each report is labeled with 31 consolidated financial KPIs to be extracted and linked to the market's reaction at the earnings date. From this data we derive three evaluation benchmarks spanning the difficulty spectrum: a pure page-level KPI retrieval task with TREC-style relevance judgments over 118,048 questions in natural language, a conversational “needle-in-a-haystack” single-value lookup, and a full KPI extraction task, both from long, numerically dense reports. We additionally provide human OCR-quality annotations with inter-annotator agreement and the complete extraction, validation, and scoring toolchain. We further demonstrate the dataset's research utility with a case study linking CEO-letter rhetoric to post-publication market impact. An extension to 291 French ESEF filers (1,153 reports with 24 KPIs) augments the corpus.
A056SHORTAdaMerge: Tuning-Free Patch Compression for Multi-Vector Visual Document Retrieval
Jianxin You (Université de Montréal) · Kun Ni (Concordia University)
Abstract
Multi-vector visual document retrieval (VDR) models such as ColPali and ColNomic achieve strong accuracy by representing each document with hundreds to thousands of patch-level embeddings, at substantial storage and latency cost. Existing compression methods either prune unimportant patches or merge similar ones into clusters; the recent state-of-the-art merging method Prune-then-Merge (PtM) consistently outperforms pruning-only baselines at high compression, but requires a per-dataset cluster budget m to be tuned by grid search. We observe that the merge-cosine sequence produced by hierarchical clustering exhibits a sharp cliff separating mergeable redundancy from salient signal, and that the location of this cliff is concentrated in a narrow band across more than 11,000 documents from 14 datasets. This suggests the merge boundary can be detected per document rather than tuned per dataset. Building on this observation, we propose AdaMerge, a plug-and-play compression method that (i) detects each document's own cliff via gap analysis on the merge-cosine trajectory, and (ii) builds attention-weighted cluster centroids to preserve salient signal. On the long-document benchmark ViDoRe-V2 (4 datasets, two backbones), AdaMerge significantly outperforms tuned PtM across the operating range (p < 10^-4); on the short-document benchmark ViDoRe-V1 (10 datasets, two backbones), where all merging methods are already near-lossless, AdaMerge matches tuned PtM without any per-dataset tuning. AdaMerge adds only about 10 ms per document and exposes a single global hyperparameter shared across all datasets and backbones.
A057FULLScalability Analysis of Cross-modal Text-to-Image Pipelines
Sanskar S. Singh (Indian Institute of Technology Delhi) · Ziv Barretto (Ashoka University) · Bharati Khanijo (Esri) · Aditya Sahu (Indian Institute of Technology Delhi) · Maya Ramanath (Indian Institute of Technology Delhi)
Abstract
Cross-modal text-to-image retrieval systems are increasingly deployed over large-scale multimedia corpora, where retrieval effectiveness must be balanced against latency, energy consumption, storage, and candidate fidelity under approximate indexing. In this paper, we present a systems-level evaluation of text-to-image retrieval pipelines under realistic deployment constraints. We study representative single-index, retrieve-and-rerank, and ensemble pipelines on MS-COCO and Flickr30K, and evaluate their scalability on a 7M-image subset of LAION using Flat, HNSW, IVFPQ, and O-IVFPQ indexes. Our results show that strong rerankers can preserve retrieval quality provided the first-stage ANN index maintains sufficient candidate fidelity, but that low-fidelity indexes create unrecoverable candidate losses. At LAION scale, O-IVFPQ provides the strongest single-index operating point, maintaining high candidate fidelity while reducing latency, energy, and storage relative to HNSW. For retrieve-and-rerank pipelines, the reranker dominates end-to-end latency and energy, making index choice less important once sufficient candidate fidelity is preserved. Overall, our study shows that scalable cross-modal retrieval requires joint reasoning about pipeline architecture, candidate fidelity, and systems cost.
A058SHORTNo Target-Language LLM? Simple English-Side Augmentations for Cross-Lingual Cross-Modal Retrieval
Rui Cai (Zhejiang Gongshang University) · Yunlong Dai (Zhejiang Gongshang University) · Jianfeng Dong (Zhejiang Gongshang University) · Xun Wang (Zhejiang Gongshang University)
Abstract
Cross-lingual cross-modal retrieval (CCR) for low-resource languages typically relies on machine-translated (MT) captions that lack diversity and carry language-specific flaws. Recent work addresses this by enriching queries with more detailed visual descriptions via multimodal LLMs and complex alignment. We instead take a data-centric view: rather than adding richer semantics, making existing supervision more challenging and diverse better strengthens the target-language encoder, without requiring any target-language LLM. Specifically, we design two lightweight English-side augmentation strategies: semantic perturbation to construct hard negatives, and semantic-preserving rewriting to foster expression robustness. Generated once in English and shared across target languages via MT, our approach is both broadly applicable and cost-efficient. An adaptive selection mechanism chooses the most suitable perturbation per sample, while a visual-guided weighting down-weights noisy rewrites. Experiments on standard CCR benchmarks show consistent improvements across target languages, confirming that simple English-side augmentations effectively boost CCR.
A059SHORTQuery-Adaptive Statutory Evidence Construction for Statutory Question Answering
Taisei Hirayama (Hokkaido University) · Akihiro Matsufuji (Panasonic Electric Works Co., Ltd.) · Yoshifumi Hirose (Panasonic Electric Works Co., Ltd.) · Hiroki Sakaji (Hokkaido University) · Itsuki Noda (Hokkaido University)
Abstract
In statutory question answering, a provision similar to the question may define an exclusion by citing other provisions elsewhere in the statute. Correct answers may therefore require scope context around the retrieved provision, other provisions listed alongside it, or provisions cited by number elsewhere in the statute. Most retrieval-augmented generation approaches either enlarge the retrieved chunk or apply a fixed neighborhood expansion. These strategies can miss provisions cited by number or include unrelated intervening text in the answer model's context. We exploit chapter, section, and article hierarchy plus parsed citation links to construct compact statutory evidence. From a single retrieved provision, the method follows only the relations the question needs: scope context, remaining items of an enumerated list, or specific cited provisions.
