We build a bilingual Japanese and English QA dataset covering these evidence types. On this QA dataset, the method gives the highest overall necessary-evidence coverage and final answer score among the tested baselines, with the clearest gains on citation-target questions. It also uses about half the broad-expansion context.
A060APPLIEDScalable Organization-Specific Language Model Adaptation for Multi-Tenant Enterprise Search
Apoorva Uday Nayak (Atlassian US, Inc.) · Chun-Chen Tu (Atlassian US, Inc.) · Hareen Venigalla (Atlassian US, Inc.) · Jianshu Ji (Atlassian US, Inc.) · Longfei Zhang (Atlassian US, Inc.)
Abstract
In multi-tenant (An architecture where a single, shared instance of software and infrastructure serves multiple independent customers (“tenants”). It maximizes resource efficiency and lowers costs, while relying on strict data isolation and access controls to keep each tenant's data secure and invisible to others. In this work, multi-tenancy refers only to shared infrastructure. It does not involve cross-organization training, gradient sharing, parameter mixing, or any form of data pooling across tenants. Every per-organization model is trained exclusively on its own organization’s data.) enterprise search, every organization brings proprietary jargon, domain-specific acronyms, entity relationships, and behavioral patterns that general-purpose language models systematically fail to capture. Bridging this organizational knowledge gap with full-parameter models is intractable at scale and further complicated by challenges unique to the multi-tenant enterprise setting: (i) strict tenant isolation at both training and serving time, (ii) eye-off development workflows that prohibit human inspection of data and customer content, (iii) cross-region data residency constraints, and (iv) scaling per-organization training to hundreds of tenants without linearly increasing inference overhead. We present a scalable system that addresses these challenges through a four-stage pipeline: (1) initialization from a pre-trained cross-encoder, (2) full-parameter masked language modeling (MLM) continual pre-training on an internal first-party corpus, (3) per-organization MLM adaptation via Low-Rank Adaptation (LoRA) on individual organization document corpora, and (4) joint per-organization LoRA ranking fine-tuning with a feature interaction layer trained on approximately 200 million behavioral query–document pairs. The underlying production infrastructure enforces security and governance (tenant isolation, eye-off development workflows, and data residency). A shared backbone serves hundreds of organizations on one GPU by routing requests to statically compiled organization-specific bundles. Online experiments show a 4.2% improvement in Query Success Rate (QSR) across 200 organizations, with MLM adaptation yielding a further 4.8% QSR improvement over ranking-only within a selected cohort of 20 organizations.
A061SHORTSCAR: Semantic Continuity-Aware Retrieval for Efficient Context Expansion in RAG
Nathanaël Langlois (Horizon Flow)
Abstract
Fixed-length chunking in Retrieval-Augmented Generation (RAG) often leads to boundary fragmentation, where critical evidence is split across segments, degrading retrieval recall. While static windowing and parent retrieval improve recall, they introduce significant token overhead. We propose SCAR (Semantic Continuity-Aware Retrieval), an adaptive retrieval policy that selectively expands neighboring chunks by weighing query-neighbor relevance against a structural continuity penalty. SCAR uses a relative expansion threshold tied to each retrieved chunk's own query-relevance, yielding an approximately scale-invariant decision rule that transfers across embedding models without recalibration. Across four diverse corpora (RFC, GDPR, a 10-K report, and a Merger agreement; N=320 queries; 160 boundary-fragmented), SCAR achieves 92.8% recall on boundary-fragmented queries with only 7.84 chunks, a 22.9% reduction compared to static windowing (10.16 chunks). Paired bootstrap tests (B=10,000) confirm the chunk reduction is highly significant (p<0.0001, Cohen's d=-1.49, large effect), with a small recall difference (Cohen's d=-0.33). The policy transfers across three embedding models (text-embedding-3-large, BGE-large-en-v1.5, zembed-1) using the same single hyperparameter setting, and downstream RAGAS evaluation on the 10-K corpus confirms SCAR preserves generation faithfulness while reducing context tokens by 27.1%.
A062SHORTFailSafe-RAG: Evidence-State-Aware Generation under Retrieval Failures
Wanjie Tao (Mashang Consumer Finance Co., Ltd) · Qun Dai (Nanjing University of Aeronautics and Astronautics) · Quan Lu (Mashang Consumer Finance Co., Ltd) · Ning Jiang (Mashang Consumer Finance Co., Ltd) · Zulong Chen (Alibaba Group)
Abstract
Retrieval-augmented generation (RAG) improves factual grounding by conditioning language models on retrieved evidence, but its reliability depends on whether the retrieved list is relevant, consistent, and semantically grounded. When retrieval fails under coverage gaps, conflicting passages, or lexical matching traps, generators may still produce definitive but unsupported answers. We propose FailSafe-RAG, a lightweight and training-free framework that treats retrieval failure as an explicit post-retrieval evidence state. Inspired by Query Performance Prediction (QPP) and retrieval-list coherence analysis, FailSafe-RAG estimates three evidence-risk indicators: coverage insufficiency, conflict risk, and evidence noise. A risk-prioritized policy maps the resulting risk state to behavior-conditioned generation, enabling clarification, abstention, cautious answering, or direct assertion without model fine-tuning or architectural changes. Experiments on failure-oriented splits derived from NQ, HotpotQA, and conflict-annotated QA instances show that FailSafe-RAG reduces overconfident failures while preserving competitive answer accuracy. The results highlight IR-based evidence assessment as a practical guardrail for reliable RAG.
A063SHORTThe Small-Model Graph-RAG Gap Is a Faithfulness Gap
Jason Thomo (University of Victoria) · Venkatesh Srinivasan (Santa Clara University) · Alex Thomo (University of Victoria)
Abstract
On multi-hop benchmarks, modern Graph-RAG retrieves the gold answer for 77-90% of questions, yet a budget open-weight 8B model answers only 31-77% correctly. We show that faithfulness (reading the retrieved evidence rather than guessing) and calibration (abstaining when it is insufficient) account for a large, recoverable part of this gap. A leak-controlled decomposition finds that on the hardest, least-contaminated benchmark (MuSiQue), 43% of questions have their supporting facts in the retrieved context yet are answered wrong, and on these the model gives a confident answer 82% of the time rather than abstaining. A grounding-and-calibration prompt makes the model answer from the retrieved context or abstain when it cannot, a more trustworthy operating point at no accuracy cost. A re-ask step then spends some of that calibration for coverage, turning abstentions into correct answers for a gain of +9 pp on KET-RAG and +13 pp on LightRAG (MuSiQue, answer-present slice) that closes about half the gap to a 70B model on KET-RAG and most of it on LightRAG. Few-shot example source moves the model along the same faithfulness-accuracy frontier, better for calibration than accuracy. Unlike structure-exploiting augmentations that degrade on uniform-relevance retrieval, grounding helps most there. For small-model Graph-RAG the target is faithful, calibrated use of retrieved evidence. Code is available at https://github.com/thomouvic/graphrag-faithfulness.
A064FULLLook Before You Leap: Teaching RAG Generators to TRACE Evidence Before Reasoning
Jingyi Ren (Tsinghua University) · Yekun Xu (Tsinghua University) · Xiaolong Wang (Tsinghua University) · Weitao Li (Tsinghua University) · Ante Wang (Tsinghua University) · Weizhi Ma (Tsinghua University) · Yang Liu (Tsinghua University)
Abstract
Retrieval-Augmented Generation (RAG) has become a powerful paradigm for knowledge-intensive applications. To maintain high recall, retrievers often return extensive context, requiring generators to distinguish truly useful evidence. Previous approaches typically couple evidence identification and reasoning. This coupling, however, hinders the model's ability to explicitly decide which evidence to use before generating a response, limiting both verifiability and effective context utilization. In this work, we propose TRACE, a reinforcement learning framework that trains RAG generators to explicitly select evidence prior to grounded reasoning. TRACE trains models under a structured protocol that separates evidence selection from subsequent reasoning, and combines task-specific rewards for correctness, relevance, and structural validity with a high-weight holistic bonus that stabilizes the joint optimization of accuracy and attribution. To further mitigate policy-update instability under multiple reward signals, we employ a stabilized KL-divergence estimator. Experiments on three multi-hop QA datasets using Qwen2.5-7B-Instruct and Llama-3.1-8B-Instruct show that TRACE improves answer accuracy by 10–30% while producing explicit, evidence-attributed reasoning traces. Its performance is competitive with advanced commercial LLMs. Further analyses demonstrate strong generalization across diverse QA datasets, retrieval settings, and an evidence-grounded summarization task. Our code is publicly available.
A065APPLIEDTRACE: Accountable Agentic Retrieval for Source Discovery in Digital Archives
Donghan Bian (école nationale des chartes - PSL) · Marie Puren (EPITA) · Florian Cafiero (EPITA)
Abstract
Historical archives pose a difficult retrieval problem for retrieval-augmented generation systems: documents are OCR-degraded, heterogeneous across genres and sources, and require strong source traceability for scholarly and institutional use. We introduce TRACE, a training-free agentic retrieval framework designed for accountable source discovery over historical corpora. The system was developed in the context of DECIDON, an interdisciplinary project on the circulation of political discourse between parliamentary debates and the press during the French Third Republic, involving digitised historical collections and institutional use cases. The prototype is currently deployed internally within the project and accessible to 24 researchers across six partner institutions. We evaluate TRACE on HistoriQA-ThirdRepublic, a benchmark of 1752 French historical questions over parliamentary debates and newspapers from 1887, with documents derived from Bibliothèque nationale de France digitised collections. TRACE achieves R@10 = 0.856 and MRR = 0.653, outperforming sparse, dense, graph-based, and agentic RAG baselines, with the largest gains on multi-hop and cross-corpus questions. At approximately $0.02 per question under the default hosted inference configuration, TRACE also remains economically feasible for heritage institutions, laboratories or companies that cannot rely on costly local GPU infrastructure. These results suggest that, for large digital libraries and archives, retrieval accountability and corpus-aware agent design can provide a practical alternative to heavier training-based or graph-construction approaches.
A066SHORTForward-Looking Guidance for Iterative RAG in Multi-Hop Question Answering
Jumin Cho (Jeonbuk National University) · Chanjun Park (Soongsil University) · Seung-Hoon Na (Ulsan National Institute of Science and Technology) · Hyun-Je Song (Jeonbuk National University)
Abstract
Multi-hop question answering aims to answer complex queries by identifying and integrating evidence distributed across multiple documents. Existing iterative RAG approaches address this task by decomposing complex questions into plans or sub-questions, followed by repeated retrieval, evidence extraction, and reasoning to accumulate the information needed for the final answer. Nevertheless, intermediate outputs produced during this iterative process are often optimized locally rather than guided by future reasoning needs, making them useful for the current iteration but suboptimal for the overall multi-hop reasoning process. We empirically investigate the potential of forward-looking guidance in iterative RAG, where the remaining planned reasoning trajectory is incorporated into each iteration. We analyze its effect across retrieval, evidence extraction, and reasoning, and find that such guidance is especially beneficial for evidence extraction and reasoning, leading to more effective intermediate outputs and consistent improvements over iterative RAG baselines.
A067SHORTHyperMind: Claim Resolution and Reputation Tracking for Trustworthy Multi-Agent LLM Aggregation
Sonia Semwal (Zysec AI Limited) · Rahul Sharma (Zysec AI Limited) · Venkatesh Siddi (Zysec AI Limited) · Subhransu Sekhar Mahapatra (Infinia Technologies)
Abstract
The quality of knowledge produced by multi-agent generative AI systems depends not on the capability of individual agents but on the reliability of the communication layer between them. When agents disagree, that reliability is entirely invisible: no outcome is recorded, no agent is accountable, and the system learns nothing. This paper presents HyperMind, a protocol that makes disagreements productive by treating each resolved dispute as a verifiable calibration event, through three co-designed components: a seven-state Claim Resolution Finite State Machine (FSM) issuing signed provenance receipts; a Beta reputation system updated exclusively from FSM-verified outcomes; and DiversityGuard, which detects and interrupts premature consensus. On a 100-question enterprise benchmark spanning five domains, HyperMind achieves the lowest Brier score on all four tested LLMs; paired-difference 95% BCa confidence intervals exclude zero on two models (Gemma-4-26B [+0.0321,+0.0913], Wilcoxon p=0.0005, surviving Bonferroni correction across four models; Qwen-3.6-35B [+0.0021,+0.0737], p=0.037, not correction-surviving), though the n=100 evaluation is underpowered for the remaining two models (5–6% power). The full run costs $0.005 per 100 questions, and every resolved claim produces an auditable chain of custody over agent reliability.
A068FULLS2R-Merge: Soft-Gated Routing with Structural Node Merge Optimization
Sanghyun Yoo (Sungkyunkwan University) · Gi Seong Kim (Sungkyunkwan University) · Jingyeong Park (Sungkyunkwan University) · Hayoung Oh (Sungkyunkwan University)
Abstract
Large Language Model (LLM)-based Multi-Agent Systems (MAS) have shown strong potential on complex reasoning tasks, but their scalability is limited by substantial communication overhead and token consumption. Recent methods reduce these costs by pruning redundant agents or edges, but such deletion-based optimization can discard role-specific information and often operates only after activating the full agent pool. To address these limitations, we propose S2R-Merge, a unified routing-and-merging framework that reframes MAS structural optimization from node deletion to information-preserving consolidation. S2R-Merge first uses an uncertainty-aware 2-Stage Soft-Gated Router to select a task-relevant agent subgraph, avoiding unnecessary full-pool activation. It then applies graph-based node merging to identify structurally inefficient agents from policy-gradient-learned communication pathways, absorbing them into strongly related partners while preserving their role-level information through Prompt-level Fusion. Experiments on six reasoning and code-generation benchmarks with Llama-3-8B-Instruct and GPT-4 show that S2R-Merge achieves the best average accuracy among all compared methods, reaching 77.22% and 92.37%, respectively. It also reduces average prompt token usage by up to 12.3× compared with full multi-agent collaboration and achieves the lowest token consumption among multi-agent graph-optimization baselines. These results demonstrate that S2R-Merge provides an effective cost-performance trade-off for scalable LLM-based MAS.
A069SHORTAdaCon: Learning Adaptive Trust Regions for Consistent LLM Agent Reasoning
Hao Chen (University of Chinese Academy of Sciences) · Xinke Jiang (Peking University) · Kaiqi Huang (University of Chinese Academy of Sciences) · Jianbin Jiao (University of Chinese Academy of Sciences)
Abstract
LLM-based agents increasingly operate over long horizons, yet they drift, contradict themselves, and abandon working strategies as interaction lengthens. At each step, an agent may produce exploratory and conservative candidates, but their disagreement alone does not reveal which one should be executed. We formulate this choice as context-conditioned online prediction using environmental feedback from executed exploratory proposals. We therefore propose Adaptive Consistency (AdaCon), which uses similarity only to identify divergent proposals and applies a critic that learns from context whether to execute them, trained online from the environment's own reward without human labels. We establish a squared-error lower bound for similarity-only rules and a no-regret guarantee for a convex linear-critic special case. On ScienceWorld, AdaCon achieves higher reported mean scores than strong reinforcement-learning, reasoning, and consistency-supervised baselines across all task horizons, with the largest gains on long-horizon tasks.
A070SHORTRedundancy-Aware Self-Consistency for Efficient LLM Reasoning
Hao Chen (University of Chinese Academy of Sciences) · Xinke Jiang (Peking University) · Kaiqi Huang (University of Chinese Academy of Sciences) · Jianbin Jiao (University of Chinese Academy of Sciences)
Abstract
Large language models increasingly solve multi-step reasoning tasks, where a single sampled chain of reasoning is frequently unreliable. Reaching a correct answer therefore requires aggregating many sampled reasoning paths into one trustworthy decision. The dominant family, self-consistency and its sampling-and-voting variants, suits such reasoning tasks, but its raw-count vote treats sampled paths as separate units of evidence, even when their reasoning is highly redundant. Within this regime, adaptive-budget methods curb the cost by deciding when to stop, yet their stopping signals are commonly based on the same redundancy-blind counts. We therefore propose Redundancy-Aware Consistency (RAC), which strengthens self-consistency by aggregating reasoning paths according to their effective support rather than their raw count. We establish the boundedness of this effective support and show that RAC recovers self-consistency when within-answer paths are mutually dissimilar. Experiments on four benchmarks with the primary backbone and a three-benchmark subset with a second backbone show that RAC achieves higher observed accuracy than the evaluated self-consistency and adaptive-budget baselines. On the primary backbone, it also uses substantially fewer samples.
A071SHORTRATED: Reliability-Aware AI Agent Tool Retrieval via Execution Dynamics
Weiliang Chen (Texas Tech University) · Song Liao (Texas Tech University)
Abstract
As AI agents increasingly rely on external tools, accurate retrieval is essential for reliable behavior. Existing methods optimize semantic relevance but largely ignore tool availability during execution. To address this gap, we propose RATED (Reliability-Aware Tool retrieval via Execution Dynamics), a retrieval framework that combines robust semantic matching with dynamic reliability adaptation. RATED employs a frozen dual-encoder with contrastive fine-tuning for semantic matching, and a lightweight contextual bandit module that re-ranks candidates based on real-time execution feedback. This design enables rapid adaptation to runtime tool failures without expensive model retraining. We introduce EcoAgent, a benchmark of 5,172 real-world tools and over 210,000 query–tool pairs for offline retrieval and dynamic reliability evaluation. Experimental results demonstrate that RATED achieves a 52.2% relative MRR improvement over the ToolLLM API retriever on real-world queries, and reduces fault selection rate from 86.2% to 2.9% under severe API outage scenarios with a 30% failure rate, while incurring negligible latency overhead of less than 1 ms over encode-only inference. Code and dataset are available at https://github.com/Elliotes/EcoAgent.
A072FULLMemDTG: Dynamic Temporal Memory Graphs for Evidence-Admissible Agent Memory
Yaxin Deng (Beijing Institute of Technology) · Hongchao Qin (Beijing Institute of Technology) · Tianyi Gao (Beijing Institute of Technology) · Guang Zeng (Ant Group) · Rong-Hua Li (Beijing Institute of Technology)
Abstract
Long-term agent memory is an online, non-monotonic retrieval problem. New interactions may reinforce, contradict, supersede, specialize, abstract, or expire earlier memories; the same fact can be a wrong current answer, a correct historical answer, or necessary transition evidence depending on query intent. Existing chunk, summary, and graph memories retrieve by semantic or graph relevance and treat time as post-hoc metadata, so they cannot determine whether a memory is observable, valid, lifecycle-admissible, and provenance-supported before it enters the candidate space. We propose MemDTG, a dynamic temporal memory graph that frames agent memory as temporal evidence admission. MemDTG separates immutable raw episodes from a mutable entity-state temporal graph and a memory-evolution graph over assertion versions. State slots localize mutable user and task states; an LLM-assisted slot-local resolver classifies semantic evolution only within bounded temporal histories; and deterministic commit rules update valid intervals, lifecycle states, and typed evolution edges. At read time, a query compiler instantiates observed-time, valid-time, version, edge-type, and role constraints before ranking, and QV-CTW retrieves evidence paths only inside the query-legal temporal subgraph. Evidence certificates record selected facts, sources, roles, and rejected stale or future alternatives, making retrieval auditable. On LongMemEval and LoCoMo, MemDTG achieves the best LLM-judge accuracy and Citation F1. Ablation and temporal error analyses confirm that provenance certificates and legal-subgraph pre-filtering are each essential for these gains, reducing stale-answer errors by 61.7% and future leaks by 80.1%.
A073FULLPrivMem: Privacy-Preserving Temporal Motif Mining over Cross-User Agent Memory Graphs
Zening Li (Beijing Institute of Technology) · Hongchao Qin (Beijing Institute of Technology) · Guang Zeng (Ant Group) · Rong-Hua Li (Beijing Institute of Technology)
Abstract
Long-lived AI agents increasingly store private memory graphs of user goals, retrieved documents, tool calls, failures, and repairs. Mining these memories across users is crucial for discovering recurrent operational patterns, yet the problem remains unsolved: raw graphs cannot be centralized, and even aggregate motifs can reveal workflows supported by only one or two users. Existing local differential privacy (LDP) frequency-estimation and pattern-mining methods optimize top-K recovery, but they have no principled release-time defense against rare-workflow disclosure. We argue that the missing axis is not a stronger randomizer but a safer server-side release policy. We present PrivMem, which extracts retrieval-causal temporal motifs on device, perturbs them with per-coordinate randomized response, and releases them through a shrinkage ranker, a public-schema risk gate, and a Benjamini–Hochberg calibrated false-discovery filter. The analysis proves per-coordinate ε-LDP, derives concentration for the unbiased support estimator, establishes a support-gap condition for top-K recovery, and shows that the release stack preserves privacy by post-processing. On a 240-user planted benchmark, PrivMem reduces in-schema rare-workflow leakage by over 35× at matched utility; at ε=1,θ=8, it keeps top-20 F1 at 0.86 while cutting leakage from 0.27 to 0.007. It also drives out-of-schema leakage to zero and improves released-subspace clustering by over 10× ARI at ε=2. On a 1,757-user real-trace corpus across eight LLM-agent domains, PrivMem releases exactly zero rare motifs at every threshold, while LDP baselines leak 0.28–0.57.
A074SHORTEntropy Interventions Do Not Transfer: Why RLVR Entropy Control Misfires in On-Policy Distillation
Xiankun Lin (Sun Yat-sen University) · Zhezheng Hao (Zhejiang University) · Lixin Liu (Tsinghua University) · Xinyi Lin (Sun Yat-sen University) · Wence Ji (University of Science and Technology of China) · Zichao Nie (Tsinghua University) · Yongkang Yang (University of Science and Technology of China)
Abstract
Reinforcement learning with verifiable rewards (RLVR) controls policy entropy by reweighting tokens against an external scalar advantage. On-policy distillation (OPD) faces the same surface problem, a student that can sharpen too fast, but it replaces that advantage with a per-token teacher target. That shared symptom makes an RLVR entropy fix look reusable. We show the reuse fails for a simple reason. Re-deriving the token-level entropy change of the OPD objective shows its governing factor is the covariance between the teacher-student probability gap and the log policy, not an advantage. The two decompositions disagree on which tokens drive entropy, so transplanting an RLVR entropy reweighting such as STEER into OPD damps exactly the teacher-corrective tokens the student must learn. A preliminary API analysis makes this failure mode visible before training, with corrective tokens over-represented in the high-entropy tail a STEER-style reweight suppresses. A controlled four-seed distillation run then confirms the prediction. Transplanting STEER collapses GSM8K accuracy from 38% to 7%, with corrective-token retention falling in step, while the MATH-500 effect stays within seed noise. We propose a corrected reweighting that reads the teacher-student sign before damping. It restores corrective-token retention and returns to the vanilla OPD band on GSM8K within seed noise.
A075SHORTSymGRPO: Preventing Mode Collapse in Group Relative Policy Optimization via Symmetric Anti-Reinforcement
Manu Ghulyani (Fujitsu Research of India) · Anuj Rathore (Fujitsu Research of India) · Amar Prakash Azad (Fujitsu Research of India) · Mahesh Chandran (Fujitsu Research of India)
Abstract
Group Relative Policy Optimization (GRPO) has become the dominant critic-free method for reinforcement learning from human feedback in large language models, with growing adoption for fine-tuning LLM-based retrievers, query reformulators, rerankers, and agentic search systems. We identify a fundamental failure mode of GRPO in multi-prompt training: prompt-blind mode collapse, where the policy converges to a single output regardless of input prompt—a critical concern for information retrieval applications where prompt-conditioned behavior is essential. We prove this arises from a quadratic gradient vanishing at the collapsed state: GRPO's entropy restoration rate is ?(?²|log ?|) where ? = 1 ? ?_max. We propose SymGRPO, which augments GRPO with an anti-reinforcement log-barrier on unchosen tokens, raising the restoration rate to ?(?|log ?|)—a diverging ratio of ?(V?1)/?. Critically, this benefit appears only when the batch advantage sum S ? 0, which holds under EMA baselines but is forced to zero by standard mean-zero normalization. Across four small-scale reasoning tasks, GRPO mode-collapses to 19–50% accuracy while SymGRPO reaches 100% on multi-solution tasks. The modification is three lines of code.
A076FULLLuWu: Adaptive Layer-wise Heterogeneous KV Cache Quantization
Hexuan Lv (Northeastern University) · Yuhai Zhao (Northeastern University) · Yuan Li (North China University of Technology)
Abstract
The KV cache is essential for efficient autoregressive inference in Large Language Models (LLMs), but its memory cost increases with context length, layer depth, and request concurrency, limiting long-context and high-throughput serving, particularly in Computing Power Network (CPN) environments. KV cache quantization reduces this cost by lowering the storage bit-width of keys and values. However, existing methods often rely on uniform precision or static mixed-precision policies, which cannot fully capture layer-wise differences in quantization sensitivity or decoding-time changes in precision requirements. This paper proposes LuWu, an adaptive layer-wise heterogeneous KV cache quantization method. LuWu first performs offline calibration to measure attention-output errors under different K/V precision pairs, clusters layers with similar error response patterns, prunes unsuitable candidate configurations, and searches an initial heterogeneous precision configuration under accuracy and bit-width objectives. During online inference, LuWu uses the Layer Activity Score (LAS) to adjust the precision of selected layers, while a hierarchical residual-code representation supports efficient promotion and demotion between precision levels. Experiments on representative reasoning, long-context, and language modeling tasks show that LuWu achieves a favorable accuracy–bitwidth trade-off. Compared with representative state-of-the-art K8V8 baselines, LuWu reduces the average equivalent bit-width by 29.5%–38.1% while maintaining competitive inference accuracy. These results highlight the effectiveness of adaptive layer-wise heterogeneous quantization for memory-efficient LLM inference.
A077SHORTTriAgent: Granularity-Stratified Multi-Agent Routing with a Multilingual Semantic Cache and a Free Trust Signal for LLM Inference Pipelines
Isabel Xu (The Overlake School) · Cynthia Xu (The Overlake School) · Rachel Ren (Edwards Vacuum Inc.) · Cong Guo (The University of Memphis) · Jiacheng Ding (The University of Memphis)
Abstract
LLM-based information pipelines—retrieval, classification, entity linking, intent inference—share a structural cost problem: the reasoner LLM dominates the per-query bill, yet a large fraction of queries are trivially handled by far cheaper specialists. We present TriAgent, a generic multi-agent inference router that stratifies agents by contextual granularity (word / sentence / cross-sentence) and gates routing with a three-way Semantic Divergence Index (SDI). On two financial testbeds we report four findings. (i) The critic plateau is calibration-conditional: on FPB (where FinBERT is well calibrated, ECE=0.016) critic protocols collapse 1.5B-7B Qwen to a single F1≈0.87 (bootstrap CIs overlap), while a same-size 3-persona vote drops to 0.66; on TFNS (where the specialist collapses to F1=0.66) the critic plateau fails, falling below the LLM-alone baseline. (ii) A Shared Consensus Dictionary on multilingual sentence-BERT answers 95% of Chinese queries from an English cache at F1=0.99 — a cross-lingual canonicaliser at zero marginal cost. (iii) The same SDI doubles as a post-hoc LLM-hallucination detector at AUC=0.90. (iv) At a 10M-user scale the architecture saves $363M/year against a GPT-4 baseline. The router, cache, and trust signal are domain-agnostic and apply directly to LLM-based IR pipelines.
A078SHORTLEAD-Route: An Adaptive Language-Calibrated and Entropy-Aware LLM Selection for Homologous Model Routing
Zhihui Liang (Yunnan University) · Sixing Wu (Yunnan University) · Yujue Zhou (Yunnan University) · Shidong Jiang (Yunnan University) · Wenhao Xue (Yunnan University) · Wei Zhou (Yunnan University)
Abstract
With the increasing language diversity on the web, the demand for multilingual Question-Answering (QA) has grown significantly. To maximize QA performance, a common way is to equip multilingual large language models (MLLMs) with more parameters, which also incurs significant costs. To improve efficiency without losing performance, we propose a novel task, Homologous Model Routing (HMR). Given a set of homologous MLLMs of varying parameter counts (such as Qwen2.5 1.5B, 3B...), HMR tries to select the minimum model that can just correctly answer the current question. Then, we propose a Language-Calibrated Entropy-Aware Dynamic Routing (LEAD-Router) that performs homologous model routing by estimating question difficulty based on response entropy and language-aware calibration. Experiments on the two datasets show that LEAD-Router achieves consistently better routing accuracy and QA performance than baselines.
A079SHORTWeight-Adjusting Binary Transformation: A Dynamic Label Ranking Model for Multi-Label Data Stream Classification
Yağız özkarahan (Bilkent University) · Fazli Can (Bilkent University)
Abstract
Multi-label data stream classification has unique challenges compared to typical classification tasks. The models do not have access to the entire data as classification is done instance by instance and the multi-label association makes predictions significantly more complex. Many of the existing solutions in this area do not scale well in terms of time efficiency and predictive accuracy when the number of labels grows. We propose Weight-Adjusting Binary Transformation (WABT), a lightweight problem transformation model which dynamically ranks labels with each arriving instance and applies binary transformation. WABT handles the problem of information loss typical in binary transformation models without increasing computational complexity. We evaluate WABT on 10 datasets, most with large numbers of labels, and compare it against four state-of-the-art problem transformation models. Overall, we demonstrate that WABT delivers the strongest average ranking across three effectiveness measures, achieves second-best performance on Hamming Score, while ranking highest in terms of time efficiency.
A080FULLDouble-down sandwiched learned Bloom filters for multiset membership query
Ming Lin (Sun Yat-sen University) · Lin Chen (Macao Polytechnic University) · Peijia Zheng (Sun Yat-sen University)
Abstract
Multi-set membership query is a core operation in network and data systems, which requires simultaneous element existence verification and set category classification. Traditional multi-set Bloom Filters rely on fixed hash mechanisms and cannot adapt to data distribution characteristics, while existing Learned Bloom Filters (LBFs) are only designed for single-set scenarios and cannot support efficient multi-set parallel queries. To address these limitations, this paper proposes Double-Down Sandwiched Learned Bloom Filters (DDSLBF), a novel learning-enhanced architecture for multi-set membership queries. DDSLBF adopts a hierarchical sandwich structure composed of dual learned oracles and parallel Bloom Filter groups, realizing collaborative pre-filtering, verification and precise classification. We conduct comprehensive theoretical analysis on error rates, space efficiency, optimal space allocation and space-accuracy trade-off, and derive the theoretical performance bounds of the model. Extensive experimental results on three real-world network datasets show that DDSLBF achieves higher classification accuracy, eliminates classification failures completely, and reduces the false positive rate significantly compared with the baselines under the same memory constraints. This work extends the application scope of LBFs and provides a lightweight, high-precision solution for multi-set query tasks in network security and data systems.
A081FULLAdaptSteer: Workload-Adaptive Optimizer Steering via Execution-Derived Preference Supervision
Syed Jalaluddin Hashmi (Kyung Hee University) · Irfan Ullah (Kyung Hee University) · Md Arif Rahman (Kyung Hee University) · Young-Koo Lee (Kyung Hee University)
Abstract
Database query optimizers often select suboptimal execution plans, and effective steering requires identifying configurations that improve query and workload performance without modifying DBMS internals. Existing external steering systems can reason over multiple optimizer configurations, but many rely on online feedback, exploration, or engine-specific steering mechanisms. More recent LLM-based SQL steering approaches avoid deeper optimizer integration, but often depend on narrow supervision and general-purpose embeddings that are costly, not explicitly aligned with execution behavior, and difficult to adapt under workload shifts. We present AdaptSteer, a novel workload-adaptive optimizer-steering framework that learns from execution-derived preference supervision. AdaptSteer converts latencies measured across diverse query–configuration pairs into preference-based contrastive training signals for a compact SQL encoder, without invasive DBMS modifications or external APIs. The resulting representation supports two lightweight decision heads: a calibrated classifier for safety-first binary steering and a pairwise Condorcet ranker that decomposes K-way configuration selection into binary execution-preference comparisons. We further apply Reptile-based meta-learning to the trained encoder, enabling few-shot adaptation to unseen workloads. Evaluations on the JOB and CEB benchmarks show that AdaptSteer reduces total workload latency by 70.1% relative to the PostgreSQL default and achieves 4.4% lower total workload latency than LLMSteer under the same binary protocol, without relying on external API calls. Beyond binary steering, AdaptSteer improves multi-action selection through pairwise preference ranking across the evaluated candidate sets and benefits from multi-configuration supervision across broader action spaces. Under CEB→JOB adaptation, AdaptSteer's meta-learned variant improves AUROC by 4.2 percentage points over the contrastive-only baseline with only 20 target-workload adaptation queries. Together, AdaptSteer unifies execution-derived preference supervision, binary and multi-action steering, and few-shot adaptation in a compact, deployable optimizer-steering framework.
A082FULLGAP: Privacy-Aware and Authenticated Knowledge Graph Queries in Hybrid-Storage Blockchains
Xi Xiao (East China Normal University) · Liang Li (East China Normal University) · Jucai Yang (East China Normal University) · Haiqin Wu (East China Normal University)
Abstract
Hybrid-storage blockchain (HSB) has been a prevailing and efficient storage model in blockchain-based applications. It retains raw data off-chain and only stores metadata on-chain for integrity check to improve scalability. However, for widely provided query services, ensuring query integrity without compromising data privacy is an ongoing challenge in HSB since the off-chain storage provider may be malicious. Existing work has largely focused on authenticated keyword search or range queries over textual data, while several studies on authenticated queries on graph data either ignore user privacy or merely enable user-side verification, with limited support for various graph queries. This paper presents GAP, the first privacy-aware and publicly authenticated scheme for rich queries, including node keyword, edge type, connectivity, and subgraph matching queries, over knowledge graphs in HSB. The core of GAP lies in a novel authenticated data structure (ADS), which incorporates our modified hybrid index and an orthogonal list encrypted with inner product encryption (IPE). With such an ADS, we efficiently perform diverse graph queries with privacy protection, meanwhile generating verification objects (VOs) for public verifiability of the query integrity. Additionally, GAP supports dynamic node/edge updates with forward privacy and update integrity. Security analysis proves that GAP achieves L-adaptive security with desired privacy and integrity. Comparative experiments on both real-world and synthetic datasets validate that GAP yields a 40%–50% reduction in trapdoor generation. It also outperforms others by over two orders of magnitude in search time, and its on-chain performance is around twice as efficient as the baselines.
A083SHORTCoordination-Free Schema Evolution for Replicated Property Graphs
Michael Landgraf (RPTU Kaiserslautern-Landau) · Annette Bieniusa (RPTU Kaiserslautern-Landau) · Stefania Dumbrava (ENSIIE, Inria Paris, IRIF, SAMOVAR (Télécom SudParis))
Abstract
Collaborative applications increasingly manage interconnected data as property graphs whose data and schema both evolve at runtime. Under concurrent updates, schema migration either incurs high latency or risks data divergence, and concurrent schema changes must be merged correctly and reflected onto the data. We present Refract, a coordination-free middleware built on conflict-free replicated data types (CRDTs). It combines a graph schema CRDT that deterministically merges concurrent Schema Modification Operators (SMOs), such as renames, property and label changes, and type splits and joins, into a single schema; a property-graph lens engine that lazily translates raw data into the current schema at query time, and a graph data CRDT that stores and merges schemaless data. To the best of our knowledge, Refract is the first system to treat property graph schema evolution itself as a replicated convergent object. Preliminary experiments on the LDBC Social Network Benchmark show that Refract matches the overhead of Cambria, the state-of-the-art document-level baseline, while adding graph-native schema merging, and cuts schema-change downtime by over two orders of magnitude compared to eager migration.
A084FULLThe Good, the Bad, and the Ugly of Markov Boundary for Tabular Prediction
Shu Wan (Arizona State University) · Abhinav Gorantla (Arizona State University) · Huan Liu (Arizona State University) · K. Selçuk Candan (Arizona State University)
Abstract
Under standard graphical assumptions, the Markov boundary of a target variable is the smallest set of features that renders every other feature redundant. Once the boundary is observed, the target is conditionally independent of the rest of the table. This is a tempting object for tabular prediction, since it names exactly the columns a model should need. Yet modern regressors are still trained on the full feature set. We ask whether the Markov boundary is genuinely useful for prediction on SCMBench, a 3,450-task synthetic SCM benchmark with feature counts from 40 to 1000 and six SCM families, evaluated with six regressors. The answer is more nuanced than the theory suggests. Restricting a regressor to the oracle boundary often improves prediction substantially, and the improvement grows as the feature space becomes larger and sparser. But the natural pipeline of recovering the boundary with causal discovery and training on the recovered mask does not deliver. Existing estimators exhaust the compute budget before reaching the regime where the boundary helps most, and even where they run they rarely beat the full feature set. We trace this to three causes. Discovery optimizes structural recovery rather than prediction. False negatives and false positives carry sharply asymmetric predictive cost. The exact boundary is only one of many feature sets that beat all features. We then develop what these facts imply for prediction-aligned feature selection and for tabular models that learn to use causal structure.
A085SHORTRelational-View Ensemble Learning for Tabular Prediction
Ji Eun Park (Chonnam National University) · Tae Jong Choi (Chonnam National University)
Abstract
Tabular prediction can benefit from relational information at multiple levels, including global feature relations, feature interactions within each sample, and relations among similar samples. Existing deep tabular methods exploit such information through attention-based, graph-based, and retrieval-based modeling. However, they often focus on only part of the relational structure or merge relational information into a shared representation, making it difficult to distinguish the predictive role of each relation type. We propose a relational-view ensemble framework for tabular prediction. Instead of simply integrating multiple relations into a single representation, the proposed model decomposes them into three distinct predictive views: global feature relations, intra-sample feature interactions, and inter-sample relations. Each view produces an independently supervised prediction logit, and the final prediction is obtained through learnable logit-level fusion. This design treats different relational axes as explicit predictive sources within a single architecture without training multiple model instances. Experiments on eight public tabular datasets show that the proposed framework achieves competitive performance against strong baselines, including gradient-boosted decision trees and recent deep tabular models, while achieving the best average rank across the evaluated methods. Ablation studies further show that the full three-view model achieves the best or tied-best performance on five of the six evaluated datasets, supporting the benefit of jointly modeling multiple relational views.
A086SHORTBenchmarking Agentic Text-to-SPARQL for Multi-Hop Scholarly Knowledge Graph Exploration
Tim Gollub (Bauhaus-Universität Weimar) · Furqan Shuja (Bauhaus-Universität Weimar) · Benno Stein (Bauhaus-Universität Weimar)
Abstract
Conversational access to scholarly knowledge graphs promises more intuitive ways of exploring research fields, but current approaches remain limited by two major barriers: the lack of realistic multi-hop benchmarks and the brittleness of Text-to-SPARQL methods over real-world schemas. We address these gaps by introducing a benchmark of challenging, researcher-authored questions grounded in a domain-specific subset of DBLP. The benchmark targets realistic multi-hop scholarly information needs rather than synthetic or template-based queries. We evaluate five large language model-based SPARQL generation pipelines with increasing levels of schema grounding, decomposition, rule guidance, and endpoint feedback. Our results show that baseline and sequential approaches remain brittle, while a rule-augmented pipeline substantially improves execution accuracy and semantic alignment with the intended information need. The study contributes both a new testbed for evaluating conversational access to scholarly knowledge graphs and practical design insights for building more reliable, schema-aware Text-to-SPARQL agents.
A087FULLMCTS-KBQA: Monte Carlo Tree Search with Information Gain Rewards for Knowledge Base Question Answering
Guanming Xiong (Peking University) · Haochen Li (AlignBase) · Zonghong Dai (Fudan University) · Liqiang Wen (Peking University) · Wen Zhao (Peking University)
Abstract
This work investigates how to improve large language model (LLM)-based reasoning for knowledge base question answering (KBQA) via Monte Carlo Tree Search (MCTS). Applying MCTS to LLM-based KBQA remains challenging because reward design is difficult and rollout-based search is computationally expensive. Existing MCTS-style methods either rely on direct LLM scoring or require substantial data to train separate reward models, and they often provide rewards only at terminal states. To address these limitations, we propose Fast MCTS, which replaces terminal rollouts with an information gain (IG) reward for intermediate states. The IG reward is implemented as a question-conditioned PPL-ratio proxy over sanitized interaction histories, computed by forward passes of an open-source instruction LLM without additional reward-model training. Experiments on four KBQA benchmarks show that Fast MCTS consistently outperforms linear baselines and generally improves the accuracy-cost trade-off relative to rollout-based Classic MCTS. (Code and data are available at https://github.com/JimXiongGM/MCTS-KBQA.)
A088FULLContinual Knowledge Graph Embedding via Community Hierarchies and Reconstruction Distillation
Lina Ge (Guangxi Minzu University) · Yongguo Yang (Guangxi Minzu University) · Qinglin Bi (Guangxi Minzu University) · Qinchun Su (Guangxi Minzu University) · Lei Tian (Guangxi Minzu University) · Chaoliang Zhou (Guangxi Minzu University)
Abstract
Continual knowledge graph embedding (CKGE) aims to incrementally learn emerging knowledge in evolving knowledge graphs while preserving previously acquired knowledge. However, existing CKGE approaches suffer from two major limitations. First, they largely overlook the explicit graph structure that is crucial for robust representation learning. Second, newly arrived triples are often learned in a stochastic order, which disrupts topological coherence and fails to preserve the structural dependencies between historical and emerging knowledge, thereby leading to severe catastrophic forgetting. We propose CHR-KGE, a structure-first framework tailored for CKGE under evolving graph scenarios. Specifically, CHR-KGE organizes newly arrived triples into a structure-guided learning order through community partition and hierarchical prioritization, while preserving cross-snapshot structural continuity via structure-constrained reconstruction and aggregation module. Meanwhile, it selectively constrains representation drift in structurally important regions through learnable mask-guided distillation, enabling effective adaptation to new knowledge without sacrificing the stability of historical representations. Experiments on six datasets show that CHR-KGE consistently outperforms strong baselines in link prediction accuracy, knowledge transferability, and training efficiency. Compared with IncDE, CHR-KGE achieves average relative improvements of 3.39% in MRR, 5.36% in Hits@1, and 2.39% in Hits@10. Compared with re-train, CHR-KGE maintains highly competitive accuracy while reducing training time by 40%–60%. These results demonstrate the effectiveness and efficiency of CHR-KGE for continual knowledge graph embedding. The code can be found at https://anonymous.4open.science/r/CHR-KGE/.
A089FULLSDiffusE: Structure-Aware Diffusion for Temporal Knowledge Graph Reasoning with Denoised Evolution
Zhongwu Chen (National University of Defense Technology) · Zhen Huang (National University of Defense Technology) · Yong Dou (National University of Defense Technology)
Abstract
Temporal Knowledge Graph (TKG) reasoning that aims to predict missing facts has been widely explored. Compared to static knowledge graphs, the introduction of temporal modalities makes reasoning about entities and relationships more challenging. Most existing methods assume that all the recorded TKG facts are credible, overlooking two critical challenges: TKGs are typically automatically constructed, thereby inevitably introducing noise; meanwhile, the temporal evolution itself inherently carries uncertainty. While recent works on KG error detection and uncertain KG have attempted to address KG errors and uncertainty, they heavily rely on hard-to-obtain labels and neglect temporal information in TKGs. In this paper, we propose SDiffusE, a novel framework that enhances TKG reasoning through Structure-aware Diffusion and denoised Evolution, addressing the above issues. SDiffusE integrates three synergistic modules: The TKG diffusion module reconstructs authentic TKG structural interactions by denoising spurious edges; The recurrent relation-aware GCN module captures temporal dependencies for both original and denoised TKG snapshots; The dual-view contrastive learning module further leverages clean denoised signals to regularize learned representations. Experiments across four datasets show the superiority of SDiffusE over five categories of baselines.
A090SHORTOntoForge: Continual Ontology and Knowledge Graph Construction via Multi-Agent Consensus and Self-Refining Procedures
Fang Guo (Shanghai Key Laboratory of Data Science, College of Computer Science and Artificial Intelligence, Fudan University) · Li Zhu (Shanghai Key Laboratory of Data Science, College of Computer Science and Artificial Intelligence, Fudan University) · Mengying Wu (JR Talent Technology Limited Company, Advantage AI Agent Lab)
Abstract
Constructing domain ontologies and knowledge graphs (KGs) remains challenging when extraction procedures must operate across heterogeneous schemas and reuse feedback over time. Fixed prompts often miss valid triples, mis-handle canonicalization, and cannot adapt to recurring errors. We propose OntoForge, a multi-agent framework for continual ontology and KG construction. OntoForge generates recall-oriented and ontology-conformant candidates, verifies them through evidence- and schema-aware consensus, and maintains a self-refining Standard Operating Procedure (SOP) memory that converts recurrent conflicts into reusable procedural rules. On Text2KGBench across four Wikidata-TEKGEN domains, OntoForge improves triple-level F1 over direct prompting and static-SOP baselines across several LLM backbones, mainly through higher recall. Ablations show that gains are not explained by extra LLM calls alone, and sequential diagnostics show that persistent SOP adaptation benefits later construction windows after cold start.
A091SHORTAutomated Construction of FAIR Digital Object Knowledge Graphs from Flat Cultural Heritage Records
Zeyd Boukhers (Fraunhofer Institute for Applied Information Technology) · Lingxiao Kong (Fraunhofer Institute for Applied Information Technology) · Xenophon Zabulis (Foundation for Research and Technology) · Georgios Toubekis (Fraunhofer Institute for Applied Information Technology FIT)
Abstract
The FAIR Digital Object (FDO) framework mandates that metadata attribute values be expressed as persistent identifiers (PIDs) wherever possible, producing a fully machine-actionable graph in which every reference is resolvable. The Europeana Data Model was designed long before the FDO specification and stores most metadata values as plain text. This supports human browsing, but gives an automated agent little to follow across records or collections. We present a pipeline that transforms flat Europeana records into an FDO-compliant knowledge graph structured with CIDOC-CRM. Following the FDO specification, we model every heritage entity as a discrete FDO with its own PID, type, profile, and metadata layer. The core technical challenge is automating the FDO-prescribed distinction between values that must become PID references (resolvable entities) and those that may remain literals (terminal leaves such as notes, measurements, and dates). We address this challenge using a large language model that classifies each metadata value, routes it to a controlled vocabulary (Getty AAT, Wikidata, VIAF, or PeriodO), and links it to a shared entity FDO. We evaluate the approach on 637 archaeological records from five Europeana providers. The pipeline links 86% of metadata slots and resolves 58.5% of values that Europeana had not already enriched. It also merges cross-lingual surface forms that byte-identical matching keeps separate; 17 of 33 such merges were correct on manual review. Graph connectivity alone does not distinguish this approach from string matching; what distinguishes the FDO graph is that every node is typed and resolvable.
A092SHORTFormal-Informal Mathematical Alignment through and beyond Human Annotations
Noah Gießing (FIZ Karlsruhe) · Ankit Satpute (FIZ Karlsruhe) · Hamid Rahkooy (FIZ Karlsruhe) · André Greiner-Petter (University of Göttingen) · Moritz Schubotz (FIZ Karlsruhe)
Abstract
Formalized mathematics libraries such as Lean's mathlib provide machine-verifiable representations of mathematical knowledge, including definitions, theorems, and their relationships. If effectively connected to informal mathematical resources, formal mathematics could help uncover previously implicit links between mathematical concepts and improve access to existing formalizations. However, connections between informal and formal mathematics libraries are currently sparse and unsystematic. In this paper, we make first strides towards better formal integration. We construct a dataset linking informal statements from the Stacks Project to their formalizations in mathlib by exploiting expert annotations. We evaluate retrieval, LLM-based reranking, and LLM-assisted verification to discover new unannotated informal-to-formal links. To facilitate exploration and reuse of formalized knowledge, we integrated the newly discovered alignments into the MaRDI knowledge graph, enabling mathematicians to find formal counterparts to informal mathematical content. We discuss the difficulties and challenges in using LLMs for linking formal and informal mathematical content. All code and data necessary for reproducing this paper can be found at: https://github.com/AnkitSatpute/Formal-Informal-Mathematical-Alignment
A093SHORTWhen One Gold Entity Is Not Enough: Label Weakening for Robust Candidate Generation
Arnab Sharma (Heinz Nixdorf Institute, Paderborn University)
Abstract
Entity linking and entity-centric question answering systems rely on candidate generation to retrieve a small set of plausible entities for a mention or question. This stage is commonly trained with hard labels, although entity annotations are often sparse, ambiguous, or noisy: semantically similar entities may be confused, plausible alternatives may be unannotated, and corrupted positives may be memorized during contrastive training. To mitigate this, in this short paper, we propose label weakening, a simple ambiguity-aware training strategy for robust entity candidate generation under noisy supervision. Instead of assuming a single reliable gold entity for each input, label weakening constructs a small set of plausible entity candidates from the observed annotation and model confidence, and optimizes a superset-ranking objective over this set. This weakens uncertain supervision without explicitly correcting labels or estimating a noise transition model. We evaluate label weakening on mention-to-entity and question-to-entity retrieval tasks. Results show that label weakening is particularly effective for preserving gold-entity Recall@10 in the candidate generation stage under high noise.
A094SHORTScaling Creative Writing Beyond Story-Centric Data with Attribute-Guided Genre Expansion
Hwan Chang (Chung-Ang University) · Yongil Kim (LG AI Research) · Heuiyeen Yeen (LG AI Research) · Yireun Kim (LG AI Research) · Jinsik Lee (LG AI Research) · Hwanhee Lee (Chung-Ang University)
Abstract
High-quality creative writing data for language models remains dominated by story-centric data, limiting models' ability to follow the structural and functional conventions of diverse creative formats. We propose an attribute-guided genre expansion framework for scaling creative writing data beyond story generation. By separating thematic breadth from genre-form control, our framework leverages human-authored story prompts as diverse creative seeds, while utilizing manually curated genre attributes to enforce distinct structural, stylistic, and formatting conventions. We combine these to prompt strong models for genre-faithful query–response pairs, which are then quality-filtered. Applying this framework, we construct the Multi-Genre Collection, a 50K-example corpus spanning 13 creative genres, including story, lyrics, game design, and other creative formats. Experiments demonstrate that models fine-tuned on our data consistently surpass not only base models and writing-specialized baselines, but also models trained on existing writing corpora. Genre-count ablations further indicate that genre expansion is a key driver of robust creative writing capability.
A095SHORTSimplify, Then Retrieve: Evaluating Meaning Preservation through Search Behavior
Claudia Nanula (University of Pisa) · Ophir Frieder (Georgetown University) · Cristina Ioana Muntean (ISTI-CNR) · Franco Maria Nardini (ISTI-CNR) · Raffaele Perego (ISTI-CNR)
Abstract
Text simplification eases document understanding while preserving meaning, but this balance remains difficult to evaluate without reference simplifications. We propose a retrieval-based perspective: if a simplified document preserves the information content of its source, it should remain retrievable for the same queries. We test this idea on BEIR collections from biomedical, news, and Wikipedia domains, comparing original and simplified documents under BM25 and dense retrieval. We analyze both retrieval effectiveness and ranking stability and relate them to a diverse set of indicators that capture different aspects of faithfulness and simplification quality. Experimental results demonstrate that simplification can substantially affect retrieval behavior, especially when models aggressively compress or delete content. Conversely, conservative simplifiers tend to better preserve search effectiveness. These findings suggest that search behavior provides a practical and complementary reference-free signal for evaluating meaning preservation in text simplification.
A096APPLIEDHIRA: A Human-in-the-Loop Retrieval-Augmented Cascade for Document Classification in Regulated Industries
Shangxuan Tian (Standard Chartered Bank) · Yanhui Chen (OCBC) · Carlos Queiroz (OCBC)
Abstract
Document classification in regulated industries is constrained by data residency, limited cold-start labels, scarce review capacity, and costly model-governance procedures. In this setting, the practical goal is not only to obtain high accuracy, but also to reduce LLM calls, avoid frequent model retraining, and send only the most ambiguous cases to human review. We present HIRA, a training-free, on-premises retrieval-augmented cascade for document classification in regulated deployments. HIRA first combines BM25 over OCR text, dense text embeddings, and image-level representations through validation-calibrated weighted reciprocal-rank fusion. Confident documents are classified directly by retrieval. Uncertain or visually confusable documents are passed to a locally hosted LLM verifier, which receives the OCR text, retrieved exemplars, label descriptions, and confusion-specific terms. When the verifier remains uncertain, the document is sent to human review. Each correction is then stored as a margin-weighted retrieval exemplar and also updates a Dirichlet-smoothed confusion graph, allowing the system to improve without updating model weights. On a private 80-class trade-finance corpus, HIRA processes the full 30,233-document production stream while requesting human correction for only 1,945 documents (6.4%), improving Macro-F1 from 0.6218 to 0.8548. On the corrected Tobacco-3482 benchmark, HIRA reaches 0.9423 Macro-F1 with a locally hosted DeepSeek-R1-Distill-Qwen-32B verifier, 17.4 percentage points above the zero-shot LLM baseline, while invoking the verifier for only about 40% of documents and therefore reducing LLM calls by approximately 60%. With 518 human corrections, corresponding to 24.8% of the pool, HIRA matches the fully labelled pool oracle in which all 2,086 pool documents are indexed with their ground-truth labels. These results show that selective human feedback and retrieval-memory adaptation can provide a practical alternative to repeated model retraining for long-tail document classification in regulated deployments.
A097SHORTFrom Preferences to Values: Evaluating Latent User Understanding and Transfer in LLMs
Taehyung Noh (Hanyang University) · Haein Yeo (Hanyang University) · Beejin Son (Hanyang University) · Kyungsik Han (Hanyang University)
Abstract
Personalized LLM agents should adapt to users who often reveal preferences through behavioral cues rather than explicit statements. Because existing benchmarks mainly evaluate surface-level profile matching, we propose PALETTE, a theory-driven benchmark designed to evaluate value-based user understanding in LLMs. Grounded in Schwartz's ten basic values, PALETTE contains 25,200 dialogues across 400 personas, pairing a historical dialogue that reveals a situational preference with a new context request that necessitates the same underlying value. We evaluate models on Dialogue-Based Understanding and New-Context Application to examine whether they can infer latent values from behavioral signals and generalize them across contexts. Our experiments with seven LLMs demonstrate that while models generate contextually appropriate dialog responses, they struggle to project an understanding of hidden values onto new contexts. PALETTE thus provides a diagnostic framework for verifying whether personalized agents can move beyond mere preference matching toward genuine, value-based user understanding. We make PALETTE publicly available at https://taehyungnoh.com/cikm26-palette/.
A098RESOURCERedditPersona: A Modular Framework for Community-Conditioned LLM Adaptation from Reddit
Amirhossein Ghaffari (Future Computing Group, University of Oulu) · Ali Goodarzi (Centre for Applied Computing, University of Oulu) · Huong Nguyen (Future Computing Group, University of Oulu) · Simo Hosio (Centre for Applied Computing, University of Oulu) · Lauri Lovén (Future Computing Group, University of Oulu) · Ekaterina Gilman (Future Computing Group, University of Oulu)
Abstract
Community-conditioned language model adaptation needs choices about data collection, community definition, and evaluation that are currently made independently in each study, making it hard to compare assumptions or reuse artifacts. We present RedditPersona, a modular framework that standardizes these choices: it collects Reddit posts and comments, profiles active users, partitions them under five grouping strategies (subreddit-based, graph-structural, semantic, hybrid, and interaction-based), trains a parameter-efficient adapter per strategy via QLoRA, and evaluates them under a shared metric suite spanning fluency, fidelity, distributional alignment, and community identifiability. Applied to 112 subreddits in the urban well-being domain (301,429 user profiles, 16M+ comments), we find that adapters' behavioral identifiability tracks each strategy's agreement with the subreddit baseline, and that a consistent trade-off between identifiability and distributional similarity to real text holds across all five strategies. The code and configuration files are available at: https://github.com/Ahghaffari/redditpersona.
A099SHORTThe Wisdom of the Right Crowd: Platform Governance via Local Vote Authority Ranking
Shayan Alipour (Toronto Metropolitan University) · Mattia Samory (Sapienza University of Rome) · Mehdi Kargar (Toronto Metropolitan University) · Morteza Zihayat (Toronto Metropolitan University)
Abstract
Online communities require governance to function, yet enforcement has not kept pace with the scale of participation. Automated classifiers struggle with community-specific nuance, while crowdsourced approaches are reactive and slow. We ask whether communities themselves hold latent moderation expertise expressed through organic voting behavior, and introduce Vote Authority Ranking (VAR), a closed-form estimator computed per community that scores users from their voting history by weighting correct votes on minority classes, applying temporal decay toward recent activity, and regularizing against sparse evidence. We evaluate our approach on 83K moderation logs and voting actions across 11 Reddit communities over three years, against nine baselines. Our findings show that community votes carry a reliable signal about moderator decisions, and that VAR identifies high-authority users more reliably than every baseline. This authority does not transfer across communities, and integrating the votes of VAR-identified users into automated classifiers improves their performance. This study offers a practical and effective path for platform governance that is based on the voting activity communities already produce.
A100FULLDisrupting Networks: Amplifying Social Dissensus via Large Language Models
Erica Coppolillo (ICAR-CNR) · Giuseppe Manco (ICAR-CNR)
Abstract
In this paper, we study how targeted content injection can strategically disrupt social networks. Specifically, we address a practical limitation of the basic variant of the Friedkin–Johnsen (FJ) model, which prevents increasing the polarization and disagreement of the network, making it unable to reproduce real-world scenarios. We overcome such limitation by using an enriched variant of the FJ model, further showing how altering a node inherent opinion to maximize disruption. Building on these preliminary considerations, we design a reinforcement learning framework to fine-tune a Large Language Model (LLM) for generating disruption-oriented text. Experiments on synthetic and real-world data confirm that tuned LLMs can approach theoretical disruption limits. Our findings raise important considerations for content moderation, adversarial information campaigns, and generative model regulation. Code is publicly available.
A101FULLKnowing When Evidence Is Insufficient: Supervising Claim-to-Evidence Reasoning for Multimodal Fact-Checking
Ziyu Yang (University of New South Wales) · Zhicheng Bao (University of New South Wales) · Jiaojiao Jiang (University of New South Wales) · Aditya Joshi (University of New South Wales)
Abstract
Not Enough Information (NEI) is the dominant failure mode in multimodal fact-checking, where current LVLMs routinely collapse NEI into Supported or Refuted. Our analysis on MOCHEG attributes this collapse to two challenges. The first challenge is a claim-driven shortcut, where supervised fine-tuning amplifies attention on claim tokens and lifts the claim-to-evidence attention ratio from 4.5 to 9.5. The second challenge is weak evidence-gap supervision, where training claims rarely expose where evidence is missing and models conflate linguistic ambiguity with genuine evidence insufficiency. To address these two challenges, we propose CEIR, a Claim-to-Evidence Insufficiency Reasoning supervision framework for multimodal fact-checking. CEIR aligns uncertainty with verified gaps between claims and evidence, helping LVLMs recognise insufficient evidence. CEIR anchors supervision by linking every atomic proposition of the claim to retrieved multimodal evidence via per-atom verification. It then rewrites only the verification-failing atoms with diverse uncertainty expressions while preserving anchor facts. Experiments on MOCHEG and Factify with advanced LVLMs show that CEIR improves NEI-F1/Macro-F1 over standard SFT by +27.5/+13.5 points on MOCHEG; on Factify, it improves merged-insufficient F1 and five-way Macro-F1 by +21.1 and +9.2 points.
A102FULLM-to-M: A Discipline-Mismatch Theory of Multimodal Fact-Checking
Abdulrahman Abdullah Alalawi (University of New South Wales) · Basem Suleiman (University of New South Wales) · Imran Razzak (Mohamed bin Zayed University of Artificial Intelligence)
Abstract
Multimodal fact-checking systems exhibit a persistent instability: an architecture that leads on one benchmark often loses ground on another, with no method best everywhere. We argue this reflects a structural property of the benchmarks themselves. Fact-checking benchmarks silently encode different verification disciplines—standards of evidential sufficiency that range from permissive, where broad multimodal consistency suffices, to strict, where each specific claim element must be independently grounded. We introduce M-to-M (Many-to-Many), a matrix-based framework that represents localized claim–evidence interactions before aggregation, and use it to instantiate two verification architectures—holistic and compositional—under identical retrieval and evidence conditions. Across three benchmarks ordered by discipline, the performance gap between the two architectures does not merely shrink but reverses sign: holistic verification wins under permissive labels, compositional verification under strict ones. We trace this reversal to a single verdict rule, show it persists when aggregation is learned rather than specified, and find that learned verdict heads fail to transfer across benchmarks. Our findings suggest that benchmark choice conditions which verification behaviors are rewarded, while M-to-M provides a methodological framework for isolating and studying these verification dynamics under controlled aggregation policies.
A103FULLInterpretation-Aware Image Manipulation Detection
Yu Li (Universitat Rovira i Virgili) · Rolando Trujillo-Rasua (Universitat Rovira i Virgili) · Depeng Chen (Universitat Rovira i Virgili)
Abstract
Image manipulation has been a common practice since the early days of photography, and has evolved into a sophisticated threat with the rise of powerful image editing tools and generative AI. It can be used to spread misinformation, manipulate public opinion, and cause harm to individuals and communities. In this article, we study the problem of determining whether an image is misleading, i.e. edited in a misleading way. We introduce a risk framework to assess the intrinsic interpretive shift (ITS) of an ordered image pair, which evaluates whether the final edited image changes the interpretation supported by a source reference image. We show our risk framework can be operationalized with the Content Provenance and Authenticity (C2PA) provenance framework. We estimate ITS with a single-call vision-language implementation of our risk framework, which first checks for meaningful visual differences, then tests whether the differences induce interpretive shift, and finally determines whether the shift is fully explained by permissible transformations rather than content-level changes. The system outputs a binary label (potentially misleading or not) together with interpretive clues and a short justification. To test the approach and show that ITS is a measurable proxy for misleading edits, we built a benchmark of 418 ordered pairs, drawn from real-world fact-check cases and meaning-preserving transformations. The best-performing model configuration (gpt-5.4) achieves 88.2% precision, 94.2% recall, and 96.5% balanced accuracy. The code is available at https://github.com/liyu0x/ITS_detection/.
A104SHORTTextZGCA: Text-Guided Zero-Gated Cross-Attention for 3D Human Motion Prediction
Guanhui Qiao (Institute of Automation Chinese Academy of Sciences) · Lu Zhou (Institute of Automation Chinese Academy of Sciences) · Ding Jiang (Wuhan Artificial Intelligence Research Institute) · Jinqiao Wang (Institute of Automation Chinese Academy of Sciences)
Abstract
3D human motion prediction (HMP) forecasts future joint trajectories from a short observed pose sequence, but pose alone is often a narrow description of human behavior. A person who is turning, sitting down, or preparing to reach can have similar short-term pose dynamics while implying different futures. Modern vision-language models can turn simple stick-figure renders into natural-language descriptions, making semantic context available without changing the motion input itself. The challenge is to use this context without overwhelming a strong pose-only predictor with heavy language-conditioning machinery. We propose TextZGCA, a text-guided zero-gated cross-attention recipe for 3D HMP. Starting from a DCT-based spatial-temporal Transformer backbone, we encode each VLM-generated caption with a frozen plain CLIP-L text tower, project it into a small set of conditioning tokens, and insert a zero-gated cross-attention adapter after every motion encoder block. Because each adapter gate is initialized to zero, the model is initially identical to the no-text baseline and can learn to use text only where it improves prediction. On Human3.6M, TextZGCA achieves the best short-horizon and overall MPJPE among representative state-of-the-art methods in our comparison, while avoiding FiLM branches, auxiliary heads, and retrieval banks. The same recipe also achieves competitive results on CMU-Mocap, supporting a simple view of language in HMP: captions are useful as a semantic prior attached to a strong motion model.
A105FULLSAVER: Selective and Adaptive Multi-View Routing for Visual Emotion Reasoning in Vision-Language Models
Yubeen Lee (Sungkyunkwan University) · Sangeun Lee (Electronics and Telecommunications Research Institute) · Junyeop Cha (Sungkyunkwan University) · Jufeng Yang (Nankai University) · Eunil Park (Sungkyunkwan University)
Abstract
Emotions elicited by visual content are formed through the interaction of multiple visual cues rather than a single visual element, and their importance varies depending on the context. This characteristic makes visual emotion analysis not merely a classification problem but a reasoning task that requires the selective integration of diverse visual cues. Existing approaches tend to represent images using a unified feature representation and fail to explicitly model the contributions of different visual cues. To capture the multifaceted nature of emotional cues, we propose SAVER, a framework for query-conditioned visual emotion reasoning. SAVER decomposes visual information into multiple view-specific representations corresponding to distinct aspects, such as facial expressions, scenes, objects, and colorfulness, enabling the explicit modeling of each cue. A semantic-aware routing mechanism dynamically selects and integrates the most relevant views by jointly considering the visual context and query semantics. This selective integration is combined with learnable soft prompts to enable structured emotion reasoning within a vision-language model. Extensive experiments on diverse emotion datasets demonstrate that the proposed method consistently outperforms both vision-based and VLM-based approaches. Qualitative analysis provides interpretable insights into how different visual cues contribute to emotion prediction, highlighting the effectiveness of SAVER in improving both its performance and interpretability. The code is available at https://github.com/leeyubin10/SAVER.git.
A106FULLWhen Explanations Seem Helpful but Fail to Help: Evaluating XAI Interfaces for Model Diagnosis Across Modalities
Sunyoung Park (Sungkyunkwan University) · Subeom Park (Sungkyunkwan University) · Sehee Kim (Sungkyunkwan University) · Eunil Park (Sungkyunkwan University)
Abstract
Explainable AI (XAI) methods, such as LIME and SHAP, are increasingly incorporated into AI-enabled information systems for model inspection, oversight, and diagnosis. However, it remains unclear whether these interfaces improve users' ability to diagnose model behavior, or whether such utility generalizes across data modalities. We report three controlled user studies comprising 108 modality-specific sessions in which participants with foundational AI knowledge diagnosed model errors across Tabular, Text, and Image settings using LIME, SHAP, or a No-Explanation baseline, jointly evaluating task-grounded behavioral outcomes and subjective perceptions. Explanation interfaces were consistently preferred and rated as more understandable and useful, and they increased completion time across modalities; however, their diagnostic utility varied by modality. Benefits were clearest in the Tabular setting, driven primarily by LIME. Explanations provided no reliable benefit in Text, and Image results reflected method-specific differences rather than a reliable advantage over the baseline. Qualitative findings suggest that explanations often strengthened users' sense of understanding but did not consistently help them detect model failures. We argue that the quality of explanations in multimodal information systems should be evaluated using task-grounded, modality-sensitive criteria rather than subjective perception alone.
A107SHORTBeyond Answer Accuracy: Diagnosing Perception Failures in Multimodal Mathematical Reasoning
