Aniket Mitra (Jio University) · Arpit Chhabra (Jio University) · Adit Desai (Jio University) · Anshu Mehta (Jio University) · Vihaan Bhulla (Jio University) · Adithya Kulkarni (Ball State University) · Sudipta Roy (Jio University) · Mohna Chakraborty (Jio University)
Abstract
Multimodal Large Language Models (MLLMs) have shown strong performance on mathematical reasoning tasks that combine textual and visual information. However, final-answer accuracy offers limited insight into whether errors arise from incorrect perception, modality-dependent information extraction, or downstream reasoning. We introduce a perception-aware diagnostic framework for bimodal mathematical reasoning that represents a model's perceived problem understanding as knowledge graph triples and evaluates them using an Auxiliary Perception Set (APS), a human-verified collection of perception-oriented questions grounded in directly observable input information. We apply the framework to Plane Geometry problems from MathVerse, evaluating three MLLMs across two input representations: text and diagram embedded in a single image, and text and diagram provided separately. We also test controlled textual and visual perturbations to examine robustness under modality-specific noise. Results show that perception accuracy and final-answer accuracy often diverge: models that generate more accurate perception triples do not necessarily achieve higher final-answer accuracy, and the same problem content can produce different behavior depending on input representation. Cross-model triple transfer further shows that downstream performance depends on both the quality of extracted perceptual structure and the model's ability to reason over it. These findings suggest that perception-aware evaluation exposes failure modes hidden by answer-only evaluation and provides a finer-grained diagnostic view of bimodal mathematical reasoning. (Detailed implementation code, prompts, our multimodal noise-variant dataset, and results are available on GitHub: https://github.com/Anshu-Mehta/CIKM-2026. An interactive project website is available at https://perception-in-mllms.netlify.app/.)
A108FULLLG-PLO: Layout-Grounded Plackett–Luce Optimization for Instance-Aware Image Generation
Yeongseung Kim (Hanyang University) · Sungwon Moon (Electronics and Telecommunications Research Institute) · Donghyeon Cho (Hanyang University)
Abstract
Layout-conditioned image generation aims to synthesize images that match specified object categories and bounding boxes. However, generated images often fail to follow the intended layout conditions, resulting in hallucinations such as missing or spurious objects and spatial misalignment. When such inconsistent image-layout pairs are used as augmented training data, they can degrade the performance of object detectors. To address this issue, we propose LG-PLO, a layout-grounded Plackett–Luce optimization framework for instance-aware image generation. LG-PLO jointly considers image- and layout-level preferences using three candidates: a preferred image with correct layout, a rejected image with correct layout, and a preferred image with incorrect layout. LG-PLO then optimizes a Plackett-Luce objective that ranks images satisfying both preferences higher than those satisfying only one. Experiments on the COCO benchmark show that LG-PLO achieves a better balance between visual fidelity and layout adherence compared to baselines, while also improving detector performance when generated images are used for data augmentation.
A109RESOURCEGround Penetrating Radar Dataset for Indoor Pipeline Detection
Jiaqin Yue (Tsinghua University) · Yingrong Qin (Tsinghua University) · Menghao Zhu (Aerospace Information Research Institute, CAS) · Shengbo Ye (Aerospace Information Research Institute, CAS) · Yue Wang (Tsinghua University)
Abstract
Locating pipelines embedded in walls indoors or buried underground outdoors using ground penetrating radar (GPR) data, especially the B-scan images, is a widely adopted non-destructive testing method. However, existing open-source datasets in this field are typically limited in scale or lack ground-truth annotations for pipelines. To address these limitations, we present P-GPR, a GPR dataset specially collected for pipeline detection tasks. The dataset was collected using two GPR devices following a two-stage data acquisition scheme: pipeline ground-truth information was first collected during the construction phase when the pipelines were exposed, and GPR data were subsequently acquired from the wall surfaces after construction was completed. This dataset covers representative indoor pipeline installation conditions, including water pipes and electrical conduits embedded in reinforced concrete walls and concrete block walls. Furthermore, to validate the value of the dataset, we annotate the data and conduct pipeline experiments using commonly adopted object detection methods. The associated data (https://doi.org/10.5281/zenodo.20575661) and code (https://github.com/aiiseverything/P-GPR-Dataset) have been made publicly available.
A110FULLLearning Video-Derived Behavioral and Physiological Representations for Automated Deception Detection
Donghui Dai (Tongji University) · Huixuechun Wang (The Hong Kong Polytechnic University) · Weijia Li (The Hong Kong Polytechnic University) · Zhimin Mei (Western University) · Boyu Wang (Western University) · Jingyu Tong (China Telecom Research Institute) · Yuanhao Feng (The University of Electro-Communications)
Abstract
Deception detection in video conferencing is increasingly important with the rise of remote interviews, online judicial hearings, and telemedicine consultations. Existing approaches either rely on observable behavioral cues (e.g., micro-expressions and head movements) or depend on specialized equipment for physiological sensing (e.g., thermal cameras or wearable devices). The former benefits from the ubiquity and non-intrusive nature of commodity RGB cameras but often suffers from limited accuracy, while the latter provides more reliable and discriminative signals at the cost of additional hardware, hindering scalability in real-world deployment. In this work, we bridge the gap between behavioral cue-based and physiological signal-based approaches and introduce DeceptSense, a video-derived multimodal framework for contactless deception detection using only RGB video. The key insight is that complementary signals, including motion dynamics, facial temperature variations, and cardiac activity, can be jointly recovered from RGB video. DeceptSense extracts these modalities using an iDT descriptor for motion dynamics, an RGB-to-thermal pipeline for temperature variation modeling, and an rPPG module for cardiac signal extraction. It then employs a cross-modal attention mechanism to align the three temporally asynchronous modalities. Extensive experiments show that DeceptSense achieves an AUC of 89.6% on the challenging Real-Life Trial dataset and AUCs of 64.5% and 65.1% on the BOL and MU3D datasets, respectively. These results demonstrate the effectiveness of the proposed video-derived multimodal framework for automated deception detection.
A111FULLTrojanShot: Reinforced Demonstrations Yield Sample-Efficient Jailbreaks and Guardrails for LLMs
Abhishek Divekar (Amazon) · Vijit Malik (Amazon)
Abstract
LLM-based applications increasingly rely on models served through third-party providers, where the model's own alignment is often the sole defense against misuse. In this regime, developers must implement both red-teaming and guardrails themselves, yet existing in-context methods address these objectives in isolation and do not refine demonstrations against the target LLM's responses. We propose TrojanShot, a unified framework that post-trains a demonstration generator via reinforcement learning to produce potent in-context examples for both attack (Trojan shots) and defense (Guardian shots), operating entirely at the prompt layer of the target LLM. On AdvBench, a single Trojan shot reaches 80.6% ASR on Mistral-7B, and averaged across four datasets TrojanShot exceeds 256-shot Many-Shot Jailbreaking by 14.6 p.p. while preserving human-readable prompts; ablations show RL post-training is the dominant factor in demonstration quality, with the untrained generator already surpassing 1-shot ICA. We demonstrate strong transferability, with a trojan-attacker trained on Mistral-7B reaching 81.2% ASR on Llama-3-70B, exceeding the 69.9% of an attacker trained on Llama-3-8B. Guardian shots reduce TrojanShot's own ASR by 48.9 p.p. with helpfulness within 1.1 p.p. of the undefended model. Our results hold for models whose intrinsic alignment is the primary defense. Warning: this paper contains harmful model responses for academic reference.
A112SHORTDirect Answers, Hidden Criteria: Empirical Trade-offs in LLM Responses to Underdetermined Prompts
Venkata Satya Satvik Viriyala (IIIT Bangalore) · Vinu Ellampallil Venugopal (IIIT Bangalore)
Abstract
Large language models are increasingly used in question answering, recommendation, and conversational decision support. In many such settings, the user asks for a single answer even though the prompt does not specify the criterion needed to justify a unique choice. We study this setting as semantic underdetermination: multiple answers remain compatible with the prompt unless an additional ranking criterion is supplied. Rather than claiming a formal impossibility result, we study an empirical tension among three properties: premise-entailment correctness, criterion neutrality, and single-turn decisiveness. We evaluate 140 manually curated underdetermined prompts across seven categories on six LLMs, from 4B to frontier scale, under four response policies that handle under-specification differently. Forcing a direct answer makes models far more decisive (decisive rate 32%→93%) but lowers judged utility (4.06→3.53 out of 5, a large effect), because a confident answer must commit to a criterion the user never gave. Asking for the missing criterion instead gives the highest judged utility (4.53/5) and LLM-predicted satisfaction (4.48/5) but is rarely decisive in one turn (5.4%). A criterion-sensitivity score supports the mechanism: differences are small in size, but every one of the six models is most criterion-sensitive when forced to answer and least when it asks for the criterion. These findings suggest that asking for the missing criterion is a practical and transparent strategy for LLM systems facing under-specified user requests.
A113FULLEvaluating Closed-Domain RAG Systems with Expert-Written MCQs
Hila Reicher (Tel Aviv University) · Stav Koren (Tel Aviv University) · Slava Novgorodov (Tel Aviv University) · Tova Milo (Tel Aviv University)
Abstract
Evaluating Retrieval-Augmented Generation (RAG) systems in closed-domain settings --- where answers must be grounded in a fixed, domain-specific corpus --- remains an open problem. Existing approaches rely on synthetic question generation, manual annotation, or general-purpose benchmarks, each with structural limitations. We propose repurposing expert-written multiple-choice questions (MCQs) as a reusable evaluation signal for closed-domain RAG. MCQs are human-authored, curriculum-aligned assessment artifacts: they test concepts domain experts consider important, are written independently of the indexed corpus, and include expert-designed distractors that distinguish correct understanding from plausible misconceptions. Our methodology decomposes each correct answer into atomic factual claims, rewrites each option as a standalone declarative probe, and evaluates the RAG system through binary per-option judgments. We instantiate the methodology on a production university tutoring system and release a publicly reproducible benchmark. The per-option evaluation exposes differences in generation accuracy, abstention behavior, and distractor credulity that are not captured by retrieval-side evaluation alone. These results show that expert-written MCQs provide a practical and diagnostically rich evaluation resource for closed-domain RAG systems.
A114SHORTBeyond Benchmark Scores: How Synthetic and Authentic Query Distributions Diverge in RAG Evaluation
Filip J. Kucia (Warsaw University of Technology) · Barbara M. Gawlik (Warsaw University of Technology)
Abstract
RAG systems are routinely evaluated using synthetic question sets generated from the target document corpus. While this practice provides a useful check on overall retrieval capability, relying exclusively on synthetic benchmarks can mislead under distribution shift and overstate deployment readiness. Synthetic generation spreads questions evenly across the corpus, formulating long, detailed queries; real users put most of their traffic on a few administrative and procedural topics in short queries, while also asking about matters the generator never covers at all. We demonstrate this gap on a university faculty information system, comparing 1,851 synthetic questions generated via Gemini Notebook against 322 authentic queries collected via a student survey. The synthetic and authentic query sets differ significantly: authentic queries average 6.8 words versus 15.7 for the synthetic ones, and draw from only 53 unique sources compared to 165. Consequently, configurations that appear highly effective on synthetic benchmarks experience a substantial performance drop on authentic queries. Importantly, optimizing on synthetic queries selected a higher-latency hybrid retriever. In our setting the sparse retrieval component benefited long synthetic questions but not short authentic ones, costing up to 8× the latency of the fastest configuration we tested. We propose treating synthetic and authentic query sets as complementary extremes of the query-quality spectrum: synthetic data verifies maximum retrieval capacity under idealized conditions, while authentic queries test system robustness to the imprecise, underspecified inputs of real users.
A115FULLTasks over Application Manuals: Revealing Gaps in Long-Horizon Procedural Reasoning for Language Models
Utkarsh Soni (Manulife) · Syed Shariyar Murtaza (Manulife) · Yifan Nie (Manulife) · Sachin Chandrasekhar (Manulife) · Eugene Wen (Manulife)
Abstract
Large language models (LLMs) have achieved strong performance on a wide range of natural language tasks, and recent benchmarks suggest that they are increasingly adept at multi-hop reasoning. However, these benchmarks are typically short-horizon, requiring only a small number of retrieval or inference steps, and provide limited evidence of reliability on real-world tasks that involve following manuals spanning hundreds of pages with complex, interdependent guidelines. In this paper, we introduce Tasks over Application Manuals (TAM), a benchmark for evaluating long-horizon procedural reasoning. We construct TAM by curating real-world tasks from two domains—ICD-10-CM clinical coding (mapping medical conditions to diagnostic codes) and U.S. federal sentencing (computing crime sentencing guideline outcomes, specifically offense levels)—with human-validated labels. Each task requires following an authoritative manual with tens of thousands of rules and executing a sequence of interdependent steps across different sections to produce an exact answer. We evaluate general-purpose prompting approaches, including retrieval-augmented generation, ReAct-style prompting, and an agent-harness baseline on GPT-5, and find that the best exact-match performance remains extremely low: 1% on ICD-10-CM coding and 15.5% on sentencing tasks. These results show that current benchmarks may overestimate LLM reasoning ability and miss a key challenge: reliably following long, rule-based procedures.
A116SHORTCite Unseen: Measuring Citation-Channel Vulnerabilities in Retrieval-Augmented Generation
Minseok Hur (Sungkyunkwan University) · Jiho Shin (Sungkyunkwan University) · Damin Kim (Sungkyunkwan University) · Moohong Min (Sungkyunkwan University)
Abstract
Citation-grounded retrieval-augmented generation (RAG) systems expose source URLs alongside answers, extending user trust to cited links. Prior corpus-poisoning research primarily targets answer corruption, overlooking cases where answers remain largely unchanged while citations route users to unsafe destinations. We identify this citation-channel vulnerability and introduce Citation-stage Attack Success Rate (C-ASR) to separate citation manipulation from answer degradation. Across four BEIR corpora, three retrievers, and four generators, changing only the source URL of a single injected document reaches 71% C-ASR on the most vulnerable generator at well under 1% corpus pollution. The attack persists with paraphrased or answer-derived content, while citation behavior differs sharply across generators under our fixed pipeline. These results expose a model-dependent safety surface missed by answer-centric RAG evaluation.
A117SHORTEmbedding-Space Attacks on Pathology Foundation Models for Histopathology Retrieval
Domenico Benfenati (University of Naples Federico II) · Antonio M. Rinaldi (University of Naples Federico II) · Cristiano Russo (University of Naples Federico II) · Cristian Tommasino (University of Naples Federico II)
Abstract
Pathology Foundation Models (PFMs) are increasingly being used as frozen encoders for content-based retrieval in histopathology archives. In this context, a malicious actor does not need to alter a class label; a slight modification to the query image can shift its embedding and change the retrieved neighbors. We examine this vulnerability within an input-only white-box threat model, wherein the adversary has access to encoder gradients, but not to labels, classifier heads, retrieval pairs or the protected gallery. We instantiate PGD attacks with embedding-space objectives, comparing them with a random-noise baseline and evaluating training-free input transformations defenses under retrieval protocols that measure both embedding stability and ranking quality. Results across recent pathology encoders and benchmark datasets show that rankings can be severely degraded without gallery access, while simple symmetric preprocessing can partially restore retrieval performance.
A118FULLLogoGate: Object-Aware Logo-Exposure Backdoor Attack for Text-to-Image Models
Jieun Yun (Ulsan National Institute of Science and Technology) · Sangah Park (Ulsan National Institute of Science and Technology) · Saerom Park (Ulsan National Institute of Science and Technology)
Abstract
As fine-tuning and customization of pre-trained T2I models have become prevalent, backdoor attacks that exploit this fine-tuning process to embed triggers have also emerged. In this context, an adversary can secretly embed a brand logo into the generation process to conduct covert advertising or brand sabotage through publicly released models. However, existing approaches do not constrain which objects carry the logo, allowing it to appear on semantically unrelated objects (e.g., a car-brand logo on a flower vase) and producing a conspicuous backdoor pattern that undermines the attack's stealthiness. To address this, we propose LogoGate, the first object-aware logo-exposure backdoor attack, which allows the adversary explicit object-level control over which objects the trigger activates on, while all other categories remain entirely inert. Specifically, LogoGate (i) identifies negative objects most strongly bound to the trigger via a memorization-based discrepancy between conditional and unconditional noise predictions, and (ii) trains the customized model with two complementary suppression objectives: one that suppresses the trigger's marginal contribution to noise prediction on negative objects, and another that aligns the trigger's classifier-free guidance direction with its trigger-free counterpart under inference-time amplification. Our experiments demonstrate that LogoGate achieves controllable logo exposure on target objects while preserving prompt fidelity and image quality. Human evaluations and qualitative results further validate the practical effectiveness of LogoGate in real-world logo-exposure backdoor attack scenarios.
A119SHORTTrigger-Invariant Contrastive Unlearning for Backdoor Removal
Santosh Chapagain (Utah State University) · Shah Muhammad Hamdi (Utah State University) · Soukaina Filali Boubrahimi (Utah State University)
Abstract
Backdoor attacks embed hidden triggers that cause malicious model behavior at inference time. Gradient-ascent-based unlearning methods attempt to remove such behavior by maximizing loss on poisoned samples, but they may redirect the trigger’s effect to other classes rather than eliminate it. We propose Trigger-Invariant Contrastive Unlearning (TICU), an invariance-based framework that constructs clean and trigger-inserted counterfactual pairs and aligns both output distributions and hidden representations. Across multiple datasets, model architectures, and attack settings, TICU reduces triggered-accuracy drift compared with strong unlearning baselines, suggesting improved mitigation of trigger shifting. However, TICU exhibits a trade-off: it often better preserves triggered-task behavior while leaving higher residual label-flip rates than some baselines. These findings highlight both the promise and limitations of invariance-based backdoor unlearning.
A120RESOURCEREMEDI: A Benchmark for Retention and Unlearning Evaluation in Multi-label Clinical Disease Inference
Anurag Sharma (Indian Institute of Technology Kharagpur) · Sai Teja Chunchu (Indian Institute of Technology Kharagpur) · Prasenjit Mitra (Carnegie Mellon University Africa) · Sandipan Sikdar (L3S Research Center, LUH) · Koustav Rudra (Indian Institute of Technology Kharagpur)
Abstract
Clinical language models are trained on patient records that hold sensitive information, and patients can ask for their data to be removed under the right to be forgotten. Retraining from scratch for each request is too costly, so machine unlearning aims to erase specific records from a trained model instead. Yet, unlearning methods are mostly evaluated on synthetic, non-medical data, leaving their behaviour on real clinical records unknown. We introduce REMEDI, a benchmark for machine unlearning in multi-label clinical disease classification, built from real MIMIC-III patient records. REMEDI defines three forget-set scenarios of increasing severity, from single-patient deletion to bulk removal, and evaluates both utility and privacy through membership inference. We benchmark four unlearning method families on two biomedical models, and we find a clear utility-privacy trade-off and show that methods succeeding on small deletions collapse under large-scale forgetting, an effect that correlated disease labels make worse. We release REMEDI publicly to support reproducible research on clinical unlearning. (Code and extended version: https://github.com/anuragiiser/REMEDI)
A121FULLFedRGP: Robust Global-Consensus Prompting for Federated Vision-Language Adaptation with Noisy Labels
Chunpei Li (Guangxi Normal University) · Jiangmai Liao (Guangxi Normal University) · Dongcheng Li (Guangxi Normal University) · Wangjie Qiu (Beihang University) · Jieyuan Sun (Guangxi Normal University) · Xianxian Li (Guangxi Normal University)
Abstract
Multimodal federated prompt learning provides a parameter-efficient pathway for adapting vision-language models in privacy-sensitive scenarios. However, most existing methods assume that client-side labels are reliable, making it difficult to suppress the propagation of noise-corrupted prompt updates during global aggregation and consequently impairing cross-modal semantic alignment and generalization performance. To address this issue, we propose FedRGP, a robust global-consensus prompting framework for federated vision-language adaptation with noisy labels. By taking the global-consensus prompt as a cross-modal semantic anchor, this framework establishes a noise-resistant prompt collaboration mechanism that integrates sample reliability estimation, dual-stream prompt decoupling, and purified aggregation of the clean prompt stream, thereby suppressing the contamination of shared prompts by label noise at both the local optimization and global aggregation levels. Furthermore, to mitigate the risk that the local clean prompt stream drifts toward the local noisy distribution, we further construct a global-consensus alignment constraint mechanism to enhance the consistency between local clean semantics and the globally shared view. In multi-random-seed experiments on seven datasets, FedRGP achieves an average improvement of 2.99 percentage points over the strongest baseline, and further enlarges the average advantage to 5.44 percentage points under the high-noise condition of 60%.The anonymized source code is available at: https://github.com/liaojiangmai/FedRGP.
A122FULLFedICL-KVc: Federated In-Context Learning via KV Cache
Yiming Chen (Tsinghua University) · Nan He (Beijing University Of Technology) · Zheng Jiang (Tsinghua University) · Lifeng Sun (Tsinghua University)
Abstract
Large language models (LLMs) are increasingly constrained by the scarcity of high-quality public data, making private data essential for further improvement. However, private data is typically distributed across resource-constrained devices and cannot be shared due to strict privacy requirements, rendering conventional federated fine-tuning of LLMs impractical under limited computation and communication budgets. To address these challenges, we propose Federated In-Context Learning via KV Cache (FedICL-KVc), a novel framework that enables effective utilization of private data without parameter updates. Instead of transmitting raw demonstrations, clients upload only the corresponding key--value (KV) caches generated during auto-regressive inference, which are compact, smaller than full-model parameter payloads, and subject to an empirical reconstruction-risk evaluation under a restricted attack model. To further enhance efficiency and effectiveness, we introduce a confidence-based demonstration selection strategy to identify informative client samples, and a server-side KV cache compression method guided by a proxy dataset to reduce inference cost and suppress irrelevant information. Experiments on multiple tasks demonstrate that FedICL-KVc achieves competitive performance without client-side parameter updates or full-model parameter transmission while avoiding direct raw-data transmission.
A123FULLFedHCA: Hierarchical Contribution-Aware Aggregation for Asynchronous Federated Class-Incremental Learning
Yan Duan (Institute of Computing Technology, Chinese Academy of Sciences) · Xin Qin (Institute of Computing Technology, Chinese Academy of Sciences) · Xiaodong Yang (Institute of Computing Technology, Chinese Academy of Sciences) · Shubai Chen (Institute of Computing Technology, Chinese Academy of Sciences)
Abstract
Federated class-incremental learning (FCIL) aims to learn emerging classes across decentralized clients while preserving previously acquired knowledge. Existing FCIL methods are often designed or evaluated under relatively synchronous new-class exposure settings, while in realistic federated systems, a new class may initially appear on only a few clients with limited samples. This creates a local-global propagation mismatch: scarce new-class samples make local updates unstable, whereas majority-dominated aggregation dilutes these updates and slows the global propagation of new-class knowledge. To address this problem, we propose Hierarchical Contribution-Aware Aggregation (FedHCA), a novel framework for FCIL under asynchronous new-class exposure. FedHCA stabilizes local new-class update formation via a prototype-guided local learning strategy, and further promotes global new-class propagation through coarse-to-fine hierarchical aggregation. Specifically, the server first distinguishes new-class-exposed clients from old-class-only clients, then groups exposed clients according to their semantic and update-direction consistency, and finally performs contribution-weighted group aggregation based on update magnitudes. This design amplifies informative new-class updates while maintaining old-class stability. Experiments on CIFAR-100, CIFAR-10, and SVHN show that FedHCA achieves the best overall accuracy and a better balance between old-class retention and new-class adaptation compared with representative baselines. Further analyses confirm its propagation efficiency, component effectiveness, and robustness under asynchronous exposure.
A124FULLHiMAC: Hierarchical Federated Learning with Mobility-Aware Collaboration
Yibo Pan (Beihang University) · Boyi Liu (Beihang University) · Zimu Zhou (City University of Hong Kong) · Fan Gao (Beihang University) · Tianyi Wang (Beihang University) · Yi Xu (Beihang University) · Yongxin Tong (Beihang University)
Abstract
Mobility-aware hierarchical federated learning (MobiHFL) is an emerging paradigm to support urban applications where clients continuously move across edge-server coverage areas. Existing methods mainly treat mobility as a scheduling challenge and often train a single global model across all edge-servers. This overlooks the spatial non-IID characteristics of urban environments, where regions exhibit distinct yet correlated data distributions. Region-wise personalization is a natural remedy, but mobility makes it difficult. Each edge model is trained on its current client population, while future arriving and departing clients may follow different distributions, causing cold-start degradation and feature-classifier mismatch after handover. We propose HiMAC, a personalized MobiHFL framework that turns predicted client movement into proactive inter-edge collaboration. HiMAC uses per-client LSTM trajectory predictors to estimate future client flows and builds a round-level transition matrix to guide collaboration. With a decoupled backbone-classifier architecture, HiMAC prepares each edge for expected incoming clients through incoming-aware classifier initialization and improves compatibility with likely destination edges through outgoing-regularized backbone training. Extensive experiments on image classification and object detection benchmarks show improvements of up to 12.18 percentage points in image-classification accuracy and 6.50 points in mAP@50 over state-of-the-art baselines across varying mobility intensities.
A125FULLFair to Federate? Two-Sided Prediction of Performance and Fairness Outcomes in Healthcare Federated Learning
Marina Ceccon (University of Padova) · Alessandro Fabris (University of Trieste) · Ornella Irrera (University of Padova) · Gianmaria Silvello (University of Padova) · Gian Antonio Susto (University of Padova)
Abstract
Federated learning (FL) has emerged as a promising paradigm for collaborative healthcare modeling under privacy constraints, yet institutions currently lack tools to anticipate how joining a federation will impact predictive performance and fairness. Existing work has primarily focused on post-hoc fairness mitigation, while overlooking the pre-collaboration decision itself. In this work, we introduce the Federation Assessment Problem, a two-sided prediction problem concerned with anticipating how federation would affect both a candidate institution seeking to join a federation and the institutions already participating in it, before collaboration occurs. To address this problem, we propose a two-stage meta-learning framework that predicts changes in performance and fairness metrics from institution-level metadata. We evaluate the framework on two healthcare imaging domains, across federations of varying sizes. Results show that federation-induced changes in both predictive performance and fairness can be estimated with high accuracy. The analysis further identifies label bias as one of the strongest predictors of fairness outcomes across both domains, often rivaling or exceeding demographic composition in importance. These findings demonstrate that informed federation assessment is possible without raw data sharing and highlight the need to explicitly measure multiple sources of bias when reasoning about fairness in healthcare FL.
A126FULLFairSEP: Harmonizing Multiple Fairness Metrics in Graph Neural Networks via Pareto Optimization
Kaixing Liang (Guilin University of Electronic Technology) · Xuemin Wang (Guilin University of Electronic Technology) · Guofeng Xia (Guilin University of Electronic Technology) · Zeyu Cao (Guilin University of Electronic Technology) · Liang Chang (Guilin University of Electronic Technology) · Tianlong Gu (Jinan University) · Yuanjing Hao (Guilin University of Electronic Technology) · Wei Chen (Guilin University of Electronic Technology)
Abstract
Group fairness in Graph Neural Networks (GNNs) aims to mitigate performance disparities across demographic groups. While existing methods primarily focus on Demographic Parity and Equal Opportunity, Predictive Equality (ΔFPR) remains under-explored, potentially leading to disparate error risks. Furthermore, these methods often rely on a single surrogate loss of fairness, which is insufficient to achieve multiple fairness criteria simultaneously. Moreover, these methods often apply uniform debiasing across different label groups, making it difficult to separately address group disparities in the positive and negative classes. Consequently, achieving an optimal trade-off between utility and multiple fairness metrics remains challenging. To address these issues, we propose FairSEP, a unified Pareto-optimized framework. Specifically, we construct a sensitive subspace from per-class centroid differences between sensitive groups, debias embeddings by removing their subspace projections, and enforce prediction consistency between original and debiased representations. On this basis, we introduce a conditional Wasserstein loss that minimizes the Wasserstein distance between predictive distributions of sensitive groups conditioned on true labels, explicitly reducing disparate error rates across groups. Finally, we design a Pareto-based strategy that automatically adjusts the loss weights to resolve conflicts between different objectives. Experiments on five benchmark datasets demonstrate that FairSEP achieves a superior trade-off compared to state-of-the-art baselines.
A127FULLVFR-Audit: Verdict-Level Reliability for Fairness Audits in Hospital Length-of-Stay Prediction
Md Jannatul Rakib Joy (Swinburne University of Technology) · Viet Vo (Swinburne University of Technology) · Caslon Chua (Swinburne University of Technology)
Abstract
Fairness audits in clinical Artificial Intelligence convert continuous fairness metrics into binary pass-or-fail verdicts against operational thresholds, where hospital governance boards, payers, and regulators act on the resulting verdicts. Such audits are repeated over time and across hospital sites, thus the same verdict can flip between pass and fail across audits. Existing uncertainty methods such as Bayesian posteriors, bootstrap confidence intervals, and permutation tests address verdict instability only at the continuous-metric level. Converting metric-level uncertainty into a verdict-stability claim remains a manual step that scales poorly across the (model, metric, attribute) cells an audit covers. Existing uncertainty methods also leave open whether bias-mitigation steps, such as reweighing or per-group threshold shifts, yield a stable passing verdict at the cost of model discrimination measured as AUROC or AUPRC. To address this verdict-stability gap, we propose VFR-Audit, a framework built around the Verdict Flip Rate (VFR), a scalar bounded between 0 and 0.5 that measures the probability of verdict reversal under stratified bootstrap resampling. VFR-Audit reports VFR alongside three reliability axes, namely within-cohort resampling stability, audit-size sensitivity, and cross-hospital verdict agreement via Fleiss' kappa. The framework was evaluated on 925,128 administrative discharge records from 441 Texas hospitals, against an intersectional adaptation of Kamiran and Calders' reweighing. On the unintervened baseline, the audit detects verdict reversal in 43.5% of cells in the cross-model audit grid. After the canonical intervention, 11 of 28 cells continue to flip. Intersectional reweighing fails the four-fifths rule on this cohort regardless of regularisation strength, while per-cell threshold shifting is the main effective component of the canonical intervention. VFR translates continuous metric uncertainty into a probability of binary-verdict reversal, and a derived-baseline comparison attributes the verdict outcome to specific intervention components, so audit reliability and intervention effects can be reported together rather than as separate claims.
A128SHORTBIRDNet: Mining and Encoding Boolean Implication Knowledge Graphs as Interpretable Deep Neural Networks
Tirtharaj Dash (BITS Pilani, K K Birla Goa Campus)
Abstract
Tabular data in knowledge-rich domains often carries a latent prior in the form of Boolean implication relationships (BIRs) between pairs of features. We mine such relationships with a sparse-exception binomial test. We encode the resulting typed graph as the connectivity of a layered neural network, called BIRDNet, in which each hidden unit corresponds to one mined rule and binds only to its two features. We show two consequences of this design: First, the architecture is sparse: at most 2/d of the weights in each BIR layer are active, where d is the input dimension. Second, the model is intrinsically interpretable: every trained unit keeps a stable symbolic identity, so rules can be read off the network without surrogate models. Unlike most neurosymbolic models, BIRDNet does not consume an external rule base; its structural prior is mined from the data. We evaluate BIRDNet on six transcriptomic and proteomic benchmarks. Our results show that BIRDNet stays within 0.02 AUROC of the strongest dense baseline, while using up to 95× fewer active parameters than an architecture-matched dense MLP. First-layer rules align with known biological signatures across multiple cancer subtypes and tissue types. Matched-topology controls show that the mined graph contributes symbolic meaning rather than predictive advantage: shuffled or random pairings match or improve AUROC but no longer correspond to mined implications. Data and code are available at: https://github.com/MAHI-Group/BIRDNet.
A129FULLContext-Aware Subgraph Explanations for Multi-Task GNNs
Yejin Yoon (Department of Statistics and Data Science, University of Seoul) · Jaesung Lim (Department of Statistics and Data Science, University of Seoul) · Jinhee Choi (School of Environmental Engineering, University of Seoul) · Jong-June Jeon (Department of Statistics, University of Seoul)
Abstract
Explanations for Graph Neural Networks (GNNs) that perform graph-level prediction generally describe how substructures in an input graph contribute to a specific output. However, in multi-task settings, the input-output relationship and important substructures are heterogeneous across tasks, limiting the effectiveness of existing explanation methods. Existing approaches typically relied on task-specific independent explainers, underutilizing the shared representations across related tasks. As a result, it remains challenging to transfer explanatory patterns to data-scarce tasks. In this paper, we propose CAMIE, a Context-Aware Motif Importance Explainer designed for multi-task molecular classification. CAMIE leverages a Knowledge Distillation-inspired pseudo target to effectively distill assay-specific motif-removal responses, transferring explanatory patterns across tasks without requiring ground-truth labels. CAMIE utilizes assay context information as an input to the explainer, jointly capturing shared explanatory structures and task-dependent mechanisms. Our experiments on the ToxCast dataset show that our proposed method flexibly adapts explanations according to assay context and provides more faithful explanations across tasks, including tasks with limited data.
A130FULLTo Rewire or Not to Rewire: Optimal Transport and the Limits of Graph Structure
Richard Serrano (Laboratoire Hubert Curien) · Charlotte Laclau (Télécom Paris, Institut Polytechnique de Paris) · Baptiste Jeudy (Laboratoire Hubert Curien) · Christine Largeron (Laboratoire Hubert Curien)
Abstract
Graph Neural Networks (GNNs) leverage message passing to learn on relational data, a mechanism that implicitly assumes homophily: connected nodes tend to share similar features. On heterophilic graphs, where this assumption breaks down, message passing can degrade node representations to the point where a simple Multi-Layer Perceptron (MLP) that ignores the graph entirely matches or outperforms spatial GNNs. While graph rewiring has emerged to address this topological misalignment, existing evaluations rarely tune rewiring hyperparameters jointly with the downstream model or include a competitive MLP baseline, which risks overestimating rewiring's benefits. We address this gap through a rigorous nested cross-validation protocol that jointly optimizes rewiring and classifier hyperparameters, guaranteeing that observed failures reflect intrinsic limitations rather than suboptimal configuration. As a practical instantiation of a rewiring approach based on joint feature-topology, we introduce OTR. It is a rewiring method based on the Multi-View Wasserstein distance that jointly models node feature similarity and graph topology via optimal transport plans, while maintaining the graph's structural density through a strict edge budget. Evaluating across the full heterophily-homophily spectrum on synthetic and real-world benchmarks, we characterize three operational regimes: rewiring is unnecessary under high homophily, beneficial in an ambiguous regime where it exposes latent homophilic structure, and insufficient under strong heterophily where a tuned MLP achieves better performance. We therefore advocate a Structure-First paradigm: establish the structure-agnostic performance ceiling before investing in topological preprocessing. Code and data are available at https://github.com/RichardSrn/GraphRewiring.
A131SHORTAdversarial Deception-based Detection of Anomalous Network Communities
Fabrizio Angiulli (University of Calabria) · Fabio Fassetti (University of Calabria) · Valeria Fionda (University of Calabria)
Abstract
Detecting anomalous communities in complex networks is a fundamental task in network science, cybersecurity, and social network analysis. In this paper, we introduce a novel framework for anomalous community detection that accounts for the intentional manipulation of community structures through adversarial deception strategies. Intuitively, our notion of anomalous community captures communities whose structure can be deliberately perturbed to evade community detection algorithms while preserving their internal cohesion. The rationale underlying this novel notion is that well-formed communities are more difficult to hide within the overall network structure and are inherently difficult to conceal, whereas anomalous ones are particularly vulnerable to deception. We formalize the notion of deception anomaly by combining community deception metrics with statistical unexpectedness measures derived from the distribution of deception scores across candidate communities. Building on these definitions, we propose DACAD (Deception-based Adversarial Community Anomaly Detection). We perform a preliminary evaluation of the proposed approach on synthetic benchmark networks, analyzing the effectiveness of the proposed approach for different network topologies and deception budgets and comparing our method with related competing approaches.
A132FULLMeta-ResGAD: Bi-Level Optimization for Topology-Adaptive Graph Anomaly Detection
ChenXuan Shan (School of Computer Science and Engineering, Northeastern University) · Minghe Yu (Software College, Northeastern University) · Zhi Dong (Software College, Northeastern University) · Songran Liu (School of Computer Science and Engineering, Northeastern University) · Tiancheng Zhang (School of Computer Science and Engineering, Northeastern University) · Ge Yu (School of Computer Science and Engineering, Northeastern University)
Abstract
Generative models have demonstrated significant potential in semi-supervised graph anomaly detection (GAD) by synthesizing pseudo-anomalies to mitigate extreme label scarcity. However, existing Generative Adversarial Network (GAN)-based frameworks face two key limitations: mode collapse during generation and poor topological adaptability. Specifically, traditional methods usually enforce rigid structural alignment, which wrongly treats normal heterophilic connections as anomalies, leading to performance degradation on heterophilic graphs. In this paper, we argue that these failures stem from indiscriminate learning, where models lack an adaptive mechanism to evaluate the quality and reliability of generated pseudo-anomalies and structural priors. To bridge this gap, we propose Meta-ResGAD, a novel bi-level optimization framework that introduces a "learning-to-reweight" paradigm into generative GAD. By reformulating GAD as a nested optimization problem, we divide the learning process into two levels: in the upper level, we utilize unrolled differentiation to optimize an upper-level Scorer using clean validation feedback; in the lower level, a structure-aware generation process explicitly decouples semantic and structural signals. Guided by meta-gradients, the Scorer acts as a dynamic sample filter that penalizes uninformative noise to prevent mode collapse, and adaptively down-weights unreliable structural priors to disentangle structural anomalies from normal heterophily. Extensive experiments on diverse real-world benchmarks demonstrate that Meta-ResGAD achieves state-of-the-art performance with robust topology-adaptive generalization, while maintaining the high inference efficiency and low memory consumption crucial for large-scale industrial deployment. Our code is now available at: https://github.com/TDSCX/AJAX.
A133FULLMETrIC-G: Multigraph Enrichment and Time-Aware Message Passing for Imbalanced Classification in Transaction Graphs
Steve Gounoue (University of Bonn) · Marco Markwald (University of Bonn) · Ashutosh Sao (Leibniz Universität Hannover) · Simon Gottschalk (Leibniz Universität Hannover) · Elena Demidova (University of Bonn)
Abstract
Modern digital ecosystems comprise entities connected through multiple directed interactions, forming complex transaction graphs. These graphs pose significant challenges for node and edge classification due to domain-specific interaction patterns spanning multiple hops and related transactions, multigraph structures with rich edge features, and often severe class imbalance. State-of-the-art graph neural networks often fail to fully exploit multigraph structures and effectively capture such structural-temporal patterns, resulting in suboptimal classification performance. To address these limitations, we introduce METrIC-G, a novel approach designed to capture multi-hop transaction patterns among connected entities occurring in close temporal proximity within a graph-neural-network-based architecture. METrIC-G builds expressive time-aware node- and edge-features from transaction sequences and time-based statistics. METrIC-G effectively identifies symbolic, class-discriminative patterns among transaction outliers to mitigate class imbalance. METrIC-G employs a time-aware message-passing mechanism that adaptively weights neighbor contributions based on a learnable temporal decay function. We experimentally demonstrate that METrIC-G outperforms all baselines by at least 5.15 percentage points (p.p.) in the minority class F1-score and at least 2.92 p.p. in macro F1-score across all datasets.
A134FULLPageRank Attributed Graph Subspace Clustering
Youness Soussou (University Mohammed VI Polytechnic) · Loubna Mekouar (University Mohammed VI Polytechnic) · Youssef Iraqi (University Mohammed VI Polytechnic) · Mohamed Nadif (Université Paris Cité)
Abstract
Attributed graph clustering aims to group nodes that are similar with respect to both graph structure and node attributes. However, effectively combining these two sources of information remains challenging, as structural proximity does not necessarily imply attribute similarity. The problem becomes even more difficult in high-dimensional settings, where clusters may depend on different subsets of features. To address these issues, we propose PRAGSC, a framework that integrates PageRank-based propagation with subspace clustering. Our propagation scheme incorporates a teleportation mechanism that mitigates over-smoothing by re-injecting the original node features at each iteration, while the subspace clustering component identifies cluster-specific attribute subsets. Experiments on six real-world benchmark datasets demonstrate that PRAGSC consistently outperforms recent state-of-the-art attributed graph clustering methods across different metrics, while enhancing interpretability through the identification of cluster-specific feature subspaces.
A135SHORTMASK: Minority-aware Semantic Alignment via Knowledge Enhancement for Long-tailed Graph Clustering
Yiwei Fu (Peking University) · Chunchun Chen (Tongji University) · Yuxing Zhang (Shanghai Jiao Tong University) · Weizhi Zhang (University of Illinois at Chicago) · Guanjie Zheng (Shanghai Jiao Tong University) · Wei Ye (Tongji University) · Xiao Luo (University of Wisconsin–Madison) · Philip S. Yu (University of Illinois at Chicago) · Minghua Deng (Peking University)
Abstract
Text-attributed graph (TAG) clustering seeks to identify node groups by jointly exploiting the semantic information encoded in textual attributes and the structural information captured by graph connectivity. Despite significant progress, their performance often becomes less satisfactory under long-tailed distributions. To address this challenge, we introduce Minority-Aware Semantic Alignment via Knowledge Enhancement (MASK), an unsupervised framework designed for long-tailed TAG clustering. The core idea of MASK is to integrate the textual understanding capability of large language models (LLMs) with canonical correlation maximization to construct minority-aware semantic groups. More specifically, MASK first leverages LLMs to augment textual attributes and generate multiple textual views, which are then aligned via canonical correlation. Subsequently, we randomly assign samples into balanced groups with mixed semantics for consistency learning and then emphasize those with higher semantic discrepancy as minority candidates. To enhance clustering with external knowledge, we leverage LLMs to fine-tune the model with ranking guidance, which is then formulated as a regularization term. Extensive experiments on four datasets under two varying imbalance ratios demonstrate the effectiveness of MASK. The implementation of MASK is publicly available at https://github.com/fuyw-aisw/MASK.
A136SHORTSparkAlign: A Star-Hopping Heuristic for Efficient Unsupervised Plain Graph Alignment
Boyan Wang (Hefei University of Technology) · Weijie Feng (Hefei University of Technology) · Jinyang Huang (Hefei University of Technology) · Dan Guo (Hefei University of Technology) · Zhi Liu (The University of Electro-Communications) · Zhuochen Fan (Pengcheng Laboratory) · Zhiyong Cheng (Hefei University of Technology)
Abstract
Unsupervised plain graph alignment (UPGA) seeks corresponding nodes between two graphs from topology alone, without attributes or seed anchors. The dominant embed-then-match paradigm is expensive on both fronts: it repeatedly retrains node embeddings and then solves a costly global assignment, so it scales poorly to large graphs. We present SparkAlign, a training-free heuristic that, inspired by star-hopping in celestial navigation, locates a node's counterpart by measuring its heat-diffusion proximity to a shared set of high-confidence landmark matches. Although heuristic in spirit, the descriptor is principled: diffusion makes structurally equivalent nodes comparable across graphs, and a short stability analysis justifies a finite diffusion depth. Matching then uses two sparse, highly parallel strategies that avoid dense global assignment, one favoring speed and one preserving one-to-one consistency on a restricted candidate set. On three benchmarks SparkAlign attains accuracy approaching a structural identifiability reference while running up to two orders of magnitude faster than the strongest baseline and seeding markedly more accurate pseudo-anchors. Our code is available at https://github.com/MaxQ545/SparkAlign.
A137FULLDegree-Mass Message Passing for Betweenness Ranking in Directed and Undirected Networks
Justin Dachille (King's College London) · Aurora Rossi (University of Bonn) · Sunil Kumar Maurya (University of Tokyo) · Frederik Mallmann-Trenn (King's College London) · Xin Liu (National Institute of Advanced Industrial Science and Technology) · Frédéric Giroire (Université Côte d'Azur, CNRS, Inria, I3S) · Tsuyoshi Murata (Institute of Science Tokyo) · Emanuele Natale (Université Côte d'Azur, CNRS, Inria, I3S)
Abstract
Computing the importance of nodes in networks is a long-standing fundamental problem that has driven extensive study of various centrality measures. A particularly well-known centrality measure is betweenness centrality, whose exact computation becomes prohibitive on large-scale networks. Graph Neural Network (GNN) models have thus been proposed to predict the ranking of nodes by betweenness centrality. However, existing GNN-based methods either have graph-size-dependent parameter counts or are limited to undirected graphs. We propose a lightweight GNN architecture that exploits the empirically observed relationship between betweenness centrality and multi-hop degree mass. This motivates the use of degree masses as size-invariant node features. To improve generalization, we train on synthetic graphs whose degree distributions more closely match those of real-world networks, including directed and undirected scale-free graphs and uniformly directed hyperbolic random graphs. We evaluate our model on 14 real-world networks spanning eight domains, including social, email, and citation networks, across both directed and undirected regimes. The experiments show that our model improves the Kendall τb correlation by up to 24.6% on undirected and 10.9% on directed graphs, while using 56× fewer parameters than the lightest competing GNN baseline and achieving competitive inference time, with up to a 24.5× speedup on selected directed graphs.
A138FULLPAGT: Prototype-Guided Adaptive Graph Transformer for Mitigating Over-Globalizing
Zanpu Wang (Xinjiang University) · Pengcheng Chen (Xinjiang University) · Xue Li (Xinjiang University) · Mohan Yang (China Agricultural University) · Ziyang Li (Xinjiang University)
Abstract
For homogeneous data node classification tasks, Graph Transformers (GTs) have become highly promising frameworks, owing to their global attention mechanism that captures long-range correlations. However, existing models suffer from the over-globalizing problem in homogeneous graphs, where global similarity aggregation triggers multi-scale feature degradation and weak alignment of semantic and structural information, consequently allowing global noise to obscure local features and impede structural discovery. To solve this problem, we propose a Prototype-Guided Adaptive Graph Transformer for mitigating over-globalizing (PAGT). Firstly, a bi-branch local propagation module enhances multi-scale graph adaptive structural representation learning by decoupling and modeling residuals hierarchically, boosting training stability. Subsequently, a prototypically guided layered adaptive query mechanism mitigates feature degradation by generating global anchors from both microscopic and macroscopic levels, reducing noise and structure-irrelevant interactions. Finally, a teacher-guided semantic and structural alignment strategy enhances alignment between local and global representations via knowledge distillation and contrastive learning, guaranteeing alignment between local topological branches and global attention branches. Experimental results show that significant improvements with strong stability are achieved on all seven datasets, improving by 2.5% and 2.6% on the CiteSeer and Cora datasets, respectively. The code will be made publicly available upon publication.
A139SHORTPRISM: Reliable LLM Knowledge Distillation from Graph-Context Perspectives for Text-Attributed Graph Learning
Jung-Hyun Kim (Hanyang University) · So-Bin Jung (Hanyang university) · David Yoon Suk Kang (Chungbuk National University) · Sang-Wook Kim (Hanyang University)
Abstract
Text-attributed graph (TAG) learning aims to leverage both textual attributes and graph structures for node classification. Recent studies have utilized Large Language Models (LLMs) to generate pseudo-labels and rationales for few-label TAG learning. However, existing approaches typically rely solely on the textual attribute of target nodes, making the generated knowledge susceptible to noise and unreliability. To address this limitation, we propose PRISM (Perspective-based Reliable Imitation with Semantic Multiplicity), a reliability-aware knowledge distillation framework for few-label TAG learning. PRISM constructs multiple structural-context perspectives for each target node and estimates the reliability of LLM-generated knowledge based on cross-perspective consistency. The resulting reliability weights are then incorporated into the distillation process, enabling GNNs to place greater emphasis on more reliable supervision signals. Extensive experiments on five TAG benchmark datasets demonstrate that PRISM consistently outperforms existing methods in few-label node classification.
A140FULLDynamic Exploitation of Source Experts for Few-Shot Node Classification on Text-Attributed Graphs
Minuk Kim (University of Seoul) · Heasoo Hwang (University of Seoul)
Abstract
Cross-graph transfer on text-attributed graphs (TAGs) is challenging because different graph domains often encode different structure-semantic relationships. Existing unified-encoder methods jointly train a single encoder using multiple source graphs, but such a unified encoder yields only marginal improvements over the best single-source encoder due to knowledge conflict across domains. Recent multi-expert methods alleviate this issue by maintaining multiple experts, yet they also require joint training over all source graphs and do not adapt routing behavior to unseen target graphs. These limit scalability, flexibility, and applicability to unseen target TAGs under two realistic constraints of a source-free environment and few-shot node classification. To overcome these limitations, we propose DARGE (Dynamic Adaptive Routing of Graph Experts), a novel source-free few-shot cross-graph transfer method for TAGs. Instead of jointly training experts and a router, DARGE independently trains source-specific experts aligned via a shared universal LLM-derived codebook, allowing their outputs to remain directly comparable. Given an unseen target graph, DARGE dynamically combines experts using a two-level routing strategy: a label-free router first adapts to the unlabeled target graph structure through self-supervision, and an episode-level calibration further refines soft expert selection using lightweight few-shot class separation signals. Experiments on seven benchmark TAG datasets demonstrate that DARGE consistently outperforms both unified-encoder methods and multi-expert baselines. Further analysis shows that our routing strategy successfully recovers target-relevant expert preferences and scales well to large expert pools through signature-based pre-screening.
A141FULLCapture Invariants from Dynamics: Temporal Graph Learning by Decoupling Graph Context and Downstream Task
Qingying Xu (Wuhan University) · Zixin Liu (Wuhan University) · Liang Hong (Wuhan University)
Abstract
Temporal graph learning aims to model the dependency between temporal graph (TG) data and downstream tasks. However, some temporal changes of nodes and edges contribute little to the essential task dependency, although they may show statistical correlations with task labels within certain time periods. Indiscriminately learning all dynamic patterns may therefore mislead the model to capture such period-specific correlations, leading to poor performance. To mask changes that could mislead model learning, we propose InvarTG, an invariance-based temporal graph learning method that decouples graph context modeling from downstream task prediction. Specifically, InvarTG first forecasts the evolving graph context by aggregating structural and temporal information through message passing and a temporal mixer, respectively. It then performs invariant task prediction by extracting invariant embeddings from multiple prediction-time graph contexts, thereby capturing invariant dependencies that consistently support downstream tasks. To preserve structural and temporal information while learning invariant dependencies, we further introduce a residual-guided joint optimization strategy to coordinate the forecasting and prediction processes. Experimental results on public datasets show that InvarTG outperforms state-of-the-art methods by at least 5.31% in F1 score.
A142SHORTHyperlink Prediction on Hypergraphs of Text
Alessia Antelmi (Università degli Studi di Torino) · Tiziano Citro (Università degli Studi di Salerno) · Dario De Maio (Università degli Studi di Salerno) · Daniele De Vinco (Università degli Studi di Salerno) · Valerio Di Pasquale (Università degli Studi di Salerno) · Mirko Polato (Università degli Studi di Torino) · Carmine Spagnuolo (Università degli Studi di Salerno)
Abstract
Hypergraphs are powerful tools for modeling high-order relationships in complex real-world data, and hyperlink prediction has emerged from the need to infer relationships that are missing or have not yet formed. Existing hyperlink prediction methods primarily emphasize the structural connectivity encoded in the network, overlooking the rich semantic information associated with nodes and hyperedges that can be expressed in text. In this work, we propose a novel framework for hyperlink prediction on Hypergraphs of Text (HoTs), where both nodes and hyperedges are enriched with textual attributes. Our model jointly leverages these semantic and structural signals by combining hypergraph convolutional operators with cross-attention mechanisms that iteratively refine node and hyperedge representations. Experimental results demonstrate that integrating semantic information from nodes and hyperedges with structural features consistently improves performance over baselines that rely solely on topology, thereby highlighting the effectiveness of contextual representations for hyperlink prediction and opening new directions for semantic-aware hypergraph learning.
A143FULLHeterogeneous Hypergraph Attention Network for Scholar Recommendation and Team Formation
Xiyao Cheng (University of Missouri Columbia) · Upasana Roy (University of Missouri Columbia) · Ashish Pandey (University Of Missouri Columbia) · Nilanjan Chakraborty (Missouri University of Science and Technology) · Sounak Chakraborty (University Of Missouri Columbia) · Prasad Calyam (University of Missouri Columbia)
Abstract
Scholar recommendation and academic team formation are critical for collaborations fostering scientific breakthroughs. However, effective team formation presents challenges of balancing expertise from diverse scientific domains. Current recommendation approaches, although reasonably effective, fail to capture higher-order group semantics inherent in co-authorship of scientific manuscripts and funding communities, and also collapse entirely for scholars lacking sufficient interaction history. To address these challenges, we propose HyTeam, a hypergraph-based method for scholar recommendation and academic team formation comprising two tightly coupled components. First, a heterogeneous hypergraph attention network with TransE-based relational scoring that encodes multi-type scholarly relationships as hyperedges and ranks candidates via learned relational translation. Second, a query-decomposed diversity-aware team formation algorithm that jointly optimises team relevance, structural diversity, and skill coverage. HyTeam derives scholar embeddings from the hypergraph co-participation structure, naturally accommodating scholars with sparse or absent collaboration records. Our evaluations on a curated NSF award dataset and the public DBLP citation network demonstrate that HyTeam outperforms all baselines, achieving Recall@10 of 0.6005 and 0.4883 on the NSF and DBLP datasets, respectively. Our team formation evaluation further achieves consistently superior team configurations, attaining the best trade-off among all baselines with a team score of 0.6740.
A144FULLResCrime: Residual Evolution Diffusion for Spatially Adaptive Multimodal Urban Crime Forecasting
Ce Zhang (Xinjiang University) · Jiaqi Duan (Xinjiang University) · Long Yu (Xinjiang University) · Shengwei Tian (Xinjiang University) · Zhezhe Zhu (Xinjiang University)
Abstract
Urban crime forecasting aims to predict future spatial risk distributions from historical crime and urban context, supporting proactive public safety allocation. Existing methods have advanced this task with multimodal urban signals, but they often use historical crime risk maps only as conditioning inputs, without explicitly modeling their evolution into future risk maps. They also provide limited adaptation of point-of-interest (POI) semantics to local historical crime context, weakening their ability to capture spatially varying predictive relevance. To address these issues, we propose ResCrime, a history-anchored residual evolution diffusion framework for spatially adaptive multimodal crime forecasting. ResCrime initializes the reverse diffusion near the observed historical risk map and models future risk as a residual evolution of historical observations. A multimodal denoising backbone integrates crime, POI, satellite, and map features to support history-to-future risk estimation, while Crime History Spatial Adaptive Reweighting (CSAR) recalibrates POI semantic channels based on local historical intensity before multimodal fusion. Experiments on New York City and Los Angeles demonstrate that ResCrime outperforms state-of-the-art baselines, improving AP over DiffCrime by 6.68% and 5.21% and reducing RMSE by 10.71% and 6.52%, while maintaining efficient inference. Code is available at https://github.com/RooB1t/ResCrime.
A145APPLIEDDelivery Scope Generation for Last-mile Delivery: Fine-grained Urban Area Segmentation, Modeling, and Optimization
Zhongkai Bao (Dingdong (Cayman) Limited) · Jing Zhao (Dingdong (Cayman) Limited) · Wei Liang (Dingdong (Cayman) Limited) · Ning Chen (Dingdong (Cayman) Limited)
Abstract
Generating non-overlapping delivery scopes is a fundamental task in last-mile delivery, requiring spatially meaningful and contiguous scopes with scalable optimization. This paper proposes a systematic framework for delivery scope generation. We first develop a fine-grained urban segmentation method that integrates road networks and Areas of Interest boundaries to generate atomic regions and construct a region connectivity graph for modeling spatial adjacency. Based on this representation, the problem is formulated as a graph-based region assignment problem. To enable large-scale planning, we design a tailored heuristic algorithm enhanced by exact local refinement. The framework supports both order-weighted delivery distance minimization and amortized delivery distance optimization via a learning-based estimator. Experiments on real-world data show that the proposed approach achieves near-optimal solutions with low computational cost and scales to mega-city instances with hundreds of stations. The system has been deployed in an online grocery platform with over 1,000 stations, demonstrating its practical effectiveness and industrial value.
A146FULLRetrieval-Corrected Conformal Prediction for Time Series
Sangjin Jin (UNIST) · Kangmin Kim (UNIST) · Junhyeong Lee (UNIST) · Yongjae Lee (UNIST)
Abstract
Conformal prediction (CP) provides distribution-free prediction intervals for fixed forecasters, but its standard calibration procedure is often inefficient for time series data, where forecast errors are temporally dependent and change across time and operating conditions. Recent time series CP methods improve local calibration using recent, weighted, or localized residuals. Yet local calibration can remain indirect, since broad residual weighting or additional adaptation procedures may dilute the evidence most relevant to the current prediction. This motivates a simple retrieval and correction strategy that selects similar past residuals as local evidence and then corrects the coverage error left by retrieval. In this paper, we propose Retrieval-Corrected Conformal Prediction (RCCP), a retrieval-augmented calibration method for time series prediction intervals. RCCP builds an asymmetric interval from retrieved one-sided residuals and calibrates its normalized retrieval error with a scalar conformal correction. Thus, retrieval provides local residual evidence, while conformal correction determines the final scale needed for coverage. We provide a coverage-gap bound based on the stability of the normalized retrieval error distribution. Across standard benchmarks and backbone forecasters, RCCP attains the target coverage in every setting and achieves the lowest Winkler scores, with fewer severe misses. RCCP also achieves low calibration and inference overhead, showing that retrieval-corrected calibration is an effective and scalable approach to uncertainty quantification in time series forecasting. Code is available at https://github.com/jinsaaang/rccp.
A147FULLReCast: Regime-aware Multi-scale Retrieval with Context--Evolution Coupling for Time Series Forecasting
Jianliang Gao (Central South University) · Zhipeng Peng (Central South University) · Yiting Shi (Central South University) · Yueyue Ma (Central South University) · Chongyun Qin (Central South University)
Abstract
Time series forecasting is essential in many real-world applications, but accurate prediction remains challenging when temporal dynamics are non-stationary and historical patterns recur at different temporal resolutions. Existing retrieval-augmented forecasting methods provide explicit historical evidence, yet they may retrieve dynamically mismatched samples and often integrate retrieved information only at the prediction stage. To address these limitations, we propose ReCast, a retrieval-augmented forecasting framework based on meta-guided multi-scale retrieval and context--evolution coupling. Specifically, we first construct lightweight statistical meta-features to characterize the global dynamics of each sample and organize historical data into latent regimes, so that retrieval is constrained to dynamically compatible candidates. We then perform retrieval across multiple temporal scales to capture recurring patterns at different resolutions. Beyond retrieved future representations, ReCast also introduces a retrieved historical context segment, termed Pre-key, which is aligned with the current input and concatenated as an informative historical prefix for encoder-side modeling. In parallel, the retrieved future representations from different scales are projected to the forecasting horizon and aggregated as a retrieval-based prediction branch. The final forecast is obtained by fusing the encoder-based parametric prediction and the retrieval-based non-parametric prediction. Experiments on both long- and short-horizon forecasting benchmarks show that ReCast consistently improves forecasting accuracy over competitive baselines, and the ablation results further demonstrate the contribution of regime-aware retrieval, multi-scale matching, and context--evolution coupling.
A148FULLMulti-Order Wavelet Derivative Transform for Multivariate Time Series Forecasting
Ziyu Zhou (The Hong Kong University of Science and Technology) · Jiaxi Hu (The Hong Kong University of Science and Technology (Guangzhou)) · Qingsong Wen (Squirrel Ai Learning) · James Kwok (The Hong Kong University of Science and Technology) · Yuxuan Liang (The Hong Kong University of Science and Technology (Guangzhou))
Abstract
In deep time series forecasting, the Fourier Transform (FT) is extensively employed for frequency pattern modeling. However, it often struggles in capturing multi-scale, time-sensitive temporal patterns. Although the Wavelet Transform (WT) can capture these patterns through frequency decomposition, its coefficients are insensitive to abrupt changes in the time series, leading to suboptimal modeling. To mitigate these limitations, we introduce the multi-order Wavelet Derivative Transform (WDT) grounded in the WT, enabling the extraction of time-aware patterns spanning both the overall trend and subtle fluctuations. Compared with the standard FT and WT, which model the raw series, WDT operates on the derivative of the series, selectively magnifying rate-of-change cues and exposing abrupt regime shifts that are particularly informative for time series modeling. Practically, we embed the WDT into a multi-branch framework named WaveTS, which decomposes the input series into multi-scale time-frequency coefficients, refines them via linear layers, and reconstructs them into the time domain via the inverse WDT. Extensive experiments on multiple benchmark datasets demonstrate that WaveTS achieves state-of-the-art forecasting accuracy while retaining high computational efficiency. The code is available at https://github.com/zhouziyu02/WaveTS.
A149FULLGDformer: Going Beyond Subsequence Isolation for Multivariate Time Series Anomaly Detection
Qingxiang Liu (The Hong Kong University of Science and Technology (Guangzhou)) · Xiaoliang Luo (China Mobile (Jiangxi) Virtual Reality Technology Co., Ltd.) · Chenghao Liu (Salesforce AI Research) · Sheng Sun (Institute of Computing Technology, Chinese Academy of Sciences) · Di Yao (Institute of Computing Technology, Chinese Academy of Sciences) · Lvchun Wang (China Mobile (Jiangxi) Virtual Reality Technology Co., Ltd.) · Wei Yu (China Mobile (Jiangxi) Virtual Reality Technology Co., Ltd.) · Yuxuan Liang (The Hong Kong University of Science and Technology (Guangzhou))
Abstract
Multivariate Time Series (MTS) anomaly detection is crucial for maintaining the reliability of real-world systems, which can identify malfunctions from operational data and mitigate the potential financial losses. Given the scarcity of anomalies and difficulty in labeling MTS data, the MTS anomaly detection task is usually framed as an unsupervised learning problem to derive a compact and distinguished detection criterion without accessing the anomaly points. The existing deep learning methods are all confined to isolated subsequences with limited and subsequence-contained horizons, hardly deriving anomaly scores with series-level knowledge and promising the unified detection criterion. In this paper, we propose the Global Dictionary-enhanced Transformer (GDformer) with a renovated dictionary-based cross attention mechanism to cultivate the global representations shared by all normal points in the entire series. Accordingly, the cross-attention maps reflect the correlation weights between the point and global representations, which naturally leads to the representation-wise similarity-based detection criterion. To foster more compact detection boundary, prototypes are introduced to capture the distribution of normal point-global correlation weights. Extensive experimental results validate the effectiveness and efficiency of GDformer, compared with state-of-the-art unsupervised anomaly detection methods on six popular benchmark datasets. The source code is available at https://github.com/yuppielqx/GDformer.
A150FULLImputation-Free Variable Subset Forecasting Based on Observed Subset Representation Enhancement
Soonhyung Kwon (Seoul National University) · Minjae Sung (Seoul National University) · Jonghun Park (Seoul National University)
Abstract
Variable subset forecasting (VSF) addresses multivariate time series forecasting when an arbitrary subset of variables is absent at inference time. Most existing methods follow an impute-then-forecast pipeline in the original variable space, in which imputation errors can propagate into forecasting. Even methods that learn latent representations typically project them back to the original variable space before forecasting, which can discard information useful for prediction. These limitations raise the question of whether imputation is necessary at all. We observed that a forecasting backbone trained with sensor dropout alone, without any imputation, matched and in some cases exceeded state-of-the-art VSF performance. This led us to hypothesize that VSF benefits more from enhancing observed-variable representations in the embedding space than from imputing missing variables in the original variable space. To this end, we propose OSRE (Observed Subset Representation Enhancement), an imputation-free, backbone-agnostic framework for VSF that operates entirely in the embedding space via two complementary branches and is trained with sensor dropout. The Observed Variable Branch enriches observed-variable representations through unified attention, while the Missing Variable Branch marks missing positions with lightweight identification tokens. The combined embedding feeds into any standard forecasting backbone. Across four datasets and four forecasting backbones, OSRE outperformed prior state-of-the-art methods on METR-LA, Traffic, and Solar by an average of 12.7% in MAE and remained robust across varying missing rates. An Integrated Gradients analysis further suggests that observation-centric processing in the embedding space is a key contributor to these gains. The code is available at https://github.com/shykwon/CIKM26-OSRE.
A151FULLQuality Heterogeneity Matters: Adaptive Harmonization for Multi-Sensor Time Series Forecasting
Jianping Zhou (Shanghai Jiao Tong University) · Bin Lu (Shanghai Jiao Tong University) · Haoyang Yue (Shanghai Jiao Tong University) · Yimian Hu (Shanghai Jiao Tong University) · Gu Tang (Shanghai Jiao Tong University) · Ze Zhao (Shanghai Jiao Tong University) · Zijun Di (Shanghai Jiao Tong University) · Xinbing Wang (Shanghai Jiao Tong University)
Abstract
Widely deployed multi-sensor networks are fundamental for the construction of digital twins. In the real-world, sensors often exhibit heterogeneous data quality due to differences in hardware designs and measurement principles. However, existing multi-sensor time series methods typically follow a quality-homogeneous modeling strategy, leading to representation aliasing and performance degradation. In this work, we propose QualityMoE, a plug-and-play quality-aware harmonization module to harmonize quality discrepancies across sensors. Specifically, we develop a quality-aware router to adaptively dispatch sensor data by integrating complementary static and dynamic quality characteristics.
