Furthermore, we employ a mixture of hybrid expert architecture where specialized experts distinguish heterogeneous qualities, while a shared expert fosters information interaction across sensors. We conduct white-box experiments to transparently validate the model's capability in perceiving quality-induced waveform heterogeneity within simulated circuits. Moreover, extensive experiments across 9 real-world datasets and 6 backbones demonstrate the effectiveness and generalizability of QualityMoE under multiple quality heterogeneity scenarios. QualityMoE further demonstrates its scalability on large-scale multi-sensor datasets and its broader applicability to another downstream task, i.e., multi-sensor time series classification.
A152FULLAPILaNet: Adaptive Physics-Informed Latent Network for Single-Sensor Forecasting
Adrian Kucia (Northumbria University) · Wai Lok Woo (Northumbria University)
Abstract
Forecasting river dynamics from sensor networks is often limited by sparse and noisy observations: in many catchments, operational monitoring provides only a single gauge and uncertain rainfall inputs. We propose an Adaptive Physics-Informed Latent Network (APILaNet), a trustworthy physics-constrained forecasting model that learns a 1-D latent dynamical field while enforcing mass conservation through a weak-form residual weighted by a learned, normalized space–time measure. The normalization stabilizes training across discretizations and concentrates constraint enforcement on transient, event-driven regimes. To improve identifiability under single-gauge supervision, APILaNet uses a monotone Lipschitz measurement layer to map latent states to observed levels, and a bounded event-aware scheduler that increases conservation and smoothness regularization during high-impact periods while preserving optimization stability. Across synthetic 1-D conservation benchmarks and multi-catchment hydrological forecasting, APILaNet improves accuracy relative to strong sequence baselines and yields markedly lower error during extreme events, with consistent gains in Nash–Sutcliffe efficiency.
A153FULLA Hybrid Framework for Time Series Anomaly Detection with LLMs
Hakan Akdag (German Aerospace Center (DLR)) · Anh Thu Bui (Cologne University of Applied Sciences) · Natalie Hußfeldt (Cologne University of Applied Sciences) · Gernot Heisenberg (Cologne University of Applied Sciences)
Abstract
Large Language Models (LLMs) are increasingly explored for time series anomaly detection (TSAD), yet their direct use often remains inferior to methods designed specifically for TSAD. In this work, we study whether this limitation arises primarily from weak forecasting or from insufficient exploitation of forecast residuals. Across LLaMA-3.1-8B-Instruct, Mistral-7B, and DeepSeek-R1-Distill-Qwen-7B, we find that parameter-efficient fine-tuning can improve forecasting accuracy, but does not consistently improve anomaly detection under fixed residual thresholding. The primary driver of detection performance is not forecasting quality, but how the resulting residuals are analyzed and refined in subsequent stages. Motivated by this finding, we propose a Forecaster–Detector–Imputer pipeline that restricts the LLM to forecasting normal temporal behavior, applies classical detectors to the resulting residuals using adaptive windowing and contamination-aware thresholding, and refines candidate detections through imputation via a time-series foundation model followed by a second detection pass. The proposed framework reaches F1 = 0.789 with LLaMA and F1 = 0.785 with Mistral, roughly doubling the zero-shot baselines, with results confirmed on an independent NAB benchmark. These results suggest that LLMs are most effective for TSAD when used as forecasting components within a hybrid residual-analysis pipeline, and that the primary bottleneck lies in post-hoc residual exploitation rather than forecasting quality alone.
A154SHORTClassification-Aware Graph Construction and Learning for Time Series Classification
Sanghun Lee (Kangwon National University) · Yang-Sae Moon (Kangwon National University)
Abstract
Recent GNN-based time series methods often fail to align graph and mini-batch construction with the classification objective, weakening target-neighbor interactions essential for accurate classification. In particular, time series similarity-based graphs may induce structural distortions by over-connecting different classes or under-connecting the same class, and random mini-batches may exclude the important neighbors of a target from the same batch. To address this, we define the Class-Discriminative Neighborhood(CDN), a graph neighborhood structure beneficial for classification, and analyze it from two perspectives: quality and connectivity. Quality refers to how strongly a target is connected to same-class neighbors and weakly to different-class ones, while connectivity refers to how sufficiently these neighbors are utilized in GNN message passing. To enhance both aspects, we propose the Classification-aware Graph Construction and Learning(CGCL) framework with two key modules. First, Embedding-Aware Graph Learning improves CDN quality by first learning embeddings from a time series graph and then further reconstructing it from more discriminative embeddings. Second, Target-Aware Mini-Batch strengthens CDN connectivity by including a target and its neighbors in the same batch. Experimental results on the UCR datasets show that CGCL improves classification accuracy by 10.7%p on average over SOTA classification models.
A155SHORTSemSTG: Semantic State Transition Graphs for Time Series Event Forecasting
Jie Zhang (Fudan University) · Peng Wang (Fudan University) · Wei Wang (Fudan University)
Abstract
Accurate time-series event prediction is critical in many real-world domains, such as web traffic monitoring and industrial system management. It relies on identifying distinct underlying states or representative patterns from observed data. However, existing studies mainly focus on state detection and pattern extraction, yet the evolutionary correlations and transition dynamics between states have largely been overlooked. In this paper, we propose a data-driven framework, called the semantic state transition graph network (SemSTGN). Specifically, SemSTGN constructs a semantic state transition graph (SemSTG) from time series with a self-supervised state recognition approach. Furthermore, we introduce a novel graph neural network to learn robust representations of the semantic state transition graph. SemSTGN can capture node-level and graph-level features in the SemSTG, then fuse such characteristics to predict future events in an end-to-end manner. Experimental results on four real-world datasets demonstrate that the proposed approach consistently outperforms 16 baseline methods.
A156SHORTICLFS:Inverted Contrastive Learning For Unsupervised Feature Selection
Utsab Ghosh (ABV IIITM Gwalior) · Roshni Chakraborty (ABV IIITM Gwalior)
Abstract
Unsupervised feature selection is important for high-dimensional data analysis, yet many existing methods rely on graph construction, spectral objectives, or reconstruction-based criteria that may be difficult to adapt across domains. We propose Inverted Contrastive Learning for Feature Selection (ICLFS), a contrastive unsupervised feature selection method that treats each feature as a training instance and learns feature representations from multiple perturbed views of its sample-profile vector. Experiments on benchmark datasets from multiple domains show that the proposed method outperforms strong classical and neural baselines on the selected evaluation suite, suggesting that feature-wise contrastive learning is a promising direction for unsupervised feature selection and other feature-related tasks.
A157FULLBridging Local Geometries via Adaptive Convex Multi-graph Fusion for Unsupervised Manifold Representation
Qirui Huang (Shenzhen University) · Xuan Yang (Shenzhen University) · Yang Zhao (Shenzhen University) · Jihong Pei (Shenzhen University)
Abstract
The quality of unsupervised manifold learning relies fundamentally on the underlying neighborhood graph. Standard linear methods utilizing a single affinity matrix often fail to capture the multiscale complexity of high-dimensional data. While multi-view algorithms integrate complementary information, additional views may be unavailable or costly to acquire in some practical scenarios. Consequently, effectively exploiting the multi-scale structural information within a single reliable view remains an important research problem. To this end, we propose Multi-Affinity Matrix Fusion-based Locality Preserving Projections (MAMF-LPP). This framework bridges fragmented local geometries through a unified joint optimization paradigm, dynamically coupling adaptive convex multi-graph fusion with manifold projection. To optimize the resulting non-convex objective, we develop an efficient Block Coordinate Descent (BCD) algorithm featuring exact row-wise probabilistic simplex projections, thereby eliminating standard heuristic approximation errors. Theoretical and empirical analysis establishes the monotonic descent of the objective, while empirical results demonstrate rapid convergence. Across multiple benchmark datasets, MAMF-LPP achieves competitive performance against representative single-graph, nonlinear, and joint-learning baselines. A case study further shows that exploiting multi-scale intra-view geometries can yield performance competitive with selected multi-view configurations under the evaluated protocol.
A158SHORTEvaluating Interestingness Functions for Automated Exploratory Clustering: A Scenario-Based Benchmark
Georg Stefan Schlake (FernUniversität in Hagen) · Christian Beecks (FernUniversität in Hagen)
Abstract
Automated Exploratory Clustering returns a set of diverse, high-quality clusterings rather than a single solution, supporting practitioners in discovering multiple valid knowledge structures within a dataset. A key open question is how to quantify the interestingness of such a clustering set, i.e., its likelihood of providing actionable insight to a user, so that it can serve as an optimization objective in an automated system. We formalize four practical usage scenarios with distinct requirements (e.g., prioritizing the best clustering vs. minimizing evaluation effort), propose four novel interestingness functions, and benchmark all six functions (including two from prior work) across 136 datasets using seven scenario-aligned evaluation measures. Our results show that the choice of interestingness function substantially impacts set composition and utility: MMR-based interestingness yields the highest-quality individual clusterings but produces unnecessarily large sets, whereas our proposed functions generate compact sets better suited to cost-sensitive or exploration-focused scenarios. We provide actionable recommendations for matching interestingness functions to usage scenarios in automated knowledge discovery systems.
A159SHORTAttribution-Aware Active Learning for Pairwise Constrained Clustering
Vincent Blase (IRIT, UMR 5505 CNRS, Université de Toulouse, UT2J) · Julien Aligon (IRIT, UMR 5505 CNRS, Université Toulouse Capitole) · Moncef Garouani (IRIT, UMR 5505 CNRS, Université Toulouse Capitole) · Isabelle Ader (Université de Toulouse, CNRS UMR 5070, INSERM U1301, EFS, ENVT, Institut RESTORE) · Olivier Teste (IRIT, UMR 5505 CNRS, Université de Toulouse, UT2J)
Abstract
Active constraint-based clustering iteratively incorporates user knowledge through pairwise constraints to improve clustering quality while minimizing annotation effort. Existing approaches rely on two main heuristics: representativeness and uncertainty. Although effective, these strategies may select constraints that do not accurately capture the underlying data structure. In this paper, we introduce a novel active constraint-based clustering approach that formulates constraint selection as a hybrid learning task. Our method first identifies a small set of representative samples to build a supervised model. We then exploit feature attribution scores derived from this model, using SHAP values to build an attribution-based representation space that captures the contribution of each feature. This space enables the identification of highly uncertain regions of the data. By jointly leveraging representativeness, uncertainty, and attributions, our approach selects pairwise constraints from the most informative regions of the data space, leading to more effective clustering guidance and improved query efficiency.
A160FULLDiagnosing and Correcting Geometric Bias in Diversity-Driven Code Instruction Data Selection
Ke Zhang (Nanjing University) · Zixian Huang (Shanghai Artificial Intelligence Laboratory) · Gong Cheng (Nanjing University)
Abstract
Diversity-driven data selection offers a scalable way to reduce code instruction-tuning costs, yet it relies on a fragile assumption: geometric spread in representation space should correspond to training-useful semantic coverage. In code data selection, our diagnosis reveals a geometric bias behind this assumption: dense embedding geometry can be strongly influenced by rare surface forms, verbose constraints, and implementation artifacts, causing diversity objectives to over-explore locally sparse or globally peripheral samples whose training utility is not guaranteed. To correct this bias, we propose Semantically Anchored Geometric Coverage (SAGC), a framework for reshaping representation geometry using LLM-generated macro-intent labels as semantic anchors for dense micro-context representations. Rather than replacing standard diversity objectives, SAGC reshapes the geometry exposed to them, using macro-intent anchors to constrain dense-space exploration toward high-level algorithmic structure without requiring downstream validation signals, gradient feedback, or evaluation results. Using only 20k samples selected from a 446k pool, SAGC reaches 0.4006 on LiveCodeBench, approaching full-data training at 0.4027. Further diagnostics and out-of-benchmark evaluations show that semantic anchoring provides a structured correction to this geometric bias.
A161SHORTLabel-Free Pairwise Embedding Comparison via Local Map Spectra
Alexander Gandlin (Independent Researcher) · Daria Denisova (Independent Researcher) · Alexey Vasilev (Independent Researcher) · Andrey Savchenko (Independent Researcher) · Aleksei Shestov (Independent Researcher)
Abstract
We study label-free pairwise comparison of embedding spaces for model selection. Existing unsupervised quality metrics usually assign one scalar score to each embedding matrix and rank candidate models by these scores. This ignores the object-level correspondence available when two embedding spaces are computed on the same unlabeled objects. Using this correspondence, we compare embedding spaces through local maps between their point clouds. Spectral summaries of these maps produce pairwise scores that are evaluated against downstream classifier accuracy differences. Across the reported matched comparisons---four spectral summaries on four datasets, plus effective-rank results on two additional datasets---the map-based score improves the matched global metric in 16/18 comparisons by correct ranking ratio. Mean signed Spearman correlation increases from 0.199 for the matched global metrics to 0.591 for the corresponding local-map scores. Ablations show the role of neighborhood scale, comparison with one-directional maps, adaptive neighborhood selection, and full-spectrum map summaries.
A162FULLEndoBudget: Capacity-Controlled Learning for Stable Information Systems under Endogenous Feedback
David Li (Yeshiva University) · Angela Li (Brown University)
Abstract
Modern information systems increasingly operate in closed feedback loops: recommenders shape exposure, retrieval and generation pipelines influence future content, agentic systems change the environments they query, and human-AI interfaces alter the logs used for subsequent training. In these settings, data are not merely sampled from an external distribution. They are endogenously produced by prior model decisions, creating deployment drift that can accumulate over time and change finite-run reliability estimates. This paper develops EndoBudget, a learning-theoretic framework for analyzing deployment discrepancy in information systems trained on feedback-generated data and for auditing explicit update budgets. We formalize closed-loop learning as a sequential process in which each deployed model induces the next data distribution. Our main generalization result bounds the long-horizon absolute deployment gap by a classical capacity-dependent estimation term plus an accumulated endogenous drift term. We further state a sufficient stability condition for temporal capacity budgeting: under an explicit update-stability condition, a summable budget yields finite feedback path length and convergence of the induced data distributions in complete metric spaces. An auxiliary continuous-time limit provides a formal view of the discrete retraining process as dynamics over probability measures. Controlled diagnostics and a semi-synthetic closed-loop recommendation study report finite-run measurements of cumulative exposure drift, absolute deployment-gap variability, exposure dispersion, and ranking utility for the compared update rules within the studied protocol. The framework provides a finite-run audit for stating, measuring, and evaluating explicit capacity and update constraints in adaptive information systems that retrain under long-term feedback, subject to the regularity assumptions made explicit below.
A163FULLSupport-Adaptive Complexity Control for Longitudinal Counterfactual Prediction
Zhe Wang (Xidian University) · Rui Wang (Alibaba Group) · Ziyu Guan (Xidian University) · Yaming Yang (Xidian University) · Bin Tong (Alibaba Group) · Wei Zhao (Xidian University) · Guan Wang (Alibaba Group) · Bo Zheng (Alibaba Group)
Abstract
Longitudinal counterfactual prediction aims to forecast future outcomes under candidate treatment sequences from observational trajectories. Existing methods mainly address time-varying confounding and temporal representation learning. We identify a complementary finite-sample challenge: counterfactual queries often lie in history-action regions with highly heterogeneous logged support. This leads to the support-complexity mismatch for the fixed-capacity prediction heads used by existing methods. Motivated by finite-sample learning theory, where reliable generalization depends on function-class complexity relative to the number of relevant samples, we propose Support-Adaptive Complexity Control (SACC) to address this issue, a backbone-agnostic method that replaces the fixed action-conditioned prediction head with a support-adaptive one. SACC estimates rollout-conditioned local support for each query and uses it to progressively activate residual prediction blocks. It shrinks toward a stable low-complexity base predictor in weakly supported regions while enabling richer corrections when support is strong. We provide theoretical analysis and experiments showing that SACC improves the finite-sample reliability of longitudinal counterfactual outcome estimation, especially for weakly supported treatment plans.
A164FULLAsymmetry-Aware Local Structure Alignment for Conditional Average Treatment Effect Estimation
Mingshu Cao (Shanxi University) · Fuyuan Cao (Shanxi University) · Shichang Qiao (Shanxi University) · Zhuhong Tan (Shanxi University)
Abstract
Estimating conditional average treatment effect (CATE) is crucial for characterizing treatment effect heterogeneity at the individual or subgroup level. Existing methods mitigate confounding bias by capturing local structures within treatment and control groups to enhance representation balancing. However, they still overlook cross-group local structure asymmetry, including capacity asymmetry from imbalanced sample sizes and semantic asymmetry from unreliable cross-group correspondences, which may induce spurious matching and ultimately compromise CATE estimation. To address these issues, we propose an Asymmetry-Aware Local Structure Alignment (ALSA) method for CATE estimation. ALSA enables reliable cross-group local alignment by modeling subgroup capacity imbalance and constructing soft barycentric correspondences. Specifically, to handle capacity asymmetry, samples within each group are clustered into prototypes, and non-uniform capacity priors are constructed based on the number of samples covered by each prototype. This enables optimal transport (OT) to explicitly account for subgroup-level capacity imbalance. Moreover, we design a prototype-guided contrastive learning strategy to encourage intra-subgroup consistency and inter-subgroup separability. To tackle semantic asymmetry, ALSA employs an OT-based bidirectional barycentric alignment mechanism, which softly aligns samples lacking reliable correspondences to the weighted barycenters of multiple relevant prototypes, thereby reducing spurious matching. Extensive experiments demonstrate that ALSA outperforms existing methods and significantly reduces CATE estimation error.
A167FULLDiscovering and Preserving Category Correlation Knowledge via Adaptive Reciprocal Knowledge Distillation
Dawen Jiang (Wuhan University of Technology) · Zhishu Shen (Wuhan University of Technology) · Zeyu Liu (Wuhan University of Technology) · Tiehua Zhang (Tongji University)
Abstract
Knowledge distillation aims to improve the performance of lightweight student models by transferring knowledge from larger and more powerful teacher models. However, a substantial size gap between teacher and student models often impedes effective knowledge transfer. Most existing approaches adopt a static, one-way teacher-to-student distillation paradigm, which overlooks the dynamic nature of student learning and fails to provide targeted guidance on hard samples. In this paper, we propose adaptive reciprocal knowledge distillation (AR-KD), a novel method that improves knowledge transfer by simplifying the teacher’s output distribution. Specifically, AR-KD performs reciprocal adaptation on the teacher by matching its class correlation matrix to the student’s relational representation, which reshapes the teacher’s prediction structure to better suit the student’s capacity. This relational alignment mitigates the collapse of inter-class dark knowledge caused by overconfident teachers, enabling the student to learn from richer and more compatible supervisory signals. We evaluate AR-KD on CIFAR-100 and ImageNet-1k classification datasets, where it outperforms state-of-the-art knowledge distillation baselines. Specifically, AR-KD improves student performance across homogeneous and heterogeneous setups: up to 7.13% accuracy gain for students, 1.42%–4.15% higher than vanilla KD on average, and further improvements when integrated with other advanced methods. Our code is available at https://anonymous.4open.science/r/ARKD/.
A168SHORTTransferability of Knowledge-Distilled Lottery Tickets Across Object Classification Tasks in Images
Daan Luyckx (KU Leuven) · Peter Karsmakers (KU Leuven)
Abstract
The Lottery Ticket Hypothesis (LTH) states that large neural networks contain sparse subnetworks, referred to as "winning tickets", that can match the performance of the original dense model when trained in isolation. Recent work has shown that knowledge distillation improves training stability and produces sparser subnetworks that retain the performance of the original ticket, leading to the Knowledge-Distilled Lottery Ticket (KDLT) framework. In this work, we investigate whether sparse subnetworks discovered using KDLT can be used effectively for downstream tasks. We evaluate the performance of these subnetworks across several vision datasets with varying levels of task similarity. Experiments are conducted on three settings: CIFAR-100 to CIFAR-10, Tiny-ImageNet to CIFAR-10, and Tiny-ImageNet to CIFAR-100. Our results show that KDLT-discovered subnetworks can be trained effectively across related vision tasks, particularly at low to medium sparsity levels. Even at high sparsities, the subnetworks retain strong performance, although, as is expected, a modest drop relative to the directly trained target-dataset tickets is observed. Furthermore, KDLT matches or modestly exceeds standard LTH in most settings.
A169RESOURCEA Benchmark & Dataset for Detecting AI-Manipulated Visual Evidence in the Court System
Kelly McConvey (University of Toronto) · Sajad Ebrahimi (University of Toronto) · Nima Jamali (University of Waterloo) · Jalehsadat Mahdavimoghaddam (University of Toronto) · Matina Mahdizadeh Sani (University of Waterloo) · Maksym Taranukhin (University of British Columbia) · Wentao Zhang (University of Waterloo) · Jaquelyn Burkell (University of Western Ontario) · Yuntian Deng (University of Waterloo) · Karen Eltis (University of Ottawa) · Maura R. Grossman (University of Waterloo) · Vered Shwartz (University of British Columbia) · Ebrahim Bagheri (University of Toronto)
Abstract
Photographic evidence is becoming increasingly vulnerable to forms of alteration and fabrication that existing legal and technical workflows are not well equipped to evaluate. Surveillance frames, dashcam stills, and phone photographs may be used to establish presence, sequence, causation, damage, or identity, yet contemporary generative systems allow non-experts to alter or fabricate such images through ordinary prompt-based interfaces. Existing image-forensics benchmarks provide important resources for face manipulation, classical tampering, and general synthetic-image detection, but they are not organized around the forms of visual evidence submitted in courts, the localized edits that can change what an exhibit appears to prove, or the consumer-tool threat model now facing the justice system. We introduce the CIFAR Synthetic Evidence Corpus for Detecting AI-Manipulated Images, a benchmark for evidentiary image authentication in court and justice-system contexts. The corpus contains 1,505 photographic items, including 720 authentic controls and 785 manipulated or fabricated images, spanning surveillance, dashcam, and consumer-photo imagery. Manipulations are organized into scene-condition edits, localized element edits, and full fabrications produced with contemporary generative systems. Each item is released with structured metadata covering source provenance, manipulation tier, subtype, generator, prompt template, and scene attributes, enabling controlled evaluation beyond aggregate binary detection. We also establish state-of-the-art baselines with publicly available image-manipulation detectors, showing that current systems exhibit error profiles that remain problematic for evidentiary use. The dataset, prompts, metadata manifest, code, and baseline evaluation scripts are released to support research on visual evidence authentication, information integrity, and trustworthy AI for the justice system.
A170SHORTJudging a Review by its Cover: A Reliability Analysis of LLM-based Peer Review Evaluation Metrics
Shakiba Amirshahi (Reviewerly) · Sajad Ebrahimi (Reviewerly) · Hai Son Le (Reviewerly) · Negar Arabzadeh (University of California, Berkeley) · Ebrahim Bagheri (University of Toronto)
Abstract
Peer-review evaluation is increasingly being automated with LLM-as-a-judge metrics, but this creates a measurement risk. A review may receive a high score because it is fluent, organized, and polished, rather than because it provides a strong evaluation of the paper. This risk is especially important in AI-assisted reviewing, where reviewers may use LLMs to improve clarity or presentation while preserving the underlying judgments. We propose a statistical framework for testing whether peer-review evaluation metrics capture substantive review quality beyond surface-level linguistic form. The framework compares original human reviews with faithful LLM rewrites that preserve the same evaluative content while changing wording and presentation. Using a dataset comprising 4,044 meaning-preserving rewrites derived from 674 human reviews from ICLR and NeurIPS, we evaluate 29 content-oriented peer-review evaluation metrics drawn from four prior works through complementary tests of surface sensitivity and robustness. Although these metrics are intended to capture review properties beyond surface-level, writing-dependent characteristics, we find that sensitivity to rewriting is widespread. Under our primary analysis, 23 metrics assign significantly different scores to reviews whose evaluative content is preserved, while only six satisfy our robustness criterion. The patterns are largely consistent across two LLM judge models, suggesting that the issue is not specific to a single judge. These findings show that many peer-review evaluation metrics partially conflate review quality with linguistic presentation, and indicate that robustness to meaning-preserving rewriting should be validated before such metrics are used to compare human-written, AI-assisted, and AI-generated reviews. All evaluation results, prompts, and implementation code are publicly available in our GitHub repository: https://github.com/Reviewerly-Inc/llm_judge_reliability_analysis.
A171SHORTVerification-Guided Specification Synthesis with Large Language Models for Intrusion Detection Rules
Kohei Yamamoto (Doshisha University) · Marie Katsurai (Doshisha University)
Abstract
Attacks against Internet-connected IoT devices continue to increase; however, transforming observed attack traffic into deployable intrusion detection system (IDS) rules remains largely a manual process. Recent studies have explored using large language models (LLMs) to generate IDS rules; nonetheless, existing approaches often require auxiliary information beyond observed traffic or generate rules without validating their detection logic against benign traffic. This study presents a verification-guided specification synthesis framework for generating Suricata rules directly from HTTP request traces. Instead of having an LLM generate IDS rules in a single step, an LLM first identifies a vulnerable parameter and synthesizes a semantic detection specification. These specifications are iteratively refined through counterexample-guided inductive synthesis (CEGIS), in which benign traffic samples serve as counterexamples during synthesis and verification. Verified specifications are then deterministically compiled into Suricata rules. Experiments on 281 real-world CVEs and benign traffic collected from real IoT devices show that the proposed method achieves a detection rate of 81.5% while maintaining a false positive rate of 0.0%. An ablation study also demonstrates that CEGIS-based verification improves detection performance while maintaining a low false positive rate.
A172FULLFinMamba: Market-Aware Graph Enhanced Multi-Level Mamba for Stock Movement Prediction
Yifan Hu (Tsinghua University) · Peiyuan Liu (Tsinghua University) · Yuante Li (Carnegie Mellon University) · Dawei Cheng (Tongji University) · Naiqi Li (Tsinghua University) · Tao Dai (Shenzhen University) · Jigang Bao (Wukong Investment) · Shu-Tao Xia (Tsinghua University)
Abstract
Recently, combining stock features with inter-stock correlations has become a common and effective approach for stock movement prediction. However, financial data presents significant challenges due to its low signal-to-noise ratio and the dynamic complexity of the market, which give rise to two key limitations in existing methods. First, the relationships between stocks are highly influenced by multifaceted factors including macroeconomic market dynamics, and current models fail to adaptively capture these evolving interactions under specific market conditions. Second, for the accuracy and timeliness required by real-world trading, existing financial data mining methods struggle to extract beneficial pattern-oriented dependencies from long historical data while maintaining high efficiency and low memory consumption. To address the limitations, we propose FinMamba, a Mamba-GNN-based framework for market-aware and multi-level hybrid stock movement prediction. Specifically, we devise a dynamic graph to learn the changing representations of inter-stock relationships by integrating a pruning module that adapts to market trends. Afterward, with a selective mechanism, the multi-level Mamba discards irrelevant information and resets states to skillfully recall historical patterns across multiple time scales with linear time costs, which are then jointly optimized for reliable prediction. Extensive experiments on U.S. and Chinese stock markets demonstrate the effectiveness of our proposed FinMamba, achieving state-of-the-art prediction accuracy and trading profitability, while maintaining low computational complexity. The code is available at https://github.com/TROUBADOUR000/FinMamba.
A173SHORTCan Frontier LLMs Capture $40 Billion in Supply Chain Value?
Chung-Chi Chen (National Institute of Informatics) · Ichiro Kobayashi (Ochanomizu University) · Yusuke Miyao (The University of Tokyo) · Hiroya Takamura (AIST)
Abstract
Large Language Models (LLMs) perform well on many NLP tasks, but their ability to reason about complex supply chain relationships remains unclear. We introduce the Supply Chain Intuition Exam (SCIE), a benchmark for evaluating whether LLMs can identify and infer direct and indirect supplier relationships. We compare standard LLMs, models with grounding-based retrieval, and deep research (DR) systems. Despite access to public financial reports and real-world data, recall remains low: standard and grounded models achieve approximately 3--16%, while the best DR systems reach only 22%. These results suggest that retrieval alone is insufficient for professional-grade supply chain reasoning. SCIE highlights the need for methods that better integrate domain knowledge, retrieval, and multi-step reasoning in business and finance applications.
A174FULLSenseFlow: A Physics-Informed and Self-Ensembling Iterative Framework for Power Flow Estimation
Zhen Zhao (Beijing Huairou Laboratory) · Wenqi Huang (Beijing Huairou Laboratory) · Zicheng Wang (University College London) · Jiaxuan Hou (Beijing Huairou Laboratory) · Peng Li (China Southern Power Grid) · Lei Bai (Shanghai AI Laborotory)
Abstract
Power flow estimation plays a vital role in ensuring the stability and reliability of electrical power systems, particularly in the context of growing network complexities and renewable energy integration. However, existing studies often fail to adequately address the unique characteristics of power systems, such as the sparsity of network connections and the critical importance of the unique Slack node, which poses significant challenges in achieving high-accuracy estimations. In this paper, we present SenseFlow, a novel physics-informed and self-ensembling iterative framework that integrates two main designs, the Physics-informed Power Flow Network (PPFNet) and Self-ensembling Iterative Estimation (SeIter), to carefully address the unique properties of the power system and thereby enhance the power flow estimation. In specific, SenseFlow enforces the PPFNet to gradually predict high-precision voltage magnitudes and phase angles through the iterative SeIter process. On the one hand, PPFNet employs the Virtual Node Attention and Slack-Gated Feed-Forward modules to facilitate efficient global-local communication in the face of network sparsity and amplify the influence of the Slack node on angle predictions, respectively. On the other hand, SeIter maintains an exponential moving average of PPFNet's parameters to create an ensemble model that refines power state predictions throughout the iterative fitting process. Experimental results demonstrate that SenseFlow outperforms existing methods, providing a promising solution for high-accuracy power flow estimation across diverse grid configurations. The code is available at https://github.com/ZhenZHAO/SenseFlow.
A175SHORTBeyond Event Prediction: A Loss Function for Operational Ordinal Wildfire Risk
Nicolas Caron (Université Marie et Louis Pasteur, CNRS, institut FEMTO-ST (UMR 6174)) · Christophe Guyeux (Université Marie et Louis Pasteur, CNRS, institut FEMTO-ST (UMR 6174)) · Hassan Noura (Université Marie et Louis Pasteur, CNRS, institut FEMTO-ST (UMR 6174)) · Benjamin Aynes (SAD Marketing)
Abstract
Wildfire prediction is often framed as classification or regression, yet operational management relies on coherent ordinal risk levels. We propose the Cluster-Centered Latent Transition Loss (CCLLT), a novel ordinal objective designed for operational wildfire risk. Rather than predicting event occurrence directly, the proposed framework learns ordinal operational risk systems whose levels correspond to increasing real-world operational consequences. CCLLT combines latent ordinal centers, hierarchical EMA priors, monotonic ranking constraints, coverage regularization, and adaptive threshold calibration to directly optimize the ordinal consistency of risk signals. Unlike standard classification, it enforces monotonic operational transitions while preventing collapse toward dominant low-risk classes. Evaluated via a monotonic explainability framework, our approach successfully moves prediction beyond event-centered metrics to produce stable, interpretable, and operationally meaningful risk signals.
A176FULLCFDA: A Plug-and-Play LLM-Driven Code Functional Diagnosis Framework for Programming Knowledge Tracing
Shixian Dong (Hubei University) · Dunhui Yu (Hubei University) · Zihao Gong (Hubei University) · Kui Xiao (Hubei University)
Abstract
Knowledge Tracing (KT) models the evolution of students' knowledge states from historical learning interactions. However, most KT models are designed for traditional subject domains and exhibit limited generalization ability in programming knowledge tracing (PKT). Programming submissions are open-ended and repeatedly revised, and the same code change may indicate an effective repair, an ineffective attempt, or a functional regression. Moreover, programming progress is functional in nature: the educational meaning of a submission depends on whether it satisfies problem requirements rather than on code structures alone. To address these issues, we propose CFDA, a plug-and-play LLM-driven Code Functional Diagnosis and calibration framework for general KT and PKT models. CFDA analyzes problem requirements and student submissions, assigning fine-grained diagnostic signals including functional completion, semantic error, skill-level application, and transition cues. These signals are then injected into existing KT backbones through a lightweight calibrator that corrects hidden knowledge states while preserving the original tracing architecture. Experiments on two public programming datasets show consistent AUC and probability-error improvements across multiple backbone models and competitive performance against 14 representative KT and PKT baselines.
A177SHORTSemIKT: Semantic-driven Inductive Knowledge Tracing
Yijun Yan (The University of New South Wales) · Sonit Singh (The University of New South Wales) · Jake Renzella (The University of New South Wales)
Abstract
Knowledge Tracing (KT) is a core component of Intelligent Tutoring Systems (ITS), enabling adaptive learning by modelling a student's evolving knowledge state to predict future performance. Most KT methods rely on question identifiers, limiting generalisability to newly introduced questions without retraining, a significant constraint for real world deployment. We present SemIKT, a semantic-driven inductive KT framework that replaces question identifiers with generalisable pretrained language-model embeddings, augmented with expert-annotated difficulty labels and contrastive auxiliary objectives. We evaluate against 16 baselines on XES3G5M, a benchmark dataset, and SFSD, a private, de-identified education dataset. SemIKT outperformed all baselines on SFSD, achieving a 1.3% AUC improvement over the strongest baseline. Under a strict unseen-question setting where 25% of questions were held out from all stages of training, SemIKT achieved an AUC of 76.10%, demonstrating viable zero-shot prediction for unseen questions.
A178FULLPsy-GRAG: Evidence-Based Subgraph-Augmented LLM Reasoning for Mental Health Attribution
Tianyi Cao (University of Bristol) · Jingyu Hu (University of Bristol) · Hongbo Bo (University of Bristol) · Weiru Liu (University of Bristol)
Abstract
Mental health disorders have emerged as a critical global public health challenge, with automated classification of social media text offering significant value for early risk detection. Fine-tuned pre-trained language models (PLMs) achieve reasonable in-domain performance but generalize poorly across tasks. Large language models (LLMs) with retrieval-augmented generation (RAG) offer improved flexibility, yet both approaches lack the structured domain knowledge required for fine-grained psychiatric reasoning. To address these gaps, we propose Psy-GRAG, an evidence-based subgraph-augmented LLM reasoning framework. First, we construct a three-layer heterogeneous knowledge graph comprising a linguistic feature layer, an intermediate semantic layer, and a task label layer, modeling the cognitive reasoning path from surface expressions to mental health classifications. Second, a multi-round graph optimization strategy iteratively refines edge confidence weights and prunes noisy connections via supervised learning. Third, a psychology-informed retrieval strategy extracts disorder-relevant reasoning paths to guide pre-trained LLMs with fixed parameters for training-free inference without further parameter updates. Extensive experiments on CAMS, SWMH, and MultiWD demonstrate that Psy-GRAG generally outperforms traditional ML models, fine-tuned PLMs, and existing graph-augmented RAG methods across Accuracy, Macro-F1, and cross-run stability.
A179SHORTAgentic Reasoning Is Not Always Better: Evidence from Clinical Time-Series Explanation
Davide Gabrielli (Sapienza University of Rome) · Paola Velardi (ISTC-CNR) · Stefano Faralli (Sapienza University of Rome) · Bardh Prenkaj (Sapienza University of Rome)
Abstract
Continuous physiological monitoring is central to emergency care, yet building trustworthy, clinically usable AI remains challenging. While LLMs translate complex physiological signals into natural-language clinical narratives, it remains unclear whether agentic reasoning frameworks improve the quality of explanations over zero-shot inference. We present Vivaldi, a role-structured multi-agent system for explaining multivariate physiological time series in emergency department settings. We evaluate through a controlled clinical pilot involving a small cohort of emergency medicine experts. Their assessments challenge the assumption that increasingly complex agentic reasoning uniformly improves performance. Our experiments show agentic pipelines substantially benefit non-reasoning and medically fine-tuned models, improving expert-rated explanation justification and relevance by +6.9 and +9.7 points, respectively. Contrarily, for reasoning models, agentic orchestration often degrades explanation quality, including a 14-point drop in relevance, while improving diagnostic precision (ESI F1 +3.6). We also find explicit tool-based computation is decisive for codifiable clinical metrics, whereas subjective targets, such as pain scores and length of stay, show limited or inconsistent changes. Expert evaluation indicates gains in clinical utility depend on visualization conventions, with medically specialized models achieving favorable trade-offs between utility and clarity. Together, these findings show that the value of agentic AI lies in the selective externalization of computation and structure rather than in maximal reasoning complexity, highlighting concrete design trade-offs that are broadly applicable to explainable AI in safety-critical healthcare settings.
A180SHORTContrastive Captioning for Clinical Time-Series: Learning Joint ECG–Text Representations through Retrieval and Generation
Letizia Rotolo (LMU Munich) · Mina Rezaei (LMU Munich) · Solveig Vieluf (LMU University Hospital, LMU Munich) · Shunjie-Fabian Zheng (LMU University Hospital, LMU Munich)
Abstract
Recent approaches to clinical time-series report generation increasingly rely on large language models (LLMs) and retrieval-augmented pipelines, achieving strong performance at the cost of substantial computational complexity. Consequently, the fundamental factors that govern effective multimodal representation learning for physiological signals remain poorly understood. We present a systematic study of contrastive captioning for electrocardiogram (ECG) report generation using a lightweight adaptation of the Contrastive Captioners (CoCa) framework. Across both the curated PTB-XL dataset and the large-scale MIMIC-IV-ECG corpus, we investigate the effects of decoder architectures, diagnostic representation quality, semantic supervision, and uncertainty-aware latent regularization on joint ECG--text representation learning. Our experiments reveal four key findings: (i) Encoder--decoder models substantially outperform decoder-only architectures for conditioning text generation on continuous physiological representations. (ii) Replacing clinical reports with demographic pseudo-text induces severe degradation in cross-modal retrieval performance, suggesting that demographic-only text is insufficient for robust ECG--text alignment at scale. (iii) Frozen contrastive ECG–text embeddings encode clinically meaningful diagnostic structure, as shown by strong linear-probe performance on PTB-XL diagnostic superclasses. (iv) While conventional latent regularization strategies improve performance in data-scarce settings, they do not transfer effectively to larger-scale datasets. We show that multimodal uncertainty conditioning alleviates this limitation and yields improved report generation performance at scale. Together, these findings establish practical design principles for scalable multimodal learning from clinical time series
A181FULLHyBrain: Spatiotemporal Hyperedges for EEG Seizure Detection and Prediction
Hyunju Kim (Georgia Institute of Technology) · Sheo Yon Jhin (Korea Advanced Institute of Science and Technology) · Noseong Park (Korea Advanced Institute of Science and Technology) · Nabil Imam (Georgia Institute of Technology)
Abstract
Seizure detection and prediction from EEG are clinically important but challenging because seizures are rare, temporally localized, and propagate as coordinated events across multiple channels. Recent dynamic graph neural networks model this by running a temporal model over a sequence of per-time-step pairwise channel edges. However, this pairwise construction misses the spatiotemporal coupling that constitutes a seizure, at substantial training cost. We propose HyBrain, which summarizes spatiotemporal EEG evidence through a small set of soft hyperedges rather than pairwise edges. A per-channel Mamba backbone produces one token per (channel, second), and a spatiotemporal hyperedge block pools these tokens into Eh shared group embeddings through soft memberships and broadcasts them back. The same encoder serves three downstream tasks: window-based detection, one-second point-wise detection, and preictal seizure prediction. On TUSZ and CHB-MIT, HyBrain achieves the best AUROC on every reported setting against ten baselines, with the largest gap on long-clip preictal prediction. It also matches the most efficient baselines in training time and peak GPU memory. A qualitative analysis shows that even a single learned hyperedge cleanly captures the preictal → ictal → postictal trajectory on a real seizure clip.
A182SHORTBERT4DTI : BERT-based Model for Predicting Drug-Protein Interactions
Thanina Hamitouch (Ecole Nationale Supérieure d'Informatique (ESI)) · Khadidja Henni (TELUQ University) · Abdelkrim Aries (Ecole Nationale Supérieure d'Informatique (ESI)) · Amina Selma Haichour (Ecole Nationale Supérieure d'Informatique (ESI)) · Neila Mezghani (Imaging and Orthopaedics Research Laboratory, CHUM Research Center) · Lina Abou-Abbas (Lebanese American University)
Abstract
Understanding how drugs interact with protein targets is fundamental to drug discovery, drug repurposing and the early identification of promising therapeutic candidates before costly experimental testing. Sequence-based DTI models face three practical limitations: labelled interactions are scarce and unevenly distributed, large pretrained chemical and protein encoders are expensive to fine-tune end-to-end, and independently encoded sequences do not capture pair-specific dependencies. We present BERT4DTI, which encodes SMILES strings with ChemBERTa and amino-acid sequences with ProtBERT, applies bidirectional mutual attention between token-level representations, and classifies the resulting interaction features using convolutional layers and a multilayer perceptron. To reduce trainable size, ProtBERT is truncated to 18 retained layers and only the last two layers of each encoder are fine-tuned. On BIOSNAP, DAVIS and BindingDB, BERT4DTI is competitive, achieving the best ROC-AUC and PR-AUC on BIOSNAP and the highest sensitivity on all three benchmarks. An ablation on DAVIS shows that mutual attention improves PR-AUC and specificity. With 125M trainable parameters compared with 353M for full BERT fine-tuning, BERT4DTI provides a favourable performance--parameter trade-off for sequence-based DTI screening, while leaving runtime profiling, calibration and leakage-audited validation for future work.
A183SHORTTG-SEG: Text-Guided and Presence-Aware Temporal Propagation for Medical Image Segmentation
Krishna Tewari (Indian Institute of Technology (BHU), Varanasi) · Shayon Dasgupta (Indian Institute of Technology (BHU), Varanasi) · Sukomal Pal (Indian Institute of Technology (BHU), Varanasi)
Abstract
Segmenting anatomical structures or lesions in medical image sequences using natural language descriptions is challenging due to subtle visual cues, ambiguous boundaries, and temporal appearance variations across frames or slices. Existing text-guided segmentation methods typically operate on individual images and lack explicit temporal modeling. This results in unstable predictions when the target is temporarily absent. In this work, we propose TG-SEG, a text-guided segmentation framework that integrates vision-language alignment with propagation-based temporal tracking and a novel presence-aware gating mechanism to ensure consistent sequence-level predictions. We evaluate our method on four medical imaging datasets with sequence characteristics, including ACDC, MSD Spleen, Prostate, and CVC-ClinicDB. Compared to existing state-of-the-art methods, TG-SEG achieves consistent improvements across all evaluated datasets, with Dice gains of upto 3.13% and IoU gains of upto 4.41%. Ablation studies show that TG-SEG reduces false negative rates by 21.8-47.5% across datasets. Furthermore, stronger visual backbones such as SwinV2 provide additional gains of up to 9.26% Dice and 13.67% IoU, demonstrating the backbone-agnostic nature of the proposed framework. These results highlight the effectiveness of presence-aware gating for accurate and reliable medical image sequence segmentation. The source code will be made publicly available at https://github.com/cse-iitbhu/TG-SEG.
A184FULLIn-Context Learning as Approximate Belief Propagation
Zehua Cheng (University of Oxford) · Wei Dai (FLock.io) · Jiahao Sun (FLock.io)
Abstract
Few-shot in-context learning (ICL) cannot revise its belief about an early demonstration once a later, contradicting one arrives, so a single misleading example can derail the prediction. Existing remedies are split: retrieval methods choose which examples to include but weight them uniformly; calibration methods adjust the output without identifying which demonstration to distrust; mechanistic interpretability reveals the latent inter-example structure but offers no way to act on it. We introduce ICL-BP, an inference-time augmentation that addresses all three. ICL-BP constructs a sparse pairwise factor graph from the model's own late-layer attention maps, runs a small fixed number of loopy belief propagation iterations to obtain per-example relevance beliefs, and uses those beliefs to additively edit the residual-stream context at the query token before decoding. Conditional on a linear-representation hypothesis, an attention–similarity alignment proxy, and a belief-collapse condition that we verify empirically rather than rate-prove, the bias of the implicit concept estimator falls quadratically in the fraction of misleading demonstrations; when no demonstration is misleading, ICL-BP reduces exactly to Standard ICL under uniform beliefs, with at most a 1/N2 noise inflation in the empirically-observed near-uniform case. On Llama-3.1-8B-Instruct with 16 demonstrations, ICL-BP improves over Standard ICL by a median +7.4 pp across eight benchmarks (+5.2 to +12.0) and over the strongest reweighting baseline BatchICL by +1.8 pp median (+1.2 to +2.4). Composed with SC-CoT on Llama-3.1-70B, it reaches 90.4% exact match on GSM8K and 80.5% on MMLU at under 10% wall-clock overhead.
A185FULLCurvature Graph Mergeability: Predicting Model Compatibility from Per-Layer Hessian Geometry
Zehua Cheng (University of Oxford) · Wei Dai (FLock.io) · Jiahao Sun (FLock.io)
Abstract
Merging independently trained neural networks — via weight averaging, model soups, or task-vector arithmetic — is increasingly central to large-scale model reuse, yet the success of any merge hinges on whether two parameter vectors occupy the same loss basin, a property currently certified only by expensive multi-point interpolation barriers. We introduce Curvature Graph Mergeability (CGM), a scoring framework that predicts the interpolation barrier from only cheap, per-layer Hessian curvature features at each endpoint. CGM extracts two scalar curvature statistics per layer using Hutchinson's trace estimator and the power method, organizes them into a chain-structured factor graph whose latent compatibility states encode qualitative regimes of layer alignment, and computes a mergeability score from the negative variational free energy of the chain. For deep linear networks under balanced factorization, we prove that the interpolation barrier is upper-bounded by a multilinear function of per-layer curvature mismatch, and we identify a diagonal-dominance condition under which the score is monotone in mismatch; the bound is stated as an implicit joint bound on the per-layer mismatch vector, with the regime of validity made explicit. Across four meta-training architectures and four held-out OOD architectures (ResNet-110, ViT-B/ImageNet, WRN-28-10, 3-layer LSTM), CGM attains Spearman ρ=0.86 on leave-models-out splits and ρ=0.81 pooled OOD, outperforming zero-order distance, CKA, Fisher overlap, REPAIR, midpoint-barrier, and architecture-agnostic curvature-MLP baselines at Holm–Bonferroni-corrected p<0.01. It is approached only by Git Re-Basin + barrier (ρ=0.90), which costs ∼14,500× more per pair; CGM closes the gap to permutation-based merging at 35× amortized speedup over direct 11-point barrier when screening 50 candidates, with negligible memory overhead. Per-layer posterior marginals additionally pinpoint specific layers that act as merge bottlenecks.

A001SHORTGroup-Relative RL Post-Training for Sequential Recommendation
Danil Gusak (AXXX) · Evgeny Frolov (AXXX)
Abstract
Sequential recommender systems are typically trained with next-item cross-entropy (CE), yet evaluated by top-N ranking metrics that reward relative item ordering in the recommendation slate. This mismatch remains unaddressed for strong collaborative sequential models. Recent group-relative reinforcement learning has shown promise for LLM alignment and LLM-based recommenders, but whether a critic-free post-training paradigm can reliably improve standard collaborative sequential recommenders remains unclear. We introduce GRFT (Group-Relative Fine-Tuning), a GRPO-style post-training framework that aligns a pretrained sequential recommender directly to slate-level ranking rewards. GRFT samples multiple top-K slates per user context via Plackett-Luce sampling without replacement, scores them with ranking rewards, and updates the model with a PPO-clipped group-relative objective anchored to the frozen supervised reference. We instantiate rankwise and listwise variants to support position-level and whole-slate credit assignment. Under leakage-resistant global temporal splits on four datasets, GRFT consistently improves a strong sequential backbone, achieving gains of up to 25.3% NDCG@20 and 19.5% Recall@20. The improvements remain complementary to stronger supervised initialization, showing that reward-aligned post-training adds value beyond better supervised training alone. GRFT thus establishes that GRPO-style, critic-free post-training can improve strong collaborative sequential recommenders.
A002APPLIEDBasketFormer: Contrastive Masked Language Modeling with Temporal Encoding and Repeat-Explore Gating for Next-Basket Recommendation
Akshay Verma (Amazon) · Sambit Das (Amazon) · Siddharth Pillai (Amazon) · Deepak Gupta (Amazon)
Abstract
Next-basket recommendation (NBR) in online grocery is a challenging task due to the dual nature of shopping behavior: customers repeat staple items while also exploring novel products. Existing approaches either treat baskets as flat item sets, losing inter-basket temporal structure, or employ sequential models that lack explicit repeat-explore decomposition. We propose BasketFormer, a Transformer-encoder architecture that unifies three complementary innovations: (1) an InfoNCE-based contrastive loss that replaces the full-vocabulary softmax with in-batch contrastive scoring, yielding stronger item representations; (2) a bucketed inter-basket gap encoding that captures purchase cadence through compact learnable embeddings without increasing sequence length; and (3) a repeat-explore gate supervised by the soft repeat ratio that learns to decompose the next-basket representation into repeat and general components. We evaluate BasketFormer on two public benchmarks (Ta-Feng, Instacart) and a large-scale proprietary grocery dataset (71K customers, 3.8M transactions). BasketFormer achieves +9.5% and +7.1% relative Recall@10 improvement over the strongest baseline on Ta-Feng and Instacart, respectively, and +28.0% over TIFU-KNN on the proprietary dataset, while boosting explore-item recall by 17×.
A003FULLRetrieve-then-Adapt: Test-Time Retrieval-Augmentation for Sequential Recommendation
Xing Tang (Shenzhen Technology University) · Jingyang Bin (Shenzhen Technology University) · Ziqiang Cui (City University of Hong Kong) · Xiaokun Zhang (City University of Hong Kong) · Fuyuan Lyu (McGill University) · Jingyan Jiang (Shenzhen Technology University) · Dugang Liu (Shenzhen University) · Chen Ma (City University of Hong Kong) · Ruiming Tang (Kuaishou Technology) · Xiuqiang He (Shenzhen Technology University)
Abstract
The sequential recommendation (SR) task aims to predict the next item based on users' historical interaction sequences. Typically trained on historical data, SR models are frozen after deployment, limiting their ability to handle test-time patterns that are rare during training. Existing approaches to address this limitation include test-time training, test-time augmentation, and retrieval-augmented fine-tuning. However, these methods either introduce significant computational overhead, rely on random augmentation strategies, or require a carefully designed two-stage training paradigm. In this paper, we argue that the key to effective test-time augmentation lies in achieving both effective retrieval and efficient fusion. To this end, we propose Retrieve-then-Adapt (ReAd), a novel framework that augments a deployed SR model through retrieved user preference signals. Specifically, given a trained SR model, ReAd first retrieves collaboratively similar items for a test user from a constructed collaborative memory. A lightweight retrieval learning module then integrates these items into an informative augmentation embedding that captures both collaborative signals and prediction-refinement cues. Finally, the initial SR prediction is refined via a fusion mechanism that incorporates this embedding. Extensive experiments across five benchmark datasets demonstrate that ReAd consistently outperforms existing SR methods. The source code is publicly available at https://github.com/xingt-tang/ReAd.
A004FULLSEDRec: Semantic Entanglement for Generative Diffusion-based Sequential Recommendation
Byungmoon Heo (Sungkyunkwan University) · Jaekwang Kim (Sungkyunkwan University)
Abstract
Sequential recommendation (SR) predicts a user’s next action by modeling their historical interaction sequence, and it underpins many real-world platforms where accuracy directly impacts engagement and conversion. Recently, diffusion-based SR has gained traction by iteratively denoising corrupted representations, improving robustness and handling uncertainty when user intent is ambiguous. However, most diffusion-based SR methods still rely mainly on item IDs and learned latent embeddings, complemented by conditioning or regularization techniques. This ID-centric design limits semantic expressiveness: semantically similar items can remain distant under sparse feedback, while unrelated items may be confounded by co-occurrence and popularity biases. Prior work has attempted to inject semantics through contrastive learning or auxiliary objectives, but semantic signals are often incorporated indirectly and can weaken along the denoising trajectory, especially at inference when generation starts from noise. To address this limitation, we make semantics an explicit denoising target by introducing a semantic token whose target is the next-item semantic embedding in the same latent space as item embeddings, and we jointly denoise the item sequence and the semantic token. Building on this idea, we propose SEDRec (Semantic Entanglement generative Diffusion for sequential Recommendation), which entangles semantic and ID-based signals through history semantic conditioning, synchronized noise levels, semantic-to-target mixing, and intermediate alignment to a fixed semantic anchor. Across multiple benchmarks and evaluation metrics, extensive experiments demonstrate that SEDRec consistently outperforms strong baselines, and ablation studies confirm the contribution of each semantic entanglement component.
A005SHORTGenerative Chain of Behavior for User Trajectory Prediction
Chengkai Huang (University of New South Wales) · Xiaodi Chen (University of New South Wales) · Hongtao Huang (University of New South Wales) · Quan Z. Sheng (Beijing Normal-Hong Kong Baptist University) · Lina Yao (University of New South Wales)
Abstract
Modeling long-term user behavior trajectories is essential for understanding evolving preferences and enabling proactive recommendations. However, most sequential recommenders focus on next-item prediction, overlooking dependencies across multiple future actions. We propose Generative Chain of Behavior (GCB), a generative framework that models user interactions as an autoregressive chain of semantic behaviors over multiple future steps. GCB first encodes items into semantic IDs via RQ-VAE with k-means refinement, forming a discrete latent space that preserves semantic proximity. On top of this space, a transformer-based autoregressive generator predicts multi-step future behaviors conditioned on user history, capturing long-horizon intent transitions and generating coherent trajectories. Experiments on benchmark datasets show that GCB achieves strong multi-step prediction performance while generating coherent long-horizon behavior trajectories. Beyond these results, GCB provides a unified generative formulation for modeling user preference evolution.
A006SHORTLeveraging Language Models for Music Recommendation with Bayesian Residual Quantization
Yi Tian (Xi'an Jiaotong University) · Jian Zhang (Xiaomi Company) · Junjie Wu (Xiaomi Company) · Hongyu Xu (Peking University) · Yajie Wang (Xiaomi Company) · Jinnan Huang (Xi'an Jiaotong University) · Jiapeng Liu (Xi'an Jiaotong University)
Abstract
Generative recommendations (GRs) reframe recommendation as autoregressive generation over Semantic IDs (SIDs), enabling Large Language Models (LLMs) to model user intent and sequential preference patterns in a unified manner. Most existing systems discretize continuous item representations into SIDs via codebook-based residual quantization, and then generate subsequent SID tokens through next-token prediction. However, conventional residual quantization relies on deterministic, hard nearest-neighbor assignments. This rigid mapping fails to account for semantic ambiguity, suffering from error propagation across quantization levels and often leading to under-utilized codebooks. To address these limitations, we propose the Bayesian Residual Quantized Variational Autoencoder (BRQ-VAE), a probabilistic reformulation of residual quantization that introduces stochastic quantization and stochastic dequantization under an ELBO-driven objective. We further develop alignment strategies to integrate language semantics and collaborative signals for end-to-end LLM-based recommendation. Experiments on public benchmarks, large-scale industrial datasets, and online A/B tests on a commercial music platform show that BRQ-VAE consistently improves codebook quality, downstream recommendation performance, and key engagement metrics over strong baselines.
A007FULLFaithful Evaluation of Semantic-ID Tokenizers for Generative Recommendation
Qian Zhang (University of Otago) · Lech Szymanski (University of Otago) · Jeremiah Deng (University of Otago) · Haibo Zhang (University of New South Wales)
Abstract
Generative recommendation based on Semantic IDs (SIDs) represents each item as a discrete sequence of SIDs and is conventionally evaluated by matching the generated SID sequence against the target item's SID sequence. This evaluation is faithful only when each SID sequence uniquely identifies one item. In practice, SID collisions violate this condition: across the evaluated SID tokenizers and datasets, collision rates reach 30.52%, and SID-level Hit@10 is inflated by up to 103.36% relative to item-level Hit@10. To address this evaluation gap, we introduce Collision-Corrected Evaluation (CCE), which defines collision-aware item-level metrics (ItemHit@K, ItemNDCG@K) computed from generated SID sequences, and Zero-Collision Reassignment (ZCR), which constructs zero-collision SID assignments for existing tokenizers via minimum-cost reassignment. Applying these methods to four datasets and five representative SID tokenizers, we find that metric inflation scales with collision rate and is large enough to flip pairwise tokenizer comparisons under item-level re-evaluation. This finding calls into question the reliability of SID-level rankings reported in prior work and indicates that faithful tokenizer evaluation requires item-level correction or zero-collision SID assignments.
A008FULLAccumulative Modality Tokenization for Multimodal Generative Recommendation
Shenghao Yang (DCST, Tsinghua University; Quan Cheng Laboratory) · Zhiqiang Guo (Quan Cheng Laboratory; DCST, Tsinghua University) · Weizhi Ma (AIR, Tsinghua University) · Min Zhang (DCST, Tsinghua University) · Lei Wang (Meituan)
Abstract
Generative recommendation has attracted widespread attention as a new paradigm in recommender systems. Its core idea is to discretize item semantic representations into semantic IDs and leverage the generative model's sequence modeling capability to predict the next item the user may prefer. Early approaches mainly focused on textual semantics, and recent multimodal generative recommendation methods incorporate additional modalities to provide richer semantics. However, existing methods typically handle modalities independently during both tokenization and generation, leading to insufficient modality fusion in semantic ID construction and inadequate cross-modal integration during recommendation. Moreover, the modality tokenizers are optimized with representation-level reconstruction or alignment objectives and lack recommendation-aware supervision, resulting in sub-optimal performance. To address these issues, we propose Accumulative Modality Tokenization for Multimodal Generative Recommendation, namely AMTGR. Specifically, we harness the Multimodal Large Language Model as the unified tokenizer to progressively accumulate and tokenize multimodal information, and design a collaborative-aware reconstruction task as the tokenizer's optimization objective to achieve recommendation-oriented multimodal semantic IDs, which will be jointly fed into the generative model to achieve effective cross-modal integration during recommendation. Experiments on public datasets demonstrate that AMTGR significantly outperforms baselines, and further analyses verify the effectiveness of high-quality multimodal semantic IDs and the unified modality integration.
A009FULLPersonalized Context-Conditioned Tokenization for Generative Recommendation
Qiyong Zhong (Zhejiang University) · Jiajie Su (Zhejiang University) · Yunshan Ma (Singapore Management University) · Julian McAuley (University of California San Diego) · Yupeng Hou (University of California San Diego)
Abstract
Generative recommendation (GR) represents user actions as sequences of discrete tokens (often referred to as semantic IDs) and predict future interactions through autoregressive generation. This paradigm offers advantages such as compact representations, scalability, and the potential to unify retrieval and ranking. However, existing tokenization schemes are typically static and agnostic to user-specific context. In most cases, semantic IDs are derived solely from item attributes, implicitly assuming a shared notion of item similarity across all users. Under autoregressive decoding, tokens with identical prefixes tend to receive similar probabilities, meaning that a fixed tokenization enforces a universal similarity structure that may not reflect individual user perspectives. In reality, users may interpret the same item in fundamentally different ways depending on their preferences and intents. To better capture such diversity, we introduce a context-conditioned tokenizer that integrates a user’s historical interactions into the tokenization process. This approach allows a single item to be mapped to multiple semantic ID sequences under different user contexts, enabling the model to represent heterogeneous interpretations and produce more personalized recommendations. Empirical results on three public benchmarks show that our method achieves up to 11.44% improvement in NDCG@10 compared with non-personalized tokenization approaches. The implementation is available at https://github.com/YoungZ365/Pctx.
A010FULLLearning from Unreachable Rewards: Hint-Conditioned Reinforcement Learning for Generative Recommendation
Kangning Zhang (Shanghai Jiao Tong University) · Haotian Fang (Shanghai Jiao Tong University) · Xukun Luo (Mei Tuan) · Hao Yin (Mei Tuan) · Yang Gao (Mei Tuan) · Peng Yan (Mei Tuan) · Weiwen Liu (Shanghai Jiao Tong University) · Weinan Zhang (Shanghai Jiao Tong University) · Yong Yu (Shanghai Jiao Tong University)
Abstract
Semantic-ID generative recommenders represent each item as a short sequence of discrete semantic tokens and predict the next item by autoregressively generating this token sequence. This paradigm enables a unified generation interface for item IDs, histories, and item text, but it also creates a structured optimization bottleneck during reward-based post-training: when an early semantic token enters the wrong branch of the item-token space, finite rollout groups rarely reach the ground-truth item, so group-relative optimization receives identical zero rewards and produces no useful advantage. We propose Hint-Conditioned Generative Recommendation (HCGRec), a semantic-ID generative recommendation framework that recovers learning signal for such hard training instances. HCGRec diagnoses each instance with checkpoint rollouts and supplies a minimal target-prefix hint only when the current generator cannot reach the correct item. The model then generates the unhinted suffix under the hinted semantic branch, turning zero-reward groups into informative comparisons over item-token completions. Hinting also changes token identity: hinted prefix tokens are oracle-provided item context, while unhinted suffix tokens are sampled generation actions. We therefore introduce hint-aware credit decomposition, using supervised learning to preserve item-semantic and prefix-structure alignment for hinted tokens and GRPO to optimize the sampled suffix. Experiments on sequential recommendation benchmarks show that HCGRec substantially improves over supervised fine-tuning and vanilla reward-based post-training, while reducing zero-advantage training samples from over 70% to below 20%. The code is accessible at https://github.com/WncFht/GRec.
A011SHORTSRCRec: Staged Reverse Curriculum Learning for Conversion-Oriented Generative Recommendation
Yulei Huang (Alibaba International Digital Commerce Group) · Hao Deng (Alibaba International Digital Commerce Group) · Jinxin Hu (Alibaba International Digital Commerce Group) · Yu Zhang (Alibaba International Digital Commerce Group) · Xiaoyi Zeng (Alibaba International Digital Commerce Group)
Abstract
Conversion-oriented generative recommendation (GR) is challenged by sparse conversion supervision, where the decoder must learn conversion targets from long interaction histories with limited positive signals. Existing multi-behavior GR methods enhance behavior-aware representation learning, but still optimize the original full-history prediction task directly, leaving the difficulty of sparse conversion modeling insufficiently addressed. Recent reverse-curriculum-inspired methods further show that conversion-related intermediate behaviors are useful, yet they mainly instantiate the curriculum as one-shot decoder-prefix conditioning, which does not provide a staged reverse curriculum process and will increase online serving latency. To address these limitations, we propose SRCRec, a staged reverse curriculum learning framework for conversion-oriented GR. SRCRec constructs difficulty-aware curriculum contexts over the historical sequence, trains the model from target-near easy contexts to harder historical contexts, and finally recovers the original no-prefix conversion objective. This staged optimization enables the model to progressively learn from curricula with increasing difficulty while keeping inference identical to standard GR. Experiments on public and industrial datasets show that SRCRec achieves superior offline performance, and online A/B tests further improve orders by 3.52% and Gross Merchandise Volume by 2.98%.
A012SHORTCDNet: Efficient Sequential-Contextual Feature Interaction via Core-Behavior Selection and Interest-Distribution Compensation
Yi Xu (Alibaba International Digital Commerce Group) · Chaofan Fan (Alibaba International Digital Commerce Group) · Moyu Zhang (Alibaba International Digital Commerce Group) · Jinxin Hu (Alibaba International Digital Commerce Group) · Jiahao Wang (Alibaba International Digital Commerce Group) · Hao Zhang (Alibaba International Digital Commerce Group) · Shizhun Wang (Alibaba International Digital Commerce Group) · Yu Zhang (Alibaba International Digital Commerce Group) · Xiaoyi Zeng (Alibaba International Digital Commerce Group)
Abstract
Effective click-through rate (CTR) prediction hinges on capturing the interactions between user behavior sequences and non-sequential contextual features. Existing approaches face a fundamental dilemma in this interaction: aggregation-based methods compress the sequence into fixed-length vectors before interacting with contextual features, sacrificing the fine-grained behavioral details critical for capturing how specific past behaviors relate to the current candidate; full sequence unrolling enables direct interaction between every behavior and every contextual feature, but incurs quadratic computational cost and allows noise from irrelevant behaviors to overwhelm the signals from the truly relevant ones. To resolve this dilemma, we propose CDNet, a Core-Behaviors and Distributional-Compensation Dual-View Interaction Network that models sequential-contextual feature interaction from two strictly complementary and mutually indispensable angles. The Fine-grained Core-Behaviors Module selects the most relevant behaviors for explicit fine-grained interaction with contextual features, providing local behavioral semantics at low computational cost. The Global Interest-Distribution Module addresses an orthogonal question that core behaviors structurally cannot answer: how broadly does the user's full history align with the candidate? This global interest-intensity signal, encoded as a compact relevance distribution over the entire sequence, enables contextual features to calibrate their interaction with the precise behavioral signals, a capacity entirely absent when only core behaviors are considered. Extensive experiments on public and industrial datasets demonstrate that both modules are necessary and their combination achieves superior accuracy and efficiency over state-of-the-art methods.
A013FULLTowards Efficient Federated Time Series Forecasting under Structural Data Heterogeneity across Nodes
Yiming Zhou (University of Science and Technology of China) · Jiahao Wang (University of Science and Technology of China) · Mingyue Cheng (University of Science and Technology of China) · Hao Wang (University of Science and Technology of China) · Defu Lian (University of Science and Technology of China) · Enhong Chen (University of Science and Technology of China)
Abstract
Time series data is highly valuable yet sharing-sensitive across nodes, making federated learning a promising paradigm to leverage distributed temporal data. However, varying sampling standards lead to heterogeneous data structures across nodes, with diverse time granularities and inconsistent variable sets being particularly prominent, posing significant challenges for conventional federated learning frameworks. In this paper, we propose PiXTime, a novel Transformer-based time series forecasting model designed to tolerate and exploit such structurally heterogeneous distributed data. Specifically, we redesign the internal modules and adopt the parameter-decoupling philosophy by carefully designating each module as either local or shared to handle the unique challenges of the federated scenario. To address granularity misalignments, PiXTime retains a personalized set of local modules for each node, acting as a crucial bridge between the node-specific raw temporal granularities and the unified feature dimension of the federated network. To tackle variable inconsistencies, we design a shared VE Table that explicitly injects globally unified variable categorical identities into specific auxiliary tokens, enhancing PiXTime's capability to collaboratively train under highly diverse auxiliary variable distributions.
