Extensive experiments demonstrate that PiXTime not only establishes state-of-the-art (SOTA) performance in handling structurally heterogeneous distributed data but also achieves superiority in conventional benchmarks. We open-source our code at https://github.com/WearTheClo/PiXTime.
A014FULLScaling Up Unified CTR Prediction via Dynamic Sequence-to-Feature Interaction
Kai Cheng (University of Science and Technology of China) · Wei Guo (HUAWEI TECHNOLOGIES CO.LTD) · Guoyuan An (HUAWEI TECHNOLOGIES CO.LTD) · Luankang Zhang (University of Science and Technology of China) · Yuyang Ye (University of Science and Technology of China) · Yong Liu (HUAWEI TECHNOLOGIES CO.LTD) · Hao Wang (University of Science and Technology of China) · Enhong Chen (University of Science and Technology of China)
Abstract
Industrial CTR prediction requires unified modeling of long user behavior histories and heterogeneous non-sequential features. Existing methods usually follow two paradigms: encode-then-concatenate methods independently encode behavior sequences and then coarsely concatenate them with non-sequential features, while token-level joint modeling methods flatten sequential and non-sequential signals into a shared interaction space. The former may ignore the heterogeneity between sequential and non-sequential representations, limiting fine-grained cross-feature interaction; the latter may suffer from capacity dilution, since behavior tokens often far outnumber high-value user, item, and contextual fields. To address these challenges, we propose Dynamic Sequence-to-Feature Interaction (DySFI), a unified sequence-conditioned dynamic feature interaction framework for CTR prediction. DySFI separately models sequential and non-sequential features with a temporal-aware sequence encoder and a DLRM backbone. The candidate-specific sequential representation generates dynamic parameters to transform the DLRM representation, enabling behavior histories to explicitly guide non-sequential feature interaction. We further introduce candidate-aware residual-update aggregation and stabilization designs to improve efficiency and training stability. Experiments on two industrial CTR scenarios show that DySFI consistently outperforms competitive baselines. Online A/B tests on Huawei AppGallery further demonstrate a 1.57% eCPM improvement over the production model, leading to full deployment.
A015FULLAlphaCast: A Human Wisdom-LLM Intelligence Co-Reasoning Framework for Time Series Forecasting
Xiaohan Zhang (State Key Laboratory of Cognitive Intelligence, University of Science and Technology of China) · Tian Gao (State Key Laboratory of Cognitive Intelligence, University of Science and Technology of China) · Mingyue Cheng (State Key Laboratory of Cognitive Intelligence, University of Science and Technology of China) · Bokai Pan (State Key Laboratory of Cognitive Intelligence, University of Science and Technology of China) · Ze Guo (State Key Laboratory of Cognitive Intelligence, University of Science and Technology of China) · Yaguo Liu (State Key Laboratory of Cognitive Intelligence, University of Science and Technology of China) · Xiaoyu Tao (State Key Laboratory of Cognitive Intelligence, University of Science and Technology of China) · Qi Liu (State Key Laboratory of Cognitive Intelligence, University of Science and Technology of China)
Abstract
Time series forecasting is typically treated as a single-pass numerical prediction task based on historical observations. However, real-world forecasting often requires expert-like reasoning, where temporal patterns, contextual cues, case-based references, and domain knowledge are jointly considered and iteratively revised. Existing statistical, deep learning, foundation, and LLM-based forecasting models mainly rely on pattern fitting, direct prompting, or static context augmentation, leaving interactive and reflective forecasting insufficiently explored. In this work, we propose AlphaCast, a human wisdom–LLM intelligence co-reasoning framework for interactive time series forecasting. AlphaCast does not require real-time human intervention; instead, it operationalizes human wisdom as structured forecasting support, including time-series features, contextual cues, case-based references, and domain knowledge. Built upon an expert-like think–forecast–reflect workflow, AlphaCast comprises three agents: an Investigator that constructs forecasting context from available evidence, a Generator that produces context-grounded forecasts, and a Reflector that evaluates plausibility and provides feedback for refinement. Extensive experiments demonstrate that AlphaCast improves forecasting accuracy and produces interpretable forecast explanations, offering a promising step toward interactive and context-aware time series forecasting (https://github.com/ustc-time-series/AlphaCast).
A016FULLLatent Residual Reasoning for Ranking in Generative Recommendation
Haihan Shi (University of Science and Technology of China) · Ruidong Han (Meituan) · Wenjie Wang (University of Science and Technology of China) · Shangyu Chen (Meituan) · Sunhao Dai (Renmin University of China) · Yongqi Li (The Hong Kong Polytechnic University) · Yangyang Li (Academy of Cyber) · Fei Jiang (Meituan) · Wei Lin (Meituan) · Fuli Feng (University of Science and Technology of China) · Xiangnan He (University of Science and Technology of China)
Abstract
Generative recommendation (GR) models for ranking typically adopt a fast-thinking direct prediction paradigm with strong practical efficiency. However, ranking requires fine-grained scoring across multiple candidate items, while existing GR models still mainly rely on one-shot prediction. This raises the question whether additional inference-time computation can further improve ranking quality. Recently, inspired by Chain-of-Thought (CoT) reasoning in large language models (LLMs), some work has begun to introduce reasoning into recommendation systems. Some of these methods rely on LLM reasoning frameworks to perform explicit reasoning in textual space, but such designs are not suitable for more widely deployed non-textual recommendation models. A more relevant direction is to introduce latent reasoning into ID-based recommendation models. Although recent work has extended latent reasoning to industrial ranking, how successive reasoning steps should improve fine-grained candidate scores remains less explored. To address this problem, we propose Refiner, a latent residual reasoning framework with parameter-efficient fine-tuning for generative ranking. Our approach introduces three key components: (1) a residual reasoning mechanism that progressively refines ranking scores through cumulative additive corrections, (2) history queries that provide condensed user behavior representations to enhance candidate-specific reasoning, and (3) a parameter-efficient fine-tuning strategy that leverages LoRA modules to adapt pre-trained models for latent reasoning. Extensive experiments on two public benchmarks, an offline industrial dataset, and an online A/B test demonstrate that Refiner consistently improves over direct prediction, validating its effectiveness and practical utility.
A017FULLTAG-Rec: Grounding LLM-based Recommendation via Trigger-Anchored GRPO
Donghee Han (Korea Advanced Institute of Science and Technology) · Jiwon Jeong (Korea Advanced Institute of Science and Technology) · Hwanjun Song (Korea Advanced Institute of Science and Technology) · Mun Yong Yi (Korea Advanced Institute of Science and Technology)
Abstract
Large Language Models (LLMs) have demonstrated significant potential in recommendation systems; however, employing Reinforcement Learning (RL) to align them with ranking metrics in the query-generation formulation of large-scale recommendation remains a critical challenge. Current RL-based approaches often suffer from reward sparsity and generating too general queries. In this paper, we propose TAG-Rec, a framework that grounds generative recommendation via Trigger-Anchored Group Relative Policy Optimization (GRPO). Built upon a verifiable-anchor training principle, TAG-Rec enforces a “Trigger-First” generation strategy in which the model explicitly identifies a salient historical item as a verifiable anchor before generating a search query, structurally transforming open-ended generation into grounded reasoning. TAG-Rec combines three components: (i) Trigger-Grounded Data Curation via reachability verification, which concentrates training supervision on samples that admit a verifiable historical anchor; (ii) the Trigger-First generation strategy that anchors generation in a salient prior interaction; and (iii) a Trigger-aware Reward that supplies dense intermediate feedback to mitigate reward sparsity. On real-world sequential recommendation benchmarks, TAG-Rec achieves up to 23.6% and 13.8% average improvement over strong SFT and RL baselines, with notable gains on long-tail and novelty metrics.
A018SHORTLearning Collaborative and Discriminative Embeddings with LLMs for Sequential Recommendation
Sijin Lu (Beijing Jiaotong University) · Jun Wu (Beijing Jiaotong University)
Abstract
Large Language Models (LLMs) have shown promise as embedding generators for sequential recommendation. Effective adaptation typically involves two stages: collaborative signal injection and discriminative representation learning. However, optimization objective and item semantic misalignments arise between these two stages, resulting in catastrophic forgetting of collaborative relationships learned in the first stage. To address these issues, we propose a novel LLM-based embedding method called GCTP, which obtains both collaborative and discriminative embeddings. Specifically, we maintain a generative training objective throughout the training process, thereby alleviating potential optimization conflicts. Moreover, we preserve local semantics to ensure semantic consistency during training, and capture global semantics with minimal modifications when extracting item embeddings. Experiments on real-world datasets show that GCTP significantly outperforms state-of-the-art LLM-based embedding methods.
A019SHORTE²L³AE: End‑to‑End Text Encoder Tuning for LLM‑Enhanced Linear Autoencoders
Maryia Kurdun (T-Bank) · Kiryl Liakhnovich (T-Bank) · Mikhail Pechatov (T-Bank) · Oleg Lashinin (Moscow Institute of Physics and Technology)
Abstract
Enriching sparse user–item interactions with semantic item knowledge is essential for robust recommendation, particularly for long-tail items where collaborative signals are weak or unreliable. L³AE integrates frozen LLM embeddings into linear autoencoders, but fixed text representations can be suboptimal for recommendation because consumption-relevant item characteristics often deviate from general textual semantics. We propose an end-to-end extension that fine-tunes the text encoder within the same linear autoencoder framework, encouraging its embeddings to reflect item relatedness derived from user–item interactions, thereby adapting pretrained textual knowledge to recommendation objectives while remaining grounded in pretrained semantic knowledge. Experiments on public datasets show that our end-to-end trained hybrid model improves upon the original L³AE and other baselines. Moreover, the fine-tuned encoder alone serves as a competitive semantic-based recommender.
A020SHORTAsk to Be Sure: Informative Interactions for Confident Multi-Turn LLM Recommendation
Cedar Site Bai (Amazon) · Duanshun Li (Amazon) · Zhenyu Liao (Amazon) · Sheikh Sarwar (Amazon) · Huiyuan Chen (Amazon) · Yuan Chen (Amazon) · Changhe Yuan (Amazon) · Haiyang Zhang (Amazon) · Qilin Qi (Amazon)
Abstract
Recent advances in large language models (LLMs) have enabled their use as conversational recommender systems (CRS), demonstrating strong recommendation accuracy and natural dialogue. However, guiding multi-turn interactions to elicit user preferences effectively remains challenging. Existing approaches either use separate reinforcement learning agents with templated interactions or optimize for interactivity judged by another LLM, without measuring how much useful information is actually gained. We propose a new approach that quantifies the effectiveness of each interaction by the reduction in the assistant’s uncertainty, measured via entropy over recommendations. We apply this entropy reduction as a reward—without relying on ground-truth recommendations, which are often unavailable in real-world scenarios—to fine-tune the LLM, enabling strategic interaction generation. Empirical results with supervised fine-tuning (SFT) and direct preference optimization (DPO) on the INSPIRED and ReDial datasets show that our method improves both recommendation quality and conversational efficiency.
A021SHORTRetrieval, Scoring, and Decoding Shape Performance and Stability in LLM-based Conversational Recommendation
Ante Kapetanovic (Infobip) · Tomislav Duricic (Infobip) · Andro Mercep (Infobip) · Emanuel Lacic (Infobip)
Abstract
Large language models (LLMs) are increasingly used as rerankers in conversational recommender systems, yet measured gains depend strongly on the retrieval and inference protocol. On the ReDial conversational movie recommendation benchmark, we compare proprietary, open-weight, and fine-tuned LLM rerankers with collaborative-filtering and sequential baselines in a shared retrieve-then-rerank pipeline. We vary candidate-pool size, first-stage retriever, and decoding temperature. With a shared semantic top-250 candidate pool and strict candidate-aware scoring, the best proprietary reranker reaches NDCG@10 of 0.1497, compared with 0.0939 for the strongest non-LLM baseline. The same reranker reaches 0.2925 in zero-shot generation, showing that unconstrained scoring can yield a much larger apparent advantage than matched-pool evaluation. No evaluated open-weight LLM outperforms the tuned shallow autoencoder baseline under this protocol. For the strongest proprietary and open-weight rerankers, switching from semantic to collaborative-filtering candidates raises NDCG@10 by more than 50%, showing that measured reranker performance is highly sensitive to candidate generation. For the best proprietary reranker, raising temperature from 0 to 1.0 increases top-10 Jaccard distance from 0.0900 to 0.1240 while mean NDCG@10 changes negligibly, whereas weaker LLMs show larger degradation. These ReDial results support treating candidate generation, candidate-pool size, scoring policy, and decoding configuration as required reporting fields rather than implementation details.
A022FULLAuditing Multimodal Claims: A Controlled Reproducibility Study of Graph-based Conversational Recommendation
Seonghyeon Park (Sungkyunkwan University) · Piao Huilin (Sungkyunkwan University) · Jeongtae Lee (Sungkyunkwan University) · Seoin Choi (Sungkyunkwan University) · Eunil Park (Sungkyunkwan University)
Abstract
Multimodal conversational recommender systems (CRS) integrate dialogue, knowledge graphs, and visual signals. Recent work reports substantial gains over the knowledge-graph baseline KGSF on the INSPIRED dataset (R@10: 0.132→0.257). However, this pipeline couples ViT-based image embeddings with zero-fill handling for 23.7% of items missing poster data and augments training with LLM-generated synthetic dialogues, failing to isolate the visual modality. We present a controlled reproducibility study, maintaining the MSCRS backbone and training fixed while intervening on data and image-embedding inputs. To isolate item-specific visual correspondence from representation-level artifacts, we replace ViT embeddings with three distractor conditions: random Gaussian vectors, zero vectors, and shuffled real ViT embeddings. We also apply an artificial 23.7% missingness mask to ReDial and probe synthetic-dialogue training using a valid-best checkpoint protocol. Across INSPIRED and ReDial, the distractor conditions do not consistently separate from the original ViT condition; the multi-seed mean R@10 spread is only 0.007. Conversely, synthetic dialogue shows a directional paired difference (Δ R@10 = +0.031 ± 0.020, Cohen's dz=1.59). Furthermore, selection bias introduces a max-test versus valid-best gap of up to +0.035 R@10. These results do not imply that images are unhelpful, but rather that modality-specific visual effects are currently confounded by missing-node graph effects and augmentation artifacts. We propose a reproducibility-oriented audit procedure for multimodal CRS evaluation, covering distractor controls, missingness validation, and strict checkpoint selection.
A023FULLLess is More: Concise Retrieval and Critic-based Re-ranking for Composed Image Retrieval
Yuqian Zheng (Sungkyunkwan University) · Hyoju Ahn (Sungkyunkwan University) · Hyeongjin Ahn (Sungkyunkwan University) · Eunil Park (Sungkyunkwan University)
Abstract
Zero-shot composed image retrieval (ZS-CIR) aims to retrieve a target image based on a reference image and modification text. Recent approaches commonly rely on large vision-language models to generate target image captions for retrieval. However, these captions may include redundant semantic details, introducing noise when retrieving the target image and leading to suboptimal retrieval results. To address this issue, we propose Less-is-More CIR, a two-stage training-free framework that combines Concise Retrieval and Critic Re-ranking. In the first stage, concise target-oriented captions are generated that preserve only the most discriminative modification semantics, thereby reducing semantic noise in the retrieval. In the second stage, a critic re-rank module further evaluates the retrieved candidates from the perspectives of modification consistency and reference preservation. Extensive experiments demonstrate the effectiveness and robustness of the proposed framework for the ZS-CIR. Our code is available at: https://github.com/dxlabskku/LM-CIR.
A024RESOURCENewsReX: An Open-Source Multi-Framework for Neural News Recommendation
Igor L.R. Azevedo (Imperial College London) · Toyotaro Suzumura (The University of Tokyo) · Yuichiro Yasui (Nikkei Inc.)
Abstract
Reproducing and comparing results in neural news recommendation research remains difficult due to fragmented codebases, inconsistent preprocessing pipelines, and tight coupling between models and deep learning frameworks. We present NewsReX (https://github.com/igor17400/NewsReX), an open-source framework that unifies multiple neural news recommendation models across two ML backends (PyTorch and JAX/Flax). Models are defined through a structured YAML specification that captures architecture, training recipe, and data contract, decoupling model definition from framework-specific implementation. A Hydra-based configuration system enables composable experiments with single-command framework switching. We provide cross-framework parity tests to verify numerical consistency across backends, allowing researchers to reproduce results from the original implementations and then transfer experiments to their preferred framework. We report comprehensive experiments on the MIND-small benchmark with multiple seeds per model and per framework, and demonstrate multilingual generalization by training on a proprietary Japanese news dataset from Nikkei News (https://nikkei.com/). We also publish pre-trained model weights on Hugging Face (https://huggingface.co/newsrex/) so that researchers can build on existing results without redundant retraining, reducing both computational cost and energy consumption. All source code, experiment configurations, and trained model weights are publicly available.
A025SHORTConformal Prediction for Statistically Reliable LLM-as-a-Judge in Recommender Systems
Maddalena Amendola (IIT-CNR) · Giacomo Medda (University of Cagliari) · Alessandro Soccol (University of Cagliari) · Ludovico Boratto (University of Cagliari) · Mirko Marras (University of Cagliari) · Raffaele Perego (ISTI-CNR)
Abstract
LLM-as-a-judge has emerged as a promising strategy for evaluating recommender systems. Yet, treating simulated ratings as real feedback can make unreliable evaluation appear reliable. This risk is especially consequential in sensitive domains such as nutrition and health. In this paper, we treat the LLM-as-a-judge paradigm as a calibrated relevance simulation problem: an LLM-based simulator predicts human preferences from user and item representations, and conformal prediction converts them into uncertainty intervals. To account for the nature of recommendation, we introduce stratified conformal calibration by user rating variance. Experiments under three LLMs and seven conformal prediction methods show that point estimates of preferences hide failures on low-rating items, while conformal interval width is driven by user-level heterogeneity. Source code and data: https://github.com/maddalena-amendola/conformal_prediction_recsys.
A026APPLIEDLossless Compression of Proximity Graph Indexes for Efficient Approximate Nearest Neighbors Search
Francesco Benocci (ISTI-CNR) · Leonard Dahlmann (eBay Inc.) · Francesco Gargiulo (University of Pisa) · Tobias Heuer (eBay Inc.) · Silvio Martinico (University of Pisa & ISTI-CNR) · Franco Maria Nardini (ISTI-CNR) · Cosimo Rulli (ISTI-CNR) · Rossano Venturini (University of Pisa)
Abstract
Graph-based Approximate Nearest Neighbor (ANN) indexes, such as HNSW, are the backbone of modern vector search. However, their massive memory footprint creates a severe infrastructure bottleneck. While vector quantization is widely adopted to reduce the memory required to store data vectors, the graph's edge structure increasingly dominates total memory usage. Compressing these adjacency lists for online search presents a critical system challenge: because decompression occurs during query processing, i.e., while navigating the graph, memory savings cannot come at the expense of query latency. In this paper, we present a compression technique explicitly tailored for live HNSW routing. By applying offline graph permutations to artificially induce structural locality, we enable the use of SIMD-accelerated integer compressors, such as Stream VByte, for rapid on-the-fly decompression. Evaluated across diverse real-world workloads, we significantly outperform the current state of the art in both compression ratio and query latency. Our experimental results show that we achieve compression ratios up to 52.7% with negligible penalties in latency compared to the uncompressed baseline. Furthermore, our technique has been effectively deployed in production at eBay, achieving up to 44.3% reduction in edge storage with no degradation in query latency.
A027SHORTA Behavioral Trait Leaks into Preferences: Diagnosing Trait Interference in LLM User Simulators
Chaehyun Kim (KAIST) · Sein Kim (KAIST) · Hongseok Kang (KAIST) · Chanyoung Park (KAIST)
Abstract
LLM-based user simulators aim to bridge the offline–online gap in recommender evaluation by emulating users through injected traits, where preference attributes determine what a user engages with and a behavioral activity trait governs how long they browse. However, we show this intended trait independence collapses during simulation, causing two failures: (i) Trait Interference, where amplified activity distorts preference boundaries and forces interactions with mismatched items to sustain browsing, and (ii) Evaluation Invalidity, where satisfaction scores inflate with activity-driven page counts despite taste mismatches, biasing evaluation toward trait distributions rather than recommender performance. To resolve this, we propose PQA, a page-level quality anchoring method that guides simulators using a personalized anchor reflecting each user's intrinsic preference standard. By assessing whether a page meets this standard before further browsing, PQA enables proactive exits from low-quality pages, letting the activity trait retain its intended role of modulating browsing depth within preference-conforming pages. Experiments show PQA mitigates trait interference and improves the reliability of LLM-based simulator evaluation under activity shifts. Our code is available at https://github.com/chaehyun1/PQA.
A028SHORTPersonalized Task Dependency Graphs for Mitigating Signal Erosion in Multi-Task Recommendation
Fuyuan Liu (Huawei Technologies Co., Ltd.) · Tiandeng Wu (Huawei Technologies Co., Ltd.) · Yaqun Fang (Huawei Technologies Co., Ltd.) · Wei Zhou (Huawei Technologies Co., Ltd.) · Zehao Zhou (Huawei Technologies Co., Ltd.) · Wenping Chen (Huawei Technologies Co., Ltd.) · Qishun Mei (Huawei Technologies Co., Ltd.) · Jiaxin Zhou (Huawei Technologies Co., Ltd.) · Heng Chang (Huawei Technologies Co., Ltd.) · Yi Cao (Huawei Technologies) · Jiandong Ding (Huawei Technologies)
Abstract
Optimizing multiple conversion objectives is a core challenge in industrial recommendation, often limited by signal erosion in rigid architectures. Existing Multi-Task Learning (MTL) methods typically enforce uniform dependency strengths across a static conversion funnel, overlooking how task correlations naturally vary based on item characteristics. Hierarchical message passing along these fixed chains leads to cumulative signal attenuation, which degrades performance on sparse, deep-funnel objectives. To address this, we propose the Personalized Task Dependency Graphs (PTDG). While respecting necessary physical causal constraints (e.g., Click → Pay), PTDG dynamically “rewires” the intensity of dependency pathways for each item via low-rank approximation to ensure structural robustness. We implement a GCN-based propagation with hard causal masking to establish adaptive information shortcuts. Additionally, we introduce an Adaptive Progressive Masking (APM) strategy that decouples shared parameters according to task sparsity, helping to stabilize optimization. Experiments on KuaiRand1K and an industrial dataset show that PTDG significantly improves AUC on sparse conversion tasks by up to 1.45%, while maintaining comparable performance on dense objectives. Online A/B testing shows PTDG improves Conversion Rate (CVR) by 1.2% and effective Cost Per Mille (eCPM) by 1.9% relative to the baseline.
A029FULLLarge Language Model-Guided Adaptive Source-Domain Weighting for Cross-Domain Sequential Recommendation
Yujie Jia (Donghua University) · Guohao Sun (Donghua University) · Xiu Fang (Donghua University) · Ge Zhang (Donghua University) · Jinhu Lu (Fuyang Normal University)
Abstract
Sequential Recommendation Systems (SRS) aim to predict the next item based on their historical interaction sequence. To address the data sparsity issue that commonly existed in SRS, Cross-Domain Sequential Recommendation (CDSR) has emerged, which aims to improve recommendation performance in a sparse domain (usually called target domain) by transferring knowledge from an information-rich domain (usually called source domain). However, existing CDSR methods mainly rely on ID-based representations and provide limited semantics across domains. With the rapid development of large language models (LLMs), recent studies have begun to incorporate LLM-generated item or user embeddings with rich semantic information into CDSR models, substantially enriching the representation space and improving modeling expressiveness. However, these LLM-enhanced methods typically treat all source domains equally and overlook the varying semantic relevance of different domains, which will lead to low-relevance domains introducing noise and consequently degrade recommendation performance. To tackle these issues, we propose LLMAW4CDSR, a Large Language Model-guided Adaptive source-domain Weighting framework. The core idea is to first leverage the semantic reasoning abilities of LLMs to produce semantically enriched user and item representations, and then use them as semantic guidance for more effective cross-domain knowledge transfer. Building on this guidance, we design an source-domain weighting mechanism that estimates the contribution of each source domain to the target domain. By integrating LLM-driven semantic alignment with adaptive domain weighting, LLMAW4CDSR highlights relevant domains while suppressing noisy ones, enabling fine-grained cross-domain knowledge transfer. Comprehensive experiments on four cross-domain datasets demonstrate that LLMAW4CDSR consistently outperforms both state-of-the-art CDSR methods and LLM-based baselines.
A030SHORTRevisiting LLM-Enhanced Collaborative Filtering: A Text-Free Alternative with Heterogeneous Interaction Signals
Jaeeun Lim (Kangwon National University) · Jae-woong Lee (Kangwon National University)
Abstract
Large language models (LLMs) have recently improved collaborative filtering (CF) by adding text-derived signals, but often require rich textual data and costly inference. In this work, we revisit RLMRec [11], a representative LLM-enhanced CF framework, and examine whether its gains come from LLM-specific knowledge or from complementary representations. Our analysis suggests that a substantial part of the improvement can be attributed to auxiliary heterogeneous signals, rather than solely to intrinsic LLM knowledge. Motivated by this, we propose HetRec (Heterogeneity-aware Recommender), a text-free, model-agnostic CF framework that replaces LLM-derived textual embeddings with interaction-derived heterogeneous signals. HetRec constructs auxiliary embeddings from heterogeneous-view CF models and enriches them via similarity-aware k-nearest neighbor aggregation, capturing neighborhood-level collaborative patterns. Under the same RLMRec-style alignment framework, HetRec improves over RLMRec variants on the Amazon-book, Yelp, and Steam datasets without textual inputs or LLM inference. Our code is available at https://github.com/Jaeeun-Lim02/HetRec.
A031SHORTTEDI: Target-Review-based Knowledge Distillation for Effective Recommendation
Jiwon Son (Hanyang University) · Bohye Han (Hanyang University) · Sang-Wook Kim (Hanyang University)
Abstract
Review-based recommendation systems (RBRS) leverage textual reviews to capture rich information about user preferences. A target review, which is directly associated with the target rating, contains highly relevant information for rating prediction but is unavailable during inference. Existing RBRS approaches try to reproduce the target review's semantic embedding by leveraging historical reviews. However, this semantic embedding often includes rating-irrelevant information, limiting its effectiveness in rating prediction. To address this issue, we propose TEDI, a novel RBRS based on privileged feature distillation (PFD). TEDI consists of a teacher module that distills rating-relevant knowledge from both target and historical reviews, and a student module that reproduces this knowledge by leveraging historical reviews during inference. Experiments on six datasets demonstrate that TEDI outperforms nine state-of-the-art RBRS methods, validating the effectiveness of utilizing knowledge from target reviews. Our code and data are available at https://github.com/Bigdasgit/TEDI.
A032FULLDREAM-CF: Diffusion-deficiency Repair via Adaptive Multi-view Semantic Bridging for Collaborative Filtering
Zhibin Chen (Heilongjiang University) · Xin Wang (Heilongjiang University) · Sida Yan (Heilongjiang University) · Wenyao Qiao (Heilongjiang University) · Nan Wang (Heilongjiang University) · Lingli Li (Heilongjiang University)
Abstract
Long-tail items are ubiquitous in collaborative filtering recommendations, and due to sparse interactions, it is difficult to extract sufficient collaborative propagation signals from the original user–item graph, leading to inadequate representation learning and a bias toward popular items. Existing Graph ODE-based collaborative filtering methods enhance propagation flexibility by continuously modeling the evolution of user and item representations. However, they typically assume that the input graph already possesses reliable information diffusion paths, thereby overlooking the issue of insufficient diffusion for long-tail items within the original interaction structure. To address this, we propose DREAM-CF, which stands for Diffusion-deficiency Repair via Adaptive Multi-view Semantic Bridging for Collaborative Filtering. DREAM-CF first integrates item text semantic representations with user historical behavior to construct a time-aware semantic initial state, thereby reducing the reliance of continuous diffusion on random ID embeddings. Subsequently, we design an ODE-aware Diffusion-deficiency Diagnosis mechanism to identify items with genuine information reception deficiencies on the original user–item graph, rather than simply classifying long-tail targets based on interaction frequency. Furthermore, DREAM-CF constructs high-confidence item-item bridge edges from three perspectives—textual semantics, co-occurrence, and metadata relationships—transforming external semantic information and behavioral priors into structured signals that can participate in graph propagation. Experimental results demonstrate that DREAM-CF effectively improves recommendation performance in long-tail and sparse interaction scenarios.Our code is publicly available at https://github.com/XiQier/Dream-CF.git.
A033SHORTNeural Tree Collaborative Filtering: Rethinking Graph Collaborative Filtering as Tree Collaborative Filtering with Curvature-Aware Propagation Depth
Jinfeng Xu (The University of Hong Kong) · Zheyu Chen (Beijing Institute of Technology) · Ziyue Peng (The Hong Kong University of Science and Technology) · Shuo Yang (The Univerisity of Hong Kong) · Jinze Li (The University of Hong Kong) · Wenhao Yuan (The University of Hong Kong) · Jian Chen (The University of Hong Kong) · Shujie Li (The University of Hong Kong) · Edith C. H. Ngai (The University of Hong Kong)
Abstract
Graph Collaborative Filtering (GCF) has become the dominant paradigm in modern recommender systems by modeling user--item interactions as a bipartite graph and propagating embeddings through a fixed number of message-passing layers. However, applying a uniform propagation depth to every node ignores a fundamental property of real interaction graphs: nodes differ substantially in their local connectivity, so peripheral nodes quickly suffer from over-smoothing while hub-like nodes remain under-explored beyond their immediate neighborhood. In this paper, we revisit GCF from a tree-structured perspective and propose Neural Tree Collaborative Filtering (NTCF), a framework that re-interprets each node's local neighborhood as a rooted tree and assigns a node-specific propagation depth based on a closed-form local-degree-imbalance score that serves as a discrete Ricci-curvature proxy. We provide a theoretical analysis showing that (i) NTCF strictly generalizes NGCF, degenerating to NGCF when all curvature-induced depth adjustments vanish (a lower bound on its representation power), and (ii) the curvature-aware schedule retains strictly more discriminative information at deep layers on positively-curved (peripheral) nodes than uniform-depth propagation. NTCF can achieve higher performance than most widely used GCF backbone models and can be integrated into existing advanced self-supervised models as a backbone, replacing their original backbone to achieve enhanced performance. Extensive experiments on three public datasets demonstrate the superiority of NTCF.
A034SHORTSequential Modality Dropout for Robust Multi-Modal Sequential Recommendation
Guanqun Yang (Stevens Institute of Technology) · Wenlong Zhang (Stevens Institute of Technology)
Abstract
Multi-modal sequential recommenders assume every item carries every modality, but real product catalogs often miss images or text, and a model trained on complete data loses much of its recommendation accuracy when a modality is unavailable at serving time. We propose Sequential Modality Dropout (SMD): during training, each modality stream (image and text) is independently erased with probability p for an entire user interaction history, so the model learns to predict the next item without relying on any single modality. We measure robustness by retention, the fraction of a model's full-modality accuracy (HR@10) that survives when a modality is removed at test time. Across four backbones (MM-SASRec, IISAN, MISSRec, and fMRLRec) on four Amazon domains, SMD raises text retention by 1.0 to 3.2× at essentially no cost to full-modality accuracy; under an extreme 95% per-item missing rate, it retains 61% of HR@10 versus 22% without (a 2.8× improvement). An optional cross-modal reconstruction loss further lifts retention from 90% to 98% on a simple additive backbone under severe text missingness. SMD is a four-line, architecture-agnostic change that makes multi-modal sequential recommenders robust to the missing modalities they actually encounter in deployment. Code: https://github.com/guanqun-yang/SMD
A035FULLMUSER: Memory-Augmented Multimodal Sequential Recommendation
Ziyi Cao (Beihang University) · Rui Liu (Beihang University) · Jiajun Lin (Beihang University) · Yi Gu (Midea AI Research Center) · Yong Chen (Beijing University of Posts and Telecommunications) · Dell Zhang (Institute of Artificial Intelligence (TeleAI), China Telecom)
Abstract
Multimodal Large Language Models offer unprecedented capabilities for sequential recommendation, yet their deployment is fundamentally bottlenecked by the conflict between finite context windows and unbounded interaction histories. Existing methods typically compress multimodal behaviors into textual summaries, inevitably precipitating semantic degradation and interest homogenization. To resolve this, we propose MUSER, a Memory-augmented framework for mUltimodal SEquential Recommendation, built upon a collaborative dual-agent architecture. Specifically, a User Agent maintains a parametric memory via structured input, forget, and rerank operations, guided by a dynamic personality parameter and an Isomorphic Consistency Planning mechanism to ensure long-term preference stability. Concurrently, a Recommendation Agent leverages this stateful memory under a decision-reason bi-objective scheme to jointly optimize recommendation accuracy and high-fidelity textual explanations. Extensive experiments on three real-world benchmarks demonstrate that MUSER significantly outperforms state-of-the-art (SoTA) baselines.
A036APPLIEDMUSE: A Simple Yet Effective Multimodal Search-Based Framework for Lifelong User Interest Modeling
Bin Wu (Wuhan University) · Feifan Yang (Taobao & Tmall Group of Alibaba) · Zhangming Chan (Taobao & Tmall Group of Alibaba) · Yu-Ran Gu (Taobao & Tmall Group of Alibaba) · Jiawei Feng (Taobao & Tmall Group of Alibaba) · Chao Yi (Taobao & Tmall Group of Alibaba) · Xiang-Rong Sheng (Taobao & Tmall Group of Alibaba) · Han Zhu (Taobao & Tmall Group of Alibaba) · Jian Xu (Taobao & Tmall Group of Alibaba) · Mang Ye (Wuhan University) · Bo Zheng (Taobao & Tmall Group of Alibaba)
Abstract
Lifelong user interest modeling is crucial for industrial recommender systems, yet existing approaches rely predominantly on ID-based features, suffering from poor generalization on long-tail items and limited semantic expressiveness. While recent work explores multimodal representations for behavior retrieval in the General Search Unit (GSU), they often neglect multimodal integration in the fine-grained modeling stage—the Exact Search Unit (ESU). In this work, we present a systematic analysis of how to effectively leverage multimodal signals across both stages of the two-stage lifelong modeling framework. Our key insight is that simplicity suffices in the GSU: lightweight cosine similarity with high-quality multimodal embeddings outperforms complex retrieval mechanisms. In contrast, the ESU demands richer multimodal sequence modeling and effective ID-multimodal fusion to unlock its full potential. Guided by these principles, we propose MUSE, a simple yet effective multimodal search-based framework. MUSE has been deployed in Taobao display advertising system, enabling 100K-length user behavior sequence modeling and delivering significant gains in top-line metrics with negligible online latency overhead. To foster community research, we share industrial deployment practices and open-source the first large-scale dataset featuring ultra-long behavior sequences paired with high-quality multimodal embeddings. Our code and dataset are available at https://taobao-mm.github.io.
A037SHORTAdaptive Preference Allocation and Semantic Hard-Negative Supervision for Multimodal Recommendation
Jicheng Sun (Nanjing University of Aeronautics and Astronautics) · Shuai Xu (Nanjing University of Aeronautics and Astronautics) · Jianqiu Xu (Nanjing University of Aeronautics and Astronautics) · Donghai Guan (Nanjing University of Aeronautics and Astronautics)
Abstract
Multimodal recommendation enhances user preference modeling by leveraging visual and textual content. However, existing methods generally adopt a unified modality fusion strategy, making it difficult to capture users’ diverse reliance on visual and textual signals. Meanwhile, random negative sampling provides limited ranking supervision and is insufficient for modeling fine-grained preference boundaries. To address these issues, we propose an Adaptive Preference allocation and Semantic Negative supervision framework called APSN, which explicitly models personalized preferences through user-level modality contribution allocation, thereby learning more fine-grained multimodal user representations. To enhance ranking supervision, APSN samples informative semantic negatives from dynamically constructed user communities, guiding the model to better capture users’ preference boundaries. In addition, APSN improves feature robustness via masked semantic consistency and complements local structural information through a sparse collaborative view. Experimental results on multiple public datasets demonstrate that APSN can achieve consistent and effective improvements in recommendation performance. Code is available at https://github.com/jcs12123/APSN.
A038SHORTSeeing Double? Multimodal Duplicate Detection for Recommendation Lists in Fashion E-Commerce
David Lapuník (Czech Technical University in Prague) · Čeněk Žid (Czech Technical University in Prague) · Antonín Hoskovec (Czech Technical University in Prague) · Rodrigo Alves (Czech Technical University in Prague) · Pavel Kordik (Czech Technical University in Prague)
Abstract
Duplicate products frequently appear in fashion e-commerce recommendation lists because the same item may be offered by multiple vendors with inconsistent product information. This paper introduces recommendation-list validation as a multimodal duplicate-detection task and presents a scalable and interpretable framework that combines visual, textual, and metadata signals through attention-based representation learning and pairwise classification. We also release the first large-scale public benchmark for list-level fashion product deduplication, comprising more than 1 million products and 800,000 validation instances. The experimental results demonstrate substantial improvements over existing baselines.
A039FULLNeutralizing Popularity Bias in LLM-based Recommendation via Counterfactual Reasoning Guidelines
Guanrong Li (Nanjing University) · Haolin Yang (Nanjing University) · Xinyu Liu (Nanjing University) · Zhen Wu (Nanjing University) · Rui Xia (Nanjing University) · Xinyu Dai (Nanjing University)
Abstract
In the era of generative AI, recommender systems are moving from precise prediction to trustworthy generation. Large language models (LLMs) support this shift by inferring user interests and producing natural-language explanations. However, LLM-based recommendation suffers from a fundamental obstacle: popularity bias. Pre-training on massive corpora, LLMs tend to rely on global statistics and trend signals, yielding recommendations that follow popularity rather than genuine preference. As this bias is entangled in model parameters and is hard to remove directly, we propose Neutralizing Popularity Bias in LLM-based Recommendation via Counterfactual Reasoning Guidelines (NPRec), a model-agnostic framework that mitigates popularity bias through external semantic intervention. NPRec performs counterfactual refinement to causally separate intrinsic user interests from popularity-driven conformity, producing debiased textual guidelines that reflect actual user preferences. These guidelines are injected at inference time to shift the LLM from unconstrained generation to guided reasoning, without any parameter updates. Serving as explicit premises, they both ground faithful explanations and improve recommendation quality. Extensive experiments on three real-world datasets demonstrate that NPRec achieves promising performance in recommendation accuracy, explanation quality and debiasing capability.
A040FULLMitigating Popularity Bias in Sequential Recommendations with Sparse Prior-Regularized Objective
Anton Pembek (Sber AI Lab) · Anton Klenitskiy (Sber AI Lab) · Alexander Savchenko (Lomonosov Moscow State University (MSU)) · Alexey Vasilev (Sber AI Lab)
Abstract
Popularity bias is a well-known challenge in recommender systems, often leading to the over-exposure of popular items and reduced catalog coverage. In this work, we propose PR-entmax, a sparse prior-regularized objective that makes popularity correction context-dependent. We derive our method from a generalized variational principle in which an item popularity prior is incorporated directly into a sparse probability mapping, yielding a popularity-aware active support: the set of items receiving non-zero probabilities and hence non-zero gradients is determined jointly by contextual relevance and item popularity. As a result, the prior affects not only item probabilities, but also which items participate in gradient updates during training. The method requires no architectural changes and can be integrated into existing training pipelines by modifying only the loss function. At inference time, the prior term is removed, and items are ranked by the learned contextual relevance alone. Experiments across multiple benchmark datasets and sequential recommendation architectures show that PR-entmax consistently reduces popularity bias while preserving or improving recommendation relevance, advancing the relevance-debiasing trade-off.
A041FULLNear In-Distribution Watermarking for Recommender Systems
Weier Bao (Shenzhen University) · Lei Li (Shenzhen University)
Abstract
Recommender systems constitute valuable intellectual property for modern platforms, driving the need for reliable ownership protection. Existing out-of-distribution (OOD) memorization-based watermarking methods for sequential recommendation preserve recommendation utility by constructing watermark sequences outside natural interaction patterns. However, this separation can introduce detectable behavioral deviations that expose new vulnerabilities under black-box deployment. We identify two such inconsistencies– distributional and trajectory inconsistency–and propose a unified inference-time attack framework that exploits them via lightweight output suppression, requiring neither retraining nor parameter modification. To mitigate these vulnerabilities while preserving watermark verifiability, we propose Near In-Distribution Watermarking (NIDW), which shifts watermark construction from extreme OOD patterns toward a controlled near-ID region. NIDW comprises three components: (1) seed prefix initialization from real user sequences, (2) near-ID sampling guided by a popularity prior and semantic smoothing, and (3) progressive multi-stage training with a lightweight OOD-retention constraint. Experiments demonstrate that the proposed attacks substantially degrade existing OOD watermarks, while NIDW maintains competitive recommendation utility and achieves improved robustness against inference-time attacks, distillation, and fine-tuning. Our code is available at https://github.com/powell4322/NIDW.
A042FULLThe Role of User-Item Connectivity in CTR Prediction
Zhongyu Ouyang (Dartmouth College) · Chunhui Zhang (Dartmouth College) · Xingjian Diao (Dartmouth College) · Yijun Tian (University of Notre Dame) · Soroush Vosoughi (Dartmouth College)
Abstract
Click-through rate (CTR) prediction is a central problem in recommendation systems. Modern CTR models are largely feature-centric. They encode users, items, and contextual variables as independent feature fields, even though the same training data also define a user-item interaction graph. Graph-based methods can exploit this structure, but less is known about the role of connectivity itself. These efforts do not ask why connectivity helps, when it produces reliable gains, and which user groups receive them. This paper studies user-item connectivity as the object of analysis rather than as another architectural component. We use a deliberately minimal message-passing (MP) operator as a controlled intervention that enriches user and item representations with graph-based information while leaving the CTR architecture unchanged. We first show that MP smooths learned representations over the interaction graph and reduces sensitivity to small input perturbations, with stronger effects for nodes with more observed interactions. Experiments across datasets with different interaction densities show that connectivity is not uniformly beneficial. Denser graphs produce more consistent gains, while sparse graphs benefit less consistently. We further find that connectivity-aware embeddings can be efficiently integrated by fine-tuning existing CTR models. Finally, we introduce the Marginal Cost of Improvement (MCI), which measures the effective effort associated with improving each user group. Across our experiments, MP shifts more predictive improvement toward under-served user groups, leading to a more balanced distribution of predictive performance.
A043SHORTPGBid: Platform-Wide Generative Auto-Bidding via Macro-Micro Decoupling
Yinqiu Huang (Meituan) · Xue Wei (Meituan) · Wenshuai Chen (Meituan) · Shuli Wang (Meituan) · Junwei Yin (Meituan) · Changhao Li (Meituan) · Yinhua Zhu (Meituan) · Haitao Wang (Meituan) · Xingxing Wang (Meituan)
Abstract
Automated bidding in Demand-Side Platforms (DSPs) aims to maximize overall value while satisfying diverse advertiser constraints. However, scaling to practical deployments reveals two structural challenges: cross-granularity constraint conflicts between advertiser-level decisions and business-line KPIs, and bid homogenization under first-price auctions that erodes platform surplus. Existing single-advertiser AI Generative Bidding (AIGB) methods fundamentally fail to address these platform-wide issues. We propose PGBid (Platform-Wide Generative Auto-Bidding), a macro-micro decoupled framework. At the macro level, a Strategist uses convex optimization to decompose global constraints into per-advertiser targets. At the micro level, a Tactician combines a conditional diffusion model with a distribution-aware inverse dynamics model to translate these targets into bidding distributions for fine-grained bid shading. Extensive offline experiments and large-scale online A/B testing demonstrate that PGBid significantly outperforms state-of-the-art baselines. Moreover, PGBid has been fully deployed on our DSP platform, reliably processing billions of bid requests daily.
A044APPLIEDSequential Multimodal Evidence Optimization for Product Media Ranking in E-Commerce
Prasenjit Dey (Amazon.com Inc.) · Frank McIntyre (Amazon.com Inc.) · Arnab Sinha (Amazon.com Inc.)
Abstract
On modern e-commerce stores, customers consume ordered slates of heterogeneous product media—such as images, videos, and 3D renders—before making purchase decisions. Existing media-ranking systems often optimize myopic engagement proxies such as clicks or dwell time, even though product media assets are cooperative informational components of the same item that together help customers find the information they need through sequential interaction. We present Sequential Multimodal Evidence Optimization (SMEO), a two-stage utility-guided framework for customer-oriented media sequencing. SMEO first learns a trajectory utility model from consumed media prefixes to estimate how ordered evidence helps customers reach a purchase decision, while mitigating position-bias and variable-depth imbalance in logged data. Recognizing that customer attention is a limited resource, it then trains an autoregressive ranking policy with survival-weighted reward-to-go that prioritizes the most decision-relevant information early, so customers can find what they need with less effort. By decoupling utility learning from policy optimization, SMEO enables stable offline learning from biased logs and post-hoc media attribution without explicit media-level labels. Evaluated offline on large-scale e-commerce sessions using doubly robust off-policy estimation, SMEO improves estimated conversion by 5.5% and helps customers reach a purchase decision with 15% fewer swipes than existing baselines.
A045SHORTWhen Is Complex Chunking Worth It? A Multi-Objective Evaluation of Chunking Methods at Scale
Laura Caspari (University of Passau) · Kanishka Ghosh Dastidar (Interdisciplinary Transformation University) · Michael Dinzinger (University of Passau) · Jelena Mitrović (University of Passau) · Michael Granitzer (University of Passau)
Abstract
Dense retrieval is commonly evaluated on benchmarks that represent each document with a single embedding, even though real-world retrieval systems often index long documents that require chunking. In these settings, the chosen chunking method not only affects retrieval quality, but also indexing throughput, query latency, and memory usage. Prior comparisons of chunking strategies have mainly focused on retrieval performance, leaving operational trade-offs underexplored. To address these issues, we evaluate eight representative chunking strategies across two scalable corpora, three embedding models, and multiple corpus sizes, measuring both retrieval effectiveness and system-level costs. Our results show that computationally expensive methods rarely provide consistent gains over simpler chunking. Instead, the best performing strategy depends on the embedding model, dataset, corpus size, and target retrieval metric. Methods with similar performance can also differ substantially in operational cost, showing that chunking should be seen as a multi-objective design decision. Our code and datasets are available on GitHub (https://github.com/casparil/chunking-eval) and Hugging Face (https://huggingface.co/datasets/PaDaS-Lab/kilt-nq) (https://huggingface.co/datasets/PaDaS-Lab/CoRE).
A046SHORTSentence Operators: Second-Order Representations for Retrieval
Panagiotis Papadakos (FORTH-ICS)
Abstract
Sentence embedding models typically compress contextual token states into a single vector and compare texts with cosine similarity. We study a second-order alternative that represents each sentence as a trace-normalized positive semidefinite (PSD) operator over normalized token directions, preserving geometry discarded by pooling. We compare mean-pooled cosine with full-operator similarities and two low-rank eigenspace scores, computed through token Gram matrices without forming dense d × d operators. We also fine-tune encoders on MS MARCO using contrastive objectives defined by these similarities. Across multiple encoder families and MTEB retrieval tasks, normalized and low-rank scores expose retrieval-relevant structure beyond pooled cosine. Unnormalized Hilbert–Schmidt overlap is generally weaker, while low-rank subspace comparison produces the strongest gains for BERT-based encoders. On frozen bert-base-cased, which lacks sentence-level training, the best projection score more than doubles average retrieval quality. The gains shrink or disappear for backbones already optimized for retrieval, indicating that the value of sentence operators is backbone-dependent. Overall, sentence operators provide a scoring and diagnostic framework for identifying when retrieval benefits from multi-directional token-state structure.
A047SHORTSeek: Self-Evaluative Exploration for Knowledge Retrieval
Amin Bigdeli (University of Waterloo) · Radin Hamidi Rad (Mila – Quebec AI Institute) · Negar Arabzadeh (University of California, Berkeley) · Sajad Ebrahimi (University of Toronto) · Hai Son Le (Toronto Metropolitan University) · Charles Clarke (University of Waterloo) · Ebrahim Bagheri (University of Toronto)
Abstract
Large Language Model (LLM)-based retrievers and rerankers have advanced passage ranking, yet both paradigms interact with the corpus in a single pass and commit to the resulting candidate set, leaving relevant documents permanently unrecoverable once missed. We introduce Seek, Self-Evaluative Exploration for Knowledge Retrieval), a training-free framework that addresses this limitation through iterative corpus interaction at test time. At each round, an LLM generates pseudo-passages conditioned on accumulated relevance feedback, a retriever surfaces fresh candidates, and a dedicated assessor assigns graded relevance judgments that guide subsequent rounds. On TREC Deep Learning, Seek matches trained rerankers in ranking quality while consistently improving Recall@100 over single-pass BM25. On the reasoning-intensive BRIGHT benchmark, Seek with Qwen2.5-7B achieves an 82% relative gain over BM25, surpassing all trained baselines, and Seek with GPT-4.1 reaches 37.4 average nDCG@10, exceeding the strongest baseline by 37%. We make our code, prompts, and data publicly available at https://github.com/aminbigdeli/SEEK.
A048SHORTReasoning About Query Difficulty to Predict Retrieval Effectiveness
Seyed Mohammad Hosseini (Toronto Metropolitan University) · Negar Arabzadeh (University of California, Berkeley) · Morteza Zihayat (Toronto Metropolitan University) · Ebrahim Bagheri (University of Toronto)
Abstract
Pre-retrieval query performance prediction methods estimate the effectiveness of a query prior to retrieval and enable control of the search pipeline through tasks such as query routing, selective expansion, and retriever selection. However, because they operate solely on query features without access to retrieved documents, pre-retrieval predictors often struggle to provide accurate predictions. They typically treat query difficulty as a latent statistical property rather than one that can be reasoned about. We propose a new pre-retrieval framework that leverages the reasoning capabilities of large language models (LLMs) to uncover and encode interpretable reasons of query difficulty. By integrating these reasons with transformer-based neural regressors, our approach allows the predictor to be both aware of and conditioned on reasons that make a query challenging. Our experiments on MS MARCO Dev, TREC DL 2019, TREC DL 2020, and DL-Hard demonstrate that our method consistently achieves reliable and stable correlations across various TREC DL datasets. Our code, models, and difficulty reason annotations are made publicly available at https://github.com/ls3-lab/draq.
A049FULLH2CE: Modeling Geo-Semantic Interactions for POI Reranking with Heterogeneous Two-Stage Cross-Encoders
Zhengwei Bai (Amazon) · Moreno D'Incà (University of Trento) · Alessandro Moschitti (Amazon) · Danielle Class (Amazon)
Abstract
Point-of-Interest (POI) reranking in local search must model query-conditioned tradeoffs among lexical semantics, geospatial proximity, and numerical quality signals such as rating and review count, while remaining practical under real-time serving constraints. A close POI may only partially satisfy the query intent, while a farther one may offer stronger semantic and quality evidence. We present H2CE, a Heterogeneous Two-stage Cross-Encoder for latency-bounded POI reranking. H2CE represents numerical attributes in two complementary ways: bucketized natural-language descriptors are inserted into the cross-encoder input to support semantic–numeric attention, while exact scalar values are processed by dedicated MLPs to preserve magnitude information. The resulting semantic and numerical embeddings are fused through latent-space aggregation, enabling nonlinear interactions beyond scalar weighted sums. H2CE then applies a two-stage architecture: Stage 1 scores all candidates pointwise for scalable filtering, and Stage 2 performs head-to-head pairwise comparison among the top-K candidates with Copeland aggregation, making fine-grained relative tradeoffs explicit while reducing pairwise cost from O(N2) to O(N+K(K-1)). On a 5,743-query local search test set, H2CE achieves 67.48% NDCG@5, improving over XGBoost LTR by +22.82% absolute and over a zero-shot LLM reranker by +35.89%. The pairwise stage adds +1.98% NDCG@5 over the pointwise model alone. Ablations confirm the value of numerical features, latent aggregation, top-K pairwise reranking, and aligned training.
A050SHORTThe Plug-and-Play Illusion: Cross-Encoder Brittleness to Retrieval Noise under Fixed Recall
Xiankun Lin (Sun Yat-sen University) · Lixin Liu (Tsinghua University) · Xinyi Lin (Sun Yat-sen University) · Zichao Nie (Tsinghua University) · Zhezheng Hao (Zhejiang University)
Abstract
Cross-encoder rerankers are often treated as safe, drop-in quality boosts once a first-stage retriever has recalled a candidate pool. The hidden assumption is simple: if the gold document is present, the reranker should still pick it out from whatever negatives the retriever supplies. We test that assumption with a recall-controlled stress test that keeps recall at 100% and varies only the distractor distribution. Under this protocol, a small cross-encoder's NDCG@10 falls by up to 50% when negatives shift from random documents to retriever-mined hard negatives. The collapse repeats across four rerankers spanning 4M-278M parameters and two training families, so it is not one weak model. We then ask whether zero-shot LLM rerankers fail in the same way. A listwise language-model reranker, with gpt-4o-mini as the strongest case, is less sensitive to BM25 hard negatives across three BEIR corpora, but the controls complicate the story. On nfcorpus, the advantage relies on the BM25-seeded listwise order. On fiqa and scifact, it survives pointwise scoring and shuffled-order controls, indicating intrinsic model robustness. Dense hard negatives still hurt all rerankers. The conclusion is therefore not that "LLMs are robust," but that negative distributions are part of the retriever-reranker interface and should be checked before deployment. We end with a no-new-label diagnostic.
A051SHORTCost-Sensitive Listwise Optimisation for Sensitivity-Aware Search
Jack McKechnie (University of Glasgow) · Graham McDonald (University of Glasgow) · Craig Macdonald (University of Glasgow)
Abstract
In typical search tasks, the goal is to return a list of k documents that are ordered by their relevance to a user-issued query. However, not all information that is contained in a collection should be made available to users, i.e., sensitive information should not be revealed. Sensitivity-Aware Search (SAS) is a bi-objective retrieval task that aims to make collections that potentially contain sensitive information safely searchable by producing a ranked list of documents that are (1) relevant to the query and (2) non-sensitive. Previous work on SAS leveraged pointwise relevance-only loss functions in combination with SAS-specific negative sampling techniques. We argue that modelling SAS in a pointwise manner at training time limits how effectively the task can be expressed to the model. Hence, we investigate listwise loss functions for SAS. Further, we propose a sensitivity-aware listwise distillation loss function that penalises the model for highly ranking sensitive documents during training. We perform experiments on two test collections labelled for relevance and different types of sensitivity, and observe that listwise loss functions outperform pointwise and pairwise losses, retrieving up to 58% fewer sensitive documents. Our proposed sensitivity-aware listwise distillation loss function outperforms a relevance-only listwise loss function by 12% and a pointwise loss function leveraging SAS training data by 15% in relevance-sensitivity tradeoff metrics. We release model checkpoints with PyTerrier integrations on HuggingFace.
A052FULLBeyond Exposure: Dynamic Income-Fair Ranking under Time-Varying Provider Value
Xuancheng Li (Tsinghua University) · Tao Yang (Amazon) · Yujia Zhou (Tsinghua University) · Yiqun Liu (Tsinghua University) · Qingyao Ai (Quancheng Laboratory)
Abstract
Ranking systems in web search and recommendation must balance relevance-based effectiveness with fairness for item providers. Exposure Fairness seeks to allocate position-induced attention according to item merit, but exposure is only an intermediate signal whose conversion into provider utility varies with context. We therefore define income as the context-dependent provider utility induced by exposure. We formalize Income Fairness, which requires cumulative provider income to be proportional to relevance, and develop a corresponding metric based on a context-dependent unit-income function. We propose DIDRF (Dynamic-Income-Derivative-aware Ranking Fairness), which exploits the quadratic structure of income-fairness violations to derive a prefix-aware, state-calibrated scoring rule that balances effectiveness and income fairness. Experiments on standard learning-to-rank datasets in semi-synthetic income environments calibrated from real advertising and e-commerce logs show that DIDRF achieves lower income unfairness than representative fair-ranking baselines while maintaining competitive effectiveness.
A053APPLIEDPersonalized Quality-Aware Reranking for Long-Term User Retention in E-commerce
Siddhant Doshi (Meesho) · Krish Rupapara (Meesho) · Bhavuk Singhal (Meesho) · Abhay Shukla (Meesho) · Ravindra Kumar Yadav (Meesho) · Debdoot Mukherjee (Meesho)
Abstract
Modern recommendation systems are predominantly optimized for short-term engagement signals such as Click-Through Rate (CTR) and Conversion Rate (CVR), often overlooking post-purchase user satisfaction. As a result, ranking systems can repeatedly promote products that drive immediate interactions but lead to poor user experiences and long-term dissatisfaction. We address this gap through a personalized quality-aware reranking framework that explicitly incorporates product quality into the ranking objective. We adopt the Net Quality Detractor (NQD) ratio, the fraction of 1–2 star post-purchase ratings, as a direct measure of severe dissatisfaction that average rating alone cannot capture. Building on this signal, we propose a dual-model architecture: Personalized NQD (PNQD), which estimates user-specific dissatisfaction risk for a user–product pair, and Retention-Driven Alpha (RDA), which adaptively controls the strength of the quality penalty based on a user's historical experience and predicted retention. Offline experiments show that PNQD captures user-level quality preferences beyond product-level signals, while large-scale online A/B experiments demonstrate a 0.48% reduction in realized post-purchase NQD and 0.47% Net Merchandise Value (NMV) uplift over a non-personalized quality baseline, with neutral impact on engagement. The system is fully deployed, serving approximately 200 million monthly active users.
A054FULLOne Metric Does Not Fit All: How Platform Type Shapes the Validity of Online Evaluation Metrics in Conversational Search
Fengxuan Lv (Wuhan University) · Yuhan Wang (Wuhan University) · Jingjing Chen (Wuhan University) · Huiyang Zhang (Wuhan University) · Fan Zhang (Wuhan University)
Abstract
The shift from traditional web search to conversational search has introduced new challenges for online evaluation. While prior work has begun to rethink evaluation for conversational search systems, the role of platform type remains underexplored. This study investigates how metric-satisfaction relationships differ between a generation-centric platform (ChatGPT) and a retrieval-centric platform (Perplexity) in conversational search. We categorize online evaluation metrics for conversational search into two categories: traditional metrics adapted to conversational contexts, and novel metrics designed specifically for conversational interactions. Through a controlled user study with 72 valid participants, we collect fine-grained interaction logs and post-task satisfaction ratings. Our results show that user behavior and the predictive power of online metrics for satisfaction differ significantly across the two platforms. Notably, novel conversational metrics exhibit stronger predictive power on generation-centric platforms, while adapted traditional metrics remain effective on retrieval-centric ones. Qualitative interviews further reveal underlying mechanisms: divergent cognitive load, verification strategies, and perceived efficiency are reflected in these cross-platform differences. Our findings highlight the necessity of context-aware evaluation frameworks tailored to platform characteristics, although the findings are based on two specific platforms and should be generalised with caution.
A055SHORTPMC: Build-Time Per-Modality Centroid Correction for Cross-Modal Binary-Quantized Retrieval
Se Hoon Kim (Korea University) · Jun Hyung Lee (Korea University) · Soonyoung Jung (Korea University)
Abstract
Approximate nearest neighbor search is a core operator in large-scale retrieval, where vector quantization is widely used to reduce memory cost. Binary quantization methods encode each dimension as a single bit, but they assume queries and database vectors share a common centroid. This assumption fails in cross-modal retrieval, where each modality clusters around a different centroid, producing a modality gap that corrupts the centroid's dual role as inverted-file routing pivot and sign-bit decision boundary. We propose Per-Modality Centroid Correction (PMC), which shifts database vectors toward the query centroid at build time, rewriting routing and code boundaries at the source rather than merely adjusting queries at serving time. A selective variant confirms that concentrated gap energy in a few dimensions drives most recall loss. PMC adds no index memory or serving overhead; at ?=1, the correction is fully absorbed into the index with zero query-time cost. Experiments on five cross-modal benchmarks, three encoders, and four binary-quantized index types show gains over uncorrected and query-shifted baselines that scale with modality-gap magnitude, up to a 400M-vector deployment. Code: https://github.com/sehoon787/PMC.
A056SHORTRecovering Graph ANN Search on Attention-Derived Workloads via a Query-Agnostic Spherical Transformation
David Procházka (Faculty of Informatics, Masaryk University) · Vlastislav Dohnal (Faculty of Informatics, Masaryk University) · Martin Aumüller (IT University of Copenhagen)
Abstract
Graph-based indexes such as HNSW are widely used for approximate nearest neighbor (ANN) search due to their strong empirical performance. Prior work (Morozov and Babenko, NeurIPS 2018) suggests that these methods remain effective even for non-metric maximum inner product search (MIPS). We show that this assumption fails for the attention-derived embeddings from modern large language models available in the recent VIBE benchmark. We trace the failure to HNSW's neighbor-selection heuristic, which prunes almost every candidate at build time and yields graphs too sparse to effectively support greedy descent. As a remedy we revisit an index-agnostic transformation that maps the database onto the unit hypersphere while preserving the inner-product ranking, without any knowledge of the query distribution. The transformation restores the assumed geometry of the datasets and raises HNSW recall above 95%. Moreover, a query-agnostic adaption of the query-aware index RoarGraph (Chen et al., VLDB 2024) stays below 40% recall. This means that RoarGraph's strong performance needs access to the query sample rather than purely relying on its bipartite graph construction.
A057SHORTCoALANN: Cross-Query Node-Fetch Coalescing for Batched Full-Precision Disk ANN Search
Hyeonbyeong Lee (Mokpo National University) · Sanghyeuk Kim (Chungbuk National University) · Wooje Sung (Chungbuk National University) · Sangho Song (Chungbuk National University) · Dojin Choi (Changwon National University) · Kyoungsoo Bok (Wonkwang University) · Jaesoo Yoo (Chungbuk National University)
Abstract
Concurrent approximate nearest-neighbor (ANN) queries over full-precision, disk-resident indexes often traverse overlapping graph regions, yet batched runtime paths can issue duplicate logical node-fetch requests independently. We study this redundancy in Vamana-style search and propose CoALANN, a traversal-round coalescer that synchronizes a batch of beam searches at bounded traversal rounds, deduplicates pending requests for the same node record, issues one deduplicated batched request set through io_uring (the Linux asynchronous I/O interface), and shares completed reads with all requesting queries. In the n = 20 headline paired runs at B = 64 across four ANN datasets (SIFT1M, DEEP1M, DEEP10M, and LastFM64) under an NVMe OS page-cache-cold stress protocol, duplicate logical node-fetch submissions account for 40.4–55.2% of requests. Relative to the same round-synchronized, batched io_uring harness with only cross-query deduplication disabled, CoALANN improves QPS by 1.09–1.35×, with identical Recall@10 in the paired runs. CoALANN leaves the index unchanged and reads full float32 vectors.
A058SHORTSurrogate Inverse-Variance Weighting for Intervention Harvesting on Heavy-Tailed Click Logs
Alessandro Magnani (Coupang) · Min Xie (Coupang)
Abstract
Under the Position-Based Model (PBM), the probability that a user clicks a document d shown for query q at position k factorises as p_k * rq,d, where p_k is the position examination probability and rq,d is the query–document relevance. Intervention harvesting estimates the ratio p_k/pk' from naturally occurring ranking variation by aggregating per-cell click-rate ratios over (q,d) cells. On real logs, cell impression counts are extremely heavy-tailed: on the full KDD Cup 2012 Track 2 log, 60% of interventional pairs have at most five impressions while 0.1% of pairs account for 42% of all impressions. The weighting of cells is therefore central to finite-sample efficiency. We study count-only weighting schemes for intervention harvesting. Beyond the uniform weighting of Agarwal et al., we propose two new count-only weights: the min-count weight omega_i = min(N_k^i, Nk'^i) and the harmonic weight omega_i = N_k^i Nk'^i / (N_k^i + Nk'^i), where N_k^i is the number of impressions of cell i at position k. The harmonic weight arises from an inverse-variance approximation to per-cell click-rate differences under PBM: after replacing the relevance-dependent variance terms with a common factor, the resulting count-only surrogate variance is minimised by harmonic weighting. A Cauchy–Schwarz argument shows that harmonic improves this surrogate variance over uniform aggregation for any impression counts. We evaluate finite-sample efficiency via the closed-form delta-method asymptotic variance of the weighted ratio estimator. On the full KDD log, harmonic weighting achieves a 4.5x asymptotic relative efficiency improvement over uniform and remains robust under weight capping. Synthetic and Yahoo-LTR semi-synthetic experiments with ground truth corroborate the prediction, with up to 54% variance reduction under high imbalance. We also make explicit an estimand caveat: under PBM mis-specification, different weights target different weighted averages of cell-specific ratios. Overall, harmonic weighting offers a simple count-only replacement for uniform intervention harvesting with a count-only surrogate-variance guarantee and consistent empirical gains; min and harmonic perform comparably, with harmonic preferred for its theoretical justification.
A059SHORTBetter Together: Human-LLM Pairs for Reliable System Rankings
Jina Lee (Waseda University) · Tetsuya Sakai (Waseda University) · Young-In Song (Naver Corporation)
Abstract
We consider the problem of assigning two bronze (i.e. "non-topic-creator") assessors per topic for constructing an IR test collection, where the quality of human assessors is unknown. Given the advent of LLM-as-a-judge strategies in IR evaluation, replacing one or both of the human assessors with an LLM certainly seems appealing. But which is the best assessor pairing strategy for the purpose of obtaining an effective system ranking that represents a collective view of human assessors? To address this question, we leverage a unique existing web search test collection whose relevance assessments were contributed by a total of 24 assessors. The collection consists of non-overlapping subcollections, each with over 50 topics. For each subcollection, our target system ranking reflects the collective view of eight assessors. We then form all possible pairs from a pool of 12—comprising the original eight assessors plus four LLMs—and evaluate how well each pair's generated ranking approximates the target ranking with only two assessors. Across the three subcollections, the best performing pair type is Human-Human (H-H), but the Human-LLM (H-LLM) pair is only 0.009 Kendall's (τ) behind on average. Two One-Sided Tests (TOST) further show that H-LLM pairs are practically equivalent to H-H pairs under a pre-defined margin. Furthermore, H-H pairs are not uniformly strong, as human assessors have larger performance variance and can occasionally underperform H-LLM pairs when a reliable LLM is used. When Llama 4—which produced output format errors during label generation—is excluded, H-LLM pairs surpass H-H on average. Our results suggest that pairing one human with a reliable LLM can closely approximate the collective view of the eight assessors for ranking systems.
A060SHORTModeling Uncertainty in LLM-Based Information Retrieval Evaluation via Hierarchical Bayesian Models
Simone Merlo (University of Padua) · Guglielmo Faggioli (University of Padua) · Stefano Marchesin (University of Padua) · Giorgio Maria Di Nunzio (University of Padua) · Nicola Ferro (University of Padua)
Abstract
Large Language Models (LLMs) are increasingly used in Information Retrieval (IR) evaluation to annotate query-document pairs for relevance, enabling significant cost reductions compared to the traditional human-only assessment process. However, LLM-generated human judgements are not error-free and, compared to humans, are more prone to introducing systematic latent biases and producing spurious results. Therefore, since the evaluation target remains the human, it is necessary to understand how to align observations derived from LLM-generated annotations with those that would have been made using human relevance judgments. This work introduces a novel framework for estimating the performance we would observe if relevance judgements were human-made, using a large amount of LLM-generated judgments with a limited pool of human-annotated queries. The proposed approach exploits hierarchical Bayesian modeling and calibration to build Credible Intervals (CrIs) providing statistical guarantees on the estimated performance.
