The obtained results show how the computed CrIs allow (a) over 95% coverage while exploiting a limited number of human annotations and (b) to jointly take into account the LLM error and the variance due to topics, enabling future use of the computed CrIs for statistical hypothesis testing.
A061RESOURCECoverage Under Contradiction: A Benchmark for Negation-Aware Retrieval
Pasha Abrishamchian (Georgetown University) · Eugene Yang (Johns Hopkins University) · Andrew Yates (Johns Hopkins University) · Nazli Goharian (Georgetown University) · Ophir Frieder (Georgetown University)
Abstract
Coverage-evaluation benchmarks quantify whether retrieved evidence covers the different pieces of information needed to satisfy an information need. Existing benchmarks mostly consider factual claims that may already be known to pretrained retrieval components, leaving open whether retrievers find corpus evidence when it contradicts those priors. We study how retrievers behave when their parametric knowledge and the information in a corpus disagrees. To do so, we develop a process to augment a nugget-based coverage benchmark with controlled contradictions. For each nugget, we create a negated counterpart and edit its supporting documents to support that negation while preserving the context. Applying this process to CoverageBench, a benchmark measuring information coverage, we create CoverageBench-Negate, spanning six datasets and roughly 63,000 original-edited evidence pairs (one per nugget-document link). We attach rich construction metadata to every pair and additionally provide out-of-family LLM judgments over all pairs and a human audit of a sample. In baseline experiments, BM25 separates original from edited near-twin evidence substantially better than dense retrievers (Qwen3 and Jina), which stay near chance. We release the benchmark on Hugging Face Datasets (nuggets, documents, pairs) together with the construction materials, including the prompts used to create it.
A062FULLCoVer-CIR: Constraint-Aware Retrieval Calibration and Self-Verification for Zero-Shot Composed Image Retrieval
Jingjing Zhang (University of Science and Technology of China) · Lei Zhang (University of Science and Technology of China) · Jiawei Huang (University of Science and Technology of China) · Bo Hu (University of Science and Technology of China) · Zhendong Mao (University of Science and Technology of China)
Abstract
Zero-shot composed image retrieval aims to retrieve a target image given a reference image and a modification instruction, without task-specific annotated triplets. Existing methods typically conflate the multimodal query into a single textual query, leveraging VLMs such as CLIP to rank candidates by overall similarity. However, this conflated representation is insufficient for CIR, where the instruction specifies multiple edit constraints relative to the reference image, such as preserving certain visual content while adding, removing, or replacing others. This makes it difficult to distinguish hard negatives that are globally plausible but violate a decisive edit constraint, especially when the violation is local and subtle. To address this limitation, we propose CoVer-CIR, a training-free framework that progressively turns edit constraints into ranking evidence. It first makes the edit constraints explicit by deriving a positive target, negative constraints, and contrastive pairs from the query. During retrieval, CoVer-CIR calibrates retrieval scores with adaptive negative penalties estimated from images favored by the positive target, producing a cleaner Top-\(K\) candidate set. For re-ranking, instead of using an expensive candidate-level verifier, CoVer-CIR performs lightweight pairwise verification with the contrastive pairs. Each pair compares a required local condition with a confusing alternative, and the resulting relative margin provides local evidence for the edit constraints. Experiments on CIRCO, CIRR, and FashionIQ show strong performance across CLIP backbones, especially in top-ranked retrieval results.
A063SHORTRemote Sensing Image-Text Retrieval via Hierarchical and Targeting Semantic Alignment
Bo Li (Guilin University of Aerospace Technology) · Xiao Zhang (Northwestern Polytechnical University) · Xing Wei (Guilin University of Aerospace Technology) · Jingyi Yan (Guilin Institute of Information Technology) · Qinghui Hu (Guilin University of Aerospace Technology) · Zhixin Li (Guangxi Normal University)
Abstract
Remote sensing image-text retrieval (RSITR) can facilitate visual language mining in spatial scenarios, which holds significant importance for aviation and aerospace applications. Existing RSITR methods often lack joint coarse-grained and fine-grained alignment, or their unified learning strategies are inefficient. Additionally, there is no analysis of remote sensing characteristics in these fine-grained feature learning. To address these issues, this paper proposes Hierarchical and Targeting Semantic Alignment (HTSA) for remote sensing image-text retrieval, which simultaneously considers the construction of global and local features. In coarse-grained semantic alignment, cross-modal classification learning and inter-modal matching learning are combined. For fine-grained semantic learning, targeted semantic alignment is introduced to highlight essential objects, which are overlooked by current RSITR methods, but crucial for remote sensing scenarios. Comprehensive experiments demonstrate the superiority of the proposed framework, while different ablation studies discuss the functions of specific components.
A064FULLProcess In-Context Learning: Confusion-Aware Demonstration Retrieval and Dynamic Insertion for Mathematical Reasoning
Ang Gao (Renmin University of China) · Changshuo Zhang (Renmin University of China) · Xiao Zhang (Renmin University of China) · Deyang Li (Huawei Poisson Lab) · Minjun Zhao (Huawei Poisson Lab) · Fangchao Liu (Huawei Poisson Lab) · Xinyu Zhang (Huawei Poisson Lab)
Abstract
In-context learning (ICL) has achieved strong results across a wide range of large language model (LLM) tasks. However, its effectiveness for problems that require step-by-step deduction, such as mathematical reasoning, is still not well understood. One major limitation of existing ICL methods is that demonstrations are chosen before inference and remain unchanged throughout reasoning. As a result, they cannot respond to confusion points that emerge during multi-step problem solving, such as uncertain calculations or missing logical transitions. When these confusion points are not resolved, they may propagate and ultimately degrade answer accuracy. To address this limitation, we propose Process In-Context Learning (PICL), a dynamic demonstration insertion framework for mathematical reasoning. PICL consists of two stages: 1) it identifies potential confusion points by analyzing semantics and entropy in the reasoning process and summarizes their core characteristics; 2) upon encountering these points, it retrieves relevant demonstrations from the demonstration pool that match the confusion context and inserts them directly into the ongoing reasoning process to guide subsequent steps. Experimental results show that PICL outperforms representative baselines by alleviating mid-process confusion, demonstrating the effectiveness of adaptive demonstration insertion for complex mathematical reasoning.
A065FULLCDAR-RAG: Cross-Distributional Alignment-Based Retriever for Online Community Jargon Understanding
Byunghwa Yoo (GIST) · Doyoung Kim (GIST) · Kyung-Joong Kim (GIST)
Abstract
Online communities often use jargon, which is a set of specialized terms that can only be understood implicitly and in context by a specific group of users. Although large language models (LLMs) have shown remarkable achievements in various tasks, understanding community jargon is challenging, as it introduces more complex, high-context comprehension. In-context learning (ICL) can help LLMs achieve better jargon understanding by providing demonstrations of jargon usage-definition pairs, yet using appropriate demonstrations is critical. However, which jargon terms are appropriate demonstrations for the given target jargon term is unclear; no true relationship between jargon terms is known. This makes typical retrieval-augmented generation (RAG) struggle to obtain appropriate demonstrations, as labeled query-document relations are often required for task-specialized RAG. For this problem, we propose CDAR (Cross-Distributional Alignment-based Retriever), a retriever training method that requires no explicit query-document relevance labels, by aligning the distribution of cosine similarities between pairs of jargon usage examples to that between their corresponding definitions. Our results show that CDAR effectively increases jargon understanding across five LLM generators of varying scales, consistently outperforming zero-shot, random, vanilla RAG, and triplet-loss baselines, and that a retriever trained on one jargon domain transfers effectively to unseen jargon domains. Notably, Qwen3 8B + CDAR significantly surpasses GPT-OSS 120B performance, showing that CDAR serves as an efficient framework, especially with smaller LLMs.
A066SHORTRankGap-RAG: Rank-Discrepancy Contrastive Feedback for Multi-Paraphrase Retrieval
Jiae Lee (Korea Institute of Energy Technology) · Seunghyun Yoon (Korea Institute of Energy Technology) · Hyuk Lim (Korea Institute of Energy Technology)
Abstract
Retrieval-Augmented Generation (RAG) is sensitive to the wording of the original query, and iterative query refinement can further amplify early retrieval errors when misleading passages are reused as feedback. We propose RankGap-RAG, a training-free query refinement framework that uses bi-encoder/cross-encoder rank discrepancy to select inference-time hard-negative feedback. Rather than treating retrieved passages as uniformly useful feedback, RankGap-RAG pairs cross-encoder-selected positive evidence with rank-gap negatives to guide the LLM toward relevant evidence while discouraging misleading semantic directions. We further introduce a Diverse Multi-Chain extension that combines contrastive feedback with multiple refinement trajectories. Experiments on SQuAD 2.0, Natural Questions, HotpotQA, 2WikiMultiHopQA, and MuSiQue show consistent gains over original-query retrieval, while component ablations on SQuAD 2.0 and Natural Questions show improvements over positive-only feedback.
A067SHORTFrom Oracle Gains to Repair Priorities: Conservative Split-Conditioned Diagnosis for Modular RAG
Chaewon Sung (Sookmyung Women's University) · Chong-Kwon Kim (Korea Institute of Energy Technology) · Yoonhyuk Choi (Sookmyung Women's University)
Abstract
Gold-evidence interventions are widely used to evaluate retrieval-augmented generation (RAG) pipelines, but they are often reduced to one average oracle gain. This aggregation mixes evidence access, context ordering, and answer-extraction failures, which can turn local evidence effects into an overinterpreted repair claim. We propose Conservative Split-Conditioned Oracle Diagnosis (CS-RAG), a compact diagnostic method that converts paired oracle traces into guarded subset-level repair priorities. CS-RAG treats each example as a bounded vector of gains from three evidence-control actions. Our method aggregates these vectors within registered splits, maps action gains to repair-label scores via a split-valid incidence map, and outputs a priority only when the support, gain, and label-margin guards all hold. On 1,500-example Natural Questions and TriviaQA diagnostic subsets, aggregate oracle probes reveal substantial headroom across stages. Preliminary repair experiments further show that retrieval repair improves both datasets, whereas conservative generation repair does not yield consistent gains. Our code is available at https://github.com/sungchaewon/rag-diagnostics.
A068SHORTRAG-X: Systematic Diagnosis of Retrieval-Augmented Generation for Medical Question Answering
Aswini Sivakumar (Oakland University) · Vijayan Sugumaran (Oakland University) · Yao Qiang (Oakland University)
Abstract
Automated question-answering (QA) systems increasingly rely on retrieval-augmented generation (RAG) to ground large language models (LLMs) in authoritative medical knowledge, ensuring clinical accuracy and patient safety in AI applications for healthcare. Despite progress in RAG evaluation, current benchmarks focus only on simple multiple-choice QA tasks and employ metrics that poorly capture the semantic precision required for complex QA tasks. These approaches fail to diagnose whether an error stems from faulty retrieval or flawed generation, limiting developers from performing targeted improvement. To address this gap, we propose RAG-X, a diagnostic framework that evaluates the retriever and generator independently across a triad of QA tasks: information extraction, short-answer generation, and multiple-choice question answering. RAG-X introduces Context Utilization Efficiency (CUE) metrics to disaggregate system success into interpretable quadrants, isolating verified grounding from deceptive accuracy. Our experiments reveal an “Accuracy Fallacy”, where a 14% gap separates perceived system success from evidence-based grounding. By surfacing hidden failure modes, RAG-X offers the diagnostic transparency needed for safe and verifiable clinical RAG systems. Our code is available at https://github.com/AswiniS94/RAG-X_Evaluation.
A069FULLA Contrastive Framework for Enhanced Automatic Attribution Evaluation Through Error Generation
Hanane Djeddal (Université Paul Sabatier, IRIT) · Karen Pinel-Sauvagnat (Université Paul Sabatier, IRIT) · Laure Soulier (Sorbonne Université, CNRS, ISIR) · Sophia Katrenko (EcoVadis) · Lynda Tamine (Université Paul Sabatier, IRIT)
Abstract
Attributed Large Language Models learn to cite supporting documents in their generated text, thus improving factuality and traceability. Research on the automatic evaluation of this capability either focuses on proposing new specialized metric-models or on defining attribution evaluation frameworks that rely on base models at a granular level, such as Natural Language Inference (NLI) models, for their implementation. While the latter have become the standard for attribution evaluation, their reliance on repurposing base models of different tasks hinders their full potential. In this work, we propose a comprehensive study that examines existing attribution evaluation solutions for a fine-grained understanding of model errors and current limitations. To achieve this, we survey existing works on attribution evaluation and construct a comprehensive taxonomy of persistent error types. We leverage this analysis to design synthetic examples that mimic error types to quantify the ability of existing models to overcome them. We additionally follow a contrastive framework and propose a new model better aligned for the attribution evaluation task that can be seamlessly integrated into existing evaluation schemes. We use two standard attribution and faithfulness evaluation benchmarks, the AttributionBench and the TRUE Benchmark, covering 18 datasets, and show that our proposed model allows for better generalization and robustness to a wide range of errors while maintaining baseline performance.
A070FULLRisk-Aware Reranking for Agentic Tool Retrieval
Qinfei Li (University of Science and Technology of China) · Xiaoxuan Dong (University of Electronic Science and Technology of China) · Jin Zhang (Lanzhou University) · Dexu Yu (Fenz.AI) · Wenhao Deng (University of Glasgow) · Junchen Fu (University of Glasgow) · Youhua Li (City University of Hong Kong) · Hanwen Du (The Ohio State University) · Chunxiao Li (University of Science and Technology of China)
Abstract
Tool retrieval determines which external tools are exposed to an LLM agent for a user query or task, making retrieval a critical pre-execution safety boundary. Unlike document retrieval, tool retrieval exposes executable actions: a tool that is useful for one task may be unnecessary or risky for another. However, existing tool-retrieval methods primarily optimize semantic relevance, and safety evaluations often focus on failures after tool execution rather than risks introduced during retrieval. We study risk-aware tool retrieval, where the goal is to retrieve useful tools while reducing exposure to higher-risk tools. We propose a lightweight reranking framework on top of a frozen first-stage retriever. The framework models query-conditioned relevance and tool-level exposure risk separately, combines them through an explicit parameter controlling the tradeoff between safety and utility, smooths scores over a ToolGraph, and optionally applies rule-based safety constraints. To support retrieval-time safety evaluation, we annotate 6,108 tools across UltraTool and Seal-Tools with five ordinal risk levels and define metrics that measure risky-tool exposure in the top-k results. Experiments on UltraTool and Seal-Tools show that our approach improves the relevance–safety tradeoff over relevance-only retrievers and reranking baselines, with the rule-filtered variant providing a conservative operating point for safety-critical deployments. These findings indicate that retrieval-stage filtering can reduce the candidate action space exposed to agents before execution, complementing downstream tool-use safeguards. The code and supplementary materials are available at: https://github.com/qli447/risk-aware-tool-retrieval-release https://github.com/qli447/risk-aware-tool-retrieval-release.
A071RESOURCEWCI: The Web Context Interface for Agentic Web Automation
Amirreza Alasti (Leibniz University Hannover) · Niloufar Ghandeharioun (Leibniz University Hannover) · Oliver Karras (TIB - Leibniz Information Centre for Science and Technology)
Abstract
Web agents struggle to interact with complex web environments designed for humans, forcing them to reverse-engineer visual and Document Object Model (DOM) structures. This discrepancy results in high token costs, hallucinated interactions, and slow runtimes, rendering reliable, large-scale web automation computationally and economically unviable. We aim to establish a machine-readable interaction layer that allows site operators to define bounded, token-efficient action spaces for web agents explicitly. We propose the Web Context Interface (WCI), a browser-native framework for agentic web automation. WCI enables site operators to expose structured interaction contracts using lightweight semantic HTML annotations and policy files, shifting web automation from a confrontational parsing paradigm to a cooperative, operator-driven ecosystem. As a comprehensive resource, we release: (1) The core WCI library, (2) An open specification for agent-directed site policies, and (3) A dataset comprising 50 multi-step task grounding scenarios across diverse web interfaces. We evaluate WCI's infrastructural utility via a static component-level grounding study across six LLMs. The WCI representations reduce token consumption by up to 8.2x. WCI also increases the success rate of target grounding from 0% on raw HTML to at least 76% for smaller open-source models, and achieves up to 96% for larger proprietary models. WCI is fully documented and open-source as an extensible foundation, lowering the economic barrier for researchers and practitioners to develop, evaluate, and deploy reproducible agentic web interaction layers at scale.
A072FULLS-VEAM: A Shared Spectral Memory for Cross-Session Retrieval in Long-Horizon LLM Agents
Jungbae Yi (Samsung Electronics) · James Geraci (Samsung Electronics)
Abstract
LLM agents in multi-session deployments must answer through a bounded prompt window while their histories grow without bound. Surfacing the right history within that budget is a retrieval and ranking problem over a state that never stops growing. We present S-VEAM, a shared spectral memory controller for long-session agents in which construction and retrieval are two phases of one persistent spectral state (P, V, ?) that unifies writing new sessions into the state and reading evidence back out. Both phases use non-generative spectral operations: the controller issues no generative-LLM call at memory-management time, and the spectral indexing rank — distinct from the retained verbatim pool — remains fixed as trajectories grow. In the tested long-session settings this yields a low-latency retrieval profile while preserving verbatim evidence for the downstream model. We evaluate S-VEAM under the Cross-Session Stress Test Protocol (CSSTP), a source-faithful evaluation over existing benchmarks with controlled long-session stress conditions. LoCoMo and LongMemEval-S provide the main long-session evidence: S-VEAM is top-ranked on both answer containment and evidence-backed answer containment on every LoCoMo cell and on LongMemEval-S native, with non-generative fixed-rank maintenance and low-latency retrieval. MuSiQue Tier 3 enters as an auxiliary multi-hop evidence-split diagnostic where S-VEAM achieves the highest evidence-backed answer containment. Stateful memory peers enter as cost-matched counterparts under the same budget and reset policy. S-VEAM thus marks a fixed-rank, non-generative indexing operating point for long-session memory under tight retrieval budgets.
A073FULLBethe Consensus Decoding: Joint Inference on Empirical Pairwise Factor Graphs for Structured LLM Outputs
Zehua Cheng (University of Oxford) · Wei Dai (FLock.io) · Jiahao Sun (FLock.io)
Abstract
Large language models increasingly serve as zero-shot extractors for structured outputs whose fields are mutually dependent: a salary range is correlated with experience level; a destination is correlated with the airline. The dominant unsupervised aggregator, independent majority voting (IMV), decodes each field marginally and therefore commits combinatorially inconsistent outputs whenever the per-field modes do not co-occur. We introduce Bethe Consensus Decoding (BCD), a training-free post-hoc aggregator that reconciles K samples drawn from a frozen LLM by minimising a Bethe free energy on a sparse pairwise factor graph. The graph is constructed from empirical mutual information using a cardinality-aware χ2 threshold, sum-product loopy belief propagation with damping yields pseudo-marginal beliefs, and a sequential greedy clamping procedure with a pairwise-belief ratio correction extracts a globally coherent output. We show that on tree-structured factor graphs in the population limit, BCD strictly dominates IMV in the induced tree distribution. On five real datasets ranging from slot filling to 15-field resume parsing, BCD with Llama-3-70B-Instruct improves average exact-match accuracy by 4.6 points over IMV and by 2.2 points over the strongest unsupervised structured baseline. We additionally evaluate BCD on Llama-3-8B, GPT-4o-mini, and Gemini-1.5-Flash and observe strong absolute performance on each (up to 44.96 EM on GPT-4o-mini), though backbone-matched IMV baselines are out of scope for this study. BCD is competitive with a supervised pairwise CRF that uses the same graph topology: the margin is small (≤ 1.3 pp) on the three data-rich benchmarks (D1, D2, D4) and substantially larger (3.7–4.7 pp, statistically significant under Holm–Bonferroni correction) on the two data-scarce benchmarks (D3, D5). Aggregation runs in milliseconds on CPU and reduces to IMV exactly when the empirical edge set is empty.
A074SHORTTraining Uncertainty-Aware Adaptive Reasoning Budgets with Policy Entropy
Kai Tian (Tsinghua University) · Sa Yang (Peking University) · Jingxuan Li (Harbin Engineering University) · Fangyuan Wang (Advanced Micro Devices, Inc.) · Yajian Huang (Advanced Micro Devices, Inc.) · Dong Li (Advanced Micro Devices, Inc.) · Jiaheng Ma (Beijing Institute of Technology) · Xinwei Long (Tsinghua University) · Guoli Jia (Tsinghua University) · Zhenzhao Yuan (Tsinghua University) · Huayong Hu (Jilin University) · Yang Liu (University of Electronic Science and Technology of China) · Emad Barsoum (Advanced Micro Devices, Inc.)
Abstract
Generative question answering and knowledge access systems increasingly use reasoning language models to synthesize retrieved or domain-specific information, but verbose rationales can raise latency and serving cost. We study whether policy entropy can serve as a training-time signal for uncertainty-aware compute allocation in such information access settings, rather than only as an online stopping heuristic. Our method estimates token-level entropy from repeated samples, assigns each question to a reasoning-budget tier, compresses traces for lower-uncertainty cases, and trains compact student models with mixed-granularity supervision and optional reinforcement learning. On five mathematical reasoning benchmarks and two knowledge-intensive QA settings in healthcare and finance, the method reduces reasoning length while preserving or improving accuracy. These results suggest that uncertainty estimates can shape supervision for resource-efficient generative AI and help models learn adaptive reasoning behavior without adding an inference-time controller.
A075FULLAegisKV: Runtime Headroom Control for Online LLM Serving via Adaptive Attention Offloading
Kihyun Kim (Sogang University) · Seong Jang (Sogang University) · Min Heo (Sogang University) · Jinwoo Kim (Sogang University) · James J. Kim (Soteria Inc.) · Youngjae Kim (Sogang University)
Abstract
This paper presents AegisKV, a runtime-adaptive attention offloading system for heterogeneous GPU environments. AegisKV dynamically offloads decode attention and KV cache at the request level based on runtime KV pressure and auxiliary GPU capability. AegisKV treats attention offloading not simply as KV-capacity expansion, but as a runtime KV headroom control mechanism for continuous batching in online LLM serving. To realize this design, AegisKV integrates (i) a pressure-aware request offloading scheduler, (ii) heterogeneous KV-cache management across serving and auxiliary GPUs, and (iii) a cross-device execution pipeline that overlaps KV transfer and decode execution. By selectively offloading only necessary requests, AegisKV mitigates preemption and recomputation while avoiding unnecessary auxiliary-path overhead. We implement AegisKV on top of vLLM and evaluate it using realistic online serving workloads on heterogeneous GPU configurations. On Llama-2-13B, AegisKV achieves up to 1.23× lower normalized token latency than baseline vLLM and 1.80× lower than static full offloading. Furthermore, on Qwen2.5-72B with MPS-based optimization, AegisKV achieves 15.07× lower TTFT and delays the onset of latency saturation by up to 1.43×.
A076SHORTLACE: Unsupervised Concept Drift Detection in Multi-Label Data Streams Through Label Cluster Evolution
Mehmet Kadri Gofralilar (Bilkent University) · Pouya Ghahramanian (Bilkent University) · Fazli Can (Bilkent University)
Abstract
Concept drift detection in multi-label data streams is challenging when true label vectors are delayed or unavailable. Most existing drift detectors monitor prediction errors, and therefore assume immediate access to ground-truth labels. This assumption is often unrealistic in stream settings, where reliable feedback may not be available at detection time. We propose LACE (Label Cluster Evolution), an unsupervised drift detector that uses changes in predicted label-dependency structure as evidence. It maintains a sliding window of recent predictions to compare label-cluster structures across consecutive subwindows. These clusters summarize evolving co-occurrence patterns among predicted labels, and changes in their structure are treated as evidence of drift in label dependencies. Cluster evolution is quantified using the Adjusted Rand Index (ARI), while Normalized Variation of Information handles degenerate cases and a Monte Carlo permutation procedure resolves ambiguous comparisons. We provide a comprehensive evaluation of LACE against several supervised error-based drift detectors and LD3, the only prior unsupervised drift detector for multi-label data streams to our knowledge. On real datasets, LACE achieves the best cumulative rank across predictive metrics despite requiring no immediate ground-truth labels. On synthetic datasets with known drift points, LACE reduces Delay For Detection by 63.51% on average relative to LD3, the next-best method, while achieving a 0% Missed Detection Rate. All code and data are publicly available at https://github.com/mehmetkadri/LACE.
A077FULLAccelerating Scientific Data Analytics Using Reconstruction-Free Error Control
Zhenlu Qin (Auburn University at Montgomery) · Qi Chen (Temple University) · Suhib Alhendi (New Jersey Institute of Technology) · Xin Liang (Oregon State University) · Weiqi Liu (Auburn University at Montgomery) · Qian Gong (Oak Ridge National Laboratory) · Qing Liu (New Jersey Institute of Technology) · Norbert Podhorszki (Oak Ridge National Laboratory) · Scott Klasky (Oak Ridge National Laboratory)
Abstract
Error-bounded lossy compression is widely used to reduce scientific data volume and alleviate storage and I/O bottlenecks. However, downstream analyses often require different accuracy levels, forcing users to rerun compression with multiple settings or store multiple compressed files. In addition, many applications focus on derived quantities of interest (QoIs), making it difficult to determine how much information should be retrieved to satisfy a prescribed QoI error bound without repeated reconstructions. In this work, we focus on QoI-aware progressive retrieval and develop reconstruction-free QoI error-control methods for both univariate and multivariate QoIs. Our approach uses basic statistics from the original data to construct conservative upper bounds, which determine a sufficient retrieval amount before reconstruction. This avoids trial-and-error reconstruction while supporting different QoI accuracy requirements from a single progressive representation. We compare our method with two categories of QoI-aware baselines: methods requiring separate compression runs for different QoI accuracy levels, and reconstruction-based progressive search methods requiring repeated reconstructions to identify a sufficient retrieval amount. The results show that our method satisfies prescribed QoI error bounds while reducing reconstruction overhead, with up to an 80.37% reduction in reconstruction time compared with the reconstruction-based search method.
A078FULLCubeFlow: Accelerating Multidimensional Query Chains for Interactive Data Analytics
Gang Qian (Nanjing University of Finance and Economics) · Qinghua Zhao (Nanjing University of Finance and Economics) · Zhengrui Qian (Xi'an Jiaotong-Liverpool University) · Hongru Chen (Xi'an Jiaotong-Liverpool University)
Abstract
Interactive data analytics tools enable users to explore data incrementally, often generating a sequence of dependent SQL queries, called a SQL chain. Even for moderately sized datasets, executing such chains on traditional database systems incurs significant overhead due to multiple rounds of intermediate aggregations, joins, and other compute-intensive operations. This paper focuses on multidimensional query chains and presents CubeFlow, an acceleration layer that sits between the analytics platform and the underlying database. By decoupling dimension columns from measure values, CubeFlow represents intermediate results as cube structures and models execution as a sequence of cube transformations along the chain. We introduce shadow dimensions to preserve regular cube structures across transformations in the chain, and propose coordinate-based aggregation and join algorithms that reuse dimension mappings and hash integer coordinates rather than raw attribute values. We implement a single-threaded prototype of CubeFlow and evaluate it on six multidimensional query chains over TPC-H, Online Retail, and Stocks. Despite the overhead of data conversion and coordination, our approach achieves average speedups of 5.4× over DuckDB and 7.6× over ClickHouse under single-threaded settings.
A079SHORTSchemaLens: Explainable Design-Space Reduction for Workload-Aware Document Schema Selection
Hudson Silva (Federal University of Santa Catarina) · Lilian Nascimento Araujo (Federal University of Santa Catarina) · Pavel Koupil (Charles University) · Irena Holubová (Charles University) · Ronaldo dos Santos Mello (Federal University of Santa Catarina)
Abstract
Document-schema design is a workload-dependent trade-off: embedding, referencing, and duplication affect latency, document growth, update cost, and the performance of other workload queries. Exhaustively benchmarking plausible MongoDB schemas is impractical, and selecting a schema too early can obscure relevant trade-offs. We present SchemaLens, an EER-guided framework for explainable design-space reduction. Rather than recommending a single schema, it extracts conceptual and workload signals and uses them to activate a compact family of MongoDB configurations for empirical benchmarking. Across representative workloads, SchemaLens reduces the benchmarked configuration space while preserving empirically competitive alternatives. The main benefit is an auditable reduction step that focuses benchmarking on semantically justified normalised, denormalised, bridge-based, and hybrid alternatives, while final schema selection remains empirical.
A080SHORTCross-Modal Attribute Consistency Verification for E-Commerce Products via Relational Graph Embedding
Ayoung Kim (Dong-A University) · Jeonghyeon Park (Dong-A University) · Wonseok Son (Dong-A University) · Sejin Chun (Dong-A University)
Abstract
Product attributes on e-commerce pages are often distributed across two modalities, textual content and embedded images. Such cross-modal presentation can introduce inconsistencies in wording, units, values, and attribute presence. Existing approaches match representations across modalities, but such alignment only indicates correspondence and cannot determine the relation type between paired attributes, such as equivalence and value conflict. We propose a framework that verifies attribute consistency at the attribute-pair level. First, it aligns cross-modal attributes by combining representation normalization with semantic embedding matching. Second, it classifies each aligned pair into four relation types. Third, it represents the inferred relations as typed triples in a relational graph for relational embedding learning. Finally, we evaluate the proposed framework on a real-world dataset in terms of relation classification, link prediction, and structural triple injection.
A081SHORTRecipeNet: A Hierarchical Transformer for Recipe Data
Pin-Yen Huang (Arizona State University) · Sachin Chhabra (Arizona State University) · Prasanth Sai Gouripeddi (Arizona State University) · Abhinav Kumar (Applied Materials) · Baoxin Li (University of Illinois Chicago)
Abstract
Recipe data arises in domains such as materials synthesis, pharmaceutical formulation, and industrial manufacturing, where procedures are represented as ordered sequences of steps containing heterogeneous structured fields. Existing tabular learning methods typically flatten this structure into fixed-schema representations, limiting their ability to capture hierarchical field interactions and procedural dependencies. We propose RecipeNet, a hierarchical Transformer architecture that encodes field-level interactions within each step and sequential dependencies across steps through stacked Transformer encoders. Experiments on multiple recipe datasets and tasks demonstrate that RecipeNet consistently outperforms existing tabular models, highlighting the value of hierarchical and sequential modeling for recipe representation learning.
A082FULLSCoP: Structured Constraint Parsing for Evidence-Space Control in Temporal Knowledge Graph Question Answering
Xiaokun Guo (Institute of Information Engineering, Chinese Academy of Sciences) · Zhen Xu (Institute of Information Engineering, Chinese Academy of Sciences) · Dongdong Huo (Institute of Information Engineering, Chinese Academy of Sciences) · Yanqiu Zhang (Institute of Information Engineering, Chinese Academy of Sciences) · Dongjin Yu (Institute of Information Engineering, Chinese Academy of Sciences) · Yu Wang (Institute of Information Engineering, Chinese Academy of Sciences)
Abstract
Temporal Knowledge Graph Question Answering (TKGQA) requires answer inference from evidence that is both structurally valid and temporally admissible. Existing methods often leave anchor-event binding, temporal admissibility, and ordinal selection implicit in model reasoning, task-specific training, or similarity-driven retrieval, allowing locally relevant but invalid facts to enter the answer context. We formulate complex TKGQA as evidence-space control and propose SCoP (Structured Constraint Parsing), a constraint-centric framework that externalizes temporal decisions before answer inference. Instead of treating retrieved facts as admissible evidence by default, SCoP separates answer-seeking event patterns from temporal anchor events, conservatively grounds them to canonical TKG entities and relations, and translates temporal intent into executable constraints with optional ranking requirements. These constraints operate over normalized point and interval ranges, enabling deterministic filtering of structurally compatible candidates and producing a compact evidence space for generation. Experiments on MultiTQ and TimelineCronQ-R assess SCoP across timestamped point-fact and interval-oriented settings with richer temporal relations and ordering dependencies. Without task-specific parameter updates, SCoP achieves 0.825 Hits@1 on MultiTQ and 0.761 Hits@1 on TimelineCronQ-R, with gains on constraint-intensive question types. These results support explicit evidence-space control over unconstrained retrieval or implicit temporal reasoning.
A083FULLIntent2Chain: Multi-Task Knowledge Graph Reasoning for Network Intent Completion
Mingyue Li (Inner Mongolia University) · Peilong Zhang (Inner Mongolia University) · Yufeng Zhao (Inner Mongolia University) · Lubing Guo (Inner Mongolia University) · Hua Li (College of Computer Science, Inner Mongolia University) · Chunyan An (College of Computer Science, Inner Mongolia University)
Abstract
Intent-Driven Networking (IDN) is important for autonomous network management. It aims to translate high-level user goals into structured network configurations. However, user intents in real-world scenarios are often incomplete. They may lack specific service functions (SFs), proper function sequences, and necessary attributes. This makes it difficult to obtain a complete Service Function Chain (SFC) representation. In this paper, we propose a multi-task knowledge graph reasoning method, named Intent2Chain, for network intent completion. We construct an Intent-Network Knowledge Graph (INKG) to unify business intents and network service knowledge in a shared semantic space. To bridge the gap between abstract intents and structured SFC representations, we decompose the completion process into three related subtasks: SF set prediction, SFC link prediction, and SF attribute completion. Specifically, we combine global attention with local graph learning to capture structural dependencies among SFs. We further introduce SFC order prior constraints and weighted topological sorting to ensure structural validity and avoid loops. Experimental results on real-world operational logs show that Intent2Chain can effectively recover missing SFs, order relations, and attributes for incomplete network intents.
A084RESOURCETempBench: A Temporal Knowledge-Graph QA Benchmark with Per-Question Gold Subgraphs and Retrieval-Quality Metrics
Guendalina Caldarini (aivancity School of AI & Data for Business & society)
Abstract
Temporal knowledge-graph question answering (TKGQA) asks systems to answer questions whose correct answer depends on when the question is asked. Existing TKGQA benchmarks ship answer strings (CronQuestions, MultiTQ, MusTQ) or, in the closest prior work (TimelineKGQA), per-question positive context facts scored by ranking - but none release per-question typed negatives or score retrieval by subgraph precision/recall against time-valid gold. We present TempBench, an 8,710-question multi-hop TKGQA benchmark over a Wikidata-derived temporal KG. Every question ships a gold supporting subgraph S* and - uniquely in this setting - same-(s,r) distractor and same-(s,r,o) stale-fact negatives (functional for 71.5% and 81.3% of questions; the interval x stale cell is structurally absent at 8.1% since interval answers are years; per-question flags released), across a 4x3 temporal-operator x hop-complexity matrix, scored by two answer-independent subgraph metrics (Temporal Retrieval Precision and Chain Consistency Rate) grounded in a forward-propagating temporal composability operator we formalise. These metrics expose retrieval quality that end-task exact-match conflates: at matched 2-hop architecture, removing the temporal filter collapses Chain Consistency Rate from 0.84 to 0.13, and deepening retrieval from two to three hops lifts 3+-hop chain coverage from 0.014 to 0.476 (paired McNemar p<10^-19 on n=143) - a retrieval gain whose end-task counterpart is single-seed-large but multi-seed-marginal. We release the benchmark, pipeline, annotation protocol, and per-question functional-negative flags.
A085SHORTLess Is More: Knowledge Graph Construction and Schema-Guided Canonicalization with LLMs
Hwangseon Park (Sungkyunkwan University) · Hayeon Yang (Sungkyunkwan University) · Dongyoung Son (Sungkyunkwan University) · Myoungseok Song (Sungkyunkwan University) · Hayoung Oh (Sungkyunkwan University)
Abstract
Knowledge graphs (KGs) are widely used in domains such as healthcare and finance, but existing LLM-based construction methods often produce redundant triples and semantically inconsistent representations. We propose a unified framework combining LLM-based triple extraction with schema-guided canonicalization. Our approach extracts triples and induces a schema to constrain canonicalization candidates, enabling consistent entity and relation merging. Experiments on five benchmark datasets show that our method produces more compact KGs with higher F1 scores than existing approaches. Ablation studies show that schema-guided canonicalization reduces redundancy with minimal loss of semantic fidelity. Our canonicalized KGs also improve retrieval-augmented generation (RAG) question-answering performance. Our code is publicly available at https://github.com/HwangSeonPark/less-is-more-kg
A086FULLFrom Ontology Alignments to Executable Code: Automating Data Integration with Fact Generating Functions
Koby Bar (University of Haifa) · Tomer Sagi (Aalborg University)
Abstract
Data integration remains labor-intensive, making projects lengthy, costly, and difficult to automate end to end. Although substantial progress has been made on core subtasks such as schema matching, ontology alignment, and entity matching, these subtasks often stop short of producing executable transformations. In ontology-based data integration, mappings can identify corresponding classes and properties, but value normalization, literal conversion, and multi-fact generation are still commonly implemented through bespoke scripts. We introduce Fact Generating Functions (FGFs), executable triple-conversion functions that transform RDF triples expressed under source semantics into semantically corresponding triples under target semantics. FGFs bridge the gap between ontology alignment and RDF materialization by making transformation logic explicit, inspectable, and executable. We present an automated pipeline that instantiates the approach by converting relational data into RDF, identifying source-to-target correspondences, generating intermediate logical rules, and materializing target triples through executable FGFs. We evaluate the method on benchmark scenarios for relational data-to-ontology integration and show competitive results across diverse mapping settings. The results demonstrate the feasibility of using FGFs as a practical abstraction to automate semantic data mapping and reduce the need for manually engineered transformation scripts.
A087SHORTBeyond Keywords: Training-Free Entity Linking for Multilingual Research Metadata
Jiayu Yang (University of Bayreuth) · Durgesh Nandini (University of Bayreuth) · Frédérick Madore (University of Bayreuth) · Neeraj Thandayan Viswajith (University of Bayreuth) · Oliver Baumann (University of Bayreuth) · Mirco Schönfeld (University of Bayreuth)
Abstract
Research collections in the humanities and social sciences describe overlapping subjects under divergent cataloguing practices, so records that belong together stay unconnected across databases. Stable identifiers would make the overlap machine-readable, but assigning them means disambiguating keywords that are short, multilingual, and largely without context. We present Context-Aware Routing for Entity Linking (CAREL), a training-free pipeline that links research metadata keywords to Wikidata QIDs through a four-layer cascade. Its core is Cross-lingual Retrieval Consensus (CRC), a novel signal that turns the agreement of retrieval ranks across language-specific queries into a measure of linking confidence without requiring annotated data. Rule-based layers resolve the clear cases, and only genuinely ambiguous keywords reach a locally deployed open-source large language model (LLM), which bounds inference cost and avoids sending research metadata to external services. On two manually verified benchmarks from multilingual African studies metadata, subject headings anchored in the Library of Congress Subject Headings (LCSH) and researcher-supplied tags, CAREL reaches 89.8% and 90.9% accuracy on the headings with Gemma4-31B-it and Qwen3.5-27B, and holds 88.8% and 89.5% on the anchor-free tags. It also detects the keywords for which no Wikidata entity exists, at an F1 of 88 on the tags.
A089APPLIEDLLM-Powered Pipeline for Web Page Classification
Jaroslav Veverka (Seznam.cz, a. s.) · Tomáš Nováčik (Seznam.cz, a. s.) · Alžbeta štajerová (Seznam.cz, a. s.) · Andrej Vojtuš (Seznam.cz, a. s.)
Abstract
We present a fully automated, end-to-end pipeline for the large-scale multi-label classification of web documents. Our approach addresses the challenge of creating production-ready classifiers without manual annotation while maintaining high classification accuracy. The pipeline combines generative and discriminative ML techniques to construct training datasets and train classifiers without human labeling. A two-stage annotation process generates the training data: semantic dense retrieval pre-selects candidate documents for each category, followed by an LLM-as-a-judge filtering step that achieves near-human annotation quality. A classification model is then trained using the task-specific fine-tuning of a semantic sentence transformer with an MLP head. We evaluate the approach by benchmarking it against the previous production baseline. Each classified pageview contributes to the aggregation of user interests aligned with the IAB Content Taxonomy. These aggregated interests enable the construction of audience segments for advertising applications and serve as features for a downstream ad ranking model. An online A/B test evaluating these system upgrades demonstrates statistically significant improvements in key business metrics (+2.73% CTR).
A090SHORTPair-Level Essay-Scale Republication and Reuse from Fragmented Historical Text Reuse: A Workflow Study on Eighteenth-Century Books and Newspapers
Ke Shu (University of Helsinki) · Kira Hinderks (University of Helsinki) · Eetu Mäkelä (University of Helsinki) · Mikko Tolonen (University of Helsinki)
Abstract
This paper addresses the recovery of essay-scale republication and reuse from fragmented text-reuse evidence, a setting whose central challenge is pair-level evidence consolidation and not fragment retrieval alone. The study focuses on a candidate set centered on essays by eighteenth-century Scottish philosopher David Hume, spanning books from ECCO (Eighteenth Century Collections Online) and historical newspapers. Because the input consists of fragmented reuse hits instead of clean document pairs, and positive coverage is inherently incomplete, we formulate the task as pair-level evidence consolidation into plausible transmission relations and compare three methodological families: a staged rule-based workflow, baselines (a decision tree and two direct LLM settings), and automated rule adaptation. On labeled ECCO--ECCO slices, pair-level feature aggregation alone already reaches 0.948 F1 on the main labeled slice, while the final workflow gives the strongest overall precision-recall trade-off among the tested rule stages. On the full ECCO--ECCO candidate universe, direct LLM baselines flag up to 14,886 pairs as reprints compared to 771 for the final workflow, behaving in this direct-prompt setup as high-recall candidate expanders rather than precision-controlled deployment classifiers. On ECCO--Newspaper, manual audit confirms all 176 predicted positives as genuine cases of republication or reuse, while issue duplication and source-side multiplicity reveal additional provenance structure. Under incomplete ground truth, auditable pair-level evidence consolidation provides a practical way to produce compact candidate spaces for historical inspection.
A091SHORTLost in Extraction: RE-ErrorTax, A Fine-Grained Taxonomy of LLM Errors in Relation Extraction Across Multiple Benchmarks
Soumya Bharadwaj (Indian Institute of Technology Guwahati) · Ashish Anand (Indian Institute of Technology Guwahati)
Abstract
Relation Extraction (RE) is a fundamental information extraction task that identifies semantic relationships between entities in text. Recent Large Language Models (LLMs) have enabled zero-shot RE, reducing the need for task-specific training data. However, existing evaluations rely primarily on aggregate metrics such as F1 score, which provide limited insight into the underlying causes of model failures. To address this limitation, we introduce RE-ErrorTax, a fine-grained error taxonomy for analyzing LLM-generated relation triples. We evaluate 13 open-source and proprietary LLMs on five widely used RE benchmarks and categorize their errors using the proposed taxonomy. Furthermore, we investigate the feasibility of using LLMs as automated error evaluators and compare their judgments against human annotations on a manually annotated subset. Our analysis reveals that relation-level errors are substantially more common than entity-level failures and that LLM judges achieve moderate agreement with a human annotator. The results demonstrate the value of taxonomy-driven evaluation for understanding LLM behavior and highlight the potential of LLM-based judges for scalable RE error analysis.
A092SHORTWhen Persona Simulations Are Informative: Graph-Structured Signals for Pluralistic Opinion Sensing
Taehyeon An (Korea Advanced Institute of Science and Technology) · Jaehyeong Park (Korea Advanced Institute of Science and Technology) · Donghyuk Shin (Korea Advanced Institute of Science and Technology)
Abstract
Persona-conditioned large language models (LLMs) are increasingly used to simulate survey responses across diverse domains. However, apparent response variation can reflect unconditioned model priors or token sampling noise rather than systematic persona conditioning. We argue that persona-conditioned variation is informative when semantically similar personas exhibit concordant response shifts. To operationalize this principle, we introduce Persona-Conditioned Informativeness (PCI), an unsupervised diagnostic metric that measures whether semantically similar personas deviate in concordant directions relative to item-level sample baselines. By modeling personas as a similarity graph, PCI uses Local Moran's I to quantify local spatial coherence and extract compact persona subsets without using construct labels. To evaluate PCI without external human benchmarks, we test its ability to recover established latent value structure using the 57-item Portrait Values Questionnaire-Revised (PVQ-RR). Confirmatory factor analysis (CFA) shows that a PCI-selected 10% subset substantially improves overall construct recovery relative to response-stability and random selection. These findings support PCI as a principled internal diagnostic for screening synthetic respondents in survey pipelines.
A093FULLWho Do We Trust? Investigating the Human-AI Trust Gap in Scientific Social Media Discourse
Yavuz Selim Kartal (GESIS - Leibniz Institute for the Social Sciences) · Dagmar Kern (GESIS - Leibniz Institute for the Social Sciences) · Kevin Schott (GESIS - Leibniz Institute for the Social Sciences) · Alisa Rieger (GESIS - Leibniz Institute for the Social Sciences)
Abstract
As social media continues to be one of the primary communication channels, it has become a critical hub for the dissemination of scientific information. The nature of these platforms allows for the quick sharing of scientific claims, even without a reference. Users often rely on contextual cues such as comments accompanying posts for validation, while some platforms are increasingly integrate LLM-based systems that participant in online discourse by generating comments, explanations, and fact-checks. In this paper, we investigate how comment attribution (Human vs. AI) affects perceived trustworthiness of comments and posts and how it changes with the presence of a reference to a scientific publication and the comment's stance. We conducted a preregistered within-subjects user study (N=152) using a web-based platform that simulates a social media timeline containing posts and comments. We compared eight conditions: two types of comment attribution (Human vs. AI), two types of comment stance (Endorsing vs. Refuting), and two types of reference existence (Reference vs. No Reference). While we did not find evidence for a difference in overall trustworthiness between Human- and AI- attributed comments, we found that comments without a reference that were attributed to an AI were perceived as more trustworthy than those attributed to a human, highlighting the risk of over-reliance on AI. Exploratory analysis further indicate differences in comment and post trustworthiness between Human- and AI-attributed comments, depending on whether posts' claims aligned with scientific consensus. These observed differences suggest a potential interplay of trust and confirmation bias in the context of AI-attributed comments, which warrants further investigation by future research.
A094FULLPACIFIER: Pacing Opinion Depolarization via a Unified Graph Learning Framework
Mingkai Liao (Shenzhen University) · Zijun Zhang (Hubei University of Police) · Mingyang Zhou (Shenzhen University)
Abstract
Online social networks often form opposing echo chambers that reinforce opinion polarization. Under the Friedkin--Johnsen (FJ) model, ModerateInternal (MI) and ModerateExpressed (ME) reduce polarization by neutralizing selected users' internal or expressed opinions, but existing solutions are largely model-specific and learning-based depolarization remains underexplored. We study FJ-based moderation as feedback-free autoregressive sequential planning and propose PACIFIER, a unified graph-learning framework that constructs ordered intervention sequences from the initial graph--opinion instance without using recomputed post-intervention expressed opinions as intermediate feedback. PACIFIER combines history-aware node representations with Greedy and RL variants for immediate and long-horizon action scoring, and supports MI, ME, continuous opinions, cost-aware moderation, and node removal. We evaluate intervention trajectories by Accumulated Normalized Polarization (ANP). Trained only on synthetic graphs with fewer than 50 nodes, PACIFIER transfers to 15 real-world Twitter networks with up to 155,599 nodes. It improves over the strongest non-PACIFIER baseline by up to 35.3%, while PACIFIER-RL improves over PACIFIER-Greedy by up to 37.69%. Compared with oracle-style Greedy, PACIFIER retains 98.94% and 97.39% near-oracle quality on MI and ME, respectively, and is about 600× faster at the 450-node range. The source code is available at https://github.com/RickyYY-SZU/PACIFIER.
A095FULLMulti-stage Interpretable Temporal Mixture of Experts for Information Diffusion Prediction
Junchang Jing (Henan Normal University) · Lingjun Wu (Henan Normal University) · Dong Liu (Henan Normal University) · Zhiyong Zhang (Henan University of Science and Technology)
Abstract
Information diffusion prediction, which aims to identify potentially infected users for a given message, is essential in domains such as public opinion analysis, fake news detection, and social recommendation. However, existing methods still suffer from several limitations: (1) They usually divide the historical cascades using a fixed time interval, ignoring the heterogeneity of multi-stage information diffusion dynamics. (2) Present methods primarily focus on sequential dependencies among users, while overlooking explicit temporal information and the interpretability of the prediction results. To address the aforementioned issues, we propose a Multi-stage Interpretable Temporal Mixture of Experts model (MITMoE). Specifically, we first introduce an adaptive temporal-scale segmentation method, which can dynamically adjust the temporal granularity according to diffusion dynamics at different stages, preserving temporal consistency while accounting for variations in diffusion density. We then present an Interpretable Temporal Mixture of Experts (ITMoE) interaction mechanism for explicit temporal information fusion, providing interpretable temporal interaction patterns at both local and global levels. Extensive experiments on four real-world datasets show that MITMoE outperforms state-of-the-art baselines, with each core component contributing effectively.
A096FULLPredicting Narrative Virality on Social Media Streams for Pre-Peak Misinformation Triage
Filipe Altoe (INESC-ID / Instituto Superior Técnico, Universidade de Lisboa) · Sérgio Miguel Gonçalves Pinto (INESC-ID / Instituto Superior Técnico, Universidade de Lisboa) · H. Sofia Pinto (INESC-ID / Instituto Superior Técnico, Universidade de Lisboa)
Abstract
Misinformation narratives that reach virality on social media typically do so within a median of 1.5 days, while professional fact-checkers require a median of 4.5 days to publish corrections. When a false claim circulates unaddressed, polarization sets in around it, eroding the corrective impact of fact-checks that arrive after peak spread. Existing virality prediction operates either on individual posts (will this tweet trend?) or on coarse events (will this topic dominate?), missing the narrative, a cluster of semantically equivalent claims, as the natural unit of analysis for fact-checking workflows. We introduce narrative-level streaming virality prediction as a new task formulation, supported by an end-to-end pipeline with four components: streaming clustering of semantically equivalent posts into evolving narratives, online kernel-density anomaly detection over cluster activity, LLM-based claim normalization, and cluster-level spread prediction via a novel Post-Detection Spread Ratio (PSR) metric that quantifies the remaining intervention window at detection time. The pipeline surfaces actionable triage decisions before peak virality. Our downstream components also advance the state of the art on two established Automatic Claim Detection (ACD) tasks. On the N=300 CT2025 English claim-normalization test subset, a contrastive few-shot approach with Mistral-7B-Instruct-v0.3 exceeds the strongest published baseline by 10.0 METEOR points despite using a smaller model than the published baselines. On CheckThat! 2024 check-worthiness, our 4-Parallel-Heads DeBERTa-v3-large achieves F1=0.833 with dimension-wise confidence decomposition, generalizing zero-shot to ClaimBuster (F1=0.973) and CheckThat! 2023 (F1=0.933). We release the first dataset and baselines for narrative-level streaming virality prediction, with virality labels, check-worthiness annotations, and intermediate features over 535 narratives derived from 1.52M tweets of a US political-event Twitter stream.
A097FULLContextClaim: A Context-Driven Paradigm for Verifiable Claim Detection
Yufeng Li (Queen Mary University of London) · Rrubaa Panchendrarajan (Queen Mary University of London) · Arkaitz Zubiaga (Queen Mary University of London)
Abstract
Automated fact-checking pipelines typically begin with a filtering stage that decides which claims are worth verifying, given that the later evidence retrieval and verification components are expensive to apply at scale. A central task in this stage is verifiable claim detection, which asks whether a statement is in principle checkable against external evidence. Prior work on this task, as well as on the closely related notion of check-worthiness, conditions its decisions only on the claim sentence itself. We argue that this is restrictive, because deciding whether a statement is checkable often depends on identifying the entities and events it mentions, and on whether external information about them is actually available in the first place. Motivated by how downstream verification systems rely on retrieved evidence, we move retrieval upstream into the detection stage and introduce ContextClaim. Given an input claim, the approach identifies entity mentions, queries Wikipedia as a structured background source, and uses large language models to compress the retrieved material into short contextual summaries that are then passed to a classifier. Experiments are conducted on two domains and genres, namely the CheckThat! 2022 Twitter collection and the PoliClaim corpus of political debates, and cover both encoder and decoder only models under fine-tuning, zero-shot, and few-shot settings. The added context yields gains on verifiable claim detection in several configurations, although the size of the improvement varies with the dataset, the backbone model, and the training setup. We further find that the same retrieved summaries are useful beyond detection. Feeding them into a downstream verification model on FEVER improves verification F1. Component level analyses, human annotation, and error inspection further clarify the conditions under which retrieved context helps, and where it does not.
A098SHORTGRAIN: Detecting AI-Generated News via Article-Level Structure
Youjin Lee (Sungkyunkwan University) · Chaewon Kang (Sungkyunkwan University) · YunSeok Choi (Sungkyunkwan University) · Jinyoung Han (Sungkyunkwan University)
Abstract
Large language models (LLMs) can generate news articles that closely resemble human-written journalism, raising concerns about misinformation and the reliability of online information. Existing AI-generated text detectors primarily rely on lexical, stylistic, or contextual representations, which often struggle to generalize to unseen generators and do not explicitly model article-level structure in news. We propose GRAIN, a framework for AI-generated news detection that jointly models semantic representations and article-level structural patterns. Through empirical analysis, we identify recurring article-level structural patterns in AI-generated news that remain consistent across multiple LLM families and a real-world AI-generated news dataset. Experiments on RAID, DetectRL, an in-house dataset comprising 157K AI-generated news articles from 11 LLMs, and the real-world NewsGPT dataset show that GRAIN improves ROC-AUC over the strongest baseline by 7.9 percentage points on average across evaluation settings. These results suggest that article-level structural patterns provide effective complementary signals for improving the robustness and generalization of AI-generated news detection. The code is available at: https://github.com/DSAIL-SKKU/GRAIN-CIKM-2026.
A099FULLHARA: A Hierarchical Artifact-Aware Residual Adapter Framework for AI-Generated Image Detection
Haowei Zhou (University of Science and Technology of China) · Long Ma (University of Science and Technology of China) · Yu Gao (University of Science and Technology of China) · Yong Liao (University of Science and Technology of China)
Abstract
With the rapid advancement of generative models, AI-generated image (AIGI) detection has become crucial. However, current pretrained encoder-based methods still face two key limitations: (i) late feature fusion, where local artifact cues are progressively suppressed by stacked ViT encoder layers before being exploited; and (ii) source-domain overfitting, which limits robustness to unseen generative models and domains. To address these challenges, we propose HARA, a Hierarchical Artifact-aware Residual Adapter framework for AIGI detection. HARA introduces a dual-branch adapter architecture that jointly models semantic representations and generation-induced artifact cues through lightweight low-rank adaptation and local convolutional feature extraction. Instead of restricting feature interaction to the final stage, HARA progressively injects adapter-enhanced features into selected shallow, intermediate, and deep ViT layers, enabling hierarchical refinement of artifact-aware representations while preserving the pretrained representation space. This progressive fusion strategy effectively preserves and exploits fine-grained artifact traces that are often diluted in deeper semantic representations. Furthermore, to improve out-of-distribution generalization, we introduce two feature-space regularization strategies: structured noise perturbation and stochastic adapter scaling. These mechanisms act as implicit feature-space augmentation, encouraging the model to learn more invariant and transferable representations under distribution shifts introduced by different generative pipelines. Extensive experiments across multiple benchmarks demonstrate that HARA consistently outperforms existing methods, particularly in challenging cross-generator and cross-domain evaluation settings.
A100FULLPrototype-Rectified Iterative Self-supervised Manifold Denoising under Severe Acoustic Shift
Ashish Anand Shukla (Indian Institute of Science Education and Research Bhopal) · Rini Smita Thakur (Indian Institute of Science Education and Research Bhopal) · Aryan Das (Vellore Institute of Technology Bhopal) · Vinod Kumar Kurmi (Indian Institute of Science Education and Research Bhopal)
Abstract
Audio-Text Foundation Models (ATMs) fail catastrophically under severe acoustic noise, yet existing adaptation strategies either rely on gradient-based Test-Time Adaptation (TTA), which reinforces noise rather than signal, or on prompt tuning that requires privileged noise annotations unavailable at inference. We address these failures with PRISM (Prototype-Rectified Iterative Self-supervised Manifold Denoising), a training-free, source-free TTA framework grounded in the Affine Noise Hypothesis: severe acoustic noise induces a low-rank affine shift in the multimodal latent space, with more than 90% of distortion energy confined to the leading 60 principal components. PRISM estimates and reverses this distortion from an unlabeled target batch using frozen text prototypes as geometric anchors via three closed-form geometric corrections compiled into a single static projection matrix by Affine Bias Regression. In inference, adaptation reduces to one matrix-vector multiplication in 9 × 10⁻⁴ ms, making it substantially faster than gradient-based TTA while requiring no additional training. On UrbanSound8K, PRISM improves over the zero-shot baseline by +12.94 pp and surpasses an oracle-assisted TTA baseline by +9.41 pp, which requires privileged augmented noise prompts PRISM never sees. We further identify the Polyphonic Trap, a principled failure mode of subspace deflation for broadband classes, and resolve it via Confidence-Aware Regression (CAR), recovering up to 8.16 pp for the worst-affected class. The code is available at https://github.com/Ashish-1108/PRISM.
A101FULLSAND-CBM: Image-Side Basis Reconstruction for Concept Bottleneck Models
Zhibo Jin (University of Technology Sydney) · Zhiyu Zhu (University of Technology Sydney) · Jiayu Zhang (Suzhou University of Technology) · Xinyi Wang (University of Malaya) · Biaoliang Chen (University of Technology Sydney) · Jianlong Zhou (University of Technology Sydney) · Fang Chen (University of Technology Sydney)
Abstract
Concept bottleneck models are only as useful as the concept space they expose. Existing concept-annotation-free CBMs often treat this space as text-pool retrieval: an image is explained by whichever prompt words score highly, so visual evidence that is fine-grained, compositional, or hard to name can be missed. We introduce SAND-CBM, which shifts the bottleneck from prompt retrieval to image-side basis reconstruction in a frozen vision–language space. Text-similarity channels are retained as named anchors, but they are complemented by learned visual-factor channels that can surface candidate evidence beyond the vocabulary. The core design is a signed–nonnegative–calibrated–shared (SNCS) representation contract: signed dictionary rows preserve CLIP-space directions, nonnegative activations give additive channel strengths, training-set calibration makes channels rankable, and a class-conditional selector reuses one shared dictionary across classes. SAND-CBM is concept-annotation-free rather than label-free: it uses no concept names, concept annotations, or concept-level targets for the learned image-side basis, while task labels train the final readout and an explicit low-bandwidth class gate. This design provides a more diagnostic interface: important channels should be removable, low-contribution or random removals should have weaker effects, discovered activations should align above null controls, and class gates should reuse rather than duplicate evidence. Across four visual benchmarks, SAND-CBM remains competitive in accuracy while showing a more concentrated and intervention-consistent concept-candidate interface than matched controls. Core code is available at https://github.com/LMBTough/SAND.
A102RESOURCEGQA-Q2Q: A Large-scale Benchmark for Entity Ambiguity Resolution in Visual Question Answering
Gyu-Min Park (Kyung Hee University) · Seong-Bae Park (Kyung Hee University)
Abstract
Vision-language models achieve remarkable results on various visual question-answering benchmarks. However, they struggle with ambiguous questions where the target entity is unclear. To address this issue, it is essential to construct a benchmark dataset that pairs ambiguous questions with entity-grounded clarifying sub-questions. This paper presents GQA-Q2Q, a large-scale dataset for resolving entity ambiguity in visual question answering via entity-grounded clarifying sub-questions. GQA-Q2Q is constructed through a template-assisted human annotation pipeline. The pipeline generates candidate sub-questions from attribute, relation, and position templates and asks human annotators to verify, select, or revise them. As a result, GQA-Q2Q contains 46,554 human-verified clarifying sub-questions with target-instance grounding. This paper also presents a proposed ambiguity-resolving VQA model that leverages the generated sub-questions before producing final answers. The experimental results show that the proposed model outperforms zero-shot and ambiguity-resolving vision-language baselines. The code and dataset are available at https://github.com/gminipark/GQA-Q2Q.git.
A103APPLIEDEfficient Frame Selection for E-Commerce Video Analysis
Arihant Jain (Amazon) · Vishnu Prabhakaran (Amazon) · Purav Aggarwal (Amazon)
Abstract
E-commerce video analysis systems---spanning fulfillment-center (FC) packaging and return-center (RC) unpackaging---face two challenges at scale: transferring and indexing full-resolution video is prohibitively expensive (evidence collection), and downstream Vision Language Model (VLM) inference requires query-specific evidence frames (evidence analysis). We propose a two-stage frame selection approach: Stage 1 is a query-agnostic on-device video summarizer that compresses each video to k keyframes via Determinantal Point Process diversity and Laplacian-variance quality scoring (8× reduction, ?1% of frames transmitted); Stage 2 is a set of domain-adapted per-category relevance rankers fine-tuned with a pairwise RankNet loss on human-verified labels. On product matching at a major e-commerce store, our approach improves over uniform sampling by +13.0pp accuracy and +11.8pp macro F1 at 3 frames, and by +21.6pp accuracy at a single frame---outperforming the best of six recent frame-selection baselines by +18.9pp.
A104FULLRobust Chart Information Extraction via an LVLM Ensemble and Pairwise Reasoning
Fahad Ahmed (TIB - Leibniz Information Centre for Science and Technology) · Matthias Springstein (TIB - Leibniz Information Centre for Science and Technology) · Anett Hoppe (Marburg University and Hessian Center for Artificial Intelligence (hessian.AI)) · Sören Auer (TIB - Leibniz Information Centre for Science and Technology) · Ralph Ewerth (Marburg University and Hessian Center for Artificial Intelligence (hessian.AI)) · Eric Müller-Budack (TIB - Leibniz Information Centre for Science and Technology)
Abstract
Data visualizations are essential for communicating findings in scientific literature since they convey significant insights such as experimental results, trends, and distributions. However, due to the diverse nature of charts in real-world settings, automatic chart information extraction (CIE) remains challenging. Current state-of-the-art models demonstrate limited generalization across a variety of charts and benchmarks, performing adequately on basic chart types but failing to recognize complex visualizations, particularly when the characteristics (e.g., resolution, axis, complexity) differ from the datasets used to train them. To address these challenges, we make several contributions. (1) We propose an ensemble-based approach that aims to leverage the synergies of models trained for CIE and general-purpose large vision-language models (LVLMs). (2) We propose several inference strategies for our ensemble approach, including a multiple choice and two binary choice approaches based on league- and tournament-style inference to prevent excessive context length and positional bias of generative AI models. (3) For a fair comparison, we suggest a novel evaluation metric that resolves fundamental problems of existing metrics used for CIE task. (4) Experimental results demonstrate that our proposed ensemble approach can efficiently leverage synergies across various models achieving superior results and generalization across four benchmarks in comparison to the state of the art.
A105FULLR2-Net: Efficient Low-Light Image Enhancement via Dynamic Routing and High-Frequency Refinement
Jiaqi Ruan (Hubei University) · Yamin Li (Hubei University) · Sihan Wu (Hubei University) · Yucheng Wan (Hubei University) · Kansong Chen (Hubei University)
Abstract
Low-light image enhancement aims to recover images with clear details and natural colors from low-light observations. However, existing enhancement algorithms often struggle to simultaneously ensure global illumination consistency, preserve local high-frequency textures, and effectively increase brightness, which is prone to noise residue or detail loss. To address these challenges, this paper proposes a novel low-light image enhancement network named R2-Net. First, to overcome the limitations of traditional Transformers, such as their high computational complexity and difficulty in adaptively capturing long-range dependencies under low-SNR conditions—we introduce the Dynamic Routing Global Block (DRGB), which adopts a content-aware dynamic routing mechanism to perform sparse global contextual modeling. Second, to alleviate the local texture blurring problem commonly observed in deep enhancement networks, we design a High-Frequency Detail Residual Refinement (HDRR) module that accurately recovers edge and texture details by selectively enhancing high-frequency responses. Extensive experiments on several real-world benchmark datasets demonstrate that the proposed method outperforms current state-of-the-art algorithms in both objective metrics and subjective visual quality, exhibiting superior enhancement performance and generalization ability. With a moderate size of only 7.37M parameters, our model achieves a superior trade-off between restoration quality and model capacity. R2-Net also serves as a robust front-end enhancement module that restores semantically meaningful visual features, improving the resilience of multimedia retrieval systems under challenging illumination conditions. Code is available at https://github.com/jiaQi224/R2-Net.
A106SHORTGrounded Distractor Probing: A Diagnostic Protocol for Hard-Distractor Sensitivity in VLM Multiple-Choice Evaluation
Seunghun Oh (Sogang University) · Ganghyeon Jeong (Sogang University) · Unsang Park (Sogang University)
Abstract
Multiple-choice evaluation for vision-language models (VLMs) increasingly relies on stronger distractors, but recent work has mostly emphasized distractor construction or generic option bias. We introduce Grounded Distractor Probing (GDP), a matched original/permutation/hard diagnostic protocol that probes how models respond to same-type, visually plausible near-miss distractors under a controlled intervention. GDP is instantiated on GDP-Slice, a manually curated 98-item diagnostic slice, and additionally characterized on an overlap-inclusive 198-item GDP-v2-lite silver set. Across four VLMs, we find that evidence-first prompting is not a universal improvement: under the same hard-distractor probe, some models improve hard-condition accuracy or reduce distractor selection, while others show lower hard-condition accuracy or increased distractor selection. We therefore argue that MCQ-based VLM evaluation should report distractor sensitivity together with model-dependent intervention response, rather than aggregate accuracy alone.
A107RESOURCEFoodVitals: A Diagnostic Benchmark for LLMs on Nutritional Literacy, Nutrient–Health Relations, and Food Safety
Nilufar Khodzhaeva (Sejong University) · Chaebin Jeong (Sejong University) · Hyeren Yu (Sejong University) · Donghyeon Park (Sejong University)
Abstract
Large Language Models (LLMs) are increasingly fine-tuned and deployed for nutrition and food-related advisory roles, yet their foundational food knowledge is rarely audited before deployment. We introduce FoodVitals, a public benchmark of 1,158 verified items spanning three high-stakes aspects of food knowledge: nutritional literacy, nutrient–health relations, and food safety. Each aspect is grounded in an authoritative source (USDA, EFSA, USDA FSIS), and the benchmark uses multiple answer formats (multiple-choice (MCQ), Yes/No (Y/N), short answer, and ranking) to characterize model performance across these aspects and assess within-aspect format sensitivity.
