Evaluating six instruction-following LLMs reveals two consistent patterns: (i) models that correctly identify the highest-nutrient food in a multiple-choice setting show markedly weaker ranking and uneven threshold-checking on the same nutrients, revealing a gap between coarse-grained nutritional knowledge and precise magnitude reasoning; and (ii) food-safety performance varies substantially across answer formats even when all formats draw from the same regulatory topic set, meaning a high score in one format does not reflect uniform competence across that topic area. Together, these patterns show that single-format evaluation gives an incomplete picture of where an LLM is unreliable and motivate multi-format auditing before high-stakes food deployment.
A108SHORTAuditing Ethical Value Misalignment in LLM-Based Human Simulation: A Dual-Metric Cross-National Study with Persona Injection
Yena Choi (Hanyang University) · Kyungsik Han (Hanyang University)
Abstract
In this paper, we propose MIRAGE (Misalignment and Representation Audit for Global Ethical Simulation), a cross-national, multi-LLM framework that empirically audits how faithfully persona-injected LLMs represent human ethical values along two axes: directional bias—a systematic skew of LLM responses toward a particular ethical direction—and distributional diversity—how well LLM responses preserve the spread of human responses. Our method (1) constructs a seven-category taxonomy from the 23 items in the World Values Survey (WVS) Wave 7 Ethical Values and Norms section, (2) generates 10,000 stratified personas per country across eight countries from WVS demographic distributions and injects them into LLMs, and (3) measures ethical value misalignment between LLM and human responses. Category-level paired tests (7 categories × 3 LLMs = 21 comparisons) reveal significant human–LLM differences in 18 of 21 for distributional diversity and 12 of 21 for directional bias, with the item-level tests (23 items × 3 LLMs = 69 comparisons) confirming that this misalignment is pervasive (44/69). LLMs show lower distributional diversity than humans across nearly all categories, indicating that they fail to represent response diversity, and LLMs show lower permissiveness in Dishonesty & Corruption, while directional bias in Political Violence varies by model. These findings demonstrate that researchers should jointly audit LLM-based personas for directional bias and distributional diversity before using them as proxies for human populations.
A109SHORTWhen Cheap Answers Are Not Delivered Answers: Contract-Aware Costing and Repair for Multilingual LLM Systems
Bowen Jiang (Shanghai Jiao Tong University) · Tao Yao (Shanghai Jiao Tong University)
Abstract
Multilingual LLM systems are often paid to deliver objects, not merely facts: localized final answers, parseable sections, visible traces, or JSON fields consumed by downstream tools. Standard cost per correct answer (CPC) prices factual correctness but can ignore whether the requested object was delivered. We operationalize Contract-Aware Delivered-Answer Evaluation: specify a visible language/format contract, label reliable delivery as correctness plus non-truncation plus contract compliance, replay deployable verifier-triggered repairs, and compare system variants by cost per reliable-correct delivered answer (CPRC). In a 5,040-output human-reviewed MGSM audit over six models, seven languages, and four requested language-path contracts, the English-trace/target-answer condition preserves 89.7% answer accuracy but falls to 53.7% visible reliable-correct delivery. Under target-final-only scoring, where the trace is ignored, delivery remains 62.0%, so the mismatch persists even without scoring the trace. Under the fixed English-trace/target deliverable, CPC and CPRC select different lowest-cost deployable prompt or visible-verifier repair variants in 19/35 complete model-language cells (problem-level bootstrap 95% interval: 16–22). DeepSeek/GPT account for 12 disagreements and the largest finite penalties, with median CPRC penalties of 3.07× and 2.77×; in 8 cells, the CPC-selected variant delivers zero reliable-correct outputs. A 500-output triple-labeled reliability check yields Fleiss' ?=0.911 for visible-contract compliance and ?=0.961 for reliable delivery. We release the ContractCostBench protocol and code, including contract specifications, prompt templates, visible-verifier logic, and rerun scripts. Belebele final-text and search-style JSON views show how the same contract-cost ledger extends to non-MGSM contracts. For the audited systems, visible compliance is not only an instruction-following label; it is a costed deployment variable.
A110SHORTWhen Is Debateability a Model Property? Cross-Interlocutor Validation in Multi-Agent Debate
Chan-Yang Ju (Hanyang University) · Jae-Young Kim (Hanyang University) · Dong-Ho Lee (Hanyang University)
Abstract
Multi-agent debate (MAD) evaluations often treat resistance to false persuasion and receptiveness to truthful correction as model-level capabilities. We test whether such persuasion-derived scores support stable target-model inference in a controlled one-turn target–interlocutor persuasion setting. Across multiple models, interlocutors, and reasoning benchmarks, single-context scores fail to identify reliable target rankings and are strongly conditioned on the interlocutor. Leave-one-interlocutor-out evaluation shows that aggregating multiple interlocutors partially recovers a transferable combined signal, but the component behaviors generalize differently, with false-attack resistance remaining weakly transferable. Independently sampled response instability predicts acceptance of both false attacks and truthful corrections, indicating that answer revision is not inherently evidence of successful deliberation. In our downstream pruning setting, fixed-interlocutor rankings do not provide consistent cross-task evidence of agent contribution. These findings establish that interlocutor sampling is part of the measurement design and that single-interlocutor persuasion scores should not be interpreted as stable target-only properties of persuasion behavior without cross-interlocutor validation.
A111SHORTHuman Indirect Prompting Vulnerabilities and Intention-Aware Conversational Defenses for Large Language Models
Unais Sait (Free University of Bozen-Bolzano) · Saravanakumar Duraisamy (University of Luxembourg)
Abstract
Large Language Models (LLMs) can explain sensitive topics across domains, but harmful goals may be concealed behind educational, fictional, historical, or research-oriented framing. We study Human Indirect Prompting (HIP), a conversation-level behavior in which a user steers an LLM toward restricted information without explicitly stating the unsafe objective. We construct a controlled, redacted dataset of 25 HIP prompts spanning five risk domains and ten prompting strategies, and evaluate five LLM families. Across 123 valid responses, indirect prompting achieves an overall attack success rate of 53.66% with substantial cross-model and cross-strategy variation. We then introduce Controller-Guided Intention-Aware Conversational Defense (IACD), a wrapper that uses structured experiment context and conversation-level control before the target model completes a request. In an ablation study using the most and least vulnerable target models from the five-model evaluation, direct harmful leakage is 88% and 20%, respectively, and falls to 0% under controller-guided conditions. Exact paired tests confirm significant reductions relative to direct prompting. These results characterize HIP and provide initial evidence for dialogue-level safety control, while the controlled use of benchmark intent metadata limits claims about autonomous intent inference.
A112FULLFortMem: Secure Stateful Data Management for Long-Term LLM Agent Memory
Zening Li (Beijing Institute of Technology) · Hongchao Qin (Beijing Institute of Technology) · Guang Zeng (Ant Group) · Rong-Hua Li (Beijing Institute of Technology)
Abstract
Long-term LLM agent memory has become a critical state layer where records are written once and reused across sessions, turning prompt poisoning from a one-shot hazard into persistent database corruption. Traditional stateless RAG defenses reset per query and fail to evaluate the trustworthiness of persistent records over time. To address this, we present FortMem, a structurally robust memory layer, and PASTP (Provenance-Anchored Signed Trust Propagation), a zero-trainable-parameter trust score that formulates provenance as the teleport vector over a signed ANN–NLI corroboration graph. Theoretically, our Closed-Coalition and Open-Boundary Trust Caps prove that adversarial coalitions can inflate trust solely via their boundary fraction, a runtime-measurable structural channel. To counter advanced provenance spoofing, an enhanced variant (PASTP+) automatically audits and demotes the priors of spoofed records contradicted by trusted neighbors. Extensive evaluations across three real-passage memory stores demonstrate that PASTP maintains resilient retrieval correctness under persistent poisoning, whereas vanilla dense retrieval degrades catastrophically. Furthermore, our boundary diagnostic accurately detects 96.3% of poisoned snapshots with zero false alarms, and downstream evaluations confirm that FortMem severely limits poisoned-answer adoption without compromising standard generative capabilities.
A113FULLSpecGuard: Source-Aware Heterogeneous Agent Placement for Defending LLM-Based Multi-Agent Systems against Adversarial Communication
Yiting Wang (Beijing Normal University) · Mingyue Wang (Beijing Normal University) · Luoxun Liu (Beijing Normal University) · Yu Guo (Beijing Normal University) · Xufeng Zhang (Ant Group) · Shuang Liu (Ant Group)
Abstract
Large Language Model based Multi-Agent Systems (LLM-MAS) have emerged as a powerful paradigm for solving complex tasks through collaboration among multiple agents. Nevertheless, this graph-structured communication inherently introduces a vulnerable attack surface, allowing adversarial instructions to propagate from compromised nodes across the entire system. Existing defenses often rely on runtime intervention or topology modification, which are often inapplicable to practical LLM-MAS deployments constrained by fixed communication structures, predefined roles, and execution protocols. A practical alternative is to selectively upgrade some agents to stronger model backbones before deployment. However, upgrading all agents to strong-tier models is costly, and the placement decision should be source-aware because adversarial content enters from specific attacker agents. To address this problem, we propose SpecGuard, a heterogeneous agent placement framework for fixed-topology LLM-MAS. SpecGuard upgrades a small set of weak agents before execution while preserving the original graph, agent set, and runtime protocol. Within SpecGuard, we design H-NetShield, a source-aware algorithm that estimates the exposure risk considering attacker locations, graph structure, deliberation horizon, and calibrated model susceptibility. It also incorporates a structural score to reduce redundant placements caused by overlapping protection. Empirical evaluations on CommonsenseQA across representative topologies demonstrate that upgrading just a single selected agent recovers 54.8%-90.3% of the defense benefit of an all-strong deployment. Moreover, H-NetShield further outperforms common graph-based baselines, and its exposure risk aligns well with empirical attack success rates.
A114FULLRevealing Hidden Vulnerabilities in Autoencoders via Gradient Signal Restoration
Chethan Krishnamurthy Ramanaik (University of the Bundeswehr Munich) · Arjun Roy (University of the Bundeswehr Munich) · Tobias Callies (University of the Bundeswehr Munich) · Eirini Ntoutsi (University of the Bundeswehr Munich)
Abstract
Adversarial robustness of deep autoencoders (AEs) has received less attention than that of discriminative models, although their compressed latent representations induce ill-conditioned mappings that can amplify small input perturbations and destabilize reconstructions. Existing white-box attacks for AEs, which optimize norm-bounded adversarial perturbations to maximize reconstruction damage, often converge to suboptimal perturbations, thereby potentially overstating AE robustness. We show that this limitation is linked to vanishing adversarial loss gradients during backpropagation through ill-conditioned layers, associated with near-zero singular values in their intermediate weight matrices. To address this, we propose GRILL (Gradient Signal Restoration in Ill-Conditioned Layers), a framework designed to mitigate gradient degradation and improve the reliability of adversarial robustness evaluation in encoder--decoder architectures. GRILL is designed to mitigate adversarial gradient degradation during optimization, enabling attacks to better approximate high-distortion perturbations under fixed norm constraints. Through extensive experiments across multiple AE architectures, under both sample-specific and universal attacks, as well as standard and adaptive attack settings, we show that GRILL significantly increases attack effectiveness, thereby exposing vulnerabilities hidden by existing attack limitations. Beyond AEs, we provide preliminary evidence that modern multimodal encoder–decoder architectures exhibit similar vulnerabilities.
A115SHORTSemantic Boundary: A Framework and Benchmark for Policy-Constrained Semantic Disclosure
Gaurav Baruah (Nimble Notions Inc.)
Abstract
Privacy-preserving AI systems must determine what information crosses from trusted collection contexts into downstream analytics, observability, evaluation, and agentic workflows. Existing approaches such as redaction, tokenization, and sanitized rewriting primarily limit disclosure by transforming surface representations. However, modern AI systems depend on feedback loops over operational traces (e.g., conversations, tool use, logs, and reports), and aggressive suppression can remove the semantic information they need for debugging, monitoring, evaluation, and learning. This challenge is particularly acute for longitudinal behavioural traces: interaction routines and inferred intent can function as identifying signatures even after explicit identifiers have been removed. Privacy and utility are therefore coupled through the semantic information that remains available after privacy-preserving transformations have been applied. We introduce Semantic Boundary, a framework for reasoning about what meaning may cross system boundaries under explicit disclosure policies and downstream purposes. Under this framework, sensitive inputs are transformed into policy-governed exports with transformation provenance before release to a downstream consumer. To evaluate alternative disclosure strategies, we construct the Semantic Boundary Benchmark (SBB), a counterfactual export-lattice benchmark over synthetic behavioural traces with injected sensitive attributes, quasi-identifiers, latent behavioural patterns, analytical tasks, and provenance targets. We find that risk-constrained selection on this lattice varies by registered purpose and linkage tolerance: surface-token suppression can coexist with persona re-linking; different tasks favour different lattice conditions; and forcing one condition across consumers incurs measurable utility regret. SBB makes these purpose-conditioned comparisons measurable and reproducible.
A116SHORTAdaptive Authorization Execution for Authorized Retrieval via TFHE-Aware Predicate Compilation
Mi Yeon Hong (Korea University) · Ji Won Yoon (Korea University)
Abstract
Modern retrieval and RAG systems commonly fill a candidate set before enforcing access, allowing unauthorized documents to consume candidate slots and displace authorized evidence. We present an authorization-aware routing operator under bitwise TFHE. Its attribute-family TFHE compiler (AFTC) reuses public predicate instances across policy templates, while repeated policy nodes can execute through a shared DAG. We evaluate two real-TFHE paths separately: a Base-ADAPT execution path that selects between per-template and shared-DAG execution, and a fixed-PT AFTC compiler ablation. We do not report an end-to-end AFTC-adaptive runtime. At the largest tested setting, Base-ADAPT achieves a 7.39±0.14× speedup over Naive-DOC, whereas AFTC-PT achieves a 1.918±0.012× speedup over Base-PT. A five-seed MS MARCO replay using the ABAC Lab E-Document workload for the view action raises Recall@10 from 0.382 to 0.513 among answerable query–user pairs (10.8% mean coverage), with a conditional mean routed-corpus fraction of 39.5% over that subset. A trusted policy enforcement point (PEP) materializes routes and performs exact final enforcement. The large-corpus experiment replays a common BM25 run with a plaintext authorization oracle; it does not measure full-corpus TFHE retrieval or physical-index latency.
A117FULLSURF: Subtractive Updates for Recommender Forgetting
Filippo Betello (Sapienza University of Rome) · Antonio Purificato (Sapienza University of Rome) · Nicola Tonellotto (University of Pisa) · Fabrizio Silvestri (Sapienza University of Rome)
Abstract
The increasing demand for user privacy and compliance with regulations such as GDPR has made machine unlearning a fundamental requirement for modern recommender systems. However, Sequential Recommender Systems (SRS) pose unique challenges for unlearning due to their reliance on temporal interaction patterns. Existing approaches either require computationally prohibitive full retraining or fail to account for the sequential nature of user behavior. We propose SURF (Subtractive Updates for Recommender Forgetting), a lightweight framework for approximate machine unlearning in SRS. SURF operates in three stages: (i) identifying the neighborhood of the entity to forget via K-nearest neighbors in the embedding space, (ii) training an auxiliary model on this compact local subset, and (iii) subtracting the auxiliary model's scores from the original model at inference time. Experiments against five baselines on 7 datasets show that SURF achieves unlearning effectiveness comparable to full retraining while substantially reducing computational cost, yielding up to a 32% improvement in NDCG and requiring as little as 0.02x of the retraining time. We share our code at https://github.com/FilippoBetello/SURF .
A118SHORTToward TabUL Rasa in Tabular Diffusion Models
Jeroen M. Galjaard (Delft University of Technology) · Chaoyi Zhu (Delft University of Technology) · Robert Birke (University of Turin) · Pin-Yu Chen (IBM Research) · Lydia Y. Chen (University of Neuchâtel)
Abstract
Generative models are increasingly adopted as they become more capable of synthesizing realistic data. Across various domains, this has urged improved control of the data that influence their behavior. Central herein is the ability to remove or alter data used during training post-hoc. While unlearning methods show promise for visual and language generators, they remain understudied in the tabular context. Both generally and specifically in attribute-level (column) data removal. In this work, we aim to empirically characterize the latter vertical unlearning using our proposed framework to quantify the ability of post-training methods to remove features (columns). Our evaluation of existing unlearners and a new variant, Vertical Negative Preference Optimization, provides insights into the dynamics of feature removal. Therewith uncovering a consistent limitation: categorical features pose an additional challenge. Our code is available online: https://gitlab.ewi.tudelft.nl/dmls/publications/tabul-rasa.
A119FULLQD-RDFL: Resources-decoupled Collaborative Computation for Data Assetization
Jianzhe Zhao (Northeastern University) · Feida Zhu (Singapore Management University) · Lingyan He (Northeastern University) · Zixin Tang (Northeastern University) · Mingce Gao (Northeastern University) · Shiyu Yang (Northeastern University) · Guibing Guo (Northeastern University)
Abstract
Computation is increasingly collaborative: data, models, and computing resources are indispensable yet rarely co-located. As their demands grow, especially the computational requirements of modern large language models, it is increasingly impractical for any participant to simultaneously possess high-quality data, advanced models, and sufficient computing resources. In settings such as federated learning (FL), participants typically control only one component; for example, a hospital may own patient data but lack powerful models or large-scale computing resources. We refer to this emerging paradigm as resource-decoupled collaborative computation. A key challenge to its sustainability is fair reward attribution, as data, ubiquitous yet critical to model quality, becomes a valuable digital asset. We propose a Resource-Decoupled FL framework (RDFL) that enables data owners, model owners, and computing centers to jointly train high-quality global models while maximizing data assetization value. We introduce a Tripartite Stackelberg Model for global utility optimization under strategic interaction and develop QD-RDFL, a Quality-aware Dynamic Resource-Decoupled FL algorithm that quantifies data-quality contributions and allocates rewards accordingly. Experiments demonstrate the effectiveness and robustness of our approach.
A120SHORTCorrelation-Guided Latent Sharing for Non-IID Federated Learning
Mahran Jazi (Tel Aviv University) · Sharva Gogawale (Tel Aviv University) · Irad Ben-Gal (Tel Aviv University)
Abstract
Federated learning (FL) enables collaborative model training across distributed clients without centralizing raw data, but its performance often degrades under non-independent and non-identically distributed (non-IID) data. This degradation is especially severe when clients observe only a limited subset of the global label space, causing biased local updates and client drift. Standard aggregation methods such as FedAvg and FedProx mainly address this problem at the optimization level, but they do not directly enrich the incomplete local data distributions that cause heterogeneity. This paper proposes Correlation-Guided Latent Sharing (CGLS), a federated learning framework that selectively augments client training using latent information received from statistically aligned peers. CGLS identifies compatible clients through gradient-direction correlation and mixes local training data with synthetic latent information from correlated neighbors. We formulate this process as a mixed-distribution federated objective and explain how targeted mixing can reduce gradient dispersion under severe label skew. Experiments on MNIST, FashionMNIST and CIFAR-10 under Dirichlet and balanced one-class non-IID partitions show that CGLS improves accuracy and macro-F1 over FedAvg and FedProx, with the largest gains appearing in the strongest heterogeneity settings.
A121FULLFedCSN: Mitigating Skewed Feature via Class-wise Selective Normalization in Federated Learning
Haojie Sun (Hohai University) · Zhihao Qu (Hohai University) · Yanyan Wang (Hohai University) · Wenxuan Zhou (Hohai University) · Ninghui Jia (Hohai University) · Baoliu Ye (Nanjing University)
Abstract
Federated learning (FL) enables multiple distributed clients to collaboratively train a shared model without directly exchanging raw data. However, heterogeneous feature distributions across clients often lead to inconsistent local optimization and degraded model performance. Existing normalization-based augmentation methods attempt to alleviate this issue through cross-client statistic sharing. Nevertheless, most existing methods do not explicitly consider class consistency during normalization perturbation, where statistics from different classes may be indiscriminately applied to local samples. Through our investigation, we observe that class-consistent statistic sharing can improve model performance, while cross-class statistic perturbation may introduce noisy augmentation under heterogeneous edge environments. Motivated by these observations, we propose FedCSN, a lightweight normalization-based augmentation framework based on class-wise selective normalization for FL under feature distribution skew. Specifically, FedCSN constructs class-wise normalization statistics from local datasets and adopts an adaptive dominant-class statistic selection strategy to improve the reliability of uploaded class-wise statistics. During local training, each sample is augmented using normalization statistics associated with its class label, thereby reducing cross-class statistic mismatch. Extensive experiments demonstrate that FedCSN achieves the highest dataset-level average accuracy among the evaluated methods across all three datasets using both AlexNet and ResNet18 under severe Non-IID settings. In particular, using AlexNet, FedCSN improves the average accuracy on Office-Caltech-10 by 6.12 percentage points compared with the state-of-the-art normalization-based augmentation method. The source code is publicly available at https://github.com/MereIN0211/FedCSN.
A122FULLFedMCS: Federated Multi-Granularity Chemical-Semantic Distillation for Molecular Graph Learning
Xingjie Zeng (School of Computer and Software Engineering, Southwest Petroleum University) · Bin Xiong (School of Computer and Software Engineering, Southwest Petroleum University) · Cheng Shi (School of Computer and Software Engineering, Southwest Petroleum University) · Shuai Wang (School of Computer and Software Engineering, Southwest Petroleum University) · Chong Zhang (School of Computer and Software Engineering, Southwest Petroleum University) · Cheng Zhong (National Key Laboratory of Oil and Gas Reservoir Geology and Exploitation, Southwest Petroleum University)
Abstract
Federated molecular learning enables collaborative molecular property prediction across distributed institutions while keeping raw molecular graphs decentralized. However, most existing federated molecular methods transfer knowledge through shared parameters, whole-molecule representations, or label-dependent prototypes. This makes collaboration vulnerable to scaffold, domain, endpoint, and label-space heterogeneity. These coarse or task-bound signals struggle to capture chemical patterns that can be reused across clients while remaining consistent with each client's local prediction objective. To address these issues, we propose Federated Multi-granularity Chemical-Semantic Distillation (FedMCS), which builds a reusable substructure-level channel regularized by a fixed fingerprint prior. FedMCS summarizes client-side substructure embeddings as compact Gaussian prototypes, allowing recurring chemical motifs to serve as transferable carriers while raw molecular graphs and task heads remain local. A gate conditioned on a client-local task embedding selectively reuses refined global mean prototypes when the same fragment has different relevance across endpoints. On the server, Soft Chemical Distillation regularizes prototype relations with fingerprint-derived similarity, encouraging the shared prototype space to preserve a fingerprint-induced neighborhood structure. Experiments on eight MoleculeNet benchmarks show that FedMCS consistently outperforms federated baselines in intra-dataset scaffold non-IID settings and obtains the best weighted average among collaborative methods in the cross-dataset setting. These results support substructure prototypes as an effective transfer granularity for federated molecular learning.
A123SHORTMany Cultures, One Label: Investigating Cultural Alignment in Harmful Meme Detection
Gian Marco Orlando (University of Naples Federico II) · Marco Perillo (University of Naples Federico II) · Diego Russo (University of Bergamo) · Ilaria Picariello (University of Naples Federico II) · Valerio La Gatta (Northwestern University) · Vincenzo Moscato (University of Naples Federico II)
Abstract
Harmful meme detection has become an important multimodal classification task. However, existing approaches are trained and evaluated against a single ground-truth binary label (harmful/not harmful), implicitly assuming a universal notion of harmfulness despite evidence that perceptions of harmful content are shaped by cultural and social context. In this paper, we investigate whether culture-aligned Large Language Model (LLM) agents can surface cross-cultural variation in harmful meme perception and reveal potential biases in benchmark annotations. To this end, we instantiate six culture-aligned LLM agents. Given a meme, each agent independently evaluates its harmfulness and provides a culturally grounded rationale. These assessments are integrated with OCR text and image captions into a concept graph representation of the meme, and combined with complementary vision language features to train a downstream classifier. Experiments on the Facebook Hateful Memes (FHM) benchmark show that the resulting model achieves competitive performance (AUC = 0.804), outperforming several baselines. More importantly, our analysis reveals substantial cross-cultural variation: the six agents disagree on 34.9% of 10,000 evaluated memes, while maintaining an overall agreement level (k = 0.690) remarkably close to that reported for human annotators (k = 0.684). We further find significant differences in alignment with the ground-truth labels, with agents representing Brazil, South Africa, and the United States exhibiting consistently higher agreement than agents representing India, Japan, and Saudi Arabia. These findings suggest that harmfulness benchmarks may implicitly privilege particular cultural interpretations of harmful content.
A124FULLAttribution as Click: Understanding and Modeling Attribution Bias in RAG
Maryam Mousavian (Università della Svizzera italiana) · Mohammad Aliannejadi (University of Amsterdam) · Chen Xu (Renmin University of China) · Fabio Crestani (Università della Svizzera italiana)
Abstract
Retrieval-augmented generation (RAG) grounds LLM outputs in retrieved documents to address hallucination, but its retrieval-and-generation pipeline could still introduce various biases. Prior work studies biases such as social bias only in generated content while overlooking the bias present in the cited references, referred to as attribution bias. In this paper, we study gender-related attribution bias in RAG, addressing three questions: (i) with the ranking fixed, how do document position and gender shape citation decisions; (ii) in a realistic ranking setup with various irrelevant documents in the ranking, how does the gender composition of irrelevant documents influence attribution; and (iii) how are relevance, position, and gender associated with attribution after conditioning on the other measured factors? Across open-ended RAG experiments with four LLMs, document position strongly affects attribution, neutral documents partially absorb gendered citation preferences, and model-specific gender preferences persist after controlling for position and relevance. Attribution bias is therefore jointly shaped by retrieval and generator behavior. Our framework positions whom a RAG system cites as an axis of fairness alongside what it says.
A125SHORTExplaining Neural Combinatorial-Optimisation Policies: LP-Weighted Attribution, CSP-Certified Counterfactuals, and Bonferroni-PAC Sufficient Subsets
Sohaib Afifi (Univ. Artois)
Abstract
Most neural policies for combinatorial optimisation (CO) rely on opaque autoregressive decoders. Operators therefore cannot tell whether a routing or scheduling choice is driven by a near-binding capacity, a tight time window, a budget envelope, or a geometric shortcut. We introduce CAX, a post-hoc explainer built around three primitives from the constraint-programming relaxation already supplied by the problem. The Λ primitive is a Lagrangian-weighted gradient × feature decomposition that scales each family's attribution by its LP shadow price. The ζ primitive is a sample-and-verify counterfactual whose accepted perturbations carry a CSP feasibility certificate. The S primitive is a Bonferroni-corrected Hoeffding sufficient-subset test. Along the greedy attribution ordering, this test bounds the smallest subset of nodes that preserves the policy's argmax, with family-wise probability 1-δ. We compare three multiplier backends using the counterfactual-derived signal on CVRPTW, OP, and FJSP, which have contrasting rank profiles. In the rank-mismatch regime, the LP-anchored backend improves over the proxy gradient by +21.5 and +42.0 percentage points on CVRPTW and OP, respectively (McNemar p ≤ 10-14 on ≥ 281 certified flips). In the rank-aligned FJSP regime, it matches the proxy, with both backends reaching 100% on the 59 certified flips. This pattern supports CAX's account of when LP duals add information and when they do not. Across a 54-configuration robustness sweep, the CF-derived top family remains unchanged on all three problems.
A126SHORTWhen Representation Drift Does Not Reflect Functional Contribution: A Regime Analysis of Prompt Tuning
Asma Ben Ali (University of Bordeaux) · Sujay Uday Rittikar (University of Winnipeg) · Sheela Ramanna (University of Winnipeg)
Abstract
Representation similarity metrics are commonly used to validate parameter-efficient fine-tuning (PEFT) methods that adapt large pre-trained language models by updating only a small subset of parameters under the implicit assumption that a large drift implies meaningful adaptation. In the encoder-based classification settings of this study, we demonstrate that this assumption is regime-dependent rather than universal. In Regime A (frozen encoder, trainable classifier), learned soft prompts exhibit drift comparable to Low-Rank Adaptation (LoRA) yet are entirely dispensable: removing, scaling, or randomizing them changes fewer than 0.3% of predictions (well within the variance of a random seed). A geometric decomposition explains this: 98% of prompt drift lies in the null space of the multi-class classifier weight matrix, computed across all heads and five seeds. In Regime B (frozen encoder, frozen task-fitted head, trainable prompts), we run two controlled variants: (B1) head taken from a converged Regime A model and (B2) head re-initialised from a different random seed. We find consistent, statistically significant gains in both, ruling out re-alignment artifacts. In Regime C, C(LoRA) and C(BitFit) produce representational drift of comparable Centered Kernel Alignment (CKA) magnitude that aligns closely with the decision boundary (orthogonal fraction 0.52–0.55), yielding large performance gains. Three similarity metrics, namely CKA, Singular Vector Canonical Correlation Analysis (SVCCA), and Projection-Weighted Canonical Correlation Analysis (PWCCA), agree on drift magnitude across every regime yet cannot distinguish functional from non-functional adaptation. We do not claim these metrics are generally invalid; rather, we characterise the specific architectural condition under which they become uninformative, that is, the presence of a free trainable component downstream of the drift source.
A127SHORTAttention to those tokens! Ensemble Clustering can explain Attention-based Text Classifiers
Fabrizio Angiulli (University of Calabria) · Francesco De Luca (University of Calabria) · Fabio Fassetti (University of Calabria)
Abstract
Recent research has questioned the reliability of attention weights as faithful explanations for Transformer-based text classifiers, showing that highly attended tokens are not necessarily responsible for model predictions and that attention distributions can be manipulated without affecting outputs. In this work, we argue that, although attention scores alone are not suitable feature-importance measures, attention patterns still encode meaningful semantic relationships among tokens that can be exploited for explainability purposes. We propose ECAM (Ensemble Clustering from Attention Maps), a novel framework for attention-based text classifiers. ECAM leverages attention maps extracted from Transformer layers to build token similarity structures and identify semantically coherent token clusters through an ensemble clustering strategy. We demonstrate that clusters produced by ECAM can be used to produce faithful explanations while requiring substantially fewer black-box evaluations than perturbation-based approaches such as LIME. Importantly, since ECAM is agnostic to the explanation task, in that it relies on semantically-driven token aggregations induced by attention patterns, our findings also provide broader evidence about the intrinsic relational properties encoded by Transformer attention mechanisms. This suggests that attention maps capture stable explainability-oriented relational structures beyond their direct use as token-importance indicators.
A128SHORTWhen Do Gradient-Based Explanations Identify Important Video Frames? A Global-Local Evaluation of Time-Series Explanations
Min Hun Lee (Singapore Management University)
Abstract
Gradient-based methods are widely used to explain deep video models, yet their ability to identify temporally important evidence remains insufficiently understood. We study gradient-based video explanation as frame-level temporal evidence detection. Using a global-local spatiotemporal attention network trained with weak video-level labels, we convert VanillaGrad, SmoothGrad, and Grad-CAM outputs into frame-level importance scores and evaluate them against annotated activity frames across four medically relevant video classification tasks. The results show that combining full-frame global views with local region-of-interest views improves both video classification and important-frame detection. The global-local model achieves 96.49 F1 for classification, and its SmoothGrad explanations achieve 86.68 F1 for important-frame detection. At the same time, the evaluation reveals failure modes: Grad-CAM is less effective for the transformer-based model, and CNN-based gradients are more reliable for long videos. These findings suggest that video explanations should be evaluated by their ability to identify relevant frames, not only by visual inspection of saliency heatmaps.
A129FULLAdversarial Edge Generation: A Generator-Discriminator Game for Sparse Graph Learning
Jianxin Ren (Harbin Engineering University) · Weining Wu (Harbin Engineering University)
Abstract
Most existing graph learning methods are limited by the sparsity of the initial graph, which leads to biased node classification on the refined graph structure. Although adversarial training has shown strong performance in computer vision tasks, there is still no study that uses adversarial training to generate edges that approximate the true data distribution on a graph. In this work, we propose AEG (Adversarial Edge Generation), a generator-discriminator game framework for sparse graph learning. By incorporating high-confidence edges and hard negative edges into adversarial training, we perform edge adversarial generation on the sparse graph. This allows us to obtain a reliable refined graph that approximates the true data distribution, and then supports the following node classification. Moreover, to address the imbalance and sparsity issues in the refined graph, we introduce a new pseudo-label evaluation strategy in which edges between unlabeled nodes and labeled nodes are added to improve connectivity on the graph, based on their prediction confidence, neighborhood information and structural centrality. Experimental results show that AEG can effectively perform both edge generation and node classification, even on extremely sparse graphs.
A130FULLRAD: Rule-Augmented Relational Anomaly Detection
Noah Dahle (Vanderbilt University) · Anne Tumlin (Vanderbilt University) · Ngoc Tran (Vanderbilt University) · Xenofon Koutsoukos (Vanderbilt University) · Tyler Derr (Vanderbilt University)
Abstract
Anomaly detection is often applied to relational databases, yet most existing methods require flattening multiple tables into a single feature matrix. This can obscure entity identity, schema structure, and multi-hop dependencies, limiting detection of anomalies that depend on relational context rather than isolated feature values. Relational anomaly detection also raises the challenge of incorporating symbolic behavioral evidence into learned relational representations. We propose RAD, a rule-augmented relational anomaly detector that combines heterogeneous graph representation learning with refined symbolic rule signals. RAD derives candidate rules from random-forest paths over flattened entity or event summaries, refines them into compact predicates, injects the resulting rule features into the graph model, and learns anomaly scores using reconstruction and pairwise-ranking supervision. We introduce a relational anomaly detection benchmark spanning three settings: LANL cybersecurity event detection and two unexpected user-churn tasks derived from Amazon and H&M relational databases. RAD improves anomaly ranking over flattened tabular detectors and relational baselines under natural class imbalance, achieving the best average rank on AUROC and AUPRC across the benchmark. Ablations show that direct rule injection and ranking-based supervision are key contributors to performance, while edge reconstruction is not uniformly beneficial. Code and data are available at https://github.com/noahd15/RAD_RelationalAnomalyDetection.
A131FULLCapturing Collaborative Structure in Graph Anomaly Detection by MoE-Gated Neural Common Neighbor
Huiling Peng (Zhejiang University) · Tongya Zheng (Hangzhou City University) · Runang He (Zhejiang University) · Jing Cao (Hangzhou City University) · Jiawei Chen (Zhejiang University) · Canghong Jin (Hangzhou City University) · Mingli Song (Zhejiang University) · Can Wang (Zhejiang University)
Abstract
In real-world graphs, anomalies usually exhibit collaborative structure, manifested as densely connected sub-graphs. Capturing multi-hop relationships is essential to identify and characterize the connections among these anomalous nodes. Existing graph anomaly detection (GAD) methods fail to capture such structures due to two core challenges: 1) standard recursive neighbor aggregation paradigm causes over-squashing of high-order neighbor information, which is vital for detecting collaborative suspicious behaviors; 2) different collaboration patterns depend on specific hop counts, with irrelevant hops introducing substantial noise. In this paper, we propose MoE-Gated Common Neighbor Attention (MCNA), an auxiliary parallel branch of the Graph Neural Network based (GNN-based) GAD backbones that can effectively distinguish collaborative structure to enhance the backbone's performance. MCNA explicitly encodes neural common neighbor information to capture the arbitrary k-hop collaborative structure among anomalies. To balance the information and noise from multi-hop neighbors, an MoE mechanism is employed to choose the valuable hops in terms of structural information. The structural collaborative patterns captured by MCNA and the attribute-based patterns captured by backbones are finally fused with a gating mechanism. Extensive experiments on 10 real-world datasets and 8 different backbones demonstrate that MCNA achieves average improvements of 5.36% on AUROC and 7.76% on AUPRC, showcasing the comprehensive universality of our proposed method.
A132SHORTMINT: Mitigating Structural Inconsistency via Attentive Message Passing for Financial Anomaly Detection
Yin-Ju Wu (National Taiwan Normal University) · Bi-Cheng Yan (National Taiwan Normal University) · Berlin Chen (National Taiwan Normal University)
Abstract
Illicit account detection is a critical task for financial risk control systems, aiming to pinpoint malicious actors within transaction networks. Existing efforts typically recast transaction networks into directed multigraphs and leverage graph neural networks (GNNs) to detect anomalies via topological structures under the homophily assumption. However, directly grafting GNNs onto transaction graphs is faced with at least two pivotal challenges, i.e., structural inconsistency and label scarcity. The former arises from deceptive connections forged by malicious actors, while the latter stems from the lack of annotated data. In light of these, we introduce MINT, a novel graph neural framework that mitigates structural inconsistency via an attentive message-passing scheme on transaction graphs. Specifically, MINT introduces a discrepancy-aware feature propagation, which tracks malicious actors by quantifying deviations between nodes across bi-directional transaction flows. A transaction salience module is proposed to mitigate structural inconsistency by adaptively regularizing the interaction strength between nodes. Furthermore, to alleviate label scarcity, MINT is optimized via Positive-Unlabeled (PU) learning, which exploits only a minority of illicit nodes coupled with a majority of unlabeled ones. Extensive experiments conducted on three financial transaction benchmarks, including two large-scale public and one in-house real-world datasets, validate the superior effectiveness of MINT over several cutting-edge baselines.
A133FULLSipu: Accurate Graph-based Positive-Unlabeled Learning under Heterophily
Shihyung Park (Seoul National University) · Junghun Kim (Seoul National University) · U Kang (Seoul National University)
Abstract
How can we accurately train a binary node classifier on heterophilic graphs when only positive and unlabeled nodes are available? This setting commonly arises in real-world applications such as fraud detection, where only detected fraudsters are labeled as positive, while the remaining users are unlabeled and may include both normal users and undetected fraudsters. The key challenge is that heterophilic edges connect nodes from different classes, causing conventional graph-based PU methods to propagate label-inconsistent information. At the same time, simply suppressing such edges discards useful higher-order homophilic information connected through heterophilic paths. This creates a trade-off between reducing negative transfer and preserving structural information, which is further complicated by the absence of negative labels. We propose Sipu, an accurate graph-based PU learning method for heterophilic graphs. Sipu models the given unsigned graph as a latent signed graph, where positive and negative signs correspond to homophilic and heterophilic relations, respectively. Through sign-aware propagation, Sipu mitigates negative transfer from heterophilic neighbors while preserving higher-order homophilic information through positive paths. To accurately estimate unobserved edge signs, Sipu iteratively refines the classifier and the edge-sign estimates using node-label and edge-homophily marginals computed via graphical inference as soft targets. Extensive experiments on multiple datasets demonstrate that Sipu gives state-of-the-art performance, consistently outperforming existing graph-based PU learning methods.
A134FULLFEIM: Fair Event-Aware Influence Maximization Over Microblogs
Chao Zhu (RMIT University) · Xiangmin Zhou (RMIT University) · Junfeng Wu (RMIT University) · Jeffrey Chan (RMIT University) · Chen Li (University of California, Irvine) · Chengkun He (Shenzhen Institute for Advanced Study, University of Electronic Science and Technology of China) · Yanchun Zhang (Victoria University)
Abstract
Microblogs have become an important source for disaster resilience (DR). A typical problem for DR is to maximize the influence of event messages to effectively engage the maximal number of social users in disaster activities. Traditional Influence Maximization (IM) approaches focus on spreading a single message to activate as many users as possible, overlooking that users vary in event sensitivity and propagation capability. As a result, existing methods may overload highly influential users with irrelevant messages while failing to activate poorly connected ones. To overcome these limitations, this paper proposes the Fair Event-aware IM (FEIM) problem and a new framework that coordinates message propagation in an event-sensitive and fair manner. We propose an event-aware social graph that captures each user’s activation probability across different events, and develop a Fair Ensemble Activation (FEA) model with seed selection and diffusion optimization algorithms to ensure equitable propagation. To further improve efficiency, we design a Dijkstra-like Fast Reachability Calculation (DFRC). Extensive tests prove the superiority of FEIM.
A135FULLLEAP: Learning Evolutionary Advantage Policies for Fixation Maximization via Deep Reinforcement Learning
Smita Ghosh (Santa Clara University) · Shivvrat Arya (New Jersey Institute of Technology)
Abstract
Diffusion processes on networks are central to social network analysis and data mining, where influence maximization provides a canonical framework for identifying influential nodes. However, many real-world diffusion processes are competitive and reversible, making classical irreversible influence maximization models inadequate. The positional Moran process captures such dynamics by modeling stochastic competition with position-dependent fitness and motivates the fixation maximization problem: selecting an initial active set that maximizes the probability of eventual population-wide dominance. Existing methods rely on static structural heuristics or simulation-intensive greedy search. These approaches either ignore long-horizon evolutionary effects or scale poorly because they require repeated stochastic simulations. This limitation raises a fundamental question: Can we learn scalable active node selection policies that capture the evolutionary dynamics governing fixation? We answer this question with LEAP, a deep reinforcement learning framework for amortized fixation maximization under the positional Moran process. LEAP formulates active node selection as a Markov decision problem and learns fixation-aware representations that combine graph structure with mutant invasion and stability signals. Its fixation-modulated message passing mechanism models selection pressure through learned fitness contrasts, while fixation-weighted pooling constructs a global evolutionary representation. Experiments on real-world networks show that LEAP matches the solution quality of simulation-based greedy methods with approximately five orders of magnitude faster inference and outperforms all baselines in at least two-thirds of experimental settings. These results show that deep reinforcement learning can optimize long-horizon competitive diffusion when equipped with fixation-aware mechanisms that capture evolutionary dynamics.
A136SHORTCARE: Calibrated Attribute Imputation with Deviation Refinement for Attribute-Missing Graph Clustering
Weilai Chi (Capital Normal University) · Shi Shi (Hangzhou Dianzi University) · Fang-Xiang Wu (University of Saskatchewan) · Yiwei Fu (Peking University) · Xiao Luo (University of Wisconsin–Madison)
Abstract
This paper studies the problem of attribute-missing graph clustering, which involves a subset of nodes with missing attributes. Existing approaches typically integrate neighborhood-aware imputation with graph autoencoders for self-supervised graph learning, resulting in suboptimal performance due to potential imputation biases and representation collapse. To address these issues, we propose Calibrated Attribute Imputation with Deviation Refinement (CARE) for attribute-missing graph clustering. The core of CARE is a self-iterative optimization scheme that jointly improves attribute imputation and graph clustering within a teacher-student framework. Specifically, our CARE introduces two complementary masking strategies, including a fixed permanent masking set and a dynamic temporal masking set, to provide reliable reconstruction supervision. The student network is optimized through attribute reconstruction over all originally observed nodes from corrupted inputs, and the teacher network is optimized using the exponential moving average of the parameters in the student network to provide stable predictions for consistency regularization. In addition, we introduce a deviation refinement strategy to iteratively update cluster prototypes and stabilize representation learning. Experiments on three benchmarks demonstrate the effectiveness and robustness of CARE against seven competing baselines.
A137FULLAligning the Spectrum: Hybrid Graph Pre-training and Prompt Tuning across Homophily and Heterophily
Haitong Luo (Institute of Computing Technology, Chinese Academy of Sciences) · Suhang Wang (The Pennsylvania State University) · Weiyao Zhang (Institute of Computing Technology, Chinese Academy of Sciences) · Ruiqi Meng (Institute of Computing Technology, Chinese Academy of Sciences) · Xuying Meng (Institute of Computing Technology, Chinese Academy of Sciences) · Yujun Zhang (Institute of Computing Technology, Chinese Academy of Sciences)
Abstract
Graph “pre-training and prompt-tuning” aligns downstream tasks with pre-trained objectives to enable efficient knowledge transfer under limited supervision. However, current methods typically rely on single-filter backbones (e.g., low-pass), whereas real-world graphs exhibit inherent spectral diversity. Our theoretical Spectral Specificity principle reveals that effective knowledge transfer requires alignment between pre-trained spectral filters and the intrinsic spectrum of downstream graphs. This identifies two fundamental limitations: (1) Knowledge Bottleneck: single-filter models suffer from irreversible information loss by suppressing signals from other frequency bands (e.g., high-frequency); (2) Utilization Bottleneck: spectral mismatches between pre-trained filters and downstream spectra lead to significant underutilization of pre-trained knowledge. To bridge this gap, we propose HS-GPPT. We utilize a hybrid spectral backbone to construct an abundant knowledge basis. Crucially, we introduce Spectral-Aligned Prompt Tuning, which learns filter-specific prompt graphs to improve spectral alignment between downstream graphs and frozen pre-trained graph filters, facilitating knowledge transfer across both homophily and heterophily. Extensive experiments validate the effectiveness under both transductive and inductive learning settings. Our code is in https://github.com/luohaitong/HS-GPPT.
A138FULLMolecular Knowledge Guided Prompt Adaptation for Pre-trained 2D Graph Encoders
Xingtong Yu (The Chinese University of Hong Kong) · Chang Zhou (University of Science and Technology of China) · Xinming Zhang (University of Science and Technology of China) · Yuan Fang (Singapore Management University)
Abstract
Pre-trained 2D graph encoders have achieved strong performance in molecular representation learning by capturing transferable topological patterns from large-scale unlabeled molecular graphs. However, downstream molecular applications often involve rich chemical and geometric information associated with atoms and bonds, which is not explicitly modeled by conventional 2D graph pre-training approaches. Existing molecular pre-training methods typically incorporate such knowledge during large-scale pre-training, requiring specialized architectures and substantial computational cost. In this paper, we investigate how to enhance pre-trained 2D graph encoders through lightweight downstream prompt adaptation with molecular knowledge. We propose a molecular prompting framework that integrates heterogeneous molecular information into downstream graph learning without modifying the pre-trained encoder parameters. Specifically, molecular knowledge is first projected into the latent space of pre-trained topological representations to reduce the discrepancy between topology and molecular semantics. Based on the aligned representations, we further employ knowledge-conditioned prompt generators to produce adaptive prompts for different molecular components, enabling fine-grained and instance-aware downstream adaptation. The proposed framework can be flexibly incorporated into existing 2D graph pre-training methods while maintaining strong parameter efficiency. Extensive experiments on molecular classification and molecular property prediction benchmarks demonstrate consistent improvements over representative graph pre-training and molecular representation learning baselines, particularly under low-resource settings.
A139FULLCausalExplainer: Causal Explanations for Temporal Graph Neural Networks
Abir Bousmina (RIADI Laboratory, National School of Computer Sciences, University of Manouba) · Mouna Selmi (RIADI Laboratory, National School of Computer Sciences, University of Manouba) · Amel Bouzeghoub (SAMOVAR, Telecom SudParis, Institut Polytechnique de Paris) · Imed Riadh Farah (RIADI Laboratory, National School of Computer Sciences, University of Manouba)
Abstract
Temporal Graph Neural Networks (TGNNs) have demonstrated remarkable performance in modeling complex dynamic interactions over evolving graphs. However, explaining their predictions remains highly challenging because asynchronous temporal dependencies often entangle causal signals with spurious patterns. We introduce CausalExplainer, a causally informed explanation framework that learns intervention-stable latent factors underlying TGNN predictions. Unlike methods that directly explain observed interactions, our approach trains a generative model to disentangle intervention-stable temporal representations from spurious variations. A multi-objective causal formulation promotes compact and faithful explanations by jointly enforcing predictive sufficiency, counterfactual necessity, and disentanglement. To further address biases arising from dynamic graph evolution, we model the confounding effects of temporal node attributes and interaction histories within a disentangled spurious latent space. We then introduce counterfactual perturbations in the learned latent causal space to encourage the identification of intervention-necessary explanatory factors and improve explanation robustness. CausalExplainer is model-agnostic, operates post-hoc on latent representations extracted from diverse TGNN architectures, and does not rely on input feature independence assumptions. Experiments conducted on real-world continuous-time dynamic graph benchmarks using TGN and TGAT demonstrate that CausalExplainer produces explanations that are more faithful and structurally cleaner than those produced by state-of-the-art baselines.
A140SHORTImproved Streaming Algorithm for Balanced Hypergraph Partitioning
Zhicheng Guo (Xidian University)
Abstract
Balanced hypergraph partitioning is an essential task for massive hypergraph analysis in distributed computing. Existing methods usually use the entire hypergraph to obtain structural information before the assignment process. However, many applications require online partitioning, motivating the development of streaming algorithms. In the streaming order, vertices are assigned in real time and their ownership does not change. Therefore, partitioning the streamed vertices under the balance constraint is challenging. In this paper, we propose a method for balanced hypergraph partitioning in the streaming mode. By defining a modularity function under the Erdos-Renyi random hypergraph model, we build the Erdos-Renyi Hypergraph Modularity Greedy. We approximate the hypergraph as a uniform hypergraph and optimize the modularity function with lower computational complexity. Compared with other modularity functions, our modularity function is more suitable for streaming algorithms. Finally, we design a data structure to reduce the execution time for finding the block with minimum capacity. Overall, our method achieves the state-of-the-art performance when evaluated with the cut-net metric.
A141FULLCHARM-Mamba: Calibrated Hierarchical Adaptive Routing Multi-Source Mamba for Cross-City Traffic Prediction
Chuanning Shi (Shanxi University) · Chao Zhang (Shanxi University) · Anna Wang (Shanxi University) · Wentao Li (Southwest University) · Deyu Li (Shanxi University)
Abstract
Cross-city transfer learning is pivotal for traffic prediction in data-scarce regions, yet impeded by structural limitations in existing frameworks. Conventional decoupled spatio-temporal modeling often struggles to fully capture the entangled, topology-dependent nature of congestion propagation. Moreover, indiscriminately aggregating heterogeneous source domains without granular pattern-specific filtering frequently induces negative transfer on incompatible data. Compounding these issues, full-parameter adaptation incurs prohibitive computational costs, severely hindering scalable few-shot deployment in dynamic real-world settings. To address these challenges, this paper proposes CHARM-Mamba, a Calibrated Hierarchical Adaptive Routing Multi-source transfer framework. First, the architecture integrates a Deep-Coupled Mamba backbone where State Space Models and dynamic spatial graphs mutually modulate to learn joint representations. Second, to mitigate negative transfer and support reliable knowledge reuse across heterogeneous sources, a routing mechanism on normalized feature spaces is introduced. By selectively retrieving compatible source prototypes via uncertainty-based calibration, it prioritizes transferable knowledge while discarding irrelevant noise. Third, to ensure parameter efficiency, a lightweight hypernetwork dynamically generates target-specific adapter parameters driven by routed patterns, facilitating pattern-aware adaptation with the backbone frozen. Extensive experiments demonstrate that CHARM-Mamba significantly outperforms state-of-the-art baselines in few-shot generalization. Notably, it achieves up to a 5.7% reduction in Mean Absolute Error (MAE) while utilizing fewer than 5% of the trainable parameters, highlighting its potential for scalable, trustworthy knowledge modeling in dynamic urban environments. The code and datasets used in this paper are available at: https://github.com/JOJOJISHENGWU/CHARM-Mamba.
A142FULLCivicPulse: Efficient Hotspot Mining and Parsing in Municipal Hotline Data
Zhiyuan Zhang (Fudan University) · Luyuan He (Fudan University) · Kai Zhang (Fudan University) · Zhenying He (Fudan University) · Yinan Jing (Fudan University) · X.Sean Wang (Fudan University)
Abstract
Municipal hotlines accumulate massive complaint narratives, yet effective governance requires more than closing individual tickets---it demands hierarchical event understanding: first surfacing recurring hotspots from complaint streams, then parsing each hotspot into actionable sub-events with distinct causes, scenarios, and citizen requests. Two challenges make this difficult. At the hotspot level, expression diversity and administrative ambiguity fragment evidence for the same civic issue, leaving conventional clustering with unstable boundaries. Within each hotspot, shared topical background overwhelms the representation space, masking the fine-grained distinctions needed for targeted intervention. We present CivicPulse, a two-stage framework that addresses both challenges. For hotspot mining, CivicPulse aggregates complementary semantic and administrative evidence to consolidate fragmented complaints into governance-aligned hotspots. For sub-event parsing, it suppresses hotspot-shared background and clusters the residual representations to expose cause- and intent-specific sub-events. On a real-world municipal hotline corpus, CivicPulse achieves a human-judged pairwise hotspot agreement of 0.7137, substantially outperforming density-based, graph-based, and taxonomy-matching baselines. Scenario-based evaluation with municipal hotline staff further confirms that its outputs are more interpretable and better support downstream dispatching and cross-department coordination.
A143FULLQuantifying Event Impacts on Time Series via Multiscale Contrastive Learning
Yiming Sun (Rutgers University) · Shengyu Chen (NEC Laboratories America) · Zhengzhang Chen (NEC Laboratories America) · Haoyu Wang (NEC Laboratories America) · Xiaowei Jia (Rutgers University) · Haifeng Chen (NEC Laboratories America)
Abstract
Shocks that spread through the web, such as cybersecurity breach disclosures, can abruptly disrupt financial time series and cause substantial abnormal losses. While these events are disclosed as discrete records through news reports, regulatory filings, or public databases, their consequences unfold through continuous market dynamics. This creates an event-conditioned impact prediction problem: given pre-event market history and limited event metadata, the goal is to estimate short-term post-disclosure abnormal loss rather than reconstruct the full post-event trajectory. However, most time-series forecasting models focus on endogenous regularities such as trend, seasonality, and autocorrelation, and thus struggle with rare and heterogeneous external events. The challenge is further amplified by sparse high-impact events and background market noise. We introduce EventTime, a multi-resolution framework that combines long-horizon market context, short-horizon pre-event dynamics, and event metadata. It incorporates an event fusion module that couples temporal representations with event attributes to identify relevant recent market patterns. To mitigate sparse supervision, EventTime further introduces a dynamic contrastive objective that constructs event- and time-series-aware positive and negative pairs during training. We also construct SECURE, a real-world dataset aligning cybersecurity incidents with stock-market time series and structured and LLM-derived semantic features. Experiments show that EventTime consistently outperforms state-of-the-art time-series and event-aware baselines in estimating post-event financial losses. Further analyses demonstrate more event-sensitive representations, greater robustness to incomplete metadata, and more interpretable estimates of short-term market impact following cybersecurity disclosures.
A144FULLForecasting Functions, Not Points: Time Series Forecasting via Polynomial-Fourier Coefficient Prediction
Yongdam Kim (Sogang University) · Joonseong Yang (Sogang University) · Hyeonji Park (Sogang University) · Sungwon Jung (Sogang University)
Abstract
Environmental sensor signals, including meteorological, air-quality, and eco-hydrological measurements, are highly characterized by a slowly varying trend and a small number of low-frequency periodic components. In long-term forecasting benchmarks for these signals, the models that explicitly capture trend and seasonality have consistently achieved strong performance. However, in practical deployments, the dominant periods of environmental signals vary between regimes, which heavily forces a deployed forecaster to operate over a wide range of varying prediction horizons H. Standard point forecasting models, such as DLinear, PatchTST, and TimeMixer, tie the output projection weights directly to H. Consequently, any change in the horizon severely increases the decoder parameter count and requires complete, expensive retraining. To the best of our knowledge, no prior studies have proposed a flexible forecasting framework that eliminates this horizon-dependent structural rigidity. Therefore, we propose a novel functional forecasting framework called the Coefficient-prediction Network, which approaches long-term time-series forecasting by predicting the coefficients of a continuous function f(t) composed of polynomial and Fourier terms. The decomposition into trend and seasonality is explicitly encoded in the structure of f(t) itself, allowing the same trained coefficients to be evaluated on any arbitrary target grid without additional parameters or retraining. Since a pure polynomial-Fourier basis captures global trend and periodicity but may not capture the detailed local variations of signals, we further propose a per-sub-window low-rank modulation scheme. This adaptable scheme captures localized fluctuations by perturbing the shared coefficients at a minimal 4% parameter overhead. As a result, the Coefficient-prediction Network successfully achieves the coarse-to-fine prediction property without requiring post-hoc interpolation. Extensive experimental results on four datasets of real-world environmental sensors demonstrate that the proposed approach is robust against varying horizons, attaining state-of-the-art performance in 13 of 16 settings against nine baselines for standard point forecasting.
A145APPLIEDCarbonMix: Exploiting Multi-Scale Dynamics in Carbon Flux Forecasting via Lightweight Slow-Fast Decoupling
Guangan Wang (Inner Mongolia University) · Ruifeng Zhang (Inner Mongolia University) · Xuefei Zhang (Jiangsu Hengwang Digital Technology Co., Ltd.) · Ming Ma (Inner Mongolia University)
Abstract
Carbon flux forecasting is a critical task in large-scale environmental information management, yet extracting actionable predictive knowledge from these datasets remains challenging. The environmental drivers of net ecosystem exchange (NEE) operate on fundamentally different timescales—radiation and turbulent fluxes cycle diurnally, while soil and thermal variables evolve over seasons to years. We present CarbonMix, a lightweight knowledge-driven framework inspired by slow-fast decomposition in dynamical systems theory. CarbonMix separates temporal modeling from cross-variable interaction: a per-variable temporal mixer captures fast periodic patterns (e.g., diurnal cycles), while a low-rank variable mixer captures slow cooperative modes among drivers, conditioned on the current regime via temporal context gating. Spectral analysis across 10 eddy covariance sites confirms that 4 principal components explain approximately 79–84% of cross-variable covariance and that driver timescales span three orders of magnitude—validating the slow-fast prior underlying our design. In our efficiency evaluation on the Weather benchmark, CarbonMix uses 434.4K parameters and 0.07G MACs, remaining substantially smaller than strong multivariate baselines while achieving the best average performance across 10 sites spanning four ecosystem types and competitive performance on public Weather data. We also release a standardized multi-site carbon flux benchmark.
A146FULLPaDi: Patch-wise Decomposition and Latent Interaction for Multivariate Time Series Forecasting
Hengyu Chang (East China Normal University) · Kun Liu (East China Normal University) · Cen Chen (East China Normal University) · Dawei Cheng (Tongji University) · Yuqi Liang (Seek Data Group, Emoney Inc.)
Abstract
Multivariate long-term time series forecasting aims to predict the future trajectories of multiple variables. However, many existing methods oversimplify temporal patches and channel interactions: they encode each raw patch as a single token and model channel relations directly in the original variable space. Such simplification leads to two limitations. At the patch level, raw-patch similarity can diverge from predictive-pattern similarity, since local state shifts may dominate the observed values, even when fluctuation patterns are similar. At the channel level, useful shared dynamics are often concentrated in compact latent structures rather than being uniformly distributed over all pairwise channel interactions. These two limitations reveal patch-level temporal heterogeneity and channel-level structural heterogeneity, suggesting that forecasting models should preserve such structures rather than force them into undifferentiated patch and channel tokens. To address these issues, we propose PaDi, a patch-based forecasting framework that captures such heterogeneity through patch-wise decomposition and latent interaction. Specifically, PaDi disentangles each input patch into base and deviation components and injects a compact base summary into future patch queries as temporal anchors, enabling stable coarse-grained cues to guide the reuse of deviation patterns. It further introduces Latent Channel Attention to exchange cross-variable information through learnable latent channel bases, thereby avoiding redundant dense channel mixing in the original variable space. Extensive experiments on seven public benchmarks under four prediction horizons demonstrate that PaDi achieves superior performance compared with several state-of-the-art baselines, highlighting its effectiveness and stability across diverse forecasting scenarios. The implementation of our model is available at: https://github.com/HYYAlex/PaDi.
A147FULLDynamic Spectral Decoupling for Time-Series Forecasting
Jaehyung Lee (Pohang University of Science and Technology) · Seungha Hong (Pohang University of Science and Technology) · Seongje Lee (Pohang University of Science and Technology) · Suyeon Kim (Kyungpook National University) · Seongku Kang (Korea University) · Hwanjo Yu (Pohang University of Science and Technology)
Abstract
While frequency-domain approaches have advanced time-series forecasting, many existing methods process spectral components through a unified pathway, despite substantial energy disparities across frequencies. High-energy components can dominate the learning process, making it difficult to capture weaker residual dynamics that may contain both predictable structure and stochastic fluctuations. To address this issue, we propose Dynamic Spectral Decoupling (DSD), a model-agnostic module that separates frequency components based on instance-wise energy concentration. DSD uses a Lorenz-curve-based adaptive mechanism to determine instance-wise separation boundaries, separates dominant components from the residual spectrum, and assigns the resulting components to separate prediction pathways. This design reduces interference between energy scales without assuming that all low-energy components are equally useful. Extensive experiments on five real-world datasets show that DSD improves the average performance of diverse forecasting backbones and outperforms existing model-agnostic methods. Our code is available at https://github.com/anthi7-google/DSD.
A148FULLTechnology Forecasting through Data-Driven Analysis of Patents
Arman Arzani (University of Duisburg-Essen) · Theodor Josef Vogl (University of Duisburg-Essen) · Marcus Handte (University of Duisburg-Essen) · Pedro José Marrón (University of Duisburg-Essen)
Abstract
Forecasting technology lifecycle phases is a key enabler of data-driven innovation scouting, helping coaches and decision makers anticipate future technological developments and plan accordingly. Patent data offers structured, time-stamped records of innovation activity, making it a valuable basis for modeling and forecasting technology lifecycle trajectories. In this paper, we propose a systematic, domain-agnostic framework for technology forecasting using patent count time series from the European Patent Office (EPO). After identifying trends that are likely to capture a complete technology lifecycle, we derive a universal eight-phase lifecycle pattern within the retained EPO series. Based on this pattern, we annotate the trends and evaluate a two-stage pipeline combining neural time series forecasting with lifecycle phase classification. The evaluation yields three key results: (1) a Transformer-seq2seq classifier achieves F1-macro 0.785 on the eight-phase labeling task using only raw patent counts; (2) the top neural forecasters converge to within MAE 7.85 patents (57% below Prophet), relative to the median per-series peak; and (3) the best combined pipeline configuration (Transformer-Direct paired with LSTM-seq2seq) predicts lifecycle phase transitions with a mean year-delta of 1.8 years and a median of 0.650 years, without relying on any domain-specific features or patent text content.
A149SHORTSBAND: Spectral Band-wise Score Debiasing for Multivariate Time Series Anomaly Detection
Seokhwan Kim (Seoul National University of Science and Technology) · Kisung Lee (Louisiana State University) · Hyuk-Yoon Kwon (Seoul National University of Science and Technology)
Abstract
Reconstruction-based multivariate time-series anomaly detection (MTSAD) typically assigns anomaly scores using the mean squared reconstruction error (MSE). We show that this score has a spectral blind spot: because MSE responds strongly to large errors, anomaly signals in low-energy bands of the training spectrum are ignored by the score. The per-dataset oracle headroom, measured on 9 of 12 well-known benchmark datasets, objectively confirms this diagnosis. From this, we propose SBAND (Spectral Band-wise Score Debiasing for Multivariate Time Series Anomaly Detection), a post-hoc correction determined in closed form from the spectrum statistics of the training input alone, without labels, validation, or separate tuning. SBAND is attached only at the scoring stage without retraining: an activation gate automatically disables the correction on diffuse datasets, and a closed-form gain determines the correction strength from the training spectrum negentropy. On the 12 benchmark datasets, SBAND, with an average AUROC of 0.802 (only 0.007 below the per-dataset oracle of 0.809), outperforms the state-of-the-art model CATCH (0.759) by +0.043 as well as all 13 external baselines. SBAND is backbone-agnostic. We apply it on CATCH, replacing the FFT with a real-valued FFT (rFFT) for efficiency, yielding a 2.6× training speedup over CATCH (6.48h vs 16.97h) and improving both accuracy and efficiency over the state of the art. The code is available at https://github.com/bigbases/SBAND.
A150FULLRNEC: Reference-Guided Neighborhood Evidence Calibration for Multivariate Time-Series Anomaly Detection
Kexuan Liu (East China Jiaotong University) · Ying Wang (East China Jiaotong University) · Qingping Li (East China Jiaotong University) · Yang Chen (East China Jiaotong University) · Tao Wan (East China Jiaotong University) · Xin Xie (East China Jiaotong University)
Abstract
Multivariate time-series anomaly detection commonly relies on reconstruction errors produced by autoencoders as anomaly scores. However, in real-world industrial systems, normal states are often heterogeneous: normal windows that are difficult to model may yield large reconstruction errors, whereas some anomalous windows can still be well reconstructed. As a result, raw reconstruction errors are not always directly comparable across different test windows. To address this issue, we propose RNEC, a post-training reference-guided neighborhood evidence calibration framework. Without modifying the parameters of a trained autoencoder, RNEC constructs a latent representation–reconstruction error reference field from training windows. During inference, it combines the relative reconstruction difficulty measured against latent neighbors with the degree to which a test window is covered by the training reference distribution, thereby producing calibrated anomaly evidence. Experiments on five public multivariate time-series anomaly detection benchmarks show that RNEC achieves the best macro-average F1, AUROC, and AUPR, with the best performance in 11 out of 15 dataset–metric combinations, while remaining lightweight and plug-and-play. The source code is publicly available at https://github.com/RNEC-code/rnec.
A151FULLGT-PSSM: Unified Probabilistic Framework for Stochastic Dynamics Modeling and Dependency Learning in Multivariate Time Series Anomaly Detection
Wonmo Koo (KAIST) · Jaeyeong Lee (KAIST) · Taeseong Yoon (KAIST) · Heeyoung Kim (KAIST)
Abstract
