Multivariate time series anomaly detection (MTAD) is crucial for ensuring the safe and reliable operation of complex systems. Many existing methods learn normal patterns by training reconstruction or forecasting models on predominantly normal data. However, a large portion of these approaches rely on deterministic models and their associated point-wise output errors for anomaly scoring. Since real-world multivariate time series are inherently stochastic due to measurement noise and intrinsic system randomness, purely error-based scores can be unreliable, as large errors may arise from benign fluctuations rather than true anomalies. Probabilistic approaches address this limitation by quantifying uncertainty in model outputs. In particular, probabilistic state-space models (PSSMs) provide a principled framework by modeling stochastic system dynamics through latent state transitions and measurement noise via emission models. Despite this advantage, existing PSSM-based MTAD methods often struggle to capture long-range temporal dependencies and inter-variable dependencies, as they typically rely on noise-sensitive recurrent architectures and lack explicit cross-variable structure modeling. To address these limitations, we propose Graph-Transformer-Enhanced Probabilistic State-Space Model (GT-PSSM), a novel PSSM-based MTAD method that tightly integrates PSSM-based probabilistic modeling of stochastic dynamics with Graph Transformer-based learning of temporal and inter-variable dependencies. Specifically, GT-PSSM leverages temporal multi-head self-attention to capture long-range temporal dependencies and graph convolution over a learnable graph to explicitly model inter-variable dependencies, while retaining principled stochastic modeling of system dynamics and measurement noise. By jointly modeling stochasticity, long-range temporal dependence, and variable interactions within a unified probabilistic framework, GT-PSSM enables more robust anomaly detection. Extensive experiments on real-world benchmark datasets demonstrate that GT-PSSM achieves state-of-the-art performance.
A152FULLS2CSR: Self-Supervised Contrastive Learning for State Recognition in Multivariate Time Series
Jie Zhang (Fudan university) · Peng Wang (Fudan university) · Wei Wang (Fudan university)
Abstract
The recent proliferation of sensors has enabled the collection of extensive time series data from cyber-physical systems. These time series can typically be segmented into distinct states, each carrying rich semantic information. For example, time series recorded during patient rehabilitation may represent sequences of activities such as standing, walking, and sitting. However, annotating these states remains both labor-intensive and costly. Although recent state-of-the-art recognition approaches utilize self-supervised learning to identify such states, many of them overlook informative frequency-domain characteristics, which are often crucial for distinguishing different states. As a result, these methods may fail to accurately identify state boundaries, particularly during periodic state transitions. In addition, existing methods often struggle to effectively capture inter-channel correlations and intra-channel temporal dependencies within multivariate time series. Furthermore, they are susceptible to false negative samples during contrastive learning, which can degrade the quality of learned representations. </par> <par>To address these limitations, we propose S2CSR, a cross-domain contrastive learning framework for multivariate time series state recognition. Specifically, S2CSR jointly performs representation learning and state discovery by introducing contrastive objectives at both the instance and temporal levels. Moreover, the framework encodes time series data in both the temporal and frequency domains, enabling the model to learn more robust and discriminative representations through cross-domain contrastive learning. To further improve representation quality, we design a false negative elimination mechanism to alleviate the adverse impact of incorrect negative samples during contrastive learning. Finally, a nonparametric clustering algorithm is employed to automatically discover latent states. Extensive experiments conducted on six benchmark datasets demonstrate that S2CSR consistently outperforms existing state-of-the-art methods in terms of both effectiveness and robustness.
A153SHORTRedundancy-Aware Sensor Array Optimization for Electronic Nose Classification
Haoxin Zhu (Beijing Technology and Business University) · Xueyi Zhou (Hanyang University) · Zhihao Hao (Beijing Technology and Business University) · Dong-Kyu Chae (Hanyang University) · Xiaoqiang Teng (Beijing Technology and Business University) · Haisheng Li (Beijing Technology and Business University)
Abstract
Electronic nose (E-nose) systems rely on multi-sensor arrays to classify gases or volatile compounds, but dense sensor arrays increase hardware cost, power consumption, and deployment complexity. This work studies compact E-nose sensor array optimization while preserving classification performance. We propose MOMENT-R3S, a redundancy-aware optimization framework based on pre-trained time-series foundation model representations. MOMENT-R3S ranks sensors by jointly considering task relevance, class separability, single-sensor utility, and inter-sensor redundancy, and determines a compact deployment budget through a performance retention constraint. Experiments on five E-nose datasets show that MOMENT-R3S reduces 40.0%–54.0% of sensors while preserving 95.61%–99.29% of full-sensor Macro-F1 performance. Under the same fixed sensor budgets, MOMENT-R3S consistently outperforms prototype-distance methods, TSelect, mutual information, and mRMR. These results show that time-series foundation model representations and redundancy-aware ranking provide an effective solution for low-cost and compact E-nose sensor array design.
A154FULLStreaming Semi-Supervised Adaptive Isolation Forest
Jia Justin Liu (University of Waikato) · Guilherme Weigert Cassales (Massey University) · Fei Tony Liu (Artificial General Intelligence Pty Ltd.,) · Sławomir Nowaczyk (Halmstad University) · Bernhard Pfahringer (University of Waikato) · Albert Bifet (University of Waikato)
Abstract
Anomaly detection in data streams is vital in areas such as network security, finance, and IoT, but it is hindered by the scarcity and cost of labels. We propose the Streaming Semi-Supervised Adaptive Isolation Forest (S3AIF), which extends the Adaptive Isolation Forest to partially labelled data, evolving streams by using discrimination power as a unifying principle to: (i) weight isolation trees when scoring; (ii) replace the least discriminative tree at each window; and (iii) select query instances for active learning by path-length disagreement. Across 22 benchmark datasets with a labelling budget below 1%, S3AIF outperforms HiLAD in both ROC-AUC and PR-AUC while running more than three times faster and ranks first against 10 unsupervised baselines in ROC-AUC. An ablation confirms that discrimination-power-based tree replacement is the main driver of S3AIF's performance.
A155SHORTXGIF: An Explanation-Guided Anomaly Detection Extention of Isolation Forest
Oloufemy Prunel Akplogan (IRIT, UMR 5505 CNRS, Université Toulouse Capitole) · Moncef Garouani (IRIT, UMR 5505 CNRS, Université Toulouse Capitole) · Julien Aligon (IRIT, UMR 5505 CNRS, Université Toulouse Capitole)
Abstract
Isolation Forest ranks among the most widely used unsupervised anomaly detection algorithms due to its simplicity, scalability, and computational efficiency. However, its tree construction process relies exclusively on randomly selected splitting features and split values, ignoring informative signals about how anomalies are characterized in the feature space. In this paper, we propose XGIF, an explanation-guided extension of Isolation Forest that exploits feature attribution signals to drive the isolation process. Our core insight is that anomalous instances tend to exhibit unstable attribution patterns across the tree ensemble, while normal instances are characterized by more consistent attributions. XGIF introduces attribution stability as a novel criterion for evaluating leaf purity and adaptively extends tree growth when unstable explanatory patterns are detected. Furthermore, the growth process is guided toward features that contribute most to anomaly characterization, enabling more effective isolation of outlying instances. By integrating explainability directly into the learning mechanism, rather than confining it to post-hoc interpretation, XGIF leverages attribution signals as an active driver of anomaly detection performance. Experiments on 20 benchmark datasets from ADBench demonstrate that XGIF significantly improves detection performance, outperforming Isolation Forest on 17 of 20 datasets.
A156FULLResilient Deep Multi-View Clustering via Dual-Time-Scale Kernel Attention
Shaojun Shi (Xi'an University of Posts and Telecommunications) · Guangbin Wang (Xi'an University of Posts and Telecommunications) · Yimeng Wang (Xi'an University of Posts and Telecommunications) · Hailong Ning (Xi'an University of Posts and Telecommunications) · Pei Li (Xi'an University of Posts and Telecommunications) · Yanping Chen (Xi'an University of Posts and Telecommunications) · Feiping Nie (Northwestern Polytechnical University)
Abstract
Multi-view clustering aims to cluster data into different groups by leveraging both the consistency and complementarity across multiple views. Nevertheless, existing methods commonly face two primary limitations. First, cross-view information fusion often lacks fine-grained sample-level modeling, leading to semantic drift during feature alignment. Second, the dynamic optimization process suffers from inherent inertia, failing to correct accumulated errors stemming from infrequent pseudo-label updating during training. To address these problems, this paper proposes a novel framework named Resilient Deep Multi-View Clustering via Dual-Time-Scale Kernel Attention (DKAMVC). Specifically, we first adopt an autoencoder coupled with a capacity-adaptive MLP to extract latent representations. Then, the unified features obtained by connecting the latent representations are fed into a dual-time-scale model which integrates slow anchor updating with fast weight learning for resilient noise suppression. Next, these reinforced features are directed into a decoupled dual-pathway architecture, which utilizes a Local Kernel Attention (LKA) module to accurately quantify localized confidence. This design completely separates distribution modeling and weighting functions to establish fine-grained sample-to-target matching in the Reproducing Kernel Hilbert Space (RKHS). Finally, the multiply-augmented global features are clustered to yield the ultimate results. Experiments conducted on eight multi-view data sets demonstrate that the clustering performance of DKAMVC outperforms state-of-the-art comparison methods.
A157FULLBeyond Local Centers toward Prototypes: Joint Learning of Self-Representation and Adaptive Clustering
Dahyun Jeong (University of Seoul) · Yunjin Choi (University of Seoul)
Abstract
In this paper, we propose a prototype-learning framework that addresses a common limitation of proximity-based methods: the need to specify proximity weights in advance. Rather than relying on a fixed proximity matrix computed from raw observations, the proposed method jointly learns the prototype representation and the proximity structure. We implement this idea by extending the convex-clustering framework, replacing the pre-specified proximity input with a self-representation matrix learned from the prototype-level representation. The resulting adaptive proximity matrix captures intrinsic relationships among prototypes, yielding prototypes that better reflect the underlying data geometry rather than merely serving as cluster centers. We solve the resulting nonconvex optimization problem using an optimization algorithm based on multiaffine ADMM. Experiments on synthetic non-Euclidean datasets and real benchmark datasets show that the proposed method learns prototypes that better cover the underlying data geometry than standard convex clustering, while removing the need to manually specify proximity weights.
A158FULLGeoHIL: Geometry-Supervised Hierarchical Invariant Learning for Molecular OOD Generalization
Li Sun (Beijing University of Posts and Telecommunications) · Lanxu Yang (North China Electric Power University) · Lu Wang (North China Electric Power University) · Junda Ye (Beijing University of Posts and Telecommunications) · Peng Tang (Shandong University) · Hao Peng (Beihang University) · Sen Su (Beijing University of Posts and Telecommunications) · Philip Yu (University of Illinois Chicago)
Abstract
Reliable molecular property prediction is fundamental to accelerating scientific discovery, yet Graph Neural Networks (GNNs) often fail to generalize when exploring new chemical spaces—a classic out-of-distribution (OOD) challenge. A popular line of research is graph invariant learning, which aims to extract environment-invariant rationales that remain stable across distribution shifts. However, existing graph invariant learning methods often rely on coarse environment partitions, which are insufficient to reflect continuous real-world shifts. Moreover, molecules are inherently 3D, and purely 2D graph-based invariant learning can extract formally invariant yet physically invalid rationales. To address these issues, inspired by 3D-enhanced graph pretraining, we propose GeoHIL, a geometric hierarchical invariant learning framework for molecular OOD generalization. GeoHIL introduces a hierarchical environment characterization, with global environments capturing dataset-level shifts and local environments capturing intra-molecular conformational variations. At the global level, GeoHIL adopts a stochastic-attention rationale learner to extract environment-robust 2D subgraphs. At the local level, we encode each conformer with a 3D encoder and aggregate the resulting representations. Then we propose geometry-supervised local invariance that uses the aggregated 3D representation as a training-time supervision signal to regularize 2D rationales to be conformation-consistent. This local invariance is instantiated with two variants: MC uses a Mahalanobis-distance consistency objective to match the conformation distribution, while vMF-C uses a von Mises--Fisher objective to enforce hyperspherical consistency. Additionally, we provide theoretical insights by interpreting the proposed local objectives as likelihood-based regularizers and providing quantitative stability insights for local invariance. Experiments on DrugOOD and GOOD-HIV show strong OOD performance, with particularly large gains in low-data settings over invariant-learning and 3D-enhanced baselines.
A159SHORTCalibration before Recognition: Sensor-Level Domain Generalization for Cross-Session HD-sEMG Gesture Recognition
Chenhao Wu (Waseda University) · Dingjie Peng (Waseda University) · Ruslan Kireev (Waseda University) · Satoshi Konishi (KDDI Research Inc.) · Wataru Kameyama (Waseda University) · Jiang Liu (Waseda University)
Abstract
Cross-session HD-sEMG gesture recognition is a zero-shot domain generalization problem central to deployable myoelectric interfaces. Existing approaches typically treat the session gap as a generic distribution mismatch and address it through larger models, uniform normalization, or latent feature alignment. We argue that, in HD-sEMG, part of this gap arises before representation learning: electrode reattachment perturbs the sensing interface, producing structured drift that is frequency-selective in amplitude and non-uniform across electrodes. Motivated by this observation, we propose a calibration-before-recognition paradigm for cross-session HD-sEMG generalization and instantiate it as Frequency–Electrode Calibration (FEC), a lightweight plug-in framework that recalibrates band-wise spectral magnitudes and down-weights unreliable electrodes before backbone feature extraction, without target-session labels or model updates. On the Hyser cross-session benchmark (20 subjects, 2 recording days separated by 3-25 days), FEC with a MobileNet3D-SE backbone achieves 70.96% zero-shot accuracy using only 99.2K parameters, improving the naive backbone by 9.33% and the strongest normalization-style calibration baseline by 4.99%. These results suggest that explicitly modeling sensor-level drift can shift cross-session generalization from purely model-centric compensation toward pre-recognition calibration, offering an interpretable view of cross-session HD-sEMG degradation and enabling a parameter-efficient framework for resource-constrained edge deployment in real-world wearable myoelectric systems.
A160FULLOnline Meta-Expert Learning
Wangyue Li (East China Normal University) · Qizhou Chen (East China Normal University) · Wei Deng (Southwestern University of Finance and Economics) · Feng Zhu (Postal Savings Bank Of China) · Xiaofeng He (East China Normal University)
Abstract
Online meta-learning combines the strengths of online learning and meta-learning to handle continuously evolving task streams. It updates the model sequentially as new data arrive, while also learning transferable knowledge that enables rapid adaptation to newly emerging tasks. However, most online meta-learning methods require explicit task boundaries, which are often unavailable in real-world scenarios such as evolving illicit transaction detection or user preference prediction. Experiments show that when tasks are blurred by injecting 20% samples from adjacent tasks into each task, the test error of online meta-learning increases by about 25.3%. Existing approaches typically either use task boundary detection to guide updates or apply threshold-based parameter adaptation, but both are highly sensitive and not robust in non-stationary environments. We address this challenge by proposing an Online Meta-Expert Learning (OMEL) framework. OMEL dynamically maintains multi-timescale experts based on geometric covering (GC) intervals and adaptively updates their weights to reduce sensitivity to task variations, guiding a meta-learner toward robust online adaptation. Because explicit parameter-space aggregation is computationally expensive, OMEL uses prediction-space distillation to efficiently transfer knowledge from the expert ensemble to the meta-learner. OMEL attains sublinear strongly adaptive regret of Õ(√τ), where τ is the interval length. Experiments on image classification and transaction anomaly detection show state-of-the-art performance.
A161SHORTNot All Segmentation Is Equal: How Quality Filters Evaluate Structure
Minju Kim (Chung-Ang university) · Hyunwook Yu (Chung-Ang University) · Mucheol Kim (Chung-Ang University)
Abstract
Classifier-based quality filtering (CQF) increasingly determines which web documents compose language-model pretraining corpora, yet its structural preferences remain poorly understood. Prior work shows that broad presentation changes can shift CQF scores, but it remains unclear how specific forms of document organization affect this judgment. This paper studies heading- and list-based organization, a common surface structure in web text, through a fact-mediated structural probe. For each source document, the probe extracts factual propositions and generates three variants from the same fact list: prose-like continuity, balanced heading/list organization, and over-segmented structure. Across examples generated from 9,973 seeds and ten public CQF and data-quality scores, CQF preferences vary sharply by objective. QuRater and several FineWeb-style educational filters favor balanced structure over Prose, while NVIDIA Quality DeBERTa and CLIMB-based scores favor Prose. Over-segmented presentation is broadly penalized relative to balanced structure, and threshold-level analyses show that structural presentation can change which documents would pass FineWeb-style educational filters. These results show that CQF models encode model-specific preferences over document organization, suggesting that data-quality filters should be evaluated not only by which documents they select, but also by which structural presentations they systematically reward. Code and artifacts are available at https://github.com/k391160334/cqf-structure-preference.
A162APPLIEDBeyond Correlation: Deploying Causal AI to Attribute E-Commerce Sales Loss at Scale
Deep Nayak (Amazon) · Mohit Kumar (Amazon) · Harsh Goel (Amazon) · Sivaramakrishnan Kaveri (Amazon)
Abstract
E-commerce stores struggle to understand the root causes of declining seller revenue, often relying on correlation-based analytics that leads to ineffective or even harmful interventions. This paper introduces the Revenue Loss Monitor (RLM), a system that uses Double Machine Learning (DML) to move from simple correlation to causal attribution of revenue loss. RLM successfully isolates the causal impact of seller-controllable factors, such as pricing, advertising, and inventory - from confounding market trends. Validated across thousands of seller accounts, RLM has demonstrably improved the accuracy of attributions. We discuss the end-to-end methodology, from our hybrid product and seller level modelling approach to the significant real-world challenges of data quality and model validation in a production environment. Online validation with domain experts shows that DML-based attributions are 19.8% more accurate than traditional correlation-based methods, with the system showing 24.9% month-over-month growth in active users. Furthermore, A/B experiments demonstrate that sellers acting on RLM-identified causal factors achieve up to 29% greater revenue recovery compared to a control group, highlighting RLM’s effectiveness as a scalable and trustworthy causal business intelligence solution.
A163FULLIncorporating Rank Distributions into Uplift Modeling
Zhuofan Sun (Tsinghua University) · Hongyan Liu (Tsinghua University) · Shuolong Huangfu (Tsinghua University) · Wei Peng (Independent Researcher) · Zhuohua Chen (Independent researcher)
Abstract
Uplift modeling estimates the individual treatment effect (ITE) by predicting the difference in outcomes between treated and control groups, enabling optimal targeting strategies in applications such as precision marketing and personalized medicine. Existing methods mainly focus on minimizing pointwise uplift errors yet fail to exploit the ranking information among samples fully. Studies in other areas have shown that ranking loss is helpful to learn more generalizable feature representations and mitigate overfitting on sparse data. Moreover, in many applications, the relative ranking often matters more than the absolute values. Thus, we propose RUM, a rank distribution-enhanced uplift modeling framework that jointly optimizes uplift estimation and ranking objectives. In the framework, we develop a full-ranking evaluation module with a SoftRank loss to enable end-to-end optimization of population-level ranking performance, which can be integrated with existing uplift models. We theoretically prove that minimizing the SoftRank loss provides a robust upper bound on ranking risk. Extensive experiments on multiple real-world datasets show that models built upon our proposed framework consistently achieve superior performance over all benchmark models.
A164SHORTDual-Level Consensus Alignment for Multi-Agent Cooperation
Hao Chen (University of Chinese Academy of Sciences) · Meiqi Wu (Tsinghua University) · Yang Yu (Beljing Academy of Artifcial Inteligence) · Kaiqi Huang (University of Chinese Academy of Sciences) · Jianbin Jiao (University of Chinese Academy of Sciences)
Abstract
Centralized training exposes cooperative agents to information that is unavailable during decentralized execution, creating a problem of representation recovery: task-relevant cooperative information must remain independently inferable from each agent's local information. Existing latent-consensus approaches commonly impose a single uniform sharing scope, although team-wide consistency and interaction-local compatibility place different requirements on a cooperative representation. We characterize this limitation as consensus-scope mismatch and introduce multi-scale cooperative sufficiency, which requires the representation at each cooperation scope to preserve task-relevant information while remaining locally recoverable. Based on this principle, we propose Dual-Level Consensus Alignment (DLCA). DLCA combines a team-level posterior aligned with a privileged global anchor and a neighborhood-level posterior aligned only across interaction-defined neighbors. Scale-specific reconstruction discourages uninformative agreement, while both posteriors are inferred locally during execution. Experiments on the discrete SMAC and SMAC-HARD benchmarks and on the continuous MAPDN benchmark show that DLCA consistently outperforms strong actor-critic and value-based baselines.
A165SHORTPrototype-Driven Multi-Agent Reinforcement Learning for Active Voltage Control via Contrastive Latent Conditioning
Hao Chen (University of Chinese Academy of Sciences) · Meiqi Wu (Tsinghua University) · Yang Yu (Beljing Academy of Artifcial Inteligence) · Kaiqi Huang (University of Chinese Academy of Sciences) · Jianbin Jiao (University of Chinese Academy of Sciences)
Abstract
Active voltage control (AVC) in low-voltage distribution networks requires cooperative multi-agent policies that adapt to highly non-stationary operating conditions driven by photovoltaic generation, load fluctuation, and topology reconfiguration. Existing centralized-training-decentralized-execution multi-agent reinforcement learning (MARL) methods rely on entangled recurrent hidden states that lack explicit semantic abstraction, while prototype-aware variants depend on manually defined discrete prototype sets that limit adaptability across diverse operating regimes. We therefore propose Prototype-Driven Multi-Agent Reinforcement Learning (PD-MARL), which equips each cooperative agent with a continuous latent task prototype that summarizes its recent operating context and conditions its policy accordingly, and we ground the design in a unified mutual-information framework that justifies the joint training objective. On the MAPDN active voltage control benchmark across 33-, 141-, and 322-bus networks, PD-MARL achieves the best overall performance among all evaluated methods.
A166FULLA Game-Theoretic Spatio-Temporal Reinforcement Learning Framework for Collaborative Public Resource Allocation
Songxin Lei (The Hong Kong University of Science and Technology (Guangzhou)) · Qiongyan Wang (The Hong Kong University of Science and Technology (Guangzhou)) · Yanchen Zhu (The Hong Kong University of Science and Technology (Guangzhou)) · Hanyu Yao (Peking University) · Sijie Ruan (Beijing Institute of Technology) · Weilin Ruan (The Hong Kong University of Science and Technology (Guangzhou)) · Yuyu Luo (The Hong Kong University of Science and Technology (Guangzhou)) · Huaming Wu (Tianjin University) · Yuxuan Liang (The Hong Kong University of Science and Technology (Guangzhou))
Abstract
Public resource allocation involves distributing resources, including urban infrastructure, energy, and transportation, which are typically limited in capacity, to meet social demands. In real-world scenarios, resources are typically limited in capacity, which makes coordination among multiple resources essential. However, existing methods often optimize resource movements in an isolated manner and do not explicitly account for capacity-aware collaboration under spatio-temporal dynamics. To address this limitation, we introduce the Collaborative Public Resource Allocation (CPRA) problem, and propose a Game-Theoretic Spatio- Temporal Reinforcement Learning (GSTRL) framework to solve it. Our contributions are twofold: 1) We formulate CPRA as a potential game and construct the potential function based on the objective function of CPRA, laying a theoretical foundation for approximating the Nash equilibrium of this NP-hard problem; and 2) Our GSTRL framework effectively captures the spatio-temporal dynamics of the overall system. We evaluate GSTRL on two real-world datasets, where experiments show its superior performance. Our source codes are available at https://github.com/thunderlrr/GSTRL.
A167FULLSpecial Orthogonal Hyper-Connections for Geometry-Preserving Deep Routing
Wei Liu (Sun Yat-sen University) · Xinyi Zhang (Sun Yat-sen University) · Wenshan Deng (Sun Yat-sen University) · Huaijie Zhu (Sun Yat-sen University) · Libin Zheng (Sun Yat-sen University) · Jianxing Yu (Sun Yat-sen University) · Jian Yin (Sun Yat-sen University)
Abstract
Deep neural networks increasingly suffer from progressive information geometry degeneration as network depth scales, manifested as gradient attenuation, representation collapse, and feature homogenization across layers. Existing connection mechanisms, including residual routing and manifold-constrained hyper-connections, primarily focus on numerical stabilization but fail to preserve the intrinsic geometric structure of feature propagation. To address this issue, we propose SOHC (Special Orthogonal Hyper-Connections), a geometry-preserving routing framework that formulates inter-layer information propagation as exact manifold transformation on the special orthogonal group. Specifically, SOHC parameterizes routing matrices through the Cayley transform, ensuring analytically exact isometric propagation along the geometry-preserving routing stream throughout network depth. This exact orthogonal residual path preserves signal energy and spectral geometry along the isometric stream, providing a stable backbone for deep information propagation. Moreover, we design a gated dual-stream architecture that combines globally stable isometric propagation with locally adaptive semantic refinement, balancing structural stability and representation expressiveness. Extensive experiments on deep language modeling and sequential recommendation benchmarks demonstrate that SOHC consistently improves optimization stability, representation diversity, and downstream performance over existing hyper-connection methods. Further analyses show that SOHC effectively mitigates representation rank degeneration and preserves stable feature geometry throughout deep signal propagation, validating the importance of geometry-preserving routing for deep neural architectures.
A168SHORTAnalyzing Stream Collapse in Hyper-Connections: From Diagnosis to Mitigation
Ekaterina Alimaskina (MIRAI) · Gleb Molodtsov (MIRAI) · Aleksandr Beznosikov (MIRAI)
Abstract
Multi-stream architectures augment standard Transformer residual pathways with several interacting streams. Focusing on Hyper-Connections (HC), we study whether residual information is distributed across streams or concentrated in a small subset. We use fine-grained diagnostics that expose both inter-stream routing and representation structure. We find that stream usage often becomes strongly imbalanced. After an early seeding stage, residual mixing tends to preserve same-stream flow, limiting exchange between streams. At the same time, representation magnitude and interpretable sparse features concentrate in a dominant stream. This indicates that the added residual pathways are used non-uniformly. Finally, symmetry-breaking stream initialization reduces dominant-stream behavior and improves validation performance across mHC variants.
A169SHORTAutomated Software Ticket Generation Using Large Language Models and Code Graphs
Timo Maximilian Sieger (Paderborn University) · Stefan Heindorf (Paderborn University)
Abstract
High-quality tickets are essential for software development, serving as a means of knowledge transfer between product owners and developers. Poorly written tickets create additional work and increase development costs. Creating tickets is time-consuming, and product owners often lack insight into the codebase, resulting in descriptions that may not reflect existing implementations. Large language models (LLMs) excel at processing natural language and possess strong programming knowledge, making them promising tools for automating ticket generation. However, research on LLM-based ticket generation remains limited. Recent work has shown that combining LLMs with code graphs improves querying of large codebases, which may benefit ticket generation. We propose TicketAgent, a repository-aware workflow for automated software ticket generation that combines LLM-based ticket writing with code-graph-based code localization and project-specific domain knowledge. We evaluate TicketAgent alongside two baselines: an LLM-only workflow and a retrieval-augmented generation (RAG) workflow. Across automated and human evaluations, providing LLMs with additional information sources consistently improves ticket quality. In particular, structured access to the source code via code-based querying yields the largest improvements, outperforming both the LLM-only and RAG baselines.
A170FULLPERO: Efficient Robust Post-Training Foundation Models for Encrypted Traffic Classification
Wumei Du (National University of Defense Technology) · Jiarong Wen (National University of Defense Technology) · Kaiyu Zhang (National University of Defense Technology) · Zi Yang (National University of Defense Technology) · Yiqin Lv (National University of Defense Technology) · Longfei Zhang (National University of Defense Technology) · Dong Liang (National University of Defense Technology) · Zheng Xie (National University of Defense Technology)
Abstract
Encrypted traffic classification is vital for network security, yet real-world deployments are inherently sensitive to rare but high-loss errors such as misclassification of malicious traffic. The encrypted traffic foundation model, as a promising general-purpose technique, can achieve impressive overall performance. However, employing standard objectives such as empirical risk minimization often overlooks high-risk tail events, and commonly used performance metrics hardly reflect robustness limitations in risk-sensitive scenarios. Directly applying robust optimization objectives, such as conditional value-at-risk, to post-training is computationally prohibitive for large models, as identifying high-loss samples exhausts substantial computation. To this end, we propose Pre-Evaluation Robust Optimization (PERO), an efficient robust post-training framework for encrypted traffic foundation models. PERO employs a lightweight proxy to estimate sample-wise risk and selects a subset of high-risk samples to update the foundation model, decoupling risk estimation from expensive large-model optimization. Extensive experiments on typical encrypted traffic datasets show that PERO achieves competitive or superior robustness and average performance compared to outstanding robust post-training methods, while significantly reducing computational and memory costs.
A171SHORTFeature or Penalty? A Placement Diagnostic for Graph-Risk Signals in Learned Portfolio Decisions
Tenghan Zhong (University of Southern California)
Abstract
Graph-derived domain signals create a placement problem in learned decision systems: they may inform the predictor, or they may enter the downstream decision layer directly. We study this question in learned portfolio contracts, where a graph-risk score can be supplied as a neural feature (Feature-only contract) or additionally priced as an explicit penalty on risky exposure (Graph-penalty contract). To separate placement from asset-specific graph-score ordering, we introduce a within-state permutation diagnostic. The control permutes the graph-risk scores across assets within each decision state, preserving the state-level marginal distribution and the explicit penalty placement while breaking the asset-specific graph-risk assignment. On Fama-French industry portfolios and an external universe of exchange-traded funds (ETFs), explicit penalty placement reduces conditional value-at-risk at the 95% level (CVaR95), crowding, and co-crash risk relative to feature-only placement over ten seeds, with essentially matched effort. All variants use matched architecture, decision rule, benchmark, and feasibility constraints. The diagnostic separates two channels: explicit penalty placement, not graph ordering, accounts for the aggregate CVaR reduction; the permutation control attains lower CVaR than the true ordering in both universes, while the true ordering helps most clearly for industry crowding. We therefore identify explicit decision-layer placement as the more reliable source of risk control in this setting.
A172APPLIEDeForecaster-MultiRegion: A Deployed Day-Ahead Load Forecasting System for Provincial Grid Operations
Qiming Chen (Alibaba Group) · Zhaoyang Zhu (Ant Group) · Linxiao Yang (Ant Group) · Zhipeng Zeng (Alibaba Group) · Peiyuan Liu (Alibaba Group) · Weiqi Chen (Alibaba Group) · Liang Sun (Ant Group)
Abstract
Accurate day-ahead electric load forecasting is critical for secure and economic dispatch of modern power grids. In this paper, we present eForecaster-MultiRegion, a deployed multi-region load forecasting system integrated into the eForecaster platform and serving a major province in Eastern China, covering 17 cities and a population of over 110 million. This setting poses practical challenges including strong regional heterogeneity (e.g., coastal vs. inland consumption patterns) and highly volatile air-conditioning-driven demand under rapidly changing weather conditions. To address these challenges, eForecaster-MultiRegion adopts a Mixture-of-Experts (MoE) architecture within a Multi-Task Learning (MTL) framework, enabling the model to share cross-city patterns while specializing to local city-level dynamics. Post-launch results show consistent improvements over the previous production system. After deployment in 2025, eForecaster-MultiRegion achieved 98.29% accuracy in summer and 98.77% accuracy in winter operations, corresponding to +1.41 and +0.68 percentage-point year-on-year improvements, respectively. In this application setting, each 1% absolute accuracy gain corresponds to an estimated RMB 500–800 million in annual economic value. These results demonstrate the effectiveness of eForecaster-MultiRegion for provincial-scale grid operations.
A173FULLMulti-View Molecular Representation Learning with Hierarchical Graphs and Contextualized Fingerprints
Gwang-Hyeon Yun (Yonsei University) · Jong-Hoon Park (Yonsei University) · Bing Hu (University of Waterloo) · Helen Chen (University of Waterloo) · Anita Layton (University of Waterloo) · Young-Rae Cho (Yonsei University - Mirae Campus)
Abstract
Molecular property prediction requires representations that generalize from limited labeled data to structurally novel compounds. Existing molecular pretraining methods often rely on a single view: graph-based approaches model atom-bond topology but provide limited fragment-level supervision, whereas fingerprint descriptors encode chemical patterns but are typically used as fixed auxiliary features. We propose HiFi-Mol, a multi-view framework that separately pretrains a hierarchical graph encoder and a contextualized fingerprint encoder before downstream integration. The graph branch uses fragment-aware masking with multi-resolution supervision to capture substructure-aware representations, while the fingerprint branch tokenizes active entries from seven fingerprint families and applies masked language modeling to learn contextualized embeddings. During fine-tuning, HiFi-Mol combines projected multi-resolution graph features with fingerprint embeddings for downstream prediction. Evaluated on MoleculeNet benchmarks under the scaffold split, HiFi-Mol achieves a 2.77% improvement in average ROC-AUC over the best baseline across eight classification tasks while maintaining competitive performance on three regression tasks. Further analyses reveal that fragment-aware masking improves graph representation quality, and classification results demonstrate dataset-dependent strengths of the individual graph and fingerprint variants, confirming that the two views provide complementary predictive signals.
A174APPLIEDImage-Based Feature Engineering for Rapid, Explainable Nanoparticle Megalibrary Screening
Alexandra L. Day (Northwestern University) · Carolin B. Wahl (Northwestern University) · Roberto dos Reis (Northwestern University) · Youjia Li (Northwestern University) · Wei-keng Liao (Northwestern University) · Vinayak P. Dravid (Northwestern University) · Alok Choudhary (Northwestern University) · Ankit Agrawal (Northwestern University)
Abstract
Advanced laboratory techniques have made it possible to synthesize up to tens of millions of nanoparticles on a single chip. Manual analysis at this scale is infeasible, necessitating the development of automated characterization procedures. This work describes the design of a rapid decision framework to perform quality assessment of grayscale nanoparticle images. Key information is extracted from experimental images and used to train decision trees for screening; model inference time is expected to be < 0.3 ms and the median feature engineering time ranges between 12.0 ms and 33.6 ms on the test set. Additionally, model precision is > 91% on all tests, with a maximum precision of 99.3%. Relative to previous studies, this work provides more explainable, interpretable models for automated nanoparticle characterization and returns decisions in a fraction of the time.
A175FULLLanguage Model-based Knowledge Tracing: A Comprehensive Study on Architectures, Domain Adaptation, and Cold Start Problem
Unggi Lee (Korea University Sejong Campus) · Dohee Kim (Enuma, Inc.) · Jaekwon Park (Enuma, Inc.) · Sookbun Lee (Opentutorials) · Taekyung Ahn (Enuma, Inc.) · Gunho Lee (Enuma, Inc.) · Jiyeong Bae (Korea University) · Hyeoncheol Kim (Korea University)
Abstract
Knowledge Tracing (KT) models student learning from interaction histories. Recent work has begun applying large language models (LLMs) to KT through prompting, option weighting, and test-time reasoning, but the resulting AUC remains substantially below ID-based KT. We propose Language Model-based Knowledge Tracing (LKT), a PLM-agnostic supervised KT framework that reformulates each interaction as a natural-language sequence of concept text, question text, and a response token, allowing any encoder-based pre-trained language model (PLM), or any decoder LLM after LLM2Vec adaptation, to be fine-tuned end-to-end under a unified protocol. Across three datasets, LKT achieves the highest supervised AUC among Language Model-based KT methods on every dataset, outperforming LOKT and Thinking-KT (best 0.7105 and 0.7185 on DBE-KT22) and frontier LLM prompting baselines (AUC near 0.5 to 0.6). Among the LKT backbones, ModernBERT provides the most cross-dataset stable performance and is our recommended deployment default. Beyond benchmark performance, we analyze LKT's behavior with performance comparisons and explainable AI (XAI) techniques, including attention maps, LIME, and t-SNE visualization of the [MASK]-position embeddings, to characterize which textual cues drive predictions and how the learned representation encodes correctness. Our work contributes a PLM-agnostic and interpretable KT framework that future PLM advances can directly plug into.
A176SHORTBeyond Rote Memorization: A Cognitive Framework for Tracing Knowledge in Open-World Scenarios
Qi Ding (East China Normal University) · Ziwei Wang (East China Normal University) · Jie Zhou (East China Normal University) · Jing Yang (East China Normal University) · Qin Chen (East China Normal University) · Qingchun Bai (Shanghai Open University) · Liang Dou (East China Normal University) · Liang He (East China Normal University)
Abstract
Knowledge Tracing (KT) models commonly represent exercises with learned problem identifiers, which limits their ability to handle new problems whose IDs have not accumulated sufficient interactions. We propose MKT-LLM, a content-aware framework for new-problem KT that combines problem-content representations with learner interaction history in an LLM-compatible latent space. The framework contains three components: (1) Perceptual Harmonization, which fuses learned problem embeddings with semantic content embeddings; (2) Adaptive Generalization, which synthesizes an ID-like representation for an unseen problem from semantically similar seen problems; and (3) Cognitive Synthesis, which models the learner's evolving knowledge state from the resulting interaction sequence. MKT-LLM uses content similarity to place new problems in the same latent space as observed problems and performs prediction from latent states rather than relying on token-level answer generation. Experiments on NIPS2020 and Junyi show consistent improvements over representative KT and cold-start baselines, and the model degrades more gracefully as the proportion of new problems increases.
A177SHORTLCSR-LLM: Longitudinal Cognitive State Reasoning for LLM-based Knowledge Tracing
Yuheng Zhang (Shanghai Jiao Tong University) · Liping Shen (Shanghai Jiao Tong University)
Abstract
Knowledge tracing aims to infer a student's evolving mastery from historical learning interactions. Recent large language model (LLM) approaches offer a natural way to encode textualized learning histories, but they are often evaluated primarily as next-step predictors. This leaves open whether the model forms a stable and diagnostically meaningful latent trajectory of student state, or merely exploits shallow statistics such as recent correctness rates. We introduce LCSR-LLM, a longitudinal cognitive state reasoning framework that uses marker-aligned LLM hidden states to estimate a soft latent cognitive-state trajectory at each prediction step. The framework combines state-conditioned prediction with trajectory-level regularization, especially dynamic consistency and entropy control, to encourage smoother and non-collapsed state posteriors. We further propose Longitudinal Aggregation Drift (LAD), a diagnostic protocol that measures sequence-level prediction drift, posterior uncertainty, and trajectory volatility. On ASSIST2012, LCSR-LLM with Qwen2.5-7B reaches 0.7684 AUC, 0.7705 ACC, and 0.8610 F1, achieving the best AUC among our controlled runs and the best F1 among the listed results, while remaining competitive in ACC. Paired trajectory diagnostics show that dynamic consistency and entropy control improve internal trajectory behavior beyond final predictive accuracy.
A178SHORTTemporal-Aware Graph Attention for Sequential Knowledge Tracing
Sunil Kumar Maurya (University of Tokyo) · Makoto Kawano (University of Tokyo) · Yusuke Iwasawa (University of Tokyo) · Yutaka Matsuo (University of Tokyo)
Abstract
Knowledge tracing aims to model student learning trajectories and predict future performance from historical question–response interactions. Many recent works approach knowledge tracing with graph-based modeling, where concept dependencies (question-concept relations) are represented as graphs and learning is driven by message passing or attention over these structures. Existing graph-based KT methods often rely on predefined or weakly learned graphs and lack a principled mechanism to jointly account for temporal distance and contextual relevance when aggregating past interactions. As a result, they may overemphasize non-informative signals while under-utilizing informative recent context. In this work, we introduce a graph attention-based knowledge tracing model, TAGAKT, and reframe the problem as implicit graph learning over a causal directed acyclic graph. Our proposed graph attention model incorporates context-aware, learnable temporal bias that adjusts the importance of historical interactions based on their distance to the current prediction point. In addition, we integrate an efficient channel recalibration module that performs lightweight cross-channel reweighting to suppress noisy feature dimensions arising from interaction aggregation, improving prediction robustness. Extensive experiments on six datasets show that TAGAKT outperforms baselines on most datasets and achieves the best overall rank.
A179FULLSynEHR: Joint Modeling Inter-visit Temporal Evolution and Intra-visit Clinical Structure for Longitudinal EHR Synthesis
Ximiao Li (Florida State University) · Lin Jiang (Florida State University) · Rongchao Xu (Florida State University) · Dahai Yu (Florida State University) · Zhe He (Florida State University) · Guang Wang (Florida State University)
Abstract
Longitudinal electronic health records (EHRs) document patients' sequences of clinical visits over time, preserving the temporal evolution of disease progression and care delivery. However, real longitudinal EHRs are difficult to access because they contain large amounts of fine-grained, patient-specific information. Synthetic EHR generation therefore provides a valuable approach for preserving the statistical patterns and clinical structure of patient visit trajectories, enabling broader modeling and analysis when real records are limited. Although recent generative models have made progress in producing future visit sequences, they remain limited in explicitly integrating inter-visit irregular temporal evolution and intra-visit clinical event structures in EHRs, leading to clinically inconsistent and temporally unrealistic visit sequences. In this work, we propose SynEHR, a lightweight adaptive LLM-based framework for longitudinal EHR synthesis. There are two novel designs in SynEHR, i.e., a Temporal State Conditioning Module captures irregular temporal states across visits and a Temporal-Relational Adaptation Module combines these states with patient history to dynamically construct patient-specific relational representations. SynEHR then builds on a parameter-efficient LoRA-adapted language-model generator with next-visit generation capability to train the two modules for temporally and clinically informed generation. Extensive experiments on real-world EHR datasets across fidelity, privacy, and downstream utility evaluations demonstrate that SynEHR outperforms state-of-the-art models by generating more clinically coherent and temporally faithful longitudinal EHR data.
A180FULLPerformance-Adaptive Instruction-Template Assignment for Clinical Reasoning in Large Language Models
Serugunda Henry Mukalazi (Makerere University) · Ouyang Jianquan (Xiangtan University) · Jacob Katende (Xiangtan University)
Abstract
Instruction-tuning corpora are commonly constructed by pairing fixed input–output examples with static or randomly sampled instruction templates. However, for clinical reasoning, different candidate instruction templates may emphasize different learning signals, including diagnostic conclusion, evidence synthesis, and explanation structure. This paper studies instruction-template assignment as a training-time corpus-construction problem: given fixed clinical input–output examples and a pool of candidate templates, can performance feedback guide template assignment during fine-tuning? This paper presents Performance-Adaptive Instruction-Template Assignment (PAITA), a framework that uses validation feedback to assign instruction templates to fixed clinical input–output examples during fine-tuning. Unlike static assignment, which repeatedly applies one template, or random assignment, which samples templates without regard to observed performance, PAITA balances exploration of alternative templates with exploitation of templates associated with stronger validation feedback. We evaluate PAITA primarily using LLaMA-3-8B and further examine instruction-template assignment across additional model settings using Qwen2.5-7B-Instruct and BioMedLM-2.7B on the Clinical Reasoning task; Clinical Diagnosis and Medical QA serve as auxiliary evaluations. PAITA improves clinical reasoning conclusion accuracy over static assignment (0.397 vs. 0.372; +2.5 percentage points, p=0.001) and random template assignment (0.397 vs. 0.383; +1.4 percentage points, p=0.044), with additional gains in several reasoning-quality metrics. Auxiliary results and template-assignment analyses further suggest that performance-adaptive assignment can provide benefits beyond instruction diversity alone. These findings support instruction-template assignment as an important design variable in supervised instruction tuning of clinical LLMs.
A181FULLPHASE: A Modular LLM Pipeline for On-Premise Phenotype Profile Extraction from Clinical Referral Reports
Matteo Bellini (ASST Papa Giovanni XXIII) · Andrea Bombarda (University of Bergamo) · Paolo Cazzaniga (University of Bergamo) · Maria Iascone (ASST Papa Giovanni XXIII) · Leonardo Sabaini (University of Bergamo) · Domenico Fabio Savo (University of Bergamo)
Abstract
The automated extraction of structured phenotypic profiles from clinical narratives is a critical step in genetic diagnosis, but it is hindered by the unstructured nature of medical reports, the contextual complexity of clinical language, and strict privacy requirements that forbid sending clinical data to external services. We present PHASE, a modular pipeline for the extraction of phenotypic profiles from clinical referral reports, designed to work under on-premise deployment constraints. Instead of using a single Large Language Model (LLM) monolithically, PHASE decomposes the task across specialized modules that interleave generative reasoning with explicit ontological alignment: a high-recall semantic extractor, a hybrid ontological aligner against the Human Phenotype Ontology (HPO), a generative concept normalizer, and an ontology-grounded validator. The resulting phenotypic profile consists of records that link each phenotype to its HPO concept, identify its subject (proband or family member) and assertion status (confirmed, negated, or suspected), and provide a natural-language rationale supporting the prediction. We further propose an ontology-aware evaluation metric that complements strict identifier matching with bounded partial credit based on HPO topology. We evaluate PHASE on a public dataset of clinical case reports, against five state-of-the-art systems, and show consistent improvements in precision, recall, and F1 score under both exact-match and ontology-aware metrics, while operating exclusively on quantized LLMs deployable on a single workstation GPU. An ablation study quantifies the antagonistic and complementary contributions of generative normalization (recall amplifier) and ontology-grounded validation (precision filter), with consistent qualitative behavior across two open-weight LLMs.
A182FULLData-Driven Near-Optimal Regional Epidemic Surveillance
Rares-Mihail Neagu (University of Iowa) · Jeffrey Keithley (University of Iowa) · Xin Zan (University of Iowa) · Sriram Pemmaraju (University of Iowa) · Bijaya Adhikari (University of Iowa)
Abstract
In the early stages of an epidemic outbreak, when the incidence data is limited, policy makers actively try to establish the scale and scope of the outbreak. Two of the most pertinent questions they seek to answer are i) has the outbreak started in a particular region (e.g. a country) and ii) how many sub-regions (e.g. a state or a county) have been affected thus far? We study these problems as a data-driven knowledge extraction task, i.e., given mobility and epidemiological data, we aim to extract actionable knowledge about which regions should receive additional surveillance resources so that an outbreak is detected early and its spatial footprint is accurately characterized. To this end, we formulate two discrete-lattice optimization objectives for epidemic surveillance, 1) maximizing the probability of detecting at least one infected sub-region and 2) maximizing the expected number of infected sub-regions detected. Both objectives turn out to be NP-hard. However, we prove that they are both submodular, which paves the way for efficient epidemic surveillance from limited data. We use this structure to derive curvature bounds for the objective. We also relate the bound with the parameters of the metapopulation disease dynamics. We propose a scalable algorithm, Lattice-Adapted Modified Greedy (LAMGreedy), that uses the curvature, and marginal-gain machinery to establish constant factor approximation guarantee. Extensive experiments on real-world mobility networks for COVID-19 and Influenza across three U.S. states show that LAMGreedy consistently outperforms natural and the state-of-the-art baselines under multiple cost models. The empirical results validate the prevalence and curvature estimates, and demonstrate that the proposed tools extract high-quality surveillance knowledge from mobility and epidemic data under realistic budget constraints.
A183FULLSTMoE: Multi-Scale Mixture-of-Experts for Single-Cell Gene Expression Prediction from Histology
Xi Li (University of California, Irvine) · Yaqi Hu (University of California, Irvine) · Ziheng Duan (University of California, Irvine) · Chaoyang Wang (University of California, Irvine) · Jing Zhang (University of California, Irvine)
Abstract
Predicting single-cell molecular state from routine histology could make spatial profiling more scalable, but existing histology-to- expression methods are mostly limited to spot-level targets, re- stricted gene panels, or organ-specific settings. This leaves three gaps for practical single-cell deployment: a lack of large aligned- cell resources, limited support for direct multi-organ prediction, and incomplete full-gene expression recovery from whole-slide images. We address these gaps by curating CellST-24M, a 23.94M- cell histology–transcriptomics resource spanning 66 studies, 25 organ categories, Visium HD, and Xenium, and by introducing STMoE, a WSI-only organ-routed prediction framework for full- gene single-cell expression inference. STMoE detects cells from H&E slides, encodes cell-centered and tissue-context crops with a frozen UNI2-h pathology foundation model, aligns image and expression embeddings with soft contrastive learning, and predicts full-gene profiles through organ-routed retrieval from training-only reference banks. On matched human lung benchmarks, STMoE achieves state-of-the-art cell-level performance, outperforming cell- adapted BLEEP, sCellST and GHIST under both in-domain and cross-patient settings. Across 22 organs, STMoE supports direct multi-organ prediction and achieves gene-wise Pearson up to 0.6451 and cell-wise Pearson up to 0.8379, while retaining approximately 60% predictive capability under cross-patient transfer. In down- stream marker-derived analysis, predicted profiles recover coarse cell-state structure with 0.5935 accuracy and 0.5922 balanced accu- racy. Together, CellST-24M and STMoE establish a benchmark and modeling framework for WSI-only, multi-organ, full-gene single- cell histology-to-expression prediction.
A184SHORTRobust Survival Analysis via Fuzzy Interval Learning
Lennart Lamberts (LMU Munich) · Andreas Bender (LMU Munich) · Bernd Bischl (LMU Munich) · Mina Rezaei (LMU Munich)
Abstract
Survival analysis plays an important role in healthcare applications, yet learning reliable time-to-event predictions remains challenging under censoring, limited data, outliers, and distributional shift. Existing uncertainty-aware approaches typically rely on Bayesian inference, ensemble methods, or higher-order probabilistic models, which often require multiple stochastic forward passes or introduce additional modeling complexity. To bridge the gap, we propose Fuzzy-AFT, a single-pass uncertainty-aware survival model that represents predictive uncertainty as output-space imprecision through fuzzy interval-valued predictions on the log-time scale. Our model is embedded within an accelerated failure time (AFT) framework and trained using a hybrid objective that combines censored likelihood estimation with interval-score-based regularization. This formulation enables direct optimization of interval-valued predictions without Bayesian sampling or second-order distributions. Experiments on two survival datasets demonstrate that Fuzzy-AFT maintains competitive predictive performance while improving robustness under covariate shift, outlier corruption, and data scarcity. Furthermore, the learned imprecision provides informative uncertainty signals for out-of-distribution detection. These results suggest that output-space imprecision offers a simple and effective alternative for robust uncertainty-aware survival analysis.
A185APPLIEDHard Rules, Soft Preferences: Bridging Reasoning, Learning, and Optimization for Personalized Packing Checklist Generation
Himel Dev (529 Tech LLC) · Madhusudan Basak (University of Massachusetts Amherst) · Tanmoy Sen (University of Wisconsin–Stout) · Paromita Shome (University of Massachusetts Amherst) · Bashima Islam (University of Massachusetts Amherst)
Abstract
Packing for air travel is recurring and error-prone: the checklist must be personal and context-aware, yet feasible under safety rules, item dependencies, and luggage limits. Existing packing assistants are template-driven or recommendation-driven but unconstrained, leaving users to deal with regulatory and capacity violations. We propose a reasoning-guided learning framework with three stages: (1) a symbolic engine that generates a regulation-compliant seed checklist with explicit dependency structure, (2) a two-stage preference learner that estimates inclusion and priority utilities from user add and remove actions, mitigating survivorship bias, and (3) a CP-SAT optimizer that selects a compact, feasible subset. On 604 labeled trip scenarios (29K inclusion labels, 343K pairwise comparisons), the symbolic engine attains 99.7% recall and 0.96 rubric validity versus 0.78 to 0.81 for frontier LLMs; gradient boosted trees and LambdaMART reach AUC-ROC 0.943 and NDCG@5 0.923; and CP-SAT attains 100% constraint satisfaction versus 28% for greedy and 10% for random. Deployment of the first two stages in FlyEnJoy, a production iOS travel app, doubled checklist completions and reduced completion time. The proposed architecture provides a general framework for constrained personalization, applicable wherever hard feasibility coexists with subjective preferences.
A186SHORTFeasible by Construction: Preference-Guided Itinerary Optimization with Cross-Entropy Search
Himel Dev (529 Tech LLC)
Abstract
Trip itinerary planning requires optimizing user preferences while satisfying hard constraints: opening hours, travel times, visit durations, daily schedule, and budget tier. We present Iterative Itinerary Optimizer, a feasibility-first framework that builds plans through projected insertions, where each proposed POI visit is retimed and kept only if the schedule stays feasible. A learned reward model trained from pairwise itinerary comparisons scores completed plans, and a cross-entropy-style update adapts the construction scorer toward high-reward candidates. Our main goal is to identify where itinerary quality actually comes from. On 891 controlled scenarios, the adaptive optimizer raises mean learned reward from 7.460 to 8.008 over the initial construction baseline. A separate equal-budget comparison attributes the improvement: most of it comes from evaluating several feasible candidates and keeping the best, while the adaptive update adds a smaller but reliable improvement over random sampling (+0.041). Because every edit is checked before it enters the plan, all variants are feasible by construction. The study positions feasible construction as a strong baseline and quantifies what an adaptive preference loop adds on top.

A001SHORTHigher Capacity Transfer into JPQ Item Codes for Scalable Sequential Recommendation
Sharare Zolghadr (University of Glasgow) · Richard Mccreadie (University of Glasgow) · Craig Macdonald (University of Glasgow)
Abstract
Although transformer models have improved the effectiveness of sequential recommendation, their computational and memory costs make it challenging to scale to item catalogues containing millions of items. To address this limitation, RecJPQ, a recommendation method based on joint product quantisation, represents each item using compact discrete codes rather than large embedding tables, substantially reducing training memory requirements. These codes are typically initialised from a memory-efficient bootstrap representation, such as truncated SVD, before being quantised. However, this process introduces an information bottleneck: because quantisation is inherently lossy, information may be lost when the bootstrap representation is mapped to the fixed-budget discrete item-code space, resulting in suboptimal code assignments. To address this capacity transfer problem, we initialise JPQ item codes using a higher-dimensional bootstrap representation and adopt product quantisation (PQ) to compress this representation into the fixed-budget discrete item-code space prior to training; we refer to this method as RecJPQ-HC (Higher Capacity). Experimental results show that RecJPQ-HC consistently improves downstream recommendation performance over the original RecJPQ code assignment strategy. Across multiple datasets and sequential recommendation models, it achieves statistically significant average relative improvements of approximately 30% in NDCG@10 while preserving memory efficiency.
A002FULLRecommender System as Slow and Fast Thinkers
Zichen Yuan (City University of Hongkong) · Xiaoxuan Dong (University of Electronic Science and Technology of China) · Linkun Dai (Shanghai Jiao Tong University) · Jinwei Yang (University of Electronic Science and Technology of China) · Jining Luan (University of Electronic Science and Technology of China) · Dexu Yu (Fenz.AI) · Chunxiao Li (University of Science and Technology of China) · Joemon M. Jose (GAIR-Lab - School of Computing Science, University of Glasgow) · Youhua Li (City University of Hong Kong) · Hanwen Du (Ohio State University) · Junchen Fu (GAIR-Lab - School of Computing Science, University of Glasgow)
Abstract
Sequential recommendation models are foundational to modern personalized services, yet their effectiveness varies substantially across heterogeneous user environments. In particular, static one-pass recommenders often perform well on common behavior patterns but degrade on operationally challenging user groups, such as users with longer histories or less mainstream item profiles. To address this limitation, we propose DS-Frame, an adaptive fast–slow inference framework for sequential recommendation. DS-Frame combines a Fast System for efficient routine prediction, a Slow System for iterative latent refinement, and a learned selector that routes each sample under a controllable computation budget. Experiments on five real-world datasets show that DS-Frame consistently improves representative sequential recommendation backbones, with larger gains on challenging groups and effective accuracy–efficiency trade-offs. This highlights the potential of adaptive inference for more efficient and robust recommendation. Code is available at https://github.com/ZichenYuan233/Recommender-System-as-Slow-and-Fast-Thinkers
A003FULLFrom Overlooked to Explored: Recovering Item Relations via Mixture of Perspectives for Sequential Recommendation
Junyoung Kim (Pohang University of Science and Technology) · Wonbin Kweon (Sungkyunkwan University) · Woojoo Kim (Pohang University of Science and Technology) · Jaehyung Lim (Pohang University of Science and Technology) · Dongha Kim (Pohang University of Science and Technology) · Hwanjo Yu (Pohang University of Science and Technology)
Abstract
Capturing user preference from a user's interaction sequence is the central challenge of Sequential Recommendation (SR). This preference intuitively emerges from inter-item relations: each item transition reflects a preference embedded in the relations between items, making the faithful capture of these relations essential for accurate recommendation. For this reason, self-attention is dominant in sequential recommendation for its ability to compute pairwise item interactions, yet our empirical analysis reveals that it consistently suffers from similarity bias across various types of transformer-based SR models: dot-product attention scores disproportionately favor similar items, systematically overlooking heterogeneous relations with meaningful preference signals and directly limiting recommendation performance. To address this, we propose PRISM (Perspective-based Relational Insight Synthesis Module), a module that re-examines item relations from multiple perspectives. PRISM employs K Perspective Lenses to calibrate attention from distinct viewpoints, combining an Affinity View that refines homogeneous relations and a Contrast View that exposes heterogeneous ones suppressed by similarity bias, enabling the model to capture the full spectrum of user preferences. Extensive experiments on seven real-world benchmarks demonstrate that PRISM consistently outperforms state-of-the-art baselines. Our code is available at https://github.com/327aem/PRISM/.
A004SHORTLatent Intent Anchoring for Robust Sequential Recommendation
Yifan Shao (The Chinese University of Hong Kong) · Peilin Zhou (New York University, Abu Dhabi) · Shoujin Wang (University of Technology Sydney) · Tuka Alhanai (New York University, Abu Dhabi)
Abstract
User behavior sequences are often driven by stable, high-level intents. Existing intent-aware sequential recommendation methods typically extract intents from derived sequence representations to serve as post-hoc supervisory signals. Although effective, this post-hoc paradigm prevents intents from explicitly participating in the semantic shaping of sequential representations. Without a structural high-level semantic anchor, the sequence representations become vulnerable to local item transitions and user behavioral noise. To overcome this challenge, we propose IASRec, an Intent-Anchored Sequential Recommendation framework that shifts user intents from post-hoc supervisors to architectural anchors. IASRec consists of three synergistic modules: (1) a Latent Intent Distiller (LID) to extract multi-faceted latent intents from interaction sequences; (2) an Intent-Anchoring Encoder (IAE) that infuses intent semantics into item representations to guide temporal dependency modeling; and (3) an Intent Consistency Regularizer (ICR) that ensures robustness across different intent views. Extensive experiments on three real-world datasets demonstrate that IASRec achieves an average 7.7% improvement over state-of-the-art baselines and exhibits superior robustness, with markedly better resilience to 20% behavioral noise compared to competing methods. The source code is available at https://github.com/x-labs-xyz/iasrec.
A005SHORTCoRe-Rec: Budgeted Consistency Policy Re-Rolling for Sequential Recommendation
Zhiyuan Zhang (The Hong Kong University of Science and Technology (Guangzhou)) · Yuxin He (The Hong Kong University of Science and Technology (Guangzhou)) · Yong Sun (The Hong Kong University of Science and Technology (Guangzhou)) · Lijiang Liu (The Hong Kong University of Science and Technology (Guangzhou)) · Junyu Shi (The Hong Kong University of Science and Technology (Guangzhou)) · Zhengjie Zhang (The Hong Kong University of Science and Technology (Guangzhou)) · Minxue Fang (Peking University) · Danqi Yan (The Hong Kong University of Science and Technology (Guangzhou)) · Qiang Nie (The Hong Kong University of Science and Technology (Guangzhou))
Abstract
Real-time sequential recommendation requires policies that are both expressive and efficient. Diffusion policies can model diverse user preferences, but their iterative denoising process introduces high serving latency. Standard reinforcement learning (RL) actors usually execute a single sampled action without checking whether the action is likely to trigger a positive user response before exposure. We propose CoRe-Rec, a budgeted consistency-policy re-rolling framework for RL-based slate recommendation. CoRe-Rec uses a shared consistency actor to generate continuous hyper-actions in one or few denoising steps. Each hyper-action induces a provisional slate through top-K item scoring. Before execution, a frozen user response model (URM) evaluates multiple low-cost candidates generated with different sampler configurations and noise seeds, and an early-stopping rule selects the best slate under an inference budget. The re-rolling step is a detached test-time search procedure: gradients are not propagated through the discrete sampler selection or the top-K slate construction; instead, the selected branch is recomputed for actor-critic learning. Experiments in simulated environments built from RL4RS, BookCrossing, and MovieLens 1M show that CoRe-Rec improves cumulative reward and episode depth while providing a favorable reward–latency trade-off.
A006FULLPRISM: Pruning-Enhanced Intent Sampling for Recommendation Multi-List Generation
Zheli Zhou (Shanghai Jiao Tong University) · Si Dong (Kuaishou Technology) · Weiwen Liu (Shanghai Jiao Tong University) · Bo Chen (Kuaishou Technology) · Jianghao Lin (Shanghai Jiao Tong University) · Weinan Zhang (Shanghai Jiao Tong University) · Chaoyi Ma (Kuaishou Technology) · Ruiming Tang (Kuaishou Technology) · Han Li (Kuaishou Technology) · Kun Gai (Kuaishou Technology)
Abstract
Generative recommendation has emerged as a prominent paradigm, unifying retrieval and ranking through large-scale sequence transducers. However, existing generative recommenders are basically pointwise: they optimize for next-item prediction, leaving the construction of the final exposure list—a slate—to heuristic post-processing. This creates a structural gap between pointwise candidate generation and industrial listwise delivery, which demands holistic reasoning over contextual opportunity, position bias, and intent uncertainty. To bridge this gap, we introduce List Composer, a decoupled module that transforms pointwise candidate pools into deliverable exposure lists within generative recommender systems. We instantiate this concept through PRISM, an autoregressive listwise generation model featuring two core mechanisms. First, a CVAE-based IntentSampler module models user interests as a latent distribution, sampling distinct intent facets as initial states averts the Deterministic Collapse phenomenon, wherein standard autoregressive generators converge onto nearly identical sequences despite repeated decoding. Second, a Listwise Pruning strategy dynamically culls low-utility beam paths using position-discounted pointwise scores, concentrating computational resources on promising trajectories. Extensive offline experiments and real-world online A/B tests validate the effectiveness of PRISM, which achieves consistent improvements in recommendation quality and serving efficiency, including a 0.288% gain in video views on a major short-video platform.
A007APPLIEDOneMall: One Architecture, More Scenarios — End-to-End Generative Recommender Family for E-commerce at Kuaishou
Kun Zhang (Kuaishou Technology) · Jingming Zhang (Kuaishou Technology) · Wei Cheng (Kuaishou Technology) · Yansong Cheng (Kuaishou Technology) · Jiaqi Zhang (Kuaishou Technology) · Jiangxia Cao (Kuaishou) · Hao Lu (Kuaishou Technology) · Xu Zhang (Kuaishou Technology) · Haixiang Gan (Kuaishou Technology) · Tenglong Wang (Kuaishou Technology) · Ximing Zhang (Kuaishou Technology) · Boyang Xia (Kuaishou Technology) · Kuo Cai (Kuaishou Technology) · Hongjian Dou (Kuaishou Technology) · Jinkai Yu (Kuaishou Technology) · Mingxing Wen (Kuaishou Technology) · Qiang Luo (Kuaishou Technology) · Zhaojie Liu (Kuaishou Technology)
Abstract
In the wave of generative recommendation, we present OneMall, an end-to-end generative recommendation framework tailored for e-commerce services at Kuaishou. Our OneMall systematically unifies the e-commerce's multiple item distribution scenarios, such as Product-card, short-video and live-streaming. Specifically, it comprises three key components, aligning the entire model training pipeline to the LLM's pre-training/post-training: (1) E-commerce Semantic Tokenizer: we provide a tokenizer solution that captures both real-world semantics and business-specific item relations across different scenarios; (2) Transformer-based Architecture: we largely utilize Transformer as our model backbone, e.g., employing Query-Former for long sequence compression, Cross-Attention for multi-behavior sequence fusion, and Sparse MoE for scalable auto-regressive generation; (3) Reinforcement Learning Pipeline: we further connect retrieval and ranking models via RL, enabling the ranking model to serve as a reward signal for end-to-end policy retrieval model optimization. Extensive experiments demonstrate that OneMall achieves consistent improvements across all e-commerce scenarios: +14.7% GMV in Product-Card, +10.3% GMV in Short-Video, and +4.9% GMV in Live-Streaming. OneMall has been deployed, serving over 400 million daily active users at Kuaishou.
A008APPLIEDBAGEL: Behavior and Preference Alignment for Generative Live-Streaming Recommendation
Shuni Chen (Kuaishou Technology) · Anjie Zhu (Kuaishou Technology) · Peilin Song (Kuaishou Technology) · Xuming Wang (Kuaishou Technology) · Fei Pan (Kuaishou Technology) · Peng Jiang (Kuaishou Technology)
Abstract
Generative recommendation represents a paradigm shift through reformulating the recommendation task as an auto-regressive token generation over discrete Semantic IDs (SIDs). However, existing SID-based approaches inadequately capture the temporal dynamics and behavioral discrimination in live-streaming recommendation, primarily due to two critical challenges: (1) dynamic content-behavior misalignment, where static SIDs fail to encode time-varying segment semantics and hierarchical behavioral intensity; (2) reward-agnostic preference alignment, where SID embedding alignment lacks fine-grained reward guidance, resulting in a significant gap between embedding and diverse online business metrics. To address these challenges, we propose a Behavior and Preference Alignment for Generative Live-Streaming Recommendation (BAGEL). First, to tackle dynamic content-behavior misalignment, we introduce real-time segment-level alignment that captures product transitions at 30-second granularity during live-streaming. Additionally, we leverage an end-to-end behavior-guided quantization that infuses hierarchical behavioral signals into residual quantization layers, enabling SIDs to integrate dynamic content and encode user preference intensity hierarchically. Second, a retrieval-based preference alignment is developed to tackle reward-agnostic preference alignment, providing multi-dimensional reward signals for end-to-end alignment optimization and advancing preference alignment from the conventional post-training stage into the representation alignment phase. Extensive experiments on industrial-scale datasets and online A/B tests on Kuaishou's local-life service demonstrate the effectiveness of BAGEL.
A009APPLIEDMERGE: Next-Generation Item Indexing Paradigm for Large-Scale Streaming Recommendation
Jing Yan (Bytedance) · Yimeng Bai (Bytedance) · Zongyu Liu (Bytedance) · Yahui Liu (Bytedance) · Junwei Wang (Bytedance) · Jingze Huang (Bytedance) · Haoda Li (Bytedance) · Sihao Ding (ByteDance) · Shaohui Ruan (ByteDance) · Yang Zhang (National University of Singapore)
Abstract
