Item indexing, which maps a large corpus of items into compact discrete representations, is critical for both discriminative and generative recommender systems, yet existing Vector Quantization (VQ)-based approaches struggle with the highly skewed and non-stationary item distributions common in industrial streaming recommenders, leading to poor assignment accuracy, imbalanced cluster occupancy, and insufficient cluster separation. To address these challenges, we propose MERGE, a next-generation item indexing paradigm that adaptively constructs clusters from scratch, dynamically monitors cluster occupancy, and forms hierarchical index structures via fine-to-coarse merging. Extensive experiments demonstrate that MERGE significantly improves assignment accuracy, cluster uniformity, and cluster separation compared with existing indexing methods, while online A/B tests show substantial gains in key business metrics, highlighting its potential as a foundational indexing approach for large-scale recommendation. Codes are available at https://github.com/baiyimeng/MERGE.
A010SHORTFrom Head to Tail: Asymmetric Knowledge Transfer in Long-tail Recommendation with Generative Semantic IDs
Chenyi Yan (Alibaba Group) · Ruocong Tang (Alibaba Group) · Xing Fang (Alibaba Group) · Yang Huang (Alibaba Group) · He Guo (Peking University) · Jing Wang (Alibaba Group)
Abstract
Long-tail recommendation in real-world e-commerce platforms remains challenging due to severe data imbalance. Existing methods often struggle to combine content-based multimodal features with collaborative signals. Many of these methods also ignore an important asymmetry in knowledge transfer between head and tail IDs: noisy signals from tail IDs can hurt representation learning for head IDs. This paper presents AKT-Rec, a framework for Asymmetric Knowledge Transfer in long-tail Recommendation that uses LLM-generated semantic IDs. AKT-Rec uses Multimodal LLMs (MLLMs) with supervised fine-tuning to align content representations with collaborative information for both items and users, producing semantic representations. It then discretizes these representations into semantic IDs with a Residual-Quantized VAE (RQ-VAE), which yields semantic clusters of similar entities. AKT-Rec has two main components: (1) Cluster-Guided Adaptive Embedding, which decomposes each ID representation into a cluster-level embedding that captures shared semantics and an individual embedding. Through an asymmetric contrastive objective and an activity-aware gating mechanism, this module directs knowledge transfer from head to tail IDs. (2) Hierarchical Feature Aggregation, which builds parallel feature views and adaptively fuses them to optimize predictions for samples with varying activity levels. Extensive experiments on both a public benchmark and a large-scale industrial dataset, together with online A/B testing on a major e-commerce platform, demonstrate the effectiveness of AKT-Rec. AKT-Rec improves offline performance by 0.35% in AUC and 1.53% in GAUC, outperforming several competitive baselines. In online A/B testing, AKT-Rec achieves a 2.76% increase in CTR and a 3.47% increase in GMV, validating its utility in real-world production environments.
A011SHORTPreference-Aligned Semantic IDs for Generative Recommendation
Valentin Tsaruk (MIRAI) · Danil Gusak (AXXX) · Rostislav Korst (MIRAI) · Evgeny Frolov (AXXX)
Abstract
Semantic IDs (SIDs) are becoming a practical interface for generative recommendation. Existing pipelines usually build them by quantizing frozen content embeddings, implicitly assuming that content similarity is the right geometry for recommendation. This assumption is often too strong: items that look similar in content space may play different roles in user behavior, while behaviorally related items may be far apart in text embedding space. We propose a simple pre-quantization alignment step for SID construction. Starting from frozen content embeddings, we train a lightweight content-to-item adapter inside a sequential next-item prediction model. The adapted vectors replace the standard item embedding table and are optimized with the recommender’s cross-entropy objective. After training, the sequential model is discarded, and the adapted item vectors are quantized using a standard SID tokenizer such as RQ-KMeans. The resulting codes preserve the content-based SID interface while aligning the underlying continuous space with user behavior. This design separates two roles that are usually coupled: learning a recommendation-useful item geometry and assigning discrete codes. It is easy to add to existing SID pipelines and requires no changes to the tokenizer or the downstream generative recommender. Experiments show that aligning embeddings before quantization improves ranking quality over content-only SIDs, collaborative-only SIDs, and compression baseline.
A012FULLCross-Domain Sequential Recommendation with Representation-Level User Transfer
Abdulaziz Samra (Skolkovo Institute of Science and Technology) · Nikita Sukhorukov (AXXX) · Alexey Grishanov (Sber AI Lab) · Alexey Vasilev (Sber AI Lab) · Evgeny Frolov (AXXX)
Abstract
Cross-domain sequential recommendation aims to improve next-item prediction in a target domain by leveraging user behavior from auxiliary source domains. However, real-world deployment faces two critical challenges: business constraints that isolate interaction data across domains, and user heterogeneity, where many users lack cross-domain activity. This makes existing cross-domain methods difficult to apply. In this paper, we propose a simple and practical framework for cross-domain sequential recommendations that transfers information exclusively through learned user representations, without sharing raw interaction data or item embeddings across domains. We introduce a lightweight adapter that projects the source-domain user representation into the target-domain embedding space and integrates it with the target interaction sequence. Importantly, when source data is unavailable (i.e., the user observed only in the target domain), the model seamlessly defaults to a robust target-only sequential recommender, retaining benefits from joint training across all users. Extensive experiments were conducted under two setups; one targets benchmarking against previous baselines, while the other focuses on realistic and scalable conditions. Both sets of experiments demonstrate consistent performance gains for shared and unshared users.
A013RESOURCESIDInspector: A Mapping-First Diagnostic Resource for Semantic-ID Tokenizers
Jiandong Ding (Huawei Technologies Co., Ltd.) · Heng Chang (Huawei Technologies Co., Ltd.) · Huijie Qin (Huawei Technologies Co., Ltd.) · Tianying Liu (Huawei Technologies Co., Ltd.)
Abstract
Semantic-ID (SID) tokenizers define the item address space consumed by generative recommenders. Yet their exported mappings remain difficult to inspect consistently before downstream training. We introduce SIDInspector, a mapping-first diagnostic resource that exposes coverage gaps, full-code aliasing, behaviorally weak prefixes, tail compression, and prefix fan-out. Its adapter contract normalizes item mappings, metadata, interactions, and optional generator traces; validation checks the resulting artifact; and mapping-level probes characterize utilization, aliasing, neighborhood alignment, popularity allocation, and structural cost. Optional interfaces extend the resource to temporal churn and generator traces. We evaluate SIDInspector on four tokenizer lines with explicit provenance. A same-item Musical study compares controlled GRID-style RQ-KMeans exports at two capacity settings with a bounded ReSID/GAOQ export; released LETTER and LC-Rec mappings test the contract on official item-index artifacts. The larger-budget GRID-style row has D2 full-code aliasing of 0.779, versus 0.977 for the width-64 row, while ReSID/GAOQ reaches 0.000. The D3 ordering differs: a deterministic category-prefix control reaches 0.447 versus 0.055–0.154 for the learned exports. Together, these results distinguish capacity, addressability, and behavioral alignment at the artifact level. Across additional datasets, D3 varies under the same category-prefix control. A bounded fixed-reranker probe links D3 to candidate exposure; ranking quality is assessed downstream.
A014SHORTDo Recommenders Need to Think in Words? Latent Reasoning for Efficient LLM-Based Recommendation
Hongyang Su (Tencent) · Beibei Kong (Tencent) · Lei Cheng (Tencent) · Chengxiang Zhuo (Tencent) · Zang Li (Tencent)
Abstract
LLM-based recommender systems increasingly generate chain-of-thought (CoT) text before each item prediction to activate the LLM's reasoning capacity, costing tens to hundreds of extra tokens per recommendation at inference. We ask whether inference-time reasoning artifacts (textual or latent) can be replaced by training-time supervision alone, without loss of accuracy. We propose LatentRec, a framework for LLM-based generative recommendation that replaces inference-time reasoning artifacts with training-time per-step head supervision. LatentRec has three components. A 2.5M-parameter Continuous Thought Module iterates K latent reasoning steps over the LLM's hidden state during training. Soft Token Selection bridges the approximately 14x norm gap between hidden states and input embeddings. A Per-step Reasoning Loss (PRL) supervises every intermediate state through the LLM's prediction head against the first token of the target Semantic ID. The trained LLM retains this accuracy without the module at inference, so the module can be discarded at deployment. On three Amazon benchmarks, LatentRec improves HR@10 by 4.0–5.0% (relative) over a CoT-distilled baseline at 18.3x lower latency (batch=1). Per-step training supervision consistently improves accuracy across three datasets, paid once at training rather than at every recommendation.
A015FULLClusterRec: Cluster-Aware Recommendation with Large Language Models for Efficient and Scalable Inference
Jingzhe Yuan (Tsinghua University) · Yongjian Zhou (School of Big Data and Software Engineering, Chongqing University) · Changxi Wen (Tsinghua University) · Shicheng Liu (Tsinghua University) · Bin Liu (Taobao & Tmall Group of Alibaba) · Ziru Xu (Taobao & Tmall Group of Alibaba) · Han Zhu (Taobao & Tmall Group of Alibaba) · Yue Wang (Department of Electronic Engineering, Tsinghua University) · Wei Zhou (School of Big Data and Software Engineering, Chongqing University) · Chen Gao (BNRist, Tsinghua University) · Yong Li (BNRist, Tsinghua University)
Abstract
Recent advances in large language models (LLMs) have significantly improved recommender systems by enabling richer semantic modeling of user preferences. However, existing LLM-based recommenders typically require expensive per-user inference over long interaction sequences, causing computational costs to scale rapidly with both model size and the number of users. To address this challenge, we propose ClusterRec, a framework that decouples LLM-based recommendation into two stages: (1) group-level preference modeling and (2) user-level personalization. Specifically, users are first clustered based on behavioral representations, and LLMs are employed to construct a group-level semantic representation for each cluster. Individual user representations are then constructed by integrating shared group representations with personalized collaborative filtering embeddings. This design amortizes LLM inference at the group level, substantially reducing computational overhead while preserving personalization. Extensive experiments on four real-world datasets demonstrate that ClusterRec achieves performance comparable to state-of-the-art methods, including conventional CF-SRec (e.g., SASRec) and recent LLM-based recommenders, while significantly reducing LLM inference cost. These results highlight that group-level semantic modeling provides an effective and scalable paradigm for integrating LLMs into practical recommender systems. The code is available at https://github.com/tsinghua-fib-lab/ClusterRec.
A016SHORTTraining-Free LLM-Based Recommendation with Post-LLM Item Refinement Using Collaborative Signals
Kyungho Kim (KAIST) · Sunwoo Kim (KAIST) · Geon Lee (KAIST) · Shinhwan Kang (KAIST) · Sojeong Kim (KAIST) · Liam Collins (Snap Inc.) · Bhuvesh Kumar (Snap Inc.) · Donald Loveland (Snap Inc.) · Kijung Shin (KAIST)
Abstract
Large language models (LLMs) have shown promise for training-free recommendation, but LLM-generated user interests are often too broad for fine-grained item retrieval. Existing methods incorporate collaborative filtering (CF) signals in a pre-LLM manner through candidate reranking or prompt augmentation, yielding limited gains. We propose CoRRe, a training-free recommendation framework with a post-LLM paradigm that injects CF signals into LLM-generated item representations, which are later matched with LLM-generated user interests for ranking. Specifically, CoRRe refines the directions of item embeddings using an item-item co-purchase graph and their magnitudes using item popularity. Experiments on real-world datasets show that CoRRe consistently outperforms existing training-free methods and achieves competitive or superior performance compared with training-based methods, without requiring any model training or task-specific fine-tuning.
A017SHORTTyped Counterfactual Preference Optimization for Multi-Turn Conversational Recommendation Agents
Hongxu Shi (Academy of Military Science) · Yi Liu (Academy of Military Science) · Kun Liu (Academy of Military Science)
Abstract
Large language models have enabled conversational recommendation agents (CRAs) that interact with users through preference clarification, tool-based retrieval, and natural-language recommendation. Existing prompt-based and preference-optimization methods can improve the interaction capabilities of CRAs, but they provide limited direct guidance for a critical multi-turn decision: when should the agent ask for more preferences, invoke the retriever, or present recommendations? To address this issue, we propose PAPO, a progress-anchored typed counterfactual preference optimization framework for multi-turn CRAs. PAPO identifies critical dialogue states where the current policy is likely to make strategically suboptimal action choices. For each critical state, PAPO constructs typed counterfactual candidates across Ask, Search, and Respond, and verifies them with action-type-specific criteria: information gain for clarification, item reachability progress for retrieval, and recommendation readiness and response grounding. The verified counterfactual actions are used to build preference pairs for direct preference optimization. Experiments in three AILO-Agent-based interactive recommendation environments show that PAPO improves recommendation-oriented performance over strong prompt-based and training-based baselines while maintaining competitive simulator-assessed satisfaction. Ablation and action timing analyses further confirm the effectiveness of typed counterfactual construction, type-specific verification, and readiness-aware recommendation.
A018SHORTFrom Counterfactual Edits to Human Narratives: LLM-Driven Interpretations for Recommender System Explanations
Vojtech Cahlik (Faculty of Information Technology, Czech Technical University in Prague) · Amir Reza Mohammadi (Department of Computer Science, University of Innsbruck) · Rodrigo Alves (Faculty of Information Technology, Czech Technical University in Prague) · Pavel Kordik (Faculty of Information Technology, Czech Technical University in Prague) · Eva Zangerle (Department of Computer Science, University of Innsbruck)
Abstract
Recommender systems increasingly influence what users discover and consume online, yet the decision logic behind their outputs often remains opaque. Counterfactual explanation (CFX) methods provide an effective way to show which changes to a user's interaction history would alter a recommendation. In recommendation settings, however, CFXs often require many edits, producing long, low-level lists that are hard for users to interpret. Moreover, most evaluations emphasize edit counts while largely overlooking whether the resulting CFXs are coherent and actionable for users. We argue that this gap between generating valid CFXs and communicating model behavior stems from the lack of user-centered abstraction and limited qualitative evaluation. To bridge this gap, we investigate large language models as mediators that summarize raw CFX interaction edit lists into concise natural language explanations describing higher-level preference patterns. We optimize these mediators for correctness, informativeness, and linguistic quality through preference optimization, and evaluate the resulting explanations with human-calibrated metrics derived from separate human-labeled datasets. On the MovieLens-1M dataset, across multiple counterfactual generators and language models, the resulting summaries achieve high overall linguistic quality, while the strongest semantic results are obtained with high-success CFX methods such as ACCENT and SPINRec. Direct Preference Optimization improves the semantic metrics in almost all evaluated settings.
A019SHORTRevisiting N2DCG: An Empirically Grounded Reformulation of Carousel Recommendation Evaluation
Jingwei Kang (University of Amsterdam) · Santiago de Leon-Martinez (Brno University of Technology) · Maarten de Rijke (University of Amsterdam) · Harrie Oosterhuis (University of Amsterdam)
Abstract
Carousel interfaces have been widely used in video and music streaming services, yet it remains unclear how to properly evaluate recommender systems in these two-dimensional layouts. N2DCG has been proposed to address this gap by adapting NDCG to carousel-based recommendation, but it relies on unverified assumptions borrowed from the single-list web-search setting that do not transfer well to two-dimensional carousel layouts. We identify two substantial limitations of N2DCG: its ideal ranking, used for normalization, violates carousel constraints, and its discount function does not reflect user browsing behavior observed in empirical data. To address both limitations, we propose a reformulation of N2DCG that normalizes appropriately by respecting constraints and uses an empirically grounded discount function. We validate the proposed metric, showing that it better reflects users' empirical behavior on real-world eye-tracking data and better predicts the comparison results of carousel layouts simulated based on empirical examination patterns.
A020SHORTDiagnosing Lexical Text-Anchor Retrievability in Sequential Recommendation Benchmarks
Keito Kozaki (Hokkaido University) · Keigo Sakurai (Hokkaido University) · Ren Togo (Hokkaido University) · Takahiro Ogawa (Hokkaido University) · Miki Haseyama (Hokkaido University)
Abstract
Aggregate accuracy on text-rich sequential recommendation benchmarks can obscure whether gains reflect broader sequential preference modeling or local item-text matching. We operationalize lexical text-anchor retrievability with a BM25-over-title diagnostic for identifying next-item cases recoverable from recent history items. On Amazon Beauty, Sports, and Toys, last-title BM25@10 retrieves the target for 6.6%, 3.6%, and 8.8% of test cases, while a recent-5 anchor-union diagnostic retrieves the target for 12.8%, 7.8%, and 14.4%; the same diagnostic is much weaker on ML-1M and Steam. As an aggregate-sensitivity test, we inject normalized recent-title evidence into ID-based sequential models without additional model training. On Amazon datasets, this bounded, validation-tuned perturbation shifts Recall@10 by an amount comparable to differences among recent learned retrieval-oriented references under our evaluation setting. These results indicate that the Amazon product benchmarks considered here contain a recency-concentrated text-anchor-retrievable regime that can disproportionately influence aggregate evaluation. We therefore recommend reporting performance separately on text-anchor-retrievable and non-retrievable cases alongside aggregate Recall/NDCG. The code is available at: https://github.com/keito0329/Retrievability.
A021SHORTCross-Country Code-Mixing for Generative Recommendation
Yuan Gao (Alibaba International Digital Commerce Group) · Hao Deng (Alibaba International Digital Commerce Group) · Haibo Xing (Alibaba International Digital Commerce Group) · Yi Xu (Alibaba International Digital Commerce Group) · Lingyu Mu (Alibaba International Digital Commerce Group) · Jinxin Hu (Alibaba International Digital Commerce Group) · Yu Zhang (Alibaba International Digital Commerce Group) · Xiaoyi Zeng (Alibaba International Digital Commerce Group)
Abstract
Cross-country recommendation on modern e-commerce platforms is typically deployed with disjoint user and item ID spaces across markets, removing the shared anchors that conventional cross-domain methods rely on. Generative recommendation (GR) mitigates this by mapping items into a shared token space and training a unified model, but existing approaches keep behavior sequences strictly country-specific, so knowledge transfer occurs only at the parameter level and remains absent at the data level. Inspired by code-switching corpora in multilingual natural language processing, we propose CMRec, a cross-country GR framework that injects cross-country supervision at the data level via dual-constrained, context-aware code-mixing. CMRec first learns a shared semantic codebook from multi-modal content and behavioral co-occurrence across countries. It then uses this codebook to synthesize mixed-country sequences via token-level substitutions that satisfy both static (content) and dynamic (e.g., price, audience, popularity) constraints. Finally, it introduces a context-aware loss that reweights mixed samples according to their plausibility in the current sequence. Experiments on two real-world multi-country datasets and an online A/B test show that CMRec substantially improves recommendation quality in data-sparse countries while preserving performance in data-rich countries, achieving +1.77% advertising revenue and +2.64% orders on a large-scale e-commerce platform.
A022APPLIEDLLM-based User-Product Relevance Evaluation for Dynamic Product Advertising
Wen Zhang (Snap Inc.) · Xiao Bai (Snap Inc.) · Hsiang-Wei Chao (Snap Inc.) · Mengfan Zhu (Snap Inc.) · Tong Zhao (Snap Inc.) · Mingxuan Ju (Snap. Inc) · Xiaodong Liu (Snap Inc.) · Congfei Zhang (Snap Inc.) · Yunzhi Zhou (Snap Inc.) · Yajun Wang (Snap Inc.) · Jinchao Li (Snap Inc.) · Yu Zhang (Snap Inc.)
Abstract
Dynamic Product Advertising (DPA) retrieval systems are a core component of modern e-commerce advertising; however, their evaluation remains challenging. Conventional offline engagement metrics are limited by sparse, biased feedback, while online evaluation is costly and time-consuming. In this work, we propose a user--product relevance metric for offline evaluation of DPA retrieval systems. The metric first compresses the engagement history into a compact set of intent representatives via Semantic-ID-grouped, event-stratified segmentation, then assesses the relevance of a recommended product to each individual intent and aggregates them as a user-level relevance score, yielding a stable and interpretable measure of retrieval quality. To compute this metric at scale, we leverage large language models (LLMs) as semantic relevance judges, capturing nuanced functional and semantic relationships that heuristic methods often miss. We propose an agentic, human-aligned prompting framework that generates multi-category relevance guidelines and distills teacher-model judgments into an efficient student model for scalable evaluation. The resulting metric strongly correlates with offline and online business metrics, enabling faster and more reliable DPA retrieval iteration before A/B testing.
A023FULLSemantic-Structural Cross-Calibration for Multi-Behavior Recommendation
Haoran Fang (Northeastern University) · Ying Yin (Northeastern University) · Chuanhou Sun (Northeastern University) · Shengjun Ma (Northeastern University) · Yuan Li (North China University of Technology) · Yuhai Zhao (Northeastern University) · Xingwei Wang (Northeastern University)
Abstract
Multi-behavior recommendation (MBR) alleviates target behavior sparsity by leveraging abundant auxiliary behaviors. However, most MBR methods are trapped in a dilemma. Separately aggregating multiple behaviors struggles to fully exploit cross-behavior interaction information, while collectively aggregating different behaviors into a unified graph may cause the target behavior to be submerged among massive auxiliary behaviors. To this end, we propose the Semantic-struCtural crOss-calibRation modEl (SCORE), a structure-conditioned calibration framework for MBR. SCORE adopts a decouple–enhance–calibrate strategy to fully exploit cross-behavior interactions while robustly reconstructing target-related user representations. Specifically, SCORE first decouples target semantics from unified representations through a shared modulation space under joint multi-behavior supervision. It then enhances unified representations through structural refinement on the target-behavior graph, reconstructing target-consistent structural context. Finally, SCORE reconciles semantic and structural references through structure-conditioned gating to obtain calibrated representations. Extensive experiments on three real-world benchmarks demonstrate that SCORE greatly improves over thirteen competitive baselines by up to 61.73% on HR@10 and 46.04% on NDCG@10.
A024SHORTTaxonomy-Guided Contrastive Learning with Competency-Calibrated Graphs for Job Recommendation
Wonseok Son (Dong-A University) · Haeyoon Koo (Konkuk University) · Jeonghyeon Park (Dong-A University) · Byungkook Oh (Konkuk University) · Sejin Chun (Dong-A University)
Abstract
The goal of job-skill matching is to predict appropriate job opportunities for job seekers based on their skill-sets. Prior studies encode unstructured skill data into latent representations using simple mappings within job classification systems. However, such approaches often fall short in capturing the multi-level and asymmetric associations between jobs and job-relevant competencies. To address these limitations, we propose TaxoCal, a Taxonomy-guided contrastive learning framework with competency-Calibrated graph propagation for skill-based job recommendation. TaxoCal combines skill-taxonomy augmentation with degree-normalized bipartite graph propagation to mitigate generic skill bias and preserve job-specific competency signals. The model learns both skill and job representations using path/depth cues from the taxonomy and competency-aware interaction patterns in the job-skill graph. Experimental results on real-world datasets show that our method improves accuracy by +13.6%, NDCG@3 by +10.6%, and MRR@3 by +11.7%, outperforming state-of-the-art baselines.
A025SHORTDualSpectralCF: Training-Free Sign-Aware Spectral Collaborative Filtering
Guanqun Yang (Stevens Institute of Technology) · Tong Qi (University of Maryland, College Park) · Xiaoxue Han (Stevens Institute of Technology)
Abstract
Real-world recommendation platforms routinely collect explicit negative feedback such as 1-star reviews, hate-button clicks, distrust between users, and very-low watch-ratio videos. Learned sign-aware recommenders exploit this signal for clear accuracy gains, but only at the cost of gradient-based training. In parallel, a line of training-free spectral collaborative filtering methods matches or beats learned graph recommenders at a fraction of the cost, yet operates on positive interactions alone. We bridge these two lines with DualSpectralCF, a training-free framework of two components that attach to any spectral backbone of the form r̂u = F(M) ru: a signed input signal ru± that encodes the user's explicit dislikes, and a signed item-item operator M± that blends like-together and dislike-together similarity. The framework is backbone-agnostic and adds just two scalar hyperparameters. We instantiate DualSpectralCF on ChebyCF, GF-CF, and Turbo-CF, and evaluate on five sign-aware benchmarks: every instance matches or beats its unsigned backbone on all 5 datasets at Recall@20 and in 14 of 15 cases at NDCG@20, with Recall@20 lifts up to +32.6% with backbone-specific (γ, κ) tuning and +1.9% to +16.0% for DualSpectralCF on ChebyCF at the fixed default (γ=-0.5, κ=0.1), and the family runs 7.7 to 155.3× faster than SIGformer while reaching 70.7% to 90.7% of its accuracy. Sign-awareness helps most for cold-start users, with up to +29.2% Recall@20 on Epinions users with 1 to 5 training items. Code: https://github.com/guanqun-yang/DualSpectralCF
A026SHORTNorm Removed, Bias Remains: Gradient-Decoupled Sampled Softmax for Collaborative Filtering
Woo-Seong Yun (WATCHA Inc.) · YeoJun Choi (Chung-Ang University) · Yoon-Sik Cho (Chung-Ang University)
Abstract
Popularity bias in collaborative filtering is known to manifest in embedding norms, which grow with interaction frequency. Sampled softmax (SSM) paired with cosine scoring addresses this by normalizing norms out of the score, and has become the dominant training objective. However, our gradient-level analysis reveals that two further mechanisms reintroduce degree bias during training. First, per-update norm drift under plain SGD recreates degree-dependent gradient magnitudes. Second, per-epoch gradient accumulation scales linearly with the interaction count, conflating genuine preference with exposure opportunity. To address these problems, we propose Gradient-Decoupled Sampled Softmax (GD-SSM). Our method combines L2 projection to stabilize per-update gradients with a closed-form degree prior that rebalances per-epoch contributions. Across three benchmarks with MF and LightGCN backbones, GD-SSM achieves the best performance in all configurations, improving over the strongest baseline by up to +33.3% and lifting the lowest-degree group by up to +114% over SSM. We further validate GD-SSM on production data from a real streaming service. Our code is available at https://github.com/yunwooseong/GD-SSM.
A027FULLBUGLE: Balanced Fusion with Graph Modality Experts for Multimodal Recommendation
Junhao Gao (Hunan University) · Chao Yang (Hunan University) · Bin Jiang (Hunan University)
Abstract
Multimodal recommendation effectively alleviates the data sparsity by integrating historical interaction behaviors with multimedia content (e.g., image, text). However, fusing these heterogeneous modalities faces two critical balance dilemmas: (1) Modality Knowledge Balance: Overemphasizing modality shared knowledge leads to homogeneous modality representations, while overemphasizing modality unique knowledge creates semantic gaps between modalities and deviates from the recommendation objective. (2) Modality Allocation Balance: Dominant modalities are often overestimated, resulting in modality bias; conversely, suppressing them may overlook their contributions to user preferences, causing excessive balance. To address these issues, we propose a novel Balanced fUsion with Graph modaLity Experts for multimodal recommendation (BUGLE). Firstly, inspired by the Mixture-of-Experts (MoE) mechanism, we design independent graph expert subnetworks for each modality to perform disentangled modeling over a shared interaction graph structure. We further introduce preference-disentangled contrastive learning to align modality representations and interaction supervision signals in the semantic spaces of each modality to enhance modality discriminability, thereby achieving a balanced utilization of both shared and unique modality knowledge. Additionally, we propose a dual-task routing balanced mechanism that combines expert routing entropy loss with result-guided loss. This mechanism ensures equitable modality allocation during fusion while highlighting the dominant contributing modalities. Extensive experiments on three real-world datasets demonstrate that BUGLE significantly outperforms various state-of-the-art methods. Our code is available at: https://github.com/GarethJellingham/BUGLE.
A028FULLGenerative Multimodal Intent Modeling with Adaptive Integration for Recommendation
Chanmi Kang (Pusan National University) · Bongguk Son (Pusan National University) · Junsu Cho (Pusan National University)
Abstract
Multimodal recommender systems have attracted increasing attention for their potential to enhance recommendation performance by leveraging textual and visual item information. However, existing approaches often treat multimodal signals as auxiliary features for item-level discrimination, overlooking two intrinsic characteristics of real-world multimodal data: 1) noise and uneven informativeness across modalities and items, and 2) fine-grained intent-related semantics embedded in multimodal representations. In this paper, we propose GEMIA, a Generative Multimodal Intent modeling framework with Adaptive integration for recommendation, which infers target-side multimodal semantic representations related to user preferences which explicitly models intent-related multimodal semantics while adaptively integrating heterogeneous modality signals. GEMIA consists of two key components: a Multimodal Semantic Inference (MSI) module that adopts a generative representation-inference approach to generate the next item’s text and image representations in a continuous multimodal semantic space, enabling the model to capture fine-grained intent-related information; and an Adaptive Multimodal Fusion (AMF) module that integrates multimodal representations via item-specific gating, accounting for item-dependent modality noise and uneven informativeness. Furthermore, GEMIA aggregates item-, text-, and image-based scores using item-wise weighting to flexibly adjust reliance on multimodal and item-level information. Extensive experiments on four real-world datasets demonstrate that GEMIA consistently outperforms state-of-the-art baselines, with more pronounced improvements in long-tail scenarios. Our code is available at https://github.com/kCMI113/GEMIA.
A029APPLIEDSA-RSQ:A Versatile Sparse Representation Framework for Multi-modal Recommender Systems
Xiang Wang (Tianjin University) · Shigang Quan (Meituan) · Tingzhen Chang (Meituan) · Kang Yang (Meituan) · Sitong Chen (Meituan) · Yabo Fan (Meituan) · Xingxing Wang (Meituan) · Zhaodian He (Institute of Software Chinese Academy of Sciences)
Abstract
Deploying high-dimensional multimodal features in industrial recommender systems incurs substantial storage and latency overhead. Hard quantization is compact but introduces boundary distortion, whereas dense soft quantization couples representation quality to the limited storage budget. We propose Sparse Activation-based Residual Soft Quantization (SA-RSQ), which uses Top-K sparse routing and softmax weights to store compact (Index, Probability) tuples. The stored tuples decouple per-item storage from codebook dimensionality; for a fixed selected support, gradients propagate through the routing weights and weighted reconstruction without relying on a straight-through estimator. Experiments on a proprietary food-delivery advertising dataset show favorable reconstruction-performance and CTR trade-offs across storage budgets of 8-48 bytes per item. A preliminary Next-Distribution Prediction study and a one-week online A/B test further demonstrate the practical potential of SA-RSQ, with relative lifts of +2.51% in CTR and +3.66% in CPM.
A031FULLBeyond Spatio-Temporal: Frequency-Gated Hypergraphs for Next-POI Recommendation
Sibo Wen (Heilongjiang university) · Rui Liu (Heilongjiang University) · Runzhe Wang (Heilongjiang University) · Nan Wang (Heilongjiang university) · Yingli Zhong (Heilongjiang University)
Abstract
Next Point-of-Interest (POI) recommendation aims to predict a user's subsequent location from historical trajectories. The task is challenging because user mobility is shaped by short-term intentions, long-term preferences, calendar effects, and structured spatial relations. Existing methods have improved sequential modeling and representation robustness, but they often treat temporal, spatial, and semantic contexts as loosely coupled signals and provide limited control over frequency-domain mobility patterns. To address these limitations, we propose ST-HFCR (Spatio-Temporal Hypergraph-enhanced Frequency-domain Contrastive Recommendation). ST-HFCR first constructs a multi-type hypergraph with time-slot, spatial-proximity, calendar-aware, and user-personalized hyperedges to model both macro-level contexts and individual preferences. It then introduces a gated frequency fusion module, GatedKAN, which learns separate gates for real and imaginary spectral components to balance amplitude- and phase-related information. Finally, ST-HFCR uses multi-level contrastive learning to align node- and graph-level representations under semantic-aware perturbations. Experiments on three real-world datasets show that ST-HFCR achieves consistent gains over competitive baselines in both HR and NDCG, suggesting that structured spatio-temporal hypergraphs and frequency-aware gated fusion provide complementary signals for next-POI recommendation. The code is available at https://github.com/MyCode12-maker/STHGCN/.
A032FULLPopularity-Aware Complementary Preference Distillation for Diffusion Recommendation
Meng Kang (University of Electronic Science and Technology of China) · Fan Li (University of Electronic Science and Technology of China) · Ping Kuang (University of Electronic Science and Technology of China)
Abstract
Diffusion recommender models have shown promising results by reconstructing user preference signals through denoising. Since user-item interactions typically follow a long-tailed distribution, the denoising process tends to favor signals from popular items with high-frequency interactions. This makes recommendation results overly concentrated on popular items and limits the exposure of long-tail items. Directly suppressing popular items may increase tail exposure, but it can weaken useful collaborative signals and degrade overall accuracy. To address this limitation, we propose Popularity-Aware Complementary Preference Distillation (PCPD), a diffusion-based recommendation method that mitigates popularity bias in the denoising process. Instead of simply suppressing popular items, PCPD incorporates mainstream collaborative signals and sparse long-tail preference signals as complementary supervision. Specifically, PCPD preserves mainstream collaborative preferences, calibrates the recovery of tail-item preferences, and distills the resulting complementary supervision into a unified diffusion recommender. At inference time, PCPD relies only on the distilled student model, without requiring auxiliary branches or online score fusion. Extensive experiments on three real-world datasets show that PCPD consistently improves long-tail recommendation performance and alleviates item-side exposure imbalance while maintaining competitive overall recommendation accuracy.
A033SHORTFairMB: A Multi-behavior Group Fairness Model for Recommendation with Representation Augmentation
Jinle He (Chongqing University of Posts and Telecommunications) · Dengping He (Chongqing University of Posts and Telecommunications) · Jian-Xun Mi (Chongqing University of Posts and Telecommunications) · Tongxin Xu (Nanjing University, State Key Laboratory of Novel Software Technology)
Abstract
Ensuring fairness in modern recommender systems is an ongoing imperative, yet current methodologies fail to effectively capture the complex interplay between long-tail distributions and biases. Specifically, sparse interactions cause tail user nodes to undergo semantic homogenization, progressively entangling their preferences with sensitive attributes. Consequently, such entanglement severely degrades recommendation utility and fairness for tail users. In this paper, we propose FairMB, a multi-behavior fairness paradigm designed to mitigate the tail-node degradation by leveraging rich collaborative signals from auxiliary behaviors. Specifically, a tail-aware aggregation mechanism exploits additional auxiliary signals to provide tail-node compensation. Furthermore, to prevent additional biases from auxiliary behaviors, a dual-guided debiasing augmentation network is employed. Driven by downstream tasks and projection-based purified residual embeddings, it constructs fair augmented targets for contrastive alignment, guiding the original representations to disentangle biases from preferences and ultimately achieving an optimal utility-fairness trade-off. Comprehensive evaluations across diverse recommendation benchmarks confirm that FairMB effectively achieves accuracy-fairness trade-off, establishing state-of-the-art standards for fair representation learning in multi-behavior environments.
A034SHORTMulti-Attribute and Intersectional Exposure Fairness in Recommender Systems
Paul Anton Bachmann (Technical University Vienna) · Hannah Eckert (Johannes Keppler University Linz) · Oleg Lesota (Johannes Kepler University Linz) · Martin Lackner (University of Applied Sciences St. Pölten) · Markus Schedl (Johannes Kepler University Linz)
Abstract
Ensuring fair exposure across demographic groups of content creators in recommender systems is crucial, as it affects the real-world visibility of minorities and underrepresented groups. Existing work on provider-side exposure fairness has primarily considered single demographic attributes, leaving multi-attribute and intersectional exposure fairness largely unexplored. Yet in real-world platforms, fairness concerns may arise simultaneously across multiple intersecting provider attributes. We introduce multi-attribute and intersectional perspectives on exposure fairness in recommender systems, propose an evaluation framework taking both perspectives into account, and present a post-processing approach for multi-attribute exposure fairness informed by online settings in social choice theory. Our experiments on real-world and synthetic datasets show a clear distinction between the two perspectives, as baseline approaches demonstrate a tendency to trade attribute-level fairness for improvements on the intersectional level. Our proposed method achieves a more favorable fairness-utility trade-off across attribute-wise exposure objectives and robust improvement of both exposure fairness aspects on the real world data. On synthetic data no method shows consistent improvement of both attribute-level and intersectional exposure fairness across all backbone models, highlighting the challenging nature of the task and the need to evaluate multi-attribute exposure fairness from both perspectives. With this work we aim to kick off the research on provider exposure fairness in recommender systems at a more granular level.
A035FULLOne Size, Many Fits: Aligning Diverse Group-Wise Click Preferences in Large-Scale Advertising Image Generation
Shuo Lu (NLPR & MAIS, CASIA) · Haohan Wang (JD.com) · Wei Feng (JD.com) · Weizhen Wang (JD.com) · Shen Zhang (JD.com) · Ke Cao (JD.com) · Jiahao Fan (JD.com) · Jingjing Lv (JD.com) · Changping Peng (JD.com) · Ching Law (JD.com) · Bing Zhan (NLPR & MAIS, CASIA) · Yuan Xu (NLPR & MAIS, CASIA) · Huizai Yao (HKUST(gz)) · Yongcan Yu (NLPR & MAIS, CASIA) · Chenyang Si (PRLab, NJU) · Jian Liang (NLPR & MAIS, CASIA)
Abstract
Advertising image generation has increasingly focused on online metrics like Click-Through Rate (CTR), yet existing approaches adopt a “one-size-fits-all” strategy that optimizes for overall CTR while neglecting preference diversity among user groups. This leads to suboptimal performance for specific groups, failing to satisfy group-wise visual preferences. To bridge this gap, we present One Size, Many Fits (OSMF), a unified framework that aligns diverse group-wise click preferences in large-scale advertising image generation. OSMF begins with product-aware adaptive grouping, which dynamically organizes users based on their attributes and product characteristics, representing each group with rich collective preference features. Building on these groups, preference-conditioned image generation employs a Group-aware Multimodal Large Language Model (G-MLLM) to generate tailored images for each group. The G-MLLM is pre-trained to simultaneously comprehend group features and generate advertising images. Subsequently, we fine-tune the G-MLLM using our proposed Group-DPO for group-wise preference alignment, which effectively enhances each group's CTR on the generated images. To further advance this field, we introduce the Grouped Advertising Image Preference Dataset (GAIP), the first large-scale public dataset of group-wise image preferences, including around 600K groups built from 40M users. Extensive experiments demonstrate that our framework achieves the state-of-the-art performance in both offline and online settings. Our code and datasets are publicly available at https://github.com/JD-GenX/OSMF.
A036FULLAn Automated Multi-Agent Search-then-Evolution Framework for Lifetime Value Prediction
Chaowei Wu (Sichuan University) · Huazhu Chen (Harbin Institute of Technology) · Qirui Yang (City University of Hong Kong) · Jiahui Li (Sichuan University) · Li Luo (Sichuan University) · Mengzhuo Guo (Sichuan University)
Abstract
Lifetime value (LTV) prediction is a key component of decision-making in online advertising, e-commerce, and recommender systems. In practice, however, LTV modeling is scenario-dependent because data distributions differ across applications. Practitioners often rely on scenario-specific pipelines with repeated feature engineering, objective adjustment, and tuning. These workflows require manual effort and are hard to transfer. We propose AgentLTV, an automated multi-agent search-then-evolution framework for lifetime value prediction. AgentLTV treats each candidate solution as an executable pipeline program. LLM-driven agents generate code, run and repair pipelines, and analyze execution feedback. Two decision agents coordinate a two-stage search. The Monte Carlo Tree Search (MCTS) stage explores a broad space of modeling choices under a fixed budget, guided by the Polynomial Upper Confidence bounds for Trees criterion and a Pareto-aware multi-metric value function. The Evolutionary Algorithm (EA) stage refines the best MCTS program via island-based evolution with crossover, mutation, and migration. Experiments on a large-scale proprietary dataset and a public benchmark show that AgentLTV consistently discovers strong models across ranking and error metrics. Online bucket-level analysis further indicates improved ranking consistency and value calibration, especially for high-value and negative-LTV segments. We summarize practitioner-oriented takeaways: use MCTS for rapid adaptation to new data patterns, use EA for stable refinement, and validate deployment readiness with bucket-level ranking and calibration diagnostics. The proposed AgentLTV has been successfully deployed online. Details of our optimal model and prompts are available at https://github.com/wuchaowei123/AgentLTV.
A037FULLCold-Start Constrained Autobidding via Implied-Dual Calibration
Andrey Pudovikov (Lomonosov Moscow State University) · Aleksandr Katrutsa (Lomonosov Moscow State University) · Egor Samosvat (Independent Researcher) · Yuriy Dorn (Lomonosov Moscow State University)
Abstract
When a new ad enters an existing auction market, an autobidding system must choose its first constrained bid before observing feedback from that ad. We study this cold-start decision under budget and CPC-style constraints. The standard warm start is to reuse a historical constrained policy, which is strong under stationarity although sensitive to shifted prices or response curves. Instead of replaying the full historical optimum, we propose implied-dual variable calibration (IDVC), which learns an admissible, low-dimensional implied-dual surface from historical contexts. For CPC constraints, the reusable margin is m=s(z)v+α(z)Cμ, where s(z)>0, α(z)∈[0,1], v=CTR·CVR, and μ=CTR. SPA/VCG auctions can bid this margin directly, and first-price/hybrid auctions require a supported map from margin to bid. We prove that calibration and bid-map error control first-period bid, reward, and constraint error under local support. On the public BAT dataset, we report benchmark-target calibration; in BAT-shaped semi-synthetic known-transform studies with validated bid maps, guarded IDVC improves early constrained bidding relative to historical reuse.
A038FULLCASTLE: Contrastive and Seed-Guided Training for Cold-Start Natural Language Search
Wendy Ran Wei (Airbnb) · Hao Li (Airbnb) · Weiwei Guo (Airbnb) · Xiaowei Liu (Airbnb) · Xueyin Chen (Airbnb) · Chun How Tan (Airbnb) · Malay Haldar (Airbnb) · Soumyadip Banerjee (Airbnb) · Kedar Bellare (Airbnb) · Huiji Gao (Airbnb) · Stephanie Moyerman (Airbnb) · Sanjeev Katariya (Airbnb)
Abstract
Deploying natural language search systems presents a critical cold-start challenge: no real user queries to learn linguistic patterns, and no relevance labels to train ranking models. We present CASTLE (Contrastive And Seed-guided Training for natural Language sEarch), an LLM-based framework for generating synthetic queries and relevance labels from structured catalog data, powering Airbnb's natural language search across its full lifecycle. CASTLE makes three contributions. First, we generate realistic queries by combining structure-guided prompting with seed queries from user research, using template, few-shot, and attribute-grounded prompt variants together with explicit variety mechanisms to prevent query collapse. Second, we produce relevance labels by construction via contrastive listing pairs derived from booking sessions---achieving near-zero false positives without LLM judgment. Third, CASTLE's structured input design is flexible: incorporating richer signals---such as guest reviews and photo captions---alongside listing attributes enables generation of niche, long-tail queries that reflect subjective user preferences (e.g. "cozy cabin with fireplace") beyond what catalog attributes alone can express. Compared against InPars-style, Promptagator, and contrastive-only baselines, CASTLE achieves KL 1.01 vs. real users---a 9.2× improvement over the best baseline (9.33)---and the lowest attribute-type KL divergence (0.08), outperforming even survey seed queries (0.09). A human evaluation on 200 sampled triplets confirms label quality: annotators agree with CASTLE labels at 91--93%. We deploy production pipelines generating synthetic examples daily for embedding-based retrieval and ranking evaluation. Synthetic data remains valuable beyond cold-start: it targets tail queries underrepresented in organic traffic and extends naturally to multi-turn conversational search.
A039APPLIEDGenerative Pseudo-Labeling for Pre-Ranking with Large Language Models
Junyu Bi (Taobao & Tmall Group of Alibaba) · Xinting Niu (Taobao & Tmall Group of Alibaba) · Daixuan Cheng (Renmin University) · Kun Yuan (Taobao & Tmall Group of Alibaba) · Tao Wang (Taobao & Tmall Group of Alibaba) · Binbin Cao (Taobao & Tmall Group of Alibaba) · Jian Wu (Taobao & Tmall Group of Alibaba) · Yuning Jiang (Taobao & Tmall Group of Alibaba)
Abstract
Pre-ranking models in industrial recommendation systems face a train--serving discrepancy: they are trained exclusively on exposed interactions yet must score all recalled candidates at serving time, including unexposed items without feedback. This induces sample selection bias that degrades generalization and suppresses long-tail content. Existing remedies introduce new biases of their own, from false negatives in negative sampling to inherited exposure bias in teacher--student distillation and training instability in adversarial domain adaptation. We propose Generative Pseudo-Labeling (GPL), which leverages large language models to assign semantically grounded pseudo-labels to unexposed items. Items are first tokenized into semantic identifiers via a frozen multimodal encoder and a Residual Quantized VAE, after which a fine-tuned language model generates user-specific interest anchors from behavioral histories. Relevance scores are computed by matching these anchors with candidates in a shared multimodal space and calibrated through uncertainty-aware weighting that accounts for semantic dispersion, historical consistency, and generation confidence. The pre-ranker is trained jointly on observed interactions and confidence-weighted pseudo-labels. All language model inference runs offline and is cached per user, imposing zero online latency. Deployed on a large-scale industrial platform, GPL achieves a 3.07% CTR lift in online A/B testing while improving recommendation diversity and long-tail coverage.
A040SHORTBandit-Quota: Latency-Budgeted Multi-Retriever Selection via Contextual Thompson Sampling
Priyank Jayraj (Birla Institute of Technology and Science, Pilani) · Poonam Goyal (Birla Institute of Technology and Science, Pilani) · Navneet Goyal (Birla Institute of Technology and Science, Pilani)
Abstract
Dense-retriever ensembles improve ranking quality but invoke every expert per query, routinely violating production latency SLAs. We present Bandit-Quota, a training-free, per-query selector that picks a budgeted subset of dense retrievers under a strict wall-clock cap. We cast multi-retriever selection as a Knapsack-constrained contextual bandit: a 16-dimensional neural–linear query sketch (PCA-projected bert-tiny [CLS], ?3 ms on CPU) feeds Linear Thompson Sampling (LinTS) posteriors, and a Lagrangian utility trades expected post-reranking quality against estimated per-arm latency, with a Jaccard coverage bonus that suppresses redundant experts. A budget-feasible greedy constructor resolves the per-query knapsack online, and a cached Reciprocal-Rank-Fusion fallback protects tail latency. Across seven BEIR collections spanning biomedical, finance, scientific and argumentative domains, Bandit-Quota reduces end-to-end latency by 2.4× to 9.3× over a 10-arm full ensemble, matches or improves nDCG@10 and MRR@10 on six of seven datasets, and outperforms a matched-capacity supervised router on all seven by adapting online to test-time query-distribution shifts. The policy exposes explicit operator knobs (B, M, ?) for the quality–latency trade-off with no retraining.
A041SHORTExploring the Capabilities and Limits of Late Interaction
Ferdinand Schlatt (Friedrich-Schiller-Universität Jena) · Gustav Arnold (Friedrich-Schiller-Universität Jena) · Matthias Hagen (Friedrich-Schiller-Universität Jena)
Abstract
Late interaction with MaxSim scoring is the ranking mechanism of the very effective multi-vector bi-encoder retrieval model ColBERT. In this paper, we investigate how important the representational capacity and ColBERT's lexically-bound token embeddings are for late interaction. Our experiments on TREC Deep Learning and on BEIR data indicate that late interaction is only more effective than a single-vector bi-encoder's dot product scoring when late interaction can use a higher representational capacity or when the embeddings are bound to lexical tokens.
A042SHORTReducing Representational Interference in Retrieval Embeddings with Trainable Prefix Tokens
Seongtae Hong (Korea University) · Youngjoon Jang (Korea University) · Jungseob Lee (Korea University) · Chanjun Park (Soongsil University) · Heuiseok Lim (Korea University)
Abstract
Embedding models compress variable-length text into fixed-size vector representations, but this compression can entangle semantic content with residual token-level information, such as artifacts arising from attention sink behavior. We propose a simple method that prepends trainable [DUMP] tokens to the input during embedding model training. The method keeps the model architecture, pooling strategy, and training loss unchanged, while optimizing the added tokens through the standard contrastive retrieval objective. By introducing trainable prefix positions that interact with regular tokens during encoding, [DUMP] tokens help reduce the influence of residual or uninformative token-level signals on the final retrieval representation. Experiments on standard retrieval and long-context benchmarks show that our method consistently improves over finetuned baselines across encoder and decoder embedding models. Further analysis shows that [DUMP] tokens alter token-level activation and attention patterns associated with low-information tokens. These results suggest that trainable prefix tokens provide a lightweight way to improve retrieval representations.
A043FULLEffective Re-Ranking with DIMEs using Few Noisy LLM-Generated Relevance Judgments
Andrea Pasin (University of Padua) · Guglielmo Faggioli (University of Padua) · Nicola Ferro (University of Padua) · Raffaele Perego (ISTI-CNR) · Nicola Tonellotto (University of Pisa)
Abstract
State-of-the-art Information Retrieval (IR) pipelines often rely on dense neural models to index and retrieve large document collections. After an initial retrieval stage, precision-oriented re-ranking approaches can further refine the ranked list. However, re-ranking quality strongly depends on the availability of reliable relevance signals. Recent work has explored the use of Large Language Models (LLMs) to automatically generate relevance judgments that can serve as such signals. However, achieving strong alignment with human gold labels generally requires either very large and complex LLMs or extensive human supervision. In this work, we investigate whether relatively small LLMs, despite producing limited and often noisy relevance assessments, can still be leveraged to improve the ranking of documents retrieved by dense bi-encoder models. Specifically, we introduce new approaches based on the recently proposed Dimension IMportance Estimators (DIMEs), incorporating LLM-generated relevance judgments into the re-ranking process. Our study assumes a practical setting: we consider access only to relatively small LLMs and to very small sets of relevance judgments generated for the top-retrieved documents of each query by dense retrieval models, and we investigate how to leverage these sparse, often noisy signals to refine the ranking of the entire retrieved set. Our method leads to substantial improvements in document ranking, boosting nDCG@10 and AP by up to 9% and 15%, respectively, across different datasets, LLMs, and bi-encoder backbone retrieval models. These results show that even a few noisy relevance judgments from small LLMs can provide a powerful signal to improve the effectiveness of IR systems.
A044FULLTree-Compatible Personalized Ranking via Linear Latent-Trait Decomposition
Pavel Metrikov (Microsoft) · Chloe Gu (Microsoft) · Xiaoyu Li (Microsoft) · Byungki Byun (Microsoft) · Swarnangsu Acharyya (Microsoft)
Abstract
Learning-to-rank systems often use a global scorer despite systematic variation in user preferences. We propose a model-agnostic latent-trait framework for probabilistic ranking objectives. A low-dimensional profile activates shared ranking directions linearly, enabling tractable profile inference with nonlinear document-feature effects. Our iterative route encodes all traits as G profile features in one ranker rather than learning or serving G factor models. Ranker fitting reuses an unmodified standard LTR package, and serving uses one model. An offline module probes the ranker to construct an additive surrogate for profile updates across neural and tree rankers. To our knowledge, this is the first continuous user-specific latent personalization under a ranking loss for standard LambdaMART without architecture changes. In simulation, the method outperforms non-personalized and history-encoder baselines, incurs a modest penalty when G is overestimated, and yields probe-surrogate updates that transfer to the trained ranker. In a retrospective offline Message Search evaluation, personalized LambdaMART outperforms its non-personalized baseline. TreeSHAP provides model-relative trait interpretations.
A045FULLEfficient Offline Learning of Ranking Policies via Top-k Policy Decomposition
Ren Kishimoto (Institute of Science Tokyo) · Koichi Tanaka (Keio University) · Haruka Kiyohara (Cornell University) · Yusuke Narita (Yale University) · Yasuo Yamamoto (LY Corporation) · Nobuyuki Shimizu (LY Corporation) · Yuta Saito (Hanjuku-kaso, Co., Ltd.)
Abstract
Many recommender systems such as for e-commerce and news platforms aim to provide users with rankings they are likely to interact with. Off-Policy Learning (OPL) of ranking policies enables us to learn new ranking policies using only historical logged data. However, ranking settings make OPL remarkably challenging because their action spaces consist of permutations of unique items, being extremely large. Existing methods primarily use either policy- or regression-based approaches. The policy-based approach, which typically uses importance-weighted policy gradients, can suffer from high variance due to large action spaces. The regression-based approach, on the other hand, estimates the expected reward using conventional machine learning methods, avoiding variance issues but potentially suffering from severe bias. To circumvent these issues of existing methods, we propose a new OPL method for ranking, named Ranking Policy Optimization via Top-k Policy Decomposition (R-POD), which combines the policy- and regression-based approaches in an effective fashion. Specifically, R-POD decomposes a ranking policy into a first-stage policy for selecting top-k actions and a second-stage policy for choosing the bottom actions given the top-k actions. It learns the first-stage policy using a new policy gradient estimator and the second-stage policy via the regression-based approach. This method can substantially reduce variance, since it applies importance weighting only to the top-k actions. We also demonstrate that our policy-gradient estimator for the first-stage policy is unbiased under a conditional pairwise correctness condition, which only requires that the expected reward differences of pairs of rankings sharing the same top-k actions can be estimated correctly. Comprehensive experiments illustrate that R-POD provides substantial improvements in OPL for ranking.
A046SHORTLLMs Propose, Verifiers Decide: Selective Intent Classification for Short Web Queries
Yihan Bai (Wuhan University) · Rongyu Luo (Wuhan University)
Abstract
Short web queries are difficult to classify: they contain few lexical cues, and query logs are dominated by informational intents. Recent work shows that LLMs improve recall on this task, but direct top-1 LLM prediction does not consistently meet the requirements of precision-sensitive annotation. We find that, in this setting, LLMs are better suited as candidate proposers than as final classifiers: their top-2 intent candidates often contain the gold label even when top-1 predictions are skewed. We introduce CAVE-NV, a selective candidate-verification framework that asks an LLM for a small candidate set, scores each candidate with a label-conditioned MiniLM verifier, and uses a split-calibrated acceptor to output a label or reject the example. On ORCAS-I-gold, GPT-4o and LLaMA-3.1-8B-Instruct reach top-2 candidate recall of 0.976 and 0.974. In the query-only setting, CAVE-NV accepts 54.8% and 45.4% of examples with 0.985 and 0.984 micro accepted precision. With clicked-URL evidence and the ranking verifier for offline query-log annotation, prediction coverage reaches 63.5% and 59.5% with 0.988 and 0.987 precision. Selective verification can therefore label a high-precision subset of query-log examples without forcing a prediction for every query.
A047SHORTEviQE: Evidence Selection for LLM-Based Query Expansion
Hai Son Le (Toronto Metropolitan University) · Amin Bigdeli (University of Waterloo) · Shirin Seyedsalehi (Toronto Metropolitan University) · Morteza Zihayat (Toronto Metropolitan University) · Ebrahim Bagheri (University of Toronto)
Abstract
LLM-based query expansion increasingly conditions reformulation on documents retrieved from the target corpus, yet most work focuses on how to generate expansions rather than which documents the model should read. We propose EviQE, which aggregates documents retrieved by multiple reformulators, selects a compact evidence set, and uses it for one grounded expansion step. This separates evidence selection from generation and treats reformulators as complementary retrieval perspectives. Across three TREC DL and five BEIR benchmarks, reformulators frequently retrieve distinct relevant documents, so pooled candidates provide higher relevant-document coverage than any individual source. The strongest gains come from relevance-based evidence selection: LLM-Score consistently outperforms direct reformulation, cold-start expansion, and single-source seeded expansion. Additional retrieval-generation rounds provide little benefit once strong conditioning evidence has been selected and can reduce effectiveness.
A048SHORTReasoning-Aware Utility Estimation for Retrieval-Augmented Generation
Abbas Salemi Nezhad (University of Toronto) · Sajad Ebrahimi (University of Toronto) · Negar Arabzadeh (University of Berkeley) · Ebrahim Bagheri (University of Toronto)
Abstract
Retrieval-Augmented Generation (RAG) systems increasingly rely on retrieved documents to ground large language model outputs, yet evaluating whether those documents are truly useful for generation remains an open challenge. Recent work has shown that retrieval quality measured by conventional relevance-based metrics does not necessarily align with end-to-end RAG performance: a document judged relevant to a query may not help the model answer correctly, while an irrelevant document may actively distract generation. Existing utility-aware evaluation methods address this limitation by estimating the utility of retrieved documents through isolated document-level probes. However, these approaches estimate document utility independently of the reasoning process. We argue that a document is useful not because it can answer a question in isolation, but because it contributes to the reasoning process that produces the final answer. To capture this behavior, we introduce Trace Utility Gain (TUG), a family of retrieval evaluation metrics that estimate document utility directly from chain-of-thought (CoT) reasoning traces generated over the full retrieval context. Specifically, TUG measures utility through three complementary signals: citation behavior, semantic alignment between retrieved documents and reasoning traces, and model self-assessment of document reliance. By estimating utility from the model's observed reasoning process, TUG captures how retrieved evidence contributes to answer generation rather than how useful it appears in isolation. We evaluate TUG on five question-answering benchmarks using three instruction-tuned large language models. Results show that TUG consistently achieves stronger correlation with end-to-end answer correctness than both traditional retrieval metrics and prior utility-aware approaches.
A049RESOURCERoute Me If You Can: A Benchmark for Query Reformulation Selection
Hai Son Le (Toronto Metropolitan University) · Negar Arabzadeh (University of California, Berkeley) · Amin Bigdeli (University of Waterloo) · Radin Hamidi Rad (Mila - Quebec AI Institute) · Sajad Ebrahimi (University of Toronto) · Charles L.A. Clarke (University of Waterloo) · Ebrahim Bagheri (University of Toronto)
Abstract
LLM-based query reformulation can improve retrieval, but no single reformulation strategy is consistently optimal across queries, domains, retrievers, or model backbones. This creates an inference-time decision problem: “Given an original query and a pool of candidate reformulations, which one should be issued to the retriever?”. Existing studies are hard to compare because they use different reformulator pools, retrievers, relevance signals, training labels, and evaluation metrics. We introduce QueryRoute, a benchmark that freezes the expensive artifacts needed to study this decision reproducibly: original queries, generated variants, ranked lists under multiple retrievers, retrieval scores, and per-query oracle labels. The benchmark contains 3,757 queries, 11 candidate systems, five reformulator backbones, and three retrievers across TREC DL, BEIR, and BRIGHT, yielding 619,905 retrieval outcomes. We benchmark supervised classification, routing, QPP, and LLM-as-judge selectors. Results show substantial oracle headroom over fixed reformulators, but current selectors recover only part of it; selector rankings change across retrievers, and similar mean effectiveness can hide different query-level behavior. The released artifacts and evaluation harness allow future selectors to be compared without regenerating variants, rerunning retrieval, or rebuilding judge pipelines. Code and data are available at https://github.com/haisonle001/QueryRoute.
A050SHORTWhat Limits Does Quantization Place on Dense Top-k Retrieval? A Theoretical Study
Koki Okajima (NTT, Inc.) · Tsukasa Yoshida (NTT, Inc.)
Abstract
We establish conditions for embedding a corpus of N documents as d-dimensional vectors such that every k-subset S ⊆ [N] is realizable as a top-k retrieval by some query vector. Recent work shows that d = O(k) suffices for such embeddings to exist in Rd, independently of N. We show that this corpus-independent bound is specific to infinite precision. With B bits per coordinate, perfect top-k retrieval requires Bd = Ω(k ln N), so at any fixed precision the dimension must grow at least logarithmically with N. Specializing to an ℓ2-normalized B-bit uniform scalar quantization model, we also identify a sharp critical precision B* = O(ln ln N) below which no dimension suffices, together with two further regimes that bound the feasible (B, d) pairs. Our result implies that in practical vector databases and dense retrieval systems where quantization is standard, the embedding dimension cannot be chosen without reference to corpus size.
A051FULLPersonalized kNN Query Execution in Vector Databases
Matúš šikyňa (Masaryk University) · Pavel Zezula (Masaryk University)
Abstract
Modern vector databases enable search over high-dimensional embeddings, but query execution engines rely on a specific similarity metric that cannot reflect how individual users perceive similarity. We advocate a metric-level perspective on personalization, keeping the shared embedding space and the underlying index unchanged, and representing each user's specific search needs by a small matrix for Mahalanobis distance learned using relevance feedback and metric learning. Using a lower bounding relationship between Mahalanobis and Euclidean distances, we propose a query execution strategy for personalized k-nearest neighbour search that retrieves an enlarged candidate set using a standard Euclidean (or inner product) index and refines it under the user’s subjective metric. Experiments on CLIP embeddings from Profiset and LAION-2B-en datasets using FAISS-based indices show that this approach can be layered on top of existing vector databases with predictable behaviour, high overlap with precise Mahalanobis kNN search results, and only a small overhead over standard Euclidean search. When the Euclidean–Mahalanobis discrepancy becomes too large for efficient refinement, we propose approximation techniques and show that a Cholesky-based whitening transformation can reorganize embeddings so that personalized search reduces to Euclidean indexing again.
A052SHORTMulti-Aspect Joint Retrieval for E-Commerce: Bridging Product Catalogs and Customer Reviews
Marco Alessio (ISTI-CNR) · Cristina Ioana Muntean (ISTI-CNR) · Franco Maria Nardini (ISTI-CNR) · Raffaele Perego (ISTI-CNR)
Abstract
E-commerce platforms support diverse retrieval needs, from finding relevant products to identifying useful information in customer reviews. In these settings, relevance depends not only on textual content, but also on structured aspects such as brand, category, price, rating, and popularity. Recent multi-aspect dense retrievers show that these signals improve product search, but they are typically designed for a single task over a single corpus, leaving open whether aspect-aware representations can be shared across related e-commerce retrieval tasks. In this paper, we study joint multi-aspect dense retrieval for e-commerce, where a single model supports retrieval over both product catalogs and customer reviews. We propose J-MADRAL, a joint dense retrieval model that learns shared aspect-aware representations from textual content and structured metadata across product and review search. To evaluate this setting, we construct Search ESCI, a novel synthetic review-search benchmark derived from Amazon Reviews 2023 and ESCI-related product resources, and evaluate on Amazon ESCI, TREC Product Search 2023, and Search ESCI. Experiments against sparse, dense, and multi-aspect retrieval baselines show that joint training substantially improves review search while maintaining competitive product search effectiveness. These results demonstrate the value of shared aspect-aware representations for integrated e-commerce search. To support reproducibility, we release the source code, data, and model weights at https://github.com/alemarco96/J-MADRAL.
A053FULLPersona Conditioning as an Assessor-Sensitivity Probe for LLM-Based IR Evaluation
Samaneh Mohtadi (The University of Queensland) · Pietro Bernardelle (The University of Queensland) · Joel Mackenzie (The University of Queensland) · Gianluca Demartini (The University of Queensland)
Abstract
Large language models (LLMs) are increasingly used as relevance assessors in information retrieval (IR) evaluation, raising questions about how assessor framing affects judgment reliability and downstream system comparison. We study persona conditioning as a diagnostic mechanism for exposing LLM assessor sensitivity. Using task-oriented personas drawn from two complementary sources (PersonaHub and NVIDIA Nemotron-Personas-USA), we instantiate five assessor roles emphasizing intent interpretation, domain expertise, contrastive judgment, evidence verification, and global search-quality assessment, compared with a standard UMBRELA baseline. Across six LLM backbones on TREC DL20 and RAG24, our analyses reveal structured rather than uniform assessor sensitivity. Judgments usually remain close to the baseline while shifting assessment strictness, evidential threshold, or interpretation emphasis rather than producing widespread relevance reversals. At the system level, high-capacity models preserve system-ranking agreement, while smaller models amplify persona-induced instability. Local rank-displacement analysis shows sensitivity concentrates on particular retrieval systems and system types, especially neural ranking/reranking systems on DL20 and RAG-oriented pipelines on RAG24. Persona source matters less than assessor role and model capacity. These findings position persona-conditioned judging as a controlled sensitivity probe for stress-testing LLM-based IR evaluation pipelines and identifying systems whose evaluation outcomes are sensitive to assessor framing.
A054SHORTRobustness of IR Models to Collection Growth
Emmanouil Georgios Lionis (University of Glasgow) · Sean MacAvaney (University of Glasgow) · Debasis Ganguly (University of Glasgow)
Abstract
Information Retrieval (IR) systems seek to identify relevant documents within a collection. In practical applications, collections are dynamic, with documents frequently added. We argue that ideally, a retriever's effectiveness should not decrease when non-relevant documents are added to a collection. This study formalises this concept and empirically evaluates it by merging two collections with negligible topic overlap. We hypothesise that the way an IR model conditions its ranking on other documents in a collection (e.g., the IDF component in BM25 or contextual documents in listwise rerankers) plays an important role in its robustness to the addition of non-relevant documents. We broadly classify models as those that do not depend on other documents (Multi-Document-Agnostic, MDA) and those that do (Multi-Document-Dependent, MDD). Our results show that neither MDD nor MDA models are fully robust to the addition of non-relevant documents, as all models exhibit some performance degradation. Interestingly, among the models we test, MDA is more effective than MDD for retrieval, whereas MDD and MDA rerankers are equally effective.
A055FULLOn Multiple Comparison Procedures Involving Multiple Measures and Collections
Tetsuya Sakai (Waseda University/Naver Corporation)
Abstract
When a researcher has m (>2) IR systems to compare and is interested in the difference in mean (say) nDCG for each of the m(m-1)/2 system pairs, a multiple comparison procedure (MCP) should be performed in order to avoid inflating the familywise error rate (FWER). However, we go beyond this rather limited view of multiple comparisons, as IR researchers often employ multiple evaluation measures and multiple test collections, and tend to make a research claim based on whatever statistically significant results found in any part of the experiment. More specifically, we consider MCPs by treating null hypotheses over multiple measures and over multiple collections as a family, using FWER-based MCPs (Holm adjustment, Tukey HSD test with Bonferroni adjustment) as well as a more recent approach of setting the desired False Discovery Rate instead of the FWER. Using real data from NTCIR and TREC with ten evaluation measures, we demonstrate the impact of introducing these more holistic MCP approaches, and provide practical recommendations for IR experimenters.
A056SHORTRetrieval-Stage Interactions in Cross-Modal Text-to-Image Retrieval Pipelines
Sanskar S. Singh (Indian Institute of Technology Delhi) · Ziv Barretto (Ashoka University) · Bharati Khanijo (Esri) · Aditya Sahu (Indian Institute of Technology Delhi) · Maya Ramanath (Indian Institute of Technology Delhi)
Abstract
Cross-modal retrieval systems enable searching content in one modality using queries from another. Recently, retrieving images using natural language queries – text-to-image retrieval – has received a lot of attention due to advances in deep learning vision models and interest in multi-modal processing in general. While several modeling approaches exist, ranging from simple keyword matching to joint embedding models and neural rerankers, there is limited understanding of how candidate generation, reranking, and fusion interact across retrieval pipelines. In this paper, we present an analysis of retrieval-stage interactions in text-to-image retrieval pipelines, spanning a comprehensive set of categories drawn from recent advances in information retrieval: single index pipelines, multi-stage retrieve and rerank pipelines, and ensemble pipelines. We compare the effectiveness of these pipelines on the MS-COCO and Flickr30K benchmarks revealing several retrieval-stage phenomena governing reranking effectiveness, candidate-set expansion, and ensemble behavior.
A057FULLBiFocus: Evidence-Grounded Patch and Query-Token Calibration for Visual Document Retrieval
Jiangyue Chen (Southeast University) · Li Yao (Southeast University) · Yuanyang Zhang (Southeast University) · Xinwei Li (Southeast University)
Abstract
