Visual document retrieval has recently shifted from OCR-heavy document parsing pipelines toward screenshot-based late-interaction retrievers such as ColPali. These models preserve fine-grained token–patch matching, but their supervision remains misaligned with their scoring mechanism: relevance is accumulated over query-token MaxSim scores, while training signals are typically page-level and, at best, patch-side. We argue that this creates a supervision asymmetry: existing methods can teach visual retrievers where to look on the page, but provide limited explicit supervision for which query tokens should drive the match. We propose BiFocus, an evidence-grounded late-interaction framework that repurposes explicit evidence boxes from BBox-DocVQA to calibrate both page-side patch grounding and query-side token contribution. The framework first converts bounding-box evidence into soft patch-level targets, then induces token-level evidence credits from token–patch alignment and uses them to train a lightweight query-token scorer. At inference time, no evidence boxes or teacher models are required; the model computes a calibrated weighted late-interaction score that emphasizes query tokens supported by document evidence while preserving the original page-level retrieval interface. On ViDoRe V2, BiFocus improves ColPali-v1.3 by +6.15 nDCG@1 and +3.80 nDCG@5, and improves ColQwen2.5-v0.2 by +7.12 nDCG@1 and +4.72 nDCG@5 under the same-backbone setting. On the more extractive and saturated ViDoRe V1 benchmark, BiFocus preserves the strong baseline performance. Code is available at https://github.com/YUEcjy13/BiFocus.
A058SHORTFirst News Report Retrieval for Short-Form Videos
Kyutae Kim (Department of Applied Artificial Intelligence, Sungkyunkwan University) · Dohun Kim (Department of Computer Education, Sungkyunkwan University) · Taesoo Park (Department of Computer Education, Sungkyunkwan University) · YunSeok Choi (Department of Immersive Media Engineering, Sungkyunkwan University)
Abstract
Short-form videos are increasingly used to consume and share news, but they often omit explicit links to the underlying articles. Tracing the first news report from these videos is challenging because the same event is often reported repeatedly across multiple news outlets and platforms, while short-form videos may summarize the event using different expressions. In this paper, we formulate First News Report Retrieval for Short-Form Videos, a task that aims to identify the first news report of the event described in a short-form video. We construct a manually verified benchmark consisting of 99 news topics and 865 Korean Shorts videos. We also introduce a stepwise retrieval-and-verification framework designed to improve first news report tracing from short-form videos. Experiments with strong frontier LLMs show that retrieving the first news report remains challenging: general tool-augmented search often returns follow-up reports or articles about related but different events. Our framework provides an initial approach for systematically investigating this task by combining structured query generation, candidate retrieval, and article-level verification.
A059SHORTPT2PR: A Benchmark for Multimodal Patent-to-Product Retrieval
Lia Shahnazaryan (Paderborn University) · Stefan Heindorf (Paderborn University)
Abstract
Detecting patent infringement requires identifying products whose design or functionality falls within the scope of a patent's claims—a task that demands sophisticated legal reasoning and is difficult not only for experts but also for LLMs. A crucial first step is to identify candidate products that are potentially related to a given patent, allowing a detailed legal analysis to focus on a small set of cases. However, patent documents and product descriptions differ substantially in language, structure, and level of abstraction, making the retrieval a challenging cross-domain problem. Yet no datasets and methods exist for this task. As a first step, this paper introduces Patent2Product (PT2PR), a benchmark for multimodal patent-to-product retrieval consisting of datasets, metrics, and baselines. Our pipeline mines patent-product pairs from patent references in product texts using high-recall rules, followed by high-precision manual validation; it can be applied to any catalog with patent references in product text. Applied to the datasets Amazon Reviews 2023 and ESCI, the pipeline yields 11,303 and 1,351 patent-product pairs, respectively. The PT2PR-Amazon dataset not only contains text, but also patent drawings and product images, enabling multimodal retrieval experiments. As baselines, we evaluate state-of-the-art LLMs, VLMs, and lexical retrieval. Our experiments show that (1) dense retrieval outperforms lexical retrieval, (2) incorporating visual information can improve retrieval, although the gains are model-dependent, and (3) the effect of using longer context windows for patent documents is also model-dependent.
A060SHORTBeyond One-Shot Expansion: Contrastive Evidence Exploration for Multi-Hop Retrieval
Jungmin Yun (Chung-Ang University) · Youngbin Kim (Chung-Ang University)
Abstract
Retrieval-augmented generation (RAG) critically depends on retrieving the evidence necessary for effective reasoning. However, this remains particularly challenging in multi-hop question answering (QA), where supporting passages are often linked through intermediate entities and relations that must be progressively uncovered. Existing retrieval approaches typically rely on a single retrieval intent or one-shot query expansion, limiting their ability to adapt to newly retrieved evidence and potentially introducing noisy or redundant retrieval signals. To address these limitations, we propose a training-free multi-hop retrieval framework that integrates evidence-conditioned exploration, passage-specific contrastive refinement, and coverage-aware final ranking. During offline indexing, the framework constructs passage-specific contrastive facets that characterize each passage relative to its semantically similar neighbors, providing fine-grained signals to distinguish closely related candidates. At inference time, the framework iteratively retrieves evidence, generates probes targeting unresolved information needs, refines candidate relevance using the contrastive facets, and selects a complementary set of passages that collectively cover diverse evidence-seeking intents. Experiments on MuSiQue, HotpotQA, and 2WikiMultihopQA demonstrate consistent improvements in retrieval quality and downstream QA performance over baselines.
A061SHORTSupport Selection Survives under Official-Context RAG: A Same-Backbone Boundary Study
Chuanheng Ma (Technology and Engineering Center for Space Utilization, Chinese Academy of Sciences) · Yizhao Wang (Technology and Engineering Center for Space Utilization, Chinese Academy of Sciences) · Shengyang Li (Technology and Engineering Center for Space Utilization, Chinese Academy of Sciences)
Abstract
We study bounded Agentic retrieval-augmented generation (RAG) for knowledge-intensive question answering. The task is to answer multi-hop or domain questions from auditable external evidence under a fixed inference budget. Existing Agentic RAG evaluations often vary the model, retriever, corpus interface, controller, training signal, and search budget together. As a result, observed gains do not show whether planning, repair, active retrieval, or support selection is the useful mechanism. We conduct a same-backbone boundary study with fixed Qwen-based retrieval, generation, evaluation, and call budgets. We decompose bounded agentic control into same-stack mechanism controls and seven ablations. The evaluation uses official-context HotpotQA, 2Wiki, and MuSiQue. It also includes a secondary native-retrieval Chinese aerospace QA stress test. Across three seeds, the full Agentic workflow is not the best answer-F1 design. Corrective achieves the highest F1 on the public benchmarks, and Active retrieval achieves the highest F1 on the domain set. In this access regime, Agentic mainly adds lexical grounding and trace structure at higher latency. The most consistent positive component is sentence-level support selection. Removing it reduces F1 on every dataset. Bootstrap CIs support this drop on HotpotQA, MuSiQue, and the domain stress test, but not on 2Wiki.
A062FULLDo RAG Systems Cite Themselves? Measuring and Preventing Source Displacement in Self-Updating Retrieval-Augmented Generation
Yajuan Wang (Shanghai Jiao Tong University)
Abstract
Self-updating retrieval-augmented generation (RAG) systems store generated answers, summaries, or evidence cards for later retrieval. We show that this reuse creates a provenance risk: generated memories can displace primary sources and later be cited without recoverable root evidence. We call these failures source displacement and citation-lineage collapse. Controlled 100-round streams on HotpotQA and 2WikiMultiHopQA show that unrestricted memory reuse places unverified generated memories in 27.6–28.4% of late-stage top-5 retrieval slots and produces citation-lineage collapse in 10.7–11.7% of answers. We then introduce LineageGuard, a lightweight provenance contract that attaches root-source metadata, admits only verified extractive memory cards, caps generated-memory exposure, and expands generated citations to primary sources. Under correct verifier and lineage metadata, LineageGuard enforces zero unverified exposure and zero collapse; these are policy guarantees rather than learned outcomes. Empirically, it improves primary-source recall by 5.0 points on HotpotQA, while lowering answer F1 on 2WikiMultiHopQA, exposing a safety–utility trade-off. An audit of 150 admitted memories finds 91.3% joint support-lineage precision. These results position LineageGuard as a practical control layer, not an accuracy-improving retrieval method, and show why self-updating RAG should treat generated memories as derived evidence rather than ordinary documents.
A063SHORTPCD-RAG: A Diagnostic Framework for Auditing Parametric Contamination in RAG Distillation
Yingying Wu (Jilin University) · Xiao Chen (The Hong Kong Polytechnic University) · Changyi Ma (Jilin University) · Xuan Song (Jilin University)
Abstract
Retrieval-Augmented Generation (RAG) distillation offers an efficient paradigm for deploying compact language models, yet it raises a critical safety concern: Does evidence-conditioned supervision inadvertently encode transient retrieved facts into the student model's parametric memory? If transient retrieved facts pollute model parameters, the core premise of externalizing knowledge in RAG is compromised. To audit this risk, we introduce PCD-RAG, a negative-control diagnostic benchmark and metric suite. By utilizing 5,000 synthetic facts with 0% pre-training exposure baseline, this atomic-level probe cleanly disentangles closed-book memorization from context-conditioned reading. Under these strictly controlled zero-exposure settings, our comprehensive evaluation across Qwen2.5 students reveals a counterintuitive finding: RAG distillation does not induce surface-level exact-match retention. Answer-only distillation leaves retrieval-free answer recovery near zero (<= 0.8%). Furthermore, extending our probe to realistic noisy multi-document distillation reveals a stark contrast in training stability: while traditional supervised fine-tuning (SFT) triggers catastrophic optimization collapse when architectural constraints are relaxed (e.g., LoRA R=16), distillation targets (Hard KD) act as an implicit regularizer that successfully stabilizes the model. By bounding parametric contamination and identifying complementary architectural safeguards, our framework lays the empirical groundwork for future community exploration of complex multi-hop reasoning, safeguarding the deployment of reliable RAG pipelines.
A064SHORTCaching Hyperedges: KV-Cache Reuse for Hypergraph RAG
Mariano Barone (University of Naples Federico II) · Francesco Di Serio (University of Naples Federico II) · Vincenzo Moscato (University of Naples Federico II) · Marco Postiglione (Northwestern University) · Giuseppe Riccio (University of Naples Federico II) · Antonio Romano (University of Naples, Federico II)
Abstract
Hypergraph-based retrieval captures the n-ary relational facts that binary-graph methods fragment, but answering a query is slow: the model must read the text of many retrieved units before it can answer. We present Cachy, which removes this reading cost by precomputing a key-value (KV) cache for each retrieval unit and reusing it whenever a query retrieves that unit. Because retrieval is hyperedge-grounded, each cached unit is a short, self-contained passage, so caches fuse at query time without fine-tuning and with no detectable loss in generation quality. To keep storage tractable, Cachy caches only the units that queries actually reach (demand caching) and compresses each cache by up to 8× with INT8/INT4 quantization and 50% K-norm token pruning. Together these cut storage from 1.9 TB to 109 GB on our workload. On UltraDomain across five domains, Cachy matches the uncached hypergraph pipeline on generation quality while cutting mean query time from 21.61 s to 8.52 s, matching the latency of lightweight RAG. Code and resources are publicly available (https://github.com/PRAISELab-PicusLab/Cachy-Hypergraphrag).
A065SHORTCiteAlign-Table: Verifying Citation Faithfulness when LLMs Attribute to Structured Data
Ashish Gupta (ServiceNow) · Manjunatha Naik Mc (ServiceNow)
Abstract
Attributed Question Answering systems increasingly ground answers in tabular structured corpora—Wikipedia infoboxes and relational tables, the dominant structured evidence in open-domain RAG—yet citation faithfulness methods remain designed for text passages. This mismatch allows LLMs to cite the correct table but the wrong row, silently aggregate values without justification, or attribute claims to schema fields that do not semantically entail them. We formalize multiple structural hallucination modes specific to structured-data attribution and introduce CiteAlign-Table, a hybrid neuro-symbolic verifier that checks schema-path validity, cell-level semantic alignment, and arithmetic consistency between claims and their cited records. A schema-aware entailment module detects entity and content misalignments, while a lightweight program synthesizer verifies numerical aggregation, temporal consistency, and unit correctness. Experiments on a hybrid benchmark of Wikipedia infoboxes and WikiTables show that CiteAlign-Table achieves 0.84 F1 in detecting unfaithful structured citations, while text-only baselines degrade to 0.61 F1. By extending citation faithfulness from passages to structured records, our work makes attributed QA trustworthy over the heterogeneous data that production RAG systems actually retrieve.
A066FULLRouting by Contract: Evidence-Gated Skill Selection for Language Agents
Shouzheng Xu (Central University of Finance and Economics) · Zonglin Feng (Central University of Finance and Economics) · Yunqi Zhou (Central University of Finance and Economics) · Yaqing Li (Central University of Finance and Economics) · Jingyi Wu (Shandong University)
Abstract
Agentic language systems increasingly rely on reusable skill libraries, but skills with similar surface descriptions often differ in their operational contracts---source of truth, recipient scope, evidence policy, and output format. We study this operational-contract under-specification problem and demonstrate its practical consequences: end-to-end agent experiments on WildClawBench, an independently published benchmark, show that incorrect skill selection causes task-completion penalties of up to 0.514 on a 0--1 verifier scale---far exceeding the offline ranking gap. To address this, we propose query-conditioned operational schema induction with evidence-gated correction. A schema induction module produces a declarative QueryRuleSpec from the query alone (without inspecting candidate skills), deterministic extraction applies the same schema to query and all candidates, and an evidence gate accepts correction only when grounded operational-contract fields are present. The correction layer works on top of any base ranker. On ContractBench, spanning 10 skill families and 6 orthogonal contract policies, schema induction reaches 0.7833 Top-1 versus 0.6917 for path-graph and 0.7167 for semantic text. Evidence-gated correction recovers 6 additional correct selections on each base ranker, empirically never reducing accuracy below the base ranker. The method is regime-aware: it preserves the strong path-graph baseline outside the contract regime and provides auditable, evidence-bearing routing decisions deployable on any base ranker.
A067SHORTThe Fellowship of the Query: Learning Retrieval Actions
Mohammed Al-Maamari (University of Passau) · Saber Zerhoudi (University of Passau) · Michael Granitzer (University of Passau) · Jelena Mitrovic (University of Passau)
Abstract
Retrieval-augmented question answering requires control decisions about when to decompose a question, search, reformulate, extract evidence, synthesize facts, verify progress, and stop. We study whether trajectory fine-tuning can improve small language models (SLMs) as next-action controllers. We additionally evaluate a low-resource setting in which a single SLM serves as both the controller and the final-answer generator. From accepted teacher search traces, we build a seven-way action-prediction task, where the model predicts the next structured teacher action from the current trajectory state, and evaluate LoRA-supervised fine-tuning across SLMs and xSLMs as controllers. On 1,646 held-out action examples, Granite 4.1 3B trained on 13,194 actions reaches macro-F1 0.6536, compared with 0.1736 for zero-shot prompting of the same model and 0.5399 for a TF-IDF logistic-regression baseline. In an end-to-end controller/generator swap evaluation over 149 held-out trajectories, using the fine-tuned model for both roles improves Exact Match from 0.7530 to 0.7946 and token F1 from 0.7783 to 0.8295 compared with using the base model as both controller and generator. The cross-role conditions show that the fine-tuned controller increases evidence-fact recording when the generator is fixed, while controller-only final-answer gains are not statistically clear. Overall, trajectory supervision improves action prediction and evidence-recording behaviour in this evaluated pipeline. The code used in this paper is publicly available.
A068FULLBringing Agentic Search to Earth Observation Data Discovery
Minghan Yu (University of Maryland, College Park) · Youran Sun (University of Maryland, College Park) · Chugang Yi (University of Maryland, College Park) · Yixin Wen (Stony Brook University) · Haizhao Yang (University of Maryland, College Park)
Abstract
NASA and its data centers hold thousands of geoscience datasets and tools like Worldview, Giovanni, the Science Discovery Engine, and Harmony. Finding the right one is hard even for domain experts. We present an agentic search framework for geoscience data discovery that takes a natural-language research query and returns matching datasets and tools. We demonstrate that, in the era of large language models, the latent value of knowledge graphs (KGs) can be substantially amplified through agentic search. From the NASA Earth Observation Knowledge Graph (NASA EO-KG) we derive NASA-EO-Bench, an open benchmark of 47k query–dataset pairs (21k task-based queries). A neural scorer fine-tuned on NASA-EO-Bench beats cosine and BM25 baselines. Further combining it with BM25 via score fusion raises both Recall@10 (R@10) and MRR to over 5× the unadapted cosine baseline. On top of this supervised pipeline, a zero-shot reranking stage lifts MRR by 16%, significant under a paired bootstrap, with no additional training, and autonomous web and arXiv tool use adds a further gain, showing that LLM reasoning is complementary to supervised retrieval.
A069SHORTRAH: Recursive Agent Harnesses for Long-Context Reasoning through Delegation-as-Code
Elias Lumer (Commercial Technology Innovation Office, PricewaterhouseCoopers, U.S.) · Sahil Sen (Commercial Technology Innovation Office, PricewaterhouseCoopers, U.S.) · Vamse Kumar Subbiah (Commercial Technology Innovation Office, PricewaterhouseCoopers, U.S.) · Kevin Paul (Commercial Technology Innovation Office, PricewaterhouseCoopers, U.S.)
Abstract
When an agent recurses over a long-context task, should the recursive unit be a bare model call or a full harness with filesystem tools, code execution, and planning? We study this question on long-context aggregation, tasks where a single instance may contain thousands of key–value pairs each requiring individual model reasoning. Coding agents reduce per-entry reasoning to regex heuristics. Recursive language models (RLMs) invoke LLMs recursively but lack tool access. We introduce the Recursive Agent Harness (RAH), in which a parent agent generates and runs an executable script that programmatically spawns full subagent harnesses in parallel for fine-grained workloads and uses structured function calls for subtasks of 1–5 entries. We call this harness recursion and study it against model recursion, recursion over bare model calls as in RLMs, on long-context aggregation. With the backbone held fixed at GPT-5 to match the published Codex and RLM baselines, RAH improves the Codex coding-agent baseline from 71.75% to 81.36% on Oolong-Synthetic (199 samples, 13 context-length buckets up to 4M tokens), a gain attributable to the harness rather than the model. With a stronger backbone, Claude Sonnet 4.5, the same design reaches 89.77%.
A070SHORTPyRAMIND: Auditable Deterministic Pyramid Memory for Long-Running LLM Agents
Anup Roy (Inception42) · Rishabh Gyanendra Upadhyay (Inception42) · Aidan Philip Millar (Mubadala Investment Company) · Larry Murray (Inception42) · Robin Mills (Inception42)
Abstract
Long-running LLM agents are increasingly considered for regulated, high-consequence domains such as finance, compliance, and audit, where memory must be accurate, traceable, replayable, and inspectable after a decision. Existing agent-memory systems often invoke an LLM during maintenance operations such as fact extraction, consolidation, updating, summarization, and forgetting. Although effective, this design makes it harder to reconstruct why a memory existed, changed, or was removed at a particular point in time. We present PyRAMIND (Pyramidal Retention with Arithmetic Memory for Inference-time Determinism), an auditable memory architecture in which write consolidation, reinforcement, forgetting, tier promotion, and retrieval scoring are closed-form arithmetic over cached embeddings. Only optional entity tagging at ingest and answer generation at query time call an external LLM. Given fixed embeddings, cached boundary-model outputs, parameters, and software, each maintenance transition is replayable from ordered inputs. PyRAMIND stores memories in a four-tier Pyramid (raw→facts→themes→worldview) and ranks them with a max-ensemble retention score modulated by local semantic density. Under a matched harness, PyRAMIND achieves competitive accuracy on long-horizon memory tasks (0.93 on LongMemEval-S) despite eliminating LLM calls from the memory-maintenance path, while reducing memory-lifecycle token expenditure to 1.4k LLM tokens per turn versus 3.1k for reproduced Mem0 OSS and 4.2k for Zep v3. Performance is weaker on temporal and multi-hop reasoning tasks (0.62 on LoCoMo), highlighting the continued value of richer relational memory structures for compositional reasoning. These results suggest that strong long-term memory performance is possible without LLM-mediated maintenance, and motivate future replayable memory systems that add temporal and relational structure while preserving auditable deterministic maintenance.
A071SHORTBeyond Uncertainty: Multi-Solver Disagreement Rewards for Self-Evolving Reasoning Curricula
Vinoth Selvendran (Independent Researcher) · Zhanming Zhang (Independent Researcher)
Abstract
Self-evolving reasoning frameworks train a Challenger to generate questions exposing a Solver's weaknesses, creating adaptive curricula without human data. However, existing approaches use a single solver's sampling uncertainty as the Challenger's reward. This creates a fundamental bottleneck: as the solver grows confident on the Challenger's question distribution, all sampled answers converge identically, collapsing the reward to zero and starving the Challenger of learning signal. Critically, this single-model reward cannot distinguish genuinely easy questions from those that merely align with one solver's learned biases. We propose a multi-solver disagreement reward using a heterogeneous ensemble varying in model capacity and sampling temperature. A normalized Shannon entropy over the ensemble's per-question plurality answers explicitly rewards questions where solvers produce conflicting solutions—capturing difficulty as inter-model divergence rather than intra-model sampling variance. This richer gradient enables the Challenger to discover questions targeting true capability boundaries, producing a curriculum that forces downstream Solvers to develop robust reasoning strategies generalizing across problem types. Our approach is a drop-in reward function replacement requiring no framework modifications or additional data. Experiments with Qwen3-4B show that Solvers trained on disagreement-Challenger questions achieve +1.34 points average improvement on competition-math benchmarks (MATH-500, AMC, Olympiad), suggesting that multi-solver disagreement provides a complementary and scalable signal for curriculum generation in self-play reasoning systems.
A072FULLDo Large Language Models have Lateral Thinking in Puzzle-Solving Games?
Yuyan Chen (Cornell University) · Zhendong Hou (University of California, Los Angeles) · Yukun Zhang (Columbia University) · Jinghan Cao (San Francisco State University) · Rui Guo (University of Southern California) · Xiong Luo (Uppsala University) · Weinan Dai (Zhejiang university) · Zhixu Li (School of Information, Renmin University of China, School of Smart Governance, Renmin University of China)
Abstract
Large Language Models (LLMs) show exceptional skills in a wide range of tasks, with their ability in lateral thinking standing out as a particularly intriguing area. Lateral thinking in LLMs allows them to understand deeper or suggested meanings from the context, which is essential for making sense of complex scenarios, especially in puzzle-solving games. To delve deeper into and improve the lateral thinking capabilities of LLMs in the realm of puzzle-solving, we introduce the “Lateral Thinking Puzzles” and construct the accompanying dataset. Our novel PuzzleVerse framework aims to enhance LLMs' lateral thinking in puzzle-solving games. Complementing this, we propose a creativity metric to ensure comprehensive evaluations. Experiments show that the selected LLMs, after being trained with PuzzleVerse, have an average improvement of 93.1% compared to their performance before PuzzleVerse training among all metrics. We also validate the robustness of PuzzleVerse that trained LLMs perform better in other reasoning tasks.
A074SHORTDetecting Routing Collapse Early and Label-Free in LLM Cascades
Xiankun Lin (Sun Yat-sen University) · Xinyi Lin (Sun Yat-sen University) · Zhezheng Hao (Zhejiang University) · Lixin Liu (Tsinghua University)
Abstract
LLM cascades save cost only when easy queries stay on the cheap model, yet learned routers often collapse and send nearly all traffic to the expensive tier. Prior work links this failure to an objective-decision mismatch; we ask why that mismatch is systematically one-sided. Under a weak per-query signal, collapse follows from regression to the mean. Even a correctly specified regression router estimates the conditional mean gain, discarding unpredictable noise and pulling predictions toward the global mean. If that mean exceeds the cost threshold, thresholding the contracted scores routes too much traffic upward. The same view predicts two counterintuitive scaling effects: collapse strengthens as the signal weakens, and more same-kind data can deepen it by removing estimation noise around an already-contracted target. It also gives a no-new-label diagnostic: compare the expensive-tier route fraction to the strong-win base rate already present in training labels. Across all 45 viable RouterBench cascades, regression over-routes by 7 to 49 points, with every bootstrap interval above zero. In 1068 real routers, 240 of 534 regression routers collapse, versus 0 of 534 decision routers. The diagnostic reaches AUROC 0.999 at convergence and 0.92 after one quarter of training. Since the failure is a rank-preserving level shift, base-rate recalibration removes it.
A075SHORTKnowing When to Correct: Cost-Aware LLM Routing for OCR Post-Correction in Historical Documents
Stergios Konstantinidis (University of Lausanne) · Hayman Lotfy (University of Lausanne) · Michalis Vlachos (University of Lausanne)
Abstract
Historical digital archives present new challenges for retrieval systems because of OCR errors introduced by degraded page quality, old typefaces, and complex page layouts. Large language models (LLMs) offer an effective means of correcting transcription errors. However, applying LLM-based correction at scale can become prohibitively expensive. We investigate a selective, cost-aware strategy for LLM-assisted OCR post-correction, using a regression-guided router to predict when LLM correction is likely to improve transcription quality, thereby reducing unnecessary LLM processing and associated costs while preserving historically valid text. We evaluate this strategy on a dataset comprising historical Swiss newspapers published between 1733 and 1945. Our results show that selective correction can retain most of the quality gains of full correction while substantially reducing the LLM token cost. Using Tesseract OCR, sending all text segments for LLM correction improves CER from 6.3% to 2.9% (best approach). In contrast, our regression-guided router achieves CER of 3.1% (0.2% worse) while avoiding routing 40% of segments for LLM correction. Finally, we show that our regression-guided LLM router closely trails the decisions of an oracle that knows in advance which segments benefit from correction.
A076SHORTConservative Hybrid SQL Rewriting with Rules, Retrieval, and LLM Reasoning
Xiangyun Zhang (Xidian University) · Wensheng Wang (Xidian University) · Cheng Wen (Xidian University) · Shengchao Qin (Xidian University)
Abstract
SQL query rewriting improves database performance by transforming queries into semantically equivalent but more efficient forms. Rule-based rewriting is reliable for standard cases, but often misses boundary scenarios involving NULL semantics, outer joins, nested queries, or workload-specific constraints. Large language models (LLMs) can reason over such cases, but direct application risks hallucinations and semantic errors. We propose Conservative Hybrid SQL Rewriting, a rule-anchored framework that combines deterministic rules, retrieval-guided LLM refinement, and verification-gated fallback. The LLM refines a rule-generated candidate, and is accepted only if validation passes; otherwise, the deterministic candidate is returned. Experiments on PostgreSQL workloads show that rules dominate standard scenarios, while constrained LLM reasoning improves boundary-case coverage. Our results suggest LLMs are most effective as conservative coverage extenders, complementing rather than replacing deterministic rules.
A077FULLGPU-Accelerated Parquet Compaction and Index Construction for High-Cardinality Time-Series Databases
Ziyue Xu (Nankai University) · Ke Wang (Nankai University) · Gang Wang (Nankai University) · Xiaoguang Liu (Nankai University)
Abstract
Time-series databases commonly employ LSM-Tree with Parquet columnar storage, where compaction and index construction act as major performance bottlenecks in high-cardinality IoT and cloud monitoring scenarios. Traditional CPU-only compaction suffers from low parallelism and high computation overhead, while mainstream GPU solutions such as cuDF fail to adapt to time-series features. They load complete Parquet files without optimization for string primary keys and lack an end-to-end accelerated index building workflow. This work presents a CPU-GPU collaborative framework for Parquet compaction and index construction. It partitions Parquet row groups into overlapping and non-overlapping segments by primary key ranges to avoid unnecessary global sorting. A global dictionary alignment scheme transforms variable-length string keys into integers to eliminate GPU warp divergence and enable efficient radix sort. Combined with lazy materialization, the framework only processes sorting keys and delays metric field parsing, significantly reducing GPU memory consumption and data transfer cost. A two-phase adaptive cost model enables effective heterogeneous task scheduling. Additionally, a parallel GPU pipeline accelerates tag inverted index construction, leaving only FST and bitmap generation to the CPU. Evaluated on the TSBS benchmark, our framework outperforms CPU baselines and cuDF substantially. It cuts compaction time by nearly an order of magnitude, speeds up index construction by 3.8×–5.2×, and boosts end-to-end throughput by 7.0%–16.0% with stable query latency.
A078FULLGSPARC: A Mode-Aware GPU-Based Method for Large-Scale Sparse Tensor Contraction
Seohyeon Kim (KAIST) · Jihye Lee (ETRI) · Sungwoo Park (KAIST) · Min-Soo Kim (KAIST)
Abstract
Sparse tensor contraction (SpTC) is a core operation for high-order sparse data analytics in recommendation, knowledge graph analytics, large-scale tensor mining, and scientific computing. Existing methods are limited by SpTC-misaligned representations, overlapping outputs across partitions, and memory-inefficient accumulation over large output spaces. We propose GSPARC, a GPU-based SpTC method that combines a new mode-aware bit-wise representation with mode-decoupled output partitioning and memory-efficient accumulation. These techniques improve index matching, eliminate inter-partition merging, and avoid full output-space allocation. Extensive experiments demonstrate that GSPARC outperforms state-of-the-art SpTC methods in contraction speed and scalability. Our code is available at this link: https://github.com/seohyeon0322/GSPARC.
A079FULLHide-And-Seek-Pair: Efficient Two-Stage Privacy-Preserving Deep Entity Resolution
Yixiang Yao (University of Southern California) · Weizhao Jin (University of Southern California) · Shanshan Han (University of California, Irvine) · Yuhang Yao (Carnegie Mellon University) · Carlee Joe-Wong (Carnegie Mellon University) · Srivatsan Ravi (University of Southern California)
Abstract
Entity resolution solutions based on deep learning have been gaining more attention due to their improved performance in linking records of the same entity. However, due to the complexity of models (especially state-of-art language models) used for entity resolution, it is challenging to provide privacy-preserving variants of deep entity resolution models to comply with data privacy constraints in applications like medical data analysis. In this paper, we propose Hide-And-Seek-Pair (HASP), an efficient privacy-preserving deep entity resolution protocol that utilizes and optimizes homomorphic encryption with deep models in a two-stage computation fashion that provides a practical balance between robust privacy guarantees and computational efficiency. Additionally, by employing Synthetic Ranging, Polynomial Degree Optimization and Differential Loss Term, HASP ensures accurate non-linear function approximation in encrypted neural networks. Overall, the framework outperforms existing state-of-the-art methods in various benchmarks while offering a secure and efficient method for privacy-preserving entity resolution.
A080FULLSeq2Synth: Benchmarking Temporal Fidelity in Synthetic Sequential Tabular Data
Kiwan Kwon (UNIST) · Kangmin Kim (UNIST) · Hojin Lee (UNIST) · Yeseong Jung (UNIST) · Hyeongwoo Kong (HUFS) · Vamsi K. Potluru (Independent Researcher) · Saerom Park (UNIST) · Yongjae Lee (UNIST)
Abstract
Synthetic sequential tabular data are increasingly used for privacy-preserving data sharing and research, yet conventional tabular metrics often overlook temporal structure. Existing single-table and relational evaluation protocols largely collapse records into static distributions, leaving key temporal properties insufficiently evaluated. We introduce Seq2Synth, a unified benchmark for assessing these properties. Its taxonomy characterizes temporal and schema properties to determine applicable evaluations, covering timestamp, cross-sectional, longitudinal, and structural fidelity, alongside trajectory-aware utility and privacy. Across seven core datasets from a 13-dataset benchmark and eight generators, models with near-perfect static fidelity still violate basic temporal constraints, producing duplicate timestamps, irregular intervals, and incomplete observation grids. Moreover, static and temporal-aware rankings diverge substantially, showing that temporal fidelity must be evaluated directly rather than inferred from static or relational scores. Project page and online appendices are available at: https://seq2synth.github.io/.
A081SHORTKITDG: Knowledge-Infused Tabular Data Generation
Daniel Gan (Deakin University) · Nayyar Zaidi (Deakin University) · Son N Tran (Deakin University)
Abstract
Tabular data generation has advanced in distributional fidelity, yet no framework systematically enforces domain-level associative structure during synthesis. We introduce KITDG (Knowledge-Infused Tabular Data Generation) – which infuses Apriori-mined association rules into a generative backbone through a differentiable Logic Tensor Network (LTN) knowledge base with gradient-isolated three-stage training, and ARFD (Association Rule Fidelity Distance) – a novel metric decomposing associative fidelity into rule preservation (P1) and rule strength (P2), applicable to any tabular generator as a drop-in evaluation complement to distributional metrics. Across 13 benchmark datasets under TSTR, KITDG matches or outperforms its backbone in 48 of 52 (dataset, classifier) pairs. We further report the top-k phenomenon, to our knowledge the first characterization of a quality-over-quantity regime in rule-infused tabular generation, supporting association rule infusion as a general, transferable principle for tabular synthesis.
A082FULLSERA: Evaluating LLM-based SEmantic RAnking over Structured Tables
Emilia Lenzi (Politecnico di Milano) · Davide Martinenghi (Politecnico di Milano) · Paolo Papotti (EURECOM) · Marco Riva (Politecnico di Milano)
Abstract
LLM-based data systems are moving beyond text-to-SQL toward semantic query processing, where natural language requests are executed through operators that combine relational processing with LLM-driven inference. A central operator in this setting is SemanticRank, or semantic top-k: given a user intent and a set of relational records, the system orders rows according to a user-defined criterion. Current systems implement this operator as a single black-box LLM prompt. This abstraction hides a key execution problem: the reliability and cost of semantic ranking depend on the criterion being evaluated, the evidence available in the table, and the physical strategy used to compare candidate records. We study semantic ranking as a logical database operator and introduce a multi-domain benchmark for identifying the factors that govern reliable execution over tabular data. Our framework evaluates five dimensions: criterion complexity and specification, computable versus semantic execution, evidence availability, and ranking strategy. We compare proprietary, open-source, and reasoning-oriented LLMs across datasets, specification regimes, evidence conditions, and execution strategies using rank-aware metrics. Our analysis shows that SemanticRank cannot be implemented reliably as a single prompting primitive. Ranking quality is shaped by criterion structure, and formula-based specifications help reasoning-oriented execution. Real-world names can introduce prior-knowledge bias that anonymisation reduces. Full execution is competitive on small candidate sets, while partitioning changes the cost-quality trade-off without consistently improving accuracy. These findings identify key factors for reliable SemanticRank execution.
A083FULLQuery-Graph Compatibility: A Formal Pre-Condition for Faithful Knowledge-Grounded Language Model Generation
Mariam ALMutairi (Virginia Tech) · Fatimah D. Alotaibi (Tuwaiq Academy) · Lulwah Alkulaib (Kuwait University) · Zhiqian Chen (Rochester Institute of Technology) · Sara Alsalamah (Imam Mohammad Ibn Saud Islamic University) · Chang-Tien Lu (Virginia Tech)
Abstract
Knowledge-graph-based retrieval-augmented generation (KG-RAG) grounds large language model (LLM) outputs in structured facts by retrieving a query-relevant subgraph before generation. However, existing KG-RAG systems often assume that the retrieved graph contains sufficient evidence to answer the query. When this assumption fails, the LLM may produce an answer that is factually plausible but not faithfully grounded in the KG. To address this problem, we introduce Query-Graph Compatibility (QGC), a formal, model-independent pre-condition for faithful KG-grounded generation. Given a natural-language query parsed into a typed conjunctive query and a KG with schema, QGC checks whether the query has a valid typed match in the graph, formalized as a typed homomorphism. If QGC=0, the KG lacks the structural evidence required by the query, so no generation model, regardless of architecture or scale, can produce a faithful answer from the KG alone-a consequence that follows directly from our definitions but yields a checkable pre-generation condition. QGC inherits the classical complexity of conjunctive-query evaluation: NP-complete in general, yet tractable for the bounded-width query structures that cover all KGQA queries in our evaluation. We validate QGC across six datasets and four domains. Under controlled edge deletion on MetaQA, QGC predicts LLM failure with AUC 0.78-0.93 for 1-2 hop queries across five LLMs, with accuracy gaps of +55 to +86 percentage points. Under natural incompleteness in clinical KGs (MIMIC-III, CORAL), all five evaluated models show positive QGC accuracy gaps (+5 to +31 percentage points), while PrimeKGQA exposes a boundary condition: structurally simpler QGC=0 contexts can yield higher correctness despite lacking faithful grounding. QGC checking runs in under 0.1 ms per query, making it practical as a real-time pre-filter or retrieval stopping criterion.
A084SHORTPROCS: Uncertainty-Aware Knowledge Graph Embeddings via Conceptual Spaces
Ubaid Azam (University of Southampton) · Imran Razzak (Mohamed Bin Zayed University of Artificial Intelligence (MBZUAI)) · Steven Schockaert (Cardiff University) · Shoaib Jameel (University of Southampton)
Abstract
While deep reasoning models (e.g., NBFNet, ULTRA) have advanced knowledge graph completion, they often sacrifice the efficiency and interpretability of geometric embeddings for increased expressivity. We present PROCS, a framework that combines the best of both worlds through region-based representations inspired by Gärdenfors' Conceptual Spaces, realised as a scalable probabilistic embedding layer. Unlike deterministic point embeddings, PROCS models entities as Gaussian distributions where variance explicitly encodes vagueness and conflict. By introducing a scalable geometric inference mechanism that avoids intractable sampling, PROCS achieves 0.417 MRR on FB15k-237, matching the performance of heavy reasoning models while retaining the O(1) inference of embedding methods. Its uncertainty estimates enable risk-aware retrieval, validated by a Defence-domain case study. Our code and data are available at https://github.com/ubaidazam/PROCS.
A085SHORTLeave-One-Signature-Out: Auditing Recurrence in Episode-Structured Temporal Benchmarks
Hyeonbyeong Lee (Mokpo National University) · Wooje Sung (Chungbuk National University) · Sanghyeuk Kim (Chungbuk National University) · Sangho Song (Chungbuk National University) · Dojin Choi (Changwon National University) · Kyoungsoo Bok (Wonkwang University) · Jaesoo Yoo (Chungbuk National University)
Abstract
Held-out train/test evaluation remains necessary, but episode-structured temporal benchmarks can preserve recurring signatures across random/time splits, so scores may partly reflect recurrence rather than broader out-of-signature generalization. We propose leave-one-signature-out evaluation (LOSO), which holds out all instances sharing a target-free structural signature. LOSO removes the audited recurrence channel by construction and enables an oracle-collapse diagnostic: the standard-to-LOSO gap indicates how strongly a score depends on the audited recurrence channel. In TKGs, repeated test triples account for 44–84% of cases against train+validation history, while LOSO audits target-free signatures such as (s,r). On UCI Diabetes EHR, LOSO exposes rank instability: temporal kNN significantly outperforms the majority baseline and logistic regression on hard folds (p = 0.004), while static kNN drops from second to last. A six-crop agricultural benchmark adds a directional case: the top random-split method drops by 0.468 macro-F1 under LOSO. We add a non-degenerate ICEWS14s (s,r)-LOSO audit to test recurrence without unseen-relation degeneracy.
A086SHORTDo General NLP Embeddings Capture Ontological Reasoning?
Hamed Babaei Giglou (TIB Leibniz Information Centre for Science and Technology) · Jennifer D'Souza (TIB Leibniz Information Centre for Science and Technology) · Sören Auer (TIB Leibniz Information Centre for Science and Technology)
Abstract
General-purpose NLP embedding models perform well on linguistic tasks, but their ability to capture symbolic ontological structure remains unclear. We introduce AVA, a systematic framework for evaluating whether embeddings distinguish logic-sensitive relational semantics in ontologies and knowledge graphs. AVA comprises 171,007 contrastive triplets derived from 163 heterogeneous ontologies using hierarchy inversion, relation substitution, and disjointness injection. Each triplet contains an ontology statement, a semantically equivalent paraphrase, and a logic-sensitive hard negative with contradictory relational meaning. We evaluate more than 25 state-of-the-art embedding models and find substantial limitations: the best model achieves only 0.739 triplet accuracy, while hard negative accuracy falls to 0.135. Fine-tuning improves discrimination by a large margin but transfers poorly to downstream Semantic Web tasks, including taxonomy discovery and ontology alignment. Further analysis suggests that improvements stem partly from perturbation-specific pattern recognition rather than robust ontological understanding. These findings reveal a persistent gap between linguistic representation learning and ontology-level discrimination, challenging the assumption that strong NLP benchmark performance translates to Semantic Web competence.
A087FULLMulti-dimensional Evolution Model with Attribute and Structure Interactions for Entity Alignment
Xiaowen Su (Peking University) · Hongzhi Liu (Peking University) · Zhonghai Wu (Peking University)
Abstract
Entity alignment aims to identify equivalent entities across different Knowledge Graphs (KGs), serving as a fundamental task for knowledge graph integration. It is inherently a multi-dimensional problem, where graph topology, entity attributes, and alignment evidence should mutually reinforce one another. However, most existing methods fail to establish such a loop. They typically expand or refine alignment supervision alone, while keeping the underlying graph structure and attribute importance static. Moreover, they lack a global view of which attributes are discriminative across the alignment set. As a result, structural sparsity persists, noisy attributes cannot be suppressed, and alignment supervision remains scarce. To solve these problems, we propose MEASI, a Multi-dimensional Evolution model with Attribute and Structure Interactions for entity alignment. MEASI comprises three evolutionary modules that establish a self-reinforcing loop. First, a Graph Structure Evolution (GSE) module progressively enhances graph topology by leveraging newly discovered alignments. Second, a Global Attribute Weight Evolution (GAWE) module iteratively updates global attribute weights via alignment feedback, emphasizing discriminative attributes and reducing the influence of attribute noise. Finally, an Alignment Signal Evolution (ASE) module continuously discovers new aligned entities from both structural and attribute views to fuel the next iteration of GSE and GAWE, compensating for limited pre-aligned entities. Extensive experiments show that MEASI outperforms state-of-the-art methods.
A088FULLCodeGraph: Open-Taxonomy Knowledge Graph for Source Code with Wikidata Grounding
Federico Pennino (Università di Bologna) · Andrea Gurioli (Università di Bologna) · Stefano Zacchiroli (LTCI, Télécom Paris, Institut Polytechnique de Paris) · Maurizio Gabbrielli (Università di Bologna) · Paolo Ferragina (Sant'Anna School of Advanced Studies)
Abstract
Public software repositories, like GitHub and Software Heritage Archive, store billions of files, yet extracting their implicit engineering knowledge ---i.e., the algorithms they implement, the paradigms they follow, the patterns they instantiate, and the application domains they serve--- remains challenging, as current tools are constrained to syntactic and token-level analysis. We present a pipeline for building an open-taxonomy semantic annotation of source code using a code-specialised Large Language Model. The extracted entities are grounded in Wikidata through a three-stage linking procedure: a deterministic SPARQL stage handles unambiguous entities, a Deep Research Agent resolves the residual long tail, and a hierarchy-rollup stage imports the parent-of closure of each resolved Wikidata identifier. The resulting annotations are materialised as a source-code-specific open-taxonomy knowledge graph. We further introduce a calibrated quality-assurance protocol that quantifies annotation precision by combining a small human gold set with an LLM-as-a-judge filter. We applied our pipeline to the 167 million files of the Stack-Edu corpus, creating the first known large-scale open-taxonomy knowledge graph for source code. Our graph, named CodeGraph, contains approximately 158 million nodes, which include around 145 million files, about 63,000 extracted concept entities (such as algorithms, paradigms, design patterns, and application domains), and roughly 19,800 grounded Wikidata entities. Furthermore, CodeGraph features approximately 1 billion typed edges that connect files to their respective concepts, link these concepts to their grounded Wikidata identifiers, and relate them to their parent categories, covering 14 programming languages.
A089RESOURCEWiCleanData: Guaranteeing the Type Consistency of Wikidata by Taxonomy Refinement and Constraint Enforcement
Yiwen Peng (Télécom Paris, Institut Polytechnique de Paris) · Marc Jeanmougin (Télécom Paris, Institut Polytechnique de Paris) · Thomas Bonald (Télécom Paris, Institut Polytechnique de Paris)
Abstract
Because of its collaborative nature, Wikidata suffers from errors, inconsistencies, and excessive complexity, such as redundant classes, ambiguity between instances and classes, wrong taxonomic paths, and type constraint violations. The manual curation of these issues is infeasible at scale. To address these challenges, we introduce WiCleanData, a refined version of Wikidata with a consistent taxonomy and free from type constraint violations. Specifically, we have designed an automated pipeline that first cleans the taxonomy with language model assistance, then simplifies type constraints by hierarchical aggregation, and finally filters facts accordingly. The resulting knowledge graph, free from any type violation, is made publicly available via a Web interface, enabling easy exploration and downstream applications.
A090RESOURCEThe EMN Country Factsheets Structured Dataset
David Alonso del Barrio (Idiap Research Institute) · Daniel Gatica-Perez (Idiap Reasearch Institute)
Abstract
Each year, the European Migration Network (EMN) country factsheets deliver an overview of key migration and international protection developments within all EMN Member States and observer countries. The factsheets include both a textual component and a visual component. In this paper, we introduce a curated dataset of the textual component of these reports over 35 countries and 13 years (2012-2024.) The dataset was created to facilitate European-level research on migration policies and developments, and promote the use of reliable sources about migration in data science and media research, particularly at a time when the spread of online misinformation about migration constitutes a serious issue. The dataset transforms the original document texts into a tabular format, with columns corresponding to country, year, section, subsection, content, and harmonized title section. We illustrate the value of the dataset with concrete analyses and propose envisioned applications and uses of the dataset. The dataset is accessible through a DOI link.
A091FULLLSRTopic: Contextual Sparse Topic Modeling via Corpus-Vocabulary Alignment
Ana Cláudia Machado (Federal University of São João del-Rei) · Celso França (Federal University of Minas Gerais) · Antônio Pereira (Federal University of São João del-Rei) · Marcos André Gonçalves (Federal University of Minas Gerais) · Leonardo Rocha (Federal University of São João del-Rei)
Abstract
Topic modeling still struggles to combine contextual expressiveness with lexical interpretability. Sparse models are transparent but semantically limited, whereas dense contextual models capture meaning at the cost of direct interpretability. We argue that Learned Sparse Representations (LSR) offer a promising alternative but remain underused in topic modeling due to a vocabulary misalignment problem: their activations are over subword vocabularies, whereas topic models require stable corpus-level terms. We introduce LSRTopic, a framework that maps and aggregates contextual sparse activations into the target corpus vocabulary, producing semantically enriched and lexically interpretable document--term matrices for factorization methods such as NMF. Experiments on six benchmark datasets against 10 baselines show that LSRTopic achieves the strongest overall performance across coherence, embedding-based proximity, topic uniqueness, and document-representation separability. Additional LLM-as-judge word-intrusion evaluation with human validation, ablations, and efficiency analysis confirms that resolving vocabulary misalignment enables topic models that jointly support contextual semantics, interpretability, and practical efficiency.
A092SHORTImproving Precision in Cluster-Level Pricing Experiments with Temporal Switchbacks
Nicolás Ferrari Ortiz (LATAM Airlines) · Sebastián Orellana Montini (LATAM Airlines) · Marie Garkavenko (ADC Consulting) · Rutger Lit (ADC Consulting) · Timur Abbiasov (ADC Consulting)
Abstract
Online pricing systems often cannot randomize treatments at the user level because prices are deployed over operational units such as routes, regions, or markets. This creates low-powered A/B tests due to persistent cluster heterogeneity, seasonality, and autocorrelated demand. We study temporal switchback designs for cluster-level pricing experiments, where each cluster alternates between treatment and control over time. Using LATAM Airlines ancillary-pricing data and calibrated simulations, we show that switchbacks can substantially reduce standard errors relative to parallel cluster designs. We further characterize how switching cadence interacts with temporal dependence, highlighting when daily or weekly switchbacks are preferable. The results provide practical guidance for experimentation in pricing and transportation platforms where fine-grained randomization is infeasible.
A093FULLAnytime-Valid Multi-Objective Online Experimentation with Contrast Certificates
Zilong Wang (Shanghai Jiao Tong University) · Penglei Zhao (Tencent, Inc) · Fang Kong (Southern University of Science and Technology) · Yong Wang (Tencent, Inc) · Shuai Li (Shanghai Jiao Tong University)
Abstract
Large-scale search and recommendation systems routinely run online experiments for ranking models, feed policies, user-interface treatments, and ad/recommendation blending strategies. These launches are rarely single-metric decisions: teams often need to improve click-through rate, conversion, dwell time, retention, or revenue while controlling negative feedback and latency. We propose AV-MO-SOPTIMA++, an anytime-valid framework for multi-objective online experimentation under adaptive traffic allocation and optional stopping. Instead of relying only on marginal arm-objective confidence sequences, AV-MO-SOPTIMA++ uses prospective two-sample contrast confidence sequences for decision-relevant arm pairs; these contrasts may be pre-activated for a fixed decision mode or activated online when new bottleneck constraints appear. The method derives Pareto and guardrail certificates from these contrasts and propagates certified dominance through a dominance graph. The framework further uses decision-specific stopping rules for full Pareto, relaxed Pareto, and guardrail launch decisions, together with a bottleneck-aware allocation policy that prioritizes comparisons currently blocking a valid decision. Experiments show that the anytime-valid controller maintains calibration under optional stopping, exposes false certificates from nominal multi-objective peeking, and supports safe guardrail launch decisions with fewer samples than fixed-horizon A/B or full-Pareto PSI in a launch benchmark. Component ablations show that contrast certificates reduce guardrail stopping time and bottleneck allocation sharply reduces bad-arm exposure. In full Pareto identification, contrast variants reduce samples on separated instances, while near-boundary instances remain challenging for all validity-first methods.
A094SHORTTMRP-Net:Temporal-Aware Multimodal Retrieval for Social Media Popularity Prediction
Chaopeng Xue (National Key Laboratory of Big Data and Decision) · Niran Deng (National Key Laboratory of Big Data and Decision) · Yang Fang (National University of Defense Technology) · Hao Xu (National Key Laboratory of Big Data and Decision) · Xiang Zhao (National Key Laboratory of Big Data and Decision)
Abstract
Predicting the popularity of user-generated content (UGC) is challenging because content diffusion depends not only on the post itself but also on its publication time and the historical performance of similar content. Retrieval provides a natural way to incorporate historical evidence, but semantic similarity alone is an insufficient proxy for retrieval utility. A retrieved post may appear relevant in content while being temporally mismatched, unavailable at prediction time, or uninformative for the target post. To address these limitations, we propose TMRP-Net, a temporally aware multimodal retrieval framework for social media popularity prediction. TMRP-Net uses CLIP-aligned image-text features and task-specific temporal representations to capture both weekly periodicity and global temporal position. It retrieves only previously published posts and ranks them according to content-time relevance, ensuring that the retrieved context is both causally valid and temporally comparable. The retrieved candidates are further refined through contribution-aware selection, modeled by a lightweight target-conditioned relational graph, and fused with the target representation using time-guided weights for final prediction. Experiments on ICIP and SMPD show that TMRP-Net consistently outperforms competitive baselines.
A095SHORTKnowing When to Escalate: Disagreement Patterns for Uncertainty-Aware Content Moderation
Michał Wawer (Warsaw University of Technology) · Jarosław A. Chudziak (Warsaw University of Technology)
Abstract
Agentic content-moderation systems increasingly rely on collective judgments from LLM agents, while aggregation methods commonly treat inter-agent disagreement as a reliability problem to be removed through consensus or voting. This framing is inappropriate for value-laden tasks, where disagreement may reflect irreducible value pluralism - a distinction standard uncertainty decompositions cannot recover, since they operate on output distributions and discard the reasoning behind each judgment. We propose Reasoning Trace Divergence Analysis (RTDA), which embeds model-generated justifications from perspective-differentiated agents and classifies each case by justification similarity and conclusion agreement. The resulting four-state taxonomy isolates convergent disagreement, where agents reasoning similarly but concluding differently, as a candidate signature of value-laden conflict. On 1,000 items from the Measuring Hate Speech corpus, this structural signal predicts human annotator disagreement better than magnitude-only and output-only baselines. We contribute a design principle: condition human escalation on the structure of disagreement, not its magnitude alone, with RTDA serving as a post-processing layer for systems that already generate reasoning traces.
A096FULLRoE-FND: Synergizing LLMs with Experiential Learning for Effective and Generalizable Evidence-Based Fake News Detection
Yuzhou Yang (Fudan University) · Qichao Ying (Fudan University) · Sheng Li (Fudan University) · Zhiying Zhu (Hohai University) · Zhenxing Qian (Fudan University) · Xinpeng Zhang (Fudan University)
Abstract
The proliferation of deceptive content in social networks necessitates robust Fake News Detection (FND) systems. Existing pipelines either train detectors on labeled data or leverage Large Language Models (LLMs) for their reasoning ability. However, current approaches remain either limited in generalizability or prone to over-commitment to persuasive yet flawed rationales, lacking systematic experience and mechanisms to expose subtle reasoning errors. We propose RoE-FND (Reason on Experiences FND), an LLM-based framework that combines self-reflective experience building with deliberation through retrieved experiences for FND. RoE-FND builds an experience bank via reflective learning that compares an unconstrained analysis with a label-conditioned analysis using the ground-truth label as posterior supervision, then summarizes their critical divergence into reusable reasoning guidelines. During inference, RoE-FND generates two opposing deductions via a flipped pseudo-label provided as posterior, retrieves the most relevant experiences for resolving their key disagreement, and adjudicates the better-supported rationale as the final prediction. Experiments across five popular benchmarks, including text-only datasets, i.e., CHEF, Snopes, PolitiFact, and multimedia datasets, i.e., FakeTT, FakeSV, demonstrate that RoE-FND outperforms strong baselines without optimizing LLM parameters on dataset distributions, while exhibiting strong cross-dataset generalization.
A097SHORTEvidence-Aware Prompting for Causal Fact Verification with Large Language Models
Joseph Mchaileh (RMIT University) · Ziqi Xu (RMIT University) · Xiuzhen Zhang (RMIT University)
Abstract
Large language models (LLMs) are increasingly integrated into information retrieval pipelines to reason over retrieved textual evidence and produce final decisions in tasks such as fact verification. However, causal fact verification presents a more specialised challenge than conventional claim verification: models must aggregate multiple pieces of evidence and assess whether the evidence supports a claimed causal relation, rather than merely verifying factual consistency. This setting is captured by CHECKWHY, which, to the best of our knowledge, is currently the only publicly available benchmark specifically designed for causal “why” fact verification. Motivated by this specialised problem, we propose Evidence-Aware Prompting (EAP), an evidence-centric framework that separates evidence selection from decision generation to enhance LLM reasoning. EAP models query-conditioned evidence selection as an explicit intermediate step and aggregates decisions over selected evidence subsets, mitigating query-only shortcuts and reducing the influence of irrelevant context. Experiments on CHECKWHY across multiple closed-source LLMs show that EAP consistently outperforms strong prompting baselines and achieves more balanced and robust evidence-grounded decisions for causal fact verification.
A098SHORTDual-Granularity Text Guidance for Dyadic Motion Generation
Xiangxi Liu (Institute of Automation, Chinese Academy of Sciences) · Lu Zhou (Institute of Automation, Chinese Academy of Sciences) · Haixin Wang (Institute of Automation, Chinese Academy of Sciences) · Yingying Chen (Institute of Automation, Chinese Academy of Sciences) · Jinqiao Wang (Institute of Automation, Chinese Academy of Sciences)
Abstract
Generating realistic dyadic motions from text is challenging due to complex inter-individual dynamics. Existing works lack in-depth exploration of input textual descriptions, leading to insufficient text-motion alignment. To address this problem, we propose DualGuidance, a diffusion model for dyadic motion generation that leverages dual-granularity text guidance, built upon three key designs. Firstly, we employ cross-modal attention to refine dyadic text features with individual motion features, obtaining coarse-grained text features that retain individual-specific motion information. Secondly, we use an LLM to generate individual textual descriptions, extract text features, and compute matching scores with individual motion features to achieve identity-aware alignment, yielding fine-grained text features. Finally, the dual-granularity text features are fused via gating mechanism to form the control signal for motion generation. Experiments on the InterHuman benchmark demonstrate that DualGuidance achieves state-of-the-art result on semantic alignment while maintaining competitive performance on other metrics, demonstrating the effectiveness of dual-granularity text guidance for dyadic motion generation. Our code and models are available at https://github.com/Xiangxi-Liu/DualGuidance.
A099FULLSADI: Spatial-Aware Dynamic Intervention for Mitigating Hallucinations in LVLMs
Yuanzhi Xu (Qilu University of Technology (Shandong Academy of Sciences)) · Qian Gao (Qilu University of Technology (Shandong Academy of Sciences)) · Jun Fan (China Telecom Digital Intelligence Technology Co, Ltd) · Guohui Ding (Shenyang Aerospace University) · Zhenyu Yang (Qilu University of Technology (Shandong Academy of Sciences)) · Sixue Lin (Qilu Institute of Technology) · Yuteng Xiao (Qilu University of Technology (Shandong Academy of Sciences))
Abstract
Large Vision-Language Models (LVLMs) persistently suffer from object hallucinations, generating plausible yet factually incorrect outputs that fabricate objects non-existent in the visual input. Existing mitigation methods typically fall into three paradigms: fine-tuning with targeted data, which incurs prohibitive computational costs; applying contrastive decoding, which introduces high inference latency and may penalize beneficial language priors; or intervening in attention weights via heuristic hard-truncation or head-homogeneous shifts, operations that may discard information from selected attention paths. Building upon the third paradigm, we present Spatial-Aware Dynamic Intervention (SADI). SADI discards conventional rigid truncations in favor of a spatial-aware soft mask to adaptively correct visual-semantic misalignments. Specifically, it establishes a robust median consensus among multiple attention heads to anchor reliable visual representations. Guided by the spatial variance across these heads, SADI dynamically allocates intervention weights and employs a soft mask to gently suppress anomalous attention distributions. As a lightweight, training-free inference solution, our method reframes attention modulation as a smooth, continuous recalibration process. Ultimately, SADI effectively rectifies semantic drift while maintaining comparable generation fluency and description richness in our evaluations. Extensive experiments demonstrate that SADI significantly reduces both sentence- and instance-level hallucinations while maintaining description richness. Across the evaluated CHAIR, POPE, and MME benchmarks, SADI shows consistent gains in the tested settings. Code is released at https://github.com/yz-8/SADI.
A100SHORTWhen Visual Frames Flip Mental-State Answers: An Item-Level Audit of Multimodal Theory-of-Mind Reasoning
Taehun Kim (Sungkyunkwan University) · Minjoo Kim (Sungkyunkwan University) · Seohyeon Hong (Sungkyunkwan University) · Hayoung Oh (Sungkyunkwan University)
Abstract
Multimodal Theory-of-Mind (ToM) evaluation often assumes that visual frames provide useful evidence for answering questions about beliefs, goals, and intentions. We test this assumption with an item-level audit of MuMA-ToM, a benchmark of 900 multiple-choice questions about multi-agent household interactions. The audit compares six settings: question-and-answer only (QA-only), video frames only (Video-only), text only (Text-only), text paired with frames (Text+Frame), generic chain-of-thought prompting (CoT), and QLogic, a structured text-only prompt that makes the question logic explicit. Across GPT-4o, Gemini 2.5 Flash, and Qwen2.5-VL-7B-Instruct, Video-only outperforms QA-only, showing that frames can be useful. However, Text+Frame does not outperform Text-only for any model, and GPT-4o shows a significant paired drop. We therefore analyze answer transitions rather than aggregate accuracy alone. The main transition is Vision-Induced ToM Degradation, defined operationally as an item that is correct under Text-only but wrong under Text+Frame. On GPT-4o degradation cases, generic CoT recovers 14 of 78 items, while QLogic recovers 62 of 78; an exact McNemar test confirms the paired recovery difference (p=2.92×10-12). Ablations show that condition tracking and candidate comparison are the most informative QLogic components. The results support a narrow conclusion suited to short-form multimodal evaluation: added visual evidence should be audited for how it changes individual mental-state answers, not only for whether it improves average accuracy.
A101SHORTText-Conditioned Scene Graph Sequence Generation via Discrete Diffusion
Bomi Kwon (Sookmyung Women's University) · Ki Yong Lee (Sookmyung Women's University)
Abstract
Scene graphs represent visual scenes as objects and their relationships. While considerable research has explored predicting scene graph sequences from images or videos, generating such sequences from text remains underexplored. In this work, we introduce a discrete diffusion framework for text-conditioned scene graph sequence generation, focusing on visual scenes centered on human--object interactions. The proposed framework represents each sequence as a fixed-slot discrete state, where each slot encodes the state of an object over time, and employs a Transformer-based denoiser to generate scene graph sequences aligned with the input text. The denoiser jointly leverages within-frame slot attention, cross-frame temporal attention, and text cross-attention to capture inter-object relationships, temporal dynamics, and text--graph correspondence. We compare the proposed framework with diverse baselines, including retrieval-based methods, scene graph parsers, large language models, sequence-to-sequence models, and non-diffusion generative models. Experimental results show that our framework improves both text--graph alignment and the accuracy of temporal dynamics represented in scene graph sequences, including object appearance, persistence, and disappearance.
A102SHORTActive Learning for Human Pose Estimation via Submodular Optimization on Latent Hyper-Ellipsoids
Kadir Rabah (AIRBUS) · Julien Aligon (Université Toulouse Capitole) · Xavier Baril (AIRBUS) · Moncef Garouani (Université Toulouse Capitole) · Olivier Teste (Université de Toulouse, UT2J)
Abstract
While deep neural networks have significantly advanced 2D Human Pose Estimation, their performance relies heavily on massive datasets with costly, dense skeletal annotations. In practical scenarios, while raw data is abundant, the high costs of manual annotation necessitate budget-constrained approaches. Active learning mitigates this annotation bottleneck, but traditional heuristics often struggle with structural overconfidence and batch redundancy when dealing with complex, articulated poses. To address this, we propose a novel, density-aware active learning framework designed to robustly explore unannotated pose distributions. By leveraging a variational auto-encoder, we map unlabeled images into a probabilistic latent space, conceptualizing instances as hyper-ellipsoids. This representation explicitly captures both local data density and epistemic uncertainty, enabling the computation of a directed Mahalanobis divergence. We then ensure diverse and highly informative batch selection by optimizing a submodular facility-location function, weighted by a "likely-miss" prediction score. Experimental results on standard Human Pose Estimation benchmarks demonstrate that our geometric approach significantly accelerates convergence, outperforming current state-of-the-art active learning methods with substantially fewer labeled samples.
A103FULLOmniHandwritingOCR: A Diagnostic Benchmark for Evaluating Multimodal LLMs in Handwritten OCR Scenarios
Zinuo Guo (East China Normal University) · Min Zhang (East China Normal University) · Bo Jiang (East China Normal University)
Abstract
Multimodal large language models (MLLMs) are increasingly used for OCR in document and knowledge-processing pipelines, yet their ability to faithfully read real handwriting remains underexplored. Existing benchmarks emphasize printed text or clean single-line inputs and provide limited coverage of multilingual handwriting, writer errors, and structurally complex mathematical expressions. We introduce OmniHandwritingOCR, a diagnostic benchmark for evaluating MLLM/OCR systems on handwritten OCR. It covers handwritten text recognition and handwritten mathematical expression recognition across six subtasks and twelve subsets, totaling 77.57K labeled images from public datasets and newly collected student writings. A difficulty-stratified multi-line formula corpus tests robustness as structural complexity increases. We evaluate thirteen open- and closed-source systems with five complementary metrics under a unified protocol. Results show that current systems remain far from faithful transcription: performance drops sharply on complex multi-line formulas, model rankings vary across language and formula settings, and several generative models hallucinate plausible but visually unsupported corrections. OmniHandwritingOCR provides a challenging testbed for diagnosing language, content, structural, and visual-grounding failures in handwritten OCR.
A104RESOURCEGeoBenchLLM: A Comprehensive Benchmark for Evaluating LLMs on Geo-Related Tasks
Rodrigo Ferreira Rodrigues (IRIT) · Karim Radouane (IRIT) · Jose G Moreno (IRIT) · Lynda Tamine (IRIT)
Abstract
In the context of geodata, existing Large Language Models have often been studied in a homogeneous setting, which has considerably limited insights into their generalization capabilities. In this paper, we present GeoBenchLLM, a comprehensive benchmark for probing LLMs on geo-related tasks. We leverage a careful selection of twelve publicly available datasets from diverse geo-related tasks and domains, and evaluate a set of LLMs on geo-spatial and temporal understanding using our benchmark. Our results show that reasoning and size have a strong impact on overall performance. GeoBenchLLM is publicly available at https://github.com/Rfr2003/GeoBenchLLM.
A105SHORTSUMO-SimQA: A Benchmark for LLM Cross-File Reasoning over Traffic Simulation Files
Jeeyun Chang (Korea Advanced Institute of Science and Technology) · Taeyoung Yun (Korea Advanced Institute of Science and Technology) · Minwoo Jeong (Korea Advanced Institute of Science and Technology) · Jinkyoo Park (Korea Advanced Institute of Science and Technology) · Yoonjin Yoon (Korea Advanced Institute of Science and Technology)
Abstract
SUMO (Simulation of Urban MObility) is a widely used open-source traffic simulator for urban mobility research, operations, and planning. While recent work has integrated SUMO with large language models (LLMs) to automate scenario generation and result interpretation, a fundamental question remains unanswered: can LLMs answer decision-relevant questions grounded in SUMO simulation files? This setting is uniquely challenging because most practitioner questions require integrating evidence across multiple files, and even a single log file can exceed the context window of current LLMs. To answer this question, we introduce SUMO-SimQA, a benchmark designed to evaluate LLM reasoning over SUMO simulation files. SUMO-SimQA comprises 480 questions that span five SUMO file types and three traffic networks, organized into three levels of reasoning complexity (retrieval, reasoning, and cross-file reasoning). We find that naive approaches fail substantially on cross-file reasoning tasks, revealing a critical gap in existing LLM-SUMO pipelines. To address this challenge, we propose Plan-Execute-Revise (PER), adapting planning and iterative revision to the large, cross-file setting of SUMO-based traffic QA. PER improves accuracy on the hardest cross-file reasoning tasks over ReAct-based approaches (56.0%?82.0%), demonstrating that structured reasoning strategies are essential for reliable performance on these tasks. Our benchmark and code are available on GitHub.
A106FULLAnchoring Bias in LLM-as-a-Judge Systems: Prior Scores Compromise Evaluation Independence
Ante Kapetanovic (Infobip) · Kemal Altwlkany (Infobip) · Andro Mercep (Infobip) · Tomislav Duricic (Infobip) · Emanuel Lacic (Infobip)
Abstract
Large language models (LLMs) increasingly assess generated content, giving rise to the LLM-as-a-Judge paradigm. These systems now score outputs, filter content, and gate iterative refinement in production pipelines, where each judgment is often assumed to be independent of earlier evaluations. We test this assumption using three prompt conditions: no metadata, revision framing, and anchored metadata containing revision, attempt, and prior-score fields. We show that prior scores, even when included only as context metadata, anchor judgments and systematically shift ratings toward their values. Across 192,000 attempted evaluations (185,271 successful) seven out of the eight evaluated models have 95% task-stratified bootstrap intervals below zero for the total anchored-metadata effect on 20 fixed texts. Cohen's d, a standardized measure of the difference between score distributions, reaches an absolute value of 0.71.
