Token-level analysis of selected model-task probes suggests a threshold-like response pattern: introducing anchored metadata produces a marked redistribution of output-score probabilities, while changing the anchor value within the tested below-threshold range produces comparatively little additional variation. On categorical industry data with human-labeled ground truth, anchored metadata blocks 48% of error corrections and flips 10.18% of correct judgments toward assigned wrong label, demonstrating the bias extends beyond numerical scoring to categorical decisions. Neither Chain-of-Thought nor a metadata-disregard warning reduces the total effect, although warning improves the paired accuracy effect relative to baseline in the industry experiment. Reliable LLM evaluation demands careful context engineering rather than passive assumption of impartiality, where effective mitigation must be validated for intended model, and specific task or domain.
A107FULLRoSafetyBench: A Culturally-Native Safety Benchmark for Romanian Language Models
Robert-Mihai Colca (West University of Timisoara)
Abstract
Romanian, like most non-English languages, has no dedicated safety benchmark for large language models—existing multilingual efforts (XSafety, M-ALERT) cover 10 and 5 languages respectively, none of them Romanian, and derive their non-English prompts by translating a source set written for other languages, which leaves culturally-specific risks like anti-Roma discrimination and Romanian profanity patterns with no source to translate from. We introduce RoSafetyBench, a Romanian-first benchmark of nearly a thousand prompts across six dimensions (toxicity, bias, hallucination, jailbreak, over-refusal, cross-lingual transfer), and evaluate 17 open-weight models (0.5B–27B) plus three frontier APIs (GPT-5.5, Claude Opus 4.7, Gemini 3.1 Pro). Methodologically we contribute a dual-judge refusal-scoring protocol pairing a primary LLM judge with a second-rater from a different vendor (? = 0.79 over 1663 responses), with bootstrap intervals on every agreement statistic. Two findings follow that the keyword protocols of prior multilingual benchmarks could not have produced: over-refusal of benign Romanian prompts spanning 0–53% and largely missed by keyword detection (? = 0.11 over all 2000 judgments); and a positive size–safety association within Gemma 3, Qwen 3, and Qwen 2.5 (with a small 14B dip), reversing an apparent inverse-scaling artefact. Independently of the scoring protocol, Romanian factual accuracy stays below 32% across the entire open-weight range. Comparing English and Romanian within prompt pairs rather than between marginal rates, the transfer gap reverses sign by category—English refuses more on harmful intent, Romanian more on bias probes—so the near-zero aggregate reported by unpaired analyses averages two opposite panel-level differences away. A scoped comparison with a 40-prompt machine-translated HarmBench control finds none of our prespecified Romanian-specific risk markers and much higher refusal than on the separate native-toxicity set; because the sets are not content-matched, this is descriptive rather than a causal translation effect. We release the benchmark, harness, all model responses, and the complete categorical judge-label table on Zenodo and Hugging Face (Section 9).
A108FULLBenchGuard: A Calibrated, Adversary-Aware Triage Layer for Reward-Hacking Agentic Trajectories
Zeming Liu (Brown University) · Hang Lyu (Brown University) · Jingtao Zhang (Georgia Institute of Technology) · Yuan Xie (Independent Researcher) · Qibai Chen (Independent Researcher)
Abstract
Agentic AI systems are increasingly evaluated on executable benchmarks, and a now well-documented failure mode is reward hacking: agents inspect graders, spoof expected outputs, hijack binaries, or extract hidden test inputs. The dominant operational response is to monitor every trajectory with a strong LLM judge, but at $0.4–$3.8 per 100 trajectories and several minutes of latency, judge-everywhere is impractical for the millions of runs produced by continuous benchmark development. We present BenchGuard, a strict command-only forensic triage layer: TF-IDF word n-grams over agent shell commands feed a class-balanced LinearSVC that is recalibrated with Platt scaling and reports prevalence-aware operating points. On Terminal Wrench's 5,984 paired trajectories, BenchGuard reaches ROC-AUC 0.928 [task-grouped bootstrap 95% CI 0.918, 0.939] at 50% prefix and TPR 0.70 at 5% FPR. We then run a head-to-head LLM judge experiment on the same balanced 100-trajectory sample under three configurations: command-only (judge AUC 0.806), full-context with a generic prompt (0.727, DeLong p=0.012 vs. BenchGuard), and full-context with a rubric-tuned prompt (0.837, p=0.237). BenchGuard is point-estimate-best across all three at $0 vs. $0.77–$1.50 per 100 trajectories. Two cheap baselines (BM25 max-similarity AUC 0.451, a distilled hashed-n-gram MLP AUC 0.931) bracket the result: pure lexical similarity is insufficient, but capacity at this scale is also not the bottleneck. Three static lexicon-evasion attacks plus an LLM-paraphrase adversary that drops token-Jaccard to 0.42 cost only 0.013–0.030 AUC (-9 pp at TPR@5%FPR for the paraphrase); adversary-aware retraining recovers the static gap. Platt-recalibrated flag rates on a 34,029-trajectory external corpus drop from 13.3% (raw) to 0.4% (Platt p >= 0.99), demonstrating calibration transfer. We document a sharp construct-validity boundary: against the realistic union-negative class (legitimate solves + no-reward attacks), AUC drops to 0.700 and operating-point precision collapses — and we translate this into a three-step deployment recommendation. All code, data extracts, judge response logs (scores and verdicts), the LLM paraphrase outputs, and calibration models are released as a reproducible artifact.
A109FULLTRACE: Graph-Aware Anomaly Detection for Trust Routing in Adversarial Decentralized Marketplaces
Nikunj Kaushik (Maharaja Agrasen Institute of Technology) · Siddhanth Gupta (Akhilesh Das Gupta Institute of Professional Studies) · Sarthak Vashisht (Vellore Institute of Technology) · Ruchi Bhatt (IGDTUW)
Abstract
Decentralized agent marketplaces route paid work to pseudonymous providers, and any trust mechanism for doing so has to balance three pressures: bound fraud exposure, stay open to newcomers, and survive coordinated graph manipulation. We introduce TRACE (Trust Routing with Adversarial Coordination Evidence), a routing policy that scores providers using uncertainty-aware evidence weighting and structural coordination detection rather than propagating trust through the graph. We compare TRACE against three baselines, reputation-only, price-only, and EigenTrust, across four attack regimes at N=1,000 agents with 30% adversaries and ten seeds per cell. Two results drive our findings. Trust propagation amplifies coordinated attacks: EigenTrust routes 81.7% of jobs to malicious agents under Sybil attack, while reputation-only contains the same attack to 29.0%. Exploration is also costly under score-based adversaries: disabling Thompson sampling in TRACE lowers mean fraud from 10.7, 46.5, 19.0, and 83.7 sats to 4.7, 6.4, 7.1, and 31.7 sats on strategic-default, collusion-ring, sybil-cluster, and game-theoretic-adversary, respectively. This greedy variant has the lowest fraud on the first three attacks; EigenTrust attains lower game-theoretic fraud (4.4 sats) but only by routing 41.2% of jobs to malicious agents. A scale run at N=5,000 (five seeds per baseline policy, ten for TRACE-no-bandit) confirms EigenTrust's pathology persists, and the same propagating-versus-non-propagating ordering replicates on two real-world signed-trust graphs (Bitcoin Over-The-Counter, Bitcoin Alpha). Together, these findings caution against trust propagation in adversarial settings and motivate risk-conditioned exploration as a principled extension.
A110FULLBackdoor Poisoning Mitigation for Federated LoRA via Structural Adaptive Control
Wenhan Hu (Jilin University) · Zhe Wang (Jilin University) · Gang Yan (Jilin University)
Abstract
Large pre-trained models are increasingly adapted on user devices, but direct fine-tuning in federated settings is constrained by computation, memory, and communication limits. These constraints have motivated the use of parameter-efficient fine-tuning methods, among which LoRA is widely adopted by concentrating adaptation in low-rank parameters. While this design improves efficiency, it also changes the security setting. In federated LoRA, backdoor behavior can exploit the low-rank adaptation structure and persist across communication rounds, making defenses designed for full-model updates less reliable. To address this gap, we propose StrAP, a server-side defense tailored to federated LoRA fine-tuning. StrAP combines reliability control before aggregation with structure-aware regulation after aggregation. Before aggregation, client updates are softly weighted based on their alignment with a clean validation gradient and tracked across rounds using a stateful trust mechanism, which suppresses persistent anomalies while allowing benign recovery. After aggregation, StrAP analyzes the LoRA parameter structure to identify suspicious rank channels using robust cross-client statistics and applies utility-calibrated structural actions guided by clean validation loss. Extensive experiments show that StrAP consistently reduces backdoor attack success rates with minimal impact on clean accuracy. Our code is available at https://github.com/HwhCN-ui/StrAP.
A111FULLCross-Architecture Semantic Backdoor Attack in Data-Driven Federated Learning
Wei Hou (Nanjing University of Posts and Telecommunications) · Yun Li (Nanjing University of Posts and Telecommunications) · Ziye Zhu (Nanjing University of Posts and Telecommunications) · Wenqiong Zhang (Nanjing University of Posts and Telecommunications)
Abstract
Traditional Federated Learning (FL) relies on iterative parameter exchange, which limits architectural flexibility and introduces high communication overhead for large foundation models. To address these issues, Data-Driven Federated Learning (DD-FL) has recently emerged as a scalable alternative. Instead of exchanging model parameters, DD-FL adopts a one-shot data-centric pipeline, where heterogeneous clients collaboratively annotate a shared unlabeled public dataset and the server performs knowledge distillation through soft-label aggregation. While DD-FL improves scalability and supports heterogeneous architectures, it also introduces a new attack surface on the shared public dataset. These public datasets are often collected from web crawlers or collaborative platforms with limited integrity validation, making data poisoning feasible. Moreover, since DD-FL removes parameter-level interactions and relies on soft-label aggregation across heterogeneous models, traditional FL backdoor attacks designed for individual models are easily diluted and exhibit poor cross-architecture transferability. In this paper, we propose a semantic backdoor attack for DD-FL. Our method generates poisoned samples by aligning image perturbations with target semantic directions in a shared vision-language space. This enables poisoned samples to induce semantically aligned target predictions across heterogeneous client models, making the backdoor more transferable during soft-label aggregation. We also study how biased aggregation weights further strengthen the attack effect. Experiments on CIFAR-10, CIFAR-100, and TinyImageNet show that our method achieves higher attack success rates and robustness than existing baselines, while maintaining high clean accuracy and strong visual stealthiness.
A112FULLDuetDP-DD: Size-Adaptive Differentially Private Dataset Distillation for Heterogeneous Users
Yukun Yan (Harbin Engineering University) · Peng Tang (Shandong University) · Rui Chen (Harbin Engineering University) · Yanru Sun (Tianjin University) · Cheng Yu (Harbin Engineering University) · Qilong Han (Harbin Engineering University) · Jie Zhang (Centre for Frontier AI Research (CFAR), Agency for Science, Technology and Research (A*STAR)) · Jing Li (Centre for Frontier AI Research (CFAR), Agency for Science, Technology and Research (A*STAR))
Abstract
Differentially private dataset distillation (DP-DD) enables privacy-preserving data sharing by releasing compact synthetic datasets with formal privacy guarantees. However, existing DP-DD methods typically optimize for a fixed images-per-class (IPC) setting, making them ill-suited to heterogeneous users who require distilled datasets with different IPC sizes. Straightforward extensions to support multiple IPC requirements either incur cumulative privacy costs across separate DP-DD runs or sacrifice adaptability by relying on a predefined maximum IPC size. To address this issue, we introduce Size-Adaptive DP-DD, a strategy that decouples private data access from the construction of IPC-specific distilled datasets under a single privacy budget. Building on this strategy, we propose DuetDP-DD, which constructs a reusable DP-synthetic candidate space and derives IPC-specific distilled datasets through tailored post-processing. DuetDP-DD employs a dual-classifier guidance scheme: the Semantic-Anchor Classifier identifies semantically central candidates within each class, while the DP-Classifier provides discriminative guidance, with its feature space supporting diversity-aware selection, thereby preserving class representativeness, inter-class discriminability, and intra-class coverage of distilled datasets across IPC settings. This design allows DuetDP-DD to serve emerging IPC requests with utility-preserving distilled datasets without additional private optimization. Extensive comparative experiments demonstrate that DuetDP-DD achieves competitive utility across IPC settings without incurring the repeated privacy cost of separate fixed-size DP-DD runs. Additional analyses confirm the effectiveness, flexibility, and cross-architecture generalization of DuetDP-DD, underscoring its applicability to privacy-preserving distilled dataset sharing for heterogeneous users.
A113FULLGraphMemShield: Auditing Cross-Session Leakage in Graph Memories
Phat T. Tran-Truong (Ho Chi Minh City University of Technology (HCMUT), Vietnam National University Ho Chi Minh City) · Xuan-Bach Le (Ho Chi Minh City University of Technology (HCMUT), Vietnam National University Ho Chi Minh City) · Son Ha (RMIT University)
Abstract
Graph-backed assistants increasingly write user utterances into a provenance-tagged knowledge-graph memory and later retrieve k-hop neighborhoods to ground responses. Because the retrieval surface is multi-user and append-only, an edge written by one session can enter the context of another. This boundary is neither model memorization nor document-RAG leakage; it is a retrieval-control problem that existing benchmarks do not isolate. We introduce GraphMemShield, a benchmark and audit suite for cross-session leakage in dynamic KG memories, packaging a JSONL trace schema, gray- and black-box leakage probes, a response-leakage scorer, and four policy baselines: global retrieval, owner-only isolation, label filtering, and bounded provenance-aware sharing. Two structural results frame the suite. First, we prove that any policy with cross-session QA accuracy a must expose at least ⌈ a Ncs/ρ⌉ victim-owned determining edges; a retrieval-time budget guard attains this bound to within 1.06× on a structured workload (the enterprise bank). Second, we apply the standard private-selection lower bound to show that post-retrieval answer-level ε-DP cannot match the deterministic guard's utility in the small-margin regime our graph-memory workloads exhibit empirically: our DP-GraphQA mechanism lands at 0.15–0.18 accuracy at usable ε on these workloads because measured margins are only 0.54–1.24. The operational rule is therefore to bound exposure before unsafe cross-session edges enter the context, and add post-retrieval DP only when the application can pay the margin cost.
A114FULLGhostEdges: Measuring Neighborhood Leakage After Deletion in Retrained GNNs
Muhammad Usman (University of Missouri-Kansas City) · Yugyung Lee (University of Missouri-Kansas City)
Abstract
The machine unlearning literature treats retraining a GNN from scratch as the gold standard for deletion privacy, yet this assumption has never been empirically tested. If even full retraining fails to prevent attackers from recovering deleted neighborhood information, then the entire framework of approximate unlearning methods built on this premise would be undermined. We formalize this question as Model-level Deleted Neighborhood Inference (M-DNI) and conduct the first systematic measurement across five attack strategies, six GNN architectures, and two signed trust networks. A key methodological challenge is that heavy-tailed degree distributions dominate the signal: simply guessing that a deleted user was connected to high-degree nodes achieves AUC 0.83, making raw attack accuracy meaningless. We therefore introduce degree-calibrated ΔAUC, defined as attack AUC minus the degree-prior baseline, as the primary metric. The strongest attack achieves raw AUC 0.761 but ΔAUC = -0.070 (p<0.0001), performing worse than naive degree guessing. Every attack and architecture yields ΔAUC ≤ 0, and after accounting for degree, the residual deletion-specific signal collapses to AUC 0.44, indistinguishable from random. Even an MLP with no access to graph structure matches the degree prior, confirming that the observable signal originates from degree features in the input, not from the GNN having memorized neighborhood structure. On the networks tested, these findings support the retraining assumption and suggest that efficient approximate unlearning methods may be sufficient for deletion privacy in GNN-based trust systems, since even the gold standard does not create exploitable neighborhood leakage.
A115FULLFUCH: Non-IID Federated Unlearning via Classification-layer Hybrid-order Constraints
Tengyuan He (School of Information Science and Technology, Yunnan Normal University) · Yunfei Zi (School of Information Science and Technology, Yunnan Normal University) · Yuelong Xia (School of Information Science and Technology, Yunnan Normal University) · Lin Liu (School of Information Science and Technology, Yunnan Normal University) · Shaojie Qiao (School of Software Engineering, Chengdu University of Information Technology) · Mingjing Tang (School of Information Science and Technology, Yunnan Normal University)
Abstract
Federated unlearning (FU) aims to support the “right to be forgotten” by reducing the influence of target samples without full retraining. However, when applied to deep neural networks (DNNs) in practical non-IID scenarios, existing FU methods suffer from low unlearning efficiency and deviate from the retraining reference's predictive behavior. Specifically, they require costly full-model updates or multi-round communication, failing to disentangle the complex coupling of target-sample influence and retained knowledge. In this work, we revisit the necessity of full-model updates for sample-level FU and investigate the formation of this complex coupling. We reveal key empirical insights: (1) updating solely the final classification layer can effectively approximate the predictive behavior of full retraining; and (2) disentangling target-sample influence under non-IID settings requires separately resolving distinct intra-client and cross-client knowledge couplings. Based on these insights, we propose FUCH, a classification-layer-based hybrid-order-constrained FU framework. To improve unlearning efficiency, FUCH freezes the feature extractor and performs a single-round update on the final classification layer. Furthermore, to disentangle the complex knowledge coupling, FUCH employs a coupling-aware hybrid-order mechanism combining local second-order and global first-order information to constrain the unlearning updates. Extensive experiments across diverse non-IID benchmarks validate our empirical insights and demonstrate that FUCH achieves efficient unlearning while significantly outperforming SOTA baselines in closely approximating the retraining reference's predictive behavior.
A116SHORTStitch the Fragments: One-Shot Hierarchical Federated Clustering
Shenghong Cai (Guangdong University of Technology) · Zihua Yang (Guangdong University of Technology) · Yuzhu Ji (Guangdong University of Technology) · Yiqun Zhang (Guangdong University of Technology) · Mengke Li (Shenzhen University) · Yang Lu (Xiamen University) · Yiu-Ming Cheung (Hong Kong Baptist University)
Abstract
Federated Clustering (FC) faces a critical bottleneck in real-world scenarios, i.e., global clusters are rarely intact, often fragmenting into incomplete, multi-granular unlabeled “clusterlets” distributed across Non-IID clients. Although hierarchical clustering is theoretically well-suited to model such nested distributions, its recursive nature strictly relies on multi-round communication, introducing prohibitive computational overhead and severe privacy vulnerabilities. This paper, therefore, proposes a novel one-shot hierarchical federated clustering framework designed to seamlessly “stitch” the fragmented local clusterlets into a holistic global distribution. Our approach enables clients to perform autonomous fine-grained distribution exploration, uploading prototype-level knowledge via a dynamic parameter-interleaving mechanism to scramble transmission trajectories, which effectively prevents the server from tracing individual client data distributions. Subsequently, a multi-granular learning mechanism at the server fuses these granularly inconsistent local clusterlets, reconstructing a coherent global hierarchy for ultimate clustering. Extensive experiments on real benchmark datasets illustrate the superiority of the proposed approach, which effectively bridges the granularity gap among heterogeneous clients while minimizing privacy exposure risks via anonymized informative one-shot communication.
A117FULLFDA-Opt: Federated Fine-Tuning via Dynamic Update Schedules
Michael Theologitis (University of Washington) · Vasilis Samoladas (Technical University of Crete) · Antonios Deligiannakis (Technical University of Crete)
Abstract
Federated Learning (FL) enables the utilization of vast, previously inaccessible data sources. At the same time, pre-trained Language Models (LMs) have taken the world by storm and for good reason. They exhibit remarkable emergent abilities and are readily adapted to downstream tasks. This opens one of the most exciting frontiers in FL: fine-tuning LMs. Yet, a persistent challenge in FL is the frequent, rigid communication of parameters—a problem magnified by the sheer size of these contemporary models. The FedOpt family of algorithms has become the go-to approach for FL, relying on fixed but arbitrary intervals for model exchanges. Recently, the FDA algorithm prescribed a dynamic approach by monitoring the training progress. However, it introduced a hard-to-calibrate parameter and imposed a rigid synchronization scheme. In this work, we address these limitations by proposing the FDA-Opt family of algorithms—a unified generalization of both FDA and FedOpt. Our experimental evaluation focuses on fine-tuning LMs on downstream NLP tasks and demonstrates that FDA-Opt outperforms FedOpt even when it is configured with hyper-parameters specifically optimized for the latter. In other words, we show that FDA-Opt is a practical, drop-in replacement for FedOpt in modern FL libraries and systems: it requires no additional configuration and delivers superior performance out of the box.
A118FULLWhen Is Shallow Enough? Adaptive Split Federated Learning with Client-Specific Sufficiency Estimation
Wenhao Yuan (The University of Hong Kong) · Chenchen Lin (Sun Yat-sen University) · Wentao Hu (The Hong Kong Polytechnic University) · Jian Chen (The University of Hong Kong) · Jinfeng Xu (The University of Hong Kong) · Shujie Li (The University of Hong Kong) · Edith Cheuk Han Ngai (The University of Hong Kong)
Abstract
Split Federated Learning (SFL) enables distributed model training by splitting networks between the server and clients. However, under client heterogeneity, the conventional static split strategy may be suboptimal because clients can differ in data distributions, adaptation dynamics, and representation learning progress, making a single split point insufficient to accommodate client-specific training states. In this paper, we propose FedSGA, a Sufficiency-Guided Adaptive split Federated learning framework that addresses this question through client-specific shallow sufficiency estimation. First, we introduce a client-specific adaptation channel based on private prompt tokens, which tracks local adaptation dynamics separately from the shared backbone and provides a lightweight signal for detecting whether client adaptation remains active. To further avoid repeated online probing over multiple candidate depths, we design a shallow sufficiency estimator that combines cross-client semantic alignment, temporal interface stability, and prompt-state variation to estimate whether the shallowest split is already sufficient. Finally, we introduce a split-compatible interface harmonization module that projects activations from different split depths into a shared semantic space, improving the comparability of heterogeneous client interfaces before server-side prediction. Extensive experiments on multiple heterogeneous benchmarks demonstrate the effectiveness of FedSGA in improving model performance compared with state-of-the-art methods while reducing unnecessary client-side computation.
A119FULLFederated Personalization of Early-Exit Networks
Boyi Liu (City University of Hong Kong Shenzhen Research Institute) · Zimu Zhou (City University of Hong Kong Shenzhen Research Institute) · Cheng Fang (City University of Hong Kong) · Yongxin Tong (Beihang University)
Abstract
Personalized Federated Learning (PFL) excels at tailoring clientspecific models, which is particularly critical for decentralized and heterogeneous data environments, yet existing methods produce static models with a fixed tradeoff between accuracy and efficiency. This inherent static nature limits their ability to adapt to inference demands that vary with context and resource availability, posing a challenge for real-world deployment. Early-exit networks (EENs), which enable adaptive inference via intermediate classifiers, offer a promising solution. However, integrating EENs into PFL introduces two intertwined conflicts: client-wise heterogeneity across clients and depth-wise interference arising from conflicting exit objectives. Prior studies fail to resolve both conflicts simultaneously, leading to suboptimal performance. In this paper, we propose X-FED, a novel Conflict-Aware Cross-Client Federated Exit Distillation framework that jointly addresses both client- and depth-wise conflicts while extending PFL to early-exit networks. At its core, X-FED employs a progressive, depth-prioritized student coordination mechanism that mitigates interference among shallow and deep exits while enabling effective personalized knowledge transfer across clients. Furthermore, we introduce a client-decoupled formulation that reduces communication overhead with theoretical soundness. Extensive evaluations on various datasets show that compared to state-of-the-art PFL and PFL-EE methods, X-FED achieves higher accuracy while reducing inference costs by 30.79%–46.86%.
A120FULLDualFed-RCGC: Dual-Track Personalized Federated Learning via Covariance-Transferred Rare-Class Geometric Completion
Qianxin Li (Sun Yat-Sen University) · Siyang Guo (Sun Yat-Sen University) · Junbo Wang (Sun Yat-Sen University)
Abstract
Personalized federated learning under extreme data heterogeneity suffers from two coupled structural issues: local majority-class gradients contaminate the globally shared representation, while rare classes lack sufficient local support, making reliable local discrimination difficult. To address these issues, we propose DualFed-RCGC, a dual-track personalized federated learning framework. First, it employs a Y-shaped architecture with explicit gradient-path isolation, decoupling global representation learning from local adaptation to mitigate majority-dominated gradients from biasing the shared backbone. Second, to improve discrimination for underrepresented classes, we introduce a Covariance-Transferred Rare-Class Geometric Completion (RCGC) module. It calibrates local decision boundaries by synthesizing geometry-aware virtual features using fixed Equiangular Tight Frame (ETF) anchors and covariance structures transferred from local majority classes. Finally, a class-aware masked distillation strategy selectively injects global knowledge to further improve rare-class discrimination. Extensive experiments on CIFAR-10, CIFAR-100, and Tiny-ImageNet demonstrate that DualFed-RCGC consistently improves personalized local accuracy while retaining a usable shared branch for federated aggregation.
A121SHORTBeyond Naive Disparity: A Size-Matched Audit of Demographic Effects in User-Agnostic Ranking
Guilherme Ramos (Instituto Superior Técnico, Universidade de Lisboa) · Ludovico Boratto (University of Cagliari) · Mirko Marras (University of Cagliari)
Abstract
User-agnostic ranking systems aggregate ratings into a single shared item ranking without consulting user attributes, motivated by privacy, manipulation resistance, and regulatory frameworks such as the EU AI Act. Prior work has reported demographic disparities in such systems using metrics that do not separate a genuine group effect from the sampling variance that small subpopulations inevitably exhibit. We propose a reusable audit combining a faithful implementation of rating-preservation disparity, a size-matched random-group null, and a stratified resampling robustness check. Applied to the UARS filter on MovieLens-100k, MovieLens-1M, and BookCrossing, the audit shows that absolute disparities are small (around 0.01 to 0.05), that ML-100k disparities largely vanish once group size is controlled, and that on the larger datasets only the youngest age groups exhibit disparity beyond what size alone produces.
A122SHORTFAIR-PIVOT: Fairness-oriented Perspective-Inversion via Viewpoint-balanced Outline-then-generaTion for Mitigating Political Bias in Web Corpora
Haneul Kim (Seoul National University of Science and Technology) · Jaebeom You (Seoul National University of Science and Technology) · Jaewon Lee (Kookmin University) · Kisung Lee (Louisiana State University) · Hyuk-Yoon Kwon (Seoul National University of Science and Technology)
Abstract
Large-scale web corpora (e.g., C4) are severely imbalanced in terms of political perspective: on the death penalty issue, e.g., left-leaning documents outnumber right-leaning ones by more than 8-fold. Such imbalances can transfer to downstream large language models, reinforcing political bias. We propose Fairness-oriented Perspective-Inversion via Viewpoint-balanced Outline-then-generaTion (simply, FAIR-PIVOT), a retrieval-augmented generation (RAG)-based two-level-agent framework that builds balanced perspective-inverted synthetic data for politically sensitive topics. After annotating web texts with multi-persona LLMs, FAIR-PIVOT retrieves documents from contrasting orientations and inverts their viewpoint, preserving authentic discourse structure rather than rephrasing the same-view text. Across nine topics, FAIR-PIVOT generates 13,954 instances and reduces the total variation distance, a measure of how far the orientation distribution deviates from uniform balance, by up to 83%, while improving linguistic fluency as measured by Perplexity (25.5→21.8). Fine-tuning small language models on the balanced corpus further shifts their downstream behavior toward the intended orientation (Gemma (L−R)% +48→+34, Qwen +55→+50), confirming that data-level balancing can yield fairer model responses. Code and scripts are available at https://github.com/bigbases/FAIR-PIVOT.
A123FULLFeature Evolution and Migration during Vision Transformer Training
Joonas Järve (University of Tartu) · Halil Ibrahim Aysel (University of Tartu) · Tarun Khajuria (University of Tartu) · Meelis Kull (University of Tartu)
Abstract
We present a novel view on feature evolution in Vision Transformers (ViTs) by visualizing the training process over two dimensions – network depth (layer) and training time (epochs). We employ Sparse Autoencoders (SAEs) to extract candidate sparse features from CLS-token representations and compare their activation profiles across epoch–layer pairs. This allows us to study feature-level dynamics that are not directly visible from representation-level similarity measures. Furthermore, we demonstrate how this framework of feature evolution allows us to describe feature migration, the change in the layer where a feature is most detectable during training. Our experiments show that migration is concentrated early in training, occurs more often toward earlier layers than toward deeper layers, and declines as feature organization stabilizes. We further find that deeper layers stabilize earlier and more strongly than shallow layers. The results show that our approach can be employed as a tool for understanding how ViTs learn and evolve.
A124FULLGroupSegment-SHAP: Shapley Value Explanations with Group-Segment Players for Multivariate Time Series
Jinwoong Kim (Hanyang University) · Sangjin Park (Hanyang University)
Abstract
Multivariate time-series models achieve strong predictive performance in healthcare, industry, energy, and finance, but how they combine cross-variable interactions with temporal dynamics remains unclear. SHapley Additive exPlanations (SHAP) has been widely used for interpretation. However, existing time-series variants typically treat the feature and time axes independently, fragmenting structural signals formed jointly by multiple variables over specific intervals. We propose GroupSegment-SHAP (GS-SHAP), which constructs explanatory units as group-segment players based on cross-variable dependence and distribution shifts over time, and then quantifies each unit's contribution via Shapley attribution. We evaluated GS-SHAP across four real-world domains: human activity recognition, power-system forecasting, medical signal analysis, and financial time series, and compared it with KernelSHAP, TimeSHAP, SequenceSHAP, WindowSHAP, and TSHAP. GS-SHAP consistently achieves the highest deletion-based faithfulness (ΔAUC) across all four benchmark datasets. In synthetic evaluations with controlled ground-truth structures, GS-SHAP achieves 24.4% higher IoU-based recovery of multivariate-temporal patterns than the strongest baseline. In addition, GS-SHAP runs on average 3.38x faster than TimeSHAP across approximation budgets in power-system forecasting, showing that it can simultaneously achieve high explanatory faithfulness and computational efficiency. In a financial case study, GS-SHAP identifies interpretable multivariate-temporal interactions among key market variables across market regimes, highlighting its potential utility for risk-aware investment analysis. Code is available at https://github.com/jirungx/GroupSegment-SHAP.
A125RESOURCESWXAI: A Unified Multimodal Explainability Library for Space Weather Forecasting and Heliophysics
Benedict Antonio Mervyn (Georgia State University) · Anli Ji (California State University, Fullerton) · Manolis K. Georgoulis (Johns Hopkins University Applied Physics Laboratory) · Berkay Aydin (Georgia State University)
Abstract
Space weather forecasting and heliophysics increasingly rely on machine learning models that process heterogeneous inputs such as multi-viewpoint multi-wavelength solar images and rasters, multivariate time series, spatial annotations, and tabular event-level data. However, explainability workflows remain fragmented across libraries, model interfaces, and output formats, limiting reuse and reproducibility. We present SWXAI, an open-source library that unifies explainable AI (XAI) workflows for image, time-series, and tabular data in space weather forecasting and heliophysics. SWXAI provides a common, extensible interface across commonly used vision, time-series, and tabular learning models, with validation, adaptation, and persistent explanation objects. It also includes domain-grounded examples, reproducible notebooks, tests, and documentation, enabling users to inspect outputs, swap models or explainers, and extend workflows to new heliophysics datasets. SWXAI reduces modality-specific engineering overhead and supports comparable, reusable explanations across heterogeneous scientific machine learning pipelines. A benchmark against direct backend implementations shows that SWXAI substantially reduces the code users write to produce an explanation, with no practical runtime cost.
A126RESOURCECFX-Bench: A Benchmark for Counterfactual Explanations
Riccardo Benassi (University of Modena and Reggio Emilia) · Federico Gualandri (University of Modena and Reggio Emilia) · Matteo Paganelli (University of Modena and Reggio Emilia) · Gennaro Aloe (CRIF S.p.A.) · Enrico Bagli (CRIF S.p.A.) · Mario Calò Carducci (CRIF S.p.A.) · Maurizio Vincini (University of Modena and Reggio Emilia) · Francesco Guerra (University of Modena and Reggio Emilia)
Abstract
Counterfactual explanations support model interpretability by identifying actionable recourse strategies, yet their evaluation remains fragmented across metrics, baselines, and experimental protocols. This paper introduces CFX-Bench, a unified benchmarking suite for comparing counterfactual explanations for tabular classification across datasets, models, and explainers. The framework integrates quantitative and qualitative metrics, local and global explanation methods, and LLM-based components for verbalization and human-centered assessment. By combining standardized benchmarking with semantic evaluation, CFX-Bench provides a reproducible environment for analyzing the quality, reliability, and coherence of counterfactual explanations, while supporting the development of new explanation methods.
A127SHORTStability Analysis of Signed Graphs under Structural Perturbations
Ning Zhang (University of Oxford) · Li Zhang (University College London)
Abstract
Signed graph learning has emerged as a powerful framework for modeling networks with both positive and negative interactions. While graph-filter-based methods have achieved promising empirical performance on signed networks, their stability to edge perturbations remains poorly understood. Existing stability analyses primarily focus on unsigned graphs and do not account for sign-flip perturbations. In this paper, we study the stability of signed graph filters under edge additions, deletions, and sign flips. Our theoretical analysis reveals how signed edge perturbations and node feature correlations jointly determine the learned representation stability. Based on this analysis, we propose a theory-guided perturbation strategy that selects structurally influential signed-edge modifications. Experiments on synthetic and real signed graphs show that the proposed method consistently induces larger embedding drift, polarity change, and downstream link prediction degradation than baselines. These results highlight the importance of sign-aware and distribution-aware stability analysis for signed graph learning.
A128FULLCurvature-Regularized Graph Autoencoders with Rewiring for Node-Level Graph Anomaly Detection
Yuejian Lan (Huazhong University of Science and Technology) · Dongmian Zou (Duke Kunshan University) · Hongfei Wang (Huazhong University of Science and Technology)
Abstract
Graph anomaly detection aims to identify nodes whose structural or relational patterns deviate from the norm. While autoencoder-based methods are widely used, reconstruction error on adjacency and node features may become unreliable if the graph exhibits large geometric curvature. In this work, we propose a curvature-regularized, plug-and-play enhancement to graph autoencoders for node-level anomaly detection. Our key idea is to encourage a near-flat latent geometry for normal regions by incorporating a curvature reconstruction penalty into the training objective. Furthermore, we present a novel curvature-based positional encoding mechanism for Graph Transformers, which encodes local topological information directly into the attention layers as node-wise geometric priors. We also introduce a curvature-guided rewiring step as preprocessing, which improves geometric consistency and enables reliable curvature regularization. Anomalous nodes are then identified through their curvature deviations, together with standard reconstruction signals. Extensive experiments demonstrate consistent performance improvements over strong baselines. In particular, applying our geometry-aware preprocessing and curvature penalty directly to the classical DOMINANT model already yields state-of-the-art results. Our code is available at https://github.com/TechnologyAiGroup/crgad.
A129FULLTowards Decoupled Contrastive Learning with Neighborhood Enhancement for Graph Anomaly Detection
Mark Junjie Li (Shenzhen University) · Jinren Li (Shenzhen University) · Sunjie Huang (Shenzhen Academy of Inspection and Quarantine) · Min Zi (Shenzhen University) · Philippe Fournier-Viger (Shenzhen University) · Shiyang He (Shenzhen University) · Yunzuo Chen (MEGATECH GROUP LIMITED) · Jun Li (Shenzhen Academy of Inspection and Quarantine)
Abstract
Unsupervised graph anomaly detection (UGAD) is crucial to identify anomalous behavior in graph-structured data. Most existing methods rely on contrastive learning, typically adopting node-subgraph and node-node contrastive paradigms. However, anomalous nodes can interfere with local neighborhood modeling, compromising node-subgraph contrast. Moreover, the training of these two paradigms is often coupled, which limits their ability to fully capture node-level anomaly cues. To address these limitations, we propose DeSEN, a novel two-stage UGAD learning framework that decouples the two contrastive learning paradigms. In Stage 1, we introduce a structural-semantic neighborhood enhancement strategy based on biased views to suppress anomalous interference during neighborhood modeling. In Stage 2, we leverage the confident node sets constructed by affinity ranking in Stage 1 to guide node-node contrast, thereby providing effective global node-level anomaly signals. Extensive experiments on eight real-world benchmark datasets, including a large-scale Open Graph Benchmark (OGB) dataset, against ten state-of-the-art baselines show that DeSEN significantly improves both AUROC and AUPRC, while the training and inference pipeline completes within a few minutes. These results validate the effectiveness and efficiency of DeSEN.
A130FULLRoleMine: Mining Behavioral Patterns in Heterogeneous Call Graphs
Koki Kawabata (SANKEN, The University of Osaka) · Pedro Fidalgo (ISCTE-IUL, Mobileum) · Mirela Teixeira Cazzolato (University of São Paulo) · Saranya Vijayakumar (Carnegie Mellon University) · Yasuko Matsubara (SANKEN, The University of Osaka) · Yasushi Sakurai (SANKEN, The University of Osaka) · Christos Faloutsos (Carnegie Mellon University)
Abstract
Large event graphs often contain rich edge attributes that describe how interactions occur. In call graphs, such attributes include response codes, durations, delays, and inter-arrival times, which are crucial for detecting suspicious entities. However, node-level anomaly detection remains challenging because anomaly labels are rarely available, normal behavior is highly heterogeneous, and operators require interpretable evidence. </par> <par>In this paper, we propose <sc>RoleMine,</sc> an unsupervised probabilistic framework for node-level anomaly detection in heterogeneous attributed call graphs. <sc>RoleMine</sc> has three key properties. (a) Accurate: it models role-dependent predictive distributions over heterogeneous edge attributes without anomaly labels. (b) Scalable: it uses observed-edge inference with linear training cost in the number of observed edges. (c) Explainable: it represents nodes by behavioral roles and explains anomalies through communication contexts and attribute-level deviations. </par> <par>Experiments on large real-world daily call graphs show that <sc>RoleMine</sc> achieves pAUC above 0.995, improves average precision by up to 2.8× over the strongest baseline, and scales linearly, easily handling 34.3M edges in our experiments.
A131FULLTASD: Temporal Adaptive Semantic Decomposition for Task-only Blockchain Graph Fraud Detection
Jianrong Wang (Tianjin University) · Wei Yao (Tianjin University) · Dengcheng Hu (Tianjin University) · Qi Li (Tianjin University) · Ju Zhang (Tianjin University of Technology)
Abstract
Blockchain fraud detection plays a critical role in online risk-control services. Constructing temporal blockchain graphs captures evolving interactions, entity behaviors, and risk propagation under causal deployment constraints. However, task-only snapshots make history-dependent temporal graph methods difficult to apply, especially when sparse fraud labels require stable fraud-discriminative semantics across evolving patterns. To fill this gap, we propose TASD, a Temporal Adaptive Semantic Decomposition framework for task-only temporal graph learning in blockchain fraud detection. In particular, TASD introduces four designs: 1) normal and abnormal semantic decomposition with alpha-guided routing for risk-aware aggregation; 2) subspace-stratified Fisher constraints to stabilize semantic parameters across time-ordered snapshots; 3) compact Gaussian prototypes to preserve historical normal and abnormal semantic distributions without historical graph replay; and 4) confidence-guided semantic distillation from the previous snapshot model to transfer reliable temporal semantic knowledge. Experimental results on Elliptic and Elliptic++ Actor demonstrate that TASD improves AUC-ROC by 3.30% and MacroF1 by 1.20% on actor/address-level risk recognition, and improves MacroF1 by 2.56% on transaction-level risk recognition when compared to state-of-the-art methods, demonstrating its effectiveness for task-only temporal blockchain fraud detection.
A132SHORTType-aware Prompting for Community Search over Heterogeneous Information Networks
Rener Zhang (Beijing Institute of Technology) · Shuheng Fang (Shenzhen Institute of Computing Sciences) · Yu Rong (The Chinese University of Hong Kong) · Kangfei Zhao (Beijing Institute of Technology)
Abstract
Community search over heterogeneous information networks (HINs) aims to identify a cohesive community of nodes sharing the same type as a given query node. Existing methods either rely on manually designed structural constraints that generalize poorly to unseen communities with diverse characteristics,or depend on query-specific supervision that is prone to overfitting under limited labels. In this paper, we study community search over HINs in an inductive learning setting, where test communities are disjoint from training ones and only a few labeled vertices are available per query. We propose HINT-CS, a type-aware prompt learning framework for community search over HINs. HINT-CS augments the original HIN with shared learnable virtual nodes: a primary virtual node that provides an explicit structural anchor to the query node and auxiliary virtual nodes that aggregate type-aware local context from heterogeneous neighbors. These prompts are inserted in a query-dependent manner and encoded by a Heterogeneous Graph Transformer (HGT), enabling the model to capture transferable community patterns. We further employ an alternating training strategy to jointly optimize the prompt nodes and the HGT encoder under limited supervision. Experiments on four real-world HIN datasets demonstrate that HINT-CS consistently outperforms five representative baselines, improving the average F1 score by 9.09% over the best baseline.
A133FULLCondensed Multi-Level Bisimulation Summaries
Ruud van Bakel (Vrije Universiteit Amsterdam) · Till Blume (Ernst & Young GmbH WPG – R&D) · Michael Cochez (ELLIS Institute Finland) · David Richerby (University of Essex) · Ansgar Scherp (Ulm University)
Abstract
Summary graphs have shown to be a valuable tool in graph analysis and processing, with applications in query optimization, retrieval, and visualization, among others. Many summarization approaches are based on the concept of stratified bisimulation, which determines vertex equivalence based on outgoing paths of length k. Summaries based on bisimulation typically also store information about all paths of length less than k, and thus explicitly encode the 1, 2, …, k bisimulations. To this end, we introduce condensed summaries: a formal model for representing stratified bisimulations in a compact manner. By leveraging repeating structures between consecutive bisimulation levels, condensed summaries represent all levels of bisimulation up to some k, while containing O(|V|) vertices, independent of k. We also prove that condensed summaries are equivalent to an established, uncondensed representation. Furthermore, we provide an algorithm for computing condensed summaries, along with an optimization that can yield a 20-fold speed-up. To demonstrate the efficacy of our model and algorithm, we provide experimental results on various edge-labelled graphs with up to 28 billion edges and a bisimulation depth of up to 4,757. All experiments successfully reached full bisimulation in less than 10 hours, while those with up to 1 billion edges only took minutes or even seconds, with no more than 64 GiB of memory. The resulting summaries were all substantially smaller than the original graphs, sometimes with a 95% reduction in vertices and edges. Code is available at: https://github.com/R-van-Bakel/Multi-Summaries.
A134FULLVisAdj: Learning Adjacency Matrices from Node-Link Images
Jiahao Xie (University of Delaware) · Guangmo Tong (University of Delaware)
Abstract
Learning adjacency matrices from node-link images is a fundamental problem for recovering structured graph information from visual observations.Existing methods typically rely on fixed KNN-based heuristics for candidate edge selection and fail to capture dependencies among edges.To overcome these limitations, we propose VisAdj, a new framework for topology-aware adjacency prediction. VisAdj introduces an attention-sparse neighbor sampler to adaptively select a high-recall set of candidate node pairs and performs joint edge inference using a line-graph transformer that treats candidate edges as tokens and explicitly models dependencies among incident edges.Extensive experiments on synthetic graphs, road networks, and vessel images demonstrate that VisAdj consistently outperforms existing baselines by clear margins.
A135FULLContinuous-Time Quantum Walks based Graph Neural Network
Yuliang Zhan (RUC) · Zefeng Gao (RUC) · Jian Li (RUC) · Yang Liu (School of Engineering Science, University of Chinese Academy of Sciences) · Hao Sun (RUC)
Abstract
Graph Neural Networks (GNNs) are widely used on graph-structured data. However, most GNNs suffer from two key weaknesses. First, message passing acts as a low-pass filter based on the homophily assumption, so it performs poorly on heterophilic graphs, where connected nodes differ. Second, stacking layers makes node features converge exponentially to constants, a problem known as over-smoothing. Existing work usually addresses the two weaknesses separately. The few methods that target both rely on empirical heuristics, and many over-smoothing solutions further sacrifice the expressive power of the model. To address both weaknesses with theoretical justification, we propose CTQW-GNN, a GNN built on Continuous-Time Quantum Walks (CTQW). The design is motivated by two properties of the CTQW propagator e-iHt. (i) It is unitary and its eigenvalues lie on the unit circle, so no frequency component is damped. This directly counters the low-pass bias. (ii) Unitarity preserves the feature norm, so the Dirichlet energy does not decay exponentially with depth. This directly counters over-smoothing. Guided by these properties, CTQW-GNN combines three aggregation modules, each motivated by a specific gap in prior work. CTQW-based Aggregation evolves node features through the unitary propagator. It captures the mid- and high-frequency signals needed for heterophilic graphs and provably keeps the Dirichlet energy from collapsing, so it addresses both weaknesses in a single branch. CTQW-Attention Aggregation builds a multi-hop neighbor graph from the CTQW amplitudes and applies attention over it, so distant homophilic nodes that single-hop aggregation misses can still be reached. LF Aggregation is a standard low-pass branch (GAT) that preserves accuracy on strongly homophilic graphs, where a pure CTQW branch is suboptimal. We further provide a spectral-gap analysis that explains the energy preservation, and a Lieb–Robinson-type bound that gives a principled rule for choosing the walk-time t. Experiments on 14 benchmarks (9 heterophilic, 5 homophilic) show that CTQW-GNN reaches state-of-the-art accuracy on every dataset. Krylov propagation and Chebyshev-based sparsification keep the CTQW-related computation linear in the number of edges under the stated sparsification rule.
A136FULLDual Prompt Adaptation for Zero-Shot Classification on Text-attributed Graphs
Yang Liu (Beijing University of Posts and Telecommunications) · Yuan Fang (Singapore Management University) · Deyu Bo (Nanyang Technological University) · Chuan Shi (Beijing University of Posts and Telecommunications)
Abstract
Graph learning plays a crucial role in capturing valuable information from both graph structures and node attributes. Despite their success, existing methods struggle to generalize to unseen datasets or classes. To achieve robust generalization, we identify two essential capabilities a graph model should possess: (1) Zero-shot inference on unseen classes, and (2) Cross-dataset adaptation under distribution shifts. Recently, Text-attributed Graphs (TAGs) have shed light on the possibility of achieving zero-shot classification due to their rich semantic information in node textual attributes. However, current studies on TAGs rely on handcrafted prompts for adaptation, which is engineering-intensive and overlooks structure shifts across different datasets. To bridge this gap, we propose ZeroPA, a dual-prompt adaptation framework for TAG methods that perform zero-shot prediction by matching node representations with label-text representations. Specifically, the textual prompt is prepended to label descriptions to enhance zero-shot classification. The graph prompt, on the other hand, is constructed as a subgraph and inserted into the original graph to calibrate node representations, thereby addressing distribution shifts. The dual prompts are optimized in an alternating and iterative manner, where each reinforces the other during adaptation. We conduct extensive experiments to verify the effectiveness of ZeroPA. The results demonstrate that ZeroPA consistently boosts the generalizability of TAG methods across diverse datasets. Our code is available at https://github.com/liuyang-tian/ZeroPA.git. (https://github.com/liuyang-tian/ZeroPA.git)
A137SHORTWho Should Teach? Confidence-Aware Dual-Teacher Learning for Few-Shot Node Classification on Text-Attributed Graphs
Hojin Kim (Chungbuk National University) · Sujin Yoon (Chungbuk National University) · Sungsu Lim (Chungnam National University) · Dongwon Lee (The Pennsylvania State University) · David Yoon Suk Kang (Chungbuk National University)
Abstract
Text-Attributed Graphs (TAGs) integrate graph structures and node-associated textual attributes, and recent studies have increasingly leveraged Large Language Models (LLMs) to improve TAG learning in few-shot settings. However, existing approaches typically utilize LLM-derived information uniformly across all nodes, despite substantial variations in its reliability, while also incurring considerable monetary costs. We argue that the most appropriate source of supervision may differ across nodes, as Graph Neural Networks (GNNs) and LLMs exhibit complementary strengths in exploiting structural and semantic information, respectively. To this end, we propose CoTeach, a Confidence-aware dual-teacher learning framework that dynamically selects the more reliable teacher for each node. Experimental results demonstrate that CoTeach consistently improves few-shot node classification performance while reducing unnecessary LLM utilization and associated monetary costs.
A138SHORTEfficient Dynamic Node Classification via Target- and Memory-Free Cross-Attention
Erfan Moshiri (Macquarie University) · Amin Beheshti (Macquarie University) · M A Hakim Newton (The University of Newcastle) · Min Li (Domain Group) · Pooyan Asgari (Domain Group)
Abstract
Dynamic graph learning faces key trade-offs: self-attention suffers from quadratic computational scaling, while memory-based methods compress interaction histories into fixed vectors, losing fine-grained temporal patterns. Furthermore, existing link prediction models rely on destination nodes as attention anchors, making them inadequate for standalone node classification. We introduce DANCE, a memory-free framework using learnable embeddings or global tokens as self-contained queries to perform identity-aware trajectory matching via linear-time asymmetric cross-attention over raw neighbor histories. This eliminates the quadratic bottleneck while preserving full per-node expressive capacity. Enriched with multi-scale temporal features, DANCE achieves state-of-the-art AUC-ROC performance (up to 6.2% relative improvement over best baselines) with significantly lower training time and memory overhead. To handle cold-start settings, our two inductive variants substitute node-specific parameters with global tokens, ensuring robust generalization on unseen nodes. Code is available on GitHub (https://github.com/erfanmoshiri/DANCE).
A139FULLID2GL: Incremental Node Representation Learning on Large-Scale Dynamic Directed Graphs
Zening Li (Beijing Institute of Technology) · Rong-Hua Li (Beijing Institute of Technology) · Yichun Yang (Beijing Institute of Technology) · Meihao Liao (Beijing Institute of Technology)
Abstract
Node representation learning on dynamic graphs is a fundamental task for numerous real-world applications. However, existing dynamic Graph Neural Networks (GNNs) face two critical challenges: (1) the inability to effectively model crucial directional information inherent in many real-world interactions, and (2) suffer from poor scalability due to the neighbor explosion problem. To address these limitations, we propose ID2GL, a novel and scalable framework for incremental node representation learning on dynamic directed graphs. ID2GL features a decoupled architecture and introduces a novel propagation mechanism based on complex-valued personalized PageRank. This mechanism not only captures directionality via complex phases but also incorporates multi-hop neighbor information, which effectively alleviates the neighbor explosion issue. To handle continuous updates efficiently, we propose an incremental update mechanism that requires only local computations on affected nodes, supported by theoretical guarantees on the post-update representation error. Finally, a transformer-based prediction module is utilized to capture the temporal evolution of node representations for various downstream tasks. Extensive experiments on multiple real-world datasets, including the massive Papers100M dataset, demonstrate that ID2GL significantly outperforms state-of-the-art baselines in both node classification and link prediction tasks, and achieves competitive efficiency and scalability.
A140FULLCounterfactual Explanations for Hypergraph Neural Networks
Fabiano Veglianti (Sapienza University) · Lorenzo Antonelli (Sapienza University) · Gabriele Tolomei (Sapienza University)
Abstract
Hypergraph Neural Networks (HGNNs) effectively model higher-order interactions in many real-world systems but remain difficult to interpret, limiting their deployment in high-stakes settings. We introduce CF-HyperGNNExplainer, a counterfactual explanation method for HGNNs that identifies the minimal structural changes required to alter a model's prediction. The method generates counterfactual hypergraphs using actionable edits limited to removing node-hyperedge incidences or deleting hyperedges, producing concise and structurally meaningful explanations. Extensive experiments on hypergraph benchmark datasets show that CF-HyperGNNExplainer generates valid and concise counterfactuals, highlighting the higher-order relations most critical to HGNN decisions.
A141FULLNetSight: Joint Spatio-Temporal Dependency Modeling for Network Traffic Prediction
Jinming Xing (North Carolina State University) · Guoheng Sun (University of Maryland College Park) · Hui Sun (North Carolina State University) · Linchao Pan (Shenzhen University) · Shakir Mahmood (North Carolina State University) · Xuanhao Luo (North Carolina State University) · Muhammad Shahzad (North Carolina State University)
Abstract
The traffic in today's networks is increasingly influenced by the interactions among network nodes as well as by the temporal fluctuations in the demands of the nodes. Traditional statistical methods to predict network traffic metrics have become obsolete due to their inability to address the non-linear and dynamic spatio-temporal dependencies present in today's network traffic. The most promising direction of research today is graph neural networks (GNNs) based prediction approaches that are naturally suited to handle graph-structured data. Unfortunately, the state-of-the-art GNN approaches separate the modeling of spatial and temporal information, resulting in the loss of important information about joint dependencies. These GNN based approaches further do not model information at both local and global scales simultaneously, leaving significant room for improvement. To address these challenges, we propose NetSight, which jointly learns spatio-temporal dependencies simultaneously at both global and local scales from the time-series of measurements of any given network metric collected at various nodes in a network. NetSight achieves this through three key innovations: a spatio-temporal adjacency matrix that fuses spatial topology with temporal similarity, a node normalization technique that enables joint spatio-temporal learning, and an architecture that applies temporal modeling directly on spatial embeddings rather than treating the two modalities independently. Through extensive evaluations and comparison with prior approaches using data from three large real-world networks, we show that NetSight significantly outperforms prior state-of-the-art approaches. All code and data used in this paper is available at [1].
A142FULLDecomposed Attention Frequency Debiased Transformer Model: Large Time-series Model for Satellite Orbit Prediction
Kangjun Lee (Sungkyunkwan University) · Seungwon Jeong (Sungkyunkwan University) · JongU Park (Sungkyunkwan University) · Youjin Shin (The Catholic University of Korea) · Simon S. Woo (Sungkyunkwan University)
Abstract
Accurate satellite orbit prediction is critical for collision avoidance and sustainable space operations. However, conventional prediction methods are constrained by coarse update intervals and orbit discontinuities. Additionally, building separate prediction models for each satellite is computationally expensive, making large-scale accurate forecasting increasingly impractical. To address the aforementioned challenges, we propose the Decomposed Attention Frequency debiased transformer (DAF) model, a large time-series prediction model that utilizes efficient Real Fast Fourier Transform (RFFT) and Inverse RFFT alongside positional embeddings. Our DAF also integrates Tensorized Multi-Head Attention based on Tensor Train Decomposition for parameter-efficient compression and improved performance. We pre-trained on a large-scale Starlink dataset comprising 6,955 satellites and evaluated zero-shot performance on seven cross-domain satellite orbit datasets and three real-world datasets. DAF achieves up to a 34.85% reduction in mean squared error and a 16.01% reduction in mean absolute error over the second-best model, using only 0.045% of its parameters while maintaining inference speed comparable to conventional neural network baselines. These results demonstrate that DAF enables zero-shot, high-precision orbit prediction not only for Starlink satellites but also for other satellite types.
A143FULLCompositional Spectral Prompts for LLM-based Online Time Series Forecasting
Seungyoon Choi (KAIST) · Hyunchul Kim (KAIST) · Jae-Gil Lee (KAIST) · Chanyoung Park (KAIST)
Abstract
To address the sequential and evolving nature of time series, the Online Time Series Forecasting (OTSF) task has been extensively studied in multiple domains. Existing research focuses on adapting to non-stationary environments by employing memory buffer-based retrieval strategies. However, we observe that such frameworks struggle with long-term adaptation and fail to generalize to unseen patterns. To this end, we introduce CoSPOT, an LLM-based online time series forecasting framework that leverages a pre-trained LLM as the backbone online forecaster, motivated by its strong few-shot capabilities. For efficient online adaptation, CoSPOT keeps the LLM frozen and employs compositional spectral prompts grounded in frequency-domain bases to guide the model with the overall distribution of the input, thereby substantially reducing the number of parameters updated during the online phase. Specifically, CoSPOT decomposes time series into frequency bases and composes the corresponding spectral basis prompts according to their amplitudes, allowing unseen patterns to be represented as new combinations of learned basis prompts. Our extensive experiments on real-world datasets demonstrate the superiority and practicality of CoSPOT across challenging online scenarios, including extended online phases and cross-dataset settings with substantial distribution shifts. Our code is available at https://github.com/seungyoon-Choi/CoSPOT.
A144FULLLSPP: Injecting Local Structural Patterns into Time Series Forecasting via Adaptive Prototype Pool
Lingling Zuo (Nanjing University of Science and Technology) · Haixiang Wu (Nanjing University of Science and Technology) · Yang Yang (Nanjing University of Science and Technology)
Abstract
Deep learning has demonstrated remarkable advancements in time series forecasting. Most existing methods formulate forecasting as a purely continuous regression task optimized by mean squared error. However, this point-wise strategy neglects underlying structural patterns, often yielding over-smoothed and unreliable predictions. To address this challenge, we propose Local Structural Prototype Pool (LSPP), a two-stage pattern-aware method that injects local structural patterns into forecasting via an adaptive prototype pool, reformulating prediction as a discrete-continuous representation learning process. Specifically, LSPP first builds a shared prototype pool through self-supervised reconstruction to compactly capture recurring structural patterns. During forecasting, LSPP encodes historical patches into global continuous representations, matches them against the prototype pool to extract local structural patterns, and fuses both global and local representations for the final prediction. A central contribution of LSPP is that the prototype pool remains learnable throughout the forecasting stage, continuously adapting to evolving temporal dynamics via a semantic alignment loss. Extensive experiments on diverse real-world benchmarks demonstrate that LSPP achieves competitive performance while maintaining favorable computational efficiency. Our code is available at https://github.com/l00907l/LSPP.
A145FULLKoopSDE: Time-Series Forecasting Under Noise with Koopman Operators and Latent Stochastic Differential Equations
Firas Yazbak (Technion - Israel Institute of Technology) · Assaf Schuster (Technion - Israel Institute of Technology)
Abstract
Long-horizon forecasting of multivariate time series is a fundamental problem in machine learning, with applications in resource planning, environmental monitoring, economic analysis, and biomedical surveillance. As the prediction horizon grows, small errors accumulate; at the same time, real measurements are rarely noise-free, and many systems show both structured dynamics and random variation. Methods based on Koopman operator theory have shown that nonlinear dynamics can be represented as linear evolution in a learned observable space, yielding models that are both accurate and mathematically interpretable. A persistent limitation of deterministic formulations is that they do not explicitly separate observation noise from the linear dynamics being learned; without such separation, noise may be absorbed into the operator and the embedding, making the true dynamics harder to recover and degrading long-range prediction. We introduce KoopSDE, a method that extends Koopman-based linear latent forecasting with a latent stochastic differential equation whose drift is tied to the Koopman generator through a matrix logarithm identity, and whose diffusion is learned from data. The model combines objectives for linear evolution and stochastic trajectories with a denoising mechanism that biases the Koopman component toward smooth dynamical structure while the SDE branch is trained against the raw observations. KoopSDE is evaluated on six standard long-horizon benchmarks and on an epidemiological series. It achieves the best or second-best mean squared error on every reported dataset and horizon, reduces the average MSE by 5.4% compared to a strong deterministic Koopman baseline across all settings, and shows growing improvement at longer horizons. Synthetic validation on a chaotic attractor with controlled noise further shows that the complete KoopSDE framework remains advantageous as controlled observation noise is introduced.
A146FULLLIPTS: LLM-enhanced Time Series Interpolation and Prediction with Incomplete Data
Zhirong Zhang (University of Bristol) · Hongrui Wang (Xi'an Jiaotong University) · Yong Fang (Chang'an University) · Zixing Song (Hong Kong Polytechnic University)
Abstract
Multivariate time series forecasting supports state estimation and trend analysis of complex dynamic systems by modeling temporal dependencies among multiple variables. However, real-world time series are often sparse and incomplete due to irregular or constrained data collection, which degrades forecasting performance. Existing methods typically adopt either imputation-then-forecasting or direct forecasting from incomplete observations. The former separates imputation from forecasting, causing interpolation errors to propagate into prediction, while the latter may overlook latent evolution patterns in missing segments. Recent advances in large language models (LLMs) suggest their potential to capture high-level sequential semantics and infer contextual patterns beyond observed numerical values, making them promising for reasoning over incomplete temporal dynamics. To address these challenges, we propose LIPTS (Large language model-based interpolation and prediction for Time Series), an end-to-end framework for time series imputation and forecasting based on LLMs. LIPTS jointly optimizes missing value interpolation and downstream forecasting within a unified framework, thereby alleviating the propagation of interpolation errors in two-stage pipelines. Moreover, it introduces an LLM-enhanced cross-modal semantic branch to infer global temporal semantics behind incomplete observations and provide complementary information for latent evolution in missing segments. The numerical branch captures historical and seasonal dependencies from observed values, while latent alignment bridges semantic representations and the numerical forecasting space, encouraging interpolated values to follow the temporal distribution required for downstream forecasting. Extensive experiments on real-world benchmarks demonstrate that LIPTS outperforms state-of-the-art baselines in prediction accuracy and robustness across different missing rates and prediction horizons.
A147FULLCross-Variable Forecasters Commit to an Arbitrary Mixing Scaffold
Seong Jin Ahn (Samsung Electronics) · Daeho Um (University of Seoul)
Abstract
Modern multivariate time-series forecasters increasingly rely on cross-variable mechanisms, with their gains commonly attributed to learning meaningful inter-variable dependency structure. This attribution is widely assumed but rarely tested at the mechanism level, since benchmark improvements may arise either from learning meaningful variable relationships or simply from the capacity to mix information across variables. To address this, we introduce a shuffle control, a per-instance random permutation applied to a model’s cross-variable operator that destroys variable identity while exactly preserving sparsity, weight distribution, row sums, and overall mixing capacity. Applying this control to representative cross-variable forecasters, we find that the learned wiring is largely interchangeable with a random one of the same shape. The dissociation is sharp: trained models strongly depend on their learned wiring, yet training from scratch on a random one recovers nearly identical accuracy. To verify that the shuffle control can detect genuine structure, we construct synthetic datasets with installed dependency patterns, where the same analysis produces strong shuffle sensitivity and the expected ordering. Overall, our study suggests that many current cross-variable forecasting gains arise primarily from mixing capacity rather than recovery of meaningful dependency structure, and we release the shuffle control as a simple mechanism-level diagnostic for evaluating future cross-variable claims. Code is available at https://github.com/SeongJinAhn/Cross-Variable-Forecasters-Commit-to-an-Arbitrary-Mixing-Scaffold.
A148FULLCausalDiff: Causality-Preserving Diffusion for Interpretable Multivariate Time-Series Generation
Ni Zhang (Taiyuan University of Technology) · Hao Miao (Taiyuan University of Technology) · Zefei Ning (Taiyuan University of Technology) · Li Wang (Taiyuan University of Technology)
Abstract
Multivariate time-series generation is important for data augmentation, simulation, and downstream analysis. Beyond the temporal dynamics of individual variables, multivariate time series also encode evolving cross-variable relationships, among which directional dependencies with temporal lags characterize how information propagates across variables over time. However, existing generative methods primarily focus on matching the distributional and temporal characteristics of real data, while the direction, strength, and temporal delay of these lagged dependencies may still be distorted in generated sequences. To address this gap, we propose CausalDiff, an interpretable nonlinear diffusion framework that explicitly models dynamic lagged causal relevance during time-series generation. Specifically, each window is represented by a historical prefix, a lagged causal-relevance tensor, and a residual sequence, corresponding to the initial temporal context, estimated lagged propagation structure, and unexplained variation, respectively. A KAN-based edge mechanism further parameterizes each estimated lagged relation with an explicit nonlinear function, making the learned edge-wise propagation patterns interpretable. For anomalous time-series generation, CausalDiff models normal-referenced shifts in causal relevance and residual variation to synthesize deviations from normal dynamics. Experiments show that CausalDiff achieves better agreement with ground-truth causal structures on causal benchmarks and stronger consistency with estimated lagged causal structures on real-world datasets while maintaining competitive distributional quality. These findings indicate that explicitly modeling lagged causal relevance helps align generated multivariate time series with the structural dynamics observed in real data while retaining edge-level interpretability. The source code is available at: https://github.com/znmiao/CausalDiff.
A149FULLDCFAD: Dual-Path Cross-Attention with Learnable Fractional Fourier Transform for Time Series Anomaly Detection
Xiaowei Jia (Shanxi University) · Shengxi Wang (Taiyuan Satellite Launch Center) · Kaikai Yang (Shanxi University of Finance and Economics) · Liang Du (Shanxi University) · Zhiguo Hu (Shanxi University)
Abstract
Multivariate time series anomaly detection is crucial for failure diagnosis, network security, and intelligent operations. Reconstruction-based approaches are well suited for unsupervised scenarios, as they detect anomalies without labeled data and model complex temporal patterns through reconstruction. However, despite recent progress in point-wise anomaly detection and frequency-enhanced representations, existing methods largely rely on fixed representation domains, which may limit their ability to separate diverse pattern-wise anomalies from normal patterns and produce robust anomaly scores. We propose DCFAD, a unified framework that integrates a learnable fractional Fourier transform (FrFT) and a dual-path cross-domain attention mechanism. DCFAD learns anomaly-sensitive intermediate representations between time and frequency domains by adaptively adjusting the fractional order of FrFT during training. Meanwhile, the dual-path cross-domain attention establishes cross-domain correspondences from temporal and variable dimensions, enabling selective fusion of time-domain and fractional-domain features for reliable anomaly reconstruction. Extensive experiments on 10 real-world datasets with multiple evaluation metrics demonstrate the state-of-the-art overall performance of DCFAD in multivariate time series anomaly detection. Notably, DCFAD achieves a 9.5 percentage-point improvement in average AUC-ROC over the strongest AUC-ROC baseline while maintaining efficient inference. The complete code has been released at https://github.com/Jia-xw1/DCFAD.
A150APPLIEDTelecomAudit: Origin-Aware Benchmark Auditing and Calibration for 5G Anomaly Detection
Chiman Salavati (University of Connecticut) · Liang Wu (Nokia) · Kelly Wan (Nokia) · Mayank Darbari (Nokia) · Liangjie Hong (Nokia)
Abstract
Modern wireless networks support reliability-critical applications, from industrial automation and autonomous mobility to UAV connectivity, making anomaly detection critical for 5G and self-optimizing 6G operations. Yet labeled telecom faults are rare, costly to annotate, and difficult to release, so telecom anomaly detectors are trained and evaluated using injected, generated, or simulated anomalies. This raises a deployment question: can strong synthetic-benchmark performance be trusted for detector selection?
