Joshua DeOliveira (Worcester Polytechnic Institute) · Ajay Bhagavatula (Worcester Polytechnic Institute) · Emily Perlow (Worcester Polytechnic Institute) · Arne Gericke (Worcester Polytechnic Institute) · Ermal Toto (Worcester Polytechnic Institute) · Elke Rundensteiner (Worcester Polytechnic Institute)
Abstract
Student attrition in higher education remains a critical problem. While existing literature has began to explore automated inference of students at risk of adverse academic outcomes, flagging and intervention diagnosis remains tenuous in practice due to the tedious manual processes, and a lack of sophisticated AI methods and automated tooling. To address this, we propose Flagger, the first academic decision-support system co-designed with domain experts that integrates a novel AI–based risk prediction engine for early identification of at-risk students automatically sifting through students' transcripts. Flagger features innovations such as a bespoke Transformer Backbone addressing dual-heterogeneity of transcripts, Modular Prediction Heads addressing evolution of at-risk predictors, and a Transcript Drill-Down and Course Dependency Engine for derived evidence for insight explanation. In this demonstration, we will feature a live exploration of transcripts guided by AI to aid advisors in understanding context, in faster triaging, and in the design of appropriate intervention. Ultimately, Flagger has been shown to increase at-risk detection rates as much as 3x in a retrospective study of 1,800 WPI students compared to current processes.

B01DEMOTS-Lens: A Zero-Shot Time-Series Pattern Search System with Inspectable Waveform Queries
Jaewon Moon (Korea Electronics Technology Institute) · Jihoon Lee (Korea Electronics Technology Institute)
Abstract
Time-series pattern exploration is central to energy monitoring, industrial diagnosis, environmental sensing, and anomaly analysis. In practice, analysts often know the pattern they want to find but do not yet have a representative query segment. Query-by-example assumes such a segment is available; sketch systems require users to draw the target shape; and recent language-based methods often depend on fixed query grammars or trained text–time-series retrievers. We present TS-Lens, an interactive web system for zero-shot time-series pattern exploration. Its core interaction is Describe–Generate–Search: rather than mapping a natural-language description directly to results or to an opaque embedding, a language model generates a normalized waveform that the user can visually inspect and edit before search, and conventional similarity search retrieves matching windows or segments. This inspectable intermediate representation sits between parse-based querying (a fixed shape grammar) and embed-based querying (a trained text–time-series space), handling the uncertainty of LLM output through user inspection instead of task-specific retriever training. The same workspace also supports sketch, sample, preset, and cluster-medoid queries, plus Time-Series-to-Text explanations and label-basket curation. Across ETT-h1, NREL Solar 2023, and UCI Air Quality scenarios, TS-Lens shows how linguistic intent and remembered visual shapes can become reusable time-series queries.
B02DEMOOrbit: Open Re-implementation of Biomedical Literature APIs
Shrestha Ghosh (University of Tübingen) · Mert Okur (University of Tübingen) · Harrisen Scells (University of Tübingen)
Abstract
Information retrieval experimentation with biomedical literature, despite an important area of research that can have a high impact, is often gated by a high barrier of entry. This is due to a variety of reasons including the requirement of bespoke document processing pipelines, complex indexing pipelines, and domain-specific query languages. While biomedical literature databases with freely available API access do exist, e.g., the Entrez API for PubMed and the ClinicalTrials.gov API, the use of such APIs is limiting: rate limits, restrictions on the number of documents that can be retrieved per request, and no way to extend or add functionality. The usual option for overcoming these limitations is to scrape or download the data, index it with an off-the-shelf search engine, and use whatever query language is implemented by the search engine. These off-the-shelf options are insufficient for reproducing retrieval in biomedical tasks, such as, systematic reviews, clinical-trial design and evidence-based clinical decision-making, that require retrieval from multiple sources and complex query mechanisms. We provide a drop-in, extendable, and open-source clean room re-implementation of two commonly used biomedical literature APIs that dramatically lowers the barrier of entry to experimentation in retrieval-based biomedical tasks. An overview of the system with example usage and video showcase is available at https://orbit.health-nlp.com.
B03DEMOPolyUQuest: Verifiable Structure-Aware Web RAG over Heterogeneous Graphs
Ying Liu (The Hong Kong Polytechnic University) · Yi Ye (The Hong Kong Polytechnic University) · Quanyu Feng (The Hong Kong Polytechnic University) · Mingxi Ye (The Hong Kong Polytechnic University) · Mingtao Zhang (The Hong Kong Polytechnic University) · Haoyang Li (The Hong Kong Polytechnic University) · Chen Jason Zhang (The Hong Kong Polytechnic University) · Qing Li (The Hong Kong Polytechnic University)
Abstract
Existing retrieval-augmented generation (RAG) systems treat web pages as flat text, losing the structural and semantic signals encoded in HTML. We present PolyUQuest, a verifiable, structure-aware web RAG framework built on a heterogeneous graph that unifies hyperlink topology between pages, DOM hierarchy within pages, and entity–relation knowledge across pages. A two-tier router dispatches each query to one of three retrieval modes matched to its structural need, including direct block retrieval, cross-page graph traversal, and multi-hop entity reasoning. Each answer carries traceable provenance: every cited block records its source page, heading path, and entity links, so users can inspect the structural evidence behind a claim. We evaluate on the official websites of the Hong Kong Polytechnic University (PolyU), comprising 4,240 pages, 31,086 DOM blocks, 29,119 entities, and 37,680 relations, together with a multi-type evaluation benchmark. PolyUQuest improves correctness, coverage, and faithfulness over the evaluated baselines while maintaining query-time token consumption comparable to ChunkRAG and substantially below the graph-based RAG baselines. The demonstration provides an interactive interface for inspecting cited answers, comparing retrieval traces across routing modes, and exploring evidence graph paths. PolyUQuest is being prepared for deployment as a student-facing QA service at PolyU. A demo video is available at https://youtu.be/thKWYaL_4rw.
B04DEMOGraphCraft: Skill-Centric Curation of Evolving GraphRAG Pipelines
Ilia Karpov (HSE University) · Ivan Chepikov (HSE University) · Denis Losev (APSolutions LLC) · Alina Avanesyan (HSE University) · Maria Godunova (HSE University) · Dmitry Ilvovsky (HSE University)
Abstract
GraphRAG pipelines build entity–relation graphs from text and use them for retrieval and question answering, but extraction noise, entity fragmentation, and unstable clustering can silently corrupt the evidence behind an answer. Correcting these errors is difficult to scale because their dominant forms depend on the corpus and repeated corrections remain manual. We present GraphCraft, an interactive system that records provenance-rich human corrections and compiles repeated corrections into reusable curation skills. Each skill identifies similar errors in subsequent corpus updates and proposes edits for curator review; proposals are previewed rather than applied automatically. The same journal links corrections and skill suggestions back to their graph context and source spans, while bi-temporal graph state distinguishes changes to the stored graph from changes in the underlying world. We evaluate a compiled skill on held-out ingestion batches and demonstrate the complete workflow from diagnosing an erroneous answer, through repairing its graph evidence, to reusing the correction on later data. GraphCraft is released as an open platform with offline deployment. Code and offline deployment: https://github.com/apsolutions/graphrag; demo video: https://vimeo.com/1141894235.
B05DEMODeepRepro: State-Aware Subplanning for Paper-to-Code Reproduction in Evolving Repositories
Hongru Song (The Institute of Computing Technology,CAS) · Ruqing Zhang (The Institute of Computing Technology,CAS) · Jiafeng Guo (The Institute of Computing Technology,CAS) · Xueqi Cheng (The Institute of Computing Technology,CAS) · Maarten de Rijke (University of Amsterdam)
Abstract
Recent advances in agentic large language models (LLMs) have enabled increasingly autonomous software engineering workflows, yet automatic machine learning (ML) paper-to-code reproduction remains a challenging long-horizon problem. Unlike conventional code generation, this task requires constructing and maintaining a fully functional repository whose state continuously evolves during execution. Existing systems typically rely on static upfront planning followed by sequential file-level generation, which often leads to inconsistencies as dependencies, interfaces, and execution feedback change over time. We propose DeepRepro, a state-aware framework for paper-to-code reproduction based on execution-state-aware subplanning. DeepRepro dynamically transforms evolving repository states and runtime feedback into fine-grained implementation subplans, keeping planning aligned with execution throughout repository construction. The framework further incorporates repository-aware orchestration and a lightweight process-aware interface for transparent monitoring of long-horizon reproduction. Experiments on PaperBench Code-Dev show that DeepRepro consistently outperforms strong scientific and commercial code-agent baselines. Code and demo are available at https://github.com/ruyisy/DeepRepro and https://youtu.be/ZvmtVX7Rleo.
B06DEMO1ShotBench: Demonstrating One-Shot Prompt Reproducibility for Autonomous Coding Agents
Neng Li (University of Waterloo) · Yijun Ge (University of Waterloo) · Xueguang Ma (University of Waterloo) · Jimmy Lin (University of Waterloo)
Abstract
The growing use of LLM agents raises a reproducibility problem: given the same task specification, different agents may follow different workflows, consume different resources, and produce varying artifacts and outcomes. We introduce the concept of One-Shot Prompt Reproducibility (1SPR): the consistency of one-shot execution across different agents given a fixed specification, without iterative human guidance. To operationalize this, we present 1ShotBench, a toolkit that repeatedly executes the same product requirement document (PRD) across isolated agent workspaces, capturing full traces, artifacts, and metadata, along with an LLM judge to evaluate results. We demonstrate a case study using software engineering tasks built around the Anserini information retrieval toolkit, though our system itself supports arbitrary tasks. 1ShotBench allows users to compare runs side by side, inspect how execution and implementation paths diverge despite a shared specification, and analyze how workflow differences relate to cost, latency, and correctness. Our central contribution is a reproducibility-oriented lens for examining agentic software development.
B07DEMOPreserving LLM Output Distributions for Probabilistic Query Evaluation
Angelo Saadeh (DI ENS, ENS, CNRS, PSL University, Inria) · Pierre Senellart (DI ENS, ENS, CNRS, PSL University, Inria)
Abstract
Language models can be used to augment databases; typically, when this is done, their top prediction is used while the uncertainty in this prediction is ignored. We propose a framework that preserves output distributions from language model predictions and uses them to evaluate SQL queries probabilistically. First, a language model is used to infer new features from existing ones. Second, ProvSQL, a PostgreSQL extension implementing a probabilistic database through data provenance, encodes the predictions as mutually exclusive events in a provenance circuit and evaluates probabilistic queries. We extend ProvSQL to support text-value comparisons and join operations on language model predictions. We demonstrate the framework on 10\,612 Amazon musical products and 230\,156 user reviews, locally augmented with the Llama 3.1 model. We show that probabilistic querying reveals contradictions between model predictions and existing labels, recovers data records otherwise missed, and propagates joint uncertainty across multi-table queries.
B08DEMOEviMap: Evidence-Grounded Hierarchical Topic Maps for Exploring Unlabeled Corpora
Zhiyin Tan (Leibniz University Hannover) · Changxu Duan (Technische Universität Darmstadt)
Abstract
Research teams and organizations often explore unfamiliar free-text collections, from survey comments and reviews to reports and domain documents, before labels, queries or coding schemes exist. At this stage, the first thematic map shapes what users notice, prioritize and carry into downstream analysis, so it should be trusted only insofar as it can be verified. Existing options force a trade-off between scale and verifiability. Qualitative coding preserves evidence but is slow. Search presupposes a query. Clustering and topic models scale but produce labels users must interpret. One-shot large language model (LLM) summaries are fluent yet difficult to reproduce or audit. We present EviMap, an interactive system providing researchers and practitioners with an auditable thematic overview of such corpora. Guided by model-generated context describing the corpus and hypothesized stakeholder concerns, EviMap extracts within-document evidence phrases and organizes them, rather than whole documents, into a three-level map of aspects, groups and fine-grained topics. Embedding-based clustering narrows the search space for finer semantic judgments by the LLM. Each node traces back to supporting phrase spans, so documents link to topics through evidence they contain and users can audit labels against the original text. Users can start from a top-level corpus map, drill into topics, inspect highlighted evidence in original documents, and combine two topics to find documents discussing both. We demonstrate this workflow across six heterogeneous corpora spanning 2,108 to 101,699 documents, with a comparison against flat and hierarchical LLM baselines. By grounding every label in verbatim source spans, EviMap makes a topic map not just readable, but verifiable. Code, demo video, and interactive dashboard are available at https://github.com/zhiyintan/EviMap.
B09DEMOSAFE-Cascade: Cost-Adaptive Vision-Language Routing for Chart Question Answering
Ayush Dwivedi (Walmart) · Qixin Wang (Walmart) · Ashvi Soni (Walmart) · Ruoteng Wang (Walmart) · Han Li (Walmart) · Animesh Mahapatra (Walmart) · Neeraj Agrawal (Walmart) · Xintao Wu (University of Arkansas)
Abstract
Vision-language models (VLMs) are powerful for chart question answering, but invoking a VLM for every query can be unnecessarily expensive when many questions are answerable from OCR text and lightweight language reasoning. We demonstrate SAFE-Cascade, an interactive system for cost-adaptive chart question answering. Given a chart image and a natural-language question, SAFE-Cascade first extracts chart text with OCR, obtains a provisional answer from a text-only language model, and then uses a learned router to decide whether to accept the text answer or escalate to a VLM. The demo exposes this decision process to users: OCR evidence, text-only answer, routing probability, escalation decision, final answer, estimated cost, and estimated latency are shown side by side. SAFE-Cascade is designed as a transparent interface for understanding when visual grounding is actually needed. Users can upload or select charts, ask questions, inspect the evidence used by each pathway, compare text-only and VLM answers, and adjust the escalation threshold to explore the accuracy-cost frontier. The system is implemented with Azure Document Intelligence for OCR, gpt-5-mini as the text-only model, gemini-2.5-flash-image as the VLM, and a Random Forest router trained on inference-time features. On a held-out ChartQA test split of 375 examples from a 2,500-example experiment, SAFE-Cascade achieves 69.1% unified accuracy with 73.1% VLM invocation, compared with 67.7% accuracy and 100% VLM invocation for the full-VLM baseline. The observed +1.4 percentage-point difference is statistically uncertain, so we interpret SAFE-Cascade as matching full-VLM performance while reducing VLM calls by 26.9% and estimated cost by 9.3%. The demonstration shows how selective modality routing can make multimodal knowledge systems more transparent, tunable, and cost-aware.
B10DEMOCali-Tree: Hierarchical Calibration for VLM Judges
Zheng Zhang (Northwestern University) · Andrew Crotty (Northwestern University) · Md. Mehrab Tanjim (Adobe Research) · Christine Dierk (Adobe Research) · Somdeb Sarkhel (Adobe Research) · Uttaran Bhattacharya (Adobe Research)
Abstract
Delegation of image assessment tasks to vision-language models (VLMs) is becoming common practice in a wide variety of domains. However, for many use cases, a significant calibration gap remains between these VLM judges and human evaluators, raising concerns about the reliability of their integration into production systems. To solve this problem, we introduce Cali-Tree, a hierarchical calibration framework for VLM judges that systematically refines rubric prompts to better align with human assessments. Starting with individual leaf prompts tuned for particular training instances, Cali-Tree iteratively clusters semantically similar nodes and merges their specialized evaluation criteria into more general parent prompts. This hierarchical training process helps mitigate destructive interference common with alternative approaches that attempt to optimize across all training instances at once. In fact, our preliminary results show that Cali-Tree can achieve an improvement of up to 30 percentage points over a baseline optimized with TextGrad. This demo will highlight the key benefits of our approach by allowing participants to interact with the Cali-Tree training pipeline for real-world image assessment tasks.
B11DEMODEP: A Decentralized Evaluation Protocol and Toolkit for Large Language Models
Jianxiang Peng (Tianjin University) · Junhao Li (Tianjin University) · Hongxiang Wang (Tianjin University) · Haocheng Lyu (Tianjin University) · Hui Guo (Tianjin University) · Siyi Hao (Tianjin University) · Shaowei Zhang (Tianjin University) · Bojian Xiong (Tianjin University) · Chuang Liu (National Supercomputing Center in Tianjin) · Yuqi Ren (Tianjin University) · Deyi Xiong (Tianjin University)
Abstract
With the rapid development of Large Language Models (LLMs), a large number of evaluation benchmarks have been proposed. However, most benchmarks lack unified evaluation standards, requiring users to manually implement customized scripts, which leads to high usage costs and difficulties in ensuring the consistency of evaluation results. Existing evaluation frameworks are typically centralized, integrating scripts, datasets, and reference answers into a single system, which not only increases system complexity but also raises the risk of benchmark leakage. To address these issues, we propose the Decentralized Evaluation Protocol (DEP), which decouples users, LLMs, and benchmarks. By associating each benchmark with a server script that can either be locally mounted or remotely deployed, DEP enables lightweight, plug-and-play, broadly compatible evaluations while preventing data leakage. Once adapted, the benchmark can be reused over the long term. To facilitate practical adoption, we developed the DEP Toolkit, a toolkit compatible with the DEP protocol that supports features such as resumable evaluation, concurrent requests, and congestion control, while also providing both a CLI and a GUI. In addition, we provide detailed documentation to guide benchmark adaptation for DEP. Using the DEP Toolkit, we validated the effectiveness of DEP in applications, demonstrating its ability to reduce the deployment cost of benchmark evaluation. As of May 2026, we have adapted more than 60 benchmarks and continue to promote community-driven collaboration to support unified evaluation across domains.
B12DEMOAEQUITAS: A Toolkit for Stock Market Prediction and Portfolio Evaluation
Sara Pederzoli (University of Modena and Reggio Emilia) · Marta Santacroce (University of Modena and Reggio Emilia) · Francesco Del Buono (Cristail Capital Scf) · Marco Bergianti (Cristail Capital Scf) · Francesco Guerra (University of Modena and Reggio Emilia)
Abstract
Stock market prediction has produced a large number of models: comparing them in practice remains difficult. Existing approaches are often released as isolated implementations, use different data construction and preprocessing pipelines, and report heterogeneous machine learning and portfolio metrics. As a result, analysts cannot easily determine whether observed performance differences are due to the models themselves or to differences in data preparation, experimental design, and evaluation protocols. To address these challenges, we present AEQUITAS, An Evaluation toolkit for QUantItative and Trading AnalySis. It supports the construction, storage, and reuse of heterogeneous financial datasets, integrates classification, regression, and ranking models under consistent settings, and links model outputs to standardized portfolio strategies. The demonstration showcases how users can configure stock prediction experiments, compare pipelines across horizons, investment universes, and portfolio settings, and interpret predictive and portfolio-level results through an interactive dashboard with LLM-based support.
B13DEMOUniTor ESG Insights: An Interactive Human-in-the-Loop System for Traceable Sustainability Report Analysis
Seyed Alireza Mousavian Anaraki (University of Rome Tor Vergata) · Danilo Croce (University of Rome Tor Vergata) · Roberta Costa (University of Rome Tor Vergata) · Luigi Tiburzi (University of Rome Tor Vergata) · Armando Calabrese (University of Rome Tor Vergata) · Roberto Basili (University of Rome Tor Vergata)
Abstract
We present UniTor ESG Insights, an interactive system for traceable sustainability report analysis. Starting from PDF reports, the system extracts paragraph-level textual units, preserves page-level provenance, and applies a set of ESG classification modules for sustainability relevance detection, GRI--SDG topic alignment, disclosure quality assessment, qualitative/quantitative evidence identification, and climate-related analysis. The system targets ESG analysts, auditors, regulators, and corporate sustainability managers who need to inspect and aggregate evidence from long and partially structured reports. Unlike approaches that return only document-level labels or aggregate ESG scores, UniTor ESG Insights follows a bottom-up workflow in which predictions are generated at paragraph level and higher-level summaries remain linked to the underlying textual evidence. Users can inspect extracted paragraphs, filter predictions, correct intermediate outputs, re-upload refined data, visualize distributions, and export structured results. The demonstration shows an end-to-end scenario in which a user uploads a sustainability report, explores paragraph-level ESG predictions, analyzes disclosure quality and evidence characteristics, and generates traceable analytical views through a Gradio interface deployed on Hugging Face Spaces.
B14DEMOSAGE: A Guardrailed LLM Tutoring System with Scaffolded Self-Regulated Learning for Adult Education
Kwan Hui Lim (Singapore University of Social Sciences) · Jing Ren (Singapore University of Social Sciences) · Yimiao Zhang (Singapore University of Social Sciences) · Stefanie Chye (Singapore University of Social Sciences) · Amy Wong (Singapore University of Social Sciences)
Abstract
We present SAGE (Scaffolded, Audited, Guided Education), a deployable guardrailed LLM tutoring system for adult learners. Left unrestricted, chat assistants often hand over the answer, which can improve in-the-moment performance but may erode the self-regulation that supports durable learning. SAGE wraps a commercial LLM in interface-level guardrails that require learners to engage before the model answers: a lightweight intent classifier routes each turn to one of three self-regulated-learning scaffolds (write-your-approach-first, paraphrase-before-proceeding, attempt-before-reveal), so a request to "just give me the answer" is held behind a guided step rather than answered outright. As a secondary safeguard, an online counterfactual fairness audit checks whether the guardrailed tutor responds differently across age band, language dominance, prior education, and digital fluency, while an agentic rectifier regenerates any flagged turn; a pseudonymous interaction log supports per-cohort analytics. The demonstration runs the same business-education prompt through an unrestricted LLM and through SAGE side by side, allowing an attendee to watch the scaffold gate hold the answer, then exercise the counterfactual swap, inspect the per-attribute audit panel, and trigger the rectifier. The system is open-source and available at https://github.com/kwanhui/public-llmLearnFair-CIKM2026 to allow other groups to deploy and audit their own scaffolds.
B15DEMOCORAL: COlonography Radiology Annotation Lab
Guanqi Cheng (University of Technology Sydney) · Zaharudin Bin Haron (National Cancer Institute Putrajaya) · Nancy Adams (University of Nebraska Medical Center College of Dentistry) · Ezequiel Zorzal (Universidade Federal de São Paulo) · Francesco Vona (Hamm-Lippstadt University of Applied Sciences) · Antoni Jaume-i-Capó (Universitat de les Illes Balears) · Mukesh Prasad (University of Technology Sydney) · Monika Sonu (NPD HealthInnovation Toolbox) · Joaquim Jorge (University of Lisbon) · Catarina Moreira (University of Technology Sydney)
Abstract
CT colonography (CTC) interpretation hinges on three intertwined structures: the colonic lumen, intracolonic fluid pockets, and polyps. Constructing voxel-level ground truth for these structures is a persistent bottleneck for computer-aided diagnosis. We present CORAL, a browser-based CT colonography annotation environment that delivers an end-to-end workflow for joint lumen, fluid-pocket, and polyp annotation, and provides a slice-level free-text comment panel for radiologists to describe their findings. CORAL parses DICOM and NIfTI volumes entirely in the browser; all image processing runs on the client and no annotation data is uploaded to a remote server. It offers six label-aware brushes, four of which encode HU-based domain knowledge (edge-aware and a fluid brush family), four in-browser refinements (GrabCut-style, Random-Walker-style, Combined, and Fluid-aware GrabCut-style), slice-to-slice mask propagation, 3D mesh visualisation, and on-image measurement. The resulting environment pairs voxel-level CTC annotations with radiologists' free-text reasoning, supporting downstream research in dataset construction and explainable medical AI. A live demo and walkthrough video are linked from our open-source repository at https://github.com/catarina-moreira/CORAL. A demo video is publicly available at https://youtu.be/hq48kqLNLD0.
Poster & Demo Session 3 · DemosWednesday, 11 Nov · 14:00 – 15:3014 demos
Demo Area · 14 demos
B01DEMOPRISM: A Personalized News Recommendation System for Mitigating Political Echo Chambers
Seongeun Ryu (Hanyang University) · Hoyeol Yang (Hanyang University) · Kayoung Lee (Hanyang University) · Sang-Wook Kim (Hanyang University)
Abstract
Personalized news recommendation systems often reinforce users' pre-existing beliefs by limiting their exposure, contributing to political echo chambers. Existing mitigation approaches—such as rewriting biased text or diversifying recommendations—risk distorting article semantics or deepening polarization, while typically offering no rationale for why content is judged biased. We present PRISM, an interactive web-based news recommendation system that mitigates political echo chambers across three levels of granularity: feed level, article level, and event level. Building on KHAN (political stance prediction) and CROWN (personalized news recommendation) from our prior work, PRISM lets users monitor the political distribution of their reading history and current recommendations, inspect each article's predicted stance with bias-indicative keywords and natural-language rationales, and voluntarily explore cross-stance coverage of the same news event, preserving user autonomy in line with self-determination theory. PRISM is available at https://github.com/Hoyeol-Yang/PRISM, with a demonstration video at https://youtu.be/NbcvHME__cI.
B02DEMODidact: A Cross-Domain Capability Discovery System for Defence
Aarya Bodhankar (University of New South Wales) · Aditya Joshi (University of New South Wales) · Bao Gia Doan (University of New South Wales) · Thomas Marchant (Cyndr.ai) · Oscar Leslie (Cyndr.ai) · Flora Salim (University of New South Wales)
Abstract
Policymakers in defence and defence-aligned sectors must monitor rapidly evolving research alongside sector priorities relevant to operational and strategic needs. In practice, these sources are fragmented across heterogeneous formats, disjoint repositories, making capability discovery slow and difficult to audit. We present Didact, a prototype that integrates two sources: publicly available defence reports and policy documents from Australia, and a purpose-built knowledge graph derived from Australian research publications. Didact provides natural language conversations for policy-oriented workflows, and devises a composite retrieval-augmented generation (RAG) pipeline that allows synthesis of information from both sources. A key feature of Didact is an interactive Evidence Rail that presents retrieved document evidence and, when research-graph retrieval is used, visualises relevant entities and relationships. Automated evaluation on DoRA-QnA50 characterises Didact's retrieval quality, response quality, and runtime. While Didact has been co-developed as an academia-industry project for the Australian defence context, it is adaptable to other domains where knowledge is similarly fragmented and reliability is critical. A demonstration video is available here: https://youtu.be/KRtlq3LQ9WA.
B03DEMOAutomatic Reference Scanner and Explainer: Don't Get Caught with Dirty References
Moritz Staudinger (TU Wien) · Wojciech Kusa (NASK National Research Institute) · Georgios Peikos (University of Milano-Bicocca) · Allan Hanbury (TU Wien)
Abstract
The growing use of large language models (LLMs) in academic writing has introduced a new failure mode: hallucinated references, citations to papers that do not exist or whose metadata is incorrect. Such fabricated references are easy to overlook during writing and review, yet they undermine the integrity of the scholarly record. The problem has reached a scale that program committees can no longer ignore: during camera-ready consistency checks for ACL 2026, over 100 already-accepted papers were found to cite non-existent literature and were rejected. We present the Automatic Reference Scanner and Explainer, a self-hostable system that parses the bibliography of a submitted PDF, cross-checks every reference against up to nine scholarly registries, and explains each verdict: every reference is labelled as matched, not found, or mismatched (e.g., incorrect authors, venue, or identifier), with the evidence per source and the reason stated explicitly, both in audit cards and as colour-coded highlights on the PDF itself. On 13 papers with all 460 references manually annotated, our tool catches 83% of fabricated references while only 1.5% of the references it clears are fabricated - turning hours of manual bibliography checking by authors, reviewers, and editors into minutes of targeted triage.
B04DEMOReLevel: A Framework for Adaptive Self-Reflection in Multi-Level Planning for Long-Horizon Agents
Hui Wei (University of California, Merced) · Xiang Chen (Adobe Research) · Sungchul Kim (Adobe Research) · Rui Wang (Adobe Research) · Raghavendra Addanki (Adobe Research) · Junda Wu (Adobe Research) · Shijia Pan (University of California, Merced) · Tong Yu (Adobe Research)
Abstract
We present ReLevel, a framework for adaptive reflection-level selection that decides at which level of an agent's plan to reflect when a failure occurs. Modern agents decompose a complex task into a hierarchy of sub-tasks down to individual actions and reflect when an action fails. The choice of reflection-level is significant: reflecting at the failed action alone is cheap but lets errors propagate to sibling steps that share the same flawed assumption, while re-planning the whole task fixes the error but discards already completed work. ReLevel instead derives three signals from each failure to adaptively select the reflection-level: the scope of invalidated assumptions, the level the model's sampled attribution points to, and the cost--benefit of regenerating each candidate level. It treats each signal as a lower bound on how coarse the reflection must be and reflects at the tightest level that satisfies all three. The lowest common ancestor of the affected steps sets a correctness floor, raised only when confidence or cost--benefit shows that a globally unsound design or an unreliable local fix requires more. An accompanying interactive system visualizes the plan tree, the failure, the three signals, and the selected level, letting users compare action-level, plan-level, and adaptive strategies on the same failure. Across six language models, ReLevel matches the repair success of whole-plan re-planning while re-executing about a third of the actions, whereas action-level reflection leaves the failure unrepaired.
B05DEMOAgent-R1: A Unified and Modular Framework for Agentic Reinforcement Learning
Mingyue Cheng (State Key Laboratory of Cognitive Intelligence, University of Science and Technology of China) · Shuo Yu (State Key Laboratory of Cognitive Intelligence, University of Science and Technology of China) · Daoyu Wang (State Key Laboratory of Cognitive Intelligence, University of Science and Technology of China) · Qingchuan Li (State Key Laboratory of Cognitive Intelligence, University of Science and Technology of China) · Xiaoyu Tao (State Key Laboratory of Cognitive Intelligence, University of Science and Technology of China) · Jie Ouyang (State Key Laboratory of Cognitive Intelligence, University of Science and Technology of China) · Yucong Luo (State Key Laboratory of Cognitive Intelligence, University of Science and Technology of China) · Yitong Zhou (State Key Laboratory of Cognitive Intelligence, University of Science and Technology of China) · Qi Liu (State Key Laboratory of Cognitive Intelligence, University of Science and Technology of China) · Enhong Chen (State Key Laboratory of Cognitive Intelligence, University of Science and Technology of China)
Abstract
LLM agents increasingly rely on reinforcement learning to improve multi-turn reasoning, tool use, and environment interaction. However, existing training pipelines often treat an agent trajectory as a flat token sequence or a reconstructed message trace, making it difficult to preserve rollout fidelity, manage long contexts, and inspect step-level credit signals. We present Agent-R1, an open-source modular framework for agentic reinforcement learning (RL). Agent-R1 uses interaction steps as the native unit for trajectory representation, replay, and environment interaction, and decouples exact trajectory storage from flexible context construction. The system supports context-management policies, step-level rollout inspection, action-mask visualization, tool-feedback analysis, and unified comparison of related RL algorithms. Through demonstrations on multiple tasks, Agent-R1 enables users to configure, train, inspect, and compare agentic RL workflows within a single interactive interface. Code and project resources are available at https://github.com/AgentR1/Agent-R1.
B06DEMOTracing the Chain Rule: Exploring Automatic Differentiation Inside a Code-Generating Database System
Clemens Ruck (University of Bamberg) · Maximilian Schüle (University of Bamberg)
Abstract
Code-generating database systems improve the runtime for automatic differentiation by eliminating function calls and storing partial derivatives within registers for reuse. This work demonstrates our extension of forward and reverse mode automatic differentiation in LingoDB. In conjunction with implemented matrix operations, the operators compute the derivatives for in-database gradient descent even for simple neural networks based on matrix multiplication. We present dsql, an interactive web interface for writing SQL queries with lambda-based loss functions and for inspecting the generated MLIR code at every compilation stage. Side-by-side comparisons show the differences in generated code size, optimisation and execution time between forward and reverse mode differentiation. Pre-loaded example workloads for linear regression and neural network training allow users to explore the interplay between automatic differentiation and compiler optimisations interactively.
B07DEMO''Will This Data Break My Task?'' Interactive Synthesis of Task-Aware Data Unit Tests
Hao Chen (BIFOLD & TU Berlin) · Arnab Phani (BIFOLD & TU Berlin) · Sebastian Schelter (BIFOLD & TU Berlin)
Abstract
Data is a central resource for modern enterprises and institutions, and data errors propagating through data pipelines lead to serious impact in production. Therefore, data validation is essential for ensuring the reliability of downstream applications. This led to the development of data unit tests, executable programs that test data before moving it around through large data pipelines. However, existing frameworks derive data unit tests from observed data alone, ignoring the semantics of the code that consumes the data downstream. To this end, we present PrismaDV, a compound AI system that synthesizes task-aware data unit tests for tabular data by jointly analyzing data and downstream task code. PrismaDV decomposes the test generation into multiple LLM-powered steps: data profiling, detection of column accesses, data flow analysis in the task code, and the inference of implicit data assumptions. It subsequently synthesizes code for the data unit test, and maintains an internal “data-code assumption graph” that links generated data constraints back to the task's source code. We demonstrate PrismaDV through an interactive web-based interface where attendees run the system on five real-world datasets with 60 downstream tasks, synthesize, inspect and refine both natural language assumptions about the data and executable data constraints. The interface allows attendees to navigate the data-code assumption graph, compare task-aware data unit tests against task-agnostic baselines on erroneous data batches, and interactively edit assumptions and data constraints. Furthermore, attendees can observe how a custom prompt optimizer adapts the system to specific datasets over time.
B08DEMOTool-supported Expert Validation of CONTEXT-sensitive Data Extraction from Scientific Articles
Diana Martínez-Minguet (Universitat Politècnica de València) · Carlo Alberto Bono (Politecnico di Milano) · Alberto García S. (Universitat Politècnica de València) · óscar Pastor (Universitat Politècnica de València) · Pietro Pinoli (Politecnico di Milano) · Anna Bernasconi (Politecnico di Milano)
Abstract
Extracting structured information from scientific literature (e.g., in life sciences) is a considerably valuable and knowledge-intensive task. Relevant target information is often highly context-sensitive and scattered across unstructured, heterogeneous documents spanning text, tables, figures, and supplementary materials. For instance, statistical measures may not be apparent in the text, requiring the interpretation of multiple methodological and experimental details across documents. Large Language Models (LLMs) offer promising support for automating this process, yet they remain prone to error, making expert curation essential. Validation is, however, expensive and time-consuming, since extracted values must be traced back to their precise location in long, multi-document sources. Here, we present CONTEXT, a domain-agnostic tool that enables in-context expert judgment over LLM-extracted outputs. Given a pipeline that returns, for each target field and scientific article, the identified value with its source location –file, section, subsection, and exact passage– our tool maps this output back to the original document, enabling efficient in-context assessment, robust to typical LLM noise such as paraphrasing and hallucination. We demonstrate CONTEXT's utility with a use case in genetics, involving the curation of metadata for polygenic risk score models. Validated extractions are exported as structured ground-truth records, providing a rich annotation format for downstream use in knowledge-intensive tasks. Demonstration video and source code are available.
B09DEMOESG-CRE: A Convert-Retrieve-Extract Framework with a Human-Guided Refinement Loop for ESG Reports
Cheng-Pei Wu (Academia Sinica) · Chih-Ming Chen (Academia Sinica) · Kuei-Ying Li (Taiwan Economic Journal Co., Ltd.) · Chuan-Ju Wang (Academia Sinica)
Abstract
Structured ESG information underpins sustainability analysis and regulatory reporting, yet ESG reports vary so widely in layout, terminology, and units that no fixed schema extracts them well. We present ESG-CRE, an interactive system for ESG report extraction built on a Convert–Retrieve–Extract pipeline: it converts PDF reports into layout-aware page artifacts, retrieves indicator-relevant contexts, and produces schema-guided, source-linked records. The core of ESG-CRE is a human-guided refinement loop that treats the schema as an editable, auditable artifact rather than a fixed input. Experts judge individual records against their source pages, and ESG-CRE compiles these judgements into versioned, additively merged schema updates that grow its domain knowledge without discarding prior rules. On public Taiwanese ESG reports, a single round of expert review yields measurable gains in extraction quality. Attendees can run the full extract–review–refine cycle live; a demo video is publicly available. (https://youtu.be/w1-iwK701Mo)
B10DEMOCivicFlow: A Human-in-the-Loop Workbench for Evolving Civic-Report Taxonomies
Jaewon Moon (Korea Electronics Technology Institute) · Seungtaek Oh (Korea Electronics Technology Institute) · Sungin Hwang (Korea Electronics Technology Institute) · Jeongcheol Yeom (Korea Electronics Technology Institute)
Abstract
Large-scale classification of civic reports is not a fixed assignment problem. Label definitions and the taxonomy keep evolving with policy and citizen language, one report often spans several departments and hierarchical paths at once, and confirmed labels are revised as administrative staff renegotiate definitions. Ground truth is therefore ongoing human judgment, not a one-shot label. We present CivicFlow, a web-based human-in-the-loop workbench for evolving civic-report taxonomies. CivicFlow keeps human-confirmed ground truth separate from model predictions, updating it only through reviewer confirmation, while keyword/entity, classifier, and retrieval-augmented large language model (LLM) evidence stays read-only. It connects taxonomy editing, active-learning simulation, quality analysis, and cluster triage in one loop. On 35,843 usable labeled Korean safety reports, operators can estimate how active-learning strategies reduce label reveals and broaden the observed label-set space before live review.
B13DEMOEd-Alpha: An Open Benchmark for Predicting Investment-Relevant Corporate Events from Open Data
Shuya Bundo (E9Technologies Inc.) · Yuki Kawashima (The University of Tokyo) · Hideaki Joko (Radboud University) · Takuya Shimano (E9Technologies Inc.)
Abstract
We present Ed-Alpha, an open benchmark platform for predicting and evaluating investment-relevant corporate events using public data. Existing event-driven investment research often relies on expensive, proprietary data, making methods difficult to reproduce or compare. Ed-Alpha addresses this challenge by providing a transparent and fully reproducible pipeline. Specifically, it uses regulatory filings from the U.S. Securities and Exchange Commission (SEC) as ground-truth event labels and combines them with high-volume news signals from the GDELT project. Using Ed-Alpha, our initial analysis reveals that even state-of-the-art LLMs achieve only limited effectiveness in predicting corporate events; we therefore expect the platform to facilitate more efficient and transparent experimentation toward future improvements in effectiveness. The benchmark platform and a demonstration video, as well as all related code and methods, are available in our repository. https://e9technologies.github.io/ED-ALPHA https://github.com/E9Technologies/ed-alpha
B14DEMOSoilCast: An Interactive Machine-Learning System for Forecasting Soil Health under Climate and Management Scenarios
Thomas Oberleitner (International Institute for Applied Systems Analysis) · Rastislav Skalsky (International Institute for Applied Systems Analysis) · Juraj Balkovic (International Institute for Applied Systems Analysis) · Artem Baklanov (International Institute for Applied Systems Analysis)
Abstract
We present SoilCast, an interactive machine-learning system for real-time exploration of long-term soil health outcomes under alternative climate and agricultural management scenarios across Europe. SoilCast replaces computationally expensive process-based environmental simulations with pretrained surrogate models learned from more than 15 million simulator-generated samples. The system employs CatBoost-based state-transition emulators that predict changes in soil organic carbon, soil nitrogen, and crop productivity over successive 20-year periods, enabling recursive multi-step forecasts through 2100. To support reliable scenario analysis, SoilCast visualizes uncertainty intervals derived from empirical rollout errors on held-out spatial test regions, capturing the accumulation of forecast error over time. The application demonstrates how scalable surrogate modeling can transform complex scientific simulators into responsive decision-support systems for sustainable land management.
B15DEMOHINTLAB: An Interactive Tool for Hint Generation, Analysis and Evaluation
Gabriel Kofler (University of Innsbruck) · Jamshid Mozafari (University of Innsbruck) · Adam Jatowt (University of Innsbruck)
Abstract
Large Language Models (LLMs) are increasingly used in educational contexts, yet their default answer-centric interaction paradigm conflicts with established principles of effective learning. Direct solution delivery can reduce productive struggle and encourage cognitive offloading rather than deep understanding. To address this tension, we present HintLab, a visualization-driven, human-in-the-loop platform for generating, analyzing, and refining LLM-generated pedagogical hints. The system operationalizes five cognitively grounded evaluation dimensions—Convergence, Relevance, Readability, Familiarity, and Leakage Avoidance—and exposes them through interactive visual analytics that support comparative inspection, manual refinement, and scaffolded sequencing of hints. Unlike standard chat interfaces, HintLab enables structured multi-model comparison, answer-space reduction analysis, and convergence-based scaffolding design without requiring domain modeling or programming expertise. A human evaluation involving 901 generated hints demonstrates favorable ratings across multiple pedagogically motivated dimensions, while a hint-assisted question answering study shows that the generated hints substantially improve users' ability to answer previously unsolved questions. The system is publicly available, with source code accessible on GitHub, and a demonstration video online.
B16DEMOShanLiangRen: A Nutrition Agent for Personalized Daily Meal Planning
Miao Xie (China Agricultural University) · Xiao Zhang (China Agricultural University) · Yuan Wang (China Agricultural University) · Ruixin Zhu (China Agricultural University) · Chunli Lv (China Agricultural University)
Abstract
Dietary nutrition planning plays an important role in chronic disease management and maintaining a healthy body. In applications, it must simultaneously satisfy personalized constraints and reasonable multidimensional nutritional goals. These two aspects often conflict, and user constraints evolve with feedback, resulting in a substantial gap between generic guidelines and executable plans. To bridge this gap, we first propose the personalized fully quantified multiobjective dietary planning problem (MDP). To tackle MDP, we develop a nutrition agent, ShanLiangRen. The system first transforms dietary specifications, nutrient data, user attributes and natural language requirements into an individualized constrained planning instance. It then employs an exact retrieval-augmented generation method to shrink the feasible candidate set from a large scale ingredient and recipe space. Finally, it adopts a refinement guided by Pareto principles, where an LLM iteratively revises candidate plans under deterministic nutrition computation and feedback from constraint verification. The system outputs fully quantified meal plans with explicit ingredients and portion sizes, together with reports on nutrition compliance that show constraint satisfaction and nutrient interval attainment. We have released the system online as a WeChat Program, ShanLiangRen. A demo video is available at https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=652OtY5VlGA.
Keynote · Catherine D’IgnazioMonday, 9 Nov · 09:00 – 10:00Sala SinopoliChair: Nicola Ferro (University of Padova)
KEYNOTEAI and Feminist Worldmaking in Technofascist Times
Catherine D’Ignazio (Massachusetts Institute of Technology, Cambridge, USA)
Abstract
Drawing on her forthcoming book, 10 Ways to Stop Technofascism (MIT Press, 2027), D'Ignazio will contextualize the rise of "technofascism" – the collusion of large technology firms with authoritarian, extractive, and anti-democratic political agendas. While we can see technofascism manifesting globally, it is not inevitable and we do not have to accept a future predicated on accumulation, violence, and exclusion. To that end, D'Ignazio will highlight the importance of feminist worldmaking through technology. Drawing from the large-scale participatory AI project described in Counting Feminicide (MIT Press, 2024), she will describe how the research team built technology with data activists and journalists to enact alternative epistemological approaches to information science that center care, memory and justice. These and other experiments in "solidarity technology" (Souza De Alvear et al. 2026) place knowledge and information in the service of informatic futures that foster life, living, and vitality.
Keynote · Paolo FerraginaTuesday, 10 Nov · 09:00 – 10:00Sala SinopoliChair: Fabrizio Silvestri (Sapienza University of Rome)
KEYNOTELearn to Compress or Compress to Learn? Shannon and Turing Meet Again in the LLM Era
Paolo Ferragina (Scuola Superiore Sant’Anna, Pisa, Italy)
Abstract
The year 1948 gave birth to two transformative pillars of modern computing: Claude Shannon's information theory, which gave rise to data compression, and Alan Turing's writings on intelligent machinery, which ignited the field of artificial intelligence. Today, nearly eight decades later, we are witnessing a profound hybridization of these once-distinct fields. As we push to efficiently store, process, and retrieve massive datasets across diverse data types, users, devices, and systems — from vector and graph databases to cutting-edge agentic memories — AI and compression can no longer operate in silos. In this talk, we investigate how Learning is fundamentally reshaping the fields of Indexing and Compression. We will focus on two challenging research directions: designing Learned Data Structures that fuse classical indexing with machine learning to achieve unprecedented efficiency, and developing next-generation Data Compressors driven by powerful autoregressive and diffusion neural models to reach new frontiers of efficacy. We will also examine the reverse direction — how Compression can reshape Learning through model compaction and comprehension. By unpacking the distinct computational advantages and current practical pitfalls of these lines of investigation, we will outline a roadmap for these research frontiers and hopefully inspire new cross-disciplinary collaborations.
Keynote · Nick KoudasWednesday, 11 Nov · 09:00 – 10:00Sala SinopoliChair: Ioana Manolescu (Inria and Institut Polytechnique de Paris)
KEYNOTEReliable by Construction: Query Processing over Unstructured Data with Guarantees
Nick Koudas (University of Toronto, Toronto, Canada)
Abstract
Most of the evidence behind real decisions, contracts, clinical narratives, filings, reports, is text. Increasingly, people want to query it the way they query a database: with selections, joins, and aggregates whose semantics they can defend. Pipelines built on large language models make this feel within reach, but they are best-effort by design: a dropped clause or misread value produces no error, it silently changes the answer. For analytics, that is not good enough. This talk argues that reliability must be engineered into the query processor rather than hoped for from the model, and proposes four principles for doing so: treat the language model as a fallible, inspectable component whose internal states reveal more than its stated confidence; convert those signals into explicit, distribution-free error contracts per operator; make abstention and human review first-class operators whose cost is minimized, not ignored; and treat the user's error allowance as a budget allocated across retrieval, extraction, filtering, and joining, much as an optimizer allocates cost. I will illustrate these principles with recent results, including our own, sketch an architecture in which they compose, and close with open problems: end-to-end guarantees, distribution shift, closed models, and evaluating systems that promise control rather than just accuracy.
Tutorials14 items
TUTORIALAmplified and Emergent Safety Risks in Multi-Agent Recommendation and Retrieval
Kurt Cutajar (Amazon) · Jas Kandola (Amazon) · Anjun Hu (University of Oxford) · Yashar Deldjoo (Politecnico di Bari)
09:00 – 13:00 · Aula 11
Abstract
Recommendation and retrieval systems are increasingly built by composition, with pipelines of LLM-powered agents that retrieve, reason, and act replacing standalone models. This shift inherits long-standing risks while introducing new ones, yet the resulting threats to robustness and safety, and the strategies to contain them, remain underexplored. Focusing on multi-agent recommender systems, this tutorial organises these threats along three tiers, from drift through misalignment to compromise, and separates risks that composition merely amplifies from those that emerge only once agents interact. Because agents that each pass their own safety checks can still interact in unsafe ways, we also show how to scope evaluation to the level at which each failure surfaces: the individual agent, the interaction, or the composed system. Interactive walkthroughs of simulated attacks illustrate how these failures propagate through complete recommender and retrieval pipelines.
TUTORIALA Tutorial on Retrieval-Augmented Generation for LLM-based Recommender Systems
Sunwoo Kim (KAIST) · Geon Lee (KAIST) · Kyungho Kim (KAIST) · Liam Collins (Snap Inc.) · Neil Shah (Snap Inc.) · Kijung Shin (KAIST)
09:00 – 13:00 · Aula 1
Abstract
Recommender systems are essential to real-world online services due to their substantial business value. Increasingly, large language models (LLMs) have been adopted for recommendation tasks, owing to their strong reasoning capabilities and their effectiveness in handling cold-start items. A large body of work has sought to adapt retrieval-augmented generation (RAG) for LLM-based recommender systems by retrieving information from external databases and integrating it into the LLM’s input to improve recommendation quality. Despite the rapid growth of the field, existing tutorials lack a clear taxonomy and a dedicated review of RAG methods for LLM-based recommender systems. To fill this gap, we present the first tutorial on this topic. First, we discuss the types of information used in LLM-based recommender systems, including target-user information and external databases for retrieval. Second, we present the design space of RAG for LLM-based recommender systems, outlining the key design choices at each stage of the pipeline: (1) retrieval, (2) augmentation, and (3) generation. Lastly, we introduce open questions for future research on this topic.
TUTORIALKnowledge Graphs Data Quality at Scale: Challenges, Solutions, and Applications
Stefano Marchesin (University of Padua) · Gianmaria Silvello (University of Padua) · Omar Alonso (Amazon)
09:00 – 13:00 · Sala del Chiostro
Abstract
Knowledge Graphs (KGs) are foundational infrastructure for search, question answering, and entity-centric applications, on the open web and within domain-specific platforms. Their lifecycle, from construction over heterogeneous sources to evaluation at scale and use in downstream tasks, raises a coupled set of data management problems that shape the reliability and utility of every system built on top of them. This tutorial offers a high-level view of KG data quality at scale, organized along KG lifecycle stages. We first frame KG construction and the open challenges that arise when facts are extracted from noisy, evolving sources. We then turn to evaluation, covering efficient quality estimation, as well as the role of Large Language Models (LLMs) as validators and auxiliary signals. We close with downstream applications, including entity-oriented search and scalable defect detection, which translate evaluation outcomes into operational decisions.
TUTORIALNeural Networks meet Explicit Knowledge Representation: Towards Mechanistic Interpretability and Neuro-symbolic Modeling by-design
Fabio Massimo Zanzotto (University of Rome Tor Vergata) · Elena Sofia Ruzzetti (University of Rome Tor Vergata) · Leonardo Ranaldi (University of Edinburgh)
09:00 – 13:00 · Aula 29
Abstract
Transformer-based Large Language Models (Tb-LLMs) demonstrate extraordinary capabilities and, thus, change the approach of conducting research even in Knowledge Representation. Building on existing research that neural networks (NNs) on discrete symbols operate as holistic reasoners over “classical” symbolic approaches, this tutorial aims to present the dominant paradigm of Tb-LLMs according to the idea that these models can be understood with neuro-symbolic, ontology-grounded approaches and controlled through mechanistic interpretable or explainable KG reasoning methods. Offering a profound understanding of the inner workings of these models, the tutorial will help practitioners build novel, transparent architectures to model symbolic knowledge in NN.
TUTORIALResource-Efficient Generative AI: Rethinking Knowledge Management and Delivery
Joao Gama (Porto University) · Arijit Ukil (Tata Consultancy Services)
09:00 – 13:00 · Aula 5
Abstract
Generative AI is increasingly embedded in information retrieval, knowledge management, and recommender systems, yet its adoption is constrained by finite compute, memory, latency, energy, and data-governance budgets. This tutorial presents a resource-aware and sovereign perspective on generative AI for scalable knowledge access, framing efficiency as a multi-objective optimization over accuracy, latency, and cost. We structure the tutorial around: intelligence building, which addresses training and adaptation under explicit resource budgets, and intelligence delivery, which focuses on serving-time inference under strict tail constraints (e.g., P99 latency, peak memory) typical of large-scale retrieval and decision-support pipelines. Core techniques, including parameter-efficient fine-tuning, sparsity and pruning, quantization, distillation, mixture-of-experts routing, and speculative decoding, are analyzed as controlled approximations that trade utility and predictive uncertainty. The tutorial equips participants with methods and deployable design patterns for building cost-efficient, privacy-preserving generative AI systems aligned with CIKM’s core themes of scalable, trustworthy knowledge access under real constraints.
TUTORIAL'Did something just break?' -- A Stream-Learning View on Monitoring: the Geometry and Causes of Change
Fabian Hinder (Bielefeld University) · Valerie Vaquet (Bielefeld University) · Philip Naumann (Technische Universität Berlin)
09:00 – 13:00 · Aula 17
Abstract
Monitoring systems analyze live data to detect and characterize anomalies and failures, enabling informed decision-making. As systems become increasingly complex, the ability to capture interactions among multiple features in real time is growing in importance across domains. In this tutorial, we approach monitoring through the lens of data streams, concept drift, and explainability. We begin with methods for automatically detecting anomalous behavior and then turn to machine-assisted analysis techniques that provide insight into observed changes, including their geometry and potential root causes. We cover both practical algorithms and theoretical foundations, and place particular emphasis on two complementary perspectives on data shift explainability: (1) the geometry of change, which introduces optimal transport as a model of data shift and leverages Wasserstein distances to characterize distributional changes; and (2) the causality of change, which extends computational causal methods for actionable root-cause analysis. Finally, we demonstrate an end-to-end workflow for critical infrastructure applications.
TUTORIALQuery Expansion Revisited: From Classical Retrieval to Agentic Search
Amin Bigdeli (University of Waterloo) · Radin Hamidi Rad (Mila – Quebec AI Institute) · Hai Son Le (Toronto Metropolitan University) · Yibin Lei (University of Amsterdam) · Andrew Yates (Johns Hopkins University) · Negar Arabzadeh (University of California, Berkeley) · Charles L. A. Clarke (University of Waterloo) · Ebrahim Bagheri (University of Toronto)
09:00 – 13:00 · Aula 7
Abstract
The emergence of large language models and agentic search systems is transforming query expansion, elevating it from a standalone preprocessing step to a central reasoning component in modern retrieval pipelines. The shift from classical term-selection methods to LLM-based generation has opened new possibilities for expansion, while deep search agents, retrieval-augmented generation, and conversational retrieval have introduced fundamentally new settings in which query expansion must operate. This tutorial offers a comprehensive treatment of query expansion methods, tracing their progression from classical statistical techniques through neural and transformer-based approaches to LLM-based generation, while covering evaluation methodology, cross-paradigm deployment, failure analysis, and emerging research opportunities. The tutorial is accompanied by hands-on experimentation for implementing and comparing expansion methods across retrieval settings.
TUTORIALGraph Correspondence Algorithms: A Comprehensive Tutorial on Graph Alignment and Subgraph Matching
Konstantinos Skitsas (Aarhus University) · Davide Mottin (Aarhus University) · Panagiotis Karras (University of Copenhagen, Aarhus University)
14:00 – 18:30 · Aula 11
Abstract
Identifying correspondences between nodes across graphs is a fundamental problem in data management, network analysis, and machine learning, with applications ranging from cross-platform social network de-anonymization to drug discovery and financial fraud detection. This half-day tutorial offers a unified, comprehensive analysis of two complementary graph correspondence paradigms: graph alignment and subgraph matching. For graph alignment, we systematically cover the major algorithmic families, including QAP-based, spectral, embedding-based, and optimal transport methods, across unrestricted, attributed, and seeded settings. For subgraph matching, we follow the canonical filter, order, enumerate pipeline, detailing state-of-the-art optimizations in each stage. Throughout the tutorial, we emphasize underlying problem formulations, algorithmic trade-offs, and practical guidance for selecting the right method for a given task.
TUTORIALAgentic Search: Foundations, Optimization, and Long-Horizons
Chuan Meng (The University of Edinburgh) · Litu Ou (The University of Edinburgh) · Sean MacAvaney (University of Glasgow) · Jeff Dalton (The University of Edinburgh)
14:00 – 18:30 · Aula 1
Abstract
The information retrieval (IR) community is moving from traditional human-driven search towards agentic search, where agents iteratively generate search queries, inspect retrieved documents, and repeat the process until sufficient evidence is gathered to produce a final answer. Agentic search is important because it can scale knowledge-intensive work, free up valuable time for humans, and enable agents to interact with external knowledge. To the best of our knowledge, this is the first dedicated tutorial on agentic search. The tutorial will cover foundations and systematic optimization paradigms, as well as advanced topics including long-horizon agentic search (deep research). It is designed for students, researchers, and practitioners from both academia and industry. Participants will gain a comprehensive understanding of agentic search, together with a live demonstration and hands-on experience in running a practical agentic search system.
TUTORIALBuilding Production LLM Agents: An Evaluation-Driven Playbook
Shao Tang (Nubank) · Aman Gupta (Nubank) · Kevin Rossell (Nubank) · Edesio Alcobaca (Nubank) · Lars Hertel (Nubank) · Imran Razzak (MBZUAI) · Flora D. Salim (University of New South Wales) · Luis Moneda (Nubank) · Herbert Fei (Nubank) · Daniel Silva (Nubank) · Rohan Ramanath (Nubank)
14:00 – 18:30 · Sala del Chiostro
Abstract
Large language model (LLM)-based agents are moving rapidly from demos to production, but the methodology for getting them there reliably remains fragmented: architecture, observability, evaluation, and online measurement are usually taught and built in isolation. This half-day tutorial presents a practical playbook for building, evaluating, and deploying LLM agents in high-stakes production settings like healthcare and finance. We cover modular context engineering, user simulation, tool and knowledge design, and - as the centerpiece - rigorous evaluation and harness optimization: calibrated LLM-as-a-judge pipelines, inter-rater reliability, and automated judge-prompt optimization, culminating in offline-online correlation that lets teams predict production impact before shipping. Principles are grounded in two regulated, high-stakes domains: customer support in finance and agentic AI in healthcare. Attendees leave with reusable recipes, evaluation code patterns, and a clear mental model connecting offline development to online outcomes. No production experience is required.
TUTORIALPath-based Reasoning on Knowledge Graphs for Explainable Recommender Systems
Ludovico Boratto (University of Cagliari) · Gianni Fenu (University of Cagliari) · Francesca Maridina Malloci (University of Cagliari) · Mirko Marras (University of Cagliari) · Giacomo Medda (University of Cagliari) · Alessandro Soccol (University of Cagliari)
14:00 – 18:30 · Aula 29
Abstract
Recommender systems are central in modern knowledge-intensive applications. Beyond predicting user-item interactions, this class of systems increasingly requires models to reason over heterogeneous entities, relations, and contextual evidence while remaining transparent, trustworthy, and reusable. Path reasoning over knowledge graphs provides a principled foundation for this goal, as it connects users, items, and knowledge through semantically meaningful chains that support explainable recommendation. However, adoption remains limited by fragmented implementations, heterogeneous preprocessing pipelines, and high coding complexity. This tutorial introduces hopwise, a framework for building explainable-by-design recommender systems through path reasoning on knowledge graphs. Participants follow a progressive hands-on workflow: transforming recommendation datasets into knowledge graphs, running reinforcement learning-based and language model-based reasoning methods, evaluating their utility and explainability, and extending the framework from multiple perspectives. Tutorial page: https://tail-unica.github.io/hopwise/cikm2026/.
TUTORIALBeyond Benchmarks: Robustness for Real-World Information Systems
Bum Jun Kim (The University of Tokyo)
14:00 – 18:30 · Aula 5
Abstract
Search, ranking, recommendation, knowledge graphs, and retrieval-augmented generation (RAG) now depend on deep neural networks, so reliability under noise, distribution shift, and adversarial manipulation is central to trustworthy deployment. This half-day lecture-primary tutorial teaches robustness as one continuous workflow: diagnose expected shifts, stress-test and measure honestly, understand failures, intervene at the data, training, and encoder levels, and report and deploy responsibly. Every stage is taught on a running CIKM system, a dense retriever with a reranker, then transferred to recommendation, knowledge graph and graph neural network robustness, and RAG. Beyond existing threat-taxonomy tutorials, attendees learn measurement forensics, training-time instability, encoder-level design, and deployment reporting, and leave with a failure-mode mental model, an evaluation toolkit, and a deployment checklist made concrete by a browser-based notebook. No robustness background is required.
TUTORIALNeural Lexical Search with Learned Sparse Retrieval
Andrew Yates (Johns Hopkins University HLTCOE) · Carlos Lassance (Cohere) · Cosimo Rulli (ISTI-CNR) · Eugene Yang (Johns Hopkins University HLTCOE) · Sean MacAvaney (University of Glasgow) · Siddharth A.K. Singh (University of Amsterdam) · Thong Nguyen (University of Amsterdam) · Yibin Lei (University of Amsterdam)
14:00 – 18:30 · Aula 17
Abstract
Learned Sparse Retrieval (LSR) techniques use neural machinery to represent queries and documents as learned bags of words. LSR has been shown to be a robust and efficient family of methods for retrieving high-quality search results. This half-day tutorial aims to provide an extensive overview of LSR, ranging from its fundamentals to the latest emerging techniques. By the end of the tutorial, attendees will be familiar with the important design decisions of an LSR model, know how to apply them to text and other modalities, and understand the latest techniques for retrieving with them efficiently. Website: https://lsr-tutorial.github.io
TUTORIALIDs That Mean Something: A Hands-On Tutorial on Semantic IDs for Recommender Systems
Roger Zhe Li (Huawei Ireland Research Center) · Aghiles Salah (Huawei Ireland Research Center) · Mete Sertkan (Huawei Ireland Research Center) · Changhong Jin (University College Dublin) · Yingjie Niu (Huawei Ireland Research Center) · Ruihai Dong (University College Dublin) · Barry Smyth (University College Dublin)
14:00 – 18:30 · Aula 7
Abstract
Traditional recommender systems rely on arbitrary integer IDs to identify items, which carry no semantic information and force models to learn representations from interaction data. While leveraging content information can partially mitigate cold-start, this paradigm inherently suffers from exploding embedding tables and scenario-specific architectures. Recent years have seen the emergence of semantic IDs, which encode semantic information directly into the item identity, reflecting content, hierarchy, and relationships. This framework addresses the above limitations by offering a principled way to encode large-scale semantic information into item identity, benefiting both generative and discriminative applications and unlocking more native unification across modalities, domains, and tasks. This tutorial traces the evolution from raw IDs to semantic IDs as a scalable means of information utilization, offering a comprehensive review of their development and applications across multi-modality, cold-start, and cross-domain recommendation. Hands-on exercises guide attendees through building and evaluating semantic IDs, training models, and exploring cross-domain transfer. We conclude by discussing open challenges, including dynamic semantic IDs and multi-stakeholder utility. All materials of the tutorial could be found at the official website https://semantic-id-tutorial.github.io.

INDUSTRYFiles Search Relevance using Wide and Deep Networks
Rajeev Gupta (Microsoft) · Sandipan Mandal (Microsoft) · Kajal Gupta (Microsoft) · Swarnangsu Acharyya (Microsoft) · Fran Martinez (Microsoft) · Nicolas Remy (Microsoft)
10:00 – 11:00
Abstract
Unlike web-search, enterprise search queries are more contextual, documents are private and heterogeneous, and ground-truth relevance labels are scarce. Production systems at this scale have long relied on gradient-boosted decision tree (GBDT) models such as LightGBM with hand-engineered features, given their speed, interpretability, and robustness on numeric features. However, high-quality semantic embeddings from large, pre-trained language models open new possibilities for neural learning-to-rank models that can jointly learn from sparse hand-crafted features (e.g., personalization signals such as user activity, document recency, and lexical matching features like BM25) and dense semantic representations. In this paper, we present our work on using wide & deep neural networks for search relevance over the enterprise files data. Due to privacy constraints on customer data, which limits direct inspection, and the lack of publicly available enterprise search datasets, we complement our private data experiments by adapting the H&M fashion recommendation dataset for experimentation. Our results show consistent and significant improvements when embedding is added as input to the ranking systems.
INDUSTRYContextual Ranker in Production: Session-Aware Similar Item Ranking for Lower-Funnel E-Commerce
Yuchen Guo (eBay Inc.) · Prudhvi Raj Dachapally (eBay Inc.)
10:00 – 11:00
Abstract
This talk presents Contextual Ranker, a production ranking system for eBay's “Similar Items” module on product detail pages. The problem sits at the lower funnel of e-commerce, where users are evaluating whether to purchase the current listing that they are viewing (the seed item) or switch to an alternative. In this setting, recommendation quality depends on preserving strong relevance to the seed item while also adapting to short-term session intent. Traditional item-to-item rankers capture seed relevance but fail to capture session dynamics, while sequential recommenders model behavior but often dilute the seed item's role as the primary anchor. Contextual Ranker addresses this balance with a seed-anchored session architecture that encodes recently viewed items with a transformer, computes both session-aware and session-independent candidate relevance, and fuses these heterogeneous signals through a multi-head attention module. We will discuss the modeling choices, latency and scaling constraints, and evaluation methodology needed to deploy this design in production. The system serves 10K+ QPS at 29 ms p99 latency on CPU-only infrastructure, improves offline purchase NDCG@4 by 3.7%, and lifts purchase-through rate by 1.5%–2.4% in online experiments.
INDUSTRYRebuilding the Content Ranking Stack for Prime Video: Lessons Learned Building from Scratch
Zhengxiang Yi (Amazon) · Fan Yang (Amazon) · Juntao Yao (Amazon) · Yinchuan Yu (Amazon) · Qisheng He (Amazon) · Songqian Chen (Amazon) · Weiming Wu (Amazon) · Lianjiang He (Amazon) · Ziwei Fan (Amazon) · Yuntian Deng (Amazon) · Zhi Zhu (Amazon) · Qilin Qi (Amazon)
10:00 – 11:00
Abstract
We present the rebuild of Prime Video’s Response Predictor (RP), the ranking stage of its recommendation system, replacing a foundation model next-item predictor with a Deep Interest Network that scores a title conditioned on context at request time. The surrounding data, feature, training, and serving stack was developed natively and validated through online experimentation. This paper concentrates on the system rather than the model and presents three lessons from building it at scale. First, label design influences business outcomes more strongly than model architecture. Second, the feature store, as the core infrastructure, must reconstruct serving-time features both correctly and efficiently at training scale. Third, offline metrics are an unreliable guide to production impact, and continuous online measurement and monitoring proved essential to identifying what improved business outcomes. In online A/B tests against the incumbent, the rebuilt RP increased total streaming hours by 0.44% in the US, with a 2.6% gain on Amazon Originals and Exclusives, alongside a 4.7% improvement in offline AUC. The system now serves Prime Video home-page recommendation traffic worldwide.We present these as practical lessons for teams building large-scale recommenders from scratch.
INDUSTRYTo Re-embedd or Not to Re-embedd
Abhishek Yadav (Pfizer)
10:00 – 11:00
Abstract
Rapid evolution of text embedding architectures, and growing size of enterprise corpora introduces a critical challenge for large-scale Dense Retrieval (DR) systems: Discrete Model Upgrades. Upgrading corpora with new or different embedding models often require full-corpus re-embedding, which is often computationally expensive, time consuming, and risks system downtime. We present AEUM - Adaptive Embedding Utility Maximizer (AEUM) framework, It intelligently decides whether an existing document should be re-embedded into a new, high-cost vector index or transitioned to a low-cost representation. By learning document utility using an "Embedding Utility Score" (EUS) for each document, the framework ensures that expensive vector resources are reserved only for high-value knowledge, minimizing migration costs while preserving search quality.
