INDUSTRYFrom Demo to Production: Generative Search Lessons from Alexa+
Jitesh Mehta (Amazon) · Rahul Joshi (Amazon) · Adarshan Naiynar Sivashunmugam (Amazon)
11:30 – 12:45
Abstract
Generative, LLM-powered search demos beautifully, then collides with production: hard latency deadlines, a bill that scales with traffic, and near-zero tolerance for failure. This experience report argues that the hidden specification for production AI search is the customer's expectation of difficulty: how hard a request looks to them. That expectation sets both the quality they demand and the latency they tolerate. Drawing on generative video search built for the launch of Alexa+, Amazon's next-generation assistant, across Fire TV and Echo Show serving millions of customers, we report six lessons. How hard a query looks is a cheap estimate, never a guarantee: "New Dean Potter documentary" tags cleanly as person and genre, yet the person is the film's subject, not cast, a relation no structured field captures and one that surfaces only at retrieval. Perceived quality is unforgiving: a title lookup looks trivial yet arrives garbled by speech recognition, cut off mid-utterance, or misremembered ("Jurassic Park Rebirth" for Jurassic World Rebirth), and must still resolve almost every time. We therefore judge relevance with an LLM-as-judge framework reporting nDCG over sets that over-sample the looks-easy tail, where graceful fallback lifts nDCG@5 from 0.51 to 0.70 with no regression on the structured head. Latency is just as decisive: customers grant seconds to queries they perceive as hard but are far less patient with ones they think simple, so perceived difficulty must set the latency budget. We cover the engineering this forces: speculative execution, predictable degradation, catalog-grounded safety, and small fine-tuned understanding models that beat a larger general LLM. Finally, the query distribution is non-stationary, so we optimize for the demand we will have, not yesterday's logs.
INDUSTRYOptimize the Harness, Not the Model: Fitting a Minimal Agent to a Self-Hostable LLM for Investigative Analysis
Shai Nahum Gefen (Dream Security) · Vered Chassida (Dream Security) · Dmitry Basin (Dream Security) · Guy Feigenblat (Dream Security)
11:30 – 12:45
Abstract
Government intelligence teams need LLM agents that can analyze large, messy evidence collections, but security and cost constraints often rule out hosted frontier models and broad, hard-to-audit tool surfaces. We report CLEO: Constrained Loop for Environment Optimization, a method for fitting a minimal agent harness to a fixed, self-hostable LLM. Given an expert-validated dataset, CLEO admits only the tools, guardrails, memory policies, and loop components that improve accuracy while remaining general and auditable. On our held-out dataset, the CLEO harness reaches an 83.8% pass rate, within 1.2 points of the strongest out-of-the-box Claude Code SDK baseline, while being two orders of magnitude smaller.
INDUSTRYEdge-Native Agentic AI for Scalable Knowledge Systems in Industrial Applications
Arijit Ukil (TCS Research, Tata Consultancy Services)
11:30 – 12:45
Abstract
Large-scale foundation models and language models provide strong general-purpose reasoning and generation capabilities, but enterprise deployment introduces additional system-level constraints beyond model accuracy. In domains such as healthcare, robotics-based automation, finance, data is heterogeneous, high-dimensional, temporally evolving, and tightly coupled with domain-specific policies and compliance constraints. Decision workflows are high-stakes and require consistency, privacy-preserving, and context-aware reasoning. Furthermore, these environments demand continuous personalization over longitudinal data and real-time contextual signals. We propose and deployed a unified edge-native agentic cognitive AI infrastructure (rolled out for digital health, in process for other use cases) that integrates locality-aware execution, dynamic context construction, and governance-aware reasoning to enable scalable, personalized, and compliant enterprise AI systems and introduce adaptive execution directly into the inference pipeline.
INDUSTRYQuery Explorer: Domain-Aware Hierarchical Query Suggestions for Exploratory Search
Hari Manikandan (Adobe) · Srinivasan Ramaswamy (Adobe) · Eshan Trivedi (Adobe)
11:30 – 12:45
Abstract
Large content catalogs present a fundamental discovery challenge: users often lack the vocabulary or domain knowledge to formulate queries that surface the most relevant content. Existing suggestion systems, built on co-occurrence data, only reflect historical search behavior, leaving vast portions of the catalog undiscovered. This paper presents Query Explorer, which uses a frontier LLM to generate domain-aware hierarchical concept trees for exploratory search, helping users both narrow broad queries into specific subcategories and discover related concepts they may not have considered. Concept trees are generated offline and surfaced as interactive suggestion pills, guiding users from broad intent toward concrete queries (e.g., food ? potluck invitation ? Thanksgiving potluck flyer). We instantiate and evaluate Query Explorer on Adobe Express, a creative template marketplace, with trees generated across five levels of specificity for 1,000 head queries scoped for an A/B test. Over 18 days, template click-through rate increased by 0.5 percentage points (99.4% confidence), while template export rate — our primary business metric — declined by 1.1 percentage points (97.6% confidence). User feedback points to the multi-level pill navigation, not the underlying suggestions, as the likely driver of this tension, a distinction with direct implications for how LLM-generated discovery interfaces should be designed. The architecture itself is domain-agnostic, adaptable to any catalog by changing only the prompt's domain constraints.
INDUSTRYSupporting Human Memory with Audiobook Recaps: From Quality Discovery to Automatic Prompt Optimization
Ekaterina Garmash (Spotify) · Claudia Hauff (Spotify) · James Jacoby (Spotify) · Gracie Beal (Spotify) · Mounia Lalmas (Spotify) · Paul Bennett (Spotify)
11:30 – 12:45
Abstract
Audiobook listeners returning after long breaks need help recovering a story. We created and deployed personalized Audiobook Recaps to address this memory barrier. Production feedback showed that good recaps are not conventional summaries: memory cues, appropriate tone, anticipation, and spoiler avoidance emerged as task-specific quality dimensions. We introduce a pairwise quality-bootstrapping method that discovers these dimensions while optimizing prompts. Annotators choose between recap pairs and explain why; an LLM induces a structured pairwise judge, replacing the missing pointwise metric in a reflective GEPA loop. From a minimal prompt, the method beat months of manual prompt engineering by 22% in pairwise win rate using ?30 annotations and no reference model. Independent evaluation found no summarization regressions and raised spoiler avoidance from 23% to 80%. This offers a general pattern for generative tasks whose quality criteria are initially unknown.

POSTERA Phased Workflow for Operating LLM-Based Coding Agents
Ante Kapetanovic (Infobip) · Tomislav Duricic (Infobip) · Andro Mercep (Infobip) · Emanuel Lacic (Infobip)
15:00 – 16:00
Abstract
LLM-based coding agents combine a foundation model with a harness that shapes agent behavior. For non-trivial tasks, how practitioners structure their work with the coding agents determines whether reliable results follow. We report on a phased workflow for operating coding agents developed by the AI research team at Infobip. The workflow structures agent-assisted development into four phases where human effort is front-loaded and delegation increases as artifacts mature. Context management is the central concern, addressed through four strategies applied at each phase to counter known failure modes. From practitioner experience, we observe that upstream errors in research and planning can compound across later phases, while correcting generated code can introduce bloat and fragility. This motivates front-loading human review. We identify two open problems: the absence of metrics for workflow effectiveness and the gap between formalized context management components and the workflow-level patterns that practitioners need.
POSTERCERTBOT: An Agentic System for Cybersecurity
Piotr Despot-Mładanowicz (NASK National Research Institute) · Mikołaj Pokrywka (NASK National Research Institute) · Grzegorz Statkiewicz (NASK National Research Institute) · Wojciech Kusa (NASK National Research Institute)
15:00 – 16:00
Abstract
In this talk, we will present the architecture of CERTBOT, a multi-agent framework acting as a search engine for a Polish Computer Emergency Response Team (CERT) website and a first triage point for incident reporting. We will provide a detailed description of the end-to-end workflow as well as the models and processing techniques that we used. We will address various challenges in ensuring high quality responses together with solutions we found to overcome them.
POSTERAligning Real-World Document Schemas to Fine-Grained Concept Vocabularies
Enver Menadjiev (KAIST) · Isaac Fisher (L2 Labs) · Kai Spicer (Columbia University) · Christos Koutras (New York University) · Andrew Bell (L2 Labs)
15:00 – 16:00
Abstract
Schema matching, or aligning semantically related elements across schemas, is a foundational task in data integration and interoperability. In this talk, we report on a year-long effort to align attributes in XML documents to a fine-grained concept vocabulary. This problem is especially important in insurance, where organizations exchange policy and claims data through legacy, proprietary, and product-specific XML schemas that must be reconciled for interoperability. This setting is understudied and differs from existing schema-matching benchmarks: source schemas contain local conventions and custom business logic, while the target vocabulary has been built over decades by many contributors, leading to inconsistencies. Building on recent work that combines smaller fine-tuned language models with larger frontier models, we propose an agent-based architecture for schema matching. The talk discusses the industrial constraints that shaped the system, failure modes of retrieval-and-re-ranking systems, and practical lessons for schema matching in the wild.
POSTERAdapting Code LLMs to Domain-specific Languages via Synthethic Instruction Generation and Reinforcement Learning with AI Feedback in Low-resource Settings
Vedad Misirlic (Graz University of Technology) · Kevin Innerebner (Graz University of Technology) · Gerald Stieglbauer (AVL List GmbH) · Elisabeth Lex (Graz University of Technology)
15:00 – 16:00
Abstract
Large Language Models (LLMs) have significantly advanced automatic code generation in mainstream, high-resource, general-purpose programming languages. These models are trained on large instruction-code datasets with executable test environments, which can benchmark the performance of the outputs. However, they typically underperform on low-resource, proprietary Domain Specific Langauges (DSLs) due to limited training data. In this work, we introduce a fully automated, two-stage training pipeline for adapting coding LLMs to low-resource and proprietary DSL scenarios. Stage 1 performs supervised fine-tuning (SFT) using multi granular instructions synthesized directly from raw code and comments. Stage 2 conducts Reinforcement Learning with AI Feedback (RLAIF) by generating new instructions, and subsequently Direct Preference Optimization (DPO) by choosing a preferred output. We evaluate our approach using parser success, similarity and fidelity metrics, complemented with walkthrough studies. Our results suggest that this fully automated, two-stage pipeline can enable effective adaptation of LLMs to low-resource and proprietary DSL settings under realistic data and evaluation constraints.
POSTERTemporal Moment Generation: A New Recommendation Task and Cost-Efficient Distillation for Outbound Marketing at Scale
Badari Udupi Bindumadhav (Amazon)
15:00 – 16:00
Abstract
Outbound marketing at scale relies on content-first programs and item-ranking pipelines that match a fixed catalog to recent activity, missing the long-horizon interests and seasonal context (e.g., back-to-school, Earth Day) that make a message relevant. Missing these signals has played a key role in engagement declines of up to 18% year-over-year, with 55% of push notifications rated irrelevant by users. We make two contributions. First, we formalize temporal moment generation as a new recommendation task, distinct from item ranking: rather than scoring a catalog against a customer, the system starts from why a specific customer should be reached now. Given a customer behavioral signal profile and reference time T, it generates temporally-grounded moments—each a name, trigger, bounded activation window, and message hook, plus tiered search phrases for product retrieval—feeding a downstream retrieval and messaging pipeline. Second, we present a cost-efficient distillation approach that makes this task viable at production scale: starting from Claude Sonnet as a teacher, we distill into a self-hosted Qwen3-32B model via supervised fine-tuning followed by ORPO preference optimization, reducing inference cost 14× while maintaining production-grade output reliability and achieving holistic quality 0.788—4% above the teacher. Together they replace the conventional item-ranking pipeline with more relevant, better-timed messaging. Offline evaluation against traditional recommendation algorithms as baseline shows 5.2× composite-score lift (conservative lower bound; see §4). The system is implemented and its scaling has been validated offline at production scale; a live A/B experiment is underway, with initial results presented at the session.
POSTERReliable Evaluation of AI Assisted Peer Review
Negar Arabzadeh (UC Berkeley) · Sajad Ebrahimi (Reviewerly) · Shakiba Amirshahi (Reviewerly) · Seyed Mohammad Hosseini (Reviewerly) · Hai Son Le (Reviewerly) · Mahdi Bashari (Reviewerly) · Ebrahim Bagheri (University of Toronto)
15:00 – 16:00
Abstract
Large language models (LLMs) are rapidly moving from experimental prototypes into operational peer review workflows, where they are used to polish, rewrite, synthesize, and generate reviews. This shift creates an urgent challenge for organizations that depend on expert assessment. Rather than asking only whether AI can improve peer review, this talk confronts a more fundamental question: can we reliably measure what makes a review useful, fair, and decision-relevant? The talk examines this question through the lens of AI-assisted peer review and shows that commonly used signals and LLM-as-a-judge evaluation often fail to capture substantive review quality. Drawing on real-world deployment experience at Reviewerly, we present case studies in which evaluation metrics reward surface-level improvements like polish and fluency while overlooking evidentiary content, correctness, and editorial usefulness. We then discuss practical lessons for building reliable evaluation systems in real peer review workflows. Although peer review is the central case study, the broader message applies to many industry and organizational settings where AI is being introduced into expert judgment workflows. Responsible automation requires more than stronger generation models. It requires evaluation methods that measure the qualities we actually want AI systems to improve.
POSTERPreserving Utility When Watermarking Fine-Tuned Vision Classifiers
Andro Merćep (Infobip) · Edvin Teskeredžić (Infobip) · Maria Ljubičić (Infobip) · Adna šestić (Infobip) · Armena Kojašević (Infobip) · Emanuel Lacić (Infobip)
15:00 – 16:00
Abstract
Open-sourcing deep learning models under non-commercial licenses raises the challenge of detecting unauthorized commercial use through black-box access alone. In this talk we show how to evaluate trigger-set watermarking for a visual content moderation classifier and embed an ownership signal during fine-tuning while preserving model utility. The trigger set is constructed by overlaying a watermark on selected training images and assigning them to a trigger class. At inference, watermarked probe inputs are classified into this class, providing a black-box ownership signal. We evaluate the approach on an 8-category content moderation dataset using a CLIP ViT-L/14 backbone with a fine-tuned MLP head. Across two held-out test sets, the watermarked model matches the reference model’s global F1 performance, achieving 0.835/0.862 versus 0.824/0.853. The trigger behavior is category-consistent and succeeds in over 98% of cases, with no evident effect on aggregate performance metrics or weight distributions. These results show that functionality-preserving watermarking is practically achievable for fine-tuned classifiers without access to pre-training data or base encoder weights.
POSTERThe Lift Is Usually Wrong: A Field Guide to Event Studies on Cross-Surface Behavioral Logs
Michael Iannelli (Scrunch AI) · Alan Ai (Scrunch Ai)
15:00 – 16:00
Abstract
A naive comparison in a panel that follows the same people across websites says information seeking rises by about 51% in the week after a person's first chat-assistant conversation. Restrict the comparison to users with prior assistant activity, key it to a random later conversation, and compare against those users' own earlier weeks: the lift falls to +5.5% [1.9, 9.4]. Nearly nine-tenths of the headline was the adoption episode, and what remains is an upper bound on the per-conversation effect rather than a clean causal point. The failure modes behind that gap are specific and transferable. Bursty activity manufactures event-time effects, first-use designs confound adoption with additional use, conclusions shift with the measurement window and with counts versus shares, and cheap intent classifiers mislead in the direction that flatters the headline. Net of the corrections, conversational AI amplifies and reroutes information-seeking episodes far more than it replaces them.
POSTERCapacity-Aligned Graph Learning for AML: From Top-K Alert Ranking to Candidate Fraud-Ring Discovery at PayPay
Naman Rai (PayPay Corporation) · Hiroyuki Ohashi (PayPay Corporation)
15:00 – 16:00
Abstract
Industrial AML systems are constrained less by “model AUC” than by investigator bandwidth: at PayPay, analysts review approximately K = 100 alerts per day, a capacity-constrained ranking setting common across fraud detection, trust & safety, and abuse monitoring. We evaluate GraphSAGE within an operational AML workflow: rule triggers ? ML ranking ? candidate organization discovery. Daily ranked alerts and graph-derived organization packets are used by analysts for triage. On a validation snapshot of 861,050 users (base rate ≈ 6.62 × 10⁻⁵), a time-safe 2-layer GraphSAGE achieves 0.212 PR-AUC versus 0.100 for LightGBM. At K = 100, GraphSAGE identifies 22/57 future positives versus 13/57 for LightGBM, yielding a 69% lift at identical analyst effort. Beyond ranking, we operationalize candidate fraud-ring discovery as knowledge discovery: seed high-risk users, expand on a filtered P2P graph, extract connected components, and rank organizations by risk and interaction strength. This yields 489 candidate organizations with investigator-ready evidence packets. The talk distills lessons for capacity-aligned evaluation, graph leakage control, drift-aware snapshots, governance, and analyst-facing evidence design.

INDUSTRYAudit-Ready RAG Retrieval in Industrial Evidence Generation: Positional HNSW and Human Review Signals
Nataraj Agaram Sundar (eBay Inc.) · Tejas Morabia (eBay Inc.)
16:30 – 17:00
Abstract
Overlapping chunks protect boundary recall in RAG, but nearest-neighbor retrieval can spend context budget on adjacent near-duplicates. We describe Self-Conditioned Positional HNSW (SCP-HNSW), an audit-oriented retrieval control that appends a two-dimensional position code to chunk vectors, estimates a query-specific position prior from a first semantic pass, re-queries the same HNSW index, and applies a logged minimum-index-gap selector. The method is an engineering proposal, not yet a causally benchmarked improvement. The accompanying 770-review generated-evidence audit and 70-case OCR audit were not produced by SCP-HNSW; they motivate review-facing metrics and failure slices rather than establish retrieval lift. We contribute a low-friction design that preserves the HNSW implementation boundary, an explicit evidence-to-claim contract, and a controlled benchmark plan against semantic HNSW, semantic HNSW plus gap filtering, MMR-style diversification, and SCP-HNSW across relevance, redundancy, coverage, latency, prompt budget, and answer utility.
INDUSTRYVector Index-Native Relevance Feedback in Production Search
Evgeniya Sukhodolskaya (Qdrant) · Till Bungert (Qdrant) · Kumar Shivendu (Qdrant) · Luis Cossio (Qdrant)
16:30 – 17:00
Abstract
Relevance feedback, using relevance judgments on initial results to refine a subsequent retrieval, has been studied for over six decades, yielding many methods for lexical and dense vector search. In dense search, however, these methods build on top of the retrieval layer, only accessed through a fixed interface. Feedback that adjusts the query–document scoring function is therefore realized as a re-scoring step over the initially retrieved documents, leaving relevant documents outside that set unreachable. We present the Relevance Feedback Query, an interface in the Qdrant open-source vector search engine that folds relevance feedback directly into scoring during vector index traversal. A feedback model assigns relevance scores to a few top results, from which the engine derives an adjusted scoring function and performs a subsequent retrieval over the full dataset. To our knowledge it is the first vector index-native relevance feedback interface in a production vector search engine. In this talk, we walk through its design and evaluation.

PHDKnowledge-Driven Recommendations in Decentralized Systems: Integrating Federated Personal Data and Public Contexts
Fernando Spadea (Rensselaer Polytechnic Institute)
09:00 – 10:45
Abstract
Modern recommendation systems force a critical trade-off between user data sovereignty and algorithmic personalization, while decentralized alternatives often struggle with data sparsity and reactive interventions that fail during high-volatility events, like decentralized finance liquidations. This doctoral research outlines a comprehensive framework that bridges sovereignty-preserving collaborative learning with predictive risk management. By fusing private personal knowledge graphs with public contextual data through computationally efficient retrieval-augmented generation and federated learning, the system generates highly tailored recommendations without exposing raw user data. Concurrently, it develops proactive, agentic architectures utilizing Survival Analysis and the physics of self-organized criticality to forecast individual time-to-event risks and systemic network fragility. By integrating these macroscopic and microscopic topological signals, the framework empowers automated agents to dynamically shift from yield-maximizing recommendations to minimally invasive, protective interventions, safeguarding users against cascading failures in decentralized ecosystems.
PHDStudying and Improving Explanation Preservation in Distilled Recommender Systems
Leonardo Di Gioia (Polytechnic of Bari)
09:00 – 10:45
Abstract
Efficiency and trustworthiness constitute two of the pivotal desiderata in modern recommender systems architecture. In this sense, increasingly large and complex models can improve recommendation quality, while explainability mechanisms provide understandable and verifiable justifications for their outputs. However, the computational cost of high-capacity models often conflicts with industrial requirements such as low-latency inference and resource-efficient deployment. Knowledge distillation (KD) addresses this trade-off by transferring the behavior of a large teacher model to a smaller, more efficient student. Existing work, however, mainly evaluates whether the student preserves the teacher's ranking performance, without assessing whether it also preserves the evidence underlying its recommendations. Students' recommendations may rely on different user-item evidence, reducing the transparency and reliability of the deployed system. My doctoral research investigates how KD affects recommendation explanations and whether explanations can actively guide distillation. Initial experiments have evaluated teacher-student explanation consistency through different post-hoc methods and comparison protocols, together with recommendation and explanation-quality metrics. They provide an empirical basis for studying how preservation depends on the model, explanation space, and evaluation setting. Building on this analysis, the next stages will investigate explanation-guided distillation strategies to improve teacher-student fidelity, recommendation performance, and explanation reliability, as well as the use of explanations to identify and reduce noisy interactions.
PHDPride in Precision, Prejudice in Prediction: Bias and Stereotyping in Recommendation Systems
Tahsin Alamgir Kheya (Deakin University)
09:00 – 10:45
Abstract
Recommendation systems are essential to digital experiences but risk perpetuating societal biases. Existing mitigation strategies to promote fairness can oversimplify the complex nature of bias, neglecting aspects like categories of items being recommended, their dynamic evolution over time, and the complexities introduced by multi-valued sensitive attributes. This doctoral research addresses these limitations by developing novel metrics to quantify social bias and model-agnostic mitigation techniques to tackle them. This work explores both in-processing and post-processing mitigation techniques, focusing on ensuring equitable exposure to different categories of items recommended to users with different sensitive attributes. This work further formalises fairness as a temporal property, demonstrating how bias accumulates through sequential user-item interactions and feedback loops, and addresses this through a reinforcement learning-based framework that jointly optimises long-term relevance and fairness. Additionally, the evaluation and mitigation of such biases in LLM-driven recommendation systems is also explored in this work. Through these fairness-aware approaches, which undergo extensive empirical evaluation on real-world datasets for both traditional and modern recommendation models, this research aims to ensure equitable, unbiased recommendations for all users.
PHDNeuro-symbolic Recommender Systems
Kevin Innerebner (Graz University of Technology)
09:00 – 10:45
Abstract
Recommender systems are a fundamental component of modern digital platforms, guiding how users discover information, products, services, and media content. Recent advances in deep learning have substantially improved recommendation performance. However, state-of-the-art approaches rely on black-box models whose limited interpretability and transparency hinder insight into their decision-making. This doctoral research investigates how symbolic methods can be integrated into neural recommender systems to improve interpretability while maintaining competitive recommendation performance. To this end, we study three complementary neuro-symbolic paradigms: (i) a hybrid model based on the cognitive architecture ACT-R; (ii) a differentiable fuzzy-logic network that learns rules describing user behavior for news recommendation; (iii) a relational transformer over knowledge-enhanced interaction graphs that enables cross-domain few-shot recommendation with feature-level attribution through in-context graph sampling. Preliminary results show that these paradigms achieve competitive accuracy while providing interpretable recommendations and transparent decision logic, highlighting the potential of neuro-symbolic paradigms as a foundation for more explainable and trustworthy recommender systems.
PHDTowards Multi-Agent Conversational Proactive Information Retrieval via Reinforcement Learning
Haoyan Zhang (Dublin City University)
09:00 – 10:45
Abstract
Conventional information retrieval systems are passive: they wait for users to issue explicit queries, yet in many tasks, user information needs are implicit, evolving, and often not yet recognised by the user. This doctoral research investigates Conversational Proactive Information Retrieval (CPIR), a paradigm that prioritises proactive retrieval and uses lightweight conversational feedback to refine its understanding of user needs. We frame the core problem in CPIR as deciding when and whether to act, which action to take (request feedback, perform a new retrieval, or reuse already-gathered evidence), and what feedback to seek when asking. We model this as a sequential decision-making problem learned with reinforcement learning, and build towards a multi-agent CPIR architecture. A preliminary ASK/PUSH/Reuse study shows that an agent can learn coherent behaviour, but also that reward design is a key challenge in aligning learned behaviour with retrieval effectiveness. We then outline a research plan towards adaptive, multi-agent CPIR under sparse, delayed feedback.
BREAKBreak
10:45 – 11:30
PHDDisentangling Capabilities and Boundaries in Tokenizer-Free Language Models
Mykola Haltiuk (AGH University of Krakow)
11:30 – 13:00
Abstract
Byte-level language models are usually argued for on the grounds of robustness, multilingual fairness, and character-level skills. We point to a different, structural advantage: because they read and write bytes, any two of them share an output space, so knowledge transfer between them is exact and independent of how either was originally tokenized. We hypothesize that the two distributions a byte-level model produces, one over the next byte, one over where its patch boundaries fall, can be disentangled and changed almost independently. A model could absorb a teacher's capability while keeping its own boundaries, or change how it places those boundaries while keeping its capabilities. We lay out the two experiments that would settle the hypothesis, alongside preliminary measurements of the properties they rest on. We argue that the community should move toward a byte-level interface as a shared standard: if the hypothesis holds, then once byte-level models are the norm, transferring capabilities and reshaping boundaries between them become cheap and routine, free of the per-model tokenizer that blocks them today.
PHDFrom Interaction Traces to Reusable Experiences for LLM Agents
Dina Fettache (CNRS)
11:30 – 13:00
Abstract
Large language model (LLM) agents act in interactive settings where they exchange messages with users, tools, and environments over multiple steps. These interactions generate rich traces that are usually treated as transient context rather than as structured data assets. This thesis investigates how to turn such traces into queryable structured data objects that can be reused to improve agents' performance by interpreting their behavior. The first part of the project introduces a data management abstraction that models tasks, interaction traces, and derived experiences as persistent, quality-aware database objects equipped with maintenance and retrieval operators. This abstraction enables agents to reuse past trajectories through examples, rules, or reflections while keeping storage and inference overhead bounded. The second part of the project extends this perspective from whole-trace reuse to decomposed reuse. It explores how to factor long interactions into reusable subtraces and how to represent these units so that agents can retrieve and compose them at appropriate levels of granularity. Planned experiments study how subtrace decomposition interacts with experience selection, which granularity levels are most beneficial, and how these mechanisms transfer across tasks and domains. The final part of the project will package these ideas into an extensible benchmark with datasets, operators, and evaluation measures that enable other researchers to design and compare new experience reuse strategies for their own agents.
PHDTowards Controllable, Stable, and Trustworthy Audio-Driven Talking-Head Generation
Zhicheng Zhang (UNSW Canberra)
11:30 – 13:00
Abstract
Audio-driven talking-head generation has become an important multimodal content generation technology for digital avatars, virtual communication, online education, and human--computer interaction. This research lies at the intersection of multimodal content generation, trustworthy generative AI, and evaluation of dynamic multimedia systems. Although recent methods have achieved progress in lip synchronization, visual realism, and identity preservation, they still face three key challenges in real-world deployment: limited controllability, temporal instability, and unreliable evaluation. First, many methods struggle to jointly control lip motion, emotional expression, and head pose in an interpretable framework. Second, pretrained generators often rely on a static reference condition throughout inference, which may become misaligned with evolving facial motion and cause identity drift, artifacts, and flickering. Third, conventional frame-wise metrics assume strict temporal alignment and may fail to fairly evaluate natural rhythm shifts and motion variations in generated videos. To address these challenges, this PhD research investigates a unified framework for controllable, stable, and trustworthy audio-driven talking-head generation through three directions: controllable and expressive facial motion generation, test-time self-adaptive conditioning for stable inference, and temporally aligned evaluation protocols for dynamic talking-head videos.
PHDPerformance Prediction for LLM-Era Information Access
Fangzheng Tian (School of Computing Science, University of Glasgow)
11:30 – 13:00
Abstract
Information access systems are being reshaped in the era of Large Language Models (LLMs). Beyond retrieving and ranking documents, modern systems are increasingly expected to understand complex information needs, reason over retrieved context, and generate coherent answers. This shift creates a new setting for performance prediction. In conventional retrieval, prediction mainly estimates whether a ranked list will satisfy an information need. In LLM-era information access, prediction also needs to explain how retrieval affects generation and reasoning. This thesis studies performance prediction as a mechanism for connecting retrieval quality with generation quality. It first investigates how LLMs can improve retrieval-performance prediction, for example by using retrieved and LLM-generated query variants for Query Performance Prediction (QPP). It then studies prediction in Retrieval-Augmented Generation (RAG), where the utility of retrieved results is defined by their influence on answer quality. Building on analyses of the relationship between IR relevance and RAG context utility, the thesis extends performance prediction from standalone retrieval systems to RAG-oriented targets, including context utility, answer quality, partial answer quality, and partial utility. The thesis further shows that such predictions can provide diagnostic signals for improving the efficiency of agentic RAG. Overall, the thesis aims to make performance prediction a practical mechanism for understanding and improving LLM-era information access systems.
PHDMulti-Mode Interest Diffusion for Online Activity Tensor Forecasting
Mizuki Yamaguchi (SANKEN, The University of Osaka)
11:30 – 13:00
Abstract
Online activity data, such as web search volumes, provide a useful signal for analyzing how public interest evolves across regions and topics. Such data are naturally represented as nonnegative tensor time series consisting of activity volumes over time and multiple categorical facets, e.g., (time, region, keyword; volume). Forecasting these tensors is challenging because latent trends evolve not only through intrinsic growth and decay, but also through interest diffusion across related regions and keywords. In this paper, we propose KronFlux, a Kronecker-structured reaction-diffusion model for online activity tensor forecasting. KronFlux has three properties: (a)Scalable: It scales linearly with respect to the number of observed tensor entries. (b)Accurate: It forecasts future tensor slices by learning latent dynamics of online activity tensors. (c)Interpretable: It separates multi-mode interest diffusion into region-mode and keyword-mode dynamics, enabling mode-wise interpretation of how latent interests evolve. Experiments on real-world datasets show that KronFlux reduces forecasting error by up to 44.8% in RMSE over a recent state-of-the-art baseline for interest-diffusion modeling in tensor data and reveals interpretable latent diffusion structures across regions and keywords.
BREAKLunch

PANELPanel
Raffaele Perego · Ophir Frieder · Oshani Seneviratne
14:00 – 15:10
PHDSensing How Users Adapt to AI Decision Support: A Multimodal Eye and Mouse Tracking Study
Yichuan Zhang (The University of Tokyo)
15:10 – 16:00
Abstract
AI decision-support systems that present data and explanations are now used in repeated, day-to-day work. Most studies, however, evaluate these systems from a single session and report static outcomes such as trust, reliance, and accuracy. My doctoral research asks a different question. How do users change the way they read and act on an AI system as they gain experience, and what does this mean for how such systems should present information and explanations? I treat this change as something to measure from behavior rather than from self-report, using eye and mouse tracking recorded at the same time. In a study where 14 users each completed three sessions of an AI-assisted forecasting task, two changes appeared together. The link between gaze and cursor position became weaker, which shows that visual attention became more independent of hand movement. Visual scanning also moved from a focal mode to an ambient mode. When I separated the two parts of this second change, it came almost entirely from longer eye movements, while the time spent on each fixation showed no reliable change. In short, users learned where to look, with no sign that they read each point faster. The largest change occurred over the panel that showed the model explanation. These early results support a thesis that uses behavioral sensing to evaluate and design AI systems that serve users from the first session through long-term use. They also point to a longer-term aim. Because users show consistent patterns in how they direct and reallocate attention, capturing these patterns is a first step toward transferring task expertise to less experienced users and, in time, to AI agents.
PHDGraph Mining and Network Reconstruction from Incomplete Information: From Missing Statistics to Fragmentary Evidence
Minh Duc Duong (University of Pisa)
15:10 – 16:00
Abstract
Many information-management and data-mining pipelines assume that the graph is already observed. In practice, relational structure may itself need to be constructed from aggregate constraints, node covariates, public signals, and partial records. My research studies graph mining and network reconstruction under incomplete information, with emphasis on how different information sources should be represented, combined, and evaluated when the adjacency matrix is hidden. Economic and financial networks serve as demanding testbeds because dyadic relations are often confidential, delayed, or only partially observable; they are not the primary object of the thesis. The dissertation is organized around four connected components: reconstruction with missing sufficient statistics, directed graph inference from public time series, information-based design of partial observations, and inference from passively observed fragmentary records. The fourth component addresses settings where researchers cannot choose what is observed: complete outgoing records may exist for some nodes and only known subsets of possible dyads for others. Together, the four components form an information-management and data-mining agenda for constructing and evaluating graph representations from incomplete data.
PHDA Knowledge Graph-Based Framework for Interoperable Supply-Chain Data Ecosystems
Mohammed Younes (ENPC, Institut Polytechnique de Paris)
15:10 – 16:00
Abstract
Cross-actor coordination in freight transportation is today impaired by the difficulty of consistently interpreting records produced by independent information systems encoded through local schemas, identifiers, validation assumptions, provenance contexts, and access regimes. However, operational visibility between actors is essential to support the implementation of services that reduce the environmental impact of freight activity. The objective of the PhD project presented in this paper is to investigate a bounded knowledge-graph-based framework for interoperable and explainable freight transport data ecosystems. It aims to assess whether shared contextual meaning over fragmented logistics records can support both the retrieval of selected cross-actor answers and the inspection of the represented identity, conformance, provenance, version, and access context supporting those answers. A planned service-fulfilment demonstrator will compare the same records with and without explicit shared graph-level conditions; this paper presents the research direction and evaluation plan rather than a completed interoperability framework.
BREAKBreak
16:00 – 16:30
PHDTowards Faithful and Actionable Explanations for Historical Handwriting Identification
Riccardo De Cesaris (Università degli Studi Roma Tre)
16:30 – 18:30
Abstract
Deep neural networks are effective tools for visual recognition and document analysis, including Historical Handwriting Identification, the task of attributing manuscript pages to the scribal hands that produced them. In paleographic practice, however, a neural prediction is useful only if the visual evidence behind it can be inspected, questioned, and related to expert criteria. A predicted hand should therefore be understood not as an autonomous attribution, but as a computational hypothesis grounded in manuscript evidence. This work investigates explanations as the interface through which such hypotheses can be examined by domain experts and transformed into signals for model improvement. It first develops post-hoc, local, feature-based explanations for neural handwriting identification models and evaluates their behavioral faithfulness through perturbation-based protocols. It then shows how positive attributions can serve as data-curation signals for a second fine-tuning stage. Preliminary results indicate that, under matched retraining budgets, explanation-guided retraining outperforms random retraining in most configurations, suggesting that faithful explanations can support model improvement as well as interpretation. Finally, the work outlines a future direction aimed at moving from low-level attribution maps to semantically richer and paleographically grounded evidence structures. The long-term goal is to develop AI-assisted handwriting identification systems whose decisions are accurate, inspectable, actionable, and supported by behaviorally faithful and domain-relevant evidence.
PHDUnsupervised clustering of longitudinal data to identify disease progression subtypes in heterogeneous diseases
Kilian Debraux (Université de Lille)
16:30 – 18:30
Abstract
Longitudinal clustering aims to identify homogeneous subgroups in repeatedly measured data over time. This approach may help unravel the heterogeneity of chronic diseases. However, several challenges must still be addressed before it can be implemented in clinical settings. This thesis proposes a new approach that simulta- neously tackles high data dimensionality, missing data, and sparse time points. The first part consists of a systematic review of exist- ing methodologies for longitudinal health data. The second part provides a comparative analysis of the identified methods. Finally, a novel approach will be developed and applied to cohorts of patients with systemic sclerosis, a rare chronic autoimmune disease.
PHDTowards Semantic Integration of Heterogeneous Energy Data
Nan Liu (Karlsruhe Institute of Technology)
16:30 – 18:30
Abstract
Heterogeneous energy data are produced across operational systems, open data platforms, and industrial applications. Their reuse remains limited by differences in schemas, vocabularies, and data representations. Knowledge graphs can provide a semantic layer for interoperability, yet their construction and maintenance still require substantial manual annotation, alignment, and integration work. This PhD research studies continuous semantic integration of heterogeneous energy data through three connected tasks: semantic interpretation, knowledge alignment, and continuous knowledge graph embedding. Preliminary work focuses on a retrieval-based DART framework that combines dense retrieval with Large Language Models (LLMs) to support semantic annotation of heterogeneous energy data. The future research will extend DART toward ontology alignment and examine how knowledge graph embeddings can be continuously updated as energy knowledge resources evolve. The expected outcome is a scalable framework that supports semantic integration, representation update, and downstream reasoning over heterogeneous energy data.
PHD · REMOTEML Inference Acceleration via Scalable In-network Computing
Shaunak Galvankar (Santa Clara University)
16:30 – 18:30
Abstract
Modern inference engines have significantly advanced the scalability of large models through innovations in serving techniques, proving instrumental in driving the widespread adoption of AI. However their true potential is constrained by traditional server architecture where reliance on host CPUs and operating systems introduces unnecessary overhead and degrades performance. We identify a significant opportunity to eliminate these bottlenecks by offloading data management directly to the network layer by proposing a unified architecture based on our previous research and ongoing work using programmable Data processing units (DPUs)/SmartNICs for in-network computing. Our previous work, NICTokenizer is a framework that offloads the initial tokenization phase to programmable network dataplane eliminating the host OS Kernel overhead lowering the overall tokenization latency by 61.3% and increasing the token throughput by 407.62% compared to conventional server based implementations and was previously published as a poster at SIGCOMM' 25. Alongside we introduce CacheFlow a disaggregated prefix cache pool which utilizes the DPU memory and GPUDirectRDMA for efficient sharing, storage and retrieval of KV cache across a cluster. CacheFlow reduces the average Time to first token (TTFT) by 82% imporves overall throughput by 39% and decreases memory storage requirements by 44% compared to standard inference engines like vLLM. As a natural progression our future research explores offloading semantic routing to a DPU enabling the network plane to dynamically select the appropriate model experts for each incoming sequence.
PHD · REMOTETowards Privacy-Preserving and Adaptive Distributed Learning for Cybersecurity Applications
Aafrin Khan (Indian Institute of Information Technology, Dharwad)
16:30 – 18:30
Abstract
Cybersecurity systems increasingly rely on machine learning models to detect malicious activities, fraud, and network intrusions. However, cybersecurity data are often distributed across multiple organizations, creating significant challenges related to privacy preservation, data sharing, scalability, and trustworthiness. While distributed learning paradigms provide opportunities for collaborative intelligence without direct data exchange, existing approaches face limitations in terms of robustness, adaptability, and explainability. This doctoral research investigates privacy-preserving and adaptive distributed learning frameworks for cybersecurity applications, with particular emphasis on explainability and trustworthy decision-making. The research aims to enable collaborative threat detection while preserving privacy and maintaining resilience against evolving cyber threats. As part of this research, an initial study on Natural Neighbor-based intrusion alert ranking was published at ACM AsiaCCS 2026. Building upon these findings, the proposed research explores distributed learning mechanisms, trustworthy artificial intelligence techniques, and adaptive cybersecurity analytics. The expected outcome is a unified framework that supports secure collaboration among distributed entities while improving detection effectiveness, explainability, and operational trust.

WORKSHOPSTMA4KD: Spatio-Temporal Data Management and Analysis for Knowledge Discovery Workshop
Workshop website: gt-gast.irisa.fr/stm4kd
Nida Meddouri (EPITA) · Juba Agoun (Université Lumière Lyon 2) · Clément Iphar (Mines Paris – PSL) · Aurélie Leborgne (Université de Strasbourg) · Loïc Salmon (Université de la Nouvelle-Calédonie) · Nazha Selmaoui (Université de la Nouvelle-Calédonie) · Assaad Oussama Zeghina (Sorbonne Université)
09:00 – 13:00 · Aula 11
Abstract
Spatial, temporal, and spatio-temporal data are central to many CIKM-relevant applications, including mobility analytics, Earth observation, environmental monitoring, maritime intelligence, healthcare, sensor platforms, and distributed information systems. Their increasing volume, diversity, and acquisition frequency create major challenges in heterogeneous data integration, scalable management, uncertainty handling, privacy, explainability, evaluation, and reproducibility. Although these challenges are shared across applications, the corresponding research remains fragmented across communities. STMA4KD is a half-day workshop dedicated to the management and analysis of spatial and temporal data across their full lifecycle, from acquisition and integration to modeling, evaluation, and dissemination. It brings together researchers and practitioners from data management, knowledge discovery, information retrieval, machine learning, and application domains through peer-reviewed papers, lightning talks, poster interactions, and a moderated open-problems session. Building on the GAST workshop series and related thematic events, STMA4KD aims to establish an international venue within CIKM for discussing methods, benchmarks, datasets, reusable evaluation protocols, and future research directions.
WORKSHOPEARL: The 3rd Workshop on Evaluating and Applying Recommender Systems with Large Language Models
Workshop website: earl-workshop.github.io
Guillaume Salha-Galvan (Shanghai Jiao Tong University) · Irene Li (University of Tokyo) · Ruihai Dong (University College Dublin) · Aonghus Lawlor (University College Dublin) · Dairui Liu (University College Dublin) · Sairamvinay Vijayaraghavan (TikTok) · Lei Li (Shenzhen University)
09:00 – 13:00 · Aula 1
Abstract
This proposal outlines the organization of the 3rd Workshop on Evaluating and Applying Recommender Systems with Large Language Models (EARL), to be co-located with the 35th International ACM Conference on Knowledge and Information Management (CIKM 2026) in Rome, Italy. Following the strong engagement of the first two EARL editions, this third installment aims to solidify the workshop as a premier venue for advancing research at the intersection of large language models (LLMs) and recommender systems (RSs). EARL 2026 will foster discussions on the evaluation and practical deployment of LLM-driven RSs, emphasizing not only methodological soundness and reproducibility, but also the responsible integration of LLMs into real-world systems. By bringing together researchers and practitioners from academia and industry, the workshop will stimulate debate, encourage critical reflection, and shape future research directions in LLM-enhanced RSs.
WORKSHOPGRAIL 2026: Workshop on Generative, Retrieval-augmented, and Agentic Intelligence for Personalization
Workshop website: grail2026.github.io
Ashish Jain (Airbnb) · Shubham Chatterjee (Missouri University of Science and Technology) · Amit Goyal (Amazon) · Xi Wang (University of Sheffield) · Marios Kokkodis (Airbnb) · Panagiotis Adamopoulos (Emory University) · Selen Uguroglu (Airbnb) · Katerina Iliakopoulou-Zanos (The Walt Disney Company) · Duong Tran (Thumbtack) · Minmin Chen (Google DeepMind)
09:00 – 13:00 · Sala del Chiostro
Abstract
Personalization is being rebuilt around generative models. Large language models, retrieval-augmented generation, and agentic systems now shape how recommenders retrieve, rank, explain, converse, and even simulate users---yet they also surface hard problems of hallucination, control, evaluation, privacy, and fairness. GRAIL 2026 brings together academic researchers and industry practitioners to advance generative, retrieval-augmented, and agentic approaches to recommendation---including LLM-based retrieval and ranking, retrieval-augmented and knowledge-grounded personalization, conversational and agentic recommenders, multimodal content generation, user simulation, and synthetic data---while giving equal attention to these open challenges and their long-term user impact.
WORKSHOPGREEN-AI: Grounding Research on Energy- and resource-Efficient Networks for sustainable AI
Workshop website: sites.google.com/uniroma1.it/green-ai-workshop/editions/cikm-2026
Filippo Betello (Sapienza University of Rome) · Antonio Purificato (Sapienza University of Rome) · Vittoria Vineis (Sapienza University of Rome) · Franco Maria Nardini (ISTI-CNR) · Fabrizio Silvestri (Sapienza University of Rome)
09:00 – 13:00 · Aula 29
Abstract
The GREEN-AI workshop addresses the growing need for environmentally sustainable Artificial Intelligence (AI). As AI models continue to scale in size and complexity, their energy consumption, carbon footprint, and resource demands raise urgent questions about the long-term ecological and social consequences of deploying large-scale AI systems at an ever-increasing pace. Distinct from workshops that apply AI to environmental or climate-related problems, GREEN-AI focuses specifically on the sustainability of AI itself—spanning its computational, methodological, and infrastructural dimensions. It offers a dedicated forum for researchers, practitioners, and policymakers to explore energy-efficient algorithms, sustainable data management and infrastructure practices, and novel evaluation metrics that explicitly incorporate environmental impact alongside traditional performance measures. By bridging academia and industry, GREEN-AI aims to catalyze actionable change and foster innovation that reconciles rapid technical advancement with global sustainability objectives. The workshop encourages contributions from diverse perspectives, including hardware-aware optimization, green computing, and responsible model development. Structured as a focused half-day event, it will feature invited talks, peer-reviewed paper presentations, and interactive panel discussions designed to shape a more responsible, resource-conscious, and ecologically aware AI ecosystem.
WORKSHOPKEEPER: Knowledge Elicitation, Externalization, and Preservation for Expert Repositories
Workshop website: cikm-keeper.ai4care.de
Nora Nahr (University of Passau) · Benedikt Elser (Deggendorf Institute of Technology) · Michael Müller (Ansbach University of Applied Sciences) · Florian Wahl (Deggendorf Institute of Technology)
09:00 – 13:00 · Aula 5
Abstract
Much of the knowledge organizations rely on is implicit: it lives in the routines, judgement, and experience of individual experts, and it is rarely written down. As workforces turn over and experts retire, this knowledge is lost before it ever reaches a database or document collection. The information and knowledge management community has strong methods for extracting and organizing knowledge that already exists in text and data, but comparatively little attention is paid to the step before that, surfacing implicit knowledge from people and work practice so that it can be represented, integrated, and preserved at all. KEEPER focuses on this gap. The workshop brings together research on eliciting implicit and expert knowledge through interactive and AI-supported methods, externalizing it into structured and reusable representations, integrating it with existing knowledge management systems, and preserving it as durable organizational memory. We treat AI as assistive and human-in-the-loop throughout. KEEPER is a half-day, on-site workshop that combines peer-reviewed contributions with an interactive session producing a shared research agenda, targeting researchers and practitioners in knowledge management, information retrieval, NLP, and human-AI interaction.
WORKSHOPVERIMEDIA: The second International Workshop on Media Verification and Integrity
Workshop website: verimedia.github.io/workshop.website
Mauro Barni (University of Siena) · Irene Amerini (Sapienza University of Rome) · Gian Luca Marcialis (University of Cagliari) · Roberto Caldelli (CNIT and Universitas Mercatorum) · Lorenzo Cirillo (Sapienza University of Rome) · Claudio Schiavella (Sapienza University of Rome) · Simone Teglia (Sapienza University of Rome) · Pietro Bongini (University of Siena) · Andrea Ciamarra (CNIT)
09:00 – 13:00 · Aula 17
Abstract
The rapid growth of generative multimodal processing and dissemination technologies has enabled the creation of an unprecedented amount of realistic synthetic media. As a result, methods for assessing the integrity and authenticity of digital media play a crucial role across scientific, industrial, and societal contexts, as the realism of altered digital content continues to challenge forensic models. In this context, multimedia forensic systems must address factors such as social media preprocessing, heterogeneous data sources, distribution shifts, adversarial perturbations, and the trustworthiness of information, as well as disinformation detection. These conditions underscore the challenges of deploying digital content integrity tools that remain effective, robust, and explainable. Therefore, this workshop will highlight research advancements in multimedia forensics, deepfake detection, adversarial machine learning, and AI-generated media attribution. Particular focus will be on the deployment of autonomous AI agents for media verification, as well as lifelong media authentication, a forward-looking perspective on AI's role in safeguarding media integrity. The workshop gathers interdisciplinary contributions that advance the foundations and practice of robust and trustworthy multimedia forensics across different modalities, such as images, text, and audio, encouraging research that challenges existing assumptions and proposes forward-looking solutions across multimedia analysis.
WORKSHOPIWILDS'26: The 6th International Workshop on Investigating Learning during Web Search and AI-Mediated Information Access
Workshop website: iwilds2026.wordpress.com
Anett Hoppe (Philipps-Universität Marburg & Hessian Center for AI) · Nilavra Bhattacharya (ABB Corporate Research Center Germany) · Jiqun Liu (University of Oklahoma) · Ran Yu (GESIS – Leibniz Institute for the Social Sciences)
09:00 – 13:00 · Aula 7
Abstract
The emergence of conversational AI, retrieval-augmented generation and adaptive recommendation systems has fundamentally reshaped how learners access, evaluate and construct knowledge from the web. Yet our understanding of how these shifts affect learning processes, and how retrieval systems should be designed to support them still remains limited. The sixth edition of the IWILDS workshop series brings together researchers from information retrieval, knowledge management, learning analytics, user modeling and educational psychology to address this gap. The workshop focuses on three interconnected research questions: how learners formulate and reformulate queries and prompts across search, RAG and conversational paradigms; what evaluation frameworks can capture learning outcomes in AI-mediated information environments; and how to construct datasets that reflect contemporary learning-in-the-wild. IWILDS'26 combines paper-based sessions (paper presentations and invited talk) with interactive phases focused on structured discussions about research questions and a collaboration fair. In its sixth year, the workshop builds on a sustained community anchored in IR and learning sciences, returning to CIKM with a sharpened focus aligned with CIKM's core interests in information retrieval, user modeling and knowledge management.
WORKSHOPLASS: The 2nd Workshop on LLM Agents for Social Simulation: Fundamental Challenges and Real-World Applications
Workshop website: lassworkshop26.github.io
Yige Yuan (Institute of Computing Technology, Chinese Academy of Sciences) · Haowen Gao (Institute of Computing Technology, Chinese Academy of Sciences) · Bingbing Xu (Institute of Computing Technology, Chinese Academy of Sciences) · Liang Pang (Institute of Computing Technology, Chinese Academy of Sciences) · Yu Zhao (Institute of Computing Technology, Chinese Academy of Sciences) · Shasha Guo (Institute of Computing Technology, Chinese Academy of Sciences) · Xiaoyan Zhao (National University of Singapore) · An Zhang (University of Science and Technology of China) · Junming Huang (Princeton University) · Zhongyu Wei (Fudan University)
09:00 – 13:00 · Aula 24
Abstract
Social simulation plays an important role in domains where human studies face practical constraints, such as sociology, psychology, medicine, and education. Conventional social simulations often rely on rule-based, statistical, or mechanistic models with predefined assumptions, which can oversimplify the complexity, diversity, and context dependence of real-world human behavior. Recent advances in Large Language Models (LLMs) offer a promising opportunity by enabling agents to interpret contextual information, perform flexible reasoning, and adapt their behaviors to evolving environments, opening new frontiers for modeling human behavior, social interactions, and collective dynamics. Despite these opportunities, LLM-agent-based social simulations raise significant challenges, including persona and domain-knowledge modeling, behavioral evaluation and analysis, safety, ethics, accountability in error-sensitive domains, and scalable infrastructure for large-scale and long-horizon simulations. To answer these questions, the second LLM Agents for Social Simulation workshop (LASS), themed Fundamental Challenges and Real-World Applications, aims to bring together researchers and practitioners from diverse disciplines and backgrounds to explore how LLM agents can be more faithfully modeled, rigorously evaluated, safely governed, and effectively applied to address real-world problems in vertical domains, with careful consideration of their unique requirements, challenges, and practical limitations, thereby promoting human well-being and broader societal benefit.
WORKSHOPKEIR @ CIKM 2026: The Third Workshop on Knowledge-Enhanced Information Retrieval
Workshop website: keir-workshop.github.io
Giacomo Frisoni (University of Bologna) · Luca Ragazzi (University of Bologna) · Gianluca Moro (University of Bologna) · Zaiqiao Meng (Huazhong University of Science and Technology) · Jinyuan Fang (University of Glasgow) · Yufang Hou (Interdisciplinary Transformation University)
14:00 – 18:30 · Aula 11
Abstract
Much of modern information retrieval (IR) now relies on pretrained language models whose parametric knowledge has driven strong gains in semantic understanding. Yet, this knowledge is frozen at training time, opaque, and limited in its coverage of long-tail, domain-specific, and fast-changing information, yielding imprecise, factually inaccurate, or poorly grounded results. Knowledge-enhanced IR addresses this by augmenting retrieval systems—and the language models that power them—with external knowledge: unstructured or structured, gold or synthetic, increasingly across modalities. Large language models are now reshaping how this knowledge is acquired and integrated—for example, autonomous agents that plan, reason, and decide what to search; automated knowledge curation and linking; and systems that interleave retrieval and generation, learning when to consult external evidence and when to answer from parametric knowledge. The Third Workshop on Knowledge-Enhanced Information Retrieval (KEIR @ CIKM 2026) gathers researchers and practitioners from IR, natural language processing, data mining, and knowledge management to advance the principled integration of external knowledge into IR. KEIR welcomes both methodological and applied contributions, with particular attention to knowledge-intensive, domain-sensitive fields such as science, medicine, law, and finance, where factuality, trust, and discovery are paramount.
WORKSHOPGraph-Augmented LLMs (GaLM): Bridging Language and Structured Knowledge
Workshop website: galm-workshop.github.io
Benyou Wang (The Chinese University of Hong Kong) · Amit Kumar Jaiswal (Indian Institute of Technology (Banaras Hindu University)) · Ruchir Gupta (Indian Institute of Technology (Banaras Hindu University)) · Jiale Han (Shenzhen Loop Area Institute) · Prayag Tiwari (Halmstad University) · Amit Agarwal (Capital One) · Shandar Ahmad (Jawaharlal Nehru University)
14:00 – 18:30 · Aula 1
Abstract
Large language models (LLMs) have demonstrated remarkable capabilities in natural language processing and other adaptable domains, yet they often struggle with knowledge grounding and reasoning. Integrating graph structures, such as knowledge graphs and graph neural networks offer a promising avenue to enhance LLMs with rich relational information. Our workshop Graph-Augmented LLMs (https://galm-workshop.github.io) explores the synergistic convergence of LLMs and graph-based methodologies and its applications with its transformative potential. This integration facilitates advancements in areas such as enhanced reasoning, improved contextual understanding, and robust generalization. We aim to foster discussions on leveraging Graph Neural Networks (GNNs) and graph representation learning to augment LLMs, as well as investigating the application of federated learning and unlearning techniques to address privacy and ethical concerns in this rapidly evolving field. This workshop aims to foster discussions on how graph structures can empower LLMs to achieve improved reasoning, knowledge integration, and data privacy in diverse applications, including but not limited to biomedical, environmental and social-economic systems, with highly structured knowledge. The proposed workshop is the second iteration of GaLM 2025 workshop (https://iitbhu.ac.in/cf/jcsic/activities/workshops), which was successfully organized at ICDM 2025 in Washington DC, USA.
WORKSHOPLLM4XAI: Generative Models for Explainable AI Narratives
Workshop website: hercolelab.github.io/LLM4XAI
Gabriele Tolomei (Sapienza University of Rome) · Ziheng Chen (Walmart Labs) · Flavio Giorgi (tellmewAI) · Vittoria Vineis (Sapienza University of Rome) · Matteo Silvestri (Sapienza University of Rome) · Fabiano Veglianti (Sapienza University of Rome) · Edoardo Gabrielli (Sapienza University of Rome) · Lorenzo Antonelli (Sapienza University of Rome)
14:00 – 18:30 · Sala del Chiostro
Abstract
As AI systems are increasingly deployed in high-stakes domains, regulatory and societal demands for transparency and interpretability continue to grow. While classical Explainable AI (XAI) methods produce structured technical artifacts (e.g., feature attributions and counterfactual examples), these remain difficult to interpret for non-technical users and only partially meet usability and legal requirements. Large Language Models (LLMs) can transform these structured outputs into accessible natural-language XAI narratives, but they introduce new challenges regarding faithfulness, hallucination, and epistemic misalignment. LLM4XAI sits at the intersection of XAI, NLP, IR, and HCI, investigating how generative systems can act as reliable mediators. The workshop provides a multidisciplinary forum for both academia and industry, focusing on the grounding, robustness, and real-world deployment of XAI narratives to ensure AI explanations bridge the gap between technical rigor and end-user accessibility.
WORKSHOPArtificial Intelligence for Data Engineering and Management Of Networked Systems (AI4DEMONS)
Workshop website: ai4demons.github.io/AI4DEMONS
Andrea Vignali (University of Naples Federico II) · Francesco Cerasuolo (University of Naples Federico II) · Giancarlo Sperlì (University of Naples Federico II) · Una-May O'Reilly (Massachusetts Institute of Technology) · Erik Hemberg (Massachusetts Institute of Technology)
14:00 – 18:30 · Aula 29
Abstract
Modern networked systems generate massive volumes of heterogeneous and continuously evolving data, creating major challenges for data management, intelligent analysis, and cybersecurity. Traditional machine learning approaches often struggle to adapt to the scale, decentralization, and dynamic nature of contemporary network environments, motivating the need for adaptive, distributed, and knowledge-driven AI solutions. This workshop explores recent advances in AI-driven network intelligence and cybersecurity, with a particular focus on information and knowledge management techniques for distributed systems. Topics include Generative AI (GenAI) for synthetic network data generation and augmentation, Large Language Models (LLMs) and Natural Language Processing (NLP) for cybersecurity intelligence and threat analysis, continual and federated learning for privacy-preserving adaptive systems, adversarial learning and trustworthy AI, and agentic AI for autonomous and human-in-the-loop security workflows. The workshop also investigates retrieval-augmented generation (RAG), knowledge graphs, reasoning over structured and unstructured security data, intelligent orchestration, and scalable AI-enabled network analytics. By bringing together researchers and practitioners from AI, cybersecurity, networking, and knowledge management, the workshop aims to foster interdisciplinary discussion on resilient, intelligent, and trustworthy networked systems.
WORKSHOPClinical-MIRF: Multimodal Information Retrieval and Fusion in Clinical Workflows
Workshop website: sites.google.com/view/clinical-mirf
Antonio Galli (University of Naples Federico II) · Michela Gravina (University of Naples Federico II) · Antonino Ferraro (Pegaso University) · Martina Iammarino (Pegaso University) · Valerio Guarrasi (UniCamillus-Saint Camillus International University of Health Sciences) · Angel Garcia-Pedrero (Universidad Politecnica de Madrid) · Consuelo Gonzalo-Martin (Universidad Politécnica de Madrid) · Paolo Soda (University of Rome Campus Bio-Medico) · Vincenzo Moscato (University of Naples Federico II) · Carlo Sansone (University of Naples Federico II)
14:00 – 18:30 · Aula 5
Abstract
Clinical decision-making increasingly depends on heterogeneous and distributed information sources, including medical images, radiology and pathology reports, electronic health records, laboratory measurements, biosignals, temporal patient trajectories, and clinical guidelines. Recent advances in multimodal learning, foundation models, and retrieval-augmented generation have opened new opportunities for Artificial Intelligence (AI) in clinical scenarios. However, current systems still struggle to support effective information access and knowledge integration across these sources, as retrieving, aligning, fusing, and reasoning over heterogeneous clinical evidence remains challenging in reliable, interpretable, and workflow-aware settings.The workshop Clinical-MIRF: Multimodal Information Retrieval and Fusion in Clinical Workflows aims to explore innovative methodologies and applications in multimodal information retrieval, cross-modal fusion, knowledge-grounded reasoning, and trustworthy information access in clinical workflows. Clinical-MIRF will bring together researchers from information retrieval, knowledge management, biomedical AI, medical imaging, natural language processing, clinical informatics, and human-centered AI. Topics include multimodal indexing and search, cross-modal representation learning, clinical Retrieval-Augmented Generation (RAG), knowledge graph-enhanced retrieval, fusion of imaging and textual evidence, evaluation protocols for multimodal clinical systems, robustness, fairness, privacy, and human-in-the-loop clinical decision support. Accepted workshop papers will be published in post-proceedings by Springer in the Lecture Notes in Computer Science (LNCS) series.
WORKSHOPREACH-AI 2026: Community-Informed Evaluation and Benchmarking of Culturally Competent Generative AI
Workshop website: samtaylek17.github.io/xaic/index.html
Jamila Smith-Loud (Google) · Andrew Smart (Google) · Lijun Qian (Prairie View A&M University) · Xishuang Dong (Prairie View A&M University)
14:00 – 18:30 · Aula 17
Abstract
Recent advances in Generative AI (GenAI) have enabled strong capabilities in language understanding, content generation, vision-language reasoning, and multimodal interaction. However, most existing benchmarks emphasize general-purpose reasoning and task performance, offering limited evaluation of whether AI systems can accurately understand, represent, retrieve, and generate culturally grounded knowledge across diverse communities and social contexts. This limitation restricts the reliable deployment of GenAI in high-impact domains such as education, healthcare, and public services. The REACH-AI 2026 Workshop brings together researchers, industry leaders, practitioners, and community stakeholders to advance community-informed approaches for evaluating culturally competent Generative AI. Motivated by the REACH GenAI Consortium, a collaboration between Google Research and twelve Historically Black Colleges and Universities (HBCUs), the workshop focuses on culturally grounded datasets, community-informed taxonomies, evaluation frameworks, benchmark development, and human-centered assessment protocols for measuring cultural competency in AI systems. It aims to foster interdisciplinary dialogue across the CIKM, information retrieval, knowledge management, multimodal AI, and responsible AI communities. Through invited talks, paper presentations, and panel discussions, participants will explore methods for assessing cultural relevance, contextual understanding, representation, and knowledge utilization in GenAI systems. Expected outcomes include a community roadmap, collaborative research opportunities, and recommendations for future datasets, benchmarks, and evaluation standards for culturally competent AI.
WORKSHOPGenAI4SG: Generative AI for Social Good and Vulnerable Populations
Workshop website: genai4sg.github.io/CIKM2026
Martino Ciaperoni (Scuola Normale Superiore) · Marco Minici (ICAR-CNR, National Research Council of Italy) · Vincenzo Moscato (University of Naples Federico II) · Marco Postiglione (Northwestern University)
14:00 – 18:30 · Aula 7
Abstract
Generative AI has become a general-purpose technology for producing text, images, code, and explanations across knowledge-intensive tasks. This opens new opportunities for social good in domains where expertise, data, and resources are scarce: rare diseases, low-resource education, accessibility, crisis response, and information integrity. Yet large-scale deployment also carries risks that fall hardest on disadvantaged communities, including hallucination, bias, privacy leakage, and high environmental cost. GenAI4SG brings together researchers working on retrieval-augmented generation, agentic systems, multimodal models, and knowledge-grounded AI to study how these technologies can be responsibly designed, evaluated, and deployed for social good, in line with the UN Sustainable Development Goals. We welcome technical, empirical, resource, demo, and position papers on methods, systems, datasets, benchmarks, and applications.
WORKSHOPSecond International Workshop on Hybrid AI for Human-Centric Personalization and Recommendation (HyPeR 2026)
Workshop website: aisocietylab.github.io/hyper26
Elisabeth Lex (Graz University of Technology) · Markus Reiter-Haas (Graz University of Technology) · Marko Tkalcic (University of Primorska) · Dietmar Jannach (University of Klagenfurt) · Markus Schedl (Johannes Kepler University Linz)
14:00 – 18:30 · Aula 24
Abstract
The increasing adoption of personalization and recommender systems in high-impact domains raises fundamental questions about how user models represent, reason about, and adapt to human behavior. While recent advances in machine learning have improved predictive accuracy, they offer limited support for explicit reasoning, interpretability, and the incorporation of cognitive and normative constraints. The Second International Workshop on Hybrid AI for Human-Centric Personalization and Recommendation (HyPeR 2026) focuses on hybrid AI as a methodological framework for user modeling, recommendations, and personalization, emphasizing the integration of learning-based approaches with symbolic knowledge, reasoning mechanisms, and cognition-informed representations. HyPeR brings together researchers and practitioners to examine architectures, methods, and evaluation strategies for hybrid user models. The workshop aims to stimulate exchange and to shape future research directions at the intersection of user modeling, hybrid AI, and human-centered recommender systems.

ANALYTICUPA Shared Task on Agentic AI in University Administration
Martin Potthast (University of Kassel, hessian.AI, and ScaDS.AI) · Udo Kruschwitz (University of Regensburg) · Michael Granitzer (University of Passau) · Arjen P. de Vries (Radboud University) · Harrisen Scells (University of Tübingen) · Maik Fröbe (Friedrich-Schiller-Universität Jena) · Andrew Parry (University of Glasgow) · Simon Ruth (University of Kassel and hessian.AI) · Clara Erner (University of Kassel)
Abstract
Agentic AI systems combine large language models, information retrieval, planning, and tool use to act on behalf of users in complex digital environments. Evaluating such systems under laboratory conditions remains challenging because real-world environments are hard to control: executing AI agents in them is neither safe nor reproducible. We show that university administration provides a particularly suitable setting for Cranfield-style evaluations of AI agents in a laboratory. By reconstructing the digital environment available to university staff, we enable the systematic evaluation of interactive AI agents within human administrative workflows. TIRA's sandboxed execution environment allows submitted agents to operate safely on institutional data. Focusing on selected workflows, such as travel reimbursement, we organize the first shared task on agentic AI in university administration and contribute a reusable benchmark with expert-judged reference solutions. The shared task comprises two subtasks: in agentic retrieval, an agent only finds the documents relevant to a task instance; in agentic task solving, the agent also performs the task and produces the solution.
